Silver King plans to emphasize local news and sports programming in some markets starting in about a year.
The stock-swap merger is valued at about $1.27 billion based on recent stock prices.
Each HSN shareholder will receive 0.45 of a share of Silver King common stock for each share of HSN stock owned.

Albert Dunlap is the chief executive of Sunbeam Corp.
Dunlap aims to halve the workforce and add $1 billion in sales.
Sunbeam's shares increased by more than 100 percent since Dunlap's appointment as CEO.
The company's shares dropped to 25-1/4 after Dunlap announced a cut of 6,000 jobs.
Analyst Daniel Noll expressed skepticism about Dunlap's plans.
Dunlap is the author of the best-selling book 'Mean Business: How I Save Bad Companies And Make Good Companies Great'.
Dunlap is credited with turning around Scott Paper Co and Lily-Tulip Co.
Dunlap plans to eliminate dozens of factories, regional administrative offices, and warehouses.
Dunlap intends to stop making more than 85 percent of Sunbeam's 11,500 products.
Dunlap promised to sell Sunbeam's furniture business and open new sales avenues.

Herbert Granath is the chairman of Disney/International Television.
Granath stated that talks with Latin America satellite-television companies are ongoing.
Granath indicated that a deal for The Disney Channel in Latin America could be reached quickly.
The potential deal for a Spanish version of The Disney Channel may be exclusive to one of two major media consortia.
One group involved in the competition for the deal is led by DirecTV of Hughes Electronics Corp.
The other group is led by News Corp Ltd.
Granath did not provide details about the Latin American DTH talks but mentioned that a deal could come together on short notice.
Granath noted that no agreement was imminent.
Disney announced a 10-year film deal with KirchGroup of Germany.
The KirchGroup deal includes an option to distribute a German version of The Disney Channel.

Anti-tobacco lawsuits brought by Florida and other state governments are intended to portray cigarette manufacturers negatively.
Tobacco-industry lawyer Irvin Nathan stated that the publicity surrounding these lawsuits aims to demonize the tobacco industry.
Nathan represented Philip Morris Cos Inc during a pre-trial hearing of a tobacco lawsuit.
Florida state lawyers claim that cigarette makers misled Americans about the health risks of smoking.
The lawsuits seek to hold the tobacco industry liable for billions of dollars in medical procedures covered by a Florida insurance program.
Nathan argued that Florida's Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) does not apply to tobacco companies.
Philip Morris and other tobacco defendants face potential penalties of $1.0 billion or more under a separate 1994 law.
Under RICO, tobacco companies could be liable for triple damages.
Robert Blakey, a law professor, stated that the RICO claim against tobacco companies fits within the law's scope.
Judge Harold Cohen indicated he was inclined to allow the Florida state lawyers to proceed with the RICO claims.

Carnival Corp is seeking acquisitions and partners in Europe and other regions to increase passenger numbers on its cruise ships.
Carnival Corp holds 28 percent of the pleasure cruise market.
The company is reportedly in talks to acquire Italy's Costa Crociere Spa.
Trading in Costa Crociere shares was suspended by Italian regulators on Monday pending information about the talks.
Edward Tavlin, an industry analyst, stated that Carnival is a natural buyer and is willing to expand globally.
A spokesman for Carnival declined to comment on the acquisition talks.
Carnival Chairman Micky Arison mentioned in a Reuters interview that he anticipates continued industry consolidation and sees potential in markets outside North America.
Carnival has formed a joint venture with Hyundai Corp to offer Asian cruises and has invested in British travel group Airtours Plc.
Analyst Jill Krutick noted that Carnival is trying to better exploit overseas markets due to capacity and pricing pressures in North America.
Carnival is profitable despite challenges in the cruise sector and expects to report record profits for the fiscal year ending November 30.

Tony O'Reilly is the chairman of Independent Newspapers Plc.
O'Reilly stated that acquisitions by Independent Newspapers Plc will slow considerably next year.
O'Reilly referred to next year as a year of consolidation.
O'Reilly's name was mentioned as a rumored buyer of Mirror Group Newspapers Plc's 46 percent stake in Independent Newspapers Plc.
Both Mirror Group and O'Reilly denied that a deal was in the works.
O'Reilly's firm owns a 46 percent stake in the British title of Independent Newspapers Plc.
O'Reilly acknowledged that his company is monitoring Australian media group John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
Conrad Black sold a 20 percent stake in Fairfax after expressing concerns about foreign ownership limits.
Some reports suggest that Fairfax may sell a top newspaper or become an acquisition target.
Rupert Murdoch sold his five percent stake in Fairfax and stated he lost interest due to foreign ownership ceilings.

$600 million is the acquisition cost of National Car Rental by Republic Industries Inc.
The acquisition would provide inventory for Republic Industries Inc's AutoNation used-car chain.
The acquisition would not significantly increase purchasing power in Detroit for Republic Industries Inc.
Maryann Keller is an automobile-industry analyst at Furman Selz in New York.
Maryann Keller stated that there is no such thing as a volume discount in car purchases.
According to Keller, it does not matter whether a buyer purchases one million cars or 20 cars.
Big Detroit manufacturers offer fleet discounts to buyers.
The terms of fleet discounts from big Detroit manufacturers have been getting tougher.

Lawyers are notifying potential claimants about a tobacco trial set to begin in June.
The mass mailing targets approximately 120,000 former and current flight attendants on U.S. airlines.
The mailing seeks to identify non-smokers suffering from ailments like lung cancer.
Print advertisements and an Internet site will follow the initial mailing over the next two months.
The class-action suit claims that second-hand smoke from cigarettes on airliners caused the illnesses.
The suit seeks unspecified damages that could total billions of dollars.
Philip Morris Cos Inc and other tobacco companies are accused of hiding the dangers of second-hand smoke.
Richard Daynard stated that this is the first time a class-action case has reached the notification stage in the tobacco industry.
Stanley Rosenblatt estimated that 25,000 to 60,000 flight attendants could be included in the suit.
The suit alleges that second-hand smoke causes various ailments, including cardiac conditions and cancer.

Quick & Reilly Group Inc. agreed to buy Nash, Weiss Inc.
The acquisition is the largest deal Quick & Reilly has completed.
Nash, Weiss buys and sells approximately 2,500 stocks listed on the Nasdaq over-the-counter electronic market.
Nash, Weiss is one of the top six independent Nasdaq market makers.
Nash, Weiss profits from the spread between seller and buyer prices.
Quick & Reilly employs about 60 people.
Quick & Reilly is known as a retail broker and is significant in backroom processing of Wall Street trading.
Quick & Reilly owns JCC Specialist Corp., the second-largest market-maker on the New York Stock Exchange.
The acquisition may lead to more deals involving market-makers in Nasdaq stocks.
Quick & Reilly plans to increase the number of securities it makes markets in from 2,500 to between 3,500 and 4,000.

A Florida judge allowed Arthur Reeves to take a back seat in a class-action trial against tobacco groups due to his complaints of intimidation.
Stanley Rosenblatt is the lawyer pursuing the class-action suit on behalf of ill and addicted smokers in Florida.
Arthur Reeves was one of the original six smokers in the class-action suit filed three years ago.
Rosenblatt stated that Reeves felt embarrassed and humiliated by investigators asking about him.
Rosenblatt claimed that private investigators for tobacco companies routinely check the backgrounds of people opposing them in court.
Rosenblatt requested that Frank Amodeo be substituted for Reeves as a witness in the trial scheduled for September 8.
Frank Amodeo began smoking at age 14 and has tried to stop smoking multiple times.
Amodeo currently smokes and receives liquid nourishment through a feeding tube.
Reeves is not withdrawing from the suit but will not act as a representative of the estimated 500,000 potential claimants.
Rosenblatt alleges that tobacco companies conspired to hide damaging medical evidence and mislead Americans about smoking dangers.

Tobacco companies are countersuing Florida regarding liability for manufacturing cigarettes in prisons.
The countersuit was filed by tobacco industry lawyers on Wednesday.
A Florida judge recently blocked the tobacco industry from using Florida's history of cigarette-making in an upcoming trial.
The Florida Department of Corrections has manufactured and distributed high-nicotine, high-tar cigarettes to inmates for decades.
State officials believed the cigarettes were particularly unhealthy but continued to distribute them.
The tobacco countersuit claims Florida should pay damages if it wins its lawsuit against cigarette makers.
Florida is suing cigarette makers for $1 billion for costs related to treating smokers through Medicaid.
Florida has the right to seek punitive damages under a state racketeering law if it proves tobacco companies conspired to hide health risks.
Florida's governor is advocating for increased cigarette taxes and restrictions on tobacco advertising.
Approximately two dozen state and local governments are suing tobacco companies for costs related to treating tobacco-related illnesses.

China accused Japan of taking an irresponsible approach to a sovereignty dispute over a group of uninhabited East China Sea islands.
The islands are known in China as the Diaoyus and in Japan as the Senkakus.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang stated that Japan's actions are damaging Sino-Japanese relations.
Tension over the islands increased when Hong Kong and Taiwan activists planted flags on one of the islets.
The activists were part of a flotilla of around 300 protesters and managed to breach Japan's maritime blockade.
An earlier protest attempt resulted in the drowning of Hong Kong activist David Chan.
Japan has condemned the landings as illegal and has not ruled out future arrests.
Japan's foreign ministry requested China and Taiwan to prevent further landings on the islands.
China claims ownership of the islands, stating it has done so for centuries, while Japan's claim dates to 1895.
Shen Guofang expressed that the actions of Japanese rightwing groups have angered the Chinese people.

Australia is determined not to let India's veto prevent a worldwide nuclear test ban treaty.
Australia plans to lead a push for a United Nations resolution to support the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT).
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer stated that Australia has launched a campaign at the United Nations to revive the CTBT draft.
A disarmament conference failed to agree on a text due to Indian opposition.
Downer emphasized the importance of not allowing the CTBT to die and noted the effort put into it.
Australia aims to achieve the treaty's endorsement during the current session of the U.N. General Assembly.
The 61-nation Conference on Disarmament in Geneva could not agree to report its failure to the General Assembly.
India blocked the treaty's progress by demanding commitments from nuclear powers towards total disarmament.
Australian ambassador for disarmament Richard Starr expressed belief that the treaty could still be salvaged.
Australia seeks to play a leading role in the campaign to end nuclear testing as a non-nuclear power.

An estimated 50,000 to 100,000 people in China are infected with the HIV virus.
Many Chinese people have limited knowledge about AIDS.
China is at a critical stage in its fight against AIDS.
Beijing's communist leadership launched a campaign to promote puritan Marxism values.
The campaign aims to reduce cases of AIDS caused by unsafe sex and drug use.
China's official total of HIV infections is around 3,400, up from 3,341 at the end of 1995.
A Ministry of Public Health official stated that tens of thousands of HIV cases are uncounted.
Experts estimate the actual number of HIV infections to be between 50,000 and 100,000.
China is implementing measures to clamp down on drug abuse and strengthen blood transfusion controls.
A three-day national meeting on AIDS is being held in Beijing.

A computer network called the China Wide Web (CWW) was launched by a subsidiary of the official news agency Xinhua.
CWW aims to take Chinese businesses online and provide them with news and economic information.
China Internet Corp created CWW to offer online services in Chinese and provide overseas subscribers access to the Chinese business world.
China Internet chief technology officer Chung-Kiu Wong stated that the objective of CWW is to increase understanding of China.
CWW will use technology developed for the World Wide Web to supply news from international economic information providers like Reuters Holdings Ltd and Bloomberg.
China Internet is a Hong Kong-registered company that is majority-owned by Xinhua news agency.
Xinhua was appointed as the government regulator for foreign suppliers of economic information in China in January.
Harry Edelson of Edelson Technology Partners stated that Xinhua's regulatory role and China Internet's market position would enhance the company's prospects.
CWW is modeled on internal company networks or 'intranets' and will provide real-time information.
China Internet will have free use of Xinhua's communications network and has access agreements with the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications.

Changing Chinese tastes and new factories have contributed to growth for Nestle SA in China.
Nestle's core products in China include milk products, instant coffee, chocolate, sugar-based confectionery, and prepared foods.
A new plant for producing mineral water is scheduled to open in China next year.
Nestle's total investment in China is expected to reach five billion yuan ($602 million) by the year 2000.
Nestle expects sales in China, excluding Hong Kong, to be 1.5 billion yuan in 1996.
Nestle has completed nine of the eleven projects planned in its initial 2.8 billion yuan investment in China.
Nestle's focus in the short term is on expanding established plants, with up to four new production projects possible by 2000.
Nestle's Nescafe brand holds a 75 percent share of the instant coffee market in China.
Theo Klauser, chief executive of Nestle (China) Investment Services Ltd, stated that the younger generation will increasingly drink coffee.
Nestle has lagged in entering China's ice cream market, facing competition from joint venture producers.

A Chinese court convicted Wang Dan of plotting to overthrow the government.
Wang Dan was sentenced to 11 years in prison.
The Beijing Number One Intermediate People's Court found Wang guilty of conspiring to subvert the Chinese government.
Wang faced a maximum penalty of death.
The court presented sufficient evidence, including written materials, witness accounts, recorded tape, and criminal technical appraisal.
Wang was deprived of his political rights for two years.
Wang confessed to receiving funds from overseas hostile forces and attempted to set up an opposition force.
Charges against Wang were supported by testimony from another dissident, Liu Xiaobo.
Liu Xiaobo was sent to a labor camp for three years.
Foreign reporters and legal experts were barred from attending the trial.

Wang Dan has received an official confirmation of his 11-year prison sentence.
A Beijing court condemned Wang Dan for plotting against the government after a trial lasting less than four hours.
Wang Dan's family received notification of the verdict, allowing him to appeal within 10 days.
Wang Dan pleaded not guilty to subversion charges that carry a maximum death sentence and a minimum of 10 years' imprisonment.
Wang Dan vowed to appeal his conviction during a brief meeting with his family after the trial.
The 11-year sentence imposed on Wang Dan is part of a series of actions against Chinese dissidents.
International human rights activists condemned Wang Dan's trial as a parody of justice.
Chinese state media described the trial as a model of fairness.
The United States and some European and Asian nations expressed concern over Wang Dan's sentencing.
Czech President Vaclav Havel called the verdict unacceptable and deeply disturbing.

Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson expressed disapproval to Chinese Premier Li Peng over the jailing of dissident Wang Dan.
Wang Dan was sentenced to 11 years in prison for plotting against the government.
A court in Beijing took less than four hours to convict Wang Dan after a trial that raised global concern.
Persson stated that human rights were discussed during official talks but Wang Dan's case was raised afterwards.
Persson had a private discussion with Premier Li Peng during a dinner where he mentioned Wang Dan's case.
Persson criticized the treatment of political and religious dissidents in China and the use of capital punishment.
Sweden and China signed an agreement for the Raoul Wallenberg Institute to arrange human rights seminars.
The jailing of Wang Dan is part of a trend of repression against China's pro-democracy movement.
Most dissidents in China have been forced into exile or are serving long prison sentences.
Persson's delegation included Swedish businessmen who were expected to sign several deals during the visit.

China congratulated U.S. President Bill Clinton on his election victory.
China stated that Clinton's victory presents an opportunity to improve ties between Washington and Beijing.
Chinese academics and officials expressed that Clinton's win is favorable for Beijing leadership.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai stated that there is a good opportunity for improving Sino-U.S. relations.
Cui Tiankai noted that some positive progress has been made in bilateral relations.
Chinese academics believe that Clinton's re-election could help stabilize Sino-U.S. relations.
Clinton's previous four years in office were marked by strained Sino-U.S. ties due to various disputes.
Chinese officials expressed cautious optimism about future relations with Clinton's re-election.
Chinese leaders prefer to deal with U.S. presidents they know personally.
Sino-U.S. economic and trade ties have grown despite recent diplomatic disputes.

Chinese leaders denounced Beijing's exclusion from the World Trade Organisation as unjust.
Minister for Economic Restructuring Li Tieying stated that China has made significant progress in opening its markets to trade and investment.
Li Tieying expressed that protectionism or trade sanctions should not be used as policy tools in a world reliant on international trade.
Li stated that a World Trade Organisation without China is incomplete.
Chinese officials believe Beijing should be allowed to join the WTO on lenient terms as a developing country.
Chinese officials blame the United States for blocking their accession to the WTO with tough demands.
Disagreement over the terms of Beijing's admission to the WTO is a point of contention in Sino-U.S. relations.
China has urged the United States to make Most Favoured Nation status permanent.
Li warned that if the United States revokes China's Most Favoured Nation treatment, U.S. consumers would incur an additional $14 billion in costs annually.
China's growing trade surplus with the United States is viewed as a barrier to improved Sino-U.S. relations.

Ablait Abdureschit is the chairman of the Xinjiang autonomous region in China.
Abdureschit accused western nations of collaborating with pro-independence activists to attempt to separate Xinjiang from China.
He stated that there is no end in sight for the war on separatism in Xinjiang.
Abdureschit claimed that activists in Xinjiang have instigated riots and committed political killings.
He asserted that the majority of people in Xinjiang oppose separatist activities.
Abdureschit accused unnamed western nations of conspiring with pro-independence activists.
He noted that separatists are against the economic progress brought by Beijing to Xinjiang.
Authorities in Xinjiang have intensified crackdowns on separatists and unauthorized religious activities this year.
Abdureschit acknowledged that the struggle against separatism is long-term and complicated.
He described Xinjiang as a region with a history of ethnic unrest between the Uighur population and the Han majority.

High-level visits have generated goodwill between China and the U.S.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin is scheduled to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton at the Asian-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in the Philippines.
Diplomats and analysts believe the meeting will address lingering disputes between the two countries.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher's recent visit to China indicated new U.S. flexibility on issues like weapons proliferation, trade, and Taiwan.
Niu Jun, a Chinese specialist on U.S. affairs, stated that progress was made on all issues during Christopher's visit.
Both China and the U.S. acknowledged the need to increase contacts and state visits.
Christopher recognized U.S. arms sales to Taiwan as a weapons proliferation issue.
The U.S. is considering starting peaceful nuclear cooperation with China before a previously signed accord is implemented.
China is interested in purchasing nuclear reactors from U.S. firms, but cooperation is hindered by U.S. concerns about nuclear technology proliferation.
China is likely to seek unilateral concessions from the U.S. regarding its accession to the World Trade Organisation, human rights, and trade.

A Japanese mission has reached basic agreement on 22 development projects proposed by China.
The projects involve infrastructure, agriculture, and environmental protection.
Shiro Sadoshima is the director of the loan aid division of Japan's Foreign Ministry.
The first year of the yen loan package is earmarked for 180 billion yen ($1.6 billion).
The yen loan package will run from 1996 to 2000.
Discussions on the projects were delayed due to faltering relations and Japanese anger at China's nuclear testing.
The 580 billion yen in Japanese soft loans to China between 1996 and 2000 were not formally affected by the protests.
No missions to approve the loan details were sent after China's nuclear test in May 1995.
Sadoshima stated that the Japanese government has never claimed that Chinese nuclear testing caused the delay.
Relations between Beijing and Tokyo have been strained by a visit by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to a war shrine and a territorial dispute.

MCI Communications Corp and Sprint Corp will have restrained third quarter results due to the cost of new ventures.
Sprint Corp's earnings per share are expected to be lower than a year ago because of investments in the Global One venture and Personal Communications Services.
Sprint's shares in issue will rise to about 435 million from 351 million a year ago due to stock issued to partners Deutsche Telekom and French Telecom.
MCI's investment in media, Internet, and satellite services with News Corp Ltd is not expected to break even for several years.
AT&T Corp warned on September 24 that its earnings per share could be as much as 10 percent below analysts' forecasts for the third quarter.
If AT&T's earnings per share are $0.83, it would be 13.5 percent below the $0.96 of a year earlier.
AT&T's problems are attributed to an expensive consumer market strategy and competition from small resellers and dial around services.
Resellers like Excel Communications Inc have achieved over 50 percent annual revenue growth by using independent sales representatives.
MCI expects higher customer turnover in consumer markets due to increased competition.
Neither MCI nor Sprint depends as heavily on the consumer market as AT&T does.

Sprint Corp showed strong performance in all businesses in the third quarter of 1996.
Analysts believe Sprint will perform better than MCI Communications Corp or AT&T Corp in long-distance telephone services.
There is uncertainty regarding the success of Sprint's new ventures and their impact on earnings.
Sprint's third-quarter earnings per share were $0.72, down from $0.76 a year ago.
The decrease in earnings per share was attributed to the cost of new ventures, a 24 percent increase in shares issued, and a two-point tax rate rise.
Call volume carried by Sprint increased by 21 percent from the previous year.
Sprint's revenues increased by 14.1 percent over the same period.
Sprint's shares rose by 1/2 to 40-3/8 by 1300 EDT/1700 GMT on Tuesday.
Sprint PCS and Global One caused earnings dilution of four and six cents per share, respectively, in the third quarter.
Sprint owns 40 percent of Sprint PCS, while Tele-Communications Inc owns 30 percent, and Comcast Corp and Cox Communications Inc each own 15 percent.

AT&T Corp's proposed successor to Robert Allen as chairman and chief executive will be a surprise candidate.
Michael Armstrong and William Esrey are not in contention for the position.
The true candidate has not been identified by sources close to the company.
AT&T's board met to examine candidates for the post of president and chief operating officer.
An announcement regarding the new candidate is expected in the next few days.
AT&T will report its third quarter results on Thursday.
The post of chairman and chief executive is vacant after Alex Mandl resigned in August.
Bob Allen may split the role of chief executive with the new candidate in the future.
AT&T is looking for a world-class marketer and technologist with considerable experience.
AT&T issued a profit warning in September, indicating earnings per share may be 10 percent below expectations.

Frontier Corp. is investing up to $500 million in a $2 billion fiber optic network in the United States.
The fiber optic network will be the largest built in the United States as a single project.
Frontier's investment will position it ahead of AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp.
Lucent Technologies Inc. will supply the network cable under a contract worth at least $100 million.
The network is being built by Qwest Communications, which has spent $500 million since beginning work in 1995.
Qwest is seeking additional telecommunications partners to help fund the remaining $1 billion of the project.
The network will connect almost 100 cities and will use the SONET technical standard.
Frontier expects to cut costs significantly and increase its network capacity forty-fold with this investment.
Robert Barrett, president of Frontier's Network Systems unit, stated that the network would begin to bring benefits in 1997.
Frontier plans to fund $350 million to $400 million of its investment from its own cash flow.

John Walter believes that making strategies work within AT&T Corp will be central to his role as chief operating officer and future chief executive in 1998.
Walter stated that execution is crucial for the success of any strategy.
Walter was appointed by AT&T as president and chief operating officer and is the heir apparent to CEO Robert Allen.
Walter will work alongside Robert Allen for 14 months to understand AT&T's operations.
Walter emphasized the importance of achieving objectives and maintaining an appropriate cost base.
Analysts have criticized AT&T's inability to meet its objectives, leading to a decline in brand value and share price.
AT&T's market share in the $75 billion market has decreased from 60 percent to around 55 percent over two years.
Consultant Chris Landis noted that AT&T has not executed effectively on the consumer side.
AT&T has sold off most of its creative content efforts and focused on Internet access.
AT&T's share price has fallen 16 percent this year, while the broader market has risen.

AT&T Corp. appointed John Walter as its new president and heir apparent to Chairman Robert Allen.
John Walter is the chairman of R.R. Donnelley and Sons.
Walter was unanimously elected to the positions of president and chief operating officer and as a member of the board, effective November 1.
Robert Allen expressed confidence in Walter's leadership qualities for AT&T's success.
Industry analysts were surprised by AT&T's choice of Walter over a more well-known executive.
Concerns were raised about the 18-month handover period not leading to a quick change in strategy.
AT&T stock closed at $37.875 on the New York Stock Exchange, down $1.875.
AT&T shares have fallen 16 percent this year, adjusted for the spin-off of Lucent Technologies Inc.
The president and COO positions were vacant after Alex Mandl resigned in August.
AT&T's board focused on Walter due to his successful track record at Donnelley.

WorldCom Inc's takeover of MFS Communications Co Inc is valued at $14 billion.
The takeover is expected to generate savings on duplicated costs.
WorldCom aims to be the first to offer end-to-end service in U.S. business telecommunications.
Bernard Ebbers, the chief executive of WorldCom, acknowledged a substantial premium in the stock terms for MFS.
Ebbers stated that savings would soon cover the cost of the deal.
MFS has local networks in numerous major U.S. cities.
MFS was positioned to compete with regional Bell companies for access to local business customers.
James Crowe, the chief executive of MFS, indicated that WorldCom had a unique opportunity to merge with MFS.
WorldCom's stock increased by 57 percent annually over the past ten years.
MFS's growth rate was 41 percent annually in the three years since its initial public offering.

British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp are considering a merger.
Analysts believe a merger would pose a significant threat in U.S. markets.
Consultant Jeffrey Kagan stated that the merger would be detrimental to AT&T Corp.
The two companies confirmed they would announce details of the merger by the end of the weekend.
A source indicated that the merger would involve a cash and stock offer from BT for MCI.
Analysts speculate the offer could be around $40 a share, valuing MCI at $28 billion.
MCI currently holds about 20 percent of the $75 billion U.S. long distance market.
AT&T has a 55 percent share of the same market.
Both companies are entering the $90 billion local calling market.
Analyst Guy Woodlief stated that the merger would provide MCI with significant resources to compete.

Telephone resellers have captured $12 billion of the $80 billion long distance market.
The merger between MFS Communications Co Inc and WorldCom Inc allows resellers to enter the telecommunications market.
MFS provides local calling networks to businesses, while WorldCom is a long distance and international carrier.
MFS WorldCom will offer end-to-end business services and allow resellers to provide their own branded telecommunication services.
Excel Communications Inc is one of over 400 resellers in the industry that has impacted the long distance telephone market.
Long distance companies and regional Bells will face increased competition and pressure on profit margins due to resellers.
Profit margins and growth rates in high speed data and broadband applications are higher than those in long distance services.
Resellers pose a threat to future growth for major firms in the telecommunications industry.
MFS WorldCom will have 2,900 salespeople available, compared to 63 previously.
GTE and some regional Bells are purchasing long distance services from WorldCom.

British Telecommunications Plc stock and cash share offer is worth between $36 and $39.60 per MCI share at Friday's closing BT share price.
MCI chief financial officer Doug Maine stated that the deal includes an offer of 0.54 new American Depositary Shares in the new combined group, named Concert, for every MCI share.
Each Concert ADS is equivalent to one BT American Depositary Share and $6 cash.
BT ADS closed at $55-1/2 in New York, giving a value of $30 per MCI share plus $6 cash per share before the effect of a buyback by BT.
BT plans to conduct a buyback of up to 10 percent of its shares after the closing of the deal.
The maximum buyback would increase the value of the deal to MCI shareholders to $39.60 per MCI share.
Maine indicated that 80 percent of MCI shares held by owners other than BT would translate into a holding of 33 percent in the combined Concert company.
The terms of the deal value MCI at a total of $25.2 billion before the effect of the buyback.
BT already owns 20 percent of MCI, so it needs to issue Concert stock and cash worth $20.1 billion.
The new Concert company will have 9.5 billion shares in issue, including 3.1 billion new shares issued for MCI.

MCI Communications Corp's merger with British Telecommunications Corp faces regulatory hurdles and a lengthy completion time of 12 months.
MCI shares were trading at 30-1/2 on Monday morning, below a theoretical value of around $39 per share.
Analyst Richard Klugman of PaineWebber stated that arbitragers are demanding between 15 and 20 percent on the deal due to uncertainties regarding U.S. regulatory approval.
The merger offer includes 0.54 new American depositary shares in the combined group, named Concert, for every MCI share.
Each Concert American depositary share is equivalent to one BT American depositary share and $6 cash.
There is a significant gap between the value of the deal using BT shares in London and the American depositary shares.
Analyst Julie Kennedy of Goldman Sachs noted that the final calculations will fluctuate with changes in BT's stock price and the exchange rate.
At the exchange rate of one pound equals $1.64, the American depositary shares appear to be overvalued.
Analysts do not expect much from a potential buyback of up to 10 percent of Concert shares after the deal closes.
Klugman mentioned that a buyback could lead to higher interest charges affecting operating earnings.

British Telecom and MCI Communications announced a $20 billion merger.
The merger is the largest cross-border takeover deal in history.
The merged company will be called Concert Plc.
Concert Plc will be the world's second-largest telecommunications group by market capitalization.
Concert Plc is valued at $54 billion based on stock prices from the previous Friday.
Concert Plc is comparable in value to AT&T Corp., which is MCI's main competitor.
The merger is expected to provide better service and lower international calling charges for customers.
Businesses will benefit from a company that can support them globally.
Analysts predict faster earnings growth for shareholders due to the merger.
The total value of MCI is $25.2 billion, with British Telecom owning 20 percent.

McDonald's Corp. created a new position of chairman of its U.S. operations.
Jack Greenberg was named chairman of McDonald's U.S.A.
Greenberg remains vice chairman of McDonald's and will relinquish the chief financial officer post.
Greenberg will continue to report to Michael Quinlan, McDonald's chairman.
Analysts stated that the creation of the new position was due to intense competition and soft sales in the U.S. market.
Analysts expect McDonald's third-quarter same store sales to be down compared to the previous year.
McDonald's has not had a single positive month in same store sales in the U.S. this year.
Margins have been under pressure for over a year in the U.S. according to analysts.
Greenberg's appointment indicates that McDonald's was not satisfied with the direction of its domestic business.
McDonald's has been introducing new offerings such as the Arch Deluxe hamburger and Deluxe Grilled Chicken.

Shedding its chemical businesses would leave Monsanto Co as a pure play in the life sciences area.
Monsanto has attractive agricultural biotechnology and pharmaceutical holdings.
NatWest Securities analyst Mark Wiltamuth stated that the entity is likely to have a higher valuation without the chemical businesses.
Mark Wiltamuth noted that the chemical business does not have the growth potential of agricultural biotechnology and pharmaceuticals.
Monsanto indicated it might spin off, sell, or merge its chemical businesses, or keep and restructure them.
Monsanto's stock rose to 42 after setting a new 52-week high of 42-3/4.
Monsanto chief economist Nicholas Filippello stated that the directions of the life sciences and chemical businesses were quite different.
Analysts expected Monsanto to shed its chemical businesses following the sale of its worldwide stryrenics plastics business.
Dain Bosworth analyst Bonnie Wittenburg suggested that the chances of keeping and restructuring the chemical businesses are slim.
The chemical businesses that may be sold or spun off include nylon and acrylic fibers, Saflex plastic interlayer, and specialty chemicals.

A federal judge accepted Archer Daniels Midland Co.'s price-fixing guilty plea.
Archer Daniels Midland Co. was ordered to pay $100 million in fines.
U.S. District Court Judge Ruben Castillo accepted ADM's guilty plea to two counts of price fixing.
The fines imposed on ADM were $70 million for fixing prices of lysine and $30 million for fixing prices on citric acid.
The fines are the largest ever in a price-fixing case.
The U.S. Justice Department is continuing its investigation of two ADM officials, Michael Andreas and Terrance Wilson.
Attorney General Janet Reno stated that the settlement should send a message to corporations about collusive behavior.
Under the plea agreement, Archer Daniels officials are required to cooperate with the Justice Department's investigation.
Archer Daniels Midland Co. reported a net income of $3.6 million for the three months ended Sept. 30.
The company's stock was unchanged at $21.625 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

Archer Daniels Midland Co.'s Chairman Dwayne Andreas apologized to shareholders for the difficult situations the company faced over the past year.
Andreas acknowledged that the company's guilty pleas to two counts of price fixing occurred during his tenure as chairman.
The company agreed to pay $100 million in fines to the U.S. government.
A proposal requiring the board to be composed of a majority of independent directors was defeated but received 42 percent of the votes cast.
ADM's slate of 12 directors was approved by about 89 percent of the votes cast.
The new board was reduced in number from 17 and is considered more independent, with only Dwayne Andreas remaining as a company executive.
William Bell of the Florida Retirement System Trust Fund expressed hope that the 42 percent vote in favor of the independent director measure would signal shareholder concerns.
The Florida trust fund and the California Public Employees Retirement System co-sponsored the independent board proposal.
Charles Valdes, chairman of Calpers, stated that Calpers will continue to pursue the wishes of shareholders for a majority of independent directors.
No mention was made of a pending U.S. Department of Justice investigation of Michael Andreas and Terrance Wilson during the meeting.

Monsanto Co exceeded analysts' expectations for its third quarter.
Nicholas Filippello is the chief economist at Monsanto.
Filippello warned analysts not to increase earnings estimates for the full year.
The First Call mean of analysts' estimates for Monsanto is $1.48 a share.
Monsanto reported third quarter earnings of $0.28 a share.
Monsanto's third quarter earnings increased from $0.23 a year ago.
Certain factors contributed to third quarter earnings exceeding First Call expectations.
Monsanto is considering options for its chemical business.
One option for the chemical business is to spin it off as a separate publicly traded company.
Filippello stated that spinning off the chemicals operation would be preferable from a tax standpoint.

Kellogg Co. reported a drop of more than 30 percent in its third quarter profits.
Kellogg's cereal volume dropped in a competitive market.
Kellogg's net income for the third quarter fell to $159.5 million from $230 million a year ago.
Kellogg's earnings per share dropped 29 percent to 75 cents from $1.05 last year.
Kellogg's overall sales slipped 9 percent to $1.68 billion from $1.84 billion.
Kellogg Chairman Arnold Langbo stated that third quarter performance was influenced by competitive conditions in the U.S. cereal category.
Analysts estimate Kellogg's domestic cereal sales volume fell 9 percent to 10 percent in the third quarter.
Kellogg's stock fell by $1 to $64.50 a share on the New York Stock Exchange.
Kellogg set a new 52-week low of $64.125.
The U.S. cereal market overall was sluggish, with sales growing about 1.5 percent.

Archer Daniels Midland Co is likely to face criminal charges in a U.S. government price-fixing investigation.
Three companies have pleaded guilty in the investigation.
Robert Stephenson, an attorney, stated that the cooperation of ADM's alleged co-conspirators increases the likelihood of charges against ADM.
An ADM spokeswoman declined to comment on the situation.
The three firms that pleaded guilty admitted to conspiracy in price-fixing of lysine, a feed additive.
Ajinomoto Co Inc, Kyowa Hakko Kogyo Co Ltd, and the U.S. unit of Sewon Co Ltd admitted to conspiring to fix prices in the world lysine market.
The three companies agreed to cooperate with the investigation by providing witnesses and documents.
Joe Sims, an attorney, indicated that the cooperation of some defendants puts pressure on remaining potential defendants like ADM.
Sims suggested that ADM may decide to enter a plea or face indictment soon.
Analysts noted that ADM could afford the $10 million fines levied against Ajinomoto and Kyowa.

American Trans Air (ATA) plans to cut back its jet capacity and some scheduled service.
ATA expects to form additional alliances with other air carriers.
Kenneth Wolff is the chief financial officer of Amtran Inc, the parent company of ATA.
ATA and Chicago Express Airlines agreed to a code-sharing agreement in late May.
Code-sharing agreements allow airlines to put their codes on each other's flights in computerized reservation systems.
Stanley Pace is the president of the Indianapolis-based company, Amtran Inc.
Pace stated that the alliance with Chicago Express has exceeded expectations.
ATA will continue to serve vacation destinations from Indianapolis, Milwaukee, and Chicago's Midway Airport.
Amtran reported a loss of $0.20 a share in the second quarter, compared to a profit of $0.29 a year ago.
ATA is cutting back scheduled service from Boston to destinations like Orlando, Florida, and Nassau, Bahamas.

Mark Whitacre, a former executive of Archer Daniels Midland Co, filed a lawsuit against ADM seeking back wages and punitive damages.
The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Central District of Illinois.
Whitacre denied charges from ADM that he stole $9.0 million from the company.
Whitacre's lawsuit claims that he was fired for assisting the FBI with its investigation into ADM, not for embezzlement.
ADM pleaded guilty to two counts of fixing prices of lysine and citric acid and agreed to pay $100 million in fines.
Whitacre seeks a judgment against ADM of more than $50,000 and punitive damages of more than $50,000.
Whitacre had previously indicated plans to file an $80 million wrongful discharge suit against ADM.
Whitacre claims lost wages from August 1995, when he was fired, until October 1995, when he was hired by Biomar International Inc.
Whitacre earned $320,000 a year at ADM, plus stock options.
Whitacre's lawsuit includes claims of denial of stock options, defamation, and mental and emotional distress.

Mark Whitacre, a former executive of Archer Daniels Midland Co., announced he is no longer cooperating with the U.S. government in its price-fixing investigation.
Whitacre was indicted along with two other former ADM executives for conspiring to fix prices of the feed additive lysine.
The other indicted executives are Michael Andreas, former executive vice president and vice chairman of ADM, and Terrance Wilson, a former group vice president.
Michael Andreas is the son of ADM Chairman Dwayne Andreas.
Whitacre stated he would not participate in what he described as the government's coverup.
Whitacre declined to comment on his indictment but suggested that the Justice Department and the FBI would have questions to answer when all evidence is revealed.
The Justice Department did not respond to Whitacre's statement.
Legal experts noted that it is common for federal informants to be indicted but often receive lenient treatment for their cooperation.
Whitacre's decision to stop cooperating could jeopardize his treatment by the Justice Department.
Whitacre's previous cooperation may still be considered in his legal proceedings.

Quaker Oats Co. is considering selling its Snapple beverage business.
Analysts suggest that Quaker may also sell its Gatorade sports drink line.
John McMillin, an analyst at Prudential Securities, believes Quaker's beverage division is up for sale.
Snapple has incurred operating losses since Quaker purchased it for $1.8 billion two years ago.
Quaker's stock price increased by $2, closing at $38.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Michael Mauboussin, an analyst at CS First Boston, stated that Quaker is likely to pursue a restructuring that includes selling undervalued assets.
Mauboussin referred to Gatorade as Quaker's 'crown jewel.'
Rumors about a potential sale of Quaker or parts of its business have circulated for about three years.
Quaker has declined to comment on speculation regarding its business.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Quaker might sell Gatorade and Snapple for prices between $3 billion and $4 billion.

The burger battle will continue in the United States next year as fast-food chains test new recipes and promotions.
McDonald's Corp has about 12,000 U.S. units and over 20,000 worldwide.
McDonald's U.S. same-store sales are below year-ago levels.
Dean Witter analyst David Adelman stated that this will be McDonald's sixth consecutive quarter of lower same-store sales in the U.S.
Wendy's International Inc has seen U.S. same-store sales rise five to six percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Wendy's had an eight percent gain in same-store sales in the third quarter of 1996.
Wendy's has about 4,425 U.S. units and 4,925 worldwide.
Burger King, a unit of Grand Metropolitan Plc, reported a 2.6 percent rise in U.S. same-store sales for fiscal 1996.
Burger King had 8,696 units worldwide at the end of fiscal 1996, including more than 6,600 in the United States.
Wendy's is testing a fresh pita sandwich in 11 U.S. markets, which may be rolled out nationally in 1997.

Monsanto Co announced its pending acquisition of Holden's Foundation Seeds for $1.0 billion.
The acquisition will dilute earnings for two or three years.
In the first year, dilution could be as much as $0.10 to $0.17 a share.
The actual dilution number could be lower due to pending accounting issues.
Nicholas Filippello, chief economist for Monsanto, stated the acquisition will be accretive by the end of the decade.
Earnings dilution may be influenced by future charges related to the Holden's deal.
Charges may include write-offs of Holden's in-process research and development.
Monsanto measures itself on an economic value added (EVA) basis.
Monsanto plans to buy Holden's for up to $945.0 million and Corn States and Corn States International for up to $75 million.
Analysts view the acquisition of Holden's as a defensive move against competitors.

Wang Xizhe is a Chinese dissident who fled to the United States via Hong Kong.
Activists and analysts believe that Wang's escape may be the last of its kind due to anticipated changes in Hong Kong's status.
Since the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989, hundreds of Chinese dissidents have escaped through Hong Kong in an operation known as Yellowbird.
Wang has not appeared in public since his arrival in the United States, and it is unconfirmed if Yellowbird facilitated his escape from Guangdong.
The escape route is expected to be closed when Hong Kong becomes part of China on July 1, ending British colonial rule.
Robin Munro, director of Human Rights Watch Asia, stated that China could prevent dissidents with asylum from leaving Hong Kong after the transition.
China has labeled Wang's escape as an illegal frontier crossing and is pursuing legal action against him and those who assisted him.
Peter Lee, a professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, indicated that it will be more difficult for dissidents to use Hong Kong as an escape route after 1997.
Lee Wing-tat, a legislator and member of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements in China, expressed concerns about potential repercussions for those aiding dissidents.

Hong Kong is observing the outcome of a Beijing gathering that will influence its post-colonial government set to take over in 1997.
The Preparatory Committee, consisting of pro-China figures from Hong Kong and mainland Chinese officials, is meeting in Beijing to elect a 400-member caucus.
This caucus will select Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader and parliament.
The transition of Hong Kong to Chinese rule is scheduled to occur in 242 days.
Gurkha soldiers, who were part of the colonial garrison, were set to bid farewell to one of their Hong Kong bases.
Concerns arose in Hong Kong regarding a potential crackdown by China following the handover, particularly after the jailing of dissident Wang Dan.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen indicated that freedom of expression in Hong Kong would be limited after the sovereignty transfer.
China barred entry to two Hong Kong politicians who intended to petition against certain policies at the Beijing meeting.
Two Hong Kong activists were expelled from Beijing on the same day.
A survey by the Better Hong Kong Foundation indicated that most Hong Kong businessmen expect a decline in press freedom, the political system, and human rights after the handover.

Hong Kong will hold an election on Friday, described by China as a 'democratic election with Hong Kong characteristics'.
Only 400 citizens out of 6.3 million in Hong Kong will be voting in this election.
A 400-member Selection Committee, formed under Beijing's control, will be inaugurated in Hong Kong.
The Selection Committee's mission is to elect the first post-colonial leader and 60 members of a new legislature.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen will appoint the committee during his first official trip to Hong Kong.
Hong Kong will become a Special Administrative Region of China after Britain hands it back at midnight on June 30.
Beijing has promised to maintain Hong Kong's capitalist system for 50 years under the 'one country two systems' policy.
Pro-democracy legislators criticized leadership candidates for not addressing human rights and democracy issues.
Trade unionist Lee Cheuk-yan described leading candidate Tung Chee-hwa as dangerous and conservative.
A motion criticizing the leadership selection was defeated by pro-Beijing legislators.

U.S. President Bill Clinton expressed new enthusiasm for Asian foreign policy issues.
Security experts in Hong Kong urged all countries to prevent conflict over Taiwan.
Experts stated that U.S. policy on China and Asia is maturing.
David Shambaugh from George Washington University identified the Taiwan Strait as a major potential security flashpoint.
Shambaugh warned that any conflict over Taiwan could harm regional commerce.
Shambaugh suggested that Taiwan's leaders should exercise restraint and wait for dialogue with Beijing after China's upcoming Communist Party congress.
Shambaugh called for China to renounce the use of force and respect Taiwan's autonomy.
China considers Taiwan a rebel province and has threatened military action if Taiwan seeks formal independence.
Tensions between China and Taiwan have increased due to pro-independence sentiment in Taiwan.
Yuan Ming from Beijing University and Masashi Nishihara from Japan's National Defence Academy advocated for maintaining the status quo regarding Taiwan.

Britain proposed new laws on subversion in Hong Kong on Tuesday.
The proposed laws aim to prevent Chinese-style jailings of dissidents after Beijing takes over Hong Kong in 1997.
The colonial government unveiled draft amendments to Hong Kong's criminal law, ordered by Governor Chris Patten's cabinet.
The bill will be presented to the Legislative Council next Wednesday.
British officials stated that the move was an effort to set legal standards for China to follow after the handover.
Chinese officials criticized Britain's proposal, claiming it violated promises regarding the transition.
A spokesman for China's de facto embassy stated that Britain must bear the consequences of its actions.
Under the Basic Law, Hong Kong must add laws against secession and subversion after the handover.
China indicated it would enact the law through a new legislature after the sovereignty transfer.
A Legislative Council motion in January urged the Hong Kong government to introduce pre-emptive laws to protect civil rights.

Tung Chee-hwa is a pro-China contender for Hong Kong's leadership.
A Beijing-controlled body conducted a three-day quiz of three candidates for Hong Kong's leadership.
The Selection Committee consists of 400 influential Hong Kong individuals chosen under China's supervision.
The committee will meet again on December 11 to select a chief executive.
Many believe Tung Chee-hwa is the likely winner of the selection process.
Tung Chee-hwa expressed loyalty to China and criticized British Governor Chris Patten during the committee's questioning.
Hong Kong will revert to Chinese rule on June 30 after being a British colony for over 150 years.
Beijing plans to establish Hong Kong as a Special Administrative Region with a promise to maintain its capitalist system for 50 years.
The Economic Journal stated that the choice of chief executive is obvious and suggested that the outcome is predetermined.
Tung Chee-hwa's responses were described as politically correct and aligned with Beijing's preferences.

The United States' top diplomat on Asia is U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord.
Winston Lord met with key officials and politicians in Hong Kong regarding the colony's 1997 return to China.
Lord had separate meetings with local political parties and with China's top official in Hong Kong, Zhou Nan.
Lord was scheduled to meet colonial Governor Chris Patten and his deputy, Anson Chan.
Lord was also set to meet shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, who is considered a candidate for Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader.
Pro-democracy parties criticized Lord for planning to meet only Tung Chee-hwa among the three candidates for the post-colonial leadership.
Legislator Emily Lau of the pro-democracy group Frontier stated that she was not invited to meet Lord.
The democracy camp accused China of preordaining Tung Chee-hwa as the winner of the leadership contest.
The leadership contest in Hong Kong is set to culminate on December 11.
Legislator Yeung Sum of the Democratic Party expressed concerns to Lord about the future of press freedom and the elected legislature.

Hong Kong democracy activists protested on Monday after 134 politicians applied to join a Beijing-controlled assembly.
The assembly is intended to replace the elected legislature in mid-1997.
Political analysts stated that the rush to join the provisional legislature may weaken the colonial legislature.
As of the registration deadline on Monday, 134 people had applied, including at least 33 members of the current Legislative Council (Legco).
Hong Kong will revert to China at midnight on June 30, and Beijing plans to replace the elected Legco with a provisional assembly on handover day.
The provisional assembly is set to be selected on December 21.
Hong Kong has a population of 6.3 million people and will have two legislatures during the final six months of British rule.
The two legislatures will have the same number of seats, which is 60.
Among the 33 incumbent lawmakers who applied is Legco speaker Andrew Wong.
Pro-democracy activists caused chaos during the registration process, burning documents and clashing with security personnel.

On the eve of a gathering in China to select Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa was favored to win.
The Selection Committee consists of 400 members, including Hong Kong business leaders and pro-China politicians.
Tung Chee-hwa received 206 votes in the first round of voting by the Selection Committee.
Sovereignty over Hong Kong will revert to China on June 30, 1997.
A poll by Lingnan College indicated that 56 percent of respondents believed the winner had been predetermined.
Martin Lee, head of the Democratic Party, expressed doubt that Tung would protect Hong Kong's freedoms and rights.
Some Hong Kong newspapers were preparing profiles of Tung Chee-hwa ahead of the selection announcement.
If elected, Tung will face a no-confidence debate from lawmaker Emily Lau.
Colonial Governor Chris Patten has pledged support for the future chief executive.
Tung has stated he will engage with Hong Kong's civil service for a smooth transition.

China and Britain are working to remove obstacles to Hong Kong's transfer to Chinese sovereignty next year.
Agreements are being formed regarding handover ceremonies and budgets.
Diplomats reported that London and Beijing are nearing an agreement on a ceremony for Hong Kong's handover to China on June 30/July 1.
A potential announcement regarding the handover ceremony deal may occur next month.
Progress in informal talks suggests a basic accord could be reached before the foreign ministers' meeting at the United Nations General Assembly next month.
Disagreements over handover ceremonies, particularly concerning Governor Chris Patten's role, are complicating negotiations.
Negotiators from Britain and China have made progress on Hong Kong's budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year.
Chinese senior official Chen Zuo'er confirmed agreements on spending guidelines, maximum spending limits, and procedures for new budget requests.
Hong Kong Treasury Secretary K.C. Kwong expressed optimism about the budget discussions, stating that the preparatory stage is nearly complete.
A Beijing official stated that the list of public nominees for the first post-colonial legislature and chief executive will not be made public.

The pro-China lobby in Hong Kong nominated Chief Justice Sir Ti Liang Yang as a candidate for leadership after the territory reverts to China in 1997.
Xu Shimin, a pro-Beijing publisher, stated he would nominate Sir Ti Liang Yang for the position.
Hong Kong will revert to China on July 1, 1997, ending 150 years of British colonial rule.
China is establishing a 400-member Selection Committee to nominate the first Chief Executive and appoint a provisional legislature.
Nominations for the Selection Committee will close in two weeks, with nearly 20,000 nomination forms requested and issued.
China has ruled out a universal democratic vote for Hong Kong's post-handover political leaders.
The Selection Committee is expected to select the Chief Executive around November.
Sir Ti Liang Yang's return to the leadership contest is surprising due to previous controversy over his remarks on human rights.
A recent poll indicated that Anson Chan is the public's favorite for post-colonial leader, receiving 60.1 percent support.
Tung Chee-hwa and Martin Lee received 10.4 percent and 10 percent support, respectively, in the same poll.

China established the Provisional Legislative Council in Shenzhen on Saturday.
The Provisional Legislative Council will take over Hong Kong's elected legislature next July.
The establishment of the new council is a significant event in Hong Kong's transition to Chinese rule.
The new legislative body consists of pro-China politicians and tycoons.
Britain, Washington, and local protesters criticized the formation of the Provisional Legislative Council.
London has challenged China to allow the International Court of Justice to rule on the council's legality.
The selection of the 60 members was conducted by a 400-member China-controlled Selection Committee.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen claimed the selection process was just, fair, and open.
The Democratic Party boycotted the selection process, labeling it anti-democratic.
Pro-democracy groups in Hong Kong protested against the Shenzhen meeting, calling it a 'fake election'.

Eurotunnel SA /Plc has agreed to a restructuring of its 69.6 billion francs of debt.
French co-chairman Patrick Ponsolle described the restructuring as a robust deal.
The restructuring will eliminate a total of 16 billion francs of debt by converting eight billion francs of loans into equity and another eight billion francs into equity notes.
The plan secures Eurotunnel's future until 2003, when the London-Folkestone high-speed rail link is expected to be built.
Ponsolle stated that after 2003, Eurotunnel expects an increase in revenues from the railways.
The interest rate for the restructuring is fixed at 5.2 percent, amounting to 3.21 billion francs for a seven-year period.
The fixed interest rate is lower than current market rates.
In case of a cash flow shortage, Eurotunnel can utilize stabilisation notes, which act as a credit line without interest until January 2006.
The restructuring extends the debt repayment periods significantly, with resettable bonds maturing in 2050 and participating loan notes in 2040.
Eurotunnel has negotiated the right to refinance its debt after 2004 without penalties.

Compagnie Generale des Eaux reported higher first half profits.
The company plans to reorganize its loss-making construction business.
The French market is currently depressed.
Chairman Jean-Marie Messier announced a first half net profit of 808 million francs.
This profit is an increase from 224 million francs a year ago.
Messier forecasted a full year net profit of about 1.8 billion francs for 1996.
This is an improvement from a net loss of 3.69 billion francs the previous year.
The results will be significantly influenced by exceptional items, including capital gains from asset sales.
Messier expects profits for 1997 to be much higher than those of 1996.
Generale des Eaux made a formal bid with Mannesmann AG to run the telecommunications operations of SNCF.

Air France is forming a transatlantic alliance with Delta Air Lines and Continental.
Air France signed letters of intent for cooperation with Delta and Continental.
The agreements are intended to help Air France compete with major European rivals.
The alliances will allow code-sharing arrangements between Air France and the U.S. carriers.
Passengers can receive a through-ticket from one airline to use on its partner airline.
The companies will harmonize flight schedules and share a frequent flyer program.
Delta operates from Atlanta, Georgia, Continental operates from Houston, Texas, and Air France operates from Paris Roissy-Charles De Gaulle airport.
Air France expects the alliances to save the airline $100 million a year.
Air France reported a net loss of more than two billion francs last year.
Air France chairman Christian Blanc has been seeking a partner to enhance the airline's global reach.

The submarine changed naval warfare in World War Two.
European shipbuilders are developing new stealth warships for the 21st century.
Three shipbuilders presented combat ship designs at a trade fair at Le Bourget airport.
Britain's Vosper Thornycroft unveiled the Sea Wraith corvette.
Brian Spilman, Vosper's manager of future projects shipbuilding, stated that the Sea Wraith could make other vessels of its class obsolete.
BAeSema presented the Cougar corvette at the trade fair.
French state-owned DCN shipyard presented the La Fayette frigate, claiming it is the first operational warship to fully use stealth features.
The La Fayette is designed for deep-water operations, unlike the other two ships designed for regional waters.
Stealth warships utilize radar-beating technology similar to that used by U.S. aircraft in the 1991 Gulf War.
The La Fayette uses a slab-sided superstructure and non-metallic materials to confuse radar.

French holding company CGIP announced it is buying 20 percent of car parts manufacturer Valeo.
The purchase addresses concerns from the French government, car makers, and Italian businessman Carlo de Benedetti.
Cerus, a French investment firm controlled by Carlo de Benedetti, sold the 20 percent stake to CGIP.
The total cost of the Valeo stake could reach 6.7 billion francs if Valeo meets its 1997 profit targets.
The Valeo stake has been available for sale for a year as Cerus aimed to reduce debts.
The sale of the Valeo stake attracted interest from U.S. investors, raising concerns among European car makers.
French industry minister Franck Borotra expressed a desire for a 'French solution' regarding the Valeo holding.
CGIP chairman Ernest-Antoine Seilliere stated that the purchase is beneficial for CGIP, its shareholders, and Valeo.
CGIP aims to rebalance its portfolio away from the packaging business, where it held 49 percent of its assets.
CGIP plans to request Valeo to adopt a more generous dividend policy and pursue acquisitions more aggressively.

The French government has allowed Air France to purchase Boeing long-haul passenger jets from the United States.
Air France is also permitted to buy similar planes from Airbus, which is based in France.
The clearance for these purchases will be discussed at a meeting of Air France's board members.
A source indicated that the French government prefers a balanced solution between Airbus and Boeing.
Les Echos reported that a committee of the Air France board is expected to recommend purchasing 10 Airbus A340-300 and 10 Boeing 777-200 jets.
Transport Minister Bernard Pons has been advocating for Air France to buy exclusively from Airbus.
Air France has received 20 billion francs in state funds.
Air France has a previous order for seven 767-300 and eight 737-500 aircraft due for delivery between 1999 and 2001.
A clause in the sale contract for the previous order allows Air France to convert these planes to other types.
The estimated cost of introducing a new plane like the Boeing 777 to the fleet is $40 million.

Eurotunnel SA/Plc operates the Channel Tunnel rail link between France and Britain.
A fire last week halted most services on the Channel Tunnel.
A minor fire broke out near the site of last week's blaze during Eurotunnel's public relations effort.
Patrick Ponsolle, French Co-Chairman of Eurotunnel, stated that the tunnel is at least as safe as other Channel transport systems.
A fire in a truck on a freight train damaged a section of the tunnel and injured 34 people.
Eurostar and Le Shuttle services have been halted, but a limited freight service has resumed.
Wednesday's fire was caused by welding work during repairs and was quickly extinguished.
Robert Malpas, British Co-Chairman of Eurotunnel, emphasized that safety is the company's first consideration.
The cause of the fire is still unknown, with sabotage being a possibility according to the investigating French magistrate.
Ponsolle estimated Eurotunnel's maximum potential loss from the fire to be between five and seven million pounds.

France's Thomson SA electronics group is considering a two-stage privatisation.
Analysts believe that separating the defence arm from the consumer goods unit makes better economic sense.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe stated that the military electronics subsidiary Thomson-CSF could be privatised separately.
The French government abandoned its plan to sell the entire Thomson group to Lagardere Groupe for one franc after the Privatisation Commission rejected it.
President Jacques Chirac's initial policy was to sell Thomson as one unit, which conflicts with the proposed break-up.
Analysts support the two-part sale and suggest restructuring the defence industry should begin immediately.
Lagardere's plan involved selling Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo Electronics while retaining Thomson-CSF.
The Privatisation Commission rejected Lagardere's bid due to concerns over technology transfers and job retention in France.
Privatising Thomson-CSF separately would help create a national champion in defence electronics.
Thomson-CSF is profitable, has low debt, and 42 percent of its capital is listed on the Paris bourse.

Airbus partners must accelerate plans to convert the consortium into a single company.
Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas announced a $13.3 billion merger plan.
The merger will create the world's largest aerospace firm with 1997 sales of about $48 billion and 200,000 employees.
Airbus historically holds around a 30 percent market share, while Boeing holds around 60 percent and McDonnell Douglas holds 10 percent.
Airbus expects to secure firm orders for more than 300 aircraft in 1996, worth around $20 billion.
Boeing reported receiving orders for 621 planes by the end of November.
Airbus partners are in discussions to change the consortium into a joint stock company.
The goal of the restructuring is to create a more competitive and responsive organization.
BAe's group managing director John Weston advocates for a large, integrated Airbus company.
Aerospatiale's chairman Yves Michot envisions Airbus as a large prime contractor directing suppliers' work.

Eurotunnel SA/Plc is a troubled Channel Tunnel operator.
Investors will vote on a complex debt deal aimed at keeping Eurotunnel afloat.
The restructuring agreement requires a two-thirds majority at an extraordinary meeting of shareholders expected by March.
Around 600,000 of Eurotunnel's estimated 750,000 small investors are French.
Albert Jauffret heads the Association de Defence des Actionnaires d'Eurotunnel (Adacte).
Sophie L'Helias is a lawyer who acted as proxy agent for more than 20,000 Eurotunnel shareholders.
Jauffret believes the restructuring gives too much to the banks.
Eurotunnel's 70 billion francs of junior-ranked loans have been marked down to about 40 percent of face value.
Jauffret argues that the 225 lending banks should cancel at least a third of the debt.
Adacte was founded in September 1995 as a breakaway from the Eurotunnel shareholders association.

French electrical equipment company Schneider aims to increase its return on equity capital to 15 percent in the next three years.
Executive vice president Michel Staib stated that the objective is to achieve a net return on capital of 15 percent before amortisation of goodwill.
Schneider's return on equity was just over eight percent in 1995.
The improvement in return on equity will come from focusing on core electrical activities and an internal re-engineering programme.
Schneider shares have risen approximately 10 percent since mid-December due to analysts considering the stock undervalued and the pending sale of the Spie Batignolles unit.
The shares closed at 255.70 francs on Wednesday.
About one-third of Schneider's capital is held by non-domestic investors.
All group companies under Schneider are profitable.
Schneider aims for Asia to contribute at least 20 percent of group turnover by the end of the decade, up from 11 percent in 1995.
Schneider has increased its number of employees in China from 200 to 2,500 over the past five years.

France's national audit office criticized the water supply market for a lack of clarity and insufficient competition.
The water supply market in France is dominated by two companies: Cie Generale des Eaux and Lyonnaise des Eaux.
Francois Logerot is the author of the Cour des Comptes report.
The report states that there is a high degree of concentration in the water supply market.
Logerot mentioned that competition in the sector is organized but not absent.
Agreements between the two dominant companies may accentuate market concentration.
The water company Societe Stephanoise des Eaux is jointly owned by Lyonnaise des Eaux Dumez and Generale des Eaux (CGE).
In 1991, the private sector held 75 percent of the supply of drinking water in France.
The price of water rose by an average of 47.7 percent from 1990 to 1994.
CGE stated that rising water prices were mainly due to higher quality and increasing investment needs.

Eurotunnel SA/Plc is set to release its first-half results on Monday.
Analysts believe forecasting Eurotunnel's figures is difficult due to uncertainties surrounding its debt restructuring.
Eurotunnel needs to refinance its $12.3 billion bank debt by the end of September.
In July, Eurotunnel requested two court-appointed mediators to assist in negotiations with its bank syndicate of approximately 220 banks.
Analysts have noted a price war between Eurotunnel and ferry companies affecting forecasts.
One analyst estimated a net loss of 2.5 billion francs ($492 million) and an operating loss of around 100 million francs.
Eurotunnel reported first-half sales of 1.79 billion francs, an increase from 806 million francs the previous year.
The company had a net loss of 7.196 billion francs on a turnover of 2.266 billion francs for the full year last year.
Jeff Summers from Klesch and Co expects a 25-30 percent improvement in underlying results compared to the previous year.
Summers projected a pretax, pre-interest loss of 22 million pounds ($34.45 million) for Eurotunnel, down from 121 million pounds the previous year.

Republic Industries Inc. is run by businessman Wayne Huizenga.
Republic Industries Inc. plans to buy security firm ADT Ltd.
A New York newspaper reported that the transaction might be called off.
Spokesman Ronald Castell stated that the deal is still moving forward.
Wayne Huizenga is the founder of Blockbuster Entertainment.
Huizenga owns the Florida Marlins, Dolphins, and Panthers professional sports teams.
Republic Industries has three major areas of business: electronic security, solid waste, and used cars.
The deal was originally valued at $5 billion when announced in July.
The deal has lost about 20 percent of its value due to a decline in Republic's share price.
At the time of the announcement, Republic shares were trading at about $29.

Shares of PepsiCo Inc rose sharply on Thursday due to rumors of a potential takeover by Philip Morris Cos Inc.
Industry experts dismissed the takeover rumor, estimating a transaction price of $60 to $80 billion.
The rumor reflects widespread dissatisfaction with PepsiCo's outlook.
Martin Romm of CS First Boston described the rumor as farfetched.
Officials from PepsiCo and Philip Morris declined to comment on the rumor.
PepsiCo shares increased by 1-3/8 to 30-1/2, while Philip Morris shares rose by 1-1/8 to 97.
The rumor gained traction after a report in the New York Post suggested Philip Morris would offer $50 a share for PepsiCo.
PepsiCo announced a plan to exit weak international beverage markets less than a month prior to the rumors.
PepsiCo's restructuring plan included a charge of over $500 million against earnings and cost-cutting targets.
Analysts expect PepsiCo to eventually sell its casual restaurant business due to its underperformance.

British Airways Plc. and USAir Group Inc. have a three-year partnership that is nearing collapse.
USAir announced the cancellation of a key marketing agreement with British Airways.
The code-sharing agreement and the link between their frequent flier programs will end on March 29, 1997.
Code-sharing allows airlines to share passengers and extend their reach to destinations they do not typically serve.
USAir cited British Airways' proposed alliance with American Airlines as a reason for the cancellation.
USAir is 24.6 percent owned by British Airways.
USAir has opposed the British Airways-American partnership and has sued both carriers.
A hearing on the lawsuit is scheduled in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.
British Airways had no immediate comment on USAir's action.
Most analysts expected USAir to maintain its relationship with British Airways until the proposed alliance was finalized.

Revco D.S. Inc. agreed to buy Big B Inc. for $380 million.
Revco will purchase all outstanding shares of Big B common stock for $17.25 per share.
Big B rejected Revco's initial offer of $15 per share last month.
Dwayne Hoven is the president and chief executive officer of Revco.
The acquisition will combine the second- and tenth-largest drug store chains in the U.S.
Big B's board of directors unanimously approved Revco's latest offer.
Big B's shareholders are recommended to tender their shares.
The sale of Big B is part of a trend of consolidation in the drugstore industry.
Revco's stock traded at $29.50 a share on the New York Stock Exchange.
Big B's shares were trading at $17 on Nasdaq.

The U.S. food industry is experiencing slow growth and is seeking new business from non-cooking consumers.
A new study predicts that consumer spending on ready-made foods will increase over the next 10 years.
John Gray is the executive director of the International Foodservice Distributors Association, which funded the study.
The study indicates that many consumers in 2005 will not have cooked meals from basic ingredients.
The food industry is projected to grow 1.6 percent per year to nearly $800 billion by 2005.
The foodservice sector is expected to capture nearly all of the anticipated incremental sales, estimated at $100 billion.
William Eacho is the president and CEO of Atlantic Food Services, which anticipates new foodservice opportunities.
Future supermarkets may include drive-up windows for ready-made meals and categorize food by meal types.
Nabisco Holdings Corp is exploring ways to maintain its product presence in stores focusing on ready-made foods.
Henry Lambert is the president of Nabisco's food service company and aims to leverage brand popularity into ready-made meals.

CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp. entered discussions about their rival offers to buy Conrail Inc.
The specific nature of the discussions between CSX and Norfolk Southern was not disclosed.
Conrail's stock fell due to views that the discussions would reduce the chances of a bidding war.
Discussions between CSX and Norfolk Southern began late last week and continued through the weekend and into Monday.
CSX agreed to buy Conrail for $8.4 billion, valuing Conrail at $92.50 per share.
Norfolk Southern launched a competing bid of $100 cash per share, totaling about $9 billion.
CSX stated that Norfolk Southern initiated the discussions regarding a possible sale of certain material assets.
Norfolk Southern confirmed its commitment to its bid for Conrail and has secured over $15 billion to finance the acquisition.
Norfolk Southern's CEO David Goode expressed concerns about maintaining a balanced competitive structure for Eastern railroad service.
Analysts noted that Pennsylvania's corporate takeover law could pose challenges to Norfolk Southern's acquisition of Conrail.

Shareholders of Conrail Inc criticized the company's revised merger agreement with CSX Corp.
Shareholders claimed the new terms do not match a rival bid from Norfolk Southern Corp.
During a conference call, some investors threatened to sell their shares for $110 and vote against the merger.
Conrail announced an amendment to the merger agreement with CSX to increase the cash portion of the deal.
Under the new terms, CSX will pay $110 cash per share for 40 percent of Conrail shares.
The remaining 60 percent of Conrail shares will be exchanged at a ratio of 1.85619 CSX shares for each Conrail share.
