The deal values Conrail shares at approximately $93 based on CSX's current stock price.
Norfolk Southern has offered to pay $100 cash per share for all of Conrail's outstanding shares.
Investors expressed dissatisfaction with a three-month extension of the merger agreement.
Conrail defended the revised transaction by stating it offers more strategic benefits than Norfolk Southern's proposal.

The outcome of a bidding war for Conrail Inc will be decided by its investors.
Conrail is considering an $8.5 billion deal with CSX Corp and a $10 billion offer from Norfolk Southern.
Wall Street experts believe Conrail is unlikely to change its planned merger with CSX.
Conrail has agreed to a stock and cash transaction with CSX valued at about $8.5 billion.
Norfolk Southern increased its all-cash offer to $10 billion.
Pennsylvania corporate law requires shareholder approval for CSX to buy more than 20 percent of Conrail in a tender offer.
A shareholder meeting for Conrail is scheduled for mid-December.
Some shareholders have expressed dissatisfaction with the proposed CSX transaction.
Arbitragers predict that Conrail will not win the shareholder vote.
Norfolk Southern chairman David Goode stated that their bid is a superior offer.

Mattel Inc. agreed to buy Tyco Toys Inc. for $755 million.
The acquisition aims to expand Mattel's market share in boys' toys.
Mattel's products include Barbie dolls, Hot Wheels, and Fisher-Price toys.
Tyco's products include Matchbox cars, Sesame Street toys, and radio-controlled vehicles.
Tyco shareholders will receive Mattel stock valued at $12.50 per Tyco share.
This stock price represents a 78 percent premium above Tyco's closing price before the announcement.
Tyco's stock price increased by $4.50 to $11.50 following the announcement.
Mattel's stock price decreased by 75 cents to $29.875 after the announcement.
The merger is expected to be completed in the first half of 1997.
Both companies' boards have approved the merger.

Conrail Inc. and CSX Corp. have received court approval for their $8.6 billion merger plan.
Shareholders are unhappy and prefer Norfolk Southern Corp.'s higher bid.
CSX's $110 cash tender offer for 19.9 percent of Conrail shares was oversubscribed.
Conrail has rejected Norfolk Southern's $110 per share offer, citing more strategic benefits from the CSX merger.
Lawyers and financial advisors are considering plans to persuade Conrail shareholders to approve the merger.
Options being considered include increasing the stock portion of the deal or setting a price volatility guard.
CSX and Conrail may revise the deal's terms to accelerate payment to investors.
There is no rush to make a decision regarding the shareholder vote, which is scheduled for mid-December.
A U.S. district court judge denied Norfolk Southern's request to block the CSX-Conrail deal.
Norfolk Southern withdrew its motion for an expedited appeal regarding the federal court ruling.

Barney's Inc. has entered a financial agreement with Dickson Concepts International Ltd.
The agreement will allow potential bidders to consider purchasing Barney's.
Barney's filed for bankruptcy nearly a year ago.
Barney's will pay Dickson up to $1 million for a financial review.
Dickson will submit a recapitalization proposal for Barney's.
Barney's will make financial information available to prospective investors.
Barney's spokeswoman Sandra Sternberg stated that the agreement provides a basis for investor due diligence.
Saks Holdings Inc. and Neiman Marcus Group Inc. have expressed interest in Barney's.
Holt Renfrew has also been cited as a potential bidder for Barney's.
Barney's has stated it is not for sale but is open to discussions with potential investors.

An independent shareholder advisory firm recommended that investors of Conrail Inc. reject a key provision in the railroad's proposed acquisition by CSX Corp.
Institutional Shareholder Services suggested that shareholders defeat a proposal that would permit CSX to pursue its proposed $8.5 billion stock and cash transaction.
Senior analyst Peter Gleason noted Norfolk Southern Corp.'s rival $10 billion cash bid that has been rejected by Conrail.
Gleason stated that all shareholders should be treated equally in any merger transaction.
Gleason expressed that it would not be in shareholders' best interest to opt out of the fair price provision at this time.
Conrail investors are being asked to waive a Pennsylvania law that requires an all-cash payment by CSX.
CSX has already bought 19.9 percent of Conrail in a cash tender offer.
CSX and Conrail announced a merger that calls for CSX to buy Conrail in a cash-and-stock deal.
CSX is offering to pay $110 in cash for 40 percent of Conrail's outstanding shares.
Institutional Shareholder Services disputed Conrail's argument that the CSX offer is a better fit than Norfolk Southern's higher bid.

The federal government's efforts to increase competition in the phone business have encountered a setback.
A federal appeals court has suspended key parts of a Federal Communications Commission rule that would open local phone monopolies to competition.
Experts believe this suspension could delay competition in the $100 billion local phone market controlled by regional Baby Bell companies.
A final decision on the case could take a year or more.
Henry Geller, a former telecommunications official, stated that 1997 will be a complicated year for the telecommunications industry.
The telecommunications law enacted in February allows Baby Bells to offer long-distance service only after opening their local markets to new competitors.
Government officials indicated that a prolonged delay of the FCC's rules would complicate the entry of Baby Bells into the long-distance market.
FCC Commissioner Susan Ness expressed concerns that the stay could hinder investment and new market entry.
The Justice Department has indicated it will be hesitant to support Baby Bell entry into long-distance service while key FCC rules are suspended.
David Turetsky from the Justice Department stated that the stay would significantly impair the Baby Bells' entry process as outlined in the telecommunications law.

The Justice Department requested the Supreme Court to lift a lower court suspension of federal rules regarding local telephone monopolies.
The request was made on behalf of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).
The Justice Department stated that the lower court's suspension could harm consumers by delaying competition in the local phone market.
A U.S. appeals court in St. Louis suspended key provisions of the FCC's interconnection order.
The interconnection order outlines how long-distance carriers and cable-TV operators can operate in the local phone market.
The rules were frozen while the appeals court considers a challenge to the FCC order by GTE Corp. and other local carriers.
Opponents of the FCC order argue that the FCC exceeded its authority granted by Congress.
The FCC ordered regional Bells and local phone companies to lease their lines to new competitors at discounts of 17 percent to 25 percent.
The appeals court panel indicated that the opponents have a strong chance of convincing the court that the FCC's rules conflict with the law.
Long-distance carriers AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp. also requested the Supreme Court to lift the stay.

Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas refused to reinstate federal rules for the local telephone market.
Thomas let stand a U.S. appeals court order suspending parts of the Federal Communications Commission's interconnection rules.
The FCC, AT&T Corp., MCI Communications Corp., and other phone companies requested Thomas to restore the rules, but he rejected the request.
The FCC and long-distance companies submitted a new request for the Supreme Court to lift the lower court's stay.
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals issued its stay on October 15 while considering a challenge to the FCC rules.
Oral arguments regarding the challenge to the rules are set for January.
GTE Corp., Baby Bell phone companies, and state regulators want to overturn the FCC rules, claiming the FCC overstepped its authority.
Local companies and state regulators requested the stay on the FCC rules.
The FCC rules require local carriers to lease their phone lines to new competitors at discounts of up to 25 percent.
With the stay in place, state regulators will determine pricing and policies for interconnection agreements.

The nation's distillers reversed their 48-year-old voluntary ban on broadcast advertising of liquor.
Distillers stated that whiskey and gin should be treated like beer and wine.
The announcement followed the presidential election and precedes the holiday season.
Seagram Co. Ltd. began airing TV ads for its Royal Crown and Chivas Regal whiskey in June.
The ad campaign has faced criticism from lawmakers, regulators, and President Clinton.
Fred Meister is the president of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States (DISCUS).
Meister claimed that the absence of spirits from advertising has led to misconceptions about their social treatment.
The reversal of the voluntary ban was included in DISCUS's 'code of good practice.'
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt opposed the decision and indicated potential new rules against liquor advertising.
Consumer advocates criticized the decision, claiming it would target children and teens.

The Supreme Court declined a request by federal regulators and long-distance phone companies to reactivate rules for local phone market competition.
The denial means that deregulation terms for the local phone market will depend on state regulators' decisions.
The denial was a defeat for the FCC and long-distance companies AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp.
Supreme Court Justice Thomas declined to restore the FCC rules.
The decision was a victory for regional 'Baby Bell' companies, GTE Corp., and other local carriers.
The regional companies argue that the FCC took away states' power to set pricing policies.
The rules detail how long-distance companies and others can access local phone networks.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt stated that states have control over prices for new entrants in local markets.
The appeals court temporarily suspended the rules, indicating the FCC may have erred in drafting them.
Justice Thomas declined a request to lift the appeals court's stay on the rules.

Regulators are initiating a two-part plan to reduce rates on overseas phone calls.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is expected to simplify negotiations for cheaper international call packages.
Next month, the FCC is expected to propose rules to reduce charges U.S. carriers pay foreign phone monopolies.
Don Gips is the head of the FCC's international bureau.
Foreign charges, known as 'accounting rates,' are reported to be five to ten times the actual costs.
Monopolies control over 90 percent of the non-U.S. phone market.
In 1995, U.S. phone companies paid $5.5 billion more to foreign companies than they received from them.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt stated that the imbalance in payments exceeds the U.S. foreign aid budget of $2 billion.
The United States has significant payment imbalances with countries including China, Jamaica, Mexico, Hong Kong, Colombia, and Argentina.
Dan Rosen from the Institute for International Economics noted that countries defending their monopolies may be concerned about the FCC's efforts.

Regulators took steps to reduce the cost of overseas phone calls for consumers and businesses.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) aims to save U.S. callers billions of dollars with new rules.
Americans spend about 16 cents a minute for domestic calls and an average of 99 cents a minute for overseas calls.
The FCC's new rules target countries with open phone markets to competition from U.S. carriers.
Countries cited by FCC officials include Canada, Britain, Chile, Sweden, Europe, and Mexico.
The FCC will waive rules that limit U.S. carriers' ability to negotiate cheaper calling rates with foreign companies.
Don Gips, head of the FCC's International Bureau, stated that the new rules will allow competitive pressures to govern the telecommunications market.
AT&T Corp. Vice President Gerry Salemme indicated that the new rules could significantly reduce costs for American consumers.
U.S. carriers paid $5.5 billion more to overseas counterparts in 1995 than foreign companies paid U.S. carriers.
International calls from the United States account for about a quarter of all international calls worldwide.

The television and entertainment industries announced plans to use their own system for rating TV programs.
The industry plans to reject any government-imposed rating system by legal means if necessary.
A group of TV and Hollywood executives will unveil a new rating system next week.
The new rating system will be based on the suitability of shows for children under 14 years of age.
The new system will be similar to the existing motion-picture rating system, which includes ratings such as G, PG, PG-13, R, and NC-17.
Jack Valenti is the chief executive of the Motion Picture Association of America and leads the implementation group for the new ratings.
Parental groups, children's advocates, educators, and some lawmakers, including Representative Edward Markey, have called for a content-based rating system.
Markey stated that the industry has not adequately addressed parents' concerns about knowing the specific content of TV shows in advance.
Valenti accused Markey of attempting to impose his own scheme through government intervention.
The Federal Communications Commission must approve the new ratings system.

Regulators approved a technology standard for high-definition digital television.
The Federal Communications Commission approved the standard after a compromise between TV manufacturers, broadcasters, and the computer industry.
Digital TV provides high-quality pictures and sound.
The new standard is expected to create a system that allows viewers to watch programs while using the Internet.
Commissioner Susan Ness stated that the decision promotes competition between computer-friendly televisions and broadcast-friendly computers.
The standard outlines how voice and video will be attached to digital signals and how those signals will be compressed and reopened at the TV receiver.
The standard does not specify the video format for displaying images.
Broadcasters wanted interlace scanning, while computer companies preferred progressive scanning or no format specification.
Progressive scanning updates every line of the TV picture, while interlaced scanning updates every other line.
The lack of a specified scanning format allows the computer industry to produce computers that use only progressive scanning.

The government's largest wireless phone auction ended with a total of $2.5 billion in bids from 125 companies.
This total was down 75 percent from a similar auction that raised $10.2 billion in May.
The average price for a license to provide personal communications services (PCS) fell more than 90 percent.
PCS technology is expected to enable various communications services through a single handheld device.
The drop in auction prices was attributed to an influx of new entrants, lack of new investment, and fewer airwaves covered by new licenses.
The top bidder was a unit of Sprint Corp., which bid $544 million for 160 licenses in cities including Chicago, Houston, and Atlanta.
The licenses acquired by Sprint cover a total population of 70 million nationwide.
AT&T Corp. was the second highest bidder, offering $407 million for 222 licenses covering 139 million people.
BellSouth Corp. was the third highest bidder, with a bid of $205 million for 39 licenses reaching nearly 12 million people.
The FCC sold 1,479 PCS licenses nationwide, making it the largest number sold at once.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has issued new rules opening the local telephone market to competition.
Lawyers predict that the FCC's new rules are likely to survive legal challenges from state regulators and local phone companies.
It is unlikely that a federal court will overturn the core of the FCC's interconnection rules.
Lawyers believe the FCC has not overstepped its legal boundaries with the new rules.
The New York Public Service Commission has asked the U.S. Court of Appeals in New York to annul the FCC's new rules.
The FCC's rules are said to intrude on the state's authority to set local telecommunications policy.
The National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners plans to ask the courts for a speedy review of the FCC's rules.
The regulations aim to break local phone monopolies and allow long-distance companies and cable firms to offer local phone service.
GTE Corp and Southern New England Telecommunications Corp plan to ask a federal appeals court to block the FCC's rules.
BellSouth Corp intends to ask a federal appeals court to overturn the FCC's rules, claiming the FCC exceeded Congressional intent.

Lawmakers and law-enforcement officials expressed support for tougher laws against eavesdropping on cellular phone calls.
The support followed the interception of Newt Gingrich's call.
A House telecommunications subcommittee is focusing on a law that bans the sale, manufacture, and importation of scanners that can intercept cellular calls.
Despite a 1992 law, many legal scanners have been modified to overhear cellular traffic.
An estimated 10 million legal scanners are currently owned by the public.
Representative Edward Markey stated the goal is to significantly reduce the sale of such equipment.
Markey referred to modified scanners as a danger to the privacy of cellular phone users.
Markey supports closing loopholes to make it harder for scanner operators to illegally intercept calls.
Representative Billy Tauzin noted issues with enforcement of anti-intercept laws.
The Federal Communications Commission refers potential criminal cases to other agencies that may prioritize other law enforcement issues.

Negotiations between American Airlines and its pilots union continued into the early hours of Friday.
Neither side reported any breakthrough that would avert a midnight strike.
A federal mediator informed the pilots that American had rejected a key union contract proposal regarding the piloting and pay of American Eagle planes.
Mediators are offering hypothetical proposals to bring the two sides closer together.
Dave Bates, a spokesman for the Allied Pilots Association, stated that the union is disappointed at the lack of progress.
Bates indicated that the pilots would go on strike at midnight if no agreement is reached.
Kenneth Hipp, chairman of the National Mediation Board, expressed hope for an agreement before the strike.
The union proposed that its pilots fly American Eagle flights with lower pay than regular American pilots.
American Airlines prefers to use lower-paid commuter pilots from a different union for smaller planes.
The average pay for pilots is about $120,000 a year, and the union had previously sought an 11.5 percent pay increase over four years.

Sun Microsystems Inc. stock declined on Wednesday despite reporting a 45 percent increase in earnings.
The company's profits rose to $123.4 million, or 63 cents a share, in its fiscal first quarter.
This profit increase was compared to $84.7 million, or 42 cents a share, in the same quarter of 1995.
Sun Microsystems cited strong sales of its computer workstations as a reason for the profit increase.
The reported earnings slightly exceeded Wall Street analysts' average forecast of 61 cents a share.
Investors began taking profits in after-hours trading following the earnings report.
The stock reached an all-time high of $70.25 before the earnings report and ended regular trading at $70.
After-hours trading saw the stock fall by $4, and it continued to decline on Wednesday.
The stock dropped as much as $7.625 to a session low of $62.375 and closed at $63.125.
Sun Chairman Scott McNealy commented on the after-hours decline, suggesting profit-taking was occurring.

Netscape Communications Corp. reported quarterly revenues of $100 million in the third quarter.
Netscape's third quarter net income was $7.7 million, or 9 cents a share.
A year ago, Netscape earned $175,000 on sales of $23.3 million.
Netscape President and Chief Executive Jim Barksdale stated that the third quarter of 1996 was a landmark quarter for the company.
Wall Street analysts had expected Netscape to report revenues of $85 million to $90 million.
Analyst Daniel Rimer noted that revenues grew 33 percent sequentially.
The quarterly revenue was above the $80.7 million posted for the whole of 1995.
For the first nine months, Netscape earned $12 million, or 14 cents a share, on sales of $231 million.
A year earlier, Netscape lost $7 million, or 10 cents a share, on sales of $44 million.
In after-hours trading, shares of Netscape reached as high as $44.875.

Sun Microsystems Inc. will unveil a network computer that it claims will cost companies up to 80 percent less to own and operate than a personal computer connected to a network.
The JavaStation network computer will be sold for as little as $750.
The unveiling will take place at a news conference in New York City.
Investors consider Sun's strategy sufficiently risky, leading to a sell-off in the company's stock earlier this month.
Microsoft and Intel announced plans to develop a competing product.
Scott McNealy, chairman and CEO of Sun, believes the company's strong financial results are related to its focus on network computing.
Sun's approach to the Network Computer targets major corporate customers for fixed-function applications.
Early applications for the JavaStation will include airline and hotel reservations, kiosks, health care systems, and stock trading.
Sun expects to highlight a dozen corporate allies, including British Telecommunications Plc, CSX Corp., Federal Express Corp., and FTD Inc.
The JavaStation will have dimensions of 8.5 by 11 inches, weigh four pounds, and have no slots, hard disk, CD-ROM, or floppy disk drive.

Stocks of high-tech companies increased on Wednesday after a ballot proposal was voted down in California.
The ballot measure, known as Proposition 211, would have made it easier for shareholders to file lawsuits.
Proposition 211 was defeated by a 3-1 margin.
John Doerr, a partner at Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, led the opposition to Proposition 211.
William Lerach, a San Diego attorney, promoted Proposition 211.
California's high-tech firms raised an estimated $38 million and mobilized 5 million employees, shareholders, and customers against Proposition 211.
Proponents of Proposition 211 spent $13 million on their campaign.
The defeat of Proposition 211 relieved Wall Street investors concerned about potential shareholder lawsuits.
Shares of Intel increased by $4.75 to an all-time high of $118.75 on Nasdaq after the news.
Texas Instruments and Microsoft also saw increases in their stock prices following the defeat of Proposition 211.

Hewlett-Packard Co. will launch a new printer called the HP LaserJet 5Si Mopier.
The Mopier is designed to reduce the need for copiers by allowing multiple original prints from a desktop.
Hewlett-Packard aims to capture a share of the $18.5 billion copier market with the new model.
Analysts expect the Mopier to challenge Xerox Corp. and other copier manufacturers.
Sales revenues of midrange copiers are projected to drop by $300 million to $1 billion by 2000.
The Mopier has a U.S. list price of $9,549, which is less than midrange copiers priced between $13,000 and $20,000.
The Mopier includes features such as stapling and collating of documents.
The printer has a user-friendly interface to assist workers with printing options.
The Mopier is designed to reduce the time spent by office workers running between printers and copiers.
The printer contains a 420 megabyte hard drive and reduces network traffic by storing print tasks.

Hewlett-Packard Co. will unveil new technology on Monday that addresses the debate over software encoding for secure data traffic.
Hewlett-Packard claims that the encryption technology has the support of industry and the U.S. and other governments.
The development of this technology could facilitate the growth of electronic commerce via the Internet.
Hewlett-Packard Chairman Lewis Platt will provide details on the technology, which includes patented technology from Hewlett-Packard and other technologies.
Technology from RSA Data Corp. will be involved in the new encryption technology.
Hewlett-Packard stock closed at $50.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Executives from Microsoft Corp. and Intel Corp. were scheduled to attend the news briefing at the National Press Club in Washington.
The new technology will allow the export of products containing strong encryption, which is currently restricted under national security laws.
National security laws have historically allowed the export of only weaker data encryption technologies.
Encryption is classified as a munition due to its potential misuse by criminals.

Intel Corp. President Andrew Grove stated that the personal computer industry must offer more than television-like features to appeal to demanding customers, specifically 10-year-old kids.
Grove delivered an opening speech at the Comdex trade show celebrating the 25th anniversary of the microprocessor invented by Intel.
He demonstrated how PCs with next-generation Intel microchips could deliver full-screen video with theater-like surround-sound stereo.
Grove emphasized that achieving this capability would only make PCs comparable to televisions as entertainment devices.
He highlighted the need for the industry to focus on satisfying demanding users, particularly children.
Using Intel chips and technology from Evans & Southerland Computer Co., Grove showcased potential improvements in graphics by the year 2000.
Grove expressed concern about the product cycle potentially slowing down and urged the industry to aggressively produce new products.
He stated that the industry should aim for annual growth of 15 percent to 17 percent, consistent with the previous decade.
Grove noted that the cost of building a semiconductor plant has significantly increased from $3 million in 1973 to $2.5 billion for the latest plant.
He mentioned that there are approximately one-third as many personal computers as televisions installed worldwide, despite annual PC sales beginning to outpace television sales.

Netscape Communications Corp. President Jim Barksdale unveiled new software called Constellation.
Constellation will allow users to receive personalized information on a computer network.
The software will enable users to merge and customize information on computer desktops and networks.
Constellation is scheduled for release in mid-1997.
Barksdale described Constellation as part of an Internet 'third wave' of information.
The third wave focuses on information finding the user rather than the user finding information.
Constellation will be part of Netscape's next-generation Netscape Communicator corporate software.
The software will allow users to log on or off computers throughout a network and see a personalized desktop.
Netscape has sold 48 million copies of its browser software, making it the most popular application ever.
Netscape holds 78 percent of the browser market, while Microsoft holds 90 percent of the operating systems market.

U.S. high tech venture fund investment increased by 50 percent in the third quarter compared to a 25 percent growth in overall U.S. venture investment from year-ago levels.
The survey was released by Price Waterhouse on a Monday.
Venture investment in high technology industries rose to $1.32 billion in the third quarter, making up two-thirds of the $2 billion total invested during that period.
Software investments more than doubled from year-ago levels to $596 million in the third quarter of 1996.
In the first nine months of 1996, software investments reached $1.74 billion, surpassing the $1.34 billion recorded for the entire year of 1995.
Total venture-backed investments in the U.S. for the first nine months of 1996 reached $7 billion, approaching the $7.5 billion reported for the full year of the previous year.
Donald McGovern, chairman of the Price Waterhouse Technology Industry Group, stated that 1996 is likely to be another record year based on current venture capital investment rates.
The total venture investment figure of $2 billion in the third quarter was a decrease from the $2.8 billion recorded in the second quarter.
Carl Thoma, president of the National Venture Capital Association, noted that third-quarter numbers are typically lower due to reduced deal flow in the summer months.
The study found that start-up and early-stage companies attracted the most venture capital, comprising 46 percent of the 444 companies receiving funds and accounting for $600 million invested.

In 1997, Internet users are expected to see more features aimed at making the Internet more lifelike.
Increased demand is likely to cause frequent communications breakdowns.
Robert Metcalfe is the inventor of Ethernet computer networking technology and founder of 3Com Corp.
Metcalfe is currently the vice president of technology at International Data Group of Boston.
Metcalfe stated that congestion is one reason many people refer to the World Wide Web as the 'World Wide Wait.'
Major outages on the Internet have been caused by minor events, such as a rodent chewing a power cable.
In the summer of 1997, more than 6 million customers of America Online Inc. were without service for 19 hours due to a software problem.
In October 1997, a failure at BBN Corp's Stanford University Internet facility cut off access for 400 high tech firms for nearly a day.
Experts predict similar types of outages in the future as telecommunications companies and Internet providers struggle to keep up with demand.
Web surfers are expected to see new features in 1997, including advanced graphics and animated characters in virtual chat rooms.

Dan Farmer is a computer security expert who conducted a study on Web site vulnerabilities.
Farmer's study claims that up to two-thirds of certain Web sites, including banks and media, are vulnerable to hacker attacks.
Farmer surveyed more than 2,200 Web sites, focusing on those where security is a concern.
The survey included 660 bank sites, 312 North American online newspaper sites, 274 credit union sites, 47 U.S. federal government sites, and 451 Internet sex clubs.
Farmer reported that over 60 percent of the approximately 1,700 Web sites he selected could be broken into or destroyed.
Farmer used non-intrusive methods and did not actually break into the sites he surveyed.
Farmer stated that with more intrusive tests, 70 percent to 80 percent of sites may have security flaws.
David Kennedy, director of research at the National Computer Security Association, found Farmer's results credible.
The study highlights a problem that is well known in the computer industry but not well understood by the public.
Deborah Triant, president of CheckPoint Software Technologies Ltd., stated that banks keep Web sites on separate computer systems.

Netscape Communications Corp. stock declined for the second time in less than a week on Tuesday.
Merrill Lynch analyst Bruce Smith expressed concerns about Netscape's ability to meet its fourth-quarter goals.
Netscape stock fell more than 10 percent, dropping $4.50 to $42.25 on the Nasdaq market.
The trading volume for Netscape stock exceeded 6.5 million shares.
Netscape's stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since the end of 1996.
The stock dropped around 19 percent after an analyst's warning last Wednesday.
Bruce Smith stated that Netscape's efforts to meet fourth-quarter numbers could negatively impact its current quarter and outlook for 1997.
A spokeswoman for Netscape denied that the company was pushing to finalize significant deals on December 31.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst William Gurley downgraded Netscape's stock rating from 'buy' to 'accumulate'.
Other analysts, including those from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, maintained 'buy' or 'strong buy' ratings on Netscape's stock.

Southern Co is the largest electricity provider in the United States.
Southern Co announced a US$2.7 billion deal to acquire Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd in Hong Kong.
Southern Co made a general offer to all CEPA's shareholders after agreeing to buy a 60.4-percent stake from Hopewell Holdings Ltd.
Ray Harris is the regional director of Southern Electric International Inc, a unit of Southern Co.
Southern Co plans to use CEPA as a growth vehicle in Asia.
Southern Co aims to acquire 80 percent of CEPA's shares at HK$18.50 per share.
Hopewell Holdings Ltd has agreed to tender 80 percent of its stake under a cash and stock option.
The cash and stock option includes one new CEPA share, cash of HK$69.50, and a contingency payment of HK$8.00 for every five CEPA shares.
Hopewell will retain between 12.1 percent and 20 percent of the new company depending on shareholder choices.
Southern's acquisition will privatize CEPA, reducing its public float below Hong Kong stock exchange requirements.

Indonesia's mutual funds industry is expected to grow rapidly.
John Booth is the Asia managing director for DST International.
A Capital Markets Law was adopted in Indonesia earlier this year.
Indonesia previously offered only one closed-end mutual fund.
Seven open-ended mutual funds, or 'reksa dana,' have been established in Indonesia with a total value of US$640 million.
Five more open-ended mutual funds are in development.
Most new mutual funds will focus on fixed income instruments rather than equities.
Four large stocks account for 25 percent of trading volume on Jakarta's stock market.
Foreign investors account for about 70 percent of trading value on Jakarta's stock market.
Felia Salim is the director of the Jakarta Stock Exchange.

Zero tax and limited regulation are attracting billions of dollars into offshore mutual funds.
The Cayman Islands is a notable location for tax-free offshore mutual funds.
Anthony Travers is a senior partner at Maples and Calder in Hong Kong.
Anecdotal evidence indicates that nearly US$900 billion has been drawn into offshore mutual funds.
The entire mutual fund industry is sometimes valued at US$5 trillion.
High taxation levels deter mutual funds from establishing in developed markets.
Offshore regions allow mutual funds to avoid tax while accessing lucrative investment areas.
Investing in offshore mutual funds can involve withholding tax and marketing issues.
Offshore mutual funds cannot market to more than 100 investors in the United States.
The United Kingdom restricts marketing of offshore retail mutual funds to designated jurisdictions.

Hong Kong is considered one of the world's most efficient economies.
Jeffrey Sachs is a Harvard-based economic adviser.
Sachs stated that Hong Kong's success as a global financial center is uncertain due to the return to Chinese rule.
Sachs mentioned that Hong Kong is currently the world's most competitive economy after Singapore.
Sachs emphasized the importance of maintaining the rule of law, media freedoms, and an open economy for Hong Kong's future success.
Sachs expressed that the future of Hong Kong's economy will depend on the independence of its judicial system and the freedom of its media after July 1997.
Sachs warned that China's economic institutions require significant reform to sustain long-term growth.
Sachs noted that China's current economic dynamism is based on a low starting point.
Sachs identified cheap labor, low taxation, and access to foreign exchange as factors fueling China's export boom.
Sachs stated that China needs to clarify property rights, develop financial markets, and establish legal certainty to maintain economic momentum.

Hong Kong funds are expected to establish 'Chinese walls' between asset management and traders.
The expectation follows revelations of unsanctioned trades at Jardine Fleming Investment Management.
Central dealing is gaining popularity in Asia after the disclosure of late allocation of trades by Colin Armstrong.
Gregory Neumann, executive director at Scudder Stevens & Clark Asia Ltd, stated there is awareness in the pension fund community regarding this issue.
Neumann believes that central dealing could become a requirement for hiring in the investment management industry.
Regulators imposed severe penalties on Colin Armstrong for delaying the allocation of his trades.
Some of Armstrong's trades involved his personal trading account.
The Investment Management Regulatory Organisation and the Securities and Futures Commission fined Jardine Fleming 700,000 stg.
Jardine Fleming also paid US$19.3 million in compensation and had its former chief executive's registration revoked.
Deborah Glass, senior director at the SFC, explained that central dealing requires fund managers to place orders through a central desk.

Hong Kong's chief immigration official, Laurence Leung, departed suddenly last July.
Anson Chan, the chief secretary of Hong Kong, is expected to resist demands to release confidential reports on Laurence Leung.
Chan will appear before a Legislative Council enquiry on Wednesday.
The Hong Kong government is facing accusations of a political cover-up regarding the Leung affair.
Legislative Council committee chairman Ip Kwok-him threatened to use an ordinance to hold Chan in contempt if she does not unveil the reports.
Civil service secretary Lam Woon-kwong stated that if the committee opens the reports, the matter will need to be resolved in court.
There are two investigations related to Leung: an anti-corruption probe and a police integrity check.
British press reports have alleged that Laurence Leung was spying for China.
Leung has denied being a spy and stated he was forced to resign, contradicting earlier claims of resigning for personal reasons.
The Hong Kong government has not yet decided whether to release the reports but emphasizes the privacy rights of civil servants.

Economic commentators in Hong Kong are expressing concerns about rising stock and property prices ahead of the British colony's return to Chinese sovereignty on July 1.
There are worries that rising price pressures could create a bubble based on the assumption that China will support Hong Kong's economy during the transition.
Ian Perkin, chief economist with the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce, stated that there is a growing belief in local markets that there is little downside risk due to China's expected support.
Domestic confidence in China's commitment to economic stability in Hong Kong is high, leading to concerns about price instability.
Economists are revising their inflation forecasts for 1997 upward due to increasing stock and luxury property prices.
Kevin Chan, an economist at Salomon Brothers, indicated that the forecast for Hong Kong's benchmark consumer price index has been raised to 7 percent from 6.6 percent.
The sudden strength in Hong Kong's stock market was initially seen as a sign of confidence in the colony's future under China.
Speculation in the luxury property market emerged in November, raising concerns among economists.
Perkin noted that both overseas and domestic investors are buying high-end properties in anticipation of short-term gains.
The Hong Kong government has supported anti-speculation measures and warned of intervention if speculation affects lower-end property markets.

A festive calm settled over Hong Kong on Thursday as people prepared to welcome the Year of the Ox.
This celebration was the last Lunar New Year under British rule.
Hong Kong people took time out from their schedules for the Chinese equivalent of a Western Christmas or American Thanksgiving.
Last-minute shoppers were seen in malls and record numbers of travelers crossed the border to visit relatives in China.
Children threw empty red 'lai see' money pockets at each other on the Star Ferry.
Ng Chak Kwong expressed a wish for a prosperous year, stating that many people were worried.
The festivities occurred amid rising political tension due to China's pledge to roll back some civil liberties laws after the handover.
The Democratic Party collected 20,000 signatures opposing the proposed legal changes.
Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa defended the proposed changes but faced skepticism.
Some families planned to watch a televised address by Governor Chris Patten, despite the diminishing relevance of British influence.

Pegged currencies are common in Asia.
Pegging a currency can have heavy consequences.
A fixed exchange rate can reassure foreign investors about currency stability.
Pegging a currency sacrifices control over inflation, according to Alan Butler-Henderson of ING Barings.
Hong Kong, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, Philippines, Singapore, and China peg their currencies to the U.S. dollar.
Pegged currencies require these countries to mimic U.S. monetary policy regardless of domestic conditions.
Many of these economies are experiencing high growth and rapid domestic consumption.
The lack of traditional inflation-fighting tools is a loss for countries trying to maintain economic progress.
Interest rate arbitrage can cause problems for small Asian countries with fixed exchange rates.
Hot money can flow into Asian banks offering higher yields due to fixed exchange rates.

Hong Kong has a large expatriate community of Filipina maids, known as amahs.
There are approximately 140,000 Filipina domestic helpers in Hong Kong, which has a population of 6.2 million.
Many families in Hong Kong rely on Filipina maids for child-care.
Filipina maids send remittances back to the Philippines, contributing significantly to the country's gross domestic product.
There are concerns that the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule may lead to the expulsion of Filipina maids in favor of mainland Chinese workers.
Chinese president Jiang Zemin and Hong Kong's chief executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa have expressed support for maintaining the current status of Filipina maids.
Dennis Suico, chairman of the Philippine Association of Hong Kong, believes that changes will occur after the handover.
Many Filipina maids in Hong Kong are college graduates, teachers, and nurses.
On Sundays, Filipina maids gather in Statue Square in Central Hong Kong for socializing.
Maria, a 30-year-old Filipina maid, stated that she works six days a week and values her time off on Sundays.

Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang presented an optimistic view of the economy on Thursday.
Economic growth in Hong Kong is forecasted at 5.5 percent for this year.
Tsang stated that Hong Kong's economy is well positioned for the transition to Chinese sovereignty on July 1.
Tsang will release the annual budget on March 12.
The government has not disclosed its fiscal reserves or commented on an expected fiscal surplus of up to HK$20 billion.
Improvements in foreign trade and rising domestic demand are expected to support Hong Kong's economy through 1997.
Consumption and investment were the main drivers of last year's economic recovery.
The unemployment rate in Hong Kong fell to 2.6 percent, and inflation was capped at 6.7 percent.
Private consumption is expected to increase by 5.5 percent this year.
Investment levels in 1996 were boosted by the airport construction project and public housing programs.

World bankers and economic chiefs held a meeting in Hong Kong on Friday.
Speakers at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) meeting emphasized the economic policies that transformed Hong Kong.
IMF managing director Michel Camdessus stated that the policy framework in Hong Kong is strong.
Joseph Yam, chief of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, invited delegates to return after the British rule ends on July 1.
Yam claimed that the 'one country, two systems' policy was working and that Hong Kong's dynamism would not change.
The IMF's decision to hold its 1997 annual meeting in Hong Kong was described as a vote of confidence in its future.
The IMF meeting will be the first major gathering in Hong Kong after China's takeover.
More than 50,000 delegates are expected to attend the meeting at a convention center still under construction.
Departing colonial governor Chris Patten attributed Hong Kong's economic success to its democratic government.
Tung Chee-hwa, the incoming chief executive, emphasized the importance of cooperation among Asian countries.

Financial Secretary Donald Tsang will reveal the size of Hong Kong's surplus and reserves on Wednesday.
The size of Hong Kong's surplus is considered a sensitive secret following recent official leaks.
Speculation about the surplus has led to controversy regarding Hong Kong's spending choices.
Hong Kong will transition from a British colony to a Special Administrative Region of China on July 1.
Debate is expected to arise when the full size of Hong Kong's cash reserves is disclosed.
China has been accused of limiting welfare spending, which has affected the relationship between colonial governor Chris Patten and Beijing.
Tsang denied that the budget was influenced by political pressure from Beijing.
Experts project a budget surplus of HK$20 billion (US$2.56 billion) for Hong Kong.
The Democratic Party has expressed concerns that social security growth will be insufficient for the elderly and disabled.
Welfare spending is expected to increase by 9.1 percent in the coming fiscal year, compared to a 20.1 percent increase in 1996/97.

China issued a warning regarding limits to freedom of expression in Hong Kong after its return to Beijing rule in 1997.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang stated that Hong Kong people will have full freedom of expression within the limits allowed by law.
Foreign Minister Qian Qichen suggested in an interview that Hong Kong may not be able to commemorate the anniversary of the 1989 crackdown on student-led protests.
Qian's comments led to public outcry in Hong Kong, where China promised a high degree of political freedoms for 50 years after the handover.
Shen Guofang emphasized that freedom of the press and speech in Hong Kong must operate within legal boundaries.
Shen stated that activities in Hong Kong must comply with legal regulations and should not interfere with mainland China's affairs.
Shen confirmed that Hong Kong would maintain its capitalist system after returning to mainland control on June 30, 1997.
Shen asserted that there would be no changes to the one nation, two systems policy after July 1, 1997.
Shen claimed that reports interpreting Qian's remarks as a ban on commemorative activities were incorrect.
Shen indicated that while people in Hong Kong could criticize Beijing, they should be cautious when commenting on Chinese leaders.

China's listed companies need to increase transparency and improve asset valuation to gain global prominence.
Arthur Levitt is the chairman of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
Levitt emphasized the importance of transparency in meetings with Chinese officials.
Levitt stated that transparency is crucial for boosting investor confidence in Chinese firms.
Chinese officials in listed firms are often reluctant to disclose company data due to competition concerns.
Levitt urged Chinese firms to view shareholders as owners rather than impediments.
Levitt called for improved disclosure, effective regulation, and a crackdown on corruption in China.
Levitt noted that the performance of Chinese companies on the New York Stock Exchange reflects a lack of investor confidence.
Levitt mentioned that the process of evaluating assets in China is uncertain and concerns many investors.
Levitt indicated that many Chinese officials were disappointed by the overseas performance of Chinese firms.

China stated that Sino-U.S. trade ties have improved.
China warned that major problems, including its entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO), still need to be resolved.
China hinted at possible retaliation against a U.S. decision to impose punitive charges on Chinese textile quotas.
Wu Yi, China's Foreign Trade Minister, stated that two major issues concerning Sino-U.S. economic links need to be settled.
The two issues are China's failure to join the WTO and the lack of permanent Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trade status for Chinese goods in the U.S. market.
High-level exchanges between Beijing and Washington have helped ease friction over various issues.
Wu stated that the tension in the Sino-U.S. relationship has been alleviated.
Wu indicated that further progress depends on Washington's stance towards China's entry into the WTO and its yearly review of MFN.
Washington annually reviews China's MFN status, which provides the lowest possible tariffs to trading partners.
China is one of the United States' largest trading partners, with U.S. companies selling about $12 billion worth of goods to China last year.

China accused foreign journalists of biased reporting.
China urged foreign journalists to learn from Edgar Snow, a U.S. reporter sympathetic to the Chinese communist cause.
A commentary in the official China Daily stated that Western reporters misjudged China based on inappropriate standards.
The commentary claimed that news reporting should provide adequate information to help audiences form correct judgments on world affairs.
The commentary encouraged Western media to emulate Edgar Snow, who portrayed Mao Zedong positively in the 1930s.
The China Daily praised Edgar Snow for his accuracy, objectivity, and impartiality in his coverage of China.
Snow's reports praised the Communist Party for its reforms and denied rumors of widespread famine in the early 1960s.
Historians estimate that more than 30 million people died from famines after Mao's Great Leap Forward.
The commentary criticized Western media for portraying China as a threat while ignoring Japan's military ambitions.
Foreign journalists are often viewed as spies in China and are frequently under police surveillance.

China criticized U.S. penalties against its textiles on Tuesday.
China stated that the U.S. did not provide sufficient evidence to support the textile sanctions.
China opposed strong-arm tactics in trade disputes.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai expressed that the U.S. had not fully consulted with China.
Cui Tiankai did not comment on whether the textile dispute would overshadow U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher's visit to China next week.
Christopher's visit to China is scheduled for November 19-21.
Cui Tiankai described Christopher's trip as an important bilateral meeting.
Cui stated that the state of relations between China and the U.S. would significantly impact the peace, stability, and prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region and the world.
Both China and the U.S. acknowledged that their ties have improved after previous disputes.
China announced a temporary ban on selected U.S. textiles and other goods in retaliation for U.S. sanctions.

North Korea expects a shortfall of two million tonnes of grain next year, which is 40 percent of the nation's needs.
A Red Cross official stated that the expected food shortage has worsened from an earlier estimate of 1.5 million tonnes.
Ole Gronning is the representative of the International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Pyongyang.
Gronning reported that North Korean officials have not been able to meet the daily food ration.
Farmers in North Korea have consumed about 400,000 tonnes of grain before it matured due to crop destruction from floods.
The floods in July destroyed approximately 373,000 tonnes of grain, worsening the food shortage.
North Korea's official figures indicate a need for 5.5 million tonnes of grain next year, while this year's harvest yielded only 3.5 million tonnes.
The federation is attempting to raise $10.5 million to buy grain for 140,000 North Koreans affected by the floods.
The summer floods submerged arable land for more than 10 days, rendering some land unusable for farming.
The federation plans to distribute a daily ration of 450 grams of grain and supplementary foods to affected individuals.

China's coal sector requires foreign funds and technology for modernization.
David Klingner, group executive of Australian mining group CRA Ltd, stated there are opportunities for billions of dollars in coal investments in China.
The development of small and inefficient mines and outdated power plants is essential for China to meet production goals and sustain economic growth.
China relies on coal for approximately 75 percent of its energy needs and produces about one-third of the world's coal output.
Rong Geng, director of the coal and oil department of China's State Development Bank, indicated that Beijing needs to create a better investment environment to attract foreign investment.
Only about 10 percent of funding for large and medium-scale coal projects in China comes from overseas.
Rong Geng emphasized the need for a sound investment environment to enhance foreign investor confidence.
Klingner noted that foreign firms require stronger legal guarantees to invest in China's coal sector.
Better risk assessment, long-term contracts, and profit assurances are necessary to attract foreign firms to China's coal industry.
China has over 80,000 small-scale mines and needs to transition to large-scale production to improve efficiency and reduce waste and pollution.

China's defence sector and state-owned heavy industries are the country's biggest loss-makers.
More than 45 percent of China's 68,800 state industrial firms posted losses from January to September.
This represents a rise of 17.6 percent in losses compared to the same period last year.
The combined losses of state firms reached 65.12 billion yuan ($7.8 billion) during the first nine months of the year.
This is a rise of 45.7 percent from the same period a year ago.
Many of China's state-run enterprises are overstaffed and unable to compete in domestic or overseas markets.
State-owned enterprises carry the burden of providing cradle-to-grave welfare services for their employees.
The net profits of China's state industries fell to 11.28 billion yuan, down 75.8 percent from the same period last year.
Reform of defence industries has proceeded slowly, with many based in remote regions and fitted with ageing technology.
China's trade unions set up a special fund to help workers in ailing state firms.

China has revived a call by Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin to eliminate poverty before the end of the century.
Jiang Zemin's speech from September calling for more funds to fight poverty was featured prominently in major newspapers.
The coverage aimed to strengthen the Communist Party's image in impoverished regions.
Chinese leaders traditionally visit poor areas to distribute gifts before the Lunar New Year.
The Lunar New Year in 2024 begins on February 7.
A Chinese analyst stated that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and causing bitterness.
China's eastern coastal provinces have experienced significant economic growth, while central and western provinces have lagged.
Beijing is concerned that the growing wealth gap could lead to social unrest.
A crucial Communist Party congress is scheduled for later this year to set national policy.
China claims to have reduced the number of people living in poverty by five million in 1995, but about 65 million still live below the official poverty line.

China posted a trade surplus of $12.24 billion in 1996.
The trade surplus was lower than recent official projections.
Predictions early in the year had forecasted a trade deficit for China.
Exports for the year totaled $151.07 billion, an increase of 1.5 percent compared to 1995.
Imports for the year were $138.83 billion, an increase of 5.1 percent.
The surplus indicated that exports declined in December, resulting in an estimated deficit of $1.74 billion for that month.
The annual surplus fell short of the State Statistical Bureau's provisional estimate of a $16 billion surplus.
The surplus was down from the $16.7 billion surplus in 1995.
Many economists had predicted a trade deficit for China in 1996 after a deficit of $1.15 billion in the first quarter.
The trade volume of overseas-funded businesses increased by 25 percent in 1996, totaling $137.1 billion.

A U.S. military honour guard took back the remains of U.S. airmen killed in World War Two.
Chinese officials handed over three black cases containing the remains of the B-24 bomber's crew to U.S. Ambassador James Sasser.
The crew died when their plane hit a steep mountain slope in China's Guangxi region 52 years ago.
The remains were placed in three body-length aluminium cases and covered with an American flag at a ceremony at Beijing's Capital Airport.
Mei Ping, director of the North American and Oceanian Affairs Office of China's Foreign Ministry, stated the ceremony was dedicated to American servicemen who sacrificed their lives.
Mei Ping also stated that the remains would be repatriated to their homeland.
The remains were loaded onto a U.S. C-141 Starlifter transport aircraft for identification at the Department of Defence's Central Identification Laboratory in Hawaii.
Alan Liotta of the MIA/POW Office stated that the remains represented more than one person, but the exact number was unknown.
Chinese and U.S. officials and soldiers saluted the dead airmen during the ceremony.
U.S. officials stated that the recovery mission was part of an effort to account for American soldiers lost in regional conflicts.

Wei Jianxing is the chairman of the Communist Party's Central Disciplinary Inspection Committee.
In 1996, China had success in battling corruption, aided by vigilant residents and income reporting rules.
Hundreds of thousands of graft cases were uncovered in 1996.
Several major officials, including Tie Ying, were involved in corruption cases that were cracked by authorities.
Several officials were dismissed during the investigation of corruption cases in 1996.
Wei Jianxing stated that more work was needed to fight corruption in 1997.
Jiang Zemin, the President and Communist Party chief, launched a crackdown on corruption in 1995.
Wei Jianxing emphasized the need to prioritize fighting random and illegal fees on public roads, schools, and for farmers.
Residents made more than 1.45 million calls to anti-graft hotlines from January to November last year.
The calls resulted in over 135,000 cases, including 5,643 involving officials at the county level or above.

The London Stock Exchange launched its new integrated trading and information computer system, Sequence 6, on Tuesday.
The launch of Sequence 6 is the last stage in a three-year programme to modernize the London stock market.
The new system completes the introduction of electronic trading that began in 1986 during the Big Bang shake-up of the London market.
Sequence 6 will facilitate the transition to electronic trading for FTSE 100 stocks next summer.
A spokeswoman for the Exchange stated that Sequence 6 was implemented successfully, on time, and under budget.
Some market-makers in London reported problems with posting prices on Tuesday due to difficulties with the Reuters system.
A Reuters spokesman indicated that the link to Sequence 6 was operating as planned but there was a temporary operational problem affecting prices.
The completion of the Sequence programme cost 81 million pounds and marks the end of a modernization process by the Exchange and Andersen Consulting.
Sequence 6 will enable electronic trading in FTSE 100 shares and the Alternative Investment Market (AIM).
The Exchange conducted extensive market testing over five weekends, during which the new platform handled up to five times the average daily activity.

The Securities and Investments Board (SIB) oversees financial regulation in Britain.
SIB has restricted the use of stockmarket derivatives to profit from inside information.
SIB stated that firms must not use derivatives to buy or sell stakes when inside information would have prohibited such actions in the open market.
The Securities and Futures Authority is responsible for enforcing the guidance on the use of inside information in the derivatives market.
Derivatives are financial instruments derived from the value of an underlying asset such as a stock or a bond.
The 1993 Criminal Justice Act criminalizes insider dealing for individuals.
Firms are expected to adhere to the spirit of the new advice from SIB regarding insider information.
Firms should not use the argument of 'equality of information' to justify stakes based on widely known information.
Firms should not rely on the defense of 'bid facilitation' if a stake only provides a cash benefit.
SIB's advice is based on standards set in criminal law regarding insider dealing.

The United Nations plans to delay Iraq's re-entry to world oil markets.
Oil shares in Europe rose on Monday due to a sharp increase in oil prices.
Iraqi military activity in the Kurdish north led the U.N. to halt a planned humanitarian oil-for-food exchange.
This halt stopped the first sales of Iraqi oil since the Gulf War six years ago.
Increased tension in the Middle East and delays to Iraqi supplies raised crude prices.
October futures for benchmark Brent crude opened 70 cents a barrel higher on London's International Petroleum Exchange.
Shares in Enterprise Oil climbed 10-1/2p to 520p.
Lasmo shares rose three to 196-1/2p.
British Petroleum shares increased by 5-1/2p to 628p.
Shell Transport shares rose 6-1/2p to 939p.

Scottish Amicable plans to shed its mutual status in favor of a stock market flotation.
The group aims to float on the London Stock Exchange in three to five years.
Scottish Amicable will pay policy-holders an initial special bonus of 75 million pounds after demutualising on May 1.
Pay-outs to policy-holders will be based on the length of time policies have been held.
The first payment will be followed by benefits worth more than 200 million pounds as a result of the flotation.
Scottish Amicable expects to have a market capitalisation of around 1.0 billion pounds on flotation.
The group believes significant opportunities exist for profitable growth in its businesses.
Scottish Amicable intends to maintain its independence and not be subject to a takeover bid.
The process of demutualisation will occur in two stages, with the business transferring to a new company, Scottish Amicable Life.
Swiss Re will provide substantial financial backing totaling 395 million pounds, including an immediate cash contribution of 350 million pounds.

Scottish Amicable rejected a takeover bid from Abbey National Plc worth up to 1.4 billion pounds.
Scottish Amicable plans to shed its mutual status and seek a stock market flotation in three to five years.
Abbey National's chief executive Peter Birch stated the offer would provide immediate value and long-term security to Scottish Amicable policyholders.
The Abbey offer includes a minimum of 400 million pounds to policyholders in cash or Abbey shares.
Abbey National plans to invest between 700 million and one billion pounds into the with-profits fund for policyholders.
Abbey National is Britain's fifth largest bank and has 14 billion pounds under management.
Abbey National's deputy chief executive Charles Toner expressed a desire to persuade Scottish Amicable to consider the offer.
Scottish Amicable described Abbey's approach as vague and unclear regarding the valuation of the group.
Scottish Amicable intends to publish detailed proposals about its transformation in 10 days.
Scottish Amicable is based in Stirling, Scotland.

Prudential Corp has made a 1.9 billion pound bid for Scottish Amicable.
The bid is considered a strong offer that may hinder competition from other bidders.
Only 250 million pounds of the bid is sourced from Prudential shareholders' funds.
Prudential shares increased by 12 pence to 566 pence following the announcement of the bid.
The offer includes a 400 million pound bonus in cash and shares for ScotAm policyholders.
Prudential plans to add an additional 150 million pounds to policies as soon as possible.
Prudential will pay 1.1 billion pounds into ScotAm's life fund as a loan from its own life fund.
Prudential intends to close ScotAm's life fund to new business.
The existing free assets of ScotAm, estimated to be at least 400 million pounds, will be paid out to policyholders.
Abbey National is expected to struggle to compete due to its lack of capital strength in its life funds.

British insurers will require individuals applying for new life insurance policies to disclose genetic test results.
The Association of British Insurers (ABI) will not require genetic tests for life insurance applications for the next two years.
The ABI's policy statement is supported by all 440 member companies.
The decision is a response to advancements in genetic testing technology.
Many U.S. insurance companies already require genetic testing for applicants.
Currently, Britons must provide results of any genetic tests they have undergone but are not required to take tests for insurance qualification.
Doctors can diagnose common single gene defects and screen for susceptibility to certain cancers.
Experts predict that it will soon be possible to assess the risk of common disorders like diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis.
Huntington's disease is identified as a rare hereditary disease that typically manifests in middle age.
Concerns have been raised about the potential creation of an underclass unable to obtain insurance due to genetic factors.

Lloyd's of London was granted judgements in two test cases against members who failed to pay debts under the reconstruction and renewal settlement.
The defendants in the cases were Dennis Leighs and David Wilkinson.
Dennis Leighs and David Wilkinson claimed they were not liable to pay their premium to Equitas.
Equitas is the company established to reinsure and run-off pre-1993 liabilities of Lloyd's syndicates.
Mr Justice Colman stated that the defendants failed to establish any arguable defences.
Lloyd's welcomed the decision and plans to pursue other non-acceptors of the settlement.
Philip Holden is the head of Lloyd's financial recovery department.
Holden stated that the pursuit of non-acceptors will be vigorous and effective due to the judgement.
Lloyd's originally brought proceedings against three Names but dropped one due to concerns over the defendant's age and ill health.
Members who have not yet accepted the settlement have until February 28 to do so.

Prudential Corp Plc is Britain's biggest life insurance group.
Prudential reported a rise in profits and expects strong performance from British operations in the coming year.
Prudential did not comment on negotiations with the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) regarding orphan assets.
Finance director Jonathan Bloomer stated that discussions with the DTI are ongoing and may take a long time.
Prudential is looking to free up around three billion pounds of orphan assets.
Pru's operating profits for the year rose over eight percent to 873 million pounds.
Profits from continuing operations were 691 million pounds.
Pru's shares increased by 11 pence to 574 pence due to confidence in new business prospects.
The dividend was raised by 10 percent to 17.3 pence per share.
Chief executive Sir Peter Davis described the year as very successful and highlighted the strength of the group's core business.

Britain's National Westminster Bank Plc announced a first half provision of 50 million pounds ($81.4 million) due to mispricing errors in its Natwest Markets unit.
A senior trader at Natwest Markets has been suspended for failure to supervise pending an internal inquiry.
A second trader, who resigned before the errors were discovered, has been reported to the Securities & Futures Authority (SFA) regulator.
NatWest stated that no clients were affected by the mispricing discovery and that the Bank of England was being kept informed.
The SFA confirmed that NatWest Markets had sent it information which is currently under review.
A spokesman for the SFA indicated that no statement was planned at that moment.
Dealers were uncertain about the transactions that led to the provision and whether they occurred on an exchange or in the over-the-counter options market.
The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange did not provide an immediate comment on the situation.
Options are contracts that give buyers the right to buy or sell an underlying security at a set price in the future.
Natwest Markets reported a 25 percent rise in profits from 'other dealing' to 171 million pounds, attributed to strong increases in rate risk management products.

B.A.T industries expressed interest in expanding its British life insurance activities through acquisition.
B.A.T was deterred from bidding for Scottish Amicable due to its price.
B.A.T Chief Executive Martin Broughton reported a three percent fall in trading profits at its financial services arm.
The trading profits included a 160 million pound charge for U.S. environmental claims dating back to the 1960s.
Broughton stated that the British American Financial Services unit would benefit from expanding in the life broker business.
Scottish Amicable was put up for sale in February and is considering bids from Prudential Corp, Abbey National, and Australian Mutual Provident.
Broughton indicated that the group wanted to increase its presence in the independent financial advice sector.
B.A.T chairman Lord Cairns did not comment on speculation regarding a partnership with Commercial Union.
Cairns mentioned that the company remained open-minded about its future structure, including the possibility of a demerger.
B.A.T owns insurance groups Allied Dunbar and Eagle Star in Britain and Farmers in the U.S.

British insurer Legal & General (L&G) reported a double digit rise in profits for 1996.
L&G provided an upbeat assessment of the outlook for the group.
L&G ruled out acquisitions in the life and pensions business.
L&G stated that rising sales and profits would continue to support strong dividend growth.
L&G chief executive David Prosser emphasized that the company's strategy is not dependent on mergers and acquisitions.
L&G shares reached an all-time high of 423 pence.
By late morning, L&G shares were trading at 415-1/2 pence, a rise of 9-1/2 pence on the day.
Analysts noted that the dividend was slightly ahead of forecast.
The value of new business for L&G increased from 20 million pounds to 60 million pounds.
L&G experienced a 54 percent jump in new business in 1996 but still had less than five percent market share.

Britannic Assurance announced plans to expedite the settlement of pension mis-selling cases.
Britannic Assurance reported a nearly 50 percent increase in profits for 1996.
The company has between 12,000 and 13,000 cases classified as priority cases.
Britannic Assurance's chief executive is Brian Shaw.
Shaw stated that the resolution of priority cases depends on both the company's resources and the response of occupational schemes.
The pension industry is in a better position to address the backlog of pension mis-selling cases.
An estimated 1.5 million people may have been misadvised to take personal pensions instead of remaining in occupational schemes.
A review of pension mis-selling was initiated in 1994, but only a small number of affected individuals have received compensation.
The Personal Investment Authority (PIA) faced criticism for its management of the pension mis-selling scandal.
Britannic Assurance reported a 47 percent increase in pre-tax profits to 93.9 million pounds.

A leading Chinese dissident, Wang Xizhe, has fled to Hong Kong.
Wang Xizhe is reported to be seeking asylum in the United States.
Wang was seen in Hong Kong and appeared to be in good health.
Wang is the second Chinese dissident to escape to the United States via Hong Kong this year.
Wang has been missing from his home in Guangdong since Liu Xiaobo was arrested.
Liu Xiaobo was ordered to serve three years in a labour camp.
Wang started planning his departure after Liu Xiaobo's arrest.
Wang approached the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of the Democratic Movement in China for help.
The Hong Kong Alliance requested the Hong Kong government to assist Wang in seeking political asylum in the United States.
Wang Xizhe had been active in recent months, sending open letters to the government.

Wang Dan was sentenced to 11 years in prison in Beijing.
The sentencing of Wang Dan raised concerns in Hong Kong about future restrictions on freedom.
More than 100 demonstrators protested against Wang Dan's verdict at China's diplomatic mission in Hong Kong.
A human rights group plans to lobby for a resolution at the United Nations condemning China's human rights record.
Protesters chanted for the release of Wang Dan during their march.
A Beijing court found Wang Dan guilty of conspiring to subvert the government after a four-hour trial.
Xinhua reported that Wang Dan received funds from hostile overseas forces and aided jailed dissidents.
Wang Dan previously served four years for his involvement in the 1989 pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing.
Legislator Bruce Liu expressed concern that the Chinese government might apply similar standards in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten acknowledged widespread concern about the sentence imposed on Wang Dan.

Air China is China's largest carrier.
Air China plans to increase its international routes next year.
Air China will add five passenger planes to its fleet.
Zhang Jinming is the general manager of Air China's publicity centre.
Air China will start flights from Beijing and Shanghai to Los Angeles on June 29, 1997.
Air China plans to start routes from Beijing to Fushan in South Korea and to Brazil next year.
The China Airshow '96 is held at Zhuhai airport in Guangdong province.
China has 30 passenger carriers.
Air China currently operates 44 international and domestic routes.
Air China has a fleet of 64 Boeing passenger jets and will receive three Airbus A340s and two Boeing 747s in 1997.

China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen arrived to open a meeting to choose Hong Kong's future leaders.
Protesters greeted Qian with anger upon his arrival.
Police clashed with demonstrators blocking access to the Convention Centre.
The meeting is part of the process for Britain to return Hong Kong to China in 228 days.
Qian will preside over a 400-member Selection Committee tasked with selecting the Chief Executive and 60 members of a new legislature.
A group of about 30 police surrounded student activists during the protests.
Hong Kong's pro-democracy lobby has criticized the selection process as undemocratic.
Protesters oppose China's plan to dissolve the elected legislature and replace it with a provisional chamber.
Demonstrators chanted slogans demanding a directly elected legislature and rejecting the deterioration of democracy.
The Selection Committee is scheduled to hold its first round of voting on Friday.

DHL Worldwide Express has operated in Eastern and Central Europe since the mid-1980s.
Peter Davies, regional director of the European rim, stated that DHL would break even in the region by the year 2000.
DHL's turnover in Eastern and Central Europe was US$155 million in 1996, up from US$110 million in 1995, and projected to reach US$200 million in 1997.
DHL experienced years of losses in the region following the fall of the Berlin Wall and the breakup of the Soviet Union.
DHL employs approximately 3,500 people in Eastern and Central Europe.
DHL holds a 75 percent market share in Eastern and Central Europe.
Foreign investments by clients in Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, and the CIS have increased DHL's business.
DHL invested US$46 million in expanding facilities and purchasing aircraft in 1996, along with an additional seven percent for training.
DHL operates in 165 locations in Eastern and Central Europe and plans to add 35 more stations in 1997.

Tung Chee-hwa made his first appearance in China as Hong Kong's leader-in-waiting on Thursday.
The Beijing-picked Preparatory Committee endorsed Tung as the successor to colonial governor Chris Patten.
Britain will hand Hong Kong back to China on July 1.
Tung was selected as the post-handover leader in Hong Kong by a 400-member body assembled by Beijing.
Tung received 80 percent of the votes in his selection process.
At the Preparatory Committee meeting, Tung was greeted with applause and smiles.
Senior Chinese envoy Lu Ping announced that Tung received the majority vote of 320.
Preparatory Committee Vice Chairman Wang Hanbin urged delegates to show support for Tung's endorsement.
Tung expressed hope that Anson Chan would remain as his deputy.
Tung stated he would work with the current British-led government to ensure a smooth transition.

China rejected a British challenge to take it to the World Court.
China staged a vote to set up a Hong Kong parliament that will oust elected lawmakers when Beijing recovers the territory next July.
An elite of 400 carefully chosen Hong Kong electors met in Shenzhen to pick new legislators for the territory.
The members of the Selection Committee cast ballots for the 60-seat legislature in big red envelopes.
Electors could choose from 130 pro-Beijing candidates who had been screened by China's representatives in Hong Kong.
The result of the vote is likely to be denounced by Britain and some of its allies as a travesty of democracy.
Britain is handing Hong Kong back to China at midnight on June 30 under a treaty that promises the territory can keep its capitalist system for 50 years.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen stated that Britain should wake up to reality regarding the situation.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind challenged China to go to the International Court of Justice to prove the legality of its provisional legislature.
Hong Kong's colonial Governor Chris Patten criticized the proposed legislature, calling it a rubber stamp and an echo chamber.

The future leader of Hong Kong, Tung Chee-hwa, announced plans to discuss the legality and funding of the territory's provisional assembly with China's legislators.
Tung Chee-hwa will meet with the National People's Congress (NPC) during his visit to Beijing this weekend.
Tung Chee-hwa did not confirm whether he would request the Chinese parliament to pass a law endorsing the provisional legislature.
The provisional legislature was formed on December 21 in Shenzhen, China.
Britain and the pro-democracy movement in Hong Kong claim the provisional legislature is illegal under the 1984 Joint Declaration.
China established the provisional legislature to reverse electoral reforms made by Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten.
The interim chamber was selected by a 400-member Selection Committee chosen by Beijing.
Tung Chee-hwa was selected by the committee to succeed Chris Patten as Chief Executive.
The provisional legislature will hold its first meeting in China to avoid legal challenges from Hong Kong's Democratic Party.
Tung Chee-hwa plans to meet with the Democratic Party to persuade them to accept the provisional legislature.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind is flying to Hong Kong earlier than expected.
This visit may be Rifkind's last before Hong Kong is handed back to China in July.
Legislators in Hong Kong are preparing to question Rifkind about the future of freedoms and human rights laws.
Rifkind's visit is shortened due to a key parliamentary vote in London.
Rifkind is expected to meet Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, and other senior officials.
Rifkind's original schedule would have caused him to miss an important parliamentary vote on 'mad cow' disease.
