Hong Kong is concerned about China's plans to replace its elected chamber with a provisional legislature.
The Democratic Party of Hong Kong has expressed the need for clarification on the operation of two legislatures before July 1.
Britain has stated that the establishment of the provisional chamber is illegal under a 1984 treaty.
A pro-China newspaper criticized the idea of letting the world court arbitrate on the provisional legislature.

Hong Kong residents lined up on Thursday to pay respects to Deng Xiaoping, China's deceased leader.
Colonial Governor Chris Patten was one of the first to offer condolences at the Xinhua news agency in Hong Kong.
Deng Xiaoping died at the age of 92 on Wednesday.
Chris Patten expressed his intention to sign a condolence book if one was opened.
Patten stated that sending flowers would not be appropriate.
During Patten's tenure as Governor, there was tension between Government House and Xinhua.
China criticized Patten for advocating democratic reforms during British rule.
China plans to dissolve Hong Kong's elected legislature and replace it with an appointed chamber.
Tung Chee-hwa, the future leader of Hong Kong, paid respects to Deng Xiaoping alongside his inner cabinet.
An elderly couple arrived early to pay respects but were asked to return later due to lack of arrangements.

Lehman Brothers and China International United Petroleum and Chemicals Co Ltd (Unipec) announced a settlement of a 22-month foreign-exchange trading dispute.
The dispute involved US$44 million over currency and swap option trading and began in November 1994.
The settlement leaves one of Lehman's three disputes with Chinese state-owned companies unresolved.
Lehman stated that it is eager to continue developing its business in China following the resolution of the dispute.
Unipec expressed anticipation of future collaboration with Lehman.
Lehman filed a US$44 million lawsuit in New York in November 1994, claiming Unipec failed to meet obligations in foreign exchange and swap transactions.
Unipec counterclaimed that Lehman took orders from Hong Kong firms not affiliated with Unipec.
A senior Unipec manager confirmed that both Lehman and Unipec have cancelled their respective lawsuits.
The dispute negatively impacted Unipec's reputation, particularly in the U.S.
Lehman has a separate US$53 million lawsuit against Minmetals International Non-Ferrous Metals Trading Co, which includes a US$128 million countersuit from Minmetals.

Tung Chee-hwa is the future leader of Hong Kong.
Tung Chee-hwa met with Democratic Party leader Martin Lee on Monday.
Tung Chee-hwa has accused Martin Lee of badmouthing Hong Kong abroad.
The meeting between Tung Chee-hwa and Martin Lee was described as cooperative.
Martin Lee provided Tung Chee-hwa with a position paper regarding key issues about Hong Kong's handover.
Martin Lee has made many trips overseas to lobby against the provisional legislature.
Tung Chee-hwa has criticized Martin Lee for his overseas criticisms of Hong Kong.
Martin Lee will receive the National Endowment for Democracy's 1997 Democracy Award on April 9.
Martin Lee stated that the Democratic Party will not censor itself in the future.
Concerns exist in Hong Kong regarding the end of its elected legislature and potential changes to laws protecting human rights.

Netscape and Microsoft agreed that the Internet browser wars were silly.
Steve Case, chairman and CEO of America Online Inc, expressed that there is silliness in the browser wars.
Case believes that Microsoft and Netscape will end up with comparable market share.
Netscape dominates the Internet browser market with its Navigator software, holding approximately 70 to 80 percent market share.
Microsoft's Internet Explorer is gaining momentum and is being bundled as the primary browser with more online services.
Internet Explorer became the preferred browser on AT&T's WorldNet Internet access service.
James Barksdale, president and CEO of Netscape, stated that 80 percent of Netscape's revenues come from the corporate network market.
Netscape is competing with Microsoft's BackOffice and IBM's Lotus Notes in the corporate network market.
Bill Gates, chairman and CEO of Microsoft, stated that competition with Netscape is beneficial for the market.
Both Gates and Barksdale agreed on the importance of the Internet.

Prodigy Inc. will launch its Internet-based version of the Prodigy online service, called Prodigy Internet, on Monday.
Prodigy Internet will have two pricing models, including a flat-rate plan of $19.95 a month for unlimited service.
Prodigy Inc. claims to be the first of the original three commercial online service companies to offer a rebuilt service that embraces Internet standards.
Prodigy plans to use its Internet focus as the basis for its international expansion, including a Spanish-language version in Mexico early next year.
The company plans to spend about $100 million in 1997 to market Prodigy Internet through various advertising channels, excluding television.
Prodigy Internet targets the 'New to the Net' market and the 90 percent of American homes that have not signed up for an online service.
Company President Paul Delacey stated that the new offering is not focused on existing subscribers but on a broader market.
Prodigy Internet aims to address limitations in navigating the Internet and the fears of Internet novices.
Prodigy Internet will offer a basic plan costing $9.95 a month for 10 hours of usage and an additional flat-rate plan for $19.95 a month.
Prodigy will continue to offer its current proprietary online service, Prodigy Classic, while providing incentives for current members to switch to Prodigy Internet.

International Business Machines Corp reported strong third quarter results.
IBM's third quarter earnings were $2.45 a share, exceeding the Wall Street consensus estimate of $2.43.
IBM's stock price fluctuated after the earnings report, initially opening lower before rising to 135-3/8 during the analysts' call.
IBM's chief financial officer expressed concerns about negative impacts from currency, memory prices, and higher expenses.
Analysts, including Jay Stevens from Dean Witter, noted cautionary comments about the fourth quarter and revised their estimates.
Some analysts reduced their fourth quarter estimates following IBM's comments about currency impact and memory chip prices.
Analysts generally viewed IBM's cost-cutting measures and product transitions positively.
IBM's revenue growth exceeded expectations, with notable growth from products other than mainframes.
IBM reported a decline in mainframe revenues during the quarter.
IBM indicated that currency and memory chip prices would have a greater negative impact than previously expected.

Ross Cooley, a top executive at Compaq Computer Corp., announced he is leaving the company to join an Internet startup called pcOrder.com.
Cooley was in charge of Compaq's $7 billion North American computer business.
At pcOrder.com, Cooley will serve as chairman and chief executive officer with a salary of $1 a year and stock options.
Cooley's departure from Compaq is similar to the recent move of Alex Mandl from AT&T.
Cooley's move is expected to provide credibility to pcOrder.com, which operates an online marketplace for personal computers and related equipment.
Cooley's retirement had been rumored for several months prior to the announcement.
James Schraith will replace Cooley at Compaq; he was formerly president of The Cerplex Group Inc. and president of AST Research Inc.
Eckhard Pfeiffer, president and CEO of Compaq, stated that Cooley's retirement had been discussed for some time.
Compaq has created a new sales infrastructure and hired Richard Snyder from Dell Computer Corp. as general manager of worldwide sales.
All heads of Compaq's five geographical sales regions will now report to Snyder instead of Pfeiffer.

America Online Inc. announced a reorganization of its business in response to competition from the Internet.
AOL introduced a flat-rate pricing plan of $19.95 per month for unlimited access.
AOL will incur $460 million in charges this year as part of its restructuring.
AOL plans to separate into three operating units: AOL Networks, AOL Studios, and ANS Communications.
Robert Pittman was named to oversee AOL Networks as part of the reorganization.
Pittman previously served as chief executive of MTV Networks and Century 21 Real Estate Corp.
AOL will take a $385 million charge in its fiscal first quarter for deferred subscriber acquisition costs.
AOL expects to incur a one-time charge of up to $75 million in the current quarter for reorganization costs.
AOL's stock price increased to $25.675 after the announcement of the reorganization.
Analysts expect some pressure on AOL's gross profits due to the new pricing strategy.

International Business Machines Corp will provide an update on its strategy for electronic commerce on Tuesday.
IBM will unveil new partners and show examples of projects already in the works.
Electronic commerce refers to buying and selling goods and services or conducting transactions over computer networks.
IBM views electronic commerce as a significant opportunity to provide products and services for online business.
An IBM spokesman stated that IBM will discuss its current status and future direction in electronic commerce.
Top executives from IBM's Lotus Development Corp unit, its Internet division, and its Network Computer unit will host a press conference.
IBM plans to announce several new partners for various applications targeted at specific industries.
IBM will unveil an application called PetroConnect for the petroleum industry to share geographical information over the Internet.
IBM is expected to add 10 new retailers to its World Mall online shopping site.
IBM will officially roll out its Network Computer division and possibly new models of the Network Station.

International Business Machines Corp announced new partnerships as part of a strategy for electronic commerce.
IBM plans to generate revenue through hardware, software, and services.
IBM's partnerships include retailers, petroleum companies, insurance companies, and a utility.
Irving Wladwasky-Berger is the general manager of IBM's Internet division.
IBM's Internet unit was established less than one year ago.
IBM is developing various electronic commerce applications, including an electronic trading system and an Internet retailing outlet.
IBM expects the worldwide information technology industry to grow from $800 billion to $1.2 trillion in the next four years.
Siemens AG is partnering with IBM to provide a service for electric utilities to sell excess power transmission capacity.
Pacific Gas and Electric Co is the first customer for the service developed with Siemens.
IBM announced 13 new retailers joining its Internet shopping mall, World Avenue.

IBM's stock is trading at historic highs.
Daniel Mandresh of Merrill Lynch raised his 12-month price target on IBM to $195 from about $155.
IBM's shares increased by 20.2 percent to 153-3/4 at Tuesday's market close.
Steve Milunovich of Morgan Stanley raised his 12-month price target for IBM to $170 from $145.
IBM's shares are trading at levels not seen since before the 1987 stock market crash.
IBM's shares have reached a nine-year high.
IBM's price/earnings ratio is about 14.2 times its trailing earnings estimates.
IBM's shares have climbed nearly 70 percent since July 15, when they were trading around 90-7/8.
Market technicians reported that IBM's shares have broken out of two previous resistance levels at 128 and 148.
Gregory Nie, a technical analyst at EVEREN Securities Inc., stated that the primary trend for IBM's stock remains up.

Several U.S. computer retailers reported a sluggish start to the holiday season.
November sales showed ongoing weakness and heavy promotions.
Retailers noted that the November holiday shopping season was shorter due to a late Thanksgiving holiday weekend.
Stephen Baker, a retail channel analyst at International Data Corp, described the situation as 'bad' rather than 'sluggish.'
Circuit City Stores Inc reported an eight percent increase over total November 1995 sales.
Circuit City's comparable store sales fell eight percent in November.
Richard Sharp, Circuit City's chairman and CEO, stated that industry sales trends remained weak and promotional activity intensified.
Best Buy Co Inc reported that the PC category became more promotional in November.
Allen Lenzmeier, Best Buy's chief financial officer, noted that third quarter sales were well below earlier expectations.
Best Buy's comparable store sales in November fell eight percent compared to an increase of 15 percent the previous November.

Home use of the Internet's World Wide Web has more than doubled in the last year.
About 11 percent of U.S. households claimed to have used the Web in the last month, according to a study by PC-Meter.
11 percent of all 98.7 million U.S. households is equivalent to about 11 million homes.
This figure is up from 4.4 percent (or 4.3 million) a year ago.
13.9 percent of households claimed to have used some type of Internet access service in the last month.
25 percent of home Web users now visit shopping sites, according to PC-Meter's audience rating reports.
62.8 percent of Web surfers were men and 37.2 percent were women in September.
The top 10 shopping sites include free software downloads, interactive auctions, clubs that sell to members, and retail operations.
Shareware.com was the top consumer shopping site on the Web, followed by Columbia House Co. and ZDNet's Software Library.
CUC International Inc. is the third most popular site and has the highest percentage of women among the top shopping sites.

Push technology broadcasts customized news directly to networked PCs.
PointCast Inc. is a privately-held company based in Santa Clara, California.
PointCast announced a major deal with Microsoft Corp on a Tuesday.
PointCast delivers customized news several times a day to users.
Ted Julian is an analyst with IDC Corp who commented on the crowded push technology market.
PointCast has 1.7 million subscribers.
PointCast delivers news from sources including the New York Times, the Boston Globe, Reuters Holdings Plc, and MSNBC.
Most push technology companies operate on an advertising-based model.
The deal with Microsoft could expand PointCast's subscriber base.
The Yankee Group predicts the Internet broadcasting market will be worth $5.7 billion by 2000.

Push technology broadcasts customized news directly to computer users connected to the Internet.
PointCast Inc. is a privately held company that announced a deal with Microsoft Corp.
PointCast and other start-ups deliver customized news to users several times a day.
The Yankee Group predicts that Internet broadcasting will generate $5.7 billion in revenues by the year 2000.
Currently, Internet broadcasting generates about $10 million in annual revenues.
Ted Julian, an analyst with IDC Corp., stated that the Internet broadcasting market is crowded.
There are between 20 to 30 start-ups in the push technology sector.
PointCast has 1.7 million subscribers and delivers news from various sources including The New York Times and MSNBC.
Most start-up companies in this sector operate on an advertising-based model, offering free services to subscribers.
The deal with Microsoft may significantly increase PointCast's subscriber base.

U.S. computer makers are expected to report solid fourth quarter earnings.
The stronger dollar will negatively impact some big systems makers.
Most U.S. PC makers, except for Apple Computer Inc and AST Research Inc, are expected to show strong sales growth.
Apple Computer Inc forecasted an operating loss for its first quarter, citing weak U.S. demand for its Performa consumer PC and shortages of notebooks.
Eugene Glazer, a Dean Witter analyst, stated that business in the PC sector, other than Apple, was strong.
Analysts expect Compaq Computer Corp to report strong earnings due to booming corporate sales.
Compaq derives about 20 percent of its revenues from the retail consumer channel.
Dell Computer Corp and Gateway 2000 Inc are benefiting from the transition to the PentiumPro chip and a hot notebook market.
Companies like International Business Machines Corp, Digital Equipment Corp, and Unisys Corp are expected to see negative impacts from a stronger dollar and sluggish sales in Europe.
Digital Equipment Corp is expected to report a slight profit as it recovers from sales force problems in Europe.

Lloyds Chemists stated it could not advise shareholders on a renewed bid offer from UniChem until it received information from Gehe AG.
Finance director Johnathan Fellows mentioned the need to ascertain Gehe's intentions.
Both UniChem's original bid and Gehe AG's rival offer lapsed in March due to referral to Britain's Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
Fellows indicated that the board needed to meet and communicate with shareholders before making recommendations.
Lloyds shares reached a record high of 523p following news of UniChem's renewed offer, before settling at 518p.
UniChem shares decreased by 6p to 250.
Gehe shares in Frankfurt fell by two marks to 109 marks.
Gehe's lapsed offer was an all-cash bid at 500 pence per share.
UniChem is offering 16 new shares and 926p in cash for every 10 Lloyds shares, valuing the company at 657.6 million pounds.
UniChem estimated cost savings and revenue benefits of over 15 million pounds in the first year after acquisition and more than 20 million pounds annually thereafter.

B.A.T Industries reported a nine percent rise in nine-month profits.
B.A.T Industries ruled out a demerger of its tobacco business.
U.S. tobacco litigation is the main issue affecting B.A.T's share price.
Chief executive Martin Broughton stated that there was no value in demerging the company.
Profits in the nine months rose to 2.04 billion pounds from 1.87 billion pounds.
Profits in the third quarter rose to 714 million pounds from 680 million pounds.
Trading profit from financial services rose by three percent.
Profits from tobacco were seven percent ahead.
Worldwide cigarette sales rose by three percent, although volumes were lower in the United States.
B.A.T shares have fallen from a high of 585 pence to below 430 pence.

Unilever Plc is an Anglo-Dutch food-to-detergent group.
Unilever is reporting third quarter results next Friday.
Analysts expect Unilever to have incurred restructuring costs for its North American industrial cleaning business Diversey.
Weak ice cream sales in Europe are anticipated due to a poor summer.
Diversey was acquired in January from Molson for 360 million stg.
Diversey was merged with Lever Industrial in October, forming a combined business with an annual turnover of 1.15 billion stg and a workforce of 13,000 in 60 countries.
Analysts predict third quarter pretax profits for Unilever to be between 760 and 820 million stg.
Charges for Diversey could range from 15 to 30 million stg, with an additional 20 million needed for restructuring other Unilever businesses.
The half-year dividend, paid in the third quarter, is expected to rise sharply due to changes in dividend policy.
Analysts forecast a 10.3p dividend payout, representing a 46 percent increase from the previous half-year's 7.05p.

Unilever Plc is expected to report third quarter results next Friday.
Analysts predict that Unilever may incur restructuring costs from its North American industrial cleaning business Diversey.
Weak ice cream sales in Europe are anticipated due to poor summer weather.
Diversey was acquired in January from Molson for 360 million stg and merged with Lever Industrial in October.
The combined business of Diversey and Lever Industrial has an annual turnover of 1.15 billion stg and a workforce of 13,000 in 60 countries.
Analysts forecast third quarter pretax profits for Unilever to be between 760 and 820 million stg.
Charges for Diversey are estimated to range from 15 to 30 million stg, with an additional 20 million needed for restructuring other Unilever businesses.
The interim dividend for the third quarter is expected to rise to 10.3p, a 46 percent increase from the previous half-year's 7.05p.
For the nine-month period, analysts forecast Unilever's pretax profits to be about 1.9 billion pounds.
The consensus forecast for Unilever's EPS in 1996 is 84.40p, increasing to 92.30p in 1997.

British consumers are spending more on leisure.
Peter Jarvis is the chief executive of Whitbread.
Whitbread reported a 14 percent rise in half-year pretax profits to 177.5 million.
Consumer confidence in Britain is expected to remain favorable for at least two to three years.
House prices are rising, the job situation is improving, and personal taxes have decreased this year.
Whitbread's workforce includes 42,000 full-time and 33,000 part-time staff.
Whitbread's hotels business doubled profits and sales in the six months to August 31.
Like-for-like sales at Whitbread were up by 11 percent.
The number of foreign tourists to Britain is increasing rapidly.
Whitbread acquired David Lloyd Leisure for 200 million stg and a chain of 16 Marriott hotels for about 185 million in August 1995.

Shares in Unilever Plc increased by 75p to 1,350 by the close of the London market.
Unilever reported a five percent rise in third-quarter profits, totaling 826 million pounds.
The profit results exceeded analysts' forecasts, which ranged from 760 million pounds to 820 million pounds.
Before an exceptional charge of 32 million pounds, Unilever's pretax profits rose six percent to 918 million pounds.
Richard Newboult, an analyst at Lehman Brothers, had predicted a total restructuring charge of 74 million pounds.
Diversey, acquired by Unilever for 360 million pounds, was merged with Lever Industrial to form a combined business with an annual turnover of 1.15 billion pounds.
Unilever owns various household brands, including Persil, OMO, Brooke Bond, Ponds, Walls, and Igloo.
Despite poor weather affecting ice-cream sales, Unilever improved its profit by 13 million pounds to 502 million in the quarter.
The Asia-Pacific region's profits increased by 20 million pounds to 108 million in the third quarter.
Latin America's profits rose by 14 million pounds to 79 million, while Africa and the Middle East saw a nine million pound increase to 56 million.

Unigate Plc is a British dairy and distribution company.
Finance director John Worby stated that Unigate is seeking to acquire food and distribution companies in Europe.
Worby mentioned that the company is looking at acquisitions of all sizes in Western Europe.
Medium-sized acquisitions are defined by Worby as being in the range of 50 to 150 million stg.
Unigate acquired Kraft's European margarine and spreads business for approximately 77 million stg in August.
As of September 30, Unigate reported net cash held of 57.9 million stg.
The cash outflow for the half year was 110.4 million stg, which included 71.4 million stg spent on acquisitions.
Unigate sold its U.S. restaurant business Black-eyed Pea for 42 million stg in July.
The company sold Taco Bueno and Casa Bonita for 27 million stg since the half-year stage.
Unigate sold its minority stake in Dutch food company Nutricia for 360 million stg in January.

Tate and Lyle Plc is expected to report a significant decline in full year profits.
Staley, Tate and Lyle's U.S. sugar unit, is projected to experience a nearly 50 percent drop in earnings.
Michael Landymore, an analyst at Henderson Crosthwaite, stated that Staley is affected by high raw material costs and low pricing for high-fructose corn syrup.
Analysts predict pretax profits for Tate and Lyle will range from 270 to 285 million stg, down from 311 million stg the previous year.
A total dividend of 17.0p is anticipated for the year, an increase of one penny.
Staley's profits were approximately 150 million stg in 1995, but are expected to be only 75 million stg this year.
Analysts believe that improvements in Tate and Lyle's North American sugar business and investments in emerging markets may offset Staley's downturn.
John Elston, an analyst at Panmure Gordon, noted that Staley's contract renegotiations are a key factor for the company.
Staley renegotiates supply contracts with soft drink companies annually at the beginning of the calendar year.
In May, Tate and Lyle warned of lower full year results due to rising grain prices.

Larry Pillard is the chief executive of Tate and Lyle.
Tate and Lyle is a British sugar and starch producer.
Larry Pillard stated that the North American unit Staley should benefit from improved market conditions this year.
Larry Pillard mentioned that corn milling companies can divert excess capacity into ethanol.
This diversion could tighten up the market.
Staley, a wet corn miller, posted a 50 percent fall in earnings.
The fall in earnings was due to a record increase in maize costs.
The increase in maize costs dragged down group pretax profits for the year by some 35 million.
The group's pretax profits for the year were 276.3 million.

Scottish and Newcastle Plc announced a 26 percent increase in half-year profits to 195.1 million pounds ($328 million).
The company reported a positive start to the second half of the year.
The acquisition of Courage from Australian brewer Fosters contributed to a 67 percent increase in trading profits from its beer divisions, totaling 89.9 million pounds.
Scottish and Newcastle Plc increased its dividend by 10 percent to 7.21 pence per share, exceeding most analysts' forecasts.
The company's shares rose by 7 pence to 647 pence.
A Reuter poll of analysts forecasted pretax profits between 178 and 198 million pounds.
Beer sales fell by just over one percent compared to the first half of 1995.
Sales of John Smith's ale increased by 17 percent, and sales of Foster's lager grew by 6.5 percent.
Profits from Center Parcs activity holiday resorts decreased by 11 percent to about 44 million pounds.
Profits from the company's pubs grew by 8.2 percent to 87 million pounds.

Sir Ian Prosser is the chairman of Bass Plc.
Bass Plc is a brewer-to-leisure group.
Bass Plc has proposed to acquire Carlsberg-Tetley.
Sir Ian Prosser stated that the acquisition would make Britain's beer market more competitive.
Prosser mentioned that the acquisition would allow Bass Plc to lower its cost base.
Lowering the cost base would provide more funds for innovation and product improvement.
The acquisition is currently being studied by the Board of Trade on competition grounds.
The Board of Trade's decision on the acquisition is expected in a few weeks.

Grand Metropolitan Plc is experiencing steady growth driven by profits from its American foods business Pillsbury and spirits arm IDV.
Gerald Corbett is the group finance director of Grand Metropolitan Plc.
Grand Metropolitan Plc announced a six percent increase in its pretax profits to 965 million stg for the year ended September 30, 1996.
GrandMet shares fell 6p to 451p after the profit figures came in below the market forecast consensus of 972 million.
The strategy of GrandMet focuses on steady, organic growth, contrasting with the previous era of frenetic acquisitions and disposals under former chairman Lord Sheppard.
Pillsbury grew operating profit by 30 percent to 431 million for the year ended September 30, 1996.
Sales at Pillsbury increased by four percent and prices rose by three percent in the same period.
U.S. operating margins for Pillsbury increased by 0.7 percentage points to 12.2 percent.
GrandMet plans to implement price rises of two to three percent on average at its spirits arm, International Distillers and Vintners (IDV), next year.
GrandMet intends to spend an additional 30 to 40 million on marketing its brands.

Ford Motor Co. has promoted Edward Hagenlocker to vice chairman from executive vice president.
Edward Hagenlocker is now in charge of a new auto components organization with 75,000 employees and revenues of $14 billion.
Jacques Nasser has been named to head Ford Automotive Operations, succeeding Hagenlocker.
Speculation exists regarding the succession of Alex Trotman, who is set to retire in July 1998.
William Clay Ford Jr. may be named a non-executive chairman or chairman when Trotman leaves.
Eugene Jennings stated that Hagenlocker's new role should not be seen as a demotion.
Nasser has worked at Ford since 1968 and has held various international assignments.
Wesley Brown noted that Nasser's new role positions him to potentially succeed Trotman.

General Motors Corp. reported a $1.3 billion profit for the third quarter.
The profit was boosted by strong automotive results and a low income tax rate.
The combined net income of GM's North American Automotive Operations and Delphi Automotive Systems was $515 million.
A year ago, these operations had a combined loss of $93 million.
GM's profit from continuing operations was $1.57 per share, compared to 39 cents per share a year ago.
Revenues increased to $39.1 billion from $35.3 billion in the same period in 1995.
GM recorded $565 million in one-time favorable items contributing to profits.
GM's effective income tax rate was 2.8 percent, adding $312 million to profits.
GM's cash balance reached $14.5 billion at the end of the quarter after adding $1.5 billion.
Analyst Ronald Glantz believes GM may raise its dividend and announce a share repurchase program.

General Motors Corp is idling 5,000 assembly workers at its Lordstown, Ohio plant for two weeks.
The Lordstown plant produces the Chevrolet Cavalier and Pontiac Sunfire small cars.
The plant has run out of transmissions supplied by a GM parts plant in Windsor, Ontario.
5,236 hourly United Auto Workers are employed at the Buick City complex in Flint, Mich.
The Buick City complex produces mid-sized cars including LeSabre, Park Avenue, Eighty Eight, and Bonneville.
As of Thursday afternoon, GM had instructed 23,801 assembly and parts workers in the United States and Mexico to stay home due to a parts shortage.
The Lordstown shutdown is the second U.S. plant where GM has completely suspended operations since the Canadian Auto Workers strike began on October 3.
The first plant to suspend operations was Detroit/Hamtramck, which produces Cadillacs.
The Lordstown plant operates with three crews, with the first crew scheduled to return on November 10.
As of the end of September, GM had between 67 and 98 days supply of mid-sized cars on dealer lots.

Union workers prepared to strike General Motors Corp for the second time this month.
Bargainers for General Motors and the United Auto Workers are struggling to reach a new contract agreement before a midnight deadline.
GM Chairman Jack Smith arrived at the automaker's headquarters early in the evening.
UAW members at pickup truck and sport/utility vehicle assembly plants in Pontiac, Mich. and Janesville, Wis. have made picket signs and drafted strike schedules.
A woman at UAW Local 95 in Janesville stated uncertainty about working in the morning.
A new labor agreement is at stake for GM's 215,000 hourly UAW workers.
General Motors employs more than half of the approximately 390,000 UAW members at Detroit's Big Three automakers.
General Motors is the only one of the Big Three without a new three-year labor contract.
Last week, General Motors settled a strike by 26,000 members of the Canadian Auto Workers union.
GM spokesman Chuck Licari expressed hope for an agreement before the termination of the current national agreement at 11:59 p.m. tonight.

General Motors Corp. faces labor costs of $43 an hour at its parts plants.
David Healy is an analyst at Burnham Securities Inc.
Joseph Phillippi is an analyst at Lehman Brothers.
Timothy Leuliette is the president and chief executive officer of ITT Automotive.
ITT Automotive Inc. paid 15 percent of its 35,000 workers less than $10 an hour in 1995.
The percentage of ITT Automotive workers earning less than $10 an hour increased from 10 percent in 1990 to 15 percent in 1995.
GM is negotiating a new three-year labor contract with the United Auto Workers union.
Delphi Automotive Systems has reported that 12 of its U.S. component facilities are underperforming.
Delphi has stated that it will pay the average U.S. parts worker nearly $19 an hour in the first year of the contract and more than $21 in the third year.
Delphi's combined hourly wage and benefit cost for a UAW worker under the 1993 national agreement is about $43.

General Motors Corp. has a potential buyer for four of its parts plants.
General Motors Corp. denied reports that it is in discussions to sell the facilities to Magna International Inc.
GM informed workers at its Delphi Interior and Lighting Systems plant in Flint, Mich., about the potential buyer.
The 1,200 workers at the Flint plant were not informed of the identity of the prospective buyer.
Tim Thompson is a district shop committee officer for United Auto Workers union Local 326.
The Detroit News reported that GM is in talks with Magna, and a deal could be announced soon.
A source told Reuters that Atoma International Inc., a division of Magna, won the bidding for the plants, but the deal is not finalized.
Delphi spokeswoman Kari Hulsey denied that Magna is a finalist to buy the plants.
The buyer wants to purchase the Flint plant, one in Livonia, Mich., and two in Canada as a group.
The four plants employ a total of 5,100 hourly workers and produce various interior parts.

A gunman in military fatigues entered a Ford Motor Co. assembly plant and opened fire on Thursday.
The gunman, identified as 29-year-old Gerald Atkins from Wixom, killed one person and wounded two others.
Gerald Atkins barricaded himself in drainage tunnels after the shooting.
Atkins shot and killed Darrell Izzard, 57, who was the Ford plant's manager of manufacturing planning.
Atkins also wounded two Oakland County sheriff's deputies during the incident.
One deputy was shot in the shoulder and the other in the leg while attempting to apprehend Atkins.
Atkins had never been employed by Ford and reportedly came to the plant to speak with a woman he was dating.
A worker at the plant reported that Atkins told her to leave before he began shooting.
Police closed adjacent Interstate 96 during the standoff and evacuated workers from the plant.
Production of Lincoln Town Cars, Continentals, and Mark VIII luxury cars was suspended until Monday.

Chrysler Corp minivans are under investigation by U.S. safety regulators.
Federal officials announced on Tuesday that they have increased probes involving the vehicles' doors.
The investigations involve nearly two million minivans.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has received reports of 39 injuries related to the rear lift-gate on 1991-1993 Caravan, Voyager, and Town & Country minivans.
The injuries are linked to retaining bolts that shear, causing the rear hatch to drop unexpectedly.
NHTSA has received a total of 477 complaints regarding the rear lift-gate issue.
An engineering analysis probe covers 1,271,575 minivans.
NHTSA upgraded a preliminary investigation into 581,686 1996-model Caravan, Voyager, and Town & Country minivans.
There have been 19 complaints about sliding doors opening while the vehicle is moving.
Chrysler was the first automaker to offer a sliding door on the left side of a minivan.

Chrysler Corp. filed an appeal against a California DMV ban on shipping new vehicles to dealers in the state.
The ban was issued due to Chrysler allegedly violating California's lemon law.
The ban allows Chrysler to delay its effects for years while pursuing an appeal.
The DMV determined that Chrysler resold 116 vehicles in 1991 and 1992 without properly disclosing their lemon status.
California's lemon law requires automakers to buy back cars from the first owner if they spend 30 days in a repair shop during the first year or if a specific problem is not fixed after three attempts.
Chrysler described the DMV's actions as a 'Draconian penalty' in its appeal.
Chrysler argued that it complied with the lemon law as it was written at the time of the vehicle sales.
Chrysler claimed the statute was vague regarding which repurchased vehicles needed to be branded as lemons.
Chrysler stated it made good-faith efforts to inform used-car buyers about the vehicles they were purchasing.
Chrysler expressed concern about the economic impact of the penalty on its 240 California dealers.

Ford Motor Co. will move 2,500 sales, marketing, and customer service workers out of the Renaissance Centre over the next two years.
Ford's office presence in downtown Detroit dates back to 1978.
General Motors Corp. purchased the Renaissance Centre in May for use as its new headquarters.
Ford agreed to sell 26 acres of land next to the Renaissance Centre to GM.
Robert Rewey is Ford's group vice president of marketing and sales.
Ford occupies about 650,000 square feet in two of the Renaissance Centre's four towers.
Most employees will be relocated to Ford's Regent Court building near its headquarters in Dearborn, Mich.
Ford decided to relocate workers due to space availability from its Ford 2000 reorganization.
Employees will begin moving by mid-1997 and should be out of the Renaissance Centre by the end of 1998.
Ford is committed to the resurgence of Detroit and is investing in local projects.

Labour lawyer James Hoffa called for a congressional investigation into the Teamsters union presidential election.
Hoffa formally asked U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno to impound the ballots and initiate an FBI investigation.
Hoffa referred to the situation as 'Teamstergate' during a news conference at the Teamsters' Detroit offices.
Incumbent Teamsters President Ron Carey claimed victory in the election by an apparent margin of about 17,000 votes.
41,002 ballots were set aside for further eligibility checks, and Hoffa claims more than 25,000 ballots may have disappeared.
Election Officer Barbara Zack Quindel accounted for 485,605 ballots returned after all eligible votes were tallied.
Quindel reported that the total number of mail-in ballots received was estimated to be 511,268.
Quindel decided to void 120 Hoffa votes due to a violation of election rules by a Hoffa backer.
The voided ballots were part of 41,002 challenged ballots that are still being checked for eligibility.
Hoffa would need to carry the challenged ballots by a better than three-to-one margin to erase Carey's lead.

Haworth Inc. received a $211.5 million payment for a patent infringement award against Steelcase Inc.
The payment ended a 17-year legal battle between Haworth and Steelcase over electrified office panels.
Steelcase paid Haworth $96.8 million in damages and $114.7 million in interest.
Steelcase is the largest office furniture maker in the world.
Haworth sued Steelcase in November 1985 for patent infringement related to pre-wired modular panel systems.
The technology in question was developed in the early 1970s and allows safe routing of electricity through office panels.
The court's decision and damage award were entered on December 23 by a special judge in U.S. District Court in Kalamazoo, Mich.
The court denied Steelcase's allegations in a 1989 suit that Haworth infringed on two patents for prewired panels.
Steelcase won the first round of the original 1985 lawsuit, but the U.S. Court of Appeals reversed that ruling in 1989.
Haworth stated that eight other companies have paid more than $75 million to settle patent infringement cases brought by them.

Chrysler Corp. expects strong December sales results for 1996.
Chrysler's total car and truck deliveries for 1996 exceeded 2.4 million units.
Chrysler's year-end sales report is expected to be released on Friday.
Analysts predict a 6 percent decline in industry volume for December compared to the previous year.
General Motors Corp.'s December sales are expected to drop by as much as 16 percent from year-ago levels.
Chrysler Vice Chairman Robert Lutz expects December vehicle sales to be several percentage points ahead of last year's record of 177,803 units.
Chrysler's 1996 sales exceeded their previous record of 2,208,057 units set in 1988.
Light truck sales for Chrysler are projected to rise by 8 percent.
Passenger car sales for Chrysler are expected to decline by 9 percent.
GM's sales of light trucks are expected to decline significantly due to tough year-ago comparisons.

China has tightened safety measures following a fatal rocket explosion earlier this year.
Chinese space officials reported the cause of another launch failure in August.
Further testing is needed for the Long March 3 rocket, which may delay China's launch schedule.
Zhang Qingwei, vice president of the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology, stated that launch vehicles will self-destruct in case of a failure.
Zhang Qingwei also mentioned that people living near space centers will be moved away during launches.
A Long March 3B rocket exploded shortly after launch in February, resulting in six deaths and 57 injuries according to official reports.
Unofficial sources reported a higher casualty toll from the February explosion.
A communications satellite failed to reach proper orbit after launch aboard a Long March 3 rocket in August.
Zhang Qingwei indicated that the August failure was caused by a faulty hydrogen valve on the third stage of the booster rocket.
An official from the China Aerospace Corporation stated that a Long March 3 rocket could be launched by the end of the year or early next year.

China is preparing to list shares of one or two of its chemical companies abroad.
Beijing plans to tighten foreign access to its chemicals market by adding new restrictions on joint ventures.
Chemical Industry Minister Gu Xiulian stated that one or two chemical companies are preparing for share offerings abroad.
Gu Xiulian mentioned that one or two Chinese companies would issue convertible bonds on a trial basis.
China's securities regulators are preparing additional companies for share offers outside the country.
Tianjin Bohai Chemical Group is listed on the Hong Kong stock market and the Shanghai exchange.
Jilin Chemical Industrial trades in Hong Kong, New York, and Shenzhen.
Gu Xiulian stated that China's chemical industry needs to raise funds for technical upgrades.
China will bar foreign companies from holding controlling stakes in joint ventures with large state enterprises in priority areas.
Gu Xiulian indicated that foreign companies may control joint ventures in areas where new technology is vital.

China's Communist leaders are concerned about the decline of the state sector in favor of private firms.
China Minsheng Banking Corporation was formally inaugurated in January.
China Minsheng aims to lend primarily to China's non-state sector.
Chairman Jing Shuping stated that many banks are unwilling to lend to the non-state sector.
China's state industry is losing money and struggling to compete in markets.
Communist leaders insist that the state sector retains a leading role in the economy.
Jing Shuping believes that a growing non-state sector will benefit the economy.
China Minsheng is a non-state entity supported by the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce.
The bank has 59 shareholders, primarily from the federation.
Guangzhou Yitong Group and Xiamen Fuxun Group hold significant stakes in China Minsheng.

China has initiated a national drive to test all blood products due to HIV contamination discovered earlier this year.
A health official from the Ministry of Public Health stated that local health authorities have been requested to inspect blood products and report results.
The HIV contamination was discovered in April in a product manufactured and sold in Guangdong province.
The contaminated product is identified as 'Wolongsong' brand blood albumin.
HIV, or Human Immunodeficiency Virus, can lead to Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS).
Following the contamination incident, a national inspection of blood products was instituted.
Results from tests conducted in several provinces have been submitted to central authorities.
Public health authorities in Guangdong have called for a halt to the sale and use of the 50-millilitre 'Wolongsong' albumin.
Officials in Beijing ordered the destruction of the 'Wolongsong' product.
Official figures indicate that China has 4,305 reported HIV cases, with projections suggesting the total could reach 5,000 by the end of the year.

China is considering listing more railway companies.
A plan is being studied to create a fund to boost foreign investment in the railway sector.
The goal of these moves is to modernize China's rail system and compete with planes and buses.
Zhang Yanzhao is a senior engineer at the Ministry of Railways.
Guangshen Railway Co Ltd is China's first railway stock offer.
The performance of Guangshen Railway is being monitored as a potential model for future stock offerings.
Guangshen Railway connects Guangzhou and Shenzhen.
Guangshen Railway's shares were listed in Hong Kong and New York as American Depositary Receipts in May.
The company's shares were trading at HK$2.925, slightly above the offer price of HK$2.91.
Future railway operations would need to be profitable and are likely to be located along the east coast.

China expects talks with the United States soon regarding U.S. sanctions on its textiles.
Beijing has not yet determined which U.S. imports would be banned if sanctions are not lifted.
An official from the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation stated that working level talks with the U.S. are anticipated.
China announced a temporary suspension of imports of certain U.S. textiles, farm goods, animal husbandry products, fruits, and alcoholic drinks in retaliation for U.S. charges on Chinese textiles.
The temporary import ban from China will take effect on December 10.
Washington imposed punitive charges against import quotas for Chinese textile goods in September, accusing China of avoiding U.S. quota restrictions.
China claims the U.S. action was taken without consultation and lacked clear evidence.
China is consulting with its enterprises to determine which products will be included in the ban, with a decision expected in 30 days.
The trade affected by U.S. actions is estimated at $19 million, a small fraction of the overall Sino-U.S. trade.
The United States reported a trade deficit with China of more than $35 billion last year.

The United States is considering peaceful nuclear cooperation with China before the full implementation of a previously signed accord.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher made this statement during a news conference in Beijing.
Christopher stated that the U.S. is prepared to consider further steps in peaceful nuclear cooperation consistent with U.S. laws.
Christopher did not specify the types of cooperation that might occur before the implementation of the 1985 agreement.
Christopher mentioned that the U.S. would consider other actions if China makes progress towards implementing the 1985 agreement.
The U.S. and China have agreed to establish a regular dialogue on arms control and non-proliferation issues.
Christopher expressed strong concern about China's nuclear cooperation with Iran.
China pledged in May not to provide assistance to any unsafeguarded nuclear facilities.
The U.S. has delayed the full implementation of the 1985 agreement due to concerns over China's nuclear sales.
Before the 1985 agreement can be implemented, the U.S. president must certify to Congress that China is not transferring nuclear technology to countries without safeguards.

China indicated that its three-year austerity program has ended.
China declared its anti-inflation efforts a success.
The new focus for China is ensuring stability as it prepares for the recovery of Hong Kong.
China's top leaders concluded four days of economic meetings.
A key goal for China next year is to accelerate the reform of struggling state enterprises.
The official Economic Daily reported that China's economy has experienced sustained, rapid, and healthy development.
The main task of controlling inflation has been achieved according to the Economic Daily.
Next year marks the recovery of Hong Kong and the 15th Communist Party congress.
China implemented strict controls on government spending in 1993 to manage inflation.
Inflation is expected to fall below 6.5 percent this year, down from 14.8 percent last year.

China should switch its fundraising efforts to longer-term bonds due to easing inflation.
The Financial News is published by the central bank of China.
The newspaper stated that reduced interest rates allow Beijing to secure long-term funds at cheaper rates.
China's retail price inflation rate was 6.9 percent for the first seven months of the year.
The inflation rate is below the target of 10 percent for the year and down from 14.8 percent for all of 1995.
The central bank cut bank interest rates once this year and analysts expect another reduction by the end of the year.
China eliminated a subsidy on new bank deposits and government debt of more than three years as of April.
The subsidy peaked at 13.24 percent in December of last year, in addition to an interest rate of 12.24 percent for three-year bank deposits.
In 1995, China issued 151 billion yuan in domestic treasury debt, which was 2.6 percent of its gross domestic product.
Beijing issued its first tranche of 10-year bonds in July, which paid annual interest of 11.83 percent without a subsidy.

Two years ago, China's second telephone network aimed to challenge the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPT).
The new network is known as China United Telecommunications Corp, or Unicom.
Li Huifen is the president of Unicom.
Unicom has struggled to compete against the MPT, which also serves as the market regulator.
Unicom has only captured a small portion of the telecommunications market.
The MPT has used its regulatory power to hinder Unicom's progress.
Unicom has 16 shareholders, with key support from the ministries of electronics industry, power, and railways.
The Ministry of Electronics Industry has manufacturing capabilities for telecommunications equipment.
The MPT's public network is overcrowded, while private networks have spare capacity.
Firms working with Unicom faced threats of blacklisting from the MPT.

China strongly opposed a visit to Jordan by Taiwan's foreign minister.
China accused Taiwan of trying to disrupt Beijing's ties with other friendly states.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang expressed strong dissatisfaction with Jordan for allowing the visit.
Shen Guofang stated that China is opposed to any official contacts with Taiwan by states that have diplomatic ties with China.
Taiwan's foreign minister John Chang arrived in Jordan on Wednesday.
Jordan has diplomatic relations with China but strong commercial ties with Taiwan.
Chang gave an economics lecture at a northern Jordanian university.
Jordanian government officials declined to comment on Chang's visit.
China has viewed Taiwan as a rebel province since 1949 and has not ruled out the use of force to recover it.
Taiwan's foreign minister was traveling to Abu Dhabi and Jordan en route to Italy.

In 1997, China celebrated the recovery of Hong Kong as a significant event in the communist era.
China Central Television aired a documentary about Deng Xiaoping, who is credited with transforming China into an economic powerhouse.
The documentary is part of a 12-day program that aims to define Deng's legacy for the upcoming Communist Party congress.
A Western diplomat stated that 1997 is an important year for the Communist Party due to the recovery of Hong Kong and the 15th party congress.
Deng Xiaoping has not been seen in public for nearly three years and appeared frail during his last public appearance.
The documentary depicted Deng as a vigorous leader and emphasized the theme of reform and market-oriented economic change.
The documentary's tone was described as adulatory, which contrasts with Deng's opposition to personality cults.
There are ongoing speculations about Deng's health, including an unconfirmed report of him briefly lapsing into unconsciousness.
Reports indicated that Deng had been admitted to a military hospital, but there were no unusual activities at the Beijing medical center.
Deng had expressed a desire to visit Hong Kong for the transfer of power on June 30, 1997, but this visit is now considered unlikely.

The U.S. Postal Service announced a plan to enhance the security and reliability of electronic mail.
The plan allows businesses and consumers to verify that e-mail has not been tampered with.
The Postal Service will offer services for electronic mail similar to those for ordinary mail, such as sending certified letters.
Robert Reisner, vice president of strategic planning, stated that security threats have hindered the transition from messaging to electronic commerce.
Cylink Corp is developing a system for the Postal Service to verify the identity of e-mail senders.
The system will allow users to register a digital signature with the Postal Service.
The Postal Service will investigate any tampering with electronic mail, similar to how it investigates tampering with regular mail.
The Postal Service is collaborating with Sun Microsystems to enhance non-electronic mail delivery.
A new online system for bulk mailers will allow them to calculate postage rates using a Java-based software application.
The Postal Service plans to offer hybrid services that combine electronic and paper mail.

A group of leading trademark specialists plans to release recommendations.
The recommendations aim to minimize disputes over Internet address names.
The International Trademark Association is working on a white paper.
The white paper will be completed in the next few months.
David Maher is the co-chair of the association's Internet issues committee.
David Maher provided this information in a telephone interview.

The Internet grew significantly in 2023, while online services struggled to gain new customers.
A survey by Louis Harris and Associates conducted in late September estimated that 35 million adults in the United States had used the Internet, up from 27 million at the beginning of the year.
Humphrey Taylor, chairman of the polling organization, stated that the number of adult Americans using computers for cyber-activities is increasing.
America Online Inc. and Compuserve Corp. reported nearly 41 million subscribers, the same level found by Harris in January.
Online services faced increased competition from companies like AT&T Corp., which offer cheaper Internet-only access.
Businesses are interested in Internet usage figures as a potential source of new revenue.
The Harris poll indicated that, although more people are getting wired, they are spending less time online.
Home users reported being online for an average of 2.8 hours a week, down from three hours in an April survey.
Business and other users reported being online for an average of 1.8 hours, down from two hours in April.
The poll found that individuals with college and graduate degrees were more likely to use computers and access the Internet compared to those who graduated from high school.

The Business Software Alliance is withdrawing its support for the Clinton Administration's new policy on encryption export rules.
The Business Software Alliance includes Microsoft Corp and International Business Machine Corp's Lotus Development.
The alliance expressed concerns that the rules implementing the new encryption export policy are flawed.
The alliance stated that significant backtracking has occurred since the October 1 announcement.
The alliance doubts that the regulations will work, meet consumer demands, or be accepted by the private sector without immediate changes.
Greg Simon, the vice president's chief domestic policy adviser, and other officials have met with the software group to discuss their criticism.
Final rules on the encryption export policy are expected by January 1.
The administration is trying to create a compromise on the export of products containing encryption.
Current laws restrict export products to very weak coding features.
U.S. software companies claim they are losing overseas sales to foreign companies not subject to export laws.

A break-in at the U.S. Justice Department's World Wide Web site occurred on August 16.
Unidentified hackers replaced the department's web page with a message labelled the 'Department of Injustice' that included a swastika and a picture of Adolf Hitler.
Justice officials quickly removed the vandalized page.
Security experts stated that the security flaws that allowed the break-in likely exist in thousands of other corporate and government web sites.
Richard Power, a senior analyst at the Computer Security Institute, claimed that the vast majority of sites are vulnerable and that the Justice Department should not be singled out.
Justice Department officials stated that the compromised web site was not connected to any computers containing sensitive files.
The web site included copies of press releases, speeches, and other publicly available information.
Bert Brandenburg, a spokesman for the Justice Department, compared the security breach to graffiti on the outside of a building.
The Nation of Islam's Million Man March web site was vandalized last year.
According to a General Accounting Office report, hackers make 250,000 attempts annually to break into U.S. military computers.

An international task force released a draft plan for expanding Internet addresses.
The International Ad Hoc Committee on domain names was formed by the Internet Society in October.
The committee recommended adding seven new top-level domains to the Internet.
Top-level domains are three-letter designations that most Internet sites end with.
The committee suggested that an unlimited number of firms be authorized to register new addresses.
The committee plans to initially approve 20 to 30 new registration services.
Network Solutions Inc. currently distributes most site addresses and charges $100 for each registration.
Network Solutions will maintain a monopoly on existing domain names until the committee's ultimate goal is achieved.
The full text of the recommendations was posted on the Internet at http://www.iahc.org.
The proposal will be open for public comment until January 17, and a final report is expected by February 3.

The Federal Communications Commission proposed to reduce the $23 billion a year that long-distance telephone companies pay to local service providers in access fees.
The FCC did not propose whether access charges should be imposed on Internet service providers and instead requested comments on the issue.
The FCC stated it could reduce access fees through a schedule of long-distance access charge reductions or by allowing market forces to lower fees.
Access charges were established after the break-up of AT&T Corp. in 1984, leading to the creation of regional local service companies known as 'Baby Bells'.
New telecommunications rules signed into law in February aim to increase competition for local and long-distance service and reduce prices.
Long-distance companies argue that access fees are excessive and support significant government-mandated cuts.
AT&T recommended that the FCC quickly eliminate $10 billion in excess access fees to benefit consumers.
Local phone companies acknowledge that access fees exceed their actual costs for carrying long-distance calls but prefer gradual reductions based on competition.
Roy Neel, president of the U.S. Telephone Association, stated that the FCC should prevent long-distance companies from benefiting at consumers' expense.
Local phone companies connect Internet users to Internet service providers over local lines without receiving access charges for those calls.

Philip Karn is a computer scientist who was barred from exporting a floppy disk containing computer encryption programming.
Karn asked a federal court to strike down the export limits, claiming they violate his right to free speech.
The State Department denied Karn's request to export the programming on disk in 1994 but allowed him to export the same material in a book.
U.S. law categorizes many types of encryption and computer coding programs as munitions.
The Clinton administration issued new rules that relaxed some export limits, but many encryption programs remain classified as munitions.
Karn's attorney, Kenneth Bass, argued that the export limits infringe on Karn's constitutional rights to free speech and due process.
Bass claimed that the First Amendment should apply equally to computer code in a book and on a floppy disk.
Karn's disk contained 'source' code, which provides directions to write software, rather than 'object' code, which is a working program.
Federal district court Judge Marilyn Patel ruled that source code should be considered a protected form of speech.
The ruling by Judge Patel is not binding on the D.C. Appeals court.

Prospects for comprehensive reform of U.S. banking and financial services laws are considered bright.
The Clinton Administration is considering a far-reaching proposal that has upset some banks.
There is a general agreement that the Glass-Steagall Act should be scrapped.
There is little consensus about removing barriers between financial firms and other commercial companies.
The Clinton Administration is actively considering reform proposals expected in the next two months.
Larry LaRocco, a former Congressman and bank lobbyist, stated that there is a strong desire for Glass-Steagall reform.
LaRocco believes that legislators have sufficient time to reach an agreement within the 105th Congress.
Federal courts and regulators have lifted many restrictions on banks' non-banking activities.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is considering recommendations to remove barriers between financial and non-financial companies.
The commerce issue is the last remaining obstacle in the reform process according to a source familiar with the administration's deliberations.

An influential global research group is preparing guidelines on encryption policy for its member countries.
The guidelines will avoid some contentious issues according to a draft report obtained by Reuters.
The Clinton administration sought support for its encryption export policy in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development guidelines but did not receive an endorsement.
The draft guidelines do not take a position on a U.S. policy requirement for data-scrambling encryption programs to provide law enforcement access to keys.
The draft states that governments should weigh the costs and benefits of key recovery without implying that they should or should not legislate for lawful access.
John Dryden, head of the OECD's Information, Computer and Communications Policy division, stated that member countries have differing views on controversial issues.
Some countries view encryption as a means to protect privacy and encourage global commerce, while others see it as a potential obstacle to law enforcement.
The guidelines suggest that encryption users should have access to cryptography that meets their needs and that government controls should be minimal.
The draft guidelines outline competing interests and do not aim to create a model national law.
The guidelines recommend that encryption standards and usage be determined by the market in an open and competitive environment.

Internet access providers and others expressed concerns about potential negative impacts of Congress on cyberspace.
Company representatives met with members of the Congressional Internet Caucus to discuss legislation related to the Internet.
Tom Evslin, vice president of AT&T Corp.'s WorldNet Internet service, stated that it is likely there will be bills introduced to legislate Internet content.
Evslin expressed that preventing Congress from making mistakes regarding Internet legislation would be challenging.
Bill Schrader, president of Internet provider PSINet Inc., warned that careless legislation could harm the Internet industry.
Members of Congress at the meeting committed to protecting the Internet.
Rep. Rick White, R-Pa., acknowledged the challenges ahead in addressing various Internet-related issues.
Sen. Conrad Burns noted that government legislation often lags behind private sector developments.
Last year, Congress passed the Communications Decency Act, which faced opposition from online companies and civil libertarians.
Congress also rejected measures that would have held Internet providers liable for copyright infringement.

A dispute has arisen between the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the state of Rhode Island regarding insurance laws.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is considering overriding a new Rhode Island insurance law.
The Rhode Island insurance law imposes different requirements on banks selling insurance compared to those on insurance agents.
National banks have the legal right to sell insurance in small towns.
State insurance regulators have historically imposed strict rules on banks selling insurance.
The Supreme Court ruled last year that states cannot significantly interfere with national banks conducting permissible activities.
Banks claim that states are attempting to evade the Supreme Court's ruling.
James McIntyre, counsel to the Association of Banks-in-Insurance, stated that the Rhode Island statute is the first successful restrictive legislation effort.
Major states such as Texas, Pennsylvania, and Illinois are expected to consider similar legislation.
The Independent Insurance Agents of America stated that preempting the Rhode Island law would be inappropriate.

Legislators introduced two bills to overturn the Clinton administration's export limits on computer encryption technology.
Encryption products scramble information and render it unreadable without a password or software key.
Encryption is used for various purposes, including keeping business emails confidential and protecting consumers' credit card numbers online.
Senators claimed that export restrictions on encryption products hindered the development of the Internet and U.S. companies' competitiveness.
The bills aim to roll back restrictions on the export of strong cryptography to allow U.S. firms to compete globally.
Sen. Pat Leahy stated that online commerce would not reach its full potential under current policies.
The bills would allow U.S. companies to export products with strong encryption if similar products are available from foreign suppliers.
Under current policy, companies can only export strong encryption if it includes a feature for the U.S. government to recover the software key.
The Clinton administration argues that it needs to crack codes to catch international criminals and terrorists.
If the bills became law, mandatory key recovery would be banned, but the government could still restrict encryption exports for military use or to certain countries.

The Czech Republic and Spain played to a scoreless draw in a World Cup group six qualifier.
The match was described as lacklustre and did not meet expectations.
The Czech Republic faced their first significant test since reaching the Euro 96 final.
Raul Gonzalez made his debut for Spain in the match.
Both teams had previously won their World Cup openers against weaker opponents.
Spain won 6-2 against the Faroe Islands, and the Czech Republic won 6-0 against Malta.
Yugoslavia and Slovakia had already secured wins against the same teams.
Both teams started the match tentatively, looking for mistakes from the opponent.
Karel Poborsky missed a scoring chance for the Czech Republic.
Pavel Srnicek, the Czech goalkeeper, made a mistake that nearly led to a goal.

Goran Ivanisevic won against Adrian Voinea with a score of 7-6 6-4 in the first round of the Czech Indoor Open.
Tim Henman defeated Nicklas Kulti with a score of 7-6 6-4 on the opening day of the tournament.
Both Ivanisevic and Henman utilized the fast carpet court to achieve multiple service winners.
Ivanisevic is ranked fifth in the world and Voinea is ranked 42nd.
Ivanisevic hit 14 aces during his match.
Ivanisevic stated that the carpet at the current venue is faster than the one used in Vienna.
Ivanisevic mentioned that winning the tournament would require defeating at least one top 10 player.
Ivanisevic is scheduled to play the winner of the match between Petr Korda and Nicolas Lapentti.
Ivanisevic may also need to compete against Boris Becker and Bohdan Ulihrach to reach the final.
Henman expressed that he felt he should have won the first set before the tiebreak.

Boris Becker withdrew from the $475,000 Czech Indoor Open due to a recurring wrist injury.
Becker tore a ligament in his right wrist during the third round at this year's Wimbledon.
Becker experienced pain after training and withdrew from his scheduled second round match against Martin Damm.
ATP Tour Supervisor Gayle Bradshaw stated that Becker's wrist was too sore for him to play.
Becker won his previous match against Frederik Fetterlein with a score of 6-3 6-4.
During the match against Fetterlein, Becker held his wrist several times.
Becker attempted to return to the circuit last month but had to retire from the first round in Bucharest.
Becker also lost in the second round in Basle and withdrew from Lyon two weeks ago.
Becker's absence has hindered his goal of qualifying for a record 12th appearance at the ATP Tour championship.
Becker currently trails Wayne Ferreira for the eighth and final spot in Hannover.

Tim Henman is the only seed to advance to the semifinals of the $475,000 Czech Indoor Open.
Tim Henman defeated Wayne Ferreira with a score of 6-4 6-3.
David Prinosil defeated Todd Martin with a score of 7-6 7-6.
Martin Damm defeated Michael Stich with a score of 5-7 6-4 6-4.
Petr Korda defeated Jiri Novak with a score of 6-1 6-0.
Tim Henman will compete against David Prinosil in the semifinals.
Petr Korda will compete against Martin Damm in the semifinals.
Wayne Ferreira is ranked seventh in the world.
Tim Henman is ranked 26th in the world.
Todd Martin is currently 199 points behind Wayne Ferreira in the race for the final spot at the ATP Tour championship.

The Prague Stock Exchange closed higher for the third consecutive session on Tuesday.
The PX50 index increased by 2.5 points, or 0.47 percent, to 537.1.
Komercni Banka, IPB, Ceska Sporitelna, and Zivnostenska Banka all gained ground.
The Reuters RPIX index climbed five points to 1,095.
A total of 188 shares rose, 121 shares lost, and 74 shares held steady.
The total volume was 701,356 shares with a turnover of 721.14 million crowns.
IPB rose 15 crowns to 331, marking its second consecutive five percent gain.
The government announced that IPB would be the first of the big four banks to undergo privatization.
Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik indicated that a strong foreign strategic partner would likely benefit from the sell-off.
Nomura and ING Bank have been rumored as frontrunners in the bid for IPB.

The Czech trade deficit fell to 10.5 billion crowns in September from 14.5 billion in August.
Analysts stated that the fall in the trade deficit buoyed market sentiment.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) reported that the January-September trade shortfall reached an all-time high of 110.7 billion crowns.
The January-September trade shortfall surpassed the full 1995 deficit of 95.7 billion crowns.
The September trade shortfall was the smallest one-month deficit of the year.
Analysts had forecasted an average trade gap of 13 to 15 billion crowns for September.
Martin Kupka, an economist at Patria Finance, expressed optimism about the September figure but did not revise the full year forecast.
Patria Finance forecasted a year-end deficit of 150-160 billion crowns.
The CSU reported that September imports rose 15.2 percent year-on-year, while exports rose 5.9 percent.
Strong growth in machinery and transport equipment imports accounted for 38.3 percent of total imports.

Czech telephone operator SPT Telecom a.s. reported a nine-month gross profit of 6.0 billion crowns.
SPT Telecom's gross profit for all of 1995 was 7.0 billion crowns.
SPT Telecom used International Accounting Standards in calculating its profit.
The company's revenues totaled 23.3 billion crowns, nearly equal to the 26.4 billion crowns for 1995.
SPT Telecom's outlays for investment in the nine-month period exceeded 20 billion crowns.
A Dutch-Swiss consortium of PTT Netherlands and Swiss Telecom bought a 27 percent stake in SPT from the government.
The consortium paid $1.32 billion for its stake in SPT Telecom.
SPT Telecom installed 272,000 new telephone lines year-to-date, bringing its total to 2.67 million lines.
SPT Telecom aims to achieve a target of over 400,000 new set lines in 1996.
SPT Telecom plans to increase its network by another 500,000 lines in 1997 and 650,000 lines in 1998.

Sepap Group a.s. reported a nine-month net profit of 188.4 million crowns, down from 520.4 million crowns in the same period in 1995.
The company's revenues decreased to 3.94 billion crowns from 5.34 billion crowns over the same nine-month period.
The shutdown of Sepap's main paper mill contributed to the decline in net profit.
The Steti mill accounts for approximately 75% of Sepap's revenues and profits.
The Steti mill's pre-tax profits fell to seven million crowns, compared to a gross profit of 95 million crowns in the same nine-month period in 1995.
Sepap's third quarter results stabilized after a downturn in the first half of the year.
The company anticipates a slight improvement in year-end earnings compared to third quarter levels.
ROTO, Sepap's second largest subsidiary, reported a nine-month pre-tax profit of 149 million crowns on sales of 1.25 billion crowns.
Michael Dingman controls 48% of Sepap through Daventree Ltd, while Assidoman holds a 39% stake in the company.
The market for pulp and paper is experiencing mixed signals for the fourth quarter.

The Czech capital market has been criticized for a lack of transparency.
An independent regulator is needed for the Czech capital market, according to a senior Finance Ministry official.
Jan Veverka stated that the creation of an independent securities committee will not immediately improve the Czech capital market.
Veverka mentioned that the independent body would create better conditions for gradual market refinement.
Foreign and domestic investors have complained about poor legislation and lack of enforcement in the Czech capital market.
The Prague Stock Exchange has declined by approximately 16 percent over the past two months due to a negative outlook from investors.
Legislation allows for near complete secrecy of off-market deals, where an estimated 70 percent of trading occurs.
Veverka noted that the original laws governing securities trading discarded the concept of regulation due to fears of abuse of power.
The mass voucher privatization resulted in shares from nearly 2,000 firms being placed on the market in a short period.
Veverka called for a higher level debate on creating a U.S.-style SEC oversight body.

The Civic Democratic Party (ODS) led in the Senate election run-offs in the Czech Republic.
Turnout for the Senate elections was 30.5 percent.
The ODS won 19 seats in the new upper house.
The opposition Social Democrats won eight seats.
The Christian Democrats won seven seats.
The Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) won two seats.
President Vaclav Havel appealed for greater voter turnout before the elections.
The Senate elections were considered important for the future of Klaus's coalition.
Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik predicted that government parties would control the Senate.
Klaus has expressed skepticism about the necessity of the Senate.

Czech share prices increased after the coalition government's victory in the Senate elections.
Analysts believe the rise in share prices is primarily due to a technical correction.
The Prague Stock Exchange's PX50 index rose 0.86 percent during the daily price fixing.
The increase was driven by gains in seven of the eight most-capitalised shares.
Brokers expressed limited optimism that the rally would continue beyond a few days.
The coalition government led by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus won 52 of 81 seats in the Senate.
The centre-left opposition Social Democrats secured 25 seats in the Senate.
Voter turnout for the Senate elections was just over 30 percent.
The Prague bourse has declined approximately 17 percent since September.
Analysts do not expect the Senate elections to lead to changes in securities laws.

The Czech trade deficit increased by nearly 16 billion crowns ($600 million) in October.
Analysts were not alarmed by the rise in the trade deficit as it aligned with their full year forecasts.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) reported that the trade gap for the first 10 months of the year reached a record 125.5 billion crowns.
The trade deficit for January-September was revised to 109.6 billion crowns.
The CSU, the Ministry of Industry and Trade, and some analysts predict the year-end deficit will be between 150-160 billion crowns.
Kamil Janacek, chief economist at Komercni Banka, stated that the year-end deficit will be 150-160 billion crowns.
Janacek noted that the economic revival of Germany will impact export growth in the first half of next year.
The CSU reported that imports rose by 14.4 percent year-on-year in the first ten months of the year.
Exports increased by 5.2 percent year-on-year after a 5.9 percent increase in January-September.
Imports of machinery and transport equipment grew by 19.1 percent year-on-year, making up 38.3 percent of total imports.

Liberty International Holdings is entering the British pensions market.
Liberty is establishing a pensions company called Liberty International Pensions.
Liberty International Pensions will target money purchase pension schemes and retail pensions.
BT Pension Scheme is paying five million pounds for 10 percent equity in Liberty International Pensions.
The remaining equity in Liberty International Pensions will be held by Liberty.
Liberty and Hermes are creating a subsidiary called Hermes Liberty International Pensions.
Hermes will act as the fund manager for Hermes Liberty International Pensions.
BT Pension Scheme will transfer 1.5 billion pounds in assets to the new funds.
Liberty's chairman Donald Gordon stated that Liberty is well positioned for changes in the UK pensions industry.
Liberty International Pensions requires approval from Britain's Department of Trade and Industry before launch.

Britain's largest cable television company was formed from the merger of Cable & Wireless, NYNEX Corp., and Bell Canada International.
The merger took five weeks to complete.
The new company surpasses Telewest as Britain's biggest cable operator.
Richard Brown is the Chief Executive of Cable & Wireless and was appointed five months prior to the merger.
C&W replaced British Telecommunications Plc in a major German alliance with RWE.
The merged company will provide integrated telecommunications, information, and entertainment services.
C&W's Mercury telephone company will have access to 18 million business and domestic customers.
30 percent of homes that can take cable have opted for one or more cable services.
Around 6 billion pounds has been invested in building the broadband fibre optic network in the U.K.
Videotron is being acquired by Bell Cablemedia in a transaction involving a $338 million equity investment from Cable & Wireless.

Halifax Building Society plans to shed its mutual status and become a publicly quoted bank in June next year.
David Gilchrist is the director of corporate affairs at Halifax.
Halifax's nine million members will vote on the conversion early next year.
