Chinese officials argue that Beijing should be allowed to join the WTO on lenient terms as a developing country.
Chinese officials have blamed the United States for blocking their accession to the WTO with tough demands for more open markets.
Chen Jinhua, chairman of the State Planning Commission, stated that China is committed to establishing a trade system in line with international practice.
China has reduced import tariffs to an average of 23 percent from 36 percent this year.
Beijing plans to continue opening its markets to foreign trade and investment.
Li Tieying warned that if the United States revokes China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) status, U.S. consumers would spend $14 billion more annually.
Disagreements over the terms of Beijing's admission to the WTO are part of ongoing disputes affecting Sino-U.S. trade relations.

China's demand for computer chips is expected to drive growth in its semiconductor industry.
Beijing aims to increase the output of advanced integrated circuits (ICs).
Import tariffs and U.S. technology export restrictions complicate access to essential equipment.
Yu Zhongyu, chief engineer of the Ministry of Electronics Industry, stated that the industry has grown rapidly in recent years.
Yu predicted that the semiconductor industry will grow even faster in the next five years.
Chip production is identified as the top priority of China's electronics industry.
Demand for ICs is driven by China's increasing need for consumer electronics and telecommunications.
China's IC output value rose to $550 million in 1995, while production was only one-fifth of demand.
China is projected to produce 700 million chips annually by the year 2000.
The value of equipment imports for chip production is expected to increase to about $700 million in 1997.

Motorola Inc is appealing to Chinese authorities over taxes on capital imports for a semiconductor plant in Tianjin.
The semiconductor plant is being built in the Xiqing district of Tianjin and has an investment of $500 million.
Construction of the plant is on schedule, with production expected to begin in the first quarter of 1998.
Motorola is appealing to China's State Council for tax exemptions on imports of vital equipment for the semiconductor plant.
Beijing abolished tax privileges for foreign-funded ventures on April 1, increasing project costs.
An official from the State Council's information office was unaware of Motorola's appeal regarding import taxes.
Work on the Xiqing project has already begun, with buildings currently being erected.
The initial investment in the Xiqing plant is expected to be around $500 million, but costs could rise to $1.0 billion.
The Xiqing plant is expected to produce 180,000 eight-inch sub-micron wafers annually.
Motorola plans to invest $1.2 billion in China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong between 1988 and 2000.

Gyaincain Norbu is the child chosen by China to be Tibet's second holiest monk.
Norbu passed the first anniversary of his selection quietly in Beijing.
Officials in Tibet concluded a six-month campaign to curb separatist sentiment in monasteries.
The campaign reportedly led to the expulsion or detention of scores of monks.
Norbu did not attend any activities on the first anniversary of his selection.
State media reported that Norbu visited Beijing's Yonghe Lamasery to celebrate his enthronement anniversary.
The exiled Dalai Lama has named another boy as the reincarnation of the 10th Panchen Lama.
Chinese sources stated that Norbu lives in Beijing under state protection.
The Tibet Information Network reported that at least 150 monks were expelled and possibly 20 arrested during the campaign.
Some monks were expelled for refusing to criticize the Dalai Lama.

AT&T Corp. Chairman Robert Allen is likely to step down early to help attract a successor.
Sources close to AT&T indicated that the successor to Alex Mandl would expect to succeed Allen before the end of his contract.
Alex Mandl resigned as AT&T president and chief operating officer in August.
AT&T would not comment on the search for Mandl's successor or whether the candidate would succeed Allen.
Analysts suggested that Allen might split the role of chief executive from his chairmanship.
Mark Bruneau from COBA MID stated that AT&T would likely want Allen to remain in a senior position for some time.
An ambitious candidate would want to make an early impact on AT&T's strategic direction.
Sources mentioned that some candidates have ruled themselves out of consideration for the position.
William Esrey from Sprint Corp. stated he was unaware of being a candidate for the AT&T job.
Michael Armstrong from Hughes Electronics Corp. also stated he was unaware of being an AT&T candidate.

Ameritech Corp. and Sprint Corp. are the two largest telecommunications companies in the Midwest.
Both companies reported double-digit profit increases in the third quarter of 1996.
Sprint's net income rose 16 percent to $312.4 million from $268.5 million in the same quarter of 1995.
Sprint's revenues grew 10.6 percent to $3.54 billion from $3.21 billion.
Sprint's earnings per share fell to 72 cents from 76 cents due to a 20 percent stake taken by France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom.
Ameritech's net income for the three months ended September 30 was $519 million, or 94 cents a share, up from $512 million, or 92 cents a share.
Ameritech's revenues rose 10 percent to $3.7 billion from $3.4 billion.
Sprint's Chief Financial Officer Arthur Krause expects double-digit volume and revenue growth in the fourth quarter.
Analysts noted Sprint's strong performance in long-distance service compared to AT&T Corp.
Sprint owns 40 percent of Sprint PCS, a wireless Personal Communications Services network.

AT&T Corp. will announce a successor to Robert Allen as chairman and chief executive.
The successor will not be one of the candidates mentioned in the press.
Michael Armstrong and William Esrey are not in contention for the position.
The true candidate has not been identified by sources close to the company.
AT&T's board met to review candidates for the post of president and chief operating officer.
An announcement regarding the new candidate is expected in the next few days.
AT&T will report its third-quarter results on Thursday.
The position became vacant after Alex Mandl resigned in August.
Bob Allen may retain his chairmanship while splitting the role of chief executive with the new candidate.
AT&T is looking for a world-class marketer and technologist with significant experience.

MCI Communications Corp is using data warehousing to target key customers in the consumer long distance telephone market.
MCI Chief Financial Officer Doug Maine stated that these customers are seeking advanced services in a package.
Maine mentioned that developing customer profiles for targeted marketing has cost tens of millions of dollars and taken many years.
Data warehousing requires powerful computers to create user profiles from individual spending decisions.
Salespeople at MCI use customer profiles to sell new services to existing customers and target potential customers from rival companies.
Churn refers to the tendency of customers to switch providers, which results in wasted marketing and administrative expenses.
MCI's third quarter results indicated benefits in the business and data markets, which account for two-thirds of its total revenues.
MCI reported that churn was higher than a year ago in the consumer market but lower than in the second quarter.
MCI has reduced its promotional spending for customer sign-ons by 70 percent compared to the previous year.
MCI One is a service package that does not offer a sign-on bonus, but half of new users opt for the Internet service.

AT&T Corp announced that John Walter will take over as chief executive from Robert Allen after a 14-month transition period.
Hal Burlingame, AT&T senior vice president for human resources, stated that the decision for the transition period made sense to both Bob Allen and John Walter.
Walter was appointed as AT&T's new president and chief operating officer effective November 1, following board approval.
Walter is currently the chairman and chief executive of R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co.
Walter will officially become chief executive of AT&T in January 1998 and will become chairman in May 1998 at the annual shareholder meeting.
During the transition period, Walter and Allen will work closely together on business issues.
Analysts had anticipated a quicker transition to a new chief executive, which contributed to a decline in AT&T's stock price.
AT&T's stock was reported down 1-7/8 at 38 during heavy trading volume.
Burlingame did not disclose Walter's compensation details but indicated it would align with the interests of AT&T shareholders.
Walter's compensation at R.R. Donnelley in 1995 included a salary of $900,000, a bonus of $555,000, and additional annual compensation of $36,427.

AT&T Corp. elected John Walter as its new president, chief operating officer, and heir apparent to Chairman Robert Allen.
John Walter was unanimously elected to the management posts and as a member of the board, effective Nov. 1.
Robert Allen expressed confidence in John Walter's leadership qualities for AT&T's success in the communications market.
Industry analysts were surprised by AT&T's choice of a less-known executive for the position.
Concerns were raised about the 18-month handover period not leading to a quick enough change in strategy.
AT&T stock fell $2 to $37.75 on the New York Stock Exchange following the announcement.
Adjusted for the split off of Lucent Technologies Inc., AT&T shares have fallen 16 percent this year.
The president and COO positions were vacant after Alex Mandl resigned in August.
AT&T's board considered multiple candidates but focused on Walter due to his track record at R.R. Donnelley.
Starting in January 1998, John Walter and Robert Allen will split the duties of chairman and chief executive.

Lucent Technologies Inc is experiencing increased orders from regional Bells customers after separating from AT&T Corp.
Lucent's final fiscal 1996 quarter reported a 42.4 percent year-on-year increase in network system sales, totaling $3.2 billion.
Don Peterson, Lucent's chief financial officer, stated that there is fundamental demand supporting the company's growth.
AT&T's divestment of Lucent was partly due to a loss of orders from the Bells, who viewed AT&T as a competitor.
Lucent changed its fiscal year end from December 31 to September 30, resulting in only three quarters for the current year.
Overall revenues for Lucent increased by 24.7 percent to $5.9 billion in the final quarter compared to the previous year.
Peterson expects the next quarter to be good but cautioned that it will be compared to a record fourth quarter in 1995.
Lucent has hired 5,000 new factory workers while planning to cut a total of 12,600 jobs from its workforce by 1998.
Net job cuts at Lucent amount to about 7,000 after accounting for new hires.
Lucent is preparing to launch new products in 1997, including a long-range cordless phone and advanced answering machines.

MCI Communications Corp. is the No. 2 long distance phone company.
MCI Communications Corp. is in talks to be acquired by British Telecommunications Plc.
The potential merger between MCI and British Telecommunications Plc could be one of the biggest ever.
British Telecommunications Plc holds a 20 percent stake in MCI.
Analysts speculate that the acquisition price could be $40 a share, valuing MCI at $28 billion.
British Telecommunications Plc would need to pay $22.1 billion for the 80 percent of MCI it does not already own.
MCI expects the talks to conclude over the weekend, but there are no guarantees of an agreement.
Analysts believe a merger would be beneficial in the competitive U.S. long distance phone industry.
A merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI would be the largest between a British and American company.
British Telecommunications Plc plans to offer a mixture of cash and stock for the remaining 80 percent of MCI.

A $22 billion merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp is nearing agreement.
This merger would be the largest international business combination in record time.
A London news conference is scheduled for 8 a.m. EST (1300 GMT) on Sunday.
MCI will hold a news conference in New York at 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT).
Consultant Jeffrey Kagan stated that the deal sounds like a done deal.
BT executives are expected to announce a $40 per share stock and cash offer for MCI.
The offer values the 80 percent of MCI that BT does not own at $22.1 billion.
The total valuation of MCI would be $28 billion.
If BT uses mainly stock for the merger, MCI shareholders could own up to 37 percent of the combined company.
The combined BT/MCI would have revenues of $38 billion, 182,000 employees, and a market value of $64 billion.

British Telecom and MCI Communications announced an agreement for British Telecom to acquire the rest of MCI for more than $20 billion.
The merged company will be called Concert Plc and will be the world's second-largest telecommunications group.
The deal values all of MCI at a total of $25.2 billion.
British Telecom already owned 20 percent of MCI and will issue Concert stock and cash worth $20.1 billion for the remaining 80 percent.
This deal is the largest between a British and American company.
Sir Iain Vallance, chairman of British Telecommunications Plc, expressed confidence in the merger's success.
Industry analysts believe the combined company will be a good fit in the U.S. long-distance phone industry.
AT&T stated it was confident that any MCI/British Telecom deal would receive proper scrutiny by the U.S. government.
MCI Chief Executive Bert Roberts expressed confidence that the merger would win federal approval.
Concert Plc would have 43 million business and residential customers in 70 countries.

The merger of MCI Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc is expected to lead to more mega-mergers among U.S. carriers.
Analyst Guy Woodlief of Dean Witter Reynolds stated that there have been four deals over $10 billion since April and more are anticipated.
Regional Bells, GTE Corp, AT&T Corp, and Sprint Corp will need to reassess their market strategies due to the merger activity.
Analysts claim that there are valuable assets, such as nationwide networks, held by carriers lacking sufficient funds.
David Goodtree, an analyst at Forrester Research, indicated that WorldCom Inc is still available for acquisition.
WorldCom is in the process of acquiring MFS Communications Co for $13.3 billion.
MFS Communications Co had recently completed its acquisition of UUNet before the WorldCom deal was announced.
Goodtree suggested that GTE or Bell Atlantic Corp could acquire WorldCom, but Cable and Wireless Plc is also a potential buyer.
GTE was rumored to be a bidder for MCI, while Bell Atlantic and NYNEX Corp merged in April.
GTE is currently offering long distance calling, while Bell Atlantic and NYNEX plan to do so after legal issues are resolved.

The wireless revolution is beginning in multiple cities across the United States.
New digital mobile phones provide clear connections, improved battery life, and fewer dropped calls.
Consumers will experience lower prices, more choices, and new features like voice mail and paging.
Wireless companies are facing increased competition to attract and retain customers.
David Roddy, chief telecommunications economist of Deloitte and Touche Consulting, stated that wireless services will become cheaper.
PrimeCo will announce its new digital Personal Communications Services in a dozen cities, reaching 32 million people.
PrimeCo will launch services in cities including Chicago, Richmond, Norfolk, Houston, Dallas/Fort Worth, San Antonio, Austin, New Orleans, and throughout Florida.
Omnipoint Corp. will announce its PCS service in metropolitan New York, competing with AT&T Corp., Bell Atlantic Corp., and NYNEX Corp.
Omnipoint plans to cover large areas in the Northeast, serving 40 million people.
PCS systems use licenses auctioned by the Federal Communications Commission in 1995.

McDonald's Corp has created a new post of chairman for its domestic business.
The company aims to address problems in the U.S. market.
Analyst Damon Brundage stated that McDonald's recognizes its problems in the U.S.
Analysts report declining same store sales in the U.S. market.
McDonald's is expected to see a decline in third-quarter same store sales compared to the previous year.
McDonald's has not had a positive month in the U.S. this year.
McDonald's does not disclose same store sales data.
Analyst Wayne Daniels noted that margins have been under pressure in the U.S. for over a year.
Jack Greenberg has been named chairman of McDonald's U.S.A.
Edward Rensi, president of McDonald's U.S.A, will report to Greenberg.

Archer Daniels Midland Co. agreed to plead guilty to two counts of federal charges of price fixing in the sale of agricultural products.
ADM will pay record fines totaling $100 million, subject to court approval.
The fines include $70 million for fixing prices for lysine and $30 million for citric acid.
The $100 million in fines is the largest ever in a criminal antitrust action.
The fines will have a minimal financial impact on ADM.
ADM has about $1.3 billion in cash and short-term securities and $1.1 billion in long-term securities.
The fate of two top ADM executives, Michael Andreas and Terrance Wilson, remains unclear regarding possible indictments.
The Justice Department's antitrust investigation into ADM is ongoing.
ADM's statement did not mention the two executives involved in the investigation.
ADM previously settled civil cases for $25 million in the lysine case and $35 million for citric acid.

Archer Daniels Midland Co pleaded guilty to price fixing.
Archer Daniels Midland Co will face criticism from shareholders at its annual meeting.
Edward Durkin is the director of special programs at the United Brotherhood of Carpenters.
The United Brotherhood of Carpenters is one of four institutional shareholders seeking changes in ADM's board.
Jon Lukomnik is the New York City deputy controller for pensions.
Jon Lukomnik stated that corporate governance issues remain at ADM despite the settlement with the U.S. Justice Department.
Archer Daniels Midland Co agreed to pay $100 million in fines as part of the settlement.
Lukomnik is looking for ADM to enact steps to make its board more independent.
Chairman Dwayne Andreas is 78 years old.
Michael Andreas, Vice Chairman of ADM, is under investigation by the Justice Department.

At Archer Daniels Midland Co.'s annual meeting last year, Chairman Dwayne Andreas did not allow shareholders to speak.
This year, shareholders are advocating for different rules at the annual meeting.
Four institutional shareholders will present proposals related to corporate governance at the meeting.
Archer Daniels Midland Co. pleaded guilty to two counts of price fixing and agreed to pay $100 million in fines.
The $100 million fine is the highest penalty ever for violating antitrust laws in the United States.
The company admitted to fixing prices for lysine and citric acid.
A proposal at this year's meeting calls for a majority of independent directors on ADM's board.
A survey indicated that about 47 percent of early votes were in favor of the independent directors proposal.
The California Public Employees Retirement System co-sponsored the independent directors proposal with the Florida Retirement System Trust Fund.
Concerns about the independence of ADM's board have been raised since a federal price-fixing investigation was disclosed in June 1995.

Quaker Oats Co. reported that its profits more than doubled in the latest quarter.
The increase in profits occurred despite a drop in sales due to lower prices for breakfast cereals and heavy spending on Snapple.
Quaker Oats purchased Snapple nearly two years ago for $1.7 billion.
The company's stock fell by $1.75 to $34.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analyst William Leach stated that the stock decline was due to the lack of announced restructuring for Snapple.
Quaker Oats reported a net income of $133 million, or 98 cents a share, for the third quarter.
This net income was an increase from $61.5 million, or 45 cents per share, from the previous year.
The latest quarter's results included a $133.6 million pretax gain from the sale of its frozen foods business and $23 million in pretax restructuring charges.
Excluding these factors, Quaker's third quarter net income was 53 cents a share, exceeding Wall Street estimates of 46 cents a share.
Chairman William Smithburg indicated that Snapple is expected to report an operating loss for 1996.

Kellogg Co is launching promotional programs to boost its sales due to declining U.S. cereal volumes.
Kellogg spokesman Richard Lovell stated that the company will take appropriate actions but did not specify the programs.
Analysts do not expect Kellogg to return to deep-discount coupons or buy-one, get-one-free promotions.
SBC Warburg analyst Chris Jakubik noted that it is uncertain what Kellogg will do next.
BT Securities analyst John O'Neil mentioned that there is no indication Kellogg has shifted from its goal to reduce inefficient promotions.
Kellogg plans to launch marketing actions in the current fourth quarter.
Kellogg cut cereal prices earlier this year to attract consumers back to the cereal aisle.
Smith Barney analyst David Rabinowitz stated that price cuts alone were not enough to increase consumer purchases.
Kellogg's third quarter operating earnings declined to $0.85 a share, down from $1.05 last year.
Kellogg's U.S. cereal sales volume declined by an estimated nine to 10 percent in the third quarter.

Kellogg Co. pledged to halt the erosion of its share of the U.S. cereal market.
Kellogg did not specify the steps it plans to take to stop market share erosion.
Kellogg's stock fell by 75 cents to $67 during afternoon trading.
Kellogg's market share has dropped to between 32.5 and 33 percent from a normal level of 35 percent.
Kellogg is the leader in the U.S. ready-to-eat cereal market.
Kellogg's spokesman stated the company will not tolerate further market share erosion.
Kellogg's long-term strategy includes lower cereal prices and reducing inefficient price promotion spending.
Analysts believe Kellogg hopes competitors will cut back on promotions to relieve pressure on its market share.
If competitors do not cut back on promotions, Kellogg will have to respond accordingly.
Kellogg's primary goal for 1997 is to increase volume in its U.S. cereal business.

Monsanto Co produces genetically altered soybeans.
Karen Marshall is the manager of public affairs for Monsanto.
Monsanto conducted approximately 1,800 tests to evaluate the safety of its soybeans.
Monsanto claims that its genetically altered soybeans are absolutely safe.
Greenpeace protests against genetically altered soybeans and criticizes Monsanto for not testing the crop for exposure to the herbicide Roundup.
Monsanto's Roundup Ready soybeans are resistant to the Roundup herbicide.
Farmers can spray Roundup on fields to kill weeds without harming Roundup Ready soybeans.
Roundup residue could be present on harvested soybeans.
Monsanto states that tolerance levels for Roundup herbicide have been established and do not require further testing.
Monsanto's testing focused on the genetic alteration of the soybeans.

McDonnell Douglas Corp's stock is near its 52-week high.
The company has a strong balance sheet and is expected to make an acquisition.
McDonnell Douglas generates approximately $1.0 billion to $1.25 billion of free cash flow annually.
This free cash flow translates into between $5 and $7 per share.
BT Securities analyst Wolfgang Demisch has a buy rating on McDonnell Douglas stock.
McDonnell Douglas lost out on a contract to build a next generation fighter for the Pentagon.
Boeing Co was awarded a 103-plane deal from AMR Corp.
McDonnell Douglas shares were down $0.25 at $52.625 on Monday.
The shares are $4.125 below a 52-week high of $56.75 and more than $10 above a low of $42.125.
Losing out on $2.2 billion in jet fighter contracts could lead McDonnell Douglas to pursue acquisitions.

Monsanto Co's board of directors is scheduled to meet on Friday.
Monsanto has expressed a desire to shed its chemical business.
A Monsanto spokeswoman confirmed the board meeting but did not comment on potential decisions.
Monsanto is considering several options for its non-agricultural chemical business, including a possible spinoff.
The remaining Monsanto company would focus on life sciences, including agricultural chemicals and pharmaceuticals.
Analysts suggest that selling or merging the chemical business is another option for Monsanto.
PaineWebber analyst Paul Raman indicated that a spinoff is likely due to significant tax liabilities associated with selling the chemical business.
Hercules Inc has been mentioned as a potential suitor for Monsanto's chemical business.
Hercules and Mallinckrodt Inc are seeking a buyer for the Tastemaker food and beverage flavors business.
A Mallinckrodt spokeswoman stated that no offers had been received for Tastemaker and no agreements had been signed.

Quaker Oats Co. is considering selling its Snapple beverage business.
Analysts suggest that Quaker may also sell its Gatorade sports drink line.
John McMillin, an analyst at Prudential Securities, believes Quaker's beverage division is up for sale.
Snapple has incurred operating losses since Quaker purchased it for $1.8 billion two years ago.
Quaker's stock price increased by $1.50 to $37.50 following speculation about the sale.
Michael Mauboussin, an analyst at CS First Boston, stated that Quaker is likely to pursue a restructuring.
Mauboussin indicated that some of Quaker's assets are currently undervalued.
Rumors about a potential sale of Quaker or parts of its business have circulated for about three years.
Quaker has a policy of not commenting on rumors and speculation, according to spokesman Ronald Bottrell.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Quaker might sell Gatorade and Snapple for prices between $3 billion and $4 billion.

Fast-food chains are testing new recipes and promotions to attract customers.
McDonald's Corp. has about 12,000 U.S. restaurants and more than 20,000 worldwide.
McDonald's U.S. same-store sales have been shrinking for six consecutive quarters as of the fourth quarter of 1996.
Wendy's International Inc. has seen U.S. same-store sales rise 5 percent to 6 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Wendy's has about 4,425 U.S. restaurants and 4,925 worldwide.
Burger King's U.S. same-store sales rose 2.6 percent for fiscal 1996 ended September 30.
Burger King had 8,696 restaurants worldwide at the end of fiscal 1996, including more than 6,600 in the United States.
Wendy's is testing fresh pita sandwiches containing grilled chicken and salads in 11 U.S. markets.
Analysts expect the pita sandwich to be launched in the United States later in 1997.
In 1996, McDonald's introduced the Arch Deluxe hamburger and new chicken and fish deluxe sandwiches.

Competitive pressures in the U.S. cereal market are expected to affect earnings for Kellogg Co and Ralcorp Holdings Inc.
Kellogg Co is the largest U.S. cereal maker.
Analysts expect Kellogg Co to report flat fourth quarter earnings, with a potential rise of one or two cents.
Ralcorp Holdings Inc is the largest maker of private-label cereals.
Analysts expect Ralcorp Holdings Inc to report lower earnings for its fiscal first quarter.
Earnings for both companies are pressured by price cuts and promotions in the U.S. cereal market.
Kellogg Co has seen a decline in market share due to heavy promotions by General Mills Inc.
General Mills Inc reported an increase in its fiscal second quarter earnings to $1.00 a share from $0.92.
Analysts expect poor pork and beef margins to hurt fourth quarter earnings for meat processor IBP Inc.
Quaker Oats Co is expected to report an operating profit for the fourth quarter compared to a year ago operating loss.

A new high-society magazine called 'The Chinese' will be launched on November 1.
The magazine is aimed at Chinese communities globally and will be published in Chinese.
The editorial operations of 'The Chinese' are based in Hong Kong.
The magazine is owned by Thailand-based M. China International and Manager Media Group.
The chairman of the publishing group is Sondhi Limthongul, who has third generation Chinese ancestry.
The launch circulation target for 'The Chinese' is 56,000 copies.
The magazine targets wealthy ethnic Chinese readers, particularly those aged 28 to 50.
The target audience has an annual personal income of at least US$120,000 or a household income of at least $150,000.
Editorial director Liu Heung Shing is a Pulitzer prize-winning photographer known for his coverage of China, Russia, and India.
John N claims that ethnic Chinese will form a powerful network of entrepreneurs in the next decade.

Hong Kong legislators plan court action and a lobbying mission to Britain to save the territory's elected legislature.
Pro-democracy leader Martin Lee stated that Britain will hand back Hong Kong to China in 238 days.
Beijing is planning to appoint a new provisional legislature to replace the fully elected Legislative Council.
A Chinese-controlled Selection Committee will name the 60 members of the new body at a meeting in Hong Kong next month.
The Selection Committee formed in Beijing is contrary to last year's election results in Hong Kong.
The Selection Committee favors pro-China factions and sidelines democracy groups.
Martin Lee is the leader of the Democratic Party in Hong Kong.
Lee stated that the government has a duty to stop Beijing's provisional legislature from being established.
Lee plans to lobby British officials, including Prime Minister John Major and opposition leader Tony Blair, regarding Hong Kong's future.
Lee has drawn up lawsuits to sue members of the provisional body if it is set up in breach of laws and treaties.

China launched a contest to select Hong Kong's future leader on Friday.
China described the contest as the birth of 'real democracy' in Hong Kong.
Pro-democracy protesters opposed the contest and stormed the voting venue.
Only 400 out of 6.3 million people in Hong Kong are participating in the voting.
The Selection Committee was established under China's close supervision.
Tung Chee-hwa and Ti Liang Yang received more than 50 votes to advance in the contest.
Tung Chee-hwa received 206 votes, leading the contest.
Peter Woo also advanced to the next round, while five other candidates were eliminated.
The run-off for the contest is scheduled for December 11.
Pro-democracy activists clashed with police during the Selection Committee gathering.

Signals from Hong Kong's likely future leader raised concerns in the pro-democracy camp about the Chinese Communist Party's future power.
Tung Chee-hwa, the favorite to become Hong Kong's chief executive, stated he would accept the Communist Party's legalisation after the British colony reverts to China.
Hong Kong will be handed back to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.
Tung Chee-hwa received 51 percent of the votes in the first round of a ballot by the 400-member selection committee organized by China.
China has promised Hong Kong wide-ranging autonomy for 50 years under a policy of 'one country, two systems'.
Emily Lau, a legislator, expressed concerns about the role of the Communist Party in Hong Kong after the handover.
There is speculation that the future Chief Executive will be influenced by a Communist official from Beijing.
Martin Lee, leader of the Democratic Party, stated that the Communist Party is already present in Hong Kong.
Christine Loh, an independent lawmaker, noted that the Communist Party dominates political and governmental institutions in China.
A Hong Kong security authority spokesman stated that the Communist Party is not legally registered in Hong Kong.

Britain and China clashed over the future of Hong Kong on Wednesday.
Britain is introducing a new law on subversion ahead of Hong Kong's return to China in 1997.
The law defines treason, sedition, subversion, and secession.
The draft bill would jail individuals who plot the violent overthrow of the government.
Chinese officials in Hong Kong criticized the new law.
Pro-China politicians believe the law will be replaced after China resumes sovereignty.
Chen Zuo'er stated that Britain should not have acted unilaterally regarding the law.
A spokesman for China's de facto embassy claimed Britain violated its promise to negotiate.
British officials expressed confidence that the bill could pass through the Legislative Council.
Tsang Yok-sing, a pro-Beijing politician, expressed skepticism about the bill's survival after the handover.

China is set to name Hong Kong's first post-colonial governor before the mid-1997 handover.
British and Chinese negotiators will meet for three days to discuss the sovereignty transfer.
Chinese sources indicated that China may respond negatively to a British proposal for a subversion law.
Britain announced a draft bill that would only classify subversion and sedition as crimes if they involved violence.
China's spokesman in Hong Kong, Zhang Junsheng, criticized the British draft bill, stating it would cause disruption and instability.
Pro-China lobby members predicted that the British law would be replaced by legislation more aligned with Chinese standards after the handover.
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord is scheduled to visit Hong Kong and China.
Lord plans to meet with Governor Chris Patten, Deputy Anson Chan, and China's envoy Zhou Nan during his visit.
Critics argue that Lord's meeting with Tung Chee-hwa sends an inappropriate signal from the U.S. regarding the leadership contest.
A Selection Committee of 400 influential Hong Kong individuals questioned Tung and his rivals about their policies.

Britain entered new talks with China on Hong Kong's future on Wednesday.
Britain admitted it could give no consular protection to Hong Kong people holding special British passports after the Chinese flag is hoisted in 1997.
Senior diplomats met to discuss handover details amid disputes over a subversion law and Chinese troop deployments in Hong Kong.
The agenda for the three-day meeting of the Joint Liaison Group (JLG) was confidential.
British chief negotiator Hugh Davies stated that significant effort was needed to address various problems before the handover in 209 days.

Hong Kong is set to become an autonomous region of China at midnight on June 30, ending over 150 years of British colonial rule.
Britain's Senior Trade Commissioner, Francis Cornish, stated that London could not provide consular protection to over 135,000 Hong Kong people holding special British passports.

More than 100 politicians have sought seats on a Beijing-controlled legislature.
112 people had applied to join the provisional legislature before a registration deadline.
33 members of the current Legislative Council (Legco) applied for the provisional legislature.

Beijing is establishing a provisional interim legislature to replace the elected Legco.
The provisional legislature will be selected on December 21.
Hong Kong has a population of 6.3 million people.
There will be two legislatures in Hong Kong for the final six months of British rule.
The number of seats on Legco and the new body is 60.
217 people had requested application forms for the provisional legislature.

Tung Chee-hwa was previously a retiring man who avoided the limelight and kept his political views secret.
Tung Chee-hwa has emerged as Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader and has become a conservative, Chinese patriot.
A 400-member Selection Committee controlled by China selected Tung Chee-hwa as chief executive to govern Hong Kong in mid-1997.
Tung Chee-hwa received 320 of the committee's 400 votes during the selection process.
Eve-of-vote polls indicated that Tung Chee-hwa had 47 percent public support compared to his nearest rival Yang Ti Liang's 29 percent.
Tung Chee-hwa stated he would legalize the Communist Party and condemned the Democratic Party for being anti-China.
Tung Chee-hwa warned foreign countries not to use Hong Kong to subvert China and stated that advocates for Taiwan or Tibet independence could not stay in Hong Kong.
Tung Chee-hwa has called for pro-China patriotism in schools and emphasized executive-led rule and a slower route to democracy.
Tung Chee-hwa has vowed to support Hong Kong's capitalist economy while also addressing social welfare needs.
Many who know Tung Chee-hwa both at home and abroad regard him as having good character.

Two hundred days before its handover to China, Hong Kong appointed Tung Chee-hwa as chief executive-designate.
Hong Kong has a population of 6.3 million people.
Tung Chee-hwa is a former shipping tycoon who resigned from his shipping empire to lead Hong Kong.
Tung Chee-hwa will take over from British Governor Chris Patten at midnight on June 30.
Anson Chan is the head of the current colonial Civil Service and is considered a popular public figure.
A senior official stated that if Tung can keep Anson Chan in her job, it would create a leadership team that satisfies both Britain and the Hong Kong community.
Tung Chee-hwa was selected by a Beijing-vetted electoral college to run the future Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China.
Tung Chee-hwa expressed his hope for a smooth transition and for most senior officials to remain in office.
Anson Chan has indicated her willingness to work for Tung Chee-hwa and has expressed her belief in libertarian values.
Anson Chan emphasized the importance of preserving freedoms and plurality of views in Hong Kong.

Britain has suggested going to the World Court regarding China's plan to disband Hong Kong's elected legislature.
The transition of Hong Kong to Chinese rule is set for midnight on June 30.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten criticized China's plans.
A Beijing-appointed legislature will replace the elected Legislative Council in Hong Kong.
Rifkind stated that there is no justification for China to replace an elected legislature.
Rifkind summoned Chinese ambassador Jiang Enzhu to express Britain's concerns.
Patten described the proposed Chinese legislature as a 'rubber stamp' chamber.
Pro-democracy groups protested against the election of the provisional legislature in Hong Kong.
Patten expressed confidence that the International Court of Justice could resolve the dispute.
Lawmaker Emily Lau stated that there is no legal basis for the proposed body.

The skyscrapers in Hong Kong are decorated with fairy lights.
Red-cloaked Santas interact with children during Christmas.
Christmas carols are played in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong features some of the most spectacular Christmas light displays in the world.
The displays include giant illuminated Santas and reindeer on skyscrapers.
Hong Kong's malls are filled with extravagant festive displays.
Shops in Hong Kong offer expensive brand names repackaged for the Christmas season.
China has promised to allow Hong Kong to maintain its capitalist system for 50 years under a 'one country two systems' policy.
Freedom of religion is expected to remain in Hong Kong after the transition to Chinese rule.
Concerns exist among Hong Kong residents about the future of pro-democracy protests and Christmas traditions.

Shares in Eurotunnel SA fell on Tuesday after being requoted following a week's suspension.
The decline was due to disappointment over the terms of its restructuring with creditor banks.
Eurotunnel SA has 69.6 billion francs ($13.50 billion) of junior-ranked bank debt.
The shares closed down 8.74 percent at 8.35 francs on a volume of 20 million shares.
The shares were suspended at 9.15 francs on September 30 before the debt deal.
Analyst Jean Borgeix stated that the market was disappointed with the 10.40 franc price for new Eurotunnel shares.
The market expected a conversion price of between 12-15 francs per share.
Current shareholders will lose 30 percent of Eurotunnel's future cashflow to pay for stabilisation notes.
Eurotunnel can issue up to 14.8 billion francs of stabilisation notes.
The restructuring will dilute current shareholders' holdings to 54.5 percent of the capital after the debt swap.

Compagnie Generale des Eaux reported a first half net profit of 808 million French francs.
The first half net profit increased from 224 million French francs the previous year.
Chairman Jean-Marie Messier forecasted a full year net profit of about 1.8 billion francs for 1996.
The company experienced a net loss of 3.69 billion francs the year before.
Messier stated that the results would be influenced by exceptional items, including capital gains from asset sales.
For 1997, Messier expected profits to be much higher than those of 1996.
The company made a net profit of 3.4 billion francs in 1994.
Generale des Eaux made a formal bid with Mannesmann to run the telecommunications operations of SNCF.
The group expects to lose 4.6 billion francs this year due to poor property assets.
The average level of property provisioning for the group was around 55-56 percent.

Air France is forming a trans-Atlantic alliance with Delta Air Lines and Continental Airlines.
Air France signed separate letters of intent to coordinate ticket booking and passenger transfers with Delta and Continental.
The agreements are intended to help Air France compete with major European rivals.
Air France and Continental previously signed a commercial accord in 1993, which was never implemented.
Continental does not have a European partner among U.S. airlines.
The alliances will allow code-sharing arrangements between Air France and the U.S. companies.
Passengers can be issued tickets by one airline to be used on its partner airline.
The companies will harmonize flight schedules, share a frequent flyer program, and provide ground facilities.
Delta operates from Atlanta, Continental operates from Houston, and Air France operates from Paris Roissy-Charles De Gaulle airport.
Air France expects the alliances to generate an additional $100 million a year in gross revenues.

The submarine changed naval warfare in World War Two.
European shipbuilders are developing new stealth warships for the 21st century.
Three shipbuilders presented combat ship designs at a trade fair at Le Bourget airport.
Britain's Vosper Thornycroft unveiled the Sea Wraith corvette.
Brian Spilman, Vosper's manager of future projects shipbuilding, stated that the Sea Wraith could make other vessels of its class obsolete.
BAeSema presented the Cougar corvette at the trade fair.
French state-owned DCN shipyard presented the La Fayette frigate, claiming it is the first operational warship to fully use stealth features.
The La Fayette frigate is designed for deep-water operations, unlike the other two corvettes.
Stealth warships utilize radar-beating technology similar to that used by U.S. aircraft in the 1991 Gulf War.
The La Fayette uses a slab-sided superstructure and non-metallic materials to confuse radar.

Airbus received a large order from USAir for 120 A320 planes and options for 280 more.
The estimated list price for the USAir order is $5.3 billion.
Emirates placed an order for 16 Airbus A330-200s worth $2 billion.
The order backlog for Airbus is considered healthy by analyst Emmanuel Dubois Pelerin.
Airbus expects to exceed 300 firm orders in 1996, compared to 106 in the previous year.
There are uncertainties regarding Airbus' future products and profitability beyond the next two to three years.
Airbus is a partnership that includes French state-owned Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA.
Airbus plans to change into a joint stock company by 1999 to improve market responsiveness and competitiveness.
Airbus aims to secure 30-40 percent of external risk sharing for the development of the A3XX plane, which is estimated to cost $8 billion.
Airbus is under pressure to develop a competitor to Boeing's large-capacity aircraft.

Air France ordered 10 Boeing jetliners and 10 Airbus jets on Wednesday.
Air France reported profits of 802 million francs ($158 million) in the first half of the year.
The profit estimate for the six months ending Sept. 30 was compared with a loss of 335 million francs ($66 million) a year ago.
Air France aims to break even in the 1996/97 fiscal year.
Air France ordered 10 Boeing 777 twinjets and has options for 10 more.
Air France ordered five Airbus A340s and confirmed five orders made in June.
Air France took options for an additional five Airbus A340s.
Air France Chairman Christian Blanc received support from French Prime Minister Alain Juppe for the Boeing purchase.
The orders for the Boeing 777-200 could be worth around $2.7 billion at list prices.
Airbus would gain $1.75 billion from the orders.

Anglo-French Eurotunnel SA/Plc sought to reassure the public about the safety of the Channel Tunnel following a fire.
The fire occurred in a truck on a freight train and seriously damaged a section of the tunnel.
The fire injured 34 people and halted most rail services between France and Britain.
French co-chairman Patrick Ponsolle stated that the tunnel is at least as safe as other Channel transport systems.
British co-chairman Robert Malpas emphasized that safety is the first consideration for Eurotunnel.
The emergency evacuation procedure worked after two other measures failed during the incident.
The cause of the fire remains unknown, with sabotage considered a possibility by the investigating French magistrate.
Legal sources indicated that the theory of deliberate fire starting is regarded as a remote possibility.
Ponsolle estimated Eurotunnel's maximum potential loss from the fire to be between five and seven million pounds.
Eurotunnel's monthly turnover before the fire was between 350 and 400 million francs.

France's Thomson SA electronics group is considering a two-stage privatisation.
Analysts believe that separating the defence arm from the consumer goods unit makes better economic sense.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe stated that Thomson-CSF could be separated from Thomson Multimedia for a quicker privatisation.
The French government abandoned its plan to sell the entire Thomson group to Lagardere Groupe for one franc after the Privatisation Commission rejected it.
President Jacques Chirac's initial policy was to restructure the French defence industry and sell Thomson as one unit.
Analysts support the two-part sale approach for restructuring the defence industry.
Lagardere planned to sell Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo Electronics while retaining Thomson-CSF.
The Privatisation Commission rejected Lagardere's bid due to concerns over technology transfers to Daewoo and job retention commitments.
Privatising Thomson-CSF separately would help create a national champion in defence electronics.
Thomson-CSF is profitable, has low debt, and 42 percent of its capital is listed on the Paris stock exchange.

The European Airbus consortium must resolve differences regarding its future structure.
Boeing and McDonnell Douglas announced a merger to create a company with annual sales of $48 billion.
Boeing currently outpaces Airbus in civilian aircraft sales.
Airbus holds 30 percent of the world civilian aircraft market, while Boeing holds around 60 percent and McDonnell Douglas holds 10 percent.
Airbus is a partnership consisting of French state-owned Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
The partners aimed to reach an agreement on restructuring Airbus Industrie by the end of 1996.
An industry source indicated that the agreement might be delayed into the new year.
Aerospatiale wants a minimal Airbus, Dasa seeks a maximum Airbus, and BAe wants a transfer of core assets to the new company.
Aerospatiale's chairman Yves Michot expressed a desire for Airbus to act as a prime contractor with more powers.
A French industry executive stated that managing marketing and manufacturing operations are distinct challenges.

A dispute over market share exists between Boeing and Airbus.
Airbus claims to have overtaken Boeing in market share.
Airbus senior vice president John Leahy stated that Boeing had 216 net new orders this year after accounting for 117 cancellations.
Leahy emphasized the importance of net orders over gross orders.
Airbus reported 221 net orders this year with 13 cancellations.
Airbus claims a 52 percent market share for planes seating between 125-350 passengers.
Boeing is credited with a 43 percent market share and McDonnell Douglas with five percent.
Leahy noted a decline in Boeing's market share since 1976 and an increase in Airbus's share.
Boeing vice-president Bruce Dennis stated that the company is exceeding its market share targets.
Dennis claimed that Airbus's market share increase has not come at Boeing's expense but rather from McDonnell Douglas's sales.

Eurotunnel Plc is the operator of the Channel Tunnel.
Eurotunnel Plc is currently in debt.
Eurotunnel Plc pledged to recover from a public relations disaster following a tunnel fire in November.
Eurotunnel Plc expects to restore lost market share in 1997.
Patrick Ponsolle is the chairman of Eurotunnel.
Eurotunnel's services experienced a partial shutdown during the Christmas period due to the fire.
Eurotunnel stated that the financial fallout from the fire would not affect its debt rescue plan.
The shareholder meeting to approve the debt plan has been delayed to June.
Eurotunnel's banking syndicate requested an extension of the debt standstill arrangement to December.
Eurotunnel reported an estimated turnover of 450 million pounds for 1996, an increase from 300 million in 1995.

France's national audit office criticized the water supply market for a lack of clarity and insufficient competition.
The water supply market in France is dominated by two companies: Cie Generale des Eaux and Lyonnaise des Eaux.
Francois Logerot authored the Cour des Comptes report on the water supply market.
The report states there is a high degree of concentration in the water supply market.

Concentration in the water supply sector may be influenced by agreements between the two dominant companies.
The water company Societe Stephanoise des Eaux is jointly owned by Lyonnaise des Eaux Dumez and Generale des Eaux.
In 1991, the private sector held 75 percent of the supply of drinking water in France.
The price of water in France rose by an average of 47.7 percent from 1990 to 1994.
Local authorities often awarded contracts to water companies in exchange for payments that were recovered in customer prices.

Airbus stated it has no evidence that Boeing is pressuring U.S. suppliers to avoid working on the A3XX project.
Manfred Bischoff, chairman of Daimler-Benz Aerospace, expressed concern that Boeing and McDonnell Douglas were signaling Northrop Grumman not to work on Airbus' A3XX project.
An Airbus spokesman confirmed there is no evidence of pressure from Boeing.
An industry source claimed that Boeing pressured Northrop Grumman to avoid involvement in the A3XX project.
Daimler-Benz Aerospace is a partner in Airbus Industrie, along with Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, and Casa of Spain.
Airbus had exploratory talks with Northrop Grumman regarding supplying engine housing sections for the A3XX, but those negotiations ended.
Airbus is seeking risk-sharing partners to cover up to 40 percent of the $8 billion development costs for the A3XX.
The A3XX is designed to seat 550 passengers and is expected to enter service in 2003.
Airbus managing director Jean Pierson plans to address competition concerns regarding the Boeing merger to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and the European Commission.
Pierson stated that the Boeing merger will pose challenges for Europe's civil aviation industry and will impact military markets.

PacifiCorp and Protection One Inc. announced a marketing alliance on Friday.
The alliance aims to boost customer loyalty in a competitive industry.
Customers of PacifiCorp subsidiaries Pacific Power and Utah Power will be offered a security system from Protection One.

Utilities are increasingly attracted to security companies as they enter new markets.
Rene Carroll, consumer products manager at PacifiCorp, mentioned they have been exploring the home security business for over a year.
The alliance provides Protection One access to 1.4 million customers served by PacifiCorp subsidiaries.
Customers accepting the offer will receive free installation of a home security system with a two-year monitoring agreement.
Protection One Chief Financial Officer John Hesse indicated that more announcements are expected in the next 12 months.

Loewen Group Inc. is the target of a $2.9 billion hostile bid by Service Corp. International.
Seven states, including Hawaii and Pennsylvania, have launched antitrust investigations into the proposed transaction.
Loewen Group Inc. is publicizing the antitrust probes as part of its takeover defense strategy.

The proposed transaction involving Loewen is also being investigated by a Canadian agency.
State authorities helped to scuttle Mattel Inc.'s unsolicited bid for Hasbro Inc. earlier this year.
State and federal complaints led to the collapse of a merger between Rite Aid Corp. and Revco D.S. Inc.
Loewen has filed a federal antitrust lawsuit against Service Corp. International.

USAir Group Inc is planning to expand overseas.
USAir Group Inc is based in Arlington, Virginia.
USAir Group Inc will terminate its passenger-sharing pact with British Airways Plc in March.
The termination of the pact is due to British Airways' proposed alliance with AMR Corp.
USAir received less revenue from the alliance with British Airways than British Airways did.
Most major airlines have established international partnerships.
USAir is seeking the right to fly to Heathrow Airport from several U.S. cities.
USAir is known for its short-haul routes on the U.S. East Coast.
USAir has the highest cost structure among major U.S. carriers.
Strong profit margins on long-haul flights may offset USAir's expenses.

Revco D.S. Inc is expected to leverage its size and experience to address problems faced by Big B Inc.
Revco is positioned to capture profits in the southeast by utilizing Big B's underused distribution center.
Revco plans to close overlapping stores in Georgia.
Big B accepted an acquisition offer from Revco valued at $380 million, or $17.25 per share.
Rite Aid Corp agreed to buy Thrifty PayLess Inc for $1.4 billion two weeks prior to the Revco-Big B deal.
Big B initially rejected Revco's unsolicited bid of $15 per share.
Big B's profit margins declined due to challenges from managed health care and discount retailers.
Big B's distribution center is operating at only 60 percent of capacity.
Revco operates 180 stores in Georgia, while Big B has 160 stores in the same area.
Revco's acquisition of Big B is expected to enhance its earnings in the first year.

Investor Carl Icahn resumed his campaign to break up RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. by nominating a slate of directors to replace the existing board members.
Icahn holds a 7.3 percent stake in RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
Icahn named his intended nominees to RJR's board in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Icahn requested that RJR spin off its Nabisco Holdings Corp. unit immediately in a letter to RJR Chairman Steven Goldstone.
Icahn stated that RJR's stock price had lost more than 20 percent recently and that the company has lost market share to Philip Morris Cos. Inc.
RJR Nabisco Holdings responded that Icahn's slate of directors was weaker than the one he submitted last year.
RJR stated that Icahn's proposed slate appears to consist mostly of lawyers, consultants, and retired individuals.
RJR, which owns 80.5 percent of Nabisco, expressed that it favors a spin-off of the food unit but believes it is not the right time to do so.
RJR warned that an attempt to spin off Nabisco in the current political and legal environment could harm the company and its shareholders.
Thomas Rattigan, former CEO of PepsiCo Bottling International, will head Icahn's proposed slate of directors.

Conrail Inc was set to formally consider a $9 billion takeover offer from Norfolk Southern Corp.
Conrail's board of directors was expected to reject the Norfolk Southern offer in favor of a friendly $8.4 billion deal with CSX Corp.
Brian Routledge of Prudential Securities predicted that Conrail would stick with the CSX proposal.
Conrail's board was scheduled to meet on Tuesday ahead of a Wednesday deadline to respond to the Norfolk Southern offer.
A Conrail spokesman declined to comment on the timing of the decision.
Conrail agreed on October 15 to be acquired by CSX in a cash and stock transaction valued at $8.4 billion, or $92.50 per share.
Norfolk Southern launched its $100-per-share bid on October 23.
Norfolk Southern and CSX have criticized each other's offers and have been involved in legal disputes.
Industry experts indicated that Conrail is likely to defend the CSX bid by citing strategic benefits and fewer legal issues.
Legal experts noted that Pennsylvania takeover law could hinder a Norfolk Southern acquisition of Conrail.

Republic Industries Inc. plans to buy Alamo-Rent-A-Car Inc. for $625 million.
Wayne Huizenga is the leader of Republic Industries Inc.
The acquisition aims to expand Republic's automobile business.
Alamo is the fourth-largest rental car company in the United States.
Alamo has a fleet of about 130,000 vehicles and operates in 42 states in the U.S.
Alamo also has operations in 10 European countries and Canada.
Michael Egan is the founder and Chairman of Alamo and owns about 94 percent of the company.
Republic's AutoNation USA car business will benefit from Alamo's relationships with manufacturers.
Republic Industries Inc. bought AutoNation earlier this year and opened its first superstore in Florida.
Republic plans to open three or four more AutoNation stores this year.

Norfolk Southern Corp. increased its hostile bid for Conrail Inc. to $10 billion in cash.
Norfolk Southern's original offer was $9.1 billion.
The proposed transaction between Conrail and CSX Corp. was valued at $8.5 billion.
Norfolk Southern's new bid values Conrail shares at $110 each.
Conrail stated it would review Norfolk Southern's new offer.
Conrail previously determined that a union with CSX was a better fit.
CSX and Conrail revised their transaction terms to provide more cash to shareholders.
The Conrail-CSX union values Conrail shares at approximately $93.
Conrail shares increased by $3.375 to $96.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
A shareholder meeting is scheduled for mid-December.

Mattel Inc announced plans to acquire Tyco Toys Inc for $755 million.
The acquisition aims to expand Mattel's market presence in boys' toys.
Mattel previously attempted to acquire Hasbro Inc but withdrew due to antitrust concerns.
Industry experts believe the Tyco acquisition will achieve similar goals to the failed Hasbro transaction.
Mattel's product line includes Barbie, Hot Wheels, and Fisher-Price.
Tyco's product line includes Matchbox, Sesame Street toys, and radio control vehicles.
Shares of Tyco increased to approximately $12.50 each following the announcement.
Tyco has been restructuring to return to profitability after cutting 10 percent of its workforce.
Analysts believe Mattel can enhance Tyco's revenue growth and expand its international reach.
Mattel president Jill Barad stated that antitrust concerns are not expected to be a major issue.

Conrail Inc. and CSX Corp. have received court approval for their $8.65 billion merger plan.
Some shareholders prefer Norfolk Southern Corp.'s larger bid over the CSX offer.
CSX's $110 cash tender offer for 19.9 percent of Conrail shares was oversubscribed.
Conrail has rejected Norfolk Southern's $110 per share offer, citing strategic benefits from the CSX merger.
Lawyers and financial advisors are considering plans to persuade investors to approve the merger.
Options being considered include increasing the stock portion of the deal or setting a price volatility guard.
CSX and Conrail may revise the deal's terms to accelerate payments to investors.
The shareholder vote on the merger is currently scheduled for mid-December.
A U.S. district court judge denied Norfolk Southern's request to block the CSX-Conrail proposal.
Pennsylvania corporate law limits cash tender offers to 20 percent of another company.

Ashland Inc. announced a restructuring programme aimed at increasing profitability.
The restructuring is in response to weak refining margins and energy industry consolidation.
The announcement led to the withdrawal of a proxy fight plan by a New York investment firm.
Ashland's Chief Executive Officer is Paul Chellgren.
The restructuring plan focuses on improving returns in Ashland's refining and marketing segment.
Ashland will form a petroleum group that includes its refining businesses, SuperAmerica retail stores, and Valvoline motor oil.
Fred Brothers will lead the new petroleum group.
Ashland will reduce its 1997 capital expenditures for Ashland Petroleum to $150 million from $175 million.
Capital expenditures for refining will be limited to $100 million.
Ashland will evaluate alternatives for its exploration unit and aims to complete this evaluation by the end of 1997.

Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp are proposing a merger.
The merger raises the stakes for survival in the defense industry.
The defense industry has experienced intense consolidation.
Global companies like Northrop Grumman Corp, Raytheon Co, and Hughes Electronics Corp are expected to seek partners for mergers.
Jon Kutler is the president of Quarterdeck Investment Partners Inc, which specializes in aerospace and defense.
The Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger is expected to trigger a resurgence of merger activity.
James Schwendinger is the director of Deloitte & Touche's aerospace and defense practice.
Northrop Grumman is considered a leading buyer of defense electronics properties.
Northrop Grumman's shares increased following news of the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger.
Lockheed Martin Corp is the current leader in the defense industry.

A part of the new telecommunications law may limit how phone companies use confidential customer data.
The law creates a conflict between consumer advocates and telecommunications carriers.
Consumer advocates are concerned about increased telemarketing and loss of personal privacy.
Telecommunications carriers want to provide customers with comprehensive service options.
Customer data includes billing records and calling patterns.
The Federal Communications Commission is creating rules regarding the use of customer proprietary network information (CPNI).
CPNI includes details about call times, destinations, frequency, length, phone lines, and billing prices.
Few restrictions on customer data usage existed before the new telecommunications law.
The FCC's new rules are expected to be released in early 1997.
Phone companies prefer less stringent rules for customer data usage to better target services.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) plans to end a rule from the Depression era that requires telephone carriers to notify the FCC before changing long-distance rates.
The new rules are intended to increase competition in the $70 billion long-distance market and reduce government regulations for long-distance carriers such as AT&T Corp, MCI Communications Corp, and Sprint Corp.
The 1934 rule required long-distance companies to submit 'tariff' filings to the FCC before changing rates or offering new services.
The original purpose of the 1934 rule was to allow regulators to review changes and provide the public with advance notice.
The FCC believes the new approach will enable companies to respond more quickly to competitors' price changes without the need for extensive paperwork.
The FCC states that the new rules will decrease the chances of companies colluding on long-distance rates.
Carriers will be required to directly notify residential customers of any rate changes instead of using complex tariff filings.
The FCC's new approach is the first significant action taken under a provision of the new telecommunications law that allows the agency to eliminate outdated rules if public interest is not harmed.
Tariff filings currently take effect one day after submission to the FCC.
AT&T previously complained that tariff filings allowed competitors to see its plans in advance, which hindered its ability to act quickly.

Federal and state regulators are working on a proposal to ensure quality and affordable phone service for all Americans.
An eight-member board is determining the size of a federal fund to subsidize universal service, with estimates ranging from $4 billion to $12 billion a year.
The proposal could affect consumer and business phone bill costs.
Mark Cooper of the Consumer Federation of America stated that consumers may have a stake depending on the dollar figures and recovery mechanism.
The panel was established by a new telecommunications law and is scheduled to unveil its plans on Thursday.
Regulators need to decide how telecommunications companies will fund affordable phone service for rural and poor urban areas.
They must also determine how schools and libraries will connect to the Internet and the associated costs.
The board must issue recommendations to the FCC by Friday, which will then finalize rules by early May.
Local phone companies currently provide universal service, funded partly by access charges paid by long-distance carriers.
In 1994, local companies received about $21 billion in interstate access charges, with seven regional Baby Bells receiving about $17 billion.

An eight-member board is determining the size of a federal fund to subsidize universal service, with estimates ranging from $4 billion to $12 billion a year.
Mark Cooper of the Consumer Federation of America stated that consumers may have a stake depending on the size of the fund and the recovery mechanism.

There is disagreement among board members regarding the extent of Internet access for schools and libraries and the discounts they should receive.

Deregulation of the local telephone market is progressing.
The Supreme Court declined to revive key parts of the FCC's rules for local phone monopolies.
Industry and government officials agree that the move towards competition is not dead.
Henry Geller, a former FCC general counsel, stated that things haven't come to a halt.
State regulators are now making many decisions regarding the opening of the local market to competition.
The states are considering the FCC's now-defunct rules on pricing for new entrants to the local business.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt expressed encouragement about the general trend in deregulation.
Long-distance carriers such as AT&T are not currently expressing alarm about the situation.
The Baby Bells and other local companies acknowledge that state decisions have been a mixed bag for them.
A U.S. appeals court in St. Louis suspended key provisions of the FCC's interconnection rules.

Federal regulators are planning a two-part initiative to reduce rates on overseas phone calls.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is expected to simplify negotiations for cheaper international call rates.
Next month, the FCC is expected to propose rules to lower charges U.S. carriers pay foreign phone monopolies.
Don Gips is the head of the FCC's international bureau.
Foreign charges, or 'accounting rates,' are reported to be five to ten times the actual costs.
Monopolies control over 90 percent of the non-U.S. phone market.
In 1995, U.S. phone companies paid $5.5 billion more to foreign carriers than they received from them.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt stated that the imbalance in payments exceeds the U.S. foreign aid budget of $2 billion.
The United States has significant imbalances in phone call charges with countries like China, Jamaica, Mexico, Hong Kong, Colombia, and Argentina.
U.S. carriers support the FCC's strategy to adjust accounting rates to reflect actual costs.

Representatives from the television and computer industries reached an agreement on a broadcast standard for high-definition digital TV.
The agreement aims to allow the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to finalize a government-prescribed standard for advanced digital TV by the end of the year.
The advanced digital TV standard offers cinema-quality pictures and CD-quality sound.
TV manufacturers hope to begin bringing digital-TV receivers to market in 1998.
The agreement calls on the FCC to issue a broadcast transmission standard but does not mandate key aspects of digital TV technology.
The market will dictate the eventual shape of the TV screen and the technology for displaying images.
FCC officials welcomed the agreement, with Commissioner Susan Ness expressing confidence that the FCC can act before the end of 1996.
Computer companies, led by Microsoft Corp. Chairman Bill Gates, objected to the initial FCC broadcast standard proposed in May.
The latest talks resolved objections from Hollywood directors, actors, and cinematographers regarding screen size affecting wide-screen films.
The initial FCC proposal was based on a recommendation from an advisory panel that included representatives from various industries.

The television and entertainment industries announced plans to use their own system for rating TV programs.
The industry plans to reject any government-imposed rating system by legal means if necessary.
A group of TV and Hollywood executives will unveil a new rating system next week.
The new rating system will be based on the suitability of shows for children under 14 years of age.
The new system will be similar to the existing motion-picture rating system, which includes ratings such as G, PG, PG-13, R, and NC-17.
Jack Valenti is the chief executive of the Motion Picture Association of America and leads the group developing the ratings.
Parental groups and some lawmakers, including Rep. Edward Markey, have called for a content-based rating system.
Markey stated that the industry has not adequately addressed parents' concerns about knowing the specific content of TV shows.
Valenti accused Markey of attempting to impose his own scheme through government intervention.
The Federal Communications Commission must approve the new ratings system.

The television industry's new rating system for programs will begin airing on ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox on Wednesday.
Broadcast and cable networks will carry the ratings, but start dates will vary.
Time Warner Inc.'s WB network began rating shows on December 22.
Black Entertainment Television does not plan to use the ratings.
The rating system includes six categories, two of which are for children's shows.
The categories are TV-Y, TV-Y7, TV-G, TV-PG, TV-14, and TV-M.
CBS rated 'Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles' as TV-Y7 and 'Chicago Hope' as TV-14.
ABC rated 'Bugs Bunny and Tweety Show' as TV-Y and 'NYPD Blue' as TV-14.
NBC will broadcast 'Schindler's List' with a TV-M rating.
Fox will rate the first episodes of 'Melrose Place' and 'The X-Files' as TV-14.

The government's largest wireless phone auction ended with a total of $2.5 billion in bids from 125 companies.
This total was down 75 percent from a similar auction that raised $10.2 billion in May.
The average price for a license to provide personal communications services (PCS) fell more than 90 percent.
PCS technology is expected to enable consumers to use multiple communications services through a single handheld device.
The drop in auction prices was attributed to an influx of new entrants, lack of new investment, and fewer airwaves covered by new licenses.
The top bidder was a unit of Sprint Corp., which bid $544 million for 160 licenses in cities including Chicago, Houston, and Atlanta.
AT&T Corp. was the second highest bidder, offering $407 million for 222 licenses in cities such as New York and Los Angeles.
BellSouth Corp. was the third highest bidder, with a bid of $205 million for 39 licenses.
The OPCSE-Galloway Consortium, consisting of Omnipoint Corp. and Galloway Entrepreneurs, bid $181 million for 109 licenses.
The FCC sold 1,479 PCS licenses nationwide, the most licenses sold at once in an auction.

President Clinton and Congress are considering airwave sales to reduce the deficit.
Analysts believe the radio spectrum is not an unlimited source of revenue.
Joe Boyer of Hatfield Associates Inc. cautioned that overselling spectrum could lower prices.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has raised about $23 billion through 12 spectrum auctions since summer 1994.
The FCC has sold licenses for personal communications services, satellite TV, and wireless cable TV.
Budget analyst Stan Collender stated that spectrum has been the most valuable asset the government has sold in decades.
President Clinton is set to unveil his fiscal 1998 budget on February 6.
White House officials indicated that spectrum auctions will be included in the fiscal 1998 budget plan.
Clinton proposed to auction the 'analog' spectrum returned by TV broadcasters in 2002, projected to raise $17 billion.
The Congressional Budget Office predicted that prices for spectrum under 3 GHz will decrease as more spectrum is sold.

The Clinton administration proposed a budget that includes a $36 billion plan to sell airwave licenses.
The administration aims to generate revenue by auctioning spectrum for new communications services.
Experts are divided on the potential success of the administration's plan to sell spectrum.
The White House proposed to auction toll-free 888 phone numbers instead of allocating them for free.
The auction plan is intended to cover a five-year period through 2002.
Many economists believe the $36 billion target is achievable due to high demand for spectrum.
James Gatusso from Citizens for a Sound Economy stated there is significant unmet demand for frequencies.
Potential new services from the auctioned spectrum include high-speed wireless internet and mobile video services.
Critics argue that aggressive spectrum sales could lower prices and harm existing license holders.
Tom Wheeler, president of the Cellular Telecommunications Industry Association, warned that selling spectrum aggressively could devalue it.

Negotiations between American Airlines and its pilots union continued into Friday morning.
Neither American Airlines nor the pilots union reported any breakthrough in the negotiations.
A federal mediator informed the pilots that American Airlines rejected a key union contract proposal regarding the operation of American Eagle planes.
Mediators are proposing hypothetical solutions to bring both sides closer together and prevent a strike.
Dave Bates, a spokesman for the Allied Pilots Association, stated that the union is disappointed at the lack of progress.
Bates indicated that the pilots would go on strike at midnight if no agreement is reached.
No face-to-face talks had been scheduled as of the time of the report.
Kenneth Hipp, chairman of the National Mediation Board, expressed hope for an agreement to avert a strike.
The union proposed that its pilots fly American Eagle flights at lower pay than regular American pilots.
American Airlines prefers to use lower-paid commuter pilots from a different union for the smaller planes.

Five major high tech companies, including Philips Electronics NV and Sony Corp., will unveil details of a new CD-ReWriteable technology.
The CD-ReWriteable technology is expected to bring re-recordable CD devices to the market in early 1997 at prices below $1,000.
The new format will allow users to store 450 times as much data as a 3.5 inch floppy diskette.
The CD-ReWriteable technology is designed to be compatible with new CD-ROM readers and upcoming DVD-ROM drives.
Dave Deane is the Future CD Writer Product Manager at Hewlett-Packard Co.'s HWP.
Hewlett-Packard, Mitsubishi Chemical Corp., and Ricoh Co. Ltd. are also involved in unveiling the new technology.
The development of the CD-ReWriteable technology has taken 18 months.
Analysts believe the CD-ROM technology could pressure other storage companies like Iomega Corp. and SyQuest Technology Inc.
Ray Freeman is the president of Freeman Associates Inc., a market research firm.
Freeman projects that the combined CD-Recordable and CD-ReWriteable market will grow to 2.9 million units in 1997.

Silicon Valley executives and venture capitalists are spending millions to defeat California's Proposition 211.
They claim Proposition 211 threatens American capitalism and could negatively impact stock prices.
California's Proposition 211 would eliminate certain legal safeguards for corporate officers and staff members.
The measure would hold corporate officers liable for incorrect projections about future results.
Opponents fear that corporate officers will stop making projections, complicating investment decisions and lowering share prices.
Proponents of Proposition 211 argue it will help victims of fraud recover losses.
Opponents describe the measure as a way for securities lawyers to profit.
A recent Los Angeles Times poll indicated that 52 percent of likely voters oppose Proposition 211.
Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt has urged voters to reject Proposition 211.
Both President Bill Clinton and Bob Dole have publicly opposed Proposition 211.

Microsoft Corp launched electronic commerce software aimed at enabling consumers and businesses to buy and sell products over the World Wide Web.
The core of the announcement is Microsoft's Merchant Server, which allows businesses to set up electronic storefronts on the Internet.
Microsoft plans to build a new channel of service providers to assist businesses in setting up electronic storefronts.
Analysts noted that Microsoft's strategy is similar to that used by Novell Inc to sell networking software.
Microsoft Chairman and Chief Executive Bill Gates stated that there will be explosive growth in the use of the Web for shopping.
Microsoft revealed that 40 companies are in the process of building Merchant Server sites.
Henry Vigil, general manager of electronic commerce services at Microsoft, expects 300 sites using the software by year-end.
The Merchant Server product competes with offerings from Netscape Communications Corp, Open Market, Oracle Corp, and International Business Machines Corp.
Microsoft and VeriFone Inc collaborated with financial institutions and payment processors to provide a secure Internet retailing and payment system.
The financial institutions involved include BankAmerica Corp, Wells Fargo & Co, Citicorp's Citibank Card Acceptance Europe, First USA Paymenteck Inc, NOVUS Services, and Royal Bank of Canada.

Stocks of high-tech companies increased significantly on Wednesday after a ballot proposal was defeated in California.
The ballot measure, known as Proposition 211, would have made it easier for shareholders to file lawsuits.
Proposition 211 was defeated by a 3-1 margin.
John Doerr, a partner at Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, led the opposition to Proposition 211.
William Lerach, a San Diego attorney, promoted Proposition 211.
California's high-tech firms raised an estimated $38 million and mobilized 5 million employees, shareholders, and customers against Proposition 211.
Proponents of Proposition 211 spent $13 million on their campaign.
The defeat of Proposition 211 relieved Wall Street investors concerned about potential shareholder lawsuits.
