Pacific Magazines and Printing Ltd informed its shareholders of an expected small rise in earnings.
Lower paper prices are increasing demand for printing work.
Earnings from magazine publishing are also growing.
Chairman Ken Cowley stated that profit will be marginally up compared to the previous year.
Cowley forecasted a tough economic environment in Australia for the current business year ending June 30.
The tough economic environment will be partly offset by a continuing cost-cutting drive.
Cowley emphasized the need to find more efficient ways of operating.

Foster's Brewing Group Ltd is seeking expansion opportunities.
The company is considering joint ventures in India and Vietnam.
Foster's executives communicated their plans at the annual meeting in Melbourne.
Foster's has faced challenges in its Canadian and Chinese operations.
The company aims to identify new direct investment opportunities after meeting current cash needs.
Foster's chairman John Ralph confirmed the consideration of joint ventures in Vietnam and India.
The Vietnamese opportunity involves an existing plant.
Foster's has breweries in Shanghai, Tianjin, and Guangdong in China.
Foster's China operations are expected to break even or turn a profit in 1998/99.
Foster's reported a loss of A$17 million for its China operations in 1995/96.

The Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd's steel division expects to increase its earnings in the 1996/97 year due to lower costs and improved operations.
BHP Steel chief executive Ron McNeilly stated that there will be no major improvement in the Australian market until possibly the second quarter of 1997.
McNeilly expects the world steel market to improve towards the end of the first half of 1997.
BHP Steel reported a 44 percent slump in profit to A$375 million before abnormals in 1995/96.
BHP Steel's profit after a write-down of the value of its Newcastle raw steel-making plant was A$153 million, a 76 percent decrease.
McNeilly described domestic demand as very patchy, with some signs of improved demand in the resource and infrastructure areas.
There is no sign of improvement in domestic housing, most of the rural sector, and general demand in Australia.
BHP's export despatches of steel have been increasing, but prices have been affected by an intensely competitive steel market.
McNeilly quoted forecasts from the International Iron and Steel Institute for strong world steel consumption over the next four years.
McNeilly anticipates that steel prices should strengthen between the first half of 1997 and the second quarter of 1998.

National Mutual Holdings Ltd is an institutional investor.
National Mutual Holdings Ltd has arranged a meeting with St George Bank Ltd.
The meeting is to discuss St George's merger with Advance Bank Australia Ltd.
National Mutual's funds management arm is a top-20 shareholder in St George.
National Mutual wants to discuss St George's decision not to put the merger proposal to a shareholders' vote.
Paul Jennings is the domestic equity investments manager at National Mutual Funds Management Ltd.
Market sources indicate that National Mutual and at least one other institution are lobbying St George to seek shareholder approval for the merger.
National Australia Bank Ltd has expressed disappointment at St George's decision regarding the merger.
The Australian Stock Exchange has approved St George's decision not to hold a shareholders' meeting.
St George's offer valued each Advance Bank share at A$7.30.

The Broken Hill Pty Co. (BHP) reported a 9.8-percent decline in first-half profits.
BHP's net profit for the six months to Nov. 30 was A$790 million ($628 million), down from A$867 million ($689.3 million) in the previous year.
BHP's profits were boosted by an abnormal gain of A$107 million ($85 million).
Analysts expressed disappointment with BHP's financial results.
BHP's operating profits fell 15.8 percent from the previous year to A$683 million ($543.0 million).
BHP's copper division showed improvement, with North American operations returning to profit.
Managing director John Prescott indicated that second-quarter figures showed faster improvement in performance.
BHP's petroleum division was the largest earner, generating A$253 million ($201.1 million), which included an abnormal gain from a tax dispute settlement.
BHP's minerals division doubled its profit contribution in the second quarter to A$154 million ($122.4 million) due to higher world prices.
BHP Copper reported a second-quarter profit of A$132 million ($104 million) due to a rise in copper prices and reduced operating costs.

Amcor Ltd announced a decline in annual profit on Monday.
The decline in profit was attributed to weak world paper prices and flat economic growth in Australia.
This was Amcor's first fall in pre-abnormal profit in over a decade.
Amcor reported a six percent drop in net profit to A$338.8 million for the year ending June 30.
The company's paper division experienced a roughly 20 percent fall in world paper prices since late 1995.
Weak economic activity in Australia and Germany negatively impacted Amcor's packaging operations.
Amcor suggested that paper prices had bottomed out and anticipated an upturn in 1997.
Amcor's managing director, Don Macfarlane, stated that all businesses have restructuring and cost-reduction programs underway.
Amcor's shares closed at A$7.62, down 12 cents from the previous close.
Analysts predict that profit will remain flat towards the end of the current year but may start to increase in 1997/98.

Australian retailers are experiencing lower profit results due to a sluggish economy and cautious consumers.
Harvey Norman Ltd reported it is not meeting its goal of 15 percent annual sales growth.
Harvey Norman Ltd described the current retail environment as the worst in its 15-year history.
David Jones Ltd and two large clothing retailers expect significant profit declines.
David Jones Ltd, Country Road Ltd, and Just Jeans Ltd warned of 50 percent drops in interim profit for the half-year ending January.
Christmas sales did not improve the financial performance of retailers.
Harvey Norman managing director Michael Harvey stated that this is the first year the company has faced a general market malaise.
Harvey Norman aims for a turnover of A$1.2 billion for the year ending June 30.
Coles Myer Ltd, Australia's largest retailer, did not provide December sales figures but expressed comfort with its performance.
Official data indicated that all areas of retailing except food weakened in the three months to November.

Over half a million people insured with National Mutual Holdings Ltd have purchased shares in the company.
National Mutual plans to list on the Australian and New Zealand exchanges next month.
Half of National Mutual's 1.2 million policy-holders have elected to take up their entitlement to shares.
National Mutual will have the largest shareholder base of any company in Australia and New Zealand.
Geoff Tomlinson is the managing director of National Mutual.
The offer price for retail investors is set at A$1.50 per share.
The price range for institutional investors is between A$1.35 and A$1.55 per share.
National Mutual will be among the top 50 companies by market capitalisation once listed.
The retail price of A$1.50 per share results in a market capitalisation of about A$2.5 billion.
National Mutual is the first major Australian life insurer to demutualise and list on the Australian market.

Australia risks losing face in Asia if it takes its overseas radio and television services off air.
An official report recommends that the government close Radio Australia and sell Australia Television.
Mark Dodgson, an expert on Australian business ties with Asia, criticized the report's recommendations as harmful to Australia's image.
Dodgson stated that Radio Australia and Australia Television are critical for Australian foreign policy and business.
Papua New Guinea has offered to reduce Australian aid if the funds could be used to ensure Radio Australia's future.
Radio Australia is often the only source of regional news in Papua New Guinea.
The report was prepared after a review of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC).
Australia Television has accumulated losses of about A$7.0 million since its establishment.
Radio Australia costs taxpayers about A$25 million per year and airs in seven Asian languages and English.
Australia Television is received in 33 countries across the region and has an option for a five-year lease on a satellite.

Pacific Dunlop Ltd is expected to announce a significant decline in first half earnings.
Analysts forecast a net profit before abnormals of around A$85 million for the six months to December 31.
This represents a 28 percent decrease compared to the previous year.
Forecasts for net profit before abnormals range between A$80 million and A$95 million.
Pacific Dunlop reported pre-abnormal net earnings of A$118 million for the first half of 1995/96.
The company experienced a 35 percent decline in pre-abnormal profit for the entire year of 1995/96.
Brokerages have been reducing their profit forecasts for Pacific Dunlop since the company warned of a weak start to the current year.
Pacific Dunlop's batteries division is facing significant issues due to problems at its U.S. lead smelter in Georgia.
The smelter has been operating below capacity and was previously shut down for redesign and modification.
The batteries division is expected to earn about half of what it did in the first half of 1995/96.

Comalco Ltd is an Australian aluminium producer.
Comalco Ltd is 67 percent owned by RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd.
Comalco is expected to report a pre-abnormal net profit of A$33 million for calendar 1996.
Comalco earned A$264.8 million in net profit in 1995.
Comalco may report a net abnormal loss of A$40 million due to its decision to end kaolin production.
Comalco was Asia's biggest supplier of kaolin clay used in paper manufacturing.
Comalco has warned of a poor second half of 1996.
Comalco's New Zealand plant is being upgraded to increase annual production by 40,000 tonnes to about 313,000 tonnes.
The average LME three-month aluminium price fell 16 percent in 1996.
Comalco's price premiums in Asia were pressured by weak demand in Europe.

Comalco Ltd is Australia's biggest aluminium producer.
Comalco announced a loss of A$16.8 million in calendar 1996.
In 1995, Comalco reported a net profit after abnormals of A$232.3 million.
Comalco's 1996 earnings before abnormals were A$32.9 million.
Comalco's share price fell eight cents following the loss announcement but ended at A$6.88.
Comalco is 67 percent owned by global mining group RTZ-CRA.
The London Metal Exchange aluminium price averaged 70 U.S. cents a pound in 1996.
The Australian dollar averaged 78 U.S. cents in 1996.
Comalco's operating profit was reduced by about A$201 due to lower aluminium prices and a strong local dollar.
Comalco predicts an increase in aluminium production and a stronger aluminium price in 1997.

Louisiana-Pacific Corp. will close its Ketchikan pulp mill in southeastern Alaska next year.
The closure follows failed negotiations with the Clinton administration over timber supply.
The company plans to take a $350 million charge against third-quarter pre-tax earnings.
The closure will idle about 500 workers in Ketchikan, a city of 15,000.
The pulp mill is set to close on March 24, 1997, after processing the existing supply of timber.
Louisiana-Pacific expects to operate two sawmills in the region for two more years under an agreement with the White House and Alaska Sen. Frank Murkowski.
The pulp mill lost an estimated $40 million in the first nine months of the year.
Louisiana-Pacific blames the closure on the Clinton administration's opposition to compromises for profitable operation.
Environmentalists claim the mill has benefited from federal timber contracts while causing pollution.
Louisiana-Pacific has filed lawsuits seeking $200 million for breach of contract.

Microsoft Corp.'s Windows 95 operating system was introduced on August 24, 1995.
More than 40 million copies of Windows 95 have been sold.
Windows 95 is the fastest-selling new software ever.
Microsoft spent tens of millions of dollars promoting Windows 95.
The product was delivered eight months late.
Analysts stated that Microsoft delivered a mixed message to business customers.
Rob Enderle is an analyst with Giga Information Group.
Scott Winkler is an analyst with Gartner Group.
Symantec Corp. posted disappointing financial results after the Windows 95 launch.
Touchstone Software Corp. settled a shareholders lawsuit for $1.3 million after sales failed to meet expectations.

Microsoft Corp. reported profits of $614 million for the latest quarter.
Earnings rose 23 percent from $499 million in the same quarter of the previous year.
Revenues increased 14 percent to $2.30 billion from $2.02 billion.
The profits exceeded Wall Street's expectations of 90 cents a share.
Shares of Microsoft rose to $136.375 in after-hours trading.
Microsoft cited strong acceptance of its Windows NT operating system.
Version 4.0 of Windows NT was shipped during the quarter.
Revenue growth for Windows NT servers and workstations was 19 percent over the previous quarter in the U.S. and Canada.
Sales of Windows NT server grew at nearly double the rate of other operating system environments.
Microsoft's Chief Financial Officer Mike Brown expects revenues to rise sequentially over the next two quarters.

A bankruptcy judge approved a reorganization plan for Morrison Knudsen Corp.
Dennis Washington will take over Morrison Knudsen Corp. for about $283 million.
Washington's main operating company is Washington Construction Group Inc.
Dennis Washington will become the non-executive chairman of Morrison Knudsen Corp.
Robert Tinstman will retain his titles as president and chief executive officer after the merger.
Washington owns 68.5 percent of Washington Construction Group shares.
The merged company will keep the Morrison Knudsen name and its Boise headquarters.
Shareholders of the old company will receive little value from the merger.
An analyst valued the distribution of stock in the new company at about 15 cents a share.
Bondholders will receive 93 to 95 percent of the $365 million they were owed.

An outbreak of bacterial food poisoning in the Seattle area has sickened at least 13 children and young adults.
The outbreak has been traced to tainted apple juice from Odwalla Inc.
Odwalla Inc is a fresh juice and beverage company based in Half Moon Bay, California.
Odwalla issued a nationwide recall of products containing fresh apple juice.
Many retailers removed all Odwalla beverages from their shelves.
Ten of the 13 confirmed cases of E. coli food poisoning were traced to unpasteurized Odwalla juice.
Three cases of E. coli food poisoning are still under investigation.
At least eight more suspected cases of food poisoning have been reported.
Six children have been hospitalized due to the outbreak, including two who required dialysis.
One 2-year-old boy remains hospitalized in satisfactory condition.

A federal appeals court overturned a jury verdict that ordered Nintendo Co. Ltd. to pay $253 million for patent infringement.
With interest, Nintendo could have been forced to pay nearly $300 million to Alpex Computer Corp.
The U.S. Court of Appeals in Washington, D.C. found a lack of substantial evidence to support a finding of infringement.
Alpex filed suit in 1986, claiming Nintendo's 8-bit game device used a patented 'bitmapping' display technology.
A U.S. District Court jury previously ordered Nintendo to pay a 6 percent royalty on over 35 million game units sold in the United States.
Alpex's technology was used in early generation video games made by Mattel, Atari, and Coleco.
Alpex previously won patent infringement settlements from Sega Enterprises Ltd. and others.
Nintendo Chairman Howard Lincoln stated that the case highlighted issues in the patent litigation system.
Lincoln expressed confidence that Nintendo would prevail if Alpex appealed to the full appeals court or the Supreme Court.
Lawyers for Alpex could not be reached for comment.

American Airlines plans to place an order for about $6 billion worth of Boeing Co. airplanes.
Airline Chairman Robert Crandall was scheduled to make a major company announcement at a news conference.
Officials of Boeing and American Airlines declined to comment on the order.
American Airlines is expected to announce an order for more than 100 new Boeing jets, including 12 wide-body 777s and 75 narrow-body 737s.
The exact size of the initial order has not been revealed.
The orders are expected to be contingent on ratification by pilots of a new six-year contract.
The board of the pilots union was voting on a tentative labor pact reached in September.
Industry analysts believe American Airlines could order hundreds of Boeing jets over the next two decades.
American Airlines currently does not operate the 737, which will replace 75 older 727 jets.
American Airlines plans to sell most of its wide-body MD-11 jets to Federal Express Corp.

Netscape Communications Corp launched its latest Navigator software on Monday.
Microsoft Corp officials stated they saw little new in Netscape's launch.
Netscape has partnered with over 20 content providers, including The New York Times and Sportsline USA.
Microsoft offered free trial subscriptions to services like The Wall Street Journal Interactive Edition and ESPN SportsZone with its Internet Explorer 3.0.
Netscape holds an estimated market share of over 80 percent in the browser market.
Industry analysts believe Microsoft's latest software poses a threat to Netscape's dominance.
More than 1 million users downloaded Microsoft's Internet Explorer since its release last Tuesday.
Netscape's stock closed at $36.50, its lowest since October, while Microsoft stock fell to $123.50.
Netscape's new Navigator features an electronic mail function that delivers information directly to users.
Microsoft referred to Netscape's electronic mail feature as 'glorified junk mail' and claimed its Internet Explorer offers faster multimedia access.

Boeing Co. agreed to acquire McDonnell Douglas Corp.
The acquisition received positive reactions from Wall Street.
Stock prices for Boeing and McDonnell Douglas increased following the announcement.
The all-stock transaction is valued at nearly $14 billion.
Boeing's workforce had been reduced by 30 percent over five years prior to the acquisition.
Boeing previously acquired Rockwell International Corp.'s defense and space business for $3.2 billion.
Boeing has received orders for $45.6 billion in new commercial jets.
Phil Condit became CEO of Boeing in April and initiated merger negotiations with McDonnell Douglas.
Executives from both companies stated the merger would enhance operating profits immediately.
Harry Stonecipher, CEO of McDonnell Douglas, stated the merger was not born of desperation.

Pyramid Breweries Inc. warned of lower-than-expected sales and earnings for the fourth quarter.
Pyramid Breweries attributed the warning to increasing competition in the craft beer industry.
Pyramid expects sales to be 20 percent to 25 percent below last year's levels on a wholesale basis.
Pyramid anticipates breaking even for the quarter, contrary to analysts' projections of earning 9 cents a share.
In last year's fourth quarter, Pyramid posted gross sales of $7 million and net income of about $1 million, or 13 cents a share.
Pyramid's stock fell 12.5 cents to $4.125 a share after the announcement.
Pyramid's stock ended an abbreviated trading session 25 cents lower at $4.
Redhook Ale Brewery Inc. warned of weak sales and was trading at $10.625 on Nasdaq.
Boston Beer Co., maker of Samuel Adams beer, was trading at $10 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Diane Daggatt of Dain Bosworth stated that not many new consumers are trying craft beers anymore.

Boeing Co. took orders for 717 jets valued at $53 billion last year.
Boeing had a 64 percent share of the world market for jets last year.
Boeing had net orders for 559 airplanes with a catalog value of $42.8 billion after excluding cancellations and conversions.
Airbus Industrie took orders for 301 jets worth $21.6 billion, giving it a 32 percent market share.
McDonnell Douglas Corp. took net orders for 38 jets valued at $2.2 billion, representing a 3 percent market share.
Boeing commercial airplane group President Ron Woodard stated that Boeing's customers put the company on top in 1996 due to the value of its airplanes.
Woodard expressed an expectation for 1997 to be as strong or stronger than 1996.
Boeing's order book exceeded analyst expectations and surpassed previous peak years from the late 1980s.
Boeing's previous best year for total orders was 1990, with 483 jets valued at $41.4 billion.
Boeing's total orders included a $6.5 billion order from American Airlines that was announced but not signed.

Microsoft Corp is expected to report modest earnings growth in the second quarter.
Analysts expect Microsoft to report earnings of $0.51 a share for the second quarter ended December 31.
This represents an increase of about 16 percent from the $0.44 a share reported a year earlier.
Revenues are expected to rise about 14 percent to more than $2.5 billion.
Last year's second quarter saw revenues soar 54 percent and net income up 48 percent.
Microsoft executives delayed the earnings report release from Thursday to Friday.
Analysts estimate that revenues from Office and its applications account for 20 to 30 percent of Microsoft's total.
Strong growth in personal computer sales and acceptance of Windows NT are contributing to Microsoft's profits.
Sales of PCs to consumers were sluggish in the quarter that just ended.
30 percent or fewer of corporate desktops have transitioned to Windows 95 or Windows NT systems.

Microsoft Corp's share price rose to record levels on Monday.
Microsoft warned of slowing growth in fiscal 1998.
Microsoft reported second-quarter earnings of $0.57 a share, up from $0.45 a year earlier.
The second-quarter earnings surpassed a consensus estimate of $0.51.
Frank Michnoff of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette commented that Microsoft had a great quarter.
Microsoft executives warned of a slowdown in growth in fiscal 1998 during an earnings statement and a conference call.
Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Mike Brown questioned the high valuation of the company's stock.
Piper Jaffray downgraded Microsoft's stock to hold from buy.
First Call reported that a consensus of 19 analysts estimated Microsoft would earn $2.33 a share for fiscal 1997.
Analysts expect Microsoft to earn $2.71 a share for fiscal 1998.

Cocoa producers have reached a compromise to oppose the use of non-cocoa fats in chocolate in the European Union.
Ivory Coast's commodities minister stated that Europeans can afford to buy pure chocolate.
Gauze, the outgoing head of the Cocoa Producers Alliance (CPA), mentioned that world cocoa demand could increase with the use of vegetable fats in some countries.
Malaysia has changed its position regarding the use of non-cocoa fats and now aligns with the CPA.
The ministers were reviewing a 1993 International Cocoa Agreement and planning to cut member output by 90,000 tonnes by the year 2000.
Gauze predicted that differences over CPA output projections for the next three years would be resolved by Tuesday.
Malaysia proposed a 1996/97 output of 120,000 tonnes, while the CPA projected 130,000 tonnes.
Ghana's output projections for 1996/97 differed from CPA projections by 20,000 tonnes.
Gauze expressed a desire to resolve all outstanding differences by the end of the meeting.
Ivory Coast opposes EU plans to allow up to five percent of non-cocoa fats in chocolate, citing potential demand reduction for cocoa.

Exporters oppose an Ivorian government plan to make them liable for income tax owed by upcountry buyers.
Tax laws approved by parliament in February allowed for deductions of about 7.5 percent of commission paid by exporters to agents buying cocoa.
Rene Ekra is the president of the GEPEX exporters' forum.
The dispute has contributed to export delays at the start of the 1996/97 marketing season.
Exporters expect a decision regarding the tax plan by the end of the week.
Exporters claim the plan means a deduction of about 2.5 CFA per kilo from buyers' commissions.
Buyers are currently paid a commission rate of about 32 CFA per kilo of collected cocoa.
Ivory Coast opened its 1996/97 cocoa marketing year on October 24 without setting new reference rates for exporters and buyers.
Exporters state that if the law is applied, the government should cover tax collection costs.
Donors indicate that the plan is part of a clampdown on tax evasion by up-country buyers.

Delayed export financing is slowing Ivory Coast cocoa arrivals.
Shipments for existing contracts will continue ahead of a government decision on licences and marketing rates.
The central bank has stopped backing private lenders.
Buying activity has slowed down in the past two days.
At least one major bank has stopped financing cocoa exports.
Exporters expect other banks to stop financing unless rates are published soon.
Exporters with licences from 1995/96 are continuing to buy and ship cocoa.
Ivory Coast opened its 1996/97 cocoa marketing season on October 24.
An announcement on guideline buyer and exporter marketing rates has been delayed.
Total port stocks are estimated to be over 100,000 tonnes.

Sporadic rain showers have continued to water Ivory Coast's cocoa belt up to the end of November.
Weather and crop analysts state that mid-crop campaign prospects are not yet clear.
A weather front expected to bring hot dry weather has backtracked to Ivory Coast's northern border.
Light rains have taken hold in dried out areas of Ivory Coast.
Rains usually fall in a sweep 200 km to the south of the weather front's position.
Crop analysts noted that the front's retreat meant no dramatic changes in cocoa pod development.
Continuing rains have been welcomed by crop analysts.
Weather data show variable rains for the last 10 days of November, with 650 percent of normal levels in Bondoukou.
An average of 30mm of rain fell at ten monitored weather stations in the last ten days of November.
Overall November rains rose from 104mm to 423mm before dropping to 295mm in the last third of the month.

Bulk cocoa shipments from West Africa are projected to exceed 325,000 tonnes in 1996/97.
This increase in shipments is attributed to a cost-cutting trend initiated by recent trial shipments.
A trader stated that most of the cocoa shipments will go to large buyers based in Amsterdam.
Ivory Coast is expected to ship approximately 270,000 tonnes of cocoa in bulk this year.
Ivory Coast was the largest producer and shipped 120,000 tonnes in bulk during 1995/96.
Of the total shipments this year, around 260,000 tonnes will be sent to two Amsterdam-based clients.
The expected crop for this year is between 900,000 and one million tonnes.
Less than half of the shipments, about 120,000 tonnes, will be shipped loose in holds.
The remainder of the shipments will be in twenty-foot bag-lined containers with drying agents.
Ghana is anticipated to increase its shipments to about 25,000 tonnes in December.

Ivorian cocoa arrivals for the 1996/97 season were around 390,000-410,000 tonnes by mid-December.
Analysts and exporters attributed the dip in December arrivals to crop profile and demand factors.
The figures for December 16 were down from an estimated 540,000 tonnes by the same date last year.
Some analysts suggested adding 50,000 tonnes to this year's total for comparative purposes due to a late season start.
Including the additional 50,000 tonnes, arrivals since October 1 would total 450,000 tonnes.
Arrivals at San Pedro since October 1 were reported to be between 130,000-140,000 tonnes.
The remainder of the cocoa arrivals went to the main port of Abidjan.
Exporters reported that subsequent arrivals up to December 22 were around 50,000 tonnes per week.
Exporters expected the deficit in arrivals compared to last year to increase in December before narrowing in January.
Rains had damaged bushtracks, causing delays in collection and raising humidity levels in some areas.

Voters in Chad participated in an election to transition to democracy.
Provisional election results are scheduled for January 15 and final results for January 25.
Runoffs for the election are scheduled for February 23.
Polling for the 125-seat assembly began last Thursday.
A total of 658 candidates from 49 parties are competing for the assembly.
The new national assembly is set to convene on March 31.
Chad has experienced coups, civil war, and conflict since its independence in 1960.
President Idriss Deby seized power in Chad in 1990 through a French-backed coup.
Approximately 3.5 million of Chad's 6.4 million people were eligible to vote.
Turnout in the capital for the election appeared lower than in previous polls.

Chad's oil production journey began in 2001 and is currently in financing and tender stages.
Chad's Foreign Minister Saleh Kebzabo expressed concerns about oil mismanagement based on experiences from other African countries.
Kebzabo stated that there have been no preparations at political and management levels regarding oil production.
Chad held its first multiparty legislative elections on January 5, marking a transition to peace after decades of civil strife.
Political leaders, including Lol Mahamet Choua, emphasized the need for laws to ensure that Chad's interests are prioritized.
Esso Exploration and Production Chad Inc. is part of a consortium with Shell and Elf, holding a 40 percent share each for Shell and Esso, and 20 percent for Elf.
The consortium sealed a deal with Chad in November regarding finance and legal terms for the main oil field located 350 miles south of N'Djamena.
The Doba oil field is expected to produce 900 million barrels over 15-20 years at a cost of $3 billion.
Chad's Gross National Product per capita income was $237 in 1995, one of the lowest in Africa.
Chad's economy relies on cotton, livestock, and gum arabic revenue and requires foreign currency after years of conflict.

Unilever subsidiary Blohorn will overhaul palm oil plantations and nine factories recently bought from Ivory Coast.
Blohorn holds a 34 percent stake in the plantations and factories, which produce a total of 190,000 tonnes of annual oil.
The plantations cover 36,000 hectares and require replanting at a rate of 4-6 percent per year due to ageing trees.
Some trees in the plantations have an average age of 22 years, necessitating extensive replanting.
Nine crop processing factories will be refurbished over two years.
Palmoil prices averaged around $380 a tonne in 1993, $680 in 1994, $650 in 1995, and $540 in 1996.
Export prices are currently around $560 a tonne, with expectations to stabilize at around $540 a tonne in 1997.
Blohorn's tender for stakes in two state-owned Palmindustrie blocks was accepted by Ivory Coast and signed on November 28 and December 27.
Blohorn partnered with SIFCA and SOCFIN SA to complete the purchase of the plantations and factories.
Output from the plantations will be used for domestic production of cooking oil and soaps, with some refined oil for export.

Demands for commodity auction rule changes will be a major topic in talks in Abidjan next week.
A World Bank official stated that they are ready to revisit the issue of amending auction rules.
Ivory Coast's Consultative Committee will meet in Abidjan from February 5-7 to review progress on the World Bank Agricultural Sector Adjustment Credit timetable.
Exporters are seeking immediate changes to the auction to ensure price competition and market transparency.
One exporter claimed that they have to pay too much and sell at a loss due to current auction rules.
The World Bank sponsored the auction as part of a $150 million loan from 1994, contingent on the application of rules and penalties.
A bank official noted that the Caistab has not provided sales data since September.
Contract allocation was previously managed by the Caistab as a state commodity marketing monopoly.
Donors agreed to two modifications in September but noted that initial overbidding had decreased since the auction system was implemented in May 1996.
One exporter expressed urgency for changes, stating that two-thirds of each year is sold forward, delaying the impact of new rules until 1999.

Port arrivals of 1996/97 Ivorian cocoa ranged between 745,000 and 755,000 tonnes by January 27.
This is a decrease from 800,000 tonnes in 1995/96.
Exporters reduced up-country buying due to a lack of storage space.
An Abidjan exporter reported having trucks waiting to unload but no space or pallets available.
Crop analysts reported heavy pod loads in southwestern Ivorian hybrid plantations.
Upcountry store managers indicated that their stocks would rise into February.
Favorable weather conditions before April could increase mid-crop cocoa volumes.
One plantation owner estimated a mid-crop forecast of 150,000 to 175,000 tonnes, depending on rain.
Others estimated the mid-crop figure at over 100,000 tonnes, with one forecaster estimating 200,000 tonnes.
The government forecasted 950,000 tonnes for 1996/97.

Delegates to Ivory Coast's cocoa Consultative Committee focused on bean quality and marketing on Thursday.
Cacao Barry managing director Alain Leblond expressed a preference for discussing cocoa quality and continuity of supply.
Ivory Coast's Consultative Committee was established in 1996 to monitor cocoa sector reforms since 1990.
International Cocoa Organization Chief Executive Edouard Kouame stated that changes must benefit farmers and local players.
Kouame emphasized the need to safeguard the legitimate interests of foreign traders, cocoa butter manufacturers, and chocolate industries.
An electronic export contract auction set up in May 1996 is seen as encouraging overbidding and concentrating export contracts.
Local exporters are allocated 85 percent of contracts, while foreign traders are allocated 15 percent.
Cocoa Association of London Chief Executive Philip Sigley raised concerns about the bidding process for export contracts.
Louis Bensdorp, Managing Director of the Netherlands Cocoa Association, noted that quality issues are linked to liberalization and the auction system.
Bensdorp highlighted the lack of quality checks and the education of farmers as major problems.

New Corp. Ltd. announced that its Fox News division will file a lawsuit against Time Warner Inc., Turner Broadcasting System Inc., and Chairman Ted Turner in U.S. District Court.
The lawsuit alleges antitrust violations related to blocking Fox News Channel in New York City.
News Corp. is led by Rupert Murdoch.
Arthur Siskind, News Corp. Group General Counsel, stated that the lawsuit will also charge Time Warner with breach of contract and fraud.
News Corp. urged city officials to void cable-TV franchises with Time Warner Inc.
News Corp. executives claimed that the pending merger of Time Warner and Turner constitutes a change of control of Time Warner's cable systems in New York City.
Time Warner holds city cable-television franchises serving 1.2 million New Yorkers that are set to expire in 1998.
Time Warner has refused to carry the 24-hour Fox News service and instead carries two Cable News Network services and MSNBC.
The merger between Turner and Time Warner is expected to occur on Thursday, creating the world's largest media organization.
Ted Turner will become vice chairman of the new company and will be its biggest shareholder.

BellSouth Corp will expand its network of wireless-telephony shops by a third.
BellSouth spends nearly $400 to acquire each new customer.
The company operates 200 or more outlets selling BellSouth Mobility cellular-telephone services.
BellSouth saves about $100 on each customer signed up by its own representatives.
BellSouth has 3.3 million U.S. cellular customers, increasing at a rate of 31 percent a year.
BellSouth has more than one million cellular customers in 11 other nations.
The share of wireless customers secured through BellSouth's directly owned shops is expected to rise.
BellSouth intends to keep the BellSouth Mobility brand for both personal communications services (PCS) and cellular.
Quarterly revenues from convenience telephone features for traditional wired telephone customers rose to $281 million in the third quarter.
Net income for BellSouth rose 12.9 percent to $631 million in the third quarter.

Silver King Communication acquired Home Shopping Network for $1.27 billion in a stock-swap deal.
The acquisition aims to advance Silver King's plans to become a conventional broadcast-TV powerhouse.
Barry Diller is the chairman of Silver King and has led the launch of the Fox network in the 1980s.
Silver King spokesman Jason Stewart stated that Diller has no firm plans to launch a new network at this time.
Silver King intends to reprogram its 12 stations currently carrying Home Shopping Network with locally oriented shows.
Some Silver King stations in major markets like New York, Los Angeles, and Miami will be converted in about a year.
The reprogramming will include local news and sports, following a common format across all Silver King stations.
Silver King plans to seek cable-system carriage for Home Shopping Network as its stations transition to traditional programming.
Diller indicated that the conversion from Home Shopping Network would take two to three years.
Analyst Alvin Mirman stated that the deal could reduce Home Shopping's distribution costs by as much as $40 million a year.

Time Warner Inc. will launch its CNN/SI sports news service on Dec. 12.
CNN/SI will combine the television apparatus of the Cable News Network and the sports expertise of Sports Illustrated.
Sports Illustrated is a weekly sports magazine published by Time Warner since 1954.
CNN will simultaneously carry a nightly sports news program for CNN/SI subscribers.
CNN reaches approximately 70 million U.S. homes.
Thirteen advertisers, including General Motors Corp., LCI International, and Delta Airlines, have signed on with CNN/SI.
ESPNEWS, majority owned by Disney, began service on Nov. 1.
CNN/SI competes against NewSport, a 24-hour sports news service owned by General Electric Co. unit NBC.
NBC, in alliance with Microsoft Corp., launched the all-news service MSNBC last summer to compete against CNN.
News Corp. has launched a general news TV service and is seeking a channel slot on Time Warner's New York cable systems.

VTR Galaxy Chile SA received government permission to offer direct-to-home (DTH) television in Chile.
DIRECTV will start selling its service in Chile by March 31.
The approval was granted by the Transportation and Telecommunications Ministry.
DIRECTV is a consortium that includes a Hughes Electronics unit and three Latin American companies.
Jose Antonio Rios is the chief executive of Galaxy Latin America.
Advertising for the service will begin around the middle of December.
Promotional methods will include billboards, newspaper ads, television, and in-store demonstrations.
VTR is a partnership between Luksic and Southwestern Bell Corp.
DIRECTV offers approximately 100 channels of video, music, and extra-fee film channels.
DIRECTV has been successful in the United States since its launch in 1994.

Grand Metropolitan Plc's Burger King is expected to post $10 billion in sales for the fiscal year ending September 30.
Burger King chief executive Robert Lowes stated that his goal for the year is to add a billion in sales.
Burger King's worldwide sales totaled $9 billion in fiscal 1996, which is a nine percent increase from the previous year.
Burger King's market share rose to 16.2 percent of all fast-food hamburger restaurant sales.
Burger King competes against McDonald's Corp and Wendy's International Inc.
Comparable store sales increased by 2.3 percent worldwide and 2.6 percent in the United States.
Operating profits at Burger King declined in the last fiscal year due to a European beef scare and a planned reduction in sales of restaurants to franchisees.
European sales were negatively impacted by a disease outbreak linked to contaminated British beef.
Burger King responded to the beef scare by introducing chicken and other food options, including a vegetarian hamburger in Britain.
Lowes mentioned that new stores, including 75 to be built along British motorways, would help increase sales.

Tony O'Reilly is the chairman of Independent Newspapers Plc.
O'Reilly stated that acquisitions by Independent Newspapers Plc will slow considerably next year.
O'Reilly referred to next year as a year of consolidation for the company.
O'Reilly's name was mentioned as a rumored buyer of Mirror Group Newspapers Plc's 46 percent stake in Independent Newspapers Plc.
Both Mirror Group and O'Reilly denied that a deal was in the works.
O'Reilly's firm owns a 46 percent stake in the British title of Independent Newspapers Plc.
O'Reilly acknowledged that his company is monitoring Australian media group John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
Conrad Black sold a 20 percent stake in Fairfax after expressing concerns about foreign ownership limits.
Rupert Murdoch sold his five percent stake in Fairfax and stated he lost interest in the company due to foreign ownership ceilings.
Independent Newspapers owns a 25 percent stake in APN, an Australian regional newspaper company.

R.J. Reynolds executives considered using additives to enhance the nicotine kick of cigarettes.
R.J. Reynolds also considered increasing marketing efforts targeted at teenagers.
R.J. Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
R.J. Reynolds turned over documents to Minnesota state lawyers in connection with a lawsuit.
Minnesota and 17 other states are suing R.J. Reynolds and other tobacco companies to recover money spent on treating smoking-related illnesses.
Trials related to these lawsuits are scheduled this year in Mississippi, Florida, and Texas.
R.J. Reynolds expects anti-tobacco information to be selectively leaked to news organizations by opposing lawyers.
R.J. Reynolds released three excerpts from 4.5 million pages of documents with its own explanations.
Two documents turned over to Minnesota lawyers suggested that R.J. Reynolds studied adding ammonia compounds to increase nicotine effects in the 1970s.
R.J. Reynolds deputy general counsel Daniel Donohue stated that the documents could be used to support claims of nicotine manipulation.

Cigarette companies dropped pre-trial opposition to punitive claims by the state of Florida in an anti-tobacco lawsuit.
Florida is seeking $1 billion or more from U.S. cigarette makers for costs incurred in its Medicaid healthcare program for treating smoking-related ailments.
Punitive damages could significantly increase potential losses for the cigarette industry if Florida wins the case.
Florida won the right to claim further damages under the state's anti-racketeering laws.
State lawyers indicated that racketeering claims could cost cigarette makers tens of billions of dollars.
A lawyer for Philip Morris Cos Inc. stated that ending pre-trial opposition had no legal effect and that the industry had never paid punitive damages in any lawsuit.
Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth described the action as a victory and a major legal concession by the industry.
Butterworth stated that he was forbidden by court order from detailing damaging information in 27,000 pages of documents to be presented on January 24.
Much of the material in the documents was gathered by other attorneys general cooperating in anti-tobacco lawsuits filed by 18 states.
Philip Morris lawyer Gregory Little expressed concern that state lawyers would present evidence against cigarette makers during the January 24 hearing.

Ryder System Inc is negotiating with several banks to create securitized financial offerings for up to 15,000 leased trucks annually.
A first offering of securitized truck leases could occur as early as March 1997.
Total offerings could reach $700 million by the end of 1997, according to Ryder's chief financial officer Ed Huston.
Huston stated that the plan involves selling a package of leases, similar to mortgage-backed securities.
No agreement has been finalized, and unforeseen issues could impede the plan.
Ryder is in the process of selecting a bank for the deal but has not disclosed which banks are being considered.
Citicorp is currently a primary financing source for Ryder.
Ryder announced a $215 million pre-tax charge related to restructuring, early retirement, and layoffs affecting approximately 2,100 employees.
The restructuring is expected to save Ryder $75 million in 1997 and $150 million annually thereafter.
Merrill Lynch analyst Jeff Kauffman noted that the charge was larger than Wall Street anticipated and reflects management's commitment to change.

Kay Koplovitz is the chief executive of U.S.A. Networks.
Koplovitz stated that Latin American television will continue to grow into the 21st century.
Pan-regional advertising in Latin America is expected to reach $1 billion within a decade.
In 1996, cross-border advertising on Latin American cable television and Direct-to-Home (DTH) was between $50 million and $75 million.
Latin America has 80 million television households.
Audiences for cable and DTH in Latin America are affluent and younger than those in North America.
Some industry analysts have questioned the appeal of pan-regional programming and advertising in Latin America.
Koplovitz compared the state of multiple-channel television in Latin America to the early days of U.S. cable television in the 1970s.
Koplovitz emphasized the need for a reliable, standardized pan-regional measuring system.
Kagan Associates projected that cable television and DTH revenues in Latin America will grow to $8.1 billion by 2001.

Florida is implementing anti-smoking measures by prohibiting cigarette promotions on state roads.
Marlboro has removed its name from banners promoting the Marlboro Grand Prix of Miami motor race.
New rules regarding banner promotions for sports events will be published on Friday and take effect in early March.
The new rules apply to banners for beer, tobacco, and other products intended for adults.
Promoters can include a product name on banners but cannot use logos or colors associated with banned products.
Department spokeswoman Lynn Holschuh stated that corporate names attached to sporting events are allowed.
Banners advertising products that cannot be sold to minors cannot contain logos or significant advertising for those products.
Advertising on billboards located on private property will not be affected by the new rules for state roadways.
The new rules do not apply to municipal, Interstate, and other roads maintained by different governments.
Philip Morris Cos. Inc. decided to drop the Marlboro name from the banners as a courtesy.

Lawyers in a class-action suit against cigarette makers won the right to question and videotape the chief executives of several top tobacco companies.
The chief executives covered in the order include those from Brown & Williamson, Philip Morris Cos Inc, RJ Reynolds Tobacco, and Lorillard.
The order was issued by Dade County Judge Robert Kaye.
Stanley Rosenblatt is one of the lawyers bringing the class-action suit on behalf of U.S. flight attendants allegedly sickened by second-hand smoke.
Rosenblatt may use the videotapes at a trial in Dade County Court scheduled to begin in June.
Rosenblatt alleges that tobacco company scientists and executives conspired to hide the dangers of smoking.
The suit covers an estimated 60,000 flight attendants who never smoked and suffer from lung ailments or other sicknesses.
Moss and other tobacco company lawyers argued that Rosenblatt had previously questioned tobacco industry chief executives.
Rosenblatt argued that many of the executives he questioned had retired and that many industry documents supporting his claims had become public.
Kaye will privately review some 1,500 industry documents for possible use by Rosenblatt in the trial.

China expressed willingness to cooperate with other countries to maintain peace on the Korean peninsula.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang stated that China is paying great attention to the situation on the Korean peninsula.
Relations between South Korea and North Korea worsened when 26 North Koreans landed in South Korea from a stranded submarine.
South Korean troops have killed or found dead 22 of the infiltrators, captured one, and are searching for three remaining infiltrators.
North Korea threatened 'merciless retaliation' for the deaths of its soldiers and demanded the return of the submarine and any survivors.
South Korea stated that any provocation from North Korea will meet 'stern punishment' and has increased security at various locations.
China was an ally of North Korea during the Korean War from 1950 to 1953 and remains one of its few diplomatic allies.
China also considers South Korea an important trading partner.
South Korea and the United States called for four-nation peace talks with North Korea and China to replace the truce that ended the Korean conflict.
North Korea has insisted on bilateral talks with the United States, claiming South Korea is not a party to the 1953 truce.

Financial analysts and economists stated that China's rising foreign debt should not cause anxiety due to a booming economy and large foreign exchange reserves.
Beijing is cautious about raising its foreign debt despite strong demand for capital.
Foreign debt in China rose 6.3 percent to $109.57 billion at the end of June compared to the previous year, according to the State Administration of Exchange Control.
Total foreign debt increased by 2.8 percent, or $2.98 billion, compared to the end of 1996.
The growth in foreign debt is lagging behind the expansion of the economy, indicating that Beijing is maintaining control over overseas borrowing.
A foreign analyst in Beijing commented that the increase in debt is not alarming relative to the size of the economy.
Beijing's tight limits on debt are influenced by the need to restrain companies seeking capital and the communist leadership's reluctance to incur foreign debt.
Demand for foreign loans and investment has increased due to China's economic growth and ambitious infrastructure plans.
China's foreign exchange reserves reached a record $95.0 billion by the end of September, allowing for increased debt levels without harming lender confidence.
A senior Chinese economist noted that the rise in total debt was a response to a slight reduction in foreign direct investment and ongoing capital demand.

China needs to make changes to its economy to join the World Trade Organisation.
James McGregor is the chairman of the American Chamber of Commerce in China.
McGregor stated that Beijing should take foreign investors' dissatisfaction seriously.
A crackdown on dissidents in China could harm relations with Washington, according to McGregor.
McGregor suggested that China should show sincerity in its business dealings.
Chinese officials have blamed the United States for blocking their entry into the WTO.
No other country wants to ease entry requirements for China to a non-viable level, according to McGregor.
The terms of China's entry into the WTO would affect other applicants.
McGregor noted that the American business community should be aware of anti-U.S. sentiments in China.
McGregor believes that China's achievements in economic reform could foster positive nationalism.

China's economy grew by 9.6 percent in the first nine months of 1996.
Many urban family incomes are lagging behind despite economic growth, according to the State Statistical Bureau.
Chinese industrial output increased and farmers were expected to achieve record grain harvests.
Inflation was reported at a year-on-year rate of 6.6 percent in the first three quarters of 1996.
Gross domestic product was 4.5675 trillion yuan ($550.3 billion) from January to September 1996.
China's GDP grew by 10.2 percent in 1995.
The average urban income rose to 3,249 yuan ($391) between January and September 1996, a year-on-year increase of 3.4 percent.
A survey indicated that the incomes per family member of around 40 percent of households had declined.
Some income decline was attributed to the birth of children or the retirement of older family members.
About half of the families surveyed experienced income falls due to inflation or stagnant income growth.

The family of jailed Chinese dissident Wei Jingsheng welcomed a decision by the European Parliament to award him a prize for freedom of thought.
Beijing criticized the award as rude interference in its internal affairs.
Wei Jingsheng has spent most of the last two decades in jail.
Wei's brother, Wei Xiaotao, expressed gratitude to the European Parliament for its support.
The Chinese foreign ministry stated that the award encouraged actions against the Chinese government.
Wei Jingsheng was jailed for 15 years in 1979 and was paroled for less than a year before being detained again in April 1994.
In December, Wei was sentenced to an additional 14 years in prison for subversion and for funding democracy activists.
The European Parliament announced that Wei won the 15,000 Ecu Sakharov prize for freedom of thought.
The award ceremony is scheduled to take place in Strasbourg in December.
Wei Jingsheng is regarded as the father of Chinese pro-democracy dissent and is a nominee for this year's Nobel Peace Prize.

Officials from the six nations of the Mekong river region arrived in southwestern China for a ministerial conference.
The conference aims to boost cooperation in the Mekong region, which has faced distrust and war.
The sixth meeting of the Greater Mekong Sub-region (GMS) programme is taking place in Kunming city.
Ministers from Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Burma, and China are reviewing regional infrastructure projects worth billions of dollars.
An environmental action plan to curb deforestation on the upper reaches of the Mekong will be considered at the meeting.
The GMS programme aims to move from project planning to implementation.
A proposed $490 million road project to connect Bangkok, Phnom Penh, and Ho Chi Minh city is expected to gain ministerial approval.
Other projects under consideration include a $1.8 to $2.1 billion railway from China to Southeast Asia and a telecommunications and power transmission network.
The GMS programme has contributed to transforming the region from a war-torn area to an attractive investment destination.
Relations between the six nations have improved, despite ongoing conflicts in Cambodia and political divides in Burma.

China has ordered two Hong Kong democracy activists, Wong Chung-ki and Chui Pak-tai, to leave the country.
The activists attempted to petition Beijing officials regarding the political future of Hong Kong.
Beijing police issued a warning to Wong and Chui, instructing them to return to Hong Kong within a specified time.
Officials at a Beijing hotel filed a public disturbance complaint against Wong and Chui for distributing materials to reporters.
Anxiety has increased in Hong Kong regarding the level of political freedom China will allow after regaining control.
Chinese dissident Wang Dan was sentenced to 11 years in prison by a Beijing court.
Chinese authorities barred two other pro-democracy advocates, Andrew To and Chan Kwok-leung, from entering the country.
To and Chan were detained for two hours at the Sha Tau Kok border post before being refused entry.
All four activists intended to lobby the China-selected Preparatory Committee regarding the selection of Hong Kong's chief executive.
The activists' statement accused China of using undemocratic methods to choose the chief executive and condemned the barring of their colleagues.

Beijing accused the United States of pursuing hostile policies towards China.
The People's Daily is the official mouthpiece of China's ruling Communist Party.
The People's Daily stated that U.S. media has attacked and sullied China.
U.S. Undersecretary of State Lynn Davis began talks on arms proliferation in Beijing.
The talks are part of a visit aimed at rebuilding strained ties between the U.S. and China.
Both sides claim that relations have improved in recent months after high-level meetings.
The Chinese state press has issued condemnations of U.S. policies and individuals seen as hostile.
People's Daily criticized a New York Times article by former U.S. ambassador James Lilley.
Lilley's opinion piece warned that nationalism in China could be dangerous.
People's Daily stated that Chinese patriotism is not the same as blind xenophobia.

A concert featuring prominent Chinese pop stars took place in Beijing on Friday.
The concert had an audience of around 18,000 people at the Capital Gymnasium.
The event was the first part of a double concert intended to celebrate the growth of the Chinese pop music industry.
The Chinese pop music industry was banned during the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976.
Some influential rock stars were excluded from the concert playlist due to political reasons.
The concert primarily featured pop songs focused on themes of love and friendship.
Harder-edged music was absent from the concert due to disapproval from communist authorities.
Cui Jian, known as the father of Chinese rock music, was not scheduled to perform at the concert.
Cui Jian's music includes politically-sensitive lyrics and has been popular among listeners.
Cui Jian has been effectively banned from performing in Beijing since 1993.

China's power minister Shi Dazhen stated that foreign investors are expected to provide one-fifth of the 700 billion yuan ($84 billion) to be invested in power generation between 1996 and 2000.
Shi Dazhen mentioned that foreign investment in the electricity generation sector would be carefully channeled to boost China's domestic industry.
A legal framework has been established in China to protect foreign investors, according to Shi Dazhen.
Beijing plans to improve its laws and regulations to ensure that the interests of investors are guaranteed.
China's electricity generating capacity is projected to reach 290,000 megawatts by the end of 2000, up from 217,000 megawatts at the end of 1995.
During the ninth five-year plan from 1996 to 2000, China will require around 700 billion yuan ($84.4 million) in investment for the power sector.
Foreign investors are expected to contribute approximately 20 percent, or around $17 billion, of the total investment needed.
The central government is expected to provide 40 percent of the investment, while local authorities and enterprises will contribute the remaining 40 percent.
Shi Dazhen stated that he was unaware of a $20 billion figure mentioned by other senior power officials regarding foreign investment needs.
Shi Dazhen acknowledged that foreign investors have expressed concerns about a 15 percent limit on returns on investment from Chinese power plant projects, but he dismissed these concerns as impractical.

China stated that a visit by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher could help maintain Sino-U.S. relations.
China warned that differences remain on sensitive issues such as trade and human rights.
Warren Christopher is the highest level U.S. official to visit Beijing in two years.
Christopher was scheduled to arrive in Beijing on Tuesday evening for meetings aimed at improving Sino-U.S. ties.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai expressed hope that Christopher's visit could aid in the healthy development of Sino-U.S. relations.
Cui Tiankai criticized U.S. policies on trade, human rights, and arms sales to Taiwan.
China has sent mixed signals to Washington prior to Christopher's visit, combining conciliatory language with tough rhetoric.
Sino-U.S. relations have been affected by disputes over trade, human rights, copyright piracy, arms proliferation, and Taiwan.
Cui Tiankai stated that differences in Sino-U.S. trade should not be resolved through threats of economic force.
Cui claimed that cases like Wang Dan's are judicial matters and not human rights issues related to Sino-U.S. relations.

China defended U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, accusing the United States of financial blackmail to prevent his re-election.
The People's Daily stated that Boutros-Ghali had contributed to world development during his five-year term.
The United States was the only country on the U.N. Security Council to oppose Boutros-Ghali's re-election.
The U.S. vetoed Boutros-Ghali's candidacy, citing slow progress on U.N. reform and linking it to delayed payment of $1.4 billion in membership dues.
People's Daily claimed that linking Boutros-Ghali's reappointment to membership dues was an attempt to blackmail the United Nations.
The editorial stated that all U.N. members are responsible for paying dues and criticized U.S. opposition to Boutros-Ghali.
People's Daily argued that the U.S. had not provided valid reasons for opposing Boutros-Ghali's renewal.
The Yangcheng Daily reported that Boutros-Ghali's opposition to U.S. hegemony was a reason for U.S. opposition to his re-election.
The U.S. Congress is delaying payment of $1.4 billion owed to the United Nations, which is affecting the organization's finances.
Diplomats indicated that African nations are advocating for Boutros-Ghali's re-election, seeking a compromise or change in U.S. policy.

There is strong demand for new telephone lines and services like caller ID at regional Bells and GTE Corp.
Earnings growth for regional Bells is expected to remain robust in the third quarter.
Bette Massick of Bear Stearns reported strong demand for new services.
Merrill Lynch analyst Dan Reingold expects third quarter average annual growth of 8.1 percent.
The expected growth of 8.1 percent is lower than the 9.6 percent growth in the second quarter.
Analysts generally favor buy ratings for Ameritech Corp, BellSouth Corp, SBC Communications Inc, and GTE.
Guy Woodlief of Dean Witter Reynolds considers Ameritech and GTE as attractive stocks.
Regional Bells have underperformed the broad market this year due to competition fears.
The Federal Communications Commission stated that the Telecom Act of 1996 requires Bells to face competition before entering long distance markets.
GTE is an exception as it already offers long distance services in 23 states with over 250,000 customers.

AT&T Corp chairman and chief executive Robert Allen will step down early to attract a successor.
Sources indicate that the successor to Alex Mandl, who resigned in August, would likely take over before Allen's contract ends.
AT&T has not commented on the search for Mandl's successor or whether that candidate would succeed Allen.
Analysts suggest that Allen may split the role of chief executive with the new candidate while retaining his chairmanship.
Mark Bruneau from COBA MID believes Allen will remain in a senior position for some time.
The telecommunications market is expected to change significantly in the coming years.
The AT&T board is scheduled to meet next Wednesday, potentially to discuss the succession issue.
Allen has expressed willingness to leave early if a suitable candidate is found.
AT&T has engaged Korn Ferry and Spencer Stuart to assist in the search for an outside candidate.
William Esry of Sprint Corp and Michael Armstrong of Hughes Electronics Corp have both stated they are not candidates for the AT&T position.

GTE Corp expects to increase earnings per share by at least 10 percent for the foreseeable future.
GTE Corp anticipates revenues to rise six to eight percent per year.
GTE reported third quarter earnings per share of $0.78, which is 10 percent higher than the previous year.
GTE's earnings per share were in line with analysts' consensus estimates.
GTE experienced a 7.4 percent rise in access lines and a 20 percent growth in cellular users.
GTE's stock price was 41-3/8 in early afternoon trading.
GTE's local calling areas are mostly suburban, where families are likely to telecommute.
GTE's areas are concentrated in economically strong regions like Florida and California.
GTE has reduced customer turnover in cellular services, resulting in lower marketing costs.
GTE's average monthly bills are $61, which is $3 above the industry average.

Regional Bells are building out more telephone lines and adding new services.
Share analysts report that the Bells and GTE Corp show strong demand.
Bill Vogel of Dillon Read characterized the quarter as a cause for celebration for regional Bell stocks.
Bell Atlantic Corp, BellSouth Corp, Pacific Telesis Group, and SBC Communications Inc reported results on Thursday.
Ameritech Corp reported results on Tuesday and GTE Corp on Wednesday.
NYNEX Corp and U S West Inc are scheduled to report next week.
Earnings per share growth averaged 8.25 percent, with a range from 3.0 percent at Ameritech to 12.5 percent at BellSouth.
Annual access line growth averaged 4.9 percent, driven by demand for Internet access and additional business lines.
Ameritech experienced a dip in line growth to 3.7 percent, attributed to a drop in advertising.
Pacific Telesis reported strong results due to a recovery in the California economy.

Robert Allen is the current chairman and chief executive of AT&T Corp.
The successor to Robert Allen will need to address AT&T's loss of market share and explore new market opportunities.
AT&T's core long distance market share has decreased from 60 percent to 55 percent in two years.
Analyst Bill Deatherage stated that AT&T needs to increase its growth rate and change its mentality.
Consultant Chris Landis emphasized that AT&T cannot win by competing solely on price.
AT&T's acquisition of McCaw Cellular was a positive move into wireless, but product integration has not yet occurred.
The new chief operating officer is expected to quickly transition to the role of chief executive and chairman.
Sources indicate that AT&T has a shortlist of candidates for the CEO position, but none have been publicly identified.
Richard Notebaert from Ameritech Corp has been mentioned as a potential successor to Robert Allen.
AT&T and the executive search firms involved have not commented on the succession issue.

AT&T Corp is losing market share and struggling in new markets.
Wall Street expected a well-known industry leader to replace Chairman Robert Allen.
AT&T appointed John Walter, chairman and chief executive of R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co, as its new president and chief operating officer.
John Walter will not take over as chief executive from Robert Allen until January 1998.
Walter will become chairman at AT&T's annual meeting four months after becoming chief executive.
Consultant Jeffrey Kagan stated that Walter may be what AT&T needs, but it will take time to know for sure.
Analysts say Walter is respected but has not faced challenges on the scale of those at AT&T.
AT&T's share in the long distance telephone market has decreased from 60 percent to around 55 percent in two years.
AT&T stock has fallen 16 percent this year, while the broad market has risen.
Barry Sine of SBC Warburg cut his rating on AT&T stock to hold from buy.

WorldCom Inc. agreed to acquire MFS Communications Co. Inc. in a stock swap worth about $14 billion.
The combined company will be called MFS WorldCom.
MFS WorldCom will provide businesses with local and long-distance telephone, data communications, and Internet services on one network.
Bernard Ebbers is the chief executive of WorldCom.
The merger is expected to create the first company since the breakup of AT&T to bundle local and long-distance services under one company.
The deregulation of the telecommunications industry is expected to enable end-to-end service.
WorldCom is the fourth largest U.S. long-distance company.
The merger will allow WorldCom to enter business markets previously dominated by regional Bells and major long-distance providers.
The merged company will have annual sales of about $5.4 billion and over 500,000 business customers in North America, Europe, and Asia.
The merger is expected to close within eight months.

Soaring Internet usage is bringing the United States phone system close to gridlock.
Industry experts and analysts report that millions of local phone lines are tied up every evening.
Amir Atai is the director of network and traffic performance at BellCore.
Atai compares the situation to gridlock on a highway, where adding more vehicles leads to congestion.
Internet use is rising at 42 percent a year according to industry studies.
NYNEX Corp. spokeswoman Susan Butta states that Internet usage on their network is growing at 10 percent a month.
Gridlock in phone networks results in fewer calls going through on the first try, more busy signals, and blocked calls.
The bottleneck is confined to local networks and does not affect long distance carriers.
Industry studies suggest that if U.S. Internet penetration reaches 15 percent, it would require a $22 billion investment by regional Bell phone companies.
California currently has the highest Internet penetration at eight percent.

MCI Communications Corp. is the No. 2 long distance phone company.
MCI Communications Corp. is in talks to be acquired by British Telecommunications Plc.
The potential merger between MCI and British Telecommunications Plc could be one of the biggest ever.
British Telecommunications Plc holds a 20 percent stake in MCI.
Analysts speculate the acquisition price could be $40 a share, valuing MCI at $28 billion.
British Telecommunications Plc would need to pay $22.1 billion for the 80 percent of MCI it does not already own.
MCI expects the acquisition talks to conclude over the weekend.
Analysts believe a merger would be beneficial in the U.S. long distance phone industry.
A merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI would be the largest between a British and American company.
British Telecommunications Plc plans to offer a mixture of cash and stock for the remaining 80 percent of MCI.

A $22 billion merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp is nearing agreement.
This merger would be the largest international business combination in record time.
A London news conference is scheduled for 8 a.m. EST (1300 GMT) on Sunday.
MCI will hold a news conference in New York at 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT).
Consultant Jeffrey Kagan stated that the deal sounds like a done deal.
BT is expected to announce a $40 per share stock and cash offer for MCI.
The offer values the 80 percent of MCI that BT does not own at $22.1 billion.
The entire company would be valued at $28 billion.
If BT uses mainly stock for the merger, MCI shareholders could own up to 37 percent of the combined company.
The combined company would have revenues of $38 billion, 182,000 employees, and a market value of $64 billion.

MCI Communications Corp announced a $20 billion merger with British Telecommunications Plc.
The merger is expected to strengthen the combined company in international calling, consulting, and U.S. local calling.
MCI Chief Financial Officer Doug Maine stated that the merger will allow them to compete with any telecommunications company globally.
Maine mentioned that combining MCI's Systemhouse with BT's Syntegra will enhance their consulting and systems integration capabilities.
Analysts believe MCI can provide significant consulting advantages to BT.
Danny Briere from Telechoice noted that BT is struggling in U.K. systems integration.
Maine predicted the merger could expedite the end of the international settlements system, which affects international call rates.
The international settlements system is facing challenges due to market liberalization in countries like Germany.
Analysts expect that as the international market opens, calling rates for customers will decrease.
Maine highlighted the potential profitability in the $90 billion U.S. local market, particularly through MCI Metro.

MCI Communications Corp. is merging with British Telecommunications Plc in a deal valued at $20 billion.
MCI is reducing its stake in a U.S. satellite joint venture with Rupert Murdoch's News Corp from 50 percent to 20 percent.
MCI Chief Executive Bert Roberts stated that no major new launches are expected from the $400 million media joint venture with News Corp.
MCI plans to sell a $700 million satellite license to Rupert Murdoch if possible.
MCI holds a stake of just under 9 percent in News Corp, which it acquired for $1.35 billion.
MCI has an option to invest an additional $1 billion to increase its stake in News Corp to 13.5 percent.
Roberts indicated that it is unlikely MCI will increase its investment in News Corp.
MCI's electronic malls on the Internet have been closed, and News Corp's plans for supermarket tabloids have been shelved.
The satellite venture American Sky Broadcasting (ASkyB) has faced development challenges and high costs.
MCI and News Corp announced plans to offer digital television direct to homes in the U.S. within two years using the $700 million license.

PrimeCo is a mobile telephone venture owned by AirTouch Communications Inc and three regional Bells.
PrimeCo expects a tougher competition with Sprint Corp in the wireless market than with AT&T Corp.
PrimeCo launched Personal Communications Services (PCS) in 16 cities on Tuesday.
PrimeCo's PCS offers smaller phones with more features, longer battery life, and clearer sound than cellular.
Ben Scott, the chief executive of PrimeCo, stated that they believe they have a quality advantage over AT&T.
Ben Scott mentioned that both PrimeCo and Sprint use code division multiple access (CDMA) technology.
Scott expressed uncertainty about whether PrimeCo can establish a better brand for wireless services than Sprint.
AT&T, Sprint, and PrimeCo are the only three firms that spent enough on Federal PCS licenses in 1995 to build national networks.
Analysts predict that significant competition will arise in one to two years when multiple PCS and digital cellular operators are present in every market.
Scott expects PrimeCo to spend about as much on advertising as AT&T Corp by mid-1997.

Stiff competition and high ingredient costs are expected to result in flat to lower earnings for several U.S. food companies.
Quaker Oats Co is expected to report flat earnings for the third quarter.
The Snapple beverage line is negatively impacting Quaker Oats Co's earnings.
Goldman Sachs analyst Nomi Ghez predicts a double-digit volume decline for Snapple.
Quaker Oats Co's new promotional campaign for Snapple was implemented too late to provide financial benefits this year.
Snapple accounts for about 10 percent of Quaker Oats Co's annual sales.
Kellogg Co projects its third quarter earnings will be about 20 percent below last year.
Ralcorp Holdings Inc is expected to incur a loss in the fiscal fourth quarter due to stiff competition.
IBP Inc is likely to see a decline in third quarter earnings due to lower profit margins and higher cattle costs.
CPC International Inc is projected to report a modest rise in third quarter earnings due to high corn prices.

Archer Daniels Midland Co has a $100 million agreement with the U.S. Justice Department.
The financial impact of the agreement on Archer Daniels Midland Co is expected to be minimal.
Archer Daniels Midland Co has approximately $1.3 billion in cash and cash equivalents.
Two top executives at Archer Daniels Midland Co may face indictments related to an antitrust investigation.
The antitrust investigation involves lysine, citric acid, and high fructose corn syrup.
Archer Daniels Midland Co has previously indicated that indictments were being considered against Michael Andreas and Terrance Wilson.
The U.S. Justice Department's investigation into Archer Daniels Midland Co is ongoing.
The $100 million in fines is a record for the Justice Department in an antitrust case.
Archer Daniels Midland Co agreed to pay $70 million for lysine and $30 million for citric acid as part of the settlement.
The settlement concludes the Justice Department's antitrust probe of high fructose corn syrup without any fines for that product.

Archer Daniels Midland Co. pleaded guilty to price fixing.
Archer Daniels Midland Co. will face criticism from shareholders at its October 17 annual meeting.
Edward Durkin is the director of special programmes at the United Brotherhood of Carpenters.
The United Brotherhood of Carpenters is one of four institutional shareholders seeking changes in ADM's board.
Jon Lukomnik is the New York City deputy controller for pensions.
Jon Lukomnik stated that corporate governance issues remain at ADM despite the settlement with the U.S. Justice Department.
Archer Daniels Midland Co. paid $100 million in fines as part of the settlement.
Dwayne Andreas is the chairman of Archer Daniels Midland Co. and is 78 years old.
Michael Andreas, the vice chairman, is under investigation by the Justice Department.
Terrance Wilson is the ADM Group Vice President also being investigated by the Justice Department.

McDonald's Corp expects its new restaurant openings for 1996 and 1997 to be at the low end of its targeted range of 2,500 to 3,200 units.
McDonald's spokesman Chuck Ebeling stated that the company will open 2,500-plus restaurants in 1996.
This will be the first time in at least three years that McDonald's has failed to exceed its expansion projections.
In 1995, McDonald's opened 2,430 units, surpassing its projection of 2,300.
In 1994, McDonald's opened 1,800 units, exceeding its projection of about 1,400 to 1,700.
McDonald's has nearly 20,000 restaurants worldwide.
McDonald's plans to open about 600-plus satellite units worldwide this year, down from an original plan of 700 to 1,000.
U.S. satellite units will account for about one-third of the total for these smaller sites, reduced from 60 percent as originally planned.
About one-third of McDonald's restaurant openings will still be in the United States.
McDonald's reported third quarter income of $0.62 a share, which was $0.01 below the consensus estimate.

McDonnell Douglas Corp. announced the resignation of Herbert Lanese, head of its aerospace business.
Speculation arose that disagreements over cost-cutting tactics contributed to Lanese's departure.
Herbert Lanese joined McDonnell Douglas in 1989 as senior vice president of finance.
Lanese left the firm after an apparent disagreement with President Harry Stonecipher.
Harry Stonecipher stated that he and Lanese had sharp differences in management and leadership styles.
Byron Callan, a Merrill Lynch analyst, described Lanese's departure as unexpected.
Lanese was tasked with reducing costs at McDonnell Douglas's military aircraft business.
Analysts noted that Lanese's focus on cost-cutting involved reducing employment.
Job security issues led to labor troubles at McDonnell Douglas, including a strike by the International Association of Machinists.
Mike Schoen from the Machinists union stated that the union was not ready for cost-cutting measures.

McDonnell Douglas Corp is cooperating with a federal investigation into the sale of $5 million of used machine tools to China.
The equipment was diverted to the site of a military plant in China.
Larry McCracken, vice president of corporate communications, stated that McDonnell Douglas violated no laws in the sale of the surplus equipment.
The machine tool sale was not directly linked to a 1994 agreement for 40 aircraft to be co-produced by McDonnell Douglas and its Chinese partner.
The machine tools were shipped to China between November 1994 and February 1995.
There are allegations that the Chinese intended to divert the equipment for military use.
