The sale of certain equipment to China requires U.S. government approval and assurances that it will not be used for military purposes.
McDonnell Douglas learned of the diversion of the equipment in March 1995 and notified the U.S. Government.
Some of the equipment was found in Nanchang, which is also the site of a Chinese commercial plant.
U.S. government officials reported evidence that some company officials may have been aware before March 1995 that China would not house the equipment in Beijing.

Kellogg Co is the leader in the U.S. ready-to-eat cereal market, valued at $9.0 billion.
Kellogg's market share has slipped to between 32.5 percent and 33 percent.
Kellogg considers a market share of 35 percent to be normal.
Kellogg does not intend to return to deep discounts and giveaways.
Kellogg's third quarter earnings were down 20 percent due to competitive pressures.
The U.S. cereal market grew by about 1.5 percent in the third quarter.
Kellogg was forced to cut prices earlier this year in response to competition.
Analysts expect Kellogg may increase promotions in 1997 if competitors do not cut back on promotions.
Kellogg aims to rebuild its market share but is currently avoiding deep discounts.
Kellogg plans to report modestly better fourth quarter earnings compared to last year's $0.77 a share.

Diana Corp announced its decision to spin off its various business holdings and retain only its Sattel Communications Inc unit.
Sattel spokesman Tony Squeglia stated that analysts on Wall Street were not interested in covering Diana due to its diverse holdings.
No analysts currently follow Diana Corp.
Diana Corp will change its name to Sattel after retaining Sattel Communications, which provides telephone and Internet switching equipment.
The other businesses, including Atlanta Provision Co Inc, C&L Communications Inc, and Valley Communications Inc, will form a new company that will trade on the Nasdaq.
Atlanta Provision, a meat and seafood distributor, is still for sale, but no imminent deal is expected.
Squeglia mentioned that Atlanta Provision accounts for about 80 percent of Diana's total revenues.
Diana's restructuring aims to make Sattel a primary business focus.
Squeglia indicated that many shareholders bought Diana stock as a proxy for Sattel.
Sattel is expected to have approximately $4.0 million in sales for its fiscal second quarter and to be modestly profitable.

Deere & Co. reported record fourth-quarter and annual earnings.
Net income for the fourth quarter increased 15 percent to $173.9 million.
Revenues for the fourth quarter rose 7 percent to $2.9 billion.
Deere's operating margins remain strong according to Chairman Hans Becherer.
Fourth quarter profits were less than some analysts had expected.
Deere's stock dropped $2.625 to $44 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Profits for the fiscal year rose 16 percent to $817.3 million.
Revenues for the fiscal year climbed 9 percent to $11.2 billion.
Operating profits for Deere's commercial and consumer equipment business fell to $1 million for the fourth quarter.
Export sales from the United States grew by 20 percent to $1.58 billion for 1996.

Oneok Inc. and Western Resources Inc. agreed to a $660 million deal that combines their natural gas assets.
The deal allows Western Resources access to a broader customer base for its electricity and security services.
Oneok will acquire all natural gas assets of Western Resources, making it the ninth largest gas distribution company in the United States.
Oneok serves 1.4 million customers and is the parent company of Oklahoma Natural Gas Co.
Western Resources will become the largest equity holder in Oneok, receiving about 3 million new shares of Oneok common stock.
Western Resources' total stake in Oneok will be about 45 percent.
The deal is expected to close by mid-1997, pending approval from Oneok shareholders and regulatory authorities.
Western Resources will focus on growing its electricity and home-security businesses after the asset swap.
Oneok's 735,000 customers could become potential clients for Western Resources' services.
The alliance positions the companies to take advantage of expected deregulation in the electricity industry.

Conseco Inc. announced it would acquire Pioneer Financial Services Inc. for approximately $417 million in stock.
Conseco will pay an additional $60 million to retire bank debt and cover other costs.
The acquisition of Pioneer is Conseco's seventh deal announced in the current year.
Conseco aims to enhance its offerings for senior citizens through this acquisition.
Conseco is a leading provider of supplemental health insurance, retirement annuities, and life insurance for consumers aged 40 and older.
James Rosensteele, a spokesman for Conseco, stated that the 65-plus consumer demographic is a key and growing market.
The merger will create the largest distribution organization for health and life insurance products in the markets where both companies operate.
Conseco Chairman Stephen Hilbert described the merger as an excellent match.
Conseco plans to use a fraction of its common stock, valued between $25 and $28, to purchase Pioneer Financial stock.
The transaction is subject to regulatory and stockholder approval and is expected to be completed within 180 days.

Kansas City Southern Industries Inc is considering options to finance its part of a joint $1.4 billion venture to control a Mexican rail line.
Michael Haverty is the president of the Kansas City Southern Railway subsidiary.
Kansas City Southern holds 49 percent of the Laredo, Texas to Mexico City rail line, known as Line 1.
Transportacion Maritima Mexicana SA de CV (TMM) holds 51 percent of Line 1.
Financing responsibility for the deal will be split according to ownership percentages.
Kansas City Southern is exploring potential equity investments from partners.
The company has discussed loaning money from strategic partners in exchange for commercial arrangements.
Analyst Steven Lewins suggested raising financing in dollars while paying for the Mexican rail stake in pesos.
Kansas City Southern's shares decreased from 50-3/8 on December 5 to 44-3/4 on the following Friday.
Haverty stated that the deal is expected to hurt earnings in the first year and be slightly dilutive in the second year, with an increase in earnings in the third year.

British Governor Chris Patten challenged business to defend the rule of law in Hong Kong.
Patten stated that the rule of law is essential for Hong Kong's success.
Britain will hand back Hong Kong to China in 264 days, ending over 150 years of colonial rule.
China has promised Hong Kong substantial autonomy under a 'one country, two systems' formula.
Patten criticized businessmen who sought favors from Beijing, which could harm Hong Kong's autonomy.
James Tien, chairman of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, stated that the chamber supports the government on key policies.
The chamber supports the pegging of Hong Kong's currency to the U.S. dollar and the rule of law.
Patten opposed the idea of cooperating with a 'provisional legislature' that China plans to establish.
Patten emphasized the importance of political opposition in Hong Kong.
A poll indicated that three-quarters of executives believed that opposition to government does not threaten Hong Kong's prospects.

Hong Kong's leadership campaign for the chief executive position has started with candidates stating their positions on key issues.
Sir Ti Liang Yang recently expressed support for China's plan to eliminate Hong Kong's elected legislature.
There are 245 days until Britain's withdrawal and Hong Kong's reversion to Chinese rule.
Political expert Michael DeGolyer stated that there is no chosen candidate in the leadership contest.
DeGolyer mentioned that different factions in Beijing are supporting various candidates in the race.
The four main contenders for the chief executive position are Sir Ti Liang Yang, Tung Chee-hwa, Peter Woo, and Simon Li.
Yang resigned as chief justice to run for the chief executive position and broke his silence on China's legislative plans.
China intends to dissolve Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council and establish a provisional legislature.
Britain and Hong Kong's democratic camp oppose China's plan for the provisional legislature.
Yang believes the provisional legislature is legally justified and necessary to avoid a legal vacuum during the transition.

Tsang Yok-sing is the leader of the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong (DAB).
Tsang stated that the China-appointed interim legislature would not clash with existing institutions before the handover.
The provisional legislature may meet on the mainland rather than in Hong Kong.
Britain is set to hand Hong Kong back to China as an autonomous Special Administrative Region in 236 days.
Hong Kong's political establishment and the governments of Britain and China are polarized over China's plan to dissolve the elected Legislative Council (Legco).
China plans to replace the Legislative Council with a provisional body until elections in 1998.
The plan is a response to an enlargement of the democratic franchise by Governor Chris Patten.
Tsang claimed that Hong Kong's constitutional arrangements do not prevent the provisional legislature from becoming the legislative body on July 1.
The Preparatory Committee has elected a 400-member body to select Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader and the provisional legislature.
Critics view the provisional legislature as a rubber-stamp body that will enact repressive laws.

Tung Chee-hwa is a shipping tycoon whose company was bailed out by Beijing years ago.
Tung Chee-hwa won 206 votes in the first round of the ballot for governing Hong Kong.
The ballot was conducted among an exclusive club of 400 rich and influential individuals in Hong Kong under Beijing's supervision.
Ti Liang Yang was the runner-up with 82 votes, and Peter Woo came in third with 54 votes.
Only Tung, Yang, and Woo received the minimum 50 votes required to advance to the deciding round on December 11.
An opinion poll indicated that if an election were held by universal suffrage, Ti Liang Yang would receive 35.7 percent of the votes and Tung Chee-hwa would receive 33.5 percent.
Tung Chee-hwa revealed that China helped salvage his family shipping empire 11 years ago with a US$120 million syndicated fund led by Henry Fok.
Henry Fok stated that the rescue package for Tung's company was above board and did not involve any political deal regarding Hong Kong's future.
Tung Chee-hwa is viewed as Beijing's favored candidate for Chief Executive of Hong Kong.
Foreign Minister Qian Qichen stated that the winner of the election had not been predetermined by Chinese leaders.

China plans to march 6,000 People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops into Hong Kong when it takes over the colony from Britain on July 1, 1997.
The Financial Times of London reported that China informed Britain of its intention to move troops into Hong Kong at the time of the handover.
Bill Dickson, a spokesman for the Foreign Office mission in Hong Kong, stated that China had not announced any such plan during ongoing handover negotiations.
Dickson mentioned that discussions about the transfer of defense responsibilities and the handover ceremony were ongoing, but no plans for troop movement were communicated by China.
Cui Tiankai, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, stated that the number of troops stationed in Hong Kong would depend on defense requirements after the transfer of power.
Cui did not specify when the troops would be moved into Hong Kong.
Diplomats in Hong Kong found the troop movement plan credible due to China's hardline stance on handover-related issues.
A British source indicated that it would be better for China to gradually build up its armed forces in Hong Kong over time.
A Western diplomat expressed concern that a sudden display of military force would raise questions about China's commitment to a smooth transition.
Hong Kong is transitioning back to Chinese sovereignty after being a British colony for 150 years.

Chief Executive candidate Tung Chee-hwa was rated by a poll as the best man to deal with China after Britain leaves Hong Kong next year.
Tung Chee-hwa stated that a proposed subversion law faces review by the post-colonial government.
Tung Chee-hwa mentioned that the Basic Law states it is up to the future government to draw up its own law on subversion.
The Special Administrative Region government will have to review subversion issues after the handover.
Britain will hand its colony back to Beijing at midnight on June 30 next year.
The China-controlled Selection Committee is vetting Tung Chee-hwa and two rivals to succeed colonial Governor Chris Patten.
The winner of the Selection Committee will be announced on December 11.
Britain began the process of bringing in a law on subversion to define treason, sedition, subversion, and secession.
China condemned Britain's move to introduce the subversion law but did not indicate whether it would be scrapped after the handover.
An opinion poll indicated that 73 percent of respondents believed Tung Chee-hwa was the candidate best able to communicate with the Chinese government.

Canadian envoys dismissed reports that thousands of Hong Kong people in Canada may be forced to return home ahead of Hong Kong's 1997 handover to China.
Canada's commissioner in Hong Kong is Garrett Lambert.
Canada's ambassador to China is Howard Balloch.
Lambert stated that he believed China would soon decide on the issue of residence rights for Hong Kong emigrants.
Lambert indicated that Hong Kong people who emigrated might have to live in Hong Kong as Canadians and lose their local voting rights after July 1, 1997.
Lambert was informed by China's envoy in Hong Kong, Zhou Nan, that progress was being made on the right of abode issue.
The right of abode issue is a major unresolved topic for the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group (JLG).
Lambert predicted that a decision on the right of abode would be announced by the JLG soon, possibly in early January.
Lambert noted that it seems unnecessary for permanent residents of Hong Kong to be physically present to protect their interests before the transition.
Questions remain about the political and working rights of Hong Kong emigrants who return after 1997.

The Hong Kong government expressed concern after Britain stated it could not protect Hong Kong holders of British passports after the Chinese takeover.
Governor Chris Patten called an urgent meeting of the Legislative Council to address the controversy.
A British envoy stated that London could not provide consular protection for Hong Kong passport holders.
Patten's spokesman noted that the issue generated considerable public interest and misunderstanding.
Patten was scheduled to answer questions from legislators at an extraordinary sitting of the Legislative Council.
The transition of Hong Kong back to Chinese rule is set to occur in 208 days.
Britain's Senior Trade Commissioner, Francis Cornish, stated that over 135,000 Hong Kong residents with British passports would not receive consular protection from Britain.
The British government offered passports to 50,000 Hong Kong households in response to demands for full British citizenship after the Tiananmen Square crackdown.
Cornish indicated that China would not recognize British consular protection for holders of dual citizenship.
Local politicians criticized Cornish's remarks as a sell-out to China.

Hong Kong is set to name its first Chinese leader after 150 years of British colonial rule.
The vote will take place under the flag of communist-ruled China.
Shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa is favored to win the leadership position.
A 400-member Chinese-controlled Selection Committee will conduct the vote.
A survey by Hong Kong University indicated that 82.2 percent of respondents expected Tung to win.
43.4 percent of respondents would support Tung if given the chance to vote.
Tung's nearest rival, Ti Liang Yang, is projected to receive 27.9 percent of popular support.
Sovereignty over Hong Kong will revert to China on June 30, 1997.
The winner of the vote will become the chief executive-designate of the Special Administrative Region of China.
Pro-democracy protesters camped outside the conference center on the eve of the vote.

Tung Chee-hwa was chosen as Hong Kong's first Chinese leader after over 150 years of British colonial rule.
Tung Chee-hwa will take office on July 1, 1997.
Governor Chris Patten stated that Tung will chart the course for Hong Kong as it enters a new era.
Hong Kong will be the first British colony to transition into a world trading economy and return to a communist-ruled country.
China has promised Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy and at least 50 more years of capitalism.
China has vowed to limit the pace of democratic reform in Hong Kong.
Tung Chee-hwa's family firm received a syndicated loan from Beijing in the 1980s to recover from financial difficulties.
Tung will face challenges from pro-democracy politicians and the departing British colonial officials.
The pro-democracy lobby plans to challenge Tung's authority with a no-confidence vote in the legislature.
Some analysts predict that the children of senior Communist Party officials will gain prominence in Hong Kong's new legislature.

Prince Andrew has arrived in Hong Kong to inspect his troops.
This visit is one of the last royal visits before Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule.
Prince Andrew is the Colonel-In-Chief of the 1st battalion of the Staffordshire regiment.
During his three-day visit, he will observe jungle training and border patrols by the soldiers.
Prince Andrew made a low-key entry to Hong Kong on Monday night.
He was entertained at Government House by Governor Chris Patten and his wife Lavender.
Prince Andrew is expected to visit Hong Kong battle positions from World War Two.
The British garrison in Hong Kong will be reduced from almost 3,000 to about 1,500 before the handover.
All remaining British troops are to be withdrawn by June 30.
Prince Andrew will attend a ceremony for the Dragon Company of the Hong Kong Military Service Corps.

Hong Kong's Governor Chris Patten criticized a legislature that Beijing plans to impose on the territory, calling it a 'rubber stamp'.
Patten suggested that Britain and China should resolve their differences in the International Court of Justice.
Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind issued a statement urging China to reconsider its legislative plan or face international pressure.
A gathering of 400 Hong Kong elites is scheduled to take place in Shenzhen to elect 60 new legislators on July 1.
On July 1, Hong Kong will revert to Chinese sovereignty after being under British rule for 150 years.
A treaty pledge from Beijing allows Hong Kong to maintain its distinct entity and capitalist system for 50 years after the handover.
The transition to Chinese sovereignty has faced challenges, including the disbandment of the elected Legislative Council.
Democrats in Hong Kong plan to mount legal challenges if the interim legislative body meets in the territory before July 1.
Patten described China's plan for the new legislature as a decision that would reduce democratic involvement in lawmaking.
Patten stated he would assist Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, in preparing for his administration.

Tung Chee-hwa is the leader-in-waiting of Hong Kong.
Tung Chee-hwa invited Anson Chan to meet him for breakfast at his villa on Hong Kong Island.
Anson Chan is the chief secretary and second-in-command to Governor Chris Patten.
Tung Chee-hwa will succeed Chris Patten after the handover of Hong Kong to China on June 30.
An opinion poll indicated that 73 percent of people in Hong Kong support Anson Chan.
Tung Chee-hwa received a 65 percent approval rating in the same opinion poll.
Tung Chee-hwa was selected by a China-controlled committee to be Hong Kong's post-colonial chief executive.
Tung Chee-hwa is the first Chinese leader in Hong Kong's history.
Tung Chee-hwa is working to assemble a cabinet and establish a relationship with a provisional legislature.
Anson Chan expressed a desire for her policy secretaries to remain in their positions for stability.

Shares in Eurotunnel SA fell on Tuesday after being requoted following a week's suspension.
The decline was due to disappointment over the terms of its restructuring with creditor banks.
Eurotunnel SA has 69.6 billion francs ($13.50 billion) of junior-ranked bank debt.
The shares were trading at 8.50 francs at 1052 GMT, with a trading volume of 16 million.
The shares were suspended at 9.15 francs on September 30.
Analyst Jean Borgeix stated that the stock market was disappointed with the conversion price of 10.40 francs for new Eurotunnel shares.
The market had expected a conversion price between 12-15 francs per share.
Current shareholders will lose 30 percent of Eurotunnel's future cashflow due to the issuance of 'stabilisation notes'.
Eurotunnel can issue up to 14.8 billion francs of stabilisation notes.
The restructuring will dilute current shareholders' holdings to 54.5 percent of the capital after the debt swap.

French aviation executives expressed concerns about renewed tensions with the United States regarding airline market access in France.
Air France is involved in a potential 'air war' related to these tensions.
The U.S. government is seeking a bilateral treaty that would provide more landing rights to American airlines in France.
France is advocating for gradual market liberalization instead of immediate changes.
A spokeswoman for the U.S. embassy in Paris stated that the U.S. had not rejected Air France's new winter schedule.
Air France has requested increased services for the winter compared to the previous year.
The U.S. Department of Transportation extended the deadline to decide on Air France's request until October 27.
The delay in approving Air France's schedule is perceived as a pressure tactic to compel France to agree to a new aviation treaty.
Air France's winter schedule is set to begin on October 27.
Air France has requested additional flights to San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Chicago for the winter season.

Air France is forming a transatlantic alliance with Delta Air Lines and Continental.
Air France signed letters of intent for cooperation with Delta and Continental.
The agreements are intended to help Air France compete with European rivals.
The alliances will allow code-sharing arrangements between Air France and the U.S. carriers.
Passengers can receive a through-ticket from one airline to use on its partner airline.
The companies will harmonize flight schedules and share a frequent flyer program.
Delta operates from Atlanta, Georgia, Continental operates from Houston, Texas, and Air France operates from Paris Roissy-Charles De Gaulle airport.
Air France expects the alliances to generate an additional $100 million in gross revenues annually.
Air France reported a net loss of over two billion francs last year.
Air France chairman Christian Blanc's search for U.S. partners was made possible by signs of financial recovery.

The submarine changed naval warfare in World War Two.
European shipbuilders are developing stealth warships for the 21st century.
Three shipbuilders presented combat ship designs at a trade fair in Le Bourget, north of Paris.
British shipbuilder Vosper Thornycroft unveiled the Sea Wraith corvette at the Euronaval exhibition.
BAeSema launched its Cougar coastal corvette project.
French state-owned DCN shipyard presented the La Fayette frigate, claiming it is the first operational warship with full stealth features.
DCN collaborates with French defence company Thomson CSF for the ship's communications, detection, and weapons control systems.
Stealth warships use radar-beating technology similar to that developed by the U.S. aircraft industry.
The La Fayette frigate uses a slab-sided superstructure and non-metallic composite materials to confuse radar and missiles.
Taiwan ordered eight La Fayette-class ships, with the second entering service last week.

The French government sold a nine percent stake in Elf-Aquitaine, raising around 10 billion francs ($2 billion).
The sale allows Elf-Aquitaine to buy back a significant portion of its own shares.
The sale follows a rise in the Paris bourse and specifically in oil stocks due to high world oil prices.
Finance minister Jean Arthuis decided to sell 24.9 million shares in Elf-Aquitaine held by the ERAP company.
The sale reduces the stake held by ERAP in Elf-Aquitaine to 0.75 percent.
The sale involved the placement of 12.5 million Elf shares at 417.50 francs per share to French and international institutions.
Elf-Aquitaine bought a 4.5 percent stake through its indirectly-owned financial Fingestval company.
The 10 billion francs will go into a government special account for share sale proceeds.
The funds will be used to recapitalise state-owned companies, particularly those being privatised.
France plans to recapitalise Thomson SA with 11 billion francs before selling it to Lagardere Groupe and Daewoo Electronics Corp.

Air France reported earnings of 802 million francs ($158 million) in the first half of the year.
The profit estimate for the six months to September 30 compared with a loss of 335 million francs a year ago.
Air France placed an order for 20 aircraft, including 10 Boeing 777 twinjets and five Airbus A340s.
Air France has options for an additional 10 Boeing 777 twinjets and five Airbus A340s.
Air France chairman Christian Blanc received support from Prime Minister Alain Juppe for the Boeing purchase.
The orders for the Boeing 777-200 version could be worth around $2.7 billion at catalogue prices.
Airbus would potentially gain $1.75 billion from the orders.
Transport Minister Bernard Pons stated that Air France is obliged to buy Boeing to meet commitments made in 1989.
Air France had outstanding orders with Boeing worth $994 million and $2 billion in options.
Air France has rationalised its fleet and restructured its network around a centralised hub at Paris Charles De Gaulle airport.

Approximately 120 Eurotunnel SA /Plc employees are working to clear wreckage from the Channel Tunnel.
A fire occurred in the Channel Tunnel two weeks ago, halting passenger services between Britain and France.
The fire started on a truck-carrying wagon on December 18, leading to the closure of Eurostar high-speed passenger trains and tourist vehicle Shuttle services.
Partial freight traffic has resumed in the Channel Tunnel.
Eurotunnel aims to restore two thirds of normal passenger and freight traffic within three to six months for repairs.
Dominique Dorso is the Eurotunnel official coordinating the clearance of wreckage.
Three wagons remain at the site of the fire in section five of the tunnel.
The fire destroyed 28 trucks, leaving no visible traces of them in the Shuttle wagons.
The fire did not penetrate the underlying 20-30 cm of injected concrete lining the tunnel.
Protective masks are required due to the lingering smell of burnt plastic and metal.

Airbus partners must accelerate plans to convert the partnership into a single company.
Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas announced a $13.3 billion merger plan.
The merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas would create the world's largest aerospace firm.
The new aerospace firm would have 1997 sales of about $48 billion and employ 200,000 people.
Airbus is a consortium made up of Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA.
Airbus partners are in discussions to change the partnership structure to a joint stock company.
The aim of the restructuring is to create a more competitive and responsive organization.
BAe's group managing director John Weston stated that future Airbus should be a large, integrated company.
Aerospatiale's chairman Yves Michot views the new Airbus as a large prime contractor directing suppliers' work.
Airbus negotiations slowed over the summer due to leadership changes.

Aerospatiale is a French state-owned aerospace group.
Aerospatiale is in merger talks with Dassault Aviation.
The merger is part of France's effort to consolidate its fragmented defense industry.
Aerospatiale is trying to maintain its role in building passenger jets for Airbus Industrie.
Jean-Marc Baron is an aerospace specialist at consultancy KPMG Peat Marwick.
Baron stated that France and Europe need to restructure due to the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger.
The merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas has prompted discussions on European consolidation.
Aerospatiale is expected to play a key role in the restructuring of Airbus.
Airbus partners BAe and Dasa are advocating for changes that could affect Aerospatiale's role in commercial aircraft production.
Aerospatiale derives 70 percent of its annual sales from the civilian sector, with half from Airbus products.

The four partners of the Airbus consortium signed an agreement to restructure Airbus into a limited liability company by 1999.
The establishment of Airbus Industrie as a single corporate entity is an initial step in the consolidation of the aerospace industry within Europe.
Airbus is currently a partnership between Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA.
The new Airbus will have a single management structure that will include engineering, testing, production, procurement, and customer service.
DASA Chairman Manfred Bischoff stated that differences remain among the partners despite the signing of the deal.
There are differing views among the partners regarding the amount of productive assets to be included in the new limited liability company.
An industry executive indicated that discussions about necessary assets would follow the signing of the agreement.
The transfer of assets will depend on their essentiality for the new Airbus functions and their valuation, to be completed by the end of 1997.
The British and Germans advocated for a high degree of integration in the new Airbus, while Aerospatiale preferred a more cautious approach.
Airbus stated that the restructured company would improve operational efficiency and allow for future strategic partnerships.

The European Airbus consortium is conducting studies on a 555-seat passenger plane.
Boeing has decided to scale back work on a larger jumbo jet, the 747-X, due to market conditions.
Boeing is diverting half of the 1,000 staff working on the 747-X project to smaller planes.
An Airbus spokesman stated that they are confident the A3XX will meet market needs.
Airbus claims that major airlines are encouraging in their collaboration on the A3XX.
Airbus believes airlines prefer an all-new plane over Boeing's 747-X, which was developed in the late 1960s.
Airbus aims to launch the A3XX product family in 1998 for service in 2003.
Airbus seeks to increase its aircraft market share from an estimated 35 percent to at least 50 percent by the end of the decade.
Airbus forecasts a market for 1,383 planes seating more than 400 passengers over the next 20 years.
Boeing estimates demand for only 470 planes seating 500 or more, which it believes would not yield a return on investment.

Canal Plus is merging with Nethold to create one of the world's largest pay-TV groups.
Nethold is jointly held by Richemont SA and MIH Holdings Ltd.
Canal Plus stated that the merger will result in over 8.5 million subscribers.
The new group will have significant positions in France, Italy, Spain, Scandinavia, the Benelux countries, and Germany.
The Paris stockmarket authorities suspended trading in Canal Plus shares on Friday morning.
Cie Generale des Eaux is a key shareholder in Canal Plus and expressed delight with the merger plan.
The merger will provide Canal Plus access to the Italian market and enhance its negotiating power for copyrights.
Canal Plus will buy 100 percent of Nethold for 6.1 million new shares and $45 million in cash.
Following the merger, Richemont and MIH will own 15 and five percent of Canal Plus, respectively.
The deal has the backing of Canal Plus's main shareholders and is subject to regulatory and shareholder approval.

Shares of American Medical Response Inc fell sharply on Wednesday for a second consecutive session.
The decline was due to concerns that the company was straying from its successful acquisition strategy.
American Medical Response announced an agreement to buy STAT Healthcare Inc in a stock transaction valued at $145 million.
The planned acquisition will move American Medical Response into hospital emergency rooms and disease management.
Shares of American Medical Response dropped 2-5/8 to 31-7/8 by midafternoon Wednesday.
The stock dropped three points after the transaction was announced on Tuesday.
Wall Street analysts stated that the deal was strategically sound from a long-term perspective.
Analysts noted that investors were wary of the company's shift into a new area.
STAT Healthcare provides staffing for hospital emergency rooms and outpatient medical services such as kidney dialysis.
American Medical Response predicted that the deal will slightly dilute earnings this year.

PacifiCorp and Protection One Inc announced a marketing alliance on Friday.
The alliance aims to boost customer loyalty in a competitive industry.
Customers of PacifiCorp subsidiaries Pacific Power and Utah Power will be offered a security system from Protection One.
The alliance is considered the first of many creative ventures in an era of deregulation.
Ron Chebra from AT&T Solutions stated that one-stop shopping is becoming key from a marketing position.
Utilities are increasingly attracted to security companies as they enter new markets.
Rene Carroll from PacifiCorp mentioned that they have been looking at entering the home security business for over a year.
The alliance will give Protection One access to 1.4 million customers served by PacifiCorp subsidiaries.
Customers accepting the offer will receive free installation of a home security system with a two-year monitoring agreement.
Protection One's chief financial officer John Hesse indicated that more announcements are expected in the next 12 months.

Mobil Corp is recognized for having the most aggressive cost-cutting program among U.S. oil companies.
Mobil Corp has implemented $760 million in cost savings in 2023 as part of a $1.3 billion plan.
Mobil Corp expects to achieve the remaining $540 million in cost savings soon.
Mobil Corp anticipates saving at least another $300 million annually by 1999 through streamlined purchases.
Mobil Corp reported a 10 percent decline in third quarter operating income due to unfavorable conditions.
Industry analysts noted that Mobil's stock price had already accounted for the earnings drop.
Jack Aydin of McDonald & Co Securities Inc stated that Mobil has done an excellent job with cost-cutting.
James Falvey of Smith Barney upgraded Mobil to a buy rating and expressed concerns about the company's cost structure.
Chairman Lucio Noto emphasized the need for changes in business operations to remain competitive.
Mobil is not expected to announce a major restructuring plan soon but anticipates future savings from purchasing and technology.

French holding company CGIP announced it may acquire a 28 percent stake in automotive parts firm Valeo SA from Carlo De Benedetti.
CGIP chairman Ernest-Antoine Seilliere stated that negotiations are nearing a conclusion.
Seilliere indicated that the acquisition would be a long-term investment for CGIP.
CGIP sold half of its 20 percent stake in Crown Cork & Seal Co Inc for $560.6 million to finance the Valeo stake.
Seilliere mentioned that CGIP is serious about acquiring Valeo but acknowledged there is still work to be done.
CGIP is a holding company with investments in industrial and information technology sectors.
Seilliere noted that 70 percent of Valeo's business is conducted outside of France.
Seilliere dismissed concerns about Valeo being affected by the cyclical nature of the automotive industry.
CGIP previously held a stake in Valeo and sold it in 1993.
Seilliere stated that CGIP does not require significant productivity or organizational changes.

Billionaire investor Marvin Davis announced an $835 million bid for Carter-Wallace Inc.
Carter-Wallace Inc. is the maker of Trojan condoms and Arrid deodorant.
Davis offered to buy outstanding stock of Carter-Wallace for $18 a share.
The offer reflects a 50 percent premium over Carter-Wallace's recent trading price.
Carter-Wallace confirmed it received the offer and will refer it to majority shareholder The CPI Development Corp.
Shares of Carter-Wallace increased by $3.875 to $15.625 on the NYSE.
Market speculation suggests that Carter-Wallace may be reluctant to sell.
Insiders control about 82 percent of Carter-Wallace via common stock and a special class of shares.
Carter-Wallace is dominated by members of the Hoyt family, with Henry Hoyt Jr. as CEO and Chairman.
Davis has been buying shares of Carter-Wallace in recent weeks and has a material interest in the company.

CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp. entered discussions about their rival offers to buy Conrail Inc.
The specific nature of the discussions between CSX and Norfolk Southern was not disclosed.
Conrail's stock fell due to views that the discussions would reduce the likelihood of a bidding war.
Discussions between CSX and Norfolk Southern began late last week and continued through the weekend and into Monday.
CSX agreed to buy Conrail in a transaction valued at $8.4 billion, or $92.50 per share.
Norfolk Southern launched a competing bid of $100 cash per share, totaling about $9 billion.
CSX stated that Norfolk Southern initiated the discussions regarding a possible sale of certain material assets.
Norfolk Southern confirmed its commitment to its bid for Conrail and has secured over $15 billion to finance the acquisition.
Norfolk Southern's CEO David Goode expressed concerns about Conrail's willingness to accept a balanced competitive structure.
Analysts noted that Pennsylvania's corporate takeover law could pose challenges to Norfolk Southern's acquisition of Conrail.

Conrail Inc. revised its takeover agreement with CSX Corp. to provide more cash to shareholders.
The proposed railroad merger is valued at nearly $8.5 billion.
Investors criticized the new terms, stating the cash-and-stock deal is below the rejected offer from Norfolk Southern Corp.
Conrail's board reaffirmed that a merger with CSX is a superior strategic combination despite the higher offer from Norfolk Southern.
Conrail Chairman David LeVan stated that the new agreement increases value for Conrail shareholders.
A source indicated that the Conrail board met late Tuesday night to finalize the new agreement with CSX.
The merger would create one of the largest transportation companies in the world with a rail system of approximately 29,000 miles in 22 eastern states.
Under the revised offer, CSX will pay $110 cash per share for 40 percent of Conrail shares.
The remaining 60 percent of Conrail shares will be exchanged at a ratio of 1.85619 CSX shares for each Conrail share.
Norfolk Southern has offered to pay $100 a share in cash for all of Conrail's outstanding shares.

Wayne Huizenga announced a deal to buy Alamo Rent-A-Car for $625 million.
The announcement was made less than six weeks after the collapse of his deal to buy ADT Ltd.
Wayne Huizenga is the founder of Blockbuster Entertainment.
Wayne Huizenga is the owner of the Florida Marlins baseball team.
Republic Industries Inc is the company making the purchase of Alamo Rent-A-Car.
The acquisition is expected to enhance Republic's automotive business.
Republic's automotive business is based on the used-car company AutoNation USA.

Norfolk Southern Corp may seek to block a proposed union between Conrail Inc and CSX Corp in a Philadelphia courtroom.
A hearing is scheduled for November 18 to address Norfolk Southern's suit regarding the Conrail-CSX merger.
Conrail rejected a $10 billion offer from Norfolk Southern and reaffirmed its commitment to the $8.5 billion transaction with CSX.
This is the second time Conrail has rejected an offer from Norfolk Southern that exceeded the CSX transaction.
Conrail shares rose earlier in the week due to speculation that CSX would improve the terms of the deal.
Analysts and traders were not surprised that the CSX deal terms were not revised.
Conrail and CSX indicated they are discussing ways to increase the value of their transaction after it is finalized.
Shareholders have expressed dissatisfaction with the Conrail-CSX deal, which values Conrail at approximately $93 per share.
Norfolk Southern's offer to buy Conrail is for $110 per share in cash.
According to Pennsylvania corporate law, Conrail can consider interests beyond shareholders when determining its best partner.

Diamond Shamrock Inc plans to close its merger with Ultramar Corp on December 3.
Diamond Shamrock Inc will announce a new organizational structure shortly after the merger.
Roger Hemminghaus is the chief executive officer of Diamond Shamrock Inc.
Diamond Shamrock is close to selling its telecommunications business and natural gas exploration and production operations in Bolivia.
The new company formed from the merger will be called Ultramar Diamond Shamrock Corp.
The merger will create a company with a combined equity value of more than $2.3 billion.
Roger Hemminghaus will become chairman and chief executive of Ultramar Diamond Shamrock Corp.
Diamond Shamrock anticipates cost savings and synergies from the merger that will add $0.20 per share to earnings in 1997 and $0.60 per share in 1998.
Diamond Shamrock's previous major transaction was the acquisition of National Convenience Stores Inc.
Cost savings from the acquisition of National Convenience Stores Inc have exceeded preliminary estimates.

Ashland Inc is facing a threatened proxy fight amid oil industry consolidation.
The company is considering strategic alternatives but has not decided on major actions.
Providence Capital Inc is expected to pressure Ashland to enhance its value by breaking up its operations.
Ashland owns 56 percent of Ashland Coal Inc, a chemicals business, and a highway construction unit.
Ashland produces Valvoline motor oils and owns SuperAmerica convenience stores.
Industry analysts believe Ashland's share value could exceed $60 if its businesses were separated.
Providence has nominated a three-man slate for election to Ashland's board at the January 30 annual shareholders' meeting.
Ashland has hired First Boston Corp for advice on the proxy issue.
Providence is not seeking control of Ashland but aims to push for restructuring.
Ashland has acknowledged Providence's interest, noting it holds 100 shares of Ashland's 64 million outstanding common shares.

Ashland Inc has restructured its core business to avoid a proxy fight.
The restructuring aims to enhance profitability amid poor profit margins in the industry.
James Falvey, an analyst at Smith Barney, expressed skepticism about Ashland's ability to deliver results.
Ashland's restructuring includes a share buyback program and evaluation of strategic alternatives for its non-core exploration unit.
Providence Capital Inc withdrew its nomination for a three-person slate for Ashland's board of directors after the restructuring announcement.
Herbert Denton, president of Providence Capital, stated that Ashland addressed major issues raised by his firm.
Ashland's stock has risen about $10 per share since September, despite little reaction to the restructuring plan.
Analysts expect Ashland to sell its exploration unit and engage in industry consolidation.
The company did not provide specific cost-cutting targets or a timeline for the restructuring actions.
Paul Chellgren, the CEO of Ashland, is set to become chairman, replacing retiring John Hall.

Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. are proposing a union that increases competition in the defence industry.
The defence industry has experienced significant consolidation in recent years.
Companies such as Northrop Grumman Corp., Raytheon Co., and Hughes Electronics Corp. are anticipated to seek partners for mergers.
Jon Kutler, president of Quarterdeck Investment Partners Inc., stated that the proposed merger has disrupted the current state of the defence industry.
Industry experts predict that the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger will lead to a resurgence in defence mergers.
James Schwendinger from Deloitte & Touche indicated that the merger could reduce the number of large firms in the industry from eight or ten to three or four.
Northrop Grumman is considered a leading buyer of defence electronics properties.
Following the merger announcement, Northrop Grumman's shares increased by $1.125 to $80.50.
A source in the defence industry noted that the merger diminishes Northrop Grumman's scale.
Northrop Grumman was formed in 1994 and acquired Westinghouse Electric Corp.'s defence business for $3.6 billion earlier this year.

A part of the new telecommunications law could restrict how phone companies use confidential customer data.
The law creates a conflict between consumer advocates and telecommunications carriers.
Consumer advocates are concerned about telemarketing and loss of personal privacy.
Telecommunications carriers want to offer customers a variety of services under the new law.
The data includes billing records and calling patterns.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is drafting rules regarding the use of customer proprietary network information (CPNI).
CPNI includes details about call times, destinations, frequency, length, phone line types, and billing prices.
Few restrictions on the use of customer data existed before the new telecommunications law.
The new FCC rules are expected to be released in early 1997.
The FCC must determine the level of customer approval required for carriers to use data for marketing purposes.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) eliminated a rule requiring phone carriers to notify the agency of rate changes.
The rule that was scrapped was established during the Great Depression.
FCC officials stated that the change aims to increase competition in the long-distance telephone market, valued at $70 billion.
The FCC's decision is intended to reduce government regulations for long-distance companies like AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp.
Industry officials and consumer advocates expressed concerns that the new approach may confuse consumers and hinder their ability to find the best deals.
The 1934 rule required long-distance carriers to submit 'tariff' filings to the FCC before changing rates or offering new services.
The FCC argued that the old rule was outdated due to increased competition in the long-distance market.
Under the new regulations, companies must disclose their rates and conditions to the public through advertising or online.
The FCC's new rules will take effect in nine months.
Mark Cooper from the Consumer Federation of America criticized the FCC's decision, stating that informed choices are necessary for consumers.

Regulators proposed to set aside $2.3 billion a year to link schools and libraries to the Internet at discounted rates.
The proposal does not endorse President Clinton's call to provide free Internet access to schools and libraries.
Eligible institutions could buy access to the computer network at discounts ranging from 20 percent to 90 percent.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt stated that schools will be able to connect every classroom to the Information Highway.
The proposed connection is described as high-speed and high-bandwidth.
The discounts will be tailored to each school's individual level of need.
The Internet proposal is part of a broader plan to overhaul the universal service program.
Officials hope the proposal will generate lower phone rates through increased competition.
Some board members expressed concerns that the plan may be too ambitious and could raise rates.
The plan includes larger discounts for less well-off institutions and those in high-cost areas.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Reed Hundt appealed to nearly 1,200 television stations to adhere to a voluntary ban on airing liquor advertisements.
Reed Hundt made this appeal after a liquor industry group announced it would end its own voluntary ban on radio and TV promotions.
Hundt stated he had no immediate plans to issue rules to block liquor ads.
Hundt plans to use his position to convince TV stations not owned by the four major networks to abstain from showing ads for spirits.
Seagram Co. Ltd. began airing TV ads for its Royal Crown whiskey in selected local markets in June.
The National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) expressed disappointment with the lifting of the voluntary ban by distillers but did not support Hundt's call for a voluntary ban.
Hundt praised the four major networks (ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox) for maintaining their policies against accepting liquor ads.
The four major networks own about 50 stations in major markets, leaving just under 1,200 commercial stations not owned by them.
NAB President Edward Frits noted that individual stations have adopted their own standards regarding hard liquor advertising.
The Distilled Spirits Council of the United States (Discus) formally ended its voluntary ban on radio and TV liquor ads, which had been in place since 1936 for radio and 1948 for TV.

Deregulation of the local telephone market is progressing.
The Supreme Court declined to revive key parts of the FCC's rules for local phone monopolies.
Industry and government officials agree that the move towards competition is not dead.
Henry Geller, a former FCC general counsel, stated that things haven't come to a halt.
State regulators are now making many decisions regarding local market competition.
States are considering the FCC's now-defunct rules on pricing for new entrants to the local market.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt expressed encouragement about the general trend in deregulation.
Long-distance carriers like AT&T Corp. are not currently expressing alarm about the situation.
The Baby Bells and other local companies acknowledge that state decisions have been mixed for them.
A U.S. appeals court in St. Louis suspended key provisions of the FCC's interconnection rules.

Federal regulators are implementing a two-part plan to reduce rates on overseas phone calls.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is expected to facilitate negotiations for cheaper international call rates.
Next month, the FCC plans to propose rules to lower charges U.S. carriers pay foreign phone monopolies for overseas calls.
Don Gips is the head of the FCC's international bureau.
Foreign charges, known as 'accounting rates,' are reported to be five to ten times the actual costs.
Monopolies control over 90 percent of the non-U.S. phone market.
In 1995, U.S. phone companies paid $5.5 billion more to foreign carriers than they received from them.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt stated that the imbalance in payments exceeds the U.S. foreign aid budget of $2 billion.
The United States has significant payment imbalances with countries including China, Jamaica, Mexico, Hong Kong, Colombia, and Argentina.
Dan Rosen from the Institute for International Economics noted that countries defending their monopolies may be concerned about the FCC's actions.

Television executives have tentatively agreed to rate shows based on their suitability for kids of different age groups.
The new ratings system is expected to be completed by the end of the year.
The new system will be similar to the existing system used by the motion-picture industry.
The Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) uses a code with letters and numbers to suggest appropriate age groups for films.
The TV industry executives rejected a content-based ratings system backed by children's advocates and educators.
An industry source stated that a content-based system would be unworkable for the numerous shows on broadcast and cable TV.
Individual networks or syndicators will rate their own shows.
The HBO system offers content-based ratings such as 'MV' for 'mild violence' and 'SC' for 'strong sexual content.'
Industry sources indicated that the TV ratings system has not been finalized and details are still being worked out.
Once completed, the ratings will be used with a 'V-chip' installed in new TV sets to allow parents to block certain shows.

A television industry group will unveil a new system for rating programs on Thursday.
The system aims to help parents control the shows their children watch.
Broadcast, cable-TV, and Hollywood executives have been meeting since March to develop the rating system.
The new system will rate shows based on their suitability for children of different ages.
The executives decided against a content-based rating system that details levels of sex, violence, and strong language.
They believe an age-based system will be easier for parents to use and understand.
Jack Valenti is the chief executive of the Motion Picture Association of America and leads the group developing the ratings.
The new ratings system is expected to include six categories, including TV-G, TV-PG, TV-14, and TV-M.
The ratings will be implemented next month, with TV networks and syndicators responsible for rating their shows.
President Clinton has given the system a conditional approval, suggesting critics allow a 10-month testing period.

Ameritech Corp. sought federal approval to offer long-distance service from its regional calling area.
The company requested permission from the Federal Communications Commission to provide long-distance service to residents in Michigan.
Ameritech has 3.5 million customers in Michigan.
Under the new telecommunications law, Ameritech can offer long-distance service if it has opened its local network to new rivals.
Ameritech has 11 million residential customers across Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Indiana, and Ohio.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt stated that Ameritech's application is significant for the implementation of the telecom law.
The application will undergo scrutiny from the FCC and other government regulators.
AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp. opposed Ameritech's application, claiming it has not opened its local phone market.
The FCC has 90 days to decide if Ameritech's entry is in the public interest.
Ameritech must meet a 14-point checklist to demonstrate it has opened its local network in Michigan.

A U.S. appeals court in St. Louis will hear arguments on a Federal Communications Commission order regarding the local phone market.
The order aims to open the $100 billion local phone market to competition.
Lawyers and analysts predict that the FCC will lose the case against GTE Corp., the Baby Bells, and other local carriers.
The appeals court suspended the FCC order in October pending the outcome of the case.
Attorney Alfred Mamlet stated that the FCC faces a difficult situation and the case may reach the Supreme Court.
The FCC's 'interconnection' order is expected to remain in legal limbo for at least a year.
Analyst Scott Cleland noted that the uncertainty surrounding the case could negatively affect the phone industry and stocks.
The order was intended to implement the 1996 communications law, which allowed competition among local and long-distance carriers.
The appeals court sided with local carriers and state regulators, arguing that the FCC overstepped its authority.
The FCC order requires local carriers to lease their phone lines to new competitors at discounts of up to 25 percent.

The U.S. communications revolution has started slowly, with more hype than competition among various carriers and firms.
Experts believe it is too early to judge the telecommunications reform bill a failure, one year after its passage.
Predictions indicate that the current lack of competition will eventually lead to increased competition, new services, and lower prices in communications.
Industry analyst Jeffrey Kagan stated that significant change in the first year is unrealistic.
Scott Cleland of Schwab Washington Research Group noted that the expectations for the bill's timeline were overly ambitious.
The Telecommunications Act of 1996 was enacted on February 8 and removed 62-year-old legal barriers in the communications industry.
The Act encourages competition among local and long-distance carriers, cable-TV operators, and electric utilities.
One-stop shopping for communication services has not yet materialized significantly, and prices have increased.
The slow start is attributed to a timetable that stretches up to 15 months and the Federal Communications Commission's delay in finalizing key rules.
The local phone market continues to be dominated by the Baby Bells one year after the reform.

Ameritech Corp. received an endorsement from Michigan regulators to offer long-distance telephone service.
The Michigan Public Service Commission voted to advise the Federal Communications Commission that Ameritech has met a 14-point checklist for opening its local phone network.
The checklist was established under last year's communications law as a requirement for local carriers to offer long-distance service.
An AT&T spokesman expressed disappointment with the decision, claiming it ignores evidence of a lack of local competition for Ameritech in Michigan.
The FCC will make the final determination on Ameritech's compliance with the technical checklist for entering the long-distance market.
The Justice Department must provide a recommendation to the FCC by February 21.
Ameritech requested permission from the FCC on January 2 to provide long-distance service in Michigan.
Ameritech has 3.5 million customers in Michigan.
Long-distance carriers like AT&T and MCI Communications Corp. have urged regulators to reject Ameritech's request.
The Michigan commission voted 2-1 to authorize comments on the Ameritech case to be filed with the FCC.

Calendar third quarter returns for Internet stocks will reflect a sacrifice of near-term profits for longer-term growth.
Many Internet startups are expected to continue posting quarterly losses while fighting to build market share.
Steve Harmon, a senior investment analyst at Mecklermedia's iWORLD, stated that technology must be digested and paid for.
Yahoo! Inc. was started by two venture-backed Stanford University students two years ago.
Yahoo! has been building on its branded media model during its second full quarter after its initial offering.
Analysts expect Yahoo! to report a $0.07 a share loss for the third quarter.
Yahoo! has begun opening metropolitan services in U.S. cities and internationally in Japan and Britain.
Yahoo! reported one billion full-page hits in the quarter.
Lycos Inc. reported a loss of $0.16 a share for its fourth fiscal quarter ended in July.
Infoseek Corp is expected to report a third quarter loss of $0.18 a share on October 21.

Wired magazine is a startup from the 1990s.
Some analysts warn that Wired magazine may be a better read than a good investment.
Steve Harmon is a senior investment analyst at Mecklermedia's iWORLD.
Wired Ventures Inc. is the publisher of Wired magazine.
The initial public offering of Wired Ventures Inc. was due to be priced late on Thursday.
Goldman Sachs is the lead underwriter for the IPO.
The IPO was initially scheduled for July but was postponed due to a decline in technology and Internet stocks.
Internet stocks have rebounded nearly 10 percent from their July lows.
Wired Ventures' revised offering has reduced its projected market capitalization by approximately $200 million.
Wired intends to sell up to 4.75 million shares at a price range of $12 to $14 per share.

Silicon Valley executives and venture capitalists are spending millions of dollars to defeat California's Proposition 211.
They claim Proposition 211 threatens American capitalism and could negatively impact stock prices.
California's Proposition 211 would eliminate certain legal safeguards for corporate officers and staff members.
The measure would hold corporate officers liable for incorrect projections about future results.
Opponents fear that corporate officers will stop making projections, complicating investment decisions and potentially lowering share prices.
Proponents of Proposition 211 argue it will help victims of fraud recover losses.
Opponents describe the measure as a way for securities lawyers to profit.
A Los Angeles Times poll indicated that 52 percent of likely voters oppose Proposition 211, an increase from five weeks prior.
Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt has urged voters to reject Proposition 211, citing concerns about increased class action suits.
Both President Bill Clinton and Bob Dole have publicly opposed Proposition 211.

Microsoft Corp launched electronic commerce software aimed at enabling consumers and businesses to buy and sell products over the World Wide Web.
The core of the announcement is Microsoft's Merchant Server, which allows businesses to set up electronic storefronts on the Internet.
Microsoft plans to build a new channel of service providers to assist businesses in setting up electronic storefronts.
Analysts noted that Microsoft's strategy is similar to that used by Novell Inc to sell networking software.
Microsoft Chairman and Chief Executive Bill Gates stated that there will be explosive growth in the use of the Web for shopping.
Microsoft revealed that 40 companies are in the process of building Merchant Server sites.
Henry Vigil, general manager of electronic commerce services at Microsoft, expects 300 sites using the software by year-end.
The Merchant Server product competes with offerings from Netscape Communications Corp, Open Market, Oracle Corp, and International Business Machines Corp.
Microsoft and VeriFone Inc collaborated with financial institutions and payment processors to provide a secure Internet retailing and payment system.
The financial institutions involved include BankAmerica Corp, Wells Fargo & Co, Citicorp's Citibank Card Acceptance Europe, First USA Paymenteck Inc, NOVUS Services, and Royal Bank of Canada.

Hewlett-Packard Co. is expected to unveil a new family of devices designed to allow people to bypass copy machines.
The new models can be used instead of a copier to make multiple printouts of a document.
The introduction of these devices poses a threat to copy machine makers such as Xerox Corp. and Canon Inc.
One source stated that this is the first direct attack at the copier market.
The initial adaptation of the technology will likely be targeted for modest printing jobs, such as three or four copies of a document.
A spokesman for Hewlett-Packard was not immediately available for comment on the new product.
The new machine, referred to internally as the 'Mopier,' is expected to be based on the LaserJet 5Si family.
The Mopier is expected to include a stapler, a multiple-slot stacker, and secure, password-protected mailboxes for confidential documents.
Hewlett-Packard announced plans to triple production of toner cartridges for its LaserJet 5Si family of network printers.
Hewlett-Packard's research indicates that pages formerly duplicated on copiers are increasingly being printed on HP printers.

The semiconductor industry reported that its key indicator rose to the highest level in almost a year.
The book-to-bill ratio increased to 1.10 in October from a revised 0.98 in September.
This is the first time the book-to-bill ratio has been over 1 since December 1995.
The Semiconductor Industry Association stated that new chip orders in October rose 17.9 percent to $3.84 billion.
Shipments increased by 5 percent from the previous month to $3.39 billion.
Analysts suggested that the surge in new orders was likely a one-time phenomenon.
Douglas Andrey, director of Information Systems and Finance at the Securities Industry Association, expressed cautious optimism for a solid fourth quarter.
Analysts expect computer chip stocks to advance further following the positive data.
Shares of Intel Corp surged to $124.69 in after-hours trade, just below its all-time trading high.
The trade group plans to phase out the North American semiconductor index in favor of a global index.

The 25th anniversary of the microprocessor is a highlight of this year's industry summit.
Senior executives predict the next 25 years of the industry will be fast-paced and competitive.
The week of the summit will feature new products, including hand-held Windows PCs and new Network Computers.
DVD technology, which holds significantly more data than conventional CD-ROMs, is expected to launch next year.
The new DVD medium will allow users to play full-length movies on laptops and is anticipated to inspire new computer games.
The annual event is expected to attract nearly a quarter of a million attendees, including executives, analysts, customers, and media.
Carl Wankowski, president of Sony Electronics Inc., stated that the convergence of television, computers, and telecommunications is redefining itself.
Sony plans to showcase products such as DVD technologies and a WebTV set-top box at the summit.
Intel CEO Andy Grove will deliver the opening keynote, discussing the history of the microprocessor and its impact on Intel.
Bill Gates, Chairman of Microsoft, is scheduled to give a keynote speech that will challenge the industry.

Microsoft Corp. Chairman Bill Gates stated that the personal computer will remain prominent for many years.
Gates made these comments during his keynote address at the annual Comdex industry trade show in Las Vegas.
He highlighted that the personal computer has survived criticisms and will continue to be used in various devices.
Microsoft unveiled its first line of handheld PC devices running on the new Windows CE operating system.
Gates mentioned that Microsoft is working on advancements for its high-end Windows NT program to improve scalability.
These technologies can store terabytes of data and process billions of transactions daily.
Currently, only around 15 companies store terabytes of data, and the billion-transaction level exceeds what phone companies, credit card firms, or airlines process.
Gates noted that the personal computer industry has grown significantly, with over 200 million PC users worldwide.
He indicated that maintaining unit sales growth above 10 percent in the future will be challenging.
Gates outlined future technologies, including three-dimensional graphics and advanced input methods like speech recognition.

U.S. high-tech venture fund investment increased by 50 percent in the third quarter.
Overall U.S. venture investment rose by 25 percent in the third quarter compared to the previous year.
High-technology industries received $1.32 billion in the third quarter, making up two-thirds of the total $2 billion invested.
Software investments more than doubled to $596 million compared to the previous year.
In the first nine months of 1996, software investments reached $1.74 billion, surpassing the $1.34 billion recorded for all of 1995.
Total venture-backed investments in the U.S. for the first nine months of 1996 reached $7 billion.
The third quarter total of $2 billion was a decrease from the $2.8 billion recorded in the second quarter.
Startup and early-stage companies received 46 percent of the venture capital investment, totaling $600 million.
On average, startup companies received more than $3.1 million in funding.
Funding for Internet-related companies continued at a high level, with 62 companies receiving funding in the third quarter.

The browser wars have shifted to a focus on delivering content efficiently over the Web.
There will be increased competition in the coming months for products that deliver information directly to computers.
The Internet is transitioning from a 'pull' model to a 'push' model for information delivery.
Eli Barkat is the chief executive of BackWeb Technologies, a start-up based in San Jose, California.
Barkat stated that people want to build relationships with information providers.
Vivek Ranadive is the president of Reuters Holdings Plc's Tibco Inc. unit.
Ranadive compared early Internet surfing to Sunday drives in the early days of the automobile.
Electronic commerce is expected to grow in 1997 and requires more efficient navigation of the Internet.
More than a dozen small high-tech start-ups are trying to define the space for efficient information delivery.
Jack Wilson is the managing editor of Technologic Partners' ComputerLetter.

A Silicon Valley company has developed a new technology to personalize the World Wide Web.
The new service is called The Angle and is available from BroadVision Inc. based in Los Altos, California.
The Angle uses BroadVision's One-to-One technology to create individual user profiles.
Users can customize their web experience by combining personal interests and preferred styles.
The service allows users to select different 'personalities' for viewing information.
Users can create different profiles for various moods, such as business or home use.
The Angle site is free to use and does not require registration.
User profiling information is stored for privacy and can be changed at any time.
Pehong Chen is the founder, president, and chief executive of BroadVision.
BroadVision is targeting large organizations for co-branded services and internal use of the technology.

Netscape Communications Corp sees no sign of a reduction in market growth for Internet and intranet.
Mike Homer is the vice president of marketing at Netscape Communications Corp.
Netscape currently has around 50 million users of its Netscape Navigator software.
Netscape Navigator comprises roughly 75 percent of the total browser market.
Critical approval for Netscape's new Communicator software has exceeded expectations.
Homer stated that Netscape is holding market share and the market is growing dramatically.
Homer declined to comment on the company's expected results for the fourth quarter or the current quarter.
Shares of Netscape closed at 47-7/8 after a downgrade from analyst William Gurley.
Gurley downgraded Netscape's stock rating due to concerns over product transition and pricing model changes.
Homer reported that 95 percent of reviews for the Communicator product are positive.

Lotus Development Corp. Chief Executive Officer Michael Zisman stated that the company will focus on the collaborative Internet software market, projected to reach $1 billion by 1999.
Lotus was acquired by International Business Machines Corp. last year in a deal valued at more than $3 billion.
Zisman emphasized that Lotus should concentrate on its core business of groupware rather than trying to serve all markets.
Zisman delivered a keynote address at a three-day Internet & Electronic Commerce conference organized by the Gartner Group.
A new version of Lotus Notes software, version 4.5, is scheduled for release in the fourth quarter and will include server software for Internet collaboration.
The new collaboration feature is based on technology called Domino, which is currently being tested.
Zisman expressed that too much focus is currently placed on browsers, which are software that help users navigate the Internet.
He noted that the server market is currently more significant than the browser market and predicted that browsers will likely be included in operating systems like Windows.
Zisman projected that the server market for collaboration through Internet sites alone will reach $1 billion by the end of the decade.
He stated that the server market will likely segment into content, collaboration, and commerce categories, with larger organizations using applications from various suppliers.

Twentieth Century Fox announced a new regional office in Hong Kong for its home entertainment division.
Jeffrey Yapp is the president of Twentieth Century Fox Home Entertainment International.
Twentieth Century Fox is owned by News Corp Ltd.
The new regional headquarters will oversee marketing and distribution for video subsidiaries in Japan, Korea, Australia, and India.
Twentieth Century Fox Home Entertainment International has restructured its business in the last two years.
The company has spent about US$2 million and hired 15 people as part of its expansion into Asia.
Asia accounts for 38 percent of the video division's revenue, with Japan being the largest territory in terms of revenue contribution.
Marc Cudennec is the senior vice-president at Fox Home International.
Fox's international focus is one of three critical strategies adopted in a restructuring 18 months ago.
The number of films in development at Fox has increased from 60 to over 450.

Indonesia issued regulations earlier this year promoting the creation of mutual funds.
The regulations have been recognized as a landmark for the local investment fund industry.
Melli Darsa from the law firm Hadiputranto, Hadinoto and Partners stated that the recognition of open-end funds by the Capital Market Law has been instrumental in the development of the industry.
Seven open-end mutual funds have already been established in Indonesia, with five more planned.
Indonesia released regulations in May outlining accounting methods, reporting procedures, and valuation methods for open-end mutual funds.
The new legal framework allows open-end mutual funds for the first time under the 1995 Capital Market Law.
Anthony Travers from the law firm Maples and Calder stated that Indonesia's financial infrastructure is more developed than that of China and India.
Delegates at the conference noted significant obstacles to the mutual fund industry, including a lack of awareness among Indonesians and restrictions on foreign investment.
Indonesian pension funds hold nearly US$2.4 billion but are prohibited from investing overseas.
Iwan Pontjowinoto, president director of P.T. Danareksa Fund Management, stated that the new rules aim to encourage domestic investment to spur the development of local capital markets.

John Greenwood is the architect of Hong Kong's currency link to the U.S. dollar.
Greenwood defended the peg's continued existence beyond Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty.
Greenwood stated that China must uphold the currency link to comply with the Basic Law.
Greenwood is the chairman and chief economist at LGT Asset Management.
The Basic Law requires China to preserve key features of the existing currency system.
Key features include maintenance of 100 percent reserves for the Hong Kong dollar float and full convertibility.
Greenwood believes it will be difficult for China to depart from the linked rate system without undermining the Basic Law.
Greenwood stated that most proposals for changing the currency peg are impractical and risky.
He argued that any change in the rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar would reduce stability.
Greenwood noted that the renminbi would need to be fully convertible to become a reserve currency.

Jardine Fleming Holdings Ltd announced an increased emphasis on regulatory compliance following revelations of front-running by a fund manager.
Alan Smith is the chairman of Jardine Fleming Holdings Ltd.
A five-month investigation by regulators in London and Hong Kong revealed irregular trades by a former senior fund manager at Jardine Fleming Investment Management Ltd.
Jardine Fleming Investment Management Ltd manages US$22 billion.
Colin Armstrong, a fund manager, delayed processing deals, which allowed for changes in trading prices.
Some irregular trades involved Colin Armstrong's personal trading account.
Jardine Fleming agreed to pay disadvantaged clients US$19.3 million as a result of the incident.
The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) in Hong Kong revoked the registration of Robert Thomas, the chief executive at Jardine Fleming Investment Management.
The SFC issued a public reprimand to Jardine Fleming.
Jardine Fleming Asset Management (JFAM) was fined 400,000 sterling and had its authorization revoked.

Hong Kong business groups oppose linking China's permanent most favoured nation (MFN) trading status to Beijing's handling of Hong Kong after its return to Chinese control.
U.S. Congressman Jim Kolbe is leading a 22-member delegation from the House of Representatives to Beijing.
The United States intends to monitor Hong Kong for at least a year before considering granting China permanent MFN status.
Mark Michelson, former chairman of the American Chamber of Commerce, stated that conditioning or removing MFN during the transition period would have a devastating effect on Hong Kong.
China currently enjoys MFN status, which is subject to annual review.
Hong Kong supports China's application for full MFN status, which would provide China with the same treatment as other major U.S. trading partners without annual review.
Selina Yen from the Hong Kong government's trade and industry branch stated that MFN should be the norm and not a privilege.
Few in Hong Kong expect China to receive full MFN status in 1997, the year of Hong Kong's return to China.
Frank Martin, president of the American Chamber of Commerce, expressed that it would have been an opportune time for Congress to extend permanent MFN status if not for the handover.
Legislation on permanent MFN has been submitted to Congress but has not yet been voted on.

The scandal involving late allocation of trades at Jardine Fleming attracted attention in Hong Kong.
Jardine Fleming did not face further sanctions and stated that business continued as usual.
A company spokesman reported that there were both redemptions and subscriptions.
Jardine Fleming retained its seat on the executive committee of the Hong Kong Investment Funds Association.
Media reports suggested that there were attempts to remove Jardine Fleming from the committee.
Jardine Fleming remains one of 12 member firms with a representative on the board of the association.
The election for the board began in early August and ballots were collected by mail.
An association spokeswoman stated there was no relationship between the elections and the scandal.
Jardine Fleming received criticism from the association regarding its past practices.
Regulators imposed heavy fines on Jardine Fleming and revoked the licence of its London-based fund management company.

The World Bank forecasts a 20-percent increase in Asian energy demand each year for the next decade.
Analysts indicate that uncertainty in the Asian power stock sector makes short-term value hard to find.
Factors contributing to uncertainty include the privatization of state utilities and the emergence of independent power producers (IPPs).
Thomas Chesser, a BZW Asia Research analyst, states that the risk/reward ratio of power investments is escalating due to industry changes.
Analysts believe that stock selection will be critical to avoid short-term hazards in the Asian power sector.
Asian power companies are expected to require an additional 2,000 megawatts of capacity each month for a decade, necessitating annual investments exceeding US$35 billion.
Up to 40 percent of new generating assets in the coming years will come from IPPs, leading to greater divergence in share price performance.
The Electric Authority of Thailand (EGAT) and National Power Corp in the Philippines are scheduled for privatization within the next two years.
A total of about US$2.5 billion in new equity is expected to enter Asian markets this year.
Goldman Sachs analyst Hilary Judis suggests that new supply may reduce premiums for already-listed companies.

Hong Kong fund managers and life insurers are optimistic about the potential of Hong Kong's public pension plan.
