The proposed Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) could lead to a tripling of Hong Kong-registered pension assets if regulations are passed by July 1.
Terry Smith is the chief executive at National Mutual Asia.
National Mutual Asia is 69-percent owned by Australia's National Mutual Holdings.
A company achieving a 10 percent market share in the pension market could receive contributions of HK$3 billion per annum.
National Mutual Asia's current premium and contribution revenue is about HK$5 billion.
Hong Kong pension assets are currently valued at about HK$100 billion, primarily held in government and corporate funds.
If MPF regulations are approved, pension assets could reach HK$300 billion within five years, with annual contributions projected at HK$30 billion.
The Big Three fund managers in Hong Kong are HSBC Asset Management, Schroders Investment Management, and Jardine Fleming Investment Management.
HSBC has US$3.5 billion under management, Schroders manages US$2.5 billion, and Jardine Fleming manages US$2.2 billion.

Many Asian fund managers welcomed stock market fluctuations related to rumors about Deng Xiaoping's health.
Asian markets have regained much of the losses incurred on Tuesday due to the rumors.
Fund managers believe that any announcement of Deng's death will have limited effect on the markets.
Christopher Day, managing director at Thornton Management (Asia) Ltd, stated that the market is filled with rumors.
Stewart Aldcroft, sales director at Templeton, indicated that immediate reactions to news will occur but will not last, especially in Hong Kong.
Tina So, associate director at Schroders Investment Management, noted that Hong Kong is trading at a discount compared to other Asian markets.
Fund managers suggested that Hong Kong could correct to 12,500 but may recover quickly.
The Hang Seng index closed at 13,106.32 on Wednesday after dropping to 12,933.98 on Tuesday.
The Taiwan market experienced a drop after reaching a six-year high due to profit-taking prompted by rumors.
Foreign investors in Taiwan warned that an announcement regarding Deng could lead to further market weakness.

Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader, died on Wednesday.
Most smaller Asian markets largely ignored the news of Deng Xiaoping's death.
Hong Kong and Taiwan experienced higher trading despite the news.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand index gained seven percent over the past eight trading days.
The increase in the Stock Exchange of Thailand index followed a previous week's decline due to a debt rating review by Moody's Investors Service Inc.
Traders reported fund flows moving out of Asia into Latin America.
Analysts expect stocks in Hong Kong to refocus on fundamentals and trade sideways.
The Hang Seng Index rose 331.59 points, or 2.53 percent, over the week to close at 13,444.85.
The Nikkei average ended down 17.17 points, or 0.09 percent, at 19,034.54 on Friday.
The Nikkei average rose 312.54 points, or 1.67 percent, during the week.

Thailand's finance sector has implemented tougher rules to boost market confidence.
Foreign investors had mixed reactions to Thailand's new finance sector rules.
Some investors welcomed Thailand's acknowledgment of asset quality problems.
Other investors criticized the timing of the announcement as too late.
Thailand's central bank ordered 10 finance companies to raise capital immediately.
The central bank also mandated provisioning levels of 115 percent for banks and 120 percent for finance companies.
Speculation about asset quality had previously caused a significant decline in the stock market.
Fund Manager Templeton called for aggressive management of the finance sector issues.
Analysts indicated that only four or five banks would need to raise provisions to meet new requirements.
Most of Thailand's 90 finance companies cannot meet the existing 100-percent provisioning requirement.

Thailand's banking sector crisis prompted calls for an upgrade of Asia's financial infrastructure at an International Monetary Fund-Hong Kong Monetary Authority meeting.
IMF managing director Michel Camdessus stated that Asia needs a stronger financial infrastructure.
The banking system in Asia has not kept pace with economic development, creating an urgent need for an overhaul.
Camdessus noted that prudential regulation and supervision have not kept pace with the complexities of the banking business.
Camdessus warned that unaddressed gaps in banking regulation could pose dangers for stability.
Thailand intervened to demand better provisioning by its banks due to asset quality problems.
Thailand's monetary policy was hampered in addressing its banking sector issues.
The baht is pegged to a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar but faced pressure from speculators.
Gerald Corrigan, managing director at Goldman Sachs, emphasized the need for stronger supervisory oversight of financial institutions.
Mahmood Pradhan, a senior economist with the IMF, stated that deregulation has increased exposure to credit and foreign exchange risk.

China confirmed that dissident Wang Xizhe fled the country.
China accused Wang Xizhe of crossing the border illegally.
Chinese authorities are pursuing those who assisted Wang Xizhe in his escape.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang stated that Wang's case involves illegal border crossing.
Wang Xizhe escaped to Hong Kong after a fellow activist was sentenced to a labour camp.
Wang has been missing from his home in Guangdong since the arrest of Liu Xiaobo.
Wang is reported to be seeking asylum in the United States.
China has not received official confirmation of Wang seeking refuge in the United States.
Wang and Liu Xiaobo accused the Communist Party of violating a 1945 pledge regarding freedom of the press.
Wang was first jailed in 1974 for advocating democracy and was paroled in 1993 after serving 12 years.

China stated that sexual contact is the leading cause of AIDS.
China warned that venereal disease could lead to an AIDS epidemic.
Health experts quoted by Xinhua urged immediate action to control the rising incidence of STDs in China.
Xinhua reported that the number of cases of eight major sexually transmitted diseases, including AIDS, gonorrhea, and syphilis, reached 362,000 last year.
Officials forecast that the number of reported cases could exceed 800,000 by the year 2000.
Minister of Public Health Chen Minzhang emphasized the importance of STD control in combating AIDS.
Ye Shunzhang, director of the National Venereal Disease Control Centre, indicated that the occurrence of HIV infection would increase with rising STDs.
Official figures show that China has 4,305 people infected with HIV, an increase from 3,341 at the end of 1995.
Experts estimate that up to 100,000 people in China could be infected with HIV.
Xinhua warned that the number of HIV cases in China could spiral out of control without prompt preventive measures.

China announced it would empower Hong Kong's courts to try off-duty Chinese soldiers after resuming control over Hong Kong in 1997.
The National People's Congress was expected to pass a law regarding criminal and civil cases involving troops in Hong Kong.
Crimes committed by off-duty personnel will be handled by the courts of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Criminal cases involving on-duty soldiers will be handled by military courts.
Civil rights offences committed by off-duty members of the Chinese garrison will be dealt with by Hong Kong courts.
Civil rights offences committed by soldiers while on duty will be referred to China's Supreme People's Court.
Chinese lawmakers referenced British army practices in Hong Kong when drafting the measures.
Defence operations of the People's Liberation Army will not be subject to Hong Kong courts.
Troops stationed in Hong Kong will notify the Hong Kong SAR government in advance of military drills involving public interest.
Military personnel will be forbidden from participating in political or religious organisations in Hong Kong.

Wang Dan, a leading Chinese activist, will go on trial on Wednesday for plotting to overthrow the government.
The Beijing Number One Intermediate People's Court informed Wang's family about the trial schedule.
Wang's mother, Wang Lingyun, plans to attend the trial to help defend her son.
Wang's family found a lawyer to defend him on most charges after being given one day to do so.
Only Wang Dan's father and sister will be allowed to attend the trial.
Wang Lingyun hopes the court will judge her son based on the facts and the law.
Wang Dan has been charged with a crime that carries a maximum penalty of death and a minimum of 10 years in prison.
Wang Dan has previously served four years in prison for counter-revolutionary crimes related to the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989.
The court is expected to limit attendance at Wang's trial to selected individuals to exclude foreign reporters and dissidents.
Wang could appeal to the Higher People's Court if convicted.

U.S. Undersecretary of State Lynn Davis has arrived in Beijing for talks with Chinese officials on arms proliferation.
Davis's visit is intended to lay the groundwork for a visit by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher later this month.
Warren Christopher's upcoming visit to China will be his first since a 1994 trip that ended due to human rights issues.
Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Robert Einhorn arrived in Beijing earlier this week for expert talks ahead of Davis's visit.
Davis will have main talks on security and proliferation issues on the 4th and 5th of the month.
Davis will return to the United States to report to the Secretary of State after her talks.
Arms control will be one of many issues that Christopher will discuss with Chinese officials.
Sino-U.S. relations have been strained by disputes over human rights, Taiwan, copyright theft, and WTO entry terms.
Washington has expressed concern over the sentencing of Chinese pro-democracy activist Wang Dan to 11 years in prison.
Davis will discuss the implementation of a peaceful nuclear cooperation pact signed in 1985.

A decade ago, Chinese publishers used manual typesetting to select characters from stereotypes.
In 1986, Wang Xuan created a software program for representing Chinese fonts on computers.
Wang's Electronic Publishing System is used by nearly all newspapers in China.
Founder Group Corp, which Wang helped launch, has 36 subsidiaries and employs over 1,000 people.
Founder is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange.
Founder's net assets were HK$494.9 million at the end of 1995.
Founder posted a net profit of HK$109 million last year on sales of HK$1.1 billion.
In the first six months of this year, Founder's net profit rose 7.0 percent to HK$55.8 million.
Founder's turnover increased by 27 percent to HK$590 million in the same period.
Founder holds 78 percent of China's publishing software market as of August, up from 70 percent at the end of 1995.

The Communist Party chief in Tibet has pledged to enhance patriotic education in the region.
The goal of patriotic education is to counter foreign forces that are hostile to China and the influence of the Dalai Lama.
The Tibet Daily reported that patriotic education is crucial in combating hostile Western forces that aim to create chaos in Tibet.
Party secretary Chen Kuiyuan stated that opposing ideological infiltration from hostile Western forces and the Dalai Lama is a significant task.
Chen Kuiyuan emphasized the need to combat the Dalai Lama's influence in Tibet.
Chen accused Western media of promoting the Dalai Lama's agenda to separate Tibet from China.
Chen claimed that the struggle against 'westernisation' and 'splitting up' will continue for a long time.
Chen stated that ideological education is necessary to combat religious and separatist ideas in Tibetan schools.
Chen described teaching love for the motherland and socialism as the primary task of ideological construction.
The Tibet Daily called for stricter controls on religion in Tibet and a crackdown on pro-independence monks and nuns.

The decision to dam the Yangtze River was made by electrical engineer-turned-premier Li Peng.
The China Three Gorges Project Development Corp officials are confident that funding shortfalls and environmental activists will not hinder the project.
The dam in Hubei faces a funding shortfall of one-sixth of its total cost.
The estimated cost of the Three Gorges Dam is at least 240 billion yuan ($29 billion) and could rise to 300 billion yuan ($36 billion).
Costs were estimated at 90 billion yuan in 1993, with additional costs from interest and inflation expected to reach at least 150 billion yuan by 2009.
The central government will cover 50 percent of the projected minimum cost, while state bank loans will account for another 20 percent.
The State Development Bank is expected to provide about 30 billion yuan in loans for the project.
Revenue from the Gezhouba dam is projected to contribute an additional 15-18 billion yuan.
The dam is expected to generate 84.7 million megawatt-hours of electricity annually.
Officials are exploring international funding options to address a shortfall of at least 40 billion yuan.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin called on Taiwanese people to offer views on reunification.
Jiang made this statement during a New Year's address broadcast on state television.
Some analysts viewed Jiang's proposal as a departure from Deng Xiaoping's 'one country, two systems' formula.
Jiang expressed a desire to secure a place in modern China's history alongside Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping.
Ties between China and Taiwan deteriorated after Beijing conducted military exercises near Taiwan.
Jiang stated that reunification was the common wish of all Chinese people.
He urged Taiwan's leadership to prioritize national interests and cease activities that could split the country.
Beijing has considered Taiwan a rebel province since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
Taipei claims it seeks reunification but under different terms than those proposed by Beijing.
China plans to continue advocating for direct transport and trade links with Taiwan.

A Russian swimmer, Nina Zhyvanevskaya, won the 100 metres backstroke event at the World Cup short-course series.
Nina Zhyvanevskaya set a new European record with a time of 59.01 seconds in the 100 metres backstroke.
The Chinese women's swimming team won eight out of nine events at the World Cup short-course series.
The only event the Chinese women's team did not win was the 100 metres backstroke.
Wang Luna won the 400 metres freestyle with a time of 4:05.45.
Chen Yan won the 400 metres individual medley and also earned a silver in the 100 metres individual medley and a bronze in the 100 metres backstroke.
Han Xie finished just 0.02 seconds shy of the world record in the 50 metres breaststroke with a time of 31.00 seconds.
Lu Bin placed sixth in the 100 metres backstroke after returning from a suspension related to a doping scandal.
Shan Ying won the 100 metres freestyle, Qu Yun won the 200 metres butterfly, and Mi Tong won the 200 metres breaststroke.
China's men's swimming team won three out of eight available golds at the World Cup short-course series.

A U.S. defence team found human remains and parts of an American bomber in southwestern China.
The team inspected a World War Two crash site on Maoer mountain in Guangxi province.
The mission was deemed a success despite an injury to a U.S. reporter.
Alan Liotta is the deputy director of the MIA/POW office under the Department of Defence.
Liotta stated that the findings confirmed information about a crash that occurred on August 31, 1944.
The B-24 bomber had a 10-man crew and did not return from a raid on Japanese ships around Taiwan.
A six-man forensic team from the Department of Defence flew into Guangxi to recover remains.
Local residents discovered the crash site last October while searching for wild herbs.
U.S. officials learned of the crash site from Chinese President Jiang Zemin during a meeting with President Bill Clinton.
Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian gave U.S. Secretary of Defence William Perry two dogtags recovered from the site.

China has launched its first survey of rural residents to assess the impact of economic reforms on agriculture.
The survey began on January 1 and involves six million officials and interviewers.
The survey aims to canvass approximately 230 million households in rural areas.
The survey is intended to gather detailed data on rural areas transformed by economic reforms initiated by Deng Xiaoping in the late 1970s.
Interviewers in Nankou township are asking residents about family size, education levels, crops grown, and occupations.
Deng Xiaoping's reforms have promoted private enterprise and rural industry, significantly changing the countryside.
Official statistics indicate that 75 percent of China's 1.2 billion people are farmers, but this figure may be misleading.
Many former farmers have transitioned to migrant labor or jobs in rural factories.
The survey aims to provide an understanding of household engagement in farming, township enterprises, and self-employment.
This is the first national rural census since the 1949 communist takeover.

China defended a proposal to roll back civil liberties in Hong Kong after its reversion to Chinese rule.
Zhou Bingxin is an official with the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office under the State Council of China.
Zhou stated that all rights and freedoms have limits.
Zhou claimed that recent British reforms to Hong Kong's civil liberties laws violated the Basic Law.
The Basic Law is the future mini-constitution of Hong Kong promulgated by Beijing.
Zhou asserted that Hong Kong's original laws align with international human rights conventions.
A panel of the Preparatory Committee listed 25 laws and articles for repeal or amendment when Beijing resumes control of Hong Kong.
The 1990 Basic Law and a 1984 Sino-British handover treaty promise a high degree of autonomy for Hong Kong's 6.3 million residents.
Zhou stated that the right to hold mass public gatherings and demonstrations in Hong Kong would be guaranteed by law after the handover.
Zhou emphasized that no rights or freedoms are absolute and all have limits.

Britain's Guardian Royal Exchange announced on Tuesday that 350 jobs will be eliminated due to a restructuring of its area and branch network.
The job losses are a result of the 48 million pound acquisition of Legal & General's commercial insurance operations in July.
Guardian stated that the restructuring aims to improve service levels and capitalize on economies of scale from the Legal & General acquisition.
The Banking, Insurance and Finance Union (BIFU) criticized the job losses as 'arbitrary' and accused Guardian of catering to industry analysts and the stock market.
The announcement follows a year of significant job cuts in the insurance industry due to consolidation efforts.
After the merger of Royal Insurance and Sun Alliance in May, it was reported that 5,000 jobs would be cut across the group, primarily in the UK.
The merger of United Friendly and Refuge Group in August is expected to result in the loss of 1,800 jobs over the next two to three years.
The insurance industry is anticipated to undergo further consolidation driven by the need for cost savings and competitive advantages.
B.A.T industries is rumored to be seeking a partner for its financial services arm, which includes Eagle Star and Allied Dunbar.
The insurance industry, which employs approximately 200,000 staff directly, has shed around 40,000 jobs between 1991 and 1995.

The insurance industry is facing overcapacity and increasing competition.
A merger between Lloyd Thompson Group and JIB Group is valued at 300 million pounds ($500 million).
This merger follows a $1.23 billion acquisition of Alexander & Alexander Services by Aon Corp.
Both mergers indicate a trend of consolidation in the insurance sector.
The Aon/A&A deal aims to reduce costs due to falling rates and declining revenues.
The merger of Lloyd Thompson and JIB is motivated by the desire to leverage complementary businesses.
Cost savings from the Lloyd Thompson and JIB merger will primarily occur in London operations.
Future growth for the merged companies will focus on opportunities in Asia Pacific.
There are rumors of Aon or Marsh & McLennan potentially launching a takeover bid for Sedgwick.
Analysts note that brokers frequently discuss mergers and consolidation in the industry.

Britain's Ladbroke Group Plc formed a global alliance with Hilton Hotels Corp on Monday.
The alliance reunites the Hilton brand worldwide for the first time in 32 years.
The agreement covers 400 hotels in 49 countries.
Ladbroke and Hilton denied any hidden agenda for a full merger.
Ladbroke chief executive Peter George stated that the alliance is a first step in bringing the hotels business closer.
Shares in Ladbroke increased by 2-1/2 pence to 236 pence following the announcement.
The deal includes sales and marketing, loyalty programs, and development to enhance growth.
Hilton has operated separately within and outside the U.S. since 1964.
HHC chief executive Stephen Bollenbach stated that customers will perceive the companies as one for the first time in 32 years.
The agreement includes a worldwide loyalty program, Hilton HHonors Worldwide, starting on February 1.

Fund manager Nicola Horlick had a public dispute with her former employer Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM).
Horlick admitted to being in talks with Dutch firm ABN AMRO until several days before her suspension.
Horlick described the talks with ABN AMRO as informal and preliminary.
Horlick stated that she did not provide confidential information about MGAM or her colleagues during the talks.
Horlick claimed her aim was to keep the clients and the team together for the benefit of all, including MGAM.
Horlick resigned from MGAM after being suspended amid allegations of planning to defect to ABN AMRO.
Horlick was promoted to managing director of MGAM shortly before her suspension.
Horlick's fight for reinstatement or compensation has received significant media attention.
Horlick expressed her determination to clear her name in a television interview.
Horlick is considering legal action against MGAM for constructive dismissal.

Scottish Amicable will provide policyholders with information about Abbey National's bid when it presents its own proposals for demutualisation.
Scottish Amicable has been campaigning against Abbey National's offer.
Scottish Amicable has refused Abbey National's requests to halt its demutualisation timetable.
Abbey National's bid values Scottish Amicable at up to 1.4 billion pounds.
Abbey National's bid includes a minimum payout of 400 million pounds to policyholders.
Abbey National has stated that policyholders should compare Scottish Amicable's proposals with alternative offers.
Scottish Amicable's public campaign included a full-page advertisement in major newspapers.
The advertisement promised to inform policyholders of any better offers before a vote on the proposals.
The ScotAm board has a fiduciary duty to its policyholders.
There is speculation that Scottish Amicable may be waiting for other bidders to emerge.

Britain's NatWest Group announced the establishment of a new business unit called NatWest Wealth Management.
NatWest Wealth Management aims to focus on private banking, long-term savings, and investment markets.
The new unit will include Gartmore, NatWest Life and Investment Services, and NatWest Ventures.
Coutts Group will join NatWest Wealth Management in January 1998 after a restructuring process.
Derek Wanless, the group chief executive of NatWest, stated that the new business has strong growth potential.
Wanless cited demographic changes and the need for savings as factors contributing to market growth potential.
NatWest Wealth Management will manage funds exceeding 60 billion pounds ($98 billion).
The unit will offer a comprehensive range of products and services to various clients, including private investors and pension fund sponsors.
Paul Myners, chairman of Gartmore, will become the chief executive of NatWest Wealth Management on April 1.
Myners indicated that the businesses in the new group are well-established and represent a significant force in long-term savings and investment products.

Britain's Britannic Assurance declared a 209 million pound special bonus for life insurance policies.
The special bonus follows discussions with the government on ownership of surplus insurance funds.
The payout will apply to all 'with profits' policies in force on February 17, 1997.
Details of the bonus will be announced with the 1996 bonus next month.
Britannic has agreed with the Department of Trade and Industry that 902 million pounds of excess assets can be attributed to shareholders.
Britannic intends to increase its dividend for the year by 82 percent to 23 pence per share.
Britannic shares rose by 29 pence to 832.5 after the announcement.
Total assets in the life funds amounted to 5.682 billion pounds at the end of 1995.
Britannic plans to restructure its long-term funds and implement new sales management and premium collection systems.
The restructuring will create two continuing 'with profits' funds for its industrial and ordinary branches.

Guardian Royal Exchange Plc reported a sharp fall in trading profits for 1996 due to competition and bad weather in the United States and Britain.
Trading profits for the year were down over 17 percent at 281 million pounds before restructuring costs.
Pre-tax profits, including investment gains, dropped to 651 million pounds from 812 million pounds the previous year.
Worldwide general insurance premium income was broadly unchanged at 2.91 billion pounds.
The dividend payout for the year was raised by 11 percent to 10.0 pence per share.
Guardian chief executive John Robins noted some hardening of premiums in selected sectors and regions.
Finance director James Morley stated that premiums in the motor and household insurance markets are expected to strengthen in the coming year.
Guardian aims to grow its business organically and by acquisition while focusing on profitability.
A new management structure was established at the beginning of 1997, and cost savings are expected to equal this year's exceptional charges.
The company plans to withdraw from non-core areas and anticipates some facility closures and staff losses.

Almost 80% of people in Britain oppose insurance companies using genetic test results to charge higher premiums or deny coverage.
The Genetics Forum commissioned an opinion poll that revealed this opposition.
The Association of British Insurers (ABI) announced that individuals seeking life insurance must report genetic test results.
The ABI's requirement aims to assess the financial impact on the insurance industry over the next two years.
The poll indicated that nearly 30% of respondents would avoid genetic testing if they had to disclose results to insurers.
This avoidance could hinder diagnosis of treatable conditions and informed family planning decisions.
ABI guidelines state that detrimental genetic test results may be considered for all types of insurance except life cover linked to mortgages under £100,000.
Standard Life has stated it will not seek genetic test results for any of its policies.
Julie Sheppard from The Genetics Forum stated that the public does not trust insurance companies with genetic information.
The poll found that nearly 40% of people would object to their anonymous tissue samples being used for research without consent.

In 1996, British insurer General Accident Plc reported a profit fall of 15 million pounds ($24.2 million) due to stiff competition and severe weather in the U.S.
Weather-related losses reduced operating profits by 30 million pounds, resulting in total operating profits of 421 million pounds for the year.
Chief executive Bob Scott described the insurance market as increasingly competitive and expressed hope for a rise in motor premiums in the coming year.
General Accident plans to raise motor rates by approximately 3.2 percent in April for about 800,000 vehicles, with a review scheduled for July.
Scott indicated that an eight percent increase for the year would be necessary given current market conditions.
Last year's four percent increase in April resulted in an eventual rise of two to three percent.
Scott noted there were no signs of rate increases in the homeowner or commercial sectors.
Despite the profit fall, the results were at the top end of market expectations, aided by a 10 million pound boost from changes in accounting for overseas earnings.
Year-end net assets per share increased to 675 pence, which later rose to 734 pence.
The dividend for the year increased by 10.5 percent to 34.25 pence per share, exceeding forecasts.

Royal & Sun Alliance Group plc is one of Britain's leading insurers.
The company unveiled its first set of annual results following a merger.
Royal & Sun Alliance Group plc will seek shareholders' permission to buy back up to five percent of its shares.
The company set aside 167 million pounds for U.S. environmental claims, primarily for asbestos.
The provisions follow a change in how the group assesses possible liabilities.
Operating profits for the year were 706 million pounds, down from 915 million pounds in 1995.
Royal & Sun shares were trading at 495 pence, down eight pence from earlier in the day.
The operating profit figure did not include 201 million pounds related to consolidating operations.
Management expressed satisfaction with the results and aims to achieve annual cost savings of 175 million pounds.
The dividend for the year was raised to 19 pence per share.

Scottish Amicable confirmed that three companies submitted final offers for the insurance group by last Friday's bid deadline.
The companies that submitted offers are Abbey National plc, Prudential Corp plc, and Australian Mutual Provident (AMP).
The bidders will find out the outcome of the bids at the end of the month.
None of the bidders have made their offers public.
Scottish Amicable's board and advisers SBC Warburg will evaluate the bids privately.
Scottish Amicable agreed to publish details of offers if requested by a bidder.
All three bidders have agreed to accept the board's decision at the end of March as final.
The board's endorsement is important for securing ownership but does not guarantee it.
Three-quarters of policyholders must approve the board's recommendation for it to be accepted.
Scottish Amicable has arranged for an independent tribunal to resolve disputes from the takeover battle.

Hong Kong's pro-Taiwan community flew Nationalist Chinese flags on Taiwan's national day.
The event took place at the Regent Hotel in Hong Kong.
Zheng An Guo is the general manager of the Chong Hua Travel Agency.
Hong Kong will revert to Chinese rule on July 1, 1997.
The Basic Law will take effect from the handover date.
The Basic Law includes a clause that Hong Kong must observe the 'one-China' principle.
Communist China considers Taiwan a rebel province.
Zhang Su Hui is a spokeswoman for Chong Hua.
Pro-Taiwan sources believe the post-handover authority will restrict celebrations of the Double-ten event.
A spokesman from Xinhua stated that Hong Kong must abide by the 'one China' principle after 1997.

The president of Sinopec, Sheng Huaren, announced plans to increase refining capacity and ethylene production in China.
Sinopec aims to support rapid economic growth and rising energy demand.
Sinopec's expansion plans are outlined in two phases.
By the year 2000, Sinopec plans to increase its refining capacity to over 200 million tonnes per year.
By 2000, Sinopec's ethylene production capacity is expected to reach around five million tonnes per year.
By 2010, Sinopec's refining capacity is projected to reach 300 to 350 million tonnes per year.
By 2010, Sinopec's ethylene production is expected to reach 8.0 to 10 million tonnes per year.
Sinopec's current crude refining capacity is 166 million tonnes per year, with ethylene output at 2.36 million tonnes per year.
China became a net oil importer in 1993 due to economic development outpacing domestic oil output.
China's biggest refinery, Yanshan in Beijing, plans to increase its capacity from 9.5 million tonnes per year to 10 million tonnes before 2000.

Royal/Dutch Shell plans to build an oil refinery in China.
Chinese oil officials revealed that Beijing is close to giving approval for the refinery.
The approval is expected to be granted before the end of 1996.
The refinery and chemical complex is planned for Huizhou in Guangdong province.
The feasibility study report for the project was presented to Beijing in February 1994.
Shell plans to hold 50 percent ownership in the complex.
China National Offshore Oil Corp (CNOOC) will hold 20 percent ownership.
The Guangdong provincial government, China Merchants Holding Company, and SINOPEC will each hold 10 percent ownership.
The Shell plant would be the second joint venture refinery in China involving foreign participation.
China's oil consumption is forecast to grow significantly due to economic reforms.

Sir Ti Liang Yang is the outgoing Chief Justice of Hong Kong.
Yang, 67, resigned as Chief Justice in September to run for Chief Executive of Hong Kong.
Yang aims to succeed Governor Chris Patten when the British leave on June 30.
Yang dropped his knighthood title 'Sir' in October and prefers to be called 'Mister'.
He was knighted in 1988 and was the first Chinese to head the judiciary under British rule.
Tung Chee-hwa is Yang's nearest rival in the Chief Executive contest.
Before Yang entered the race, Tung faced businessman Peter Woo as his main competitor.
A recent public popularity poll showed Yang with 42.6 percent support, ahead of Tung's 32.9 percent.
Woo and former appeals court judge Simon Li are considered unlikely winners by the public.
The winner of the Chief Executive contest will be chosen by a 400-member Selection Committee controlled by China.

Britain and China have agreed to work on a new anti-espionage law in Hong Kong.
The new law will take effect after Hong Kong is handed back to Beijing next year.
Chinese Ambassador Zhao Jihua stated that Britain's official secrets act would be localized for Hong Kong.
Hong Kong currently does not have its own official secrets act.
Zhao warned Britain against making major legal changes before the handover of Hong Kong.
Zhao reassured Hong Kong residents that their freedom of movement will continue after 1997.
Chinese negotiators protested to Britain about a draft anti-subversion bill unveiled by the colonial administration.
Britain has accused China of blocking efforts to draft laws on subversion, sedition, and treason for the handover.
Zhao claimed that Britain violated the 1984 Joint Declaration and Hong Kong's Basic Law.
Zhao stated that Britain's actions represent a unilateral change in the law without consultation with China.

Emily Lau is a pro-democracy politician in Hong Kong.
Emily Lau was removed by police during a protest against China's election methods.
Up to 40 pro-democracy activists clashed with riot police outside the Hong Kong Convention Centre.
A committee of 400 chosen by Beijing voted for a chief executive to rule Hong Kong.
29 demonstrators were arrested for obstruction and were to be released on bail later.
A dozen activists protested by lying down on the road.
Witnesses reported that Emily Lau was among those carried away by police.
Andrew Cheng and Lee Cheuk-yan were also removed by police during the protest.
John Wing-ling Tse expressed that it was a sad day for Hong Kong and noted that ordinary citizens could not vote.
Protesters erected a 'tomb of democracy' outside the Hong Kong Convention Centre.

Taiwan proposed a joint-venture bank called 'Greater China' on Wednesday.
Analysts and businessmen in Hong Kong expressed caution about the proposal.
Carmel Wellso, a regional banking analyst with ING-Barings, stated that more details are needed to assess feasibility.
Wellso noted that large corporations likely have existing relationships with current banks.
Hsu Sheng-fa, chairman of Taiwan's Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry, mentioned that business leaders from Taiwan, China, and Hong Kong are considering the bank.
Hsu proposed the idea during a meeting with business delegations from Hong Kong and mainland China.
The meeting occurred during an unofficial economic forum in Taipei.
Taiwan has banned direct contact with China since the civil war in 1949, requiring third-region communication.
Despite the ban, around 30,000 Taiwan-funded businesses have invested over US$20 billion in China since the late 1980s.
Hong Kong will revert to Chinese control on June 30.

Hong Kong's colonial Governor Chris Patten refused a request by future leader Tung Chee-hwa for support of the interim legislature.
Tung Chee-hwa was chosen by a China-controlled committee to lead Hong Kong starting July 1.
Tung stated that Patten's position was clear and he was unable to convince him to provide help.
Patten and Tung met for 1.5 hours and exchanged handshakes and brief speeches to the press.
Both Patten and Tung described the discussion as long and constructive.
The meeting occurred amid strained Sino-British relations following China's naming of the provisional legislature.
The interim assembly is set to replace the current elected Legislative Council when Hong Kong returns to Chinese control.
The new assembly was designed by China to reverse electoral reforms introduced by Patten.
British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind challenged China regarding the legality of the new assembly.
Patten criticized the new lawmaking body, calling its appointment a bizarre farce.

China's Zhenhai Refining & Chemical Co Ltd experienced a significant drop in its stock price due to U.S. missile attacks on Iraq.
Zhenhai Refining & Chemical Co Ltd stated that investors had over-reacted to the situation.
A senior manager from Zhenhai Refining & Chemical Co Ltd claimed that the stock market reaction was psychological and had minimal real impact.
The share price of Zhenhai Refining & Chemical Co Ltd fell almost 10 percent to HK$2.05 intraday on Tuesday.
The share price closed at HK$2.075, down 20 cents, due to investor fears regarding crude oil price hikes.
On Wednesday, the share price partially recovered to close at HK$2.175.
After the first U.S. missile attack, oil prices reached their highest level since Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
Zhenhai Refining & Chemical Co Ltd runs predominantly on imported crudes and sells most of its output in China's domestic markets.
The company has an eight-million tonne per year refining capacity and had stopped buying crude oil cargoes since the start of the Iraqi crisis.
Zhenhai Refining & Chemical Co Ltd has a crude stockpile that can last for two months.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind met future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa for the first time since Tung was chosen.
The meeting did not narrow the differences between the outgoing and incoming governments.
Tung Chee-hwa stated that London refused to change its objections to China's plans for an interim appointed legislature.
Tung supports China's plans, which are opposed by Hong Kong's pro-democracy lobby.
Rifkind criticized skeptics who believe Britain cannot influence China's plans for Hong Kong after the handover on June 30.
Rifkind stated that Britain would maintain pressure until June 30 and would monitor China's compliance with the Joint Declaration.
The 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration commits Britain to restoring Hong Kong to China in mid-1997 and China to maintaining Hong Kong's freedoms for 50 years.
Tung expressed hope that Britain would reconsider its position regarding cooperation with China's provisional legislature.
Britain argues that the formation of the provisional legislature is illegal under the terms of the Joint Declaration.
Rifkind's visit to Hong Kong was cut short for him to return to London for a key parliamentary vote.

Newspapers in Hong Kong reacted to the death of Deng Xiaoping on Friday.
Many newspapers praised Deng Xiaoping's reformist policies.
The South China Morning Post stated that Deng Xiaoping raised the material standards of living for many people.
The South China Morning Post editorial claimed Deng Xiaoping would be considered one of the leading figures of the century.
Newspapers published full-colour photographs of mourners in Hong Kong and Shenzhen.
Some newspapers mentioned Deng's role in the military crackdown during the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests.
The Hongkong Standard referred to Deng Xiaoping as one of China's greatest leaders.
Deng Xiaoping died at the age of 92 from complications related to Parkinson's disease and a lung infection.
Deng Xiaoping was credited with transforming China into an emerging economic powerhouse.
Deng Xiaoping's policies contributed to the economic growth of Hong Kong.

China has allowed Hong Kong to manage media coverage of its handover to Beijing.
The agreement was announced by Chinese and British negotiators after recent talks.
Hugh Davies is the British team chief at the Joint Liaison Group (JLG).
The JLG is responsible for negotiating the details of Hong Kong's transfer of sovereignty.
Concerns were raised by human rights activists and pro-democracy politicians about potential restrictions on media access.
A joint statement confirmed that the Hong Kong government will handle media coverage arrangements.
The Hong Kong government will receive and process applications from journalists for media accreditation.
Application forms for media accreditation will be available from March 15 and must be returned by April 7.
Hong Kong will revert to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
The government expects 6,000 foreign and local media representatives to cover the handover event.

Ominous gray clouds were present over Hong Kong on Sunday.
Hong Kong marked the 100-day countdown to the handover to China.
More than 7,000 people participated in a street celebration in Hong Kong.
The celebration was in anticipation of the reunion with China on June 30, 1997.
Thousands of westerners attended the annual international Rugby seven-a-side tournament.
The Rugby tournament was designated as a world cup event this year.
Chris Patten was the 28th and last British governor of Hong Kong.
Patten described Hong Kong as running smoothly but warned against changes from China.
For many residents, it was a normal Sunday with family gatherings and a day off work.
Emotions in Hong Kong were mixed as the handover approached.

U.S. computer hardware makers are expected to report mixed results for the third quarter.
Some companies are undergoing product transitions while a few are expected to have solid earnings.
International Business Machines Corp is expected to have good results for the third quarter.
Digital Equipment Corp is expected to report a loss for the third quarter.
Gary Helmig, a SoundView Financial Group analyst, mentioned product transitions and U.S. strength as issues for the third quarter.
Currency will have less impact on earnings than in the previous two quarters.
John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst, stated that the negative impact from currency exchange rates is reduced from June-quarter results.
Europe remains a concern for some companies, including Digital Equipment Corp.
Steve Milunovich, a Morgan Stanley analyst, noted that Digital has significant exposure to Europe.
Digital recently revamped its sales force and distribution channel in Europe to address sluggish sales.

IBM reports earnings on Monday.
Analysts expect growth of about 5 percent for the third quarter.
Sales of personal computers, other hardware, and the service business are expected to boost growth.
International Business Machines Corp. had a difficult second quarter.
A product transition depressed results in IBM's mainframe business.
The strong dollar will constrain IBM's results, but not as much as in the second quarter.
John Jones at Salomon Brothers stated that he does not expect a blowout or soft results.
IBM is expected to earn $2.43 a share on average, up from $2.30 a share in the 1995 quarter.
Estimates for IBM's earnings range from $2.17 a share to $2.60 a share.
In the third quarter of 1995, IBM earned $1.3 billion excluding a one-time charge of $1.8 billion from the acquisition of Lotus Development Corp.

Unisys Corp. reported a third quarter profit of $14.2 million.
Unisys Corp. had a loss of 9 cents a share after paying $30.2 million in dividends on preferred stock.
Unisys Corp. had a net loss of $32.2 million, or 36 cents a share, in the same quarter a year ago.
Revenues for Unisys Corp. in the third quarter were $1.63 billion, up 9 percent from $1.49 billion in the year-ago quarter.
Unisys Corp. reported revenue increases in its three business units: information services, computer systems, and computer services.
James Unruh is the chairman and CEO of Unisys Corp.
Unisys shares closed at $6.875, up 37.5 cents, on the New York Stock Exchange.
Unisys Corp.'s computer systems group reported a 14 percent increase in sales.
Stratus Computer Inc. reported third quarter income of $10.8 million, or 45 cents a share.
Stratus Computer Inc. had a loss of $9.3 million, or 40 cents a share, in the third quarter of 1995.

Sun Microsystems Inc. introduced its first network computer, the JavaStation, on Tuesday.
The JavaStation is designed to challenge Microsoft and Intel, the dominant players in the industry.
Scott McNealy is the Chief Executive Officer of Sun Microsystems.
The JavaStation is a charcoal-grey device measuring about nine inches by 12 inches.
The JavaStation has no disk drives, slots, or floppy disks and costs $742.
Sun, Oracle Corp., and International Business Machines Corp. are challenging the Wintel architecture.
The JavaStation is targeted at businesses but may eventually be offered to consumers.
Java allows software applications to be written in one language and distributed across various computing environments.
Ed Zander is the president of Sun Micro's Computer Co.
Sun introduced three versions of the JavaStation, with the lowest cost version priced at $742 and lacking a monitor or keyboard.

EchoStar Communications Corp began operations in March.
EchoStar Communications Corp cut prices sharply in the satellite industry.
Thomson matched EchoStar's price of $199 for satellite TV dishes.
Thomson executives believe the new price will impact the industry and increase sales.
Joe Clayton is an executive vice president at Thomson, a unit of Thomson-CSF in France.
Thomson's price cut reduced the RCA brand digital satellite system price by up to $200.
DirecTV and U.S. Satellite Broadcasting Co offered a $200 cash back promotion.
The total price for consumers who pre-pay for one year of programming is $199.
Thomson holds an estimated 45 percent market share of the digital satellite system dish market.
As of July, there were approximately 3.4 million digital satellite system dishes in the market.

International Business Machines Corp. will update its strategy for electronic commerce on Tuesday.
IBM will unveil new partners and show examples of ongoing projects.
Electronic commerce refers to buying and selling goods and services over computer networks, including the Internet.
IBM sees electronic commerce as a significant opportunity to provide products and services for online business.
An IBM spokesman stated that the company will provide an update on its current and future electronic commerce plans.
Top executives from IBM's Lotus Development Corp., its Internet division, and its Network Computer unit will hold a news conference.
Analysts expect IBM to announce several new partners for various applications targeted at specific industries.
IBM plans to unveil an application called PetroConnect for the petroleum industry to share geological information online.
IBM is expected to add 10 new retailers to its World Mall shopping site on the Internet.
IBM will officially launch its Network Computer division and possibly new models of the Network Station.

International Business Machines Corp. unveiled its Internet strategy on Tuesday.
IBM announced partnerships with retailers, oil companies, and other companies to enhance business over the Internet and corporate intranets.
Irving Wladwasky-Berger is the general manager of IBM's Internet division.
The Internet unit of IBM was formed less than a year ago and is a key strategic business for the company.
IBM is assisting customers in developing various electronic commerce applications.
IBM's revenue will primarily come from hardware, software, and services.
IBM expects the worldwide information technology industry to grow from $800 billion to $1.2 trillion in the next four years.
Siemens AG is a partner with IBM for the electric utility industry.
Pacific Gas and Electric Co. is the first customer for IBM and Siemens' service for electric utilities.
IBM announced 13 new retailers joining its Internet shopping mall, World Avenue.

CompuServe Corp is expected to announce the dissolution of its Wow! consumer online service.
The company is shifting its focus from the consumer market to the corporate market.
A spokesman for CompuServe declined to comment before a strategic announcement planned for Thursday.
CompuServe has faced increased competition from America Online Inc, Microsoft Corp Network, and other Internet access providers.
The company plans to stop marketing to consumers and will emphasize corporate customers in the U.S. and Europe.
CompuServe aims to convert its 100,000 Wow! users to its core CompuServe Information Service.
CompuServe will not abandon its current consumer users but will not prioritize the consumer business.
Wall Street analysts suggest that CompuServe's shift may lead to layoffs and a restructuring charge.
CompuServe's Wow! service is priced at $17.95 a month.
CompuServe's stock price has fallen from its initial offering price of $30 a share to around $11-5/8.

Philip Zimmermann is a computer programmer and cryptographer.
Zimmermann was investigated by the U.S. government for three years due to his encryption software being classified as a weapon.
Zimmermann's company is called Pretty Good Privacy Inc.
Zimmermann will unveil two security software products at the Internet World trade show in New York.
Zimmermann's original encryption software has over 2 million users since its distribution began in 1991.
PGP Mail is a product that scrambles electronic mail for privacy.
The U.S. Justice Department and the Department of Commerce investigated Zimmermann's software due to its strong encryption.
The United States dropped its investigation of Zimmermann in January after three years.
Pretty Good Privacy Inc. is privately funded and has not accepted venture capital.
PGP has acquired ViaCrypt, a company that enhances PGP Mail.

Sun Microsystems Inc will announce an initiative on Wednesday to standardize the Java programming language.
The initiative is supported by International Business Machines Corp, Apple Computer Inc, Netscape Communications Corp, Oracle Corp, and others.
The initiative aims to ensure that a program is 'pure Java.'
There are concerns in the industry that the Java language could become fragmented with multiple versions.
Java allows software developers to write an application that runs on any computer system.
There are currently at least twenty different versions of the UNIX operating system.
Jon Kannegaard, vice president of software at Sun, expressed concern about Java splintering.
The initiative will include education for the industry, developer assistance, and program certification.
In the first quarter of 1997, Sun will introduce testing, certification, and branding for applications that meet its criteria.
A survey by Morgan Stanley indicated that 75 percent of corporations interviewed were developing or planning to develop applications using Java.

Electronic commerce over the Internet includes buying airplane tickets, music CDs, and clothes with a credit card.
In 1996, security concerns hindered the growth of Internet commerce.
Delays in developing software for secure credit card transactions affected e-commerce in 1996.
E-commerce was not as robust in 1996 as some firms had anticipated.
Scott Smith, a Jupiter Communications analyst, described 1996 as a 'building year' for e-commerce.
According to Jupiter, total revenues from consumer shopping over the Internet were about $1.2 billion in 1996.
Jupiter forecasts that e-commerce revenues will increase to $2.3 billion in 1997.
Jupiter predicts revenues will reach $5.5 billion in 1999 and $7.3 billion in 2000.
Travel and direct distribution of electronic products are the two largest categories of electronic commerce in 1996.
Travel accounted for about half of the $1.2 billion in e-commerce revenues in 1996.

Many personal computer makers will roll out multimedia PCs designed around a new chip by Intel Corp.
Intel will launch its P55C microprocessor using MMX technology.
Several companies will unveil new consumer PCs, notebooks, and desktops using the new chip.
The new chip is expected to offer faster performance.
An Intel spokesman stated that the new chip will provide a richer experience.
International Business Machines Corp., Compaq Computer Corp., Dell Computer Corp., Gateway 2000 Inc., Toshiba America Corp., and Sony Corp. are expected to unveil new high-end PCs.
Most new machines are expected to be priced over $3,000.
Intel claims that an MMX-based PC will provide sharper images, three-dimensional graphics, faster audio, and television-like video.
The Intel spokesman noted that expectations for PCs are increasing due to influences from movies and television.
Rod Schrock, a vice president of Compaq's Presario division, stated that the entire line of Presarios was redesigned for the new MMX processor.

Peter Jarvis is the chief executive of Whitbread Plc.
Whitbread Plc is experiencing strong growth in consumer spending on leisure.
Consumer spending has been positive for the last 12 months.
Expenditure on the National Lottery took out 5.0 billion stg from the economy last year.
The National Lottery expenditure accounted for about 5.0 percent of total leisure spending in Britain.
The absence of the Lottery effect has allowed for strong growth in leisure expenditure.
Jarvis is particularly encouraged by the performance of the hotels business.
The hotel market in Britain is described as very buoyant.
Whitbread acquired David Lloyd Leisure for about 200 million stg.
Whitbread also acquired a chain of 16 Marriott hotels in Britain for about 185 million stg.

B.A.T Industries is a British tobacco and insurance conglomerate.
B.A.T Industries will report its third quarter results on Wednesday.
There is increasing scientific evidence linking smoking to lung cancer.
Charles Pick is an analyst at Panmure Gordon.
B.A.T shares are vulnerable to litigation issues.
Standard & Poor's revised its outlook for B.A.T to negative due to litigation claims.
Analysts expect B.A.T's pretax profits for the quarter to be between 650 and 715 million stg.
B.A.T's tobacco sales in emerging markets are expected to remain strong.
B.A.T's shares have fallen from 585p on February 2 to 434p recently.
Some UK shareholders are calling for a demerger of B.A.T's two component businesses.

A planned merger between British brewer Bass and Carlsberg-Tetley is expected to face scrutiny from Britain's competition authorities.
Ralph Findlay, finance director of Wolverhampton & Dudley Breweries, believes the merger will likely be referred to competition authorities.
Bass confirmed details of the merger with Carlsberg-Tetley, which would give Carlsberg a 20 percent stake in the merged entity if approved.
If Bass cannot merge with Carlsberg-Tetley within 16 months, it can sell its entire shareholding to Carlsberg.
Carlsberg has the option to sell 15 percent of Carlsberg-Tetley to Allied Domecq under the merger terms.
Bass lost its position as Britain's leading brewer last year when Scottish & Newcastle acquired Courage, giving S&N a 31 percent market share.
A merger between Bass and Carlsberg-Tetley would result in Bass controlling 35 percent of Britain's beer market.
Britain's competition authorities are concerned that the merger could give Bass and S&N excessive control over beer prices.
Roger Young, retail director at Greenalls Group, anticipates a referral of the merger due to concerns about competition.
Many brewing analysts argue that the duopoly between Bass and S&N in Scotland leads to higher prices for consumers.

Associated British Foods reported a 15 percent increase in its full year profits.
Chairman Garry Weston expressed caution about future forecasts due to upcoming elections in the United States and Britain.
ABF posted pretax profits of 430 million pounds for the year ended September 14.
Worldwide sales for ABF increased by 17 percent to 5.707 billion pounds.
Profits were driven by strong performance from ABF's retail operations in Britain and Ireland.
Operating profits rose 25 percent to 69 million pounds.
Primark's results included contributions from One Up stores acquired from Storehouse.
ABF's food manufacturing and processing operations in Britain showed an 8.0 percent sales growth to 3.11 billion pounds.
Profits from British Sugar fell to 183 million pounds due to European community quotas and currency strength.
ABF's profits from its Australia and New Zealand operations increased by 20 percent to 38 million pounds.

John McGrath is the chief executive of Grand Metropolitan Plc.
Grand Metropolitan Plc aims to reduce production to lower costs.
McGrath stated that controlling quality is more important than owning production.
Grand Metropolitan is considering further deals where third parties handle production.
Last year, Grand Metropolitan contracted Seneca for processing and packaging Green Giant's canned vegetables.
Green Giant was acquired by Grand Metropolitan as part of Pillsbury in 1989.
Pillsbury currently produces approximately 75 percent of its products.
McGrath indicated that if a product is protected by patent, Grand Metropolitan would prefer to produce it in-house.
McGrath believes that certain products, like whisky, require skilled production that should remain in-house.
McGrath acknowledged the contributions of former chairman Lord Sheppard in transforming Grand Metropolitan.

Burton reported a 54 percent increase in full year profit.
Pretax profits rose to 151.6 million pounds in the year to August 31.
Sales increased by 7.1 percent to 2.0 billion pounds.
The group raised its full-year dividend by 27 percent to 2.8 pence a share.
All divisions of Burton reported an increase in full-year profits.
Burton's Debenhams department store chain saw a 21 percent increase in profits to 102.8 million pounds.
Burton Menswear and Principles returned to profitability after previous losses.
Burton's shares rose by 1.5 pence to 146.5 pence following the results.
Burton acquired mail order group Innovations in August and Racing Green in October.
The main focus of Burton will remain on its core retail division.

Shares in Unilever Plc rose sharply after the group posted a five percent rise in third quarter profits.
David Lang, an analyst at Henderson Crosthwaite, expressed surprise at the positive results.
Unilever's shares increased by 42-1/2p to 1,317-1/2p following the profit announcement.
Unilever's profits for the quarter reached 826 million pounds ($1.36 billion).
The profit results exceeded analysts' forecasts, which ranged from 760 million pounds to 820 million pounds.
Before an exceptional charge of 32 million pounds, Unilever's pretax profits rose six percent to 918 million pounds.
Richard Newboult, an analyst at Lehman Brothers, noted that the total charges were lower than expected.
Diversey, acquired by Unilever for 360 million pounds, was merged with Lever Industrial to form a combined business with annual turnover of 1.15 billion pounds.
Unilever owns various household brands, including OMO, Brooke Bond, Ponds, and several ice-cream products.
Despite poor weather affecting ice-cream sales, Unilever improved its profit by 13 million pounds to 502 million in the quarter.

Britain's Northern Foods does not expect world dairy commodity prices to improve in the second half of the year.
Jo Stewart is the managing director of Northern Foods' prepared food division.
In the first half, prices for butter, skimmed milk, and bulk cream on world commodity markets decreased by approximately 20 percent compared to the previous year.
Weakening world demand for dairy products and the rise in the value of sterling against other major European currencies did not lead to a reduction in Northern's cost of milk.
Eden Vale Food Ingredients, a division of Northern Foods, was significantly affected by the decline in commodity prices.
Margins on Northern's prepared foods business increased by one percentage point to 8.0 percent in the first half.
Northern Foods achieved a four percent price inflation on its prepared foods in the first half, compared to zero percent the previous year.
A typical pack of Northern's biscuits increased in price by 2p to 51p over the past six months.
Sales of Northern's meat products decreased by 6.8 percent in the first half due to consumer concerns about mad-cow disease.
Northern Foods estimated that the beef crisis cost the company approximately 3.0 million pounds in the first half.

Luxury goods maker Vendome reported a 4.6 percent drop in first half profits.
Vendome attributed the profit decline to poor tourist spending in the Far East.
The company's pretax profits fell to 113 million pounds from 118.5 million pounds.
Sales increased to 703.6 million pounds from 699.5 million pounds.
Interest income decreased to 3.2 million pounds from 5.7 million pounds.
Chairman Joseph Kanoui expressed belief that the drop in Far East demand was temporary.
Vendome's profits fell short of market expectations, which anticipated earnings between 125 million and 135 million pounds.
Vendome is 70 percent owned by Richemont Securities and was established three years ago.
In Swiss francs, pretax profits fell 2.1 percent to 214.7 million francs in the six months to September 30.
Sales of jewellery decreased by 17.4 percent and leather goods fell by 2.3 percent in the first half.

Grand Metropolitan Plc will report a significant increase in its underlying business performance in its full-year results.
The increase is driven by its North American foods business, Pillsbury.
Grand Metropolitan Plc is expected to incur a loss of 522 million stg on disposals.
Analysts' forecasts for pretax profits range from 948 to 999 million stg, excluding the loss on disposals.
Grand Metropolitan Plc posted pre-tax profits of 920 million stg last year.
Dividend forecasts for Grand Metropolitan Plc are centered on 15.8p, an increase from 14.9p.
The loss on disposals includes 265 million stg of goodwill from the sale of its optician business Pearle.
The loss also includes a 36 million stg hit from the disposal of William Hill and Mecca to Brent Walker.
Additionally, there is a 14 million stg loss on the disposal of its Erasco food business in Germany to Campbell Soup Company.
Grand Metropolitan Plc aims to focus on its major international brands in Europe, including Pillsbury, Green Giant, Haagen-Dazs, and Old El Paso.

Marston, Thompson & Evershad Plc reported an 8.5 percent decline in sales of its key brand ale Marston Pedigree in the first half of the year.
The decline in sales of Marston Pedigree was attributed to the rising popularity of nitrokegs.
Marston Pedigree increased its market share by one percent despite the sales decline.
Overall sales of the company's brewed beers rose by 0.5 percent.
Marston, Thompson & Evershad Plc launched its own nitrokeg, Marston's Bitter Smoothbrewed, in the Spring.
David Gordon, the chief executive, stated that nitrokeg is affecting market share.
The company's shares were 5p lower at 275p.
Scottish & Newcastle and Bass saw their shares rise despite Marston's decline.
Scottish & Newcastle announced a 26 percent rise in its half year profits.
Marston, Thompson reported a 5.3 percent increase in pretax profits to 14.7 million stg for the half year ended September 28.

Grand Metropolitan Plc reported a six percent increase in annual profits before tax, totaling 965 million pounds.
Chairman George Bull stated that trading for the current year had started satisfactorily.
Profits at Pillsbury, GrandMet's North American foods business, increased by 30 percent to 431 million pounds.
International Distillers and Vitners (IDV) reported a four percent increase in trading profit to 471 million pounds.
GrandMet shares decreased by 8p to 448p due to investor concerns about the impact of a strong pound against the dollar on future profits.
Pillsbury and Burger King account for approximately 60 percent of GrandMet's group earnings in dollars.
The pound's value increased from $1.493 on May 1 to $1.6477.
An unnamed analyst indicated that currency translation would likely lead to downgrades in profit forecasts for next year.
Group finance director Gerald Corbett mentioned that GrandMet is focused on steady, organic growth driven by profits from Pillsbury and IDV.
Sales at Pillsbury rose by four percent, prices increased by three percent, and margins improved by 0.7 percentage points to 12.2 percent.

Britain referred Bass Plc's acquisition of Carlsberg-Tetley to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission for investigation.
Analysts believe the deal will go through once certain conditions are met.
The British Trade & Industry Minister, Mr. Lang, has competition concerns regarding the merger due to increased concentration in the UK brewing industry.
Bass acquired half of Carlsberg-Tetley from Allied Domecq for 200 million pounds in August.
Bass plans to buy the rest of Carlsberg-Tetley from Carlsberg A/S in exchange for Carlsberg taking a 20 percent stake in the merged company.
The Monopolies and Mergers Commission will investigate if the merger operates against the public interest and will report by March 24, 1997.
If approved, the merger would create Britain's largest brewer with at least 35 percent market share.
Bass currently has a 23 percent market share.
Rival brewers and analysts expected a referral to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission due to the dominance the merger would create.
Bass shares fell about 6p on the news but closed 14-1/2p higher as analysts expected the deal to go through with conditions.

The race to succeed Alex Trotman for the top office at Ford Motor Co. has begun.
Ford promoted Edward Hagenlocker to vice chairman and put him in charge of a new auto components organization.
The new auto components organization has 75,000 employees and revenues of $14 billion.
Jacques Nasser was named to head Ford Automotive Operations, replacing Hagenlocker.
Speculation exists about how Ford's board will handle Trotman's succession as he approaches retirement in July 1998.
William Clay Ford Jr. may be named a non-executive chairman or chairman when Trotman leaves.
Hagenlocker's tenure at Ford Automotive Operations has faced challenges, including slumping profits.
Hagenlocker has overseen the successful launch of the new F-Series pickup trucks and the Ford Expedition.
Eugene Jennings stated that Hagenlocker's new role could provide valuable experience for running the company.
Jacques Nasser has been with Ford since 1968 and has held various international assignments.

Ford Motor Co. reported third-quarter profits of $686 million.
Ford's profits nearly doubled compared to the previous year.
The company experienced a loss of $619 million from non-U.S. regions.
Ford's worldwide automotive operations generated a profit of $15 million.
Ford's third-quarter profits amounted to 56 cents a share on a fully diluted basis.
Ford's Financial Services Group earned $671 million in the third quarter.
Ford Credit's earnings decreased to $299 million from $357 million a year ago.
Ford incurred a $39 million charge for early retirements of U.S. salaried employees.
Ford expects to report additional charges of $300 million to $400 million in the fourth quarter for early retirements.
Ford lost $226 million from its South American operations in the third quarter.

Bargainers for the United Auto Workers union and General Motors Corp. continued bargaining on Sunday.
General Motors spokesman Ray Deibel stated that talks resumed at midmorning Sunday after adjourning Saturday evening.
The deadline for a new labour pact is set for midnight (0500 GMT).
General Motors employs more than half of the 390,000 UAW members who work at Detroit's Big Three automakers.
General Motors is the only one of the Big Three not to have a new three-year labour contract.
Analysts speculated that negotiators could be discussing contract language regarding job guarantees.
Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp. have agreed to contracts that promise to keep 95 percent of their current UAW hourly workforces.
General Motors is trying to shed 12 unprofitable parts plants and wants to exclude certain facilities from employment guarantees.
UAW President Stephen Yokich set a deadline for contract extension expiration at midnight Sunday.
There is speculation that the UAW could initiate a plant-specific strike if sufficient progress is not made by the deadline.

By the year 2000, nearly one quarter of ITT Automotive Inc's workers worldwide will be paid a combined hourly and benefit rate of less than $10 an hour.
In 1995, ITT Automotive paid 15 percent of its 35,000 workers less than $10 an hour.
In 1990, ITT Automotive paid 10 percent of its workers less than $10 an hour.
Timothy Leuliette is the president and chief executive officer of ITT Automotive.
Leuliette stated that auto suppliers need to continue slashing costs to remain independent in the industry.
Leuliette mentioned that a 3-4 percent price reduction is necessary to promise customers.
The global hourly rate for labor-intensive assemblies such as wiring harnesses is $1 to $2.
More technical products are made for $10 to $12 an hour.
Leuliette indicated that suppliers must be globally competitive to supply ITT.
J.T. Battenberg advised suppliers to focus on a few product areas, stress quality, and pursue international alliances.

Ford Motor Co. launched a new computer-aided design project called C3P.
C3P is based on a computer program from Structural Dynamics Research Corp.
Ford claims C3P will cut prototype costs by up to 50 percent.
Ford states C3P will improve investment efficiency by 20 percent to 30 percent.
Ford asserts C3P will eliminate half of costly late development changes.
Paul Blumberg is the director of product development systems at Ford's Product Development Center.
Three new vehicle programs started in 2023 will use C3P.
Ford plans to merge computer-aided design, manufacturing, and engineering functions into a unified system by 2000.
Structural Dynamics Research Corp. is considered a small player in the CAD/CAM market.
Chrysler Corp. launched a similar design program seven years prior to Ford's C3P announcement.

Chairman Jack Smith oversaw the rollout of General Motors Corp.'s first electric vehicle, the EV1.
The EV1 was loaded onto an auto-hauling truck at the Lansing Craft Centre for transport to the West Coast.
The EV1 will go on sale on December 5 at 26 Saturn dealerships in Los Angeles, San Diego, Phoenix, and Tucson.
GM invested $350 million and over six years to develop the EV1, a two-passenger coupe.
The EV1 is the first GM vehicle to carry a GM badge instead of a name from one of its other divisions.
GM claims the EV1 is the first vehicle designed from the ground up as an electric car.
The EV1 incorporates 23 new patents and is described by Smith as the most technologically advanced vehicle platform in the world.
The EV1 is powered by 26 12-volt lead-acid batteries and can travel up to 90 miles before recharging.
The EV1 can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in less than nine seconds and has a top speed of 80 mph.
GM will sell the EV1 through a 36-month lease at a price of $33,995, with monthly payments of $480 for buyers receiving a $5,000 state credit.

General Motors Corp. agreed to sell four parts plants to Peregrine Inc.
Peregrine Inc. plans to become a major player in the automotive interior supply industry.
The automotive interior supply industry is valued at $22 billion.
Peregrine Inc. is funded by Joseph Littlejohn & Levy and Edward Gulda.
No terms were announced for the sale of the plants.
Peregrine Inc. is expected to have more than $1 billion in annual revenues.
Peregrine Inc. will be based in Southfield, Mich.
Peregrine Inc. plans to pursue contracts with car and truck manufacturers in North America and overseas.
The four plants produce hinges, door and instrument panels, and other interior parts, generating about $1 billion in annual revenue.
The plants employ approximately 5,500 workers.

Chrysler Corp filed an appeal against a California Department of Motor Vehicle (DMV) ban on shipping new vehicles to dealers.
The ban was issued as a penalty for allegedly violating California's lemon law.
The ban was determined after the DMV found that Chrysler resold 116 vehicles in 1991 and 1992 without proper disclosure.
Chrysler described the DMV's actions as a 'draconian penalty' in its appeal to California's New Motor Vehicle Board.
Chrysler argues that it complied with the lemon law as it was written at the time of the vehicle sales.
Chrysler stated that the statute in effect was vague regarding which repurchased vehicles needed to be branded as lemons.
Chrysler claimed it made good faith efforts to inform used car buyers about the vehicles they were purchasing.
Chrysler expressed concerns about the economic impact of the penalty on its 240 California dealers.
The New Motor Vehicle Board can reverse or amend the DMV's decision.
Chrysler sold nearly 170,000 new cars and trucks in California in 1995, which was about eight percent of its annual volume.

The president of Ford Motor Co.'s automotive operations is Jacques Nasser.
Jacques Nasser denied that Ford is considering plant closures in North America.
Ford is seeking to reduce an additional $2.5 billion from its 1997 spending plans.
Nasser stated that Ford is always studying alternatives for its manufacturing facilities.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Ford was considering closing its Lorain, Ohio, car plant.
Ford is consolidating its Explorer production into a single plant in Louisville, Kentucky.
Nasser said Ford has no plans to reduce capacity for its Explorer sport utility vehicle.
Nasser described the Wall Street Journal report as surprising and lacking substance.
An industry source indicated that Ford has considered closing the Lorain plant to boost profits.
Ford announced it has achieved the industry's top quality certification on a global basis.

The U.S. auto industry celebrated its 100th birthday in 1996.
The U.S. auto industry experienced higher sales and a new labor accord in 1996.
The U.S. auto industry faces tough competition from foreign automakers, particularly from Japan.
The Japanese yen has weakened from a high of 80 to about 114 to the dollar since April 1995.
A weaker yen allows Japanese firms to produce vehicles more cheaply in Japan and sell them in the United States.
Van Bussman, Chrysler Corp.'s top economist, predicts the yen will remain in the 110-115 range for the first half of 1997.
Bussman believes the weakened yen will provide Japanese automakers with significant profit potential in North America.
In 1996, the average price increase for Detroit's Big Three automakers was $386, while Japanese automakers raised prices by only $8.
Ford Motor Co. Chairman Alex Trotman stated that the weaker yen will make competition tougher in 1997.
Forecasts for 1997 project total vehicle sales to be similar to the 15.4 million expected for 1996.

Peregrine Inc. may let go up to half of its 5,500 hourly employees at the four former General Motors Corp. component plants it purchased.
Peregrine Chief Executive Officer Edward Gulda stated that workers not needed at Peregrine could transfer back to GM.
Employees who remain with Peregrine will be paid according to the terms of the new United Auto Worker and Canadian Auto Worker contracts established with GM.
Peregrine was formed by the New York investment firm Joseph Littlejohn & Levy to purchase the four plants from GM's Delphi Automotive Systems unit.
Peregrine will formally take over the plants on January 1.
The four plants are located in Michigan and Ontario and produce various parts including window regulators and metal stampings.
Gulda outlined steps to streamline cost structures and expand operations from an annual revenue base of about $1 billion.
Three of the four plants are expected to turn a profit in 1997, while the fourth is expected to break even.
Peregrine plans to make annual capital investments of at least $20 million into the four facilities.
UAW parts workers earn about $43 an hour, including benefits, which is higher than what non-union companies pay.

Sales of light vehicles in December are expected to be down as much as 6 percent from December of the previous year.
Analysts project that the total sales for 1996 will match industry projections of 15.1 million units.
General Motors Corp. is expected to experience the largest sales drop among the Big Three automakers, with a daily sales rate estimated to be down 16 percent from December 1995.
GM's sales of light trucks, including pickup trucks, sport/utility vehicles, and minivans, are expected to decline significantly due to tough comparisons from the previous year.
Car sales for GM are estimated to drop by as much as 20 percent, attributed to the impact of labor strikes that affected production.
GM is scheduled to report its sales on January 3.
Chrysler Corp. is expected to report flat or slightly increased sales compared to December of the previous year.
Chrysler's light truck sales, which account for about 70 percent of its total sales, are projected to rise by 8 percent, while passenger car sales are expected to decline by 9 percent.
Ford Motor Co. is scheduled to release its sales results on January 6 and is expected to see sales rise between 8 percent and 9 percent compared to December 1995.
Ford's car sales are forecast to dip by 3 percent to 4 percent, while light truck sales are expected to rise by 20 percent.

Officials with Volkswagen-First Automotive Works in northeastern China dismissed a report about the joint venture facing possible closure.
A spokeswoman for the joint venture stated that the report by Der Spiegel is incorrect.
Production at the joint venture is continuing.
The joint venture has a 25-year agreement.
If the German side withdrew unilaterally, they would have to pay compensation.
A ceremony marking the full implementation of the joint venture project will be held soon.
A spokesman for Volkswagen AG's Volkswagen Asia-Pacific arm stated that production at the joint venture would continue.
The Changchun plant produced 14,700 Jetta cars in the first eight months of this year, which is a 10 percent increase from the previous year.
The Jetta is not selling as well as the Volkswagen Santana produced at Volkswagen's Shanghai joint venture.
Changes in the joint venture agreement are being negotiated, including new car models and the possibility of Volkswagen taking over sales and after-sales service.

China plans to develop bigger rockets to carry heavier payloads into space.
Chinese aerospace officials stated that the goal is to build rockets capable of carrying 20-tonne payloads.
