The current capacity of China's most powerful launch vehicles is less than 10 tonnes.
A spokeswoman for China Aerospace Corp mentioned that this goal could extend into the second decade of the next century.
China needs rockets to launch multiple satellites for domestic use and to enhance its position in the commercial space market.
China's existing rockets can carry payloads of 9.2 tonnes for lower earth orbits and 3.4-5.0 tonnes for geosynchronous orbits.
Li Jianzhong, president of the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology, stated that a development program will begin soon.
China will develop key technologies for a heavy lift launch vehicle with a payload of 20 tonnes.
China has been trying to expand its role in the commercial space market despite recent setbacks.
A Long March 3 rocket failed to put a U.S.-built satellite into orbit due to a valve leakage.

China is planning to issue rules to speed development of its power sector with an expanded role for foreign companies.
Wang Hong is a planning official from the State Planning Commission.
Beijing is reviewing rules governing build-operate-transfer (BOT) projects for major power projects.
The State Council is considering temporary regulations regarding BOT projects.
China needs $20 billion in foreign capital through the year 2000 for power industry development.
The BOT rules will not be ready in time for the first power sector project, which is expected to cost between $600 million and $700 million.
China is evaluating tenders for the Laibin power project in Guangxi province.
The Laibin project involves the construction and operation of two 350-megawatt power units.
Major bidders for the Laibin project include ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG, Siemens AG, and China Light & Power Co Ltd.
The rules under review will define BOT projects, specify the approval process, and determine risk apportioning between China and foreign companies.

China has announced new rules on direct shipping links to Taiwan.
Analysts state that Beijing is far from achieving direct shipping with Taiwan.
Fan Xizhou is the head of the Taiwan Research Institute at Xiamen University.
Fan Xizhou believes that the new rules have put pressure on Taiwan authorities.
Beijing views Taiwan as a renegade province.
Taiwan's Nationalist government has banned direct air and shipping links with China since 1949.
Taiwanese businessmen have invested over $20 billion into China.
Taiwanese authorities have been reluctant to lift the ban on direct transport links.
The latest news has raised hopes among Taiwanese businessmen for eased restrictions.
China specifies that only Taiwanese or Chinese companies can conduct business on the new shipping routes.

China International Trust and Investment Corp is focusing its domestic operations on the financial sector.
CITIC hopes to see 70 percent of its profits from the financial sector.
Chang Zhenming is the group executive director of CITIC.
CITIC reported a profit of 2.05 billion yuan in the last year, up from 1.67 billion yuan in 1994.
CITIC Industrial Bank is the main contributor to CITIC's domestic operations, accounting for net profits of about 1.0 billion yuan last year.
Profits from CITIC Industrial Bank were up 20 percent over 1994.
CITIC expects profits from the bank to climb another 20 percent this year.
CITIC has a good base of corporate clients, providing a reliable source of low-cost call-money deposits.
CITIC has been able to hold the line on bad debts, having fewer bad loans than some other banks.
CITIC has diversified domestic interests including power projects, telecommunications, automotive production, and real estate.

China signaled to U.S. President Bill Clinton that trade disputes remained unresolved after the election.
China planned to impose temporary curbs on American imports as retaliation for U.S. charges on Chinese textiles.
Beijing announced a temporary suspension of imports of some U.S. textiles, farm goods, and alcoholic drinks.
The import ban was set to take effect on December 10.
China accused the U.S. of severe violations of a bilateral textile accord.
The U.S. imposed punitive charges on 1996 import quotas for Chinese textile goods in September.
The U.S. action was expected to cost China about $19 million.
China claimed the U.S. move was made without full consultation and lacked clear supporting evidence.
China stated it had urged the U.S. to withdraw the penalties but received no response.
China's import suspension would also apply to U.S. fruits and animal husbandry products.

China stated that the United States is trying to contain it.
China called for a shift in U.S. policies to improve bilateral ties.
China accused the United States of being self-righteous and alienating in its foreign policy.
The Business Weekly claimed that the U.S. must drop the idea of containing China to expect progress in relations.
The United States is employing a strategy of containment linked to South Korea, Japan, the Philippines, and Thailand.
The newspaper cited Chen Bingcai, an economist at a think-tank linked to the State Planning Commission.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher is scheduled to arrive in China on Tuesday.
The visit is the first senior-level contact between the two nations since the re-election of U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Relations between China and the U.S. have been strained by disputes over Taiwan, human rights, trade, and arms proliferation.
China held war games and missile tests off Taiwan earlier this year, prompting a U.S. military response.

China called on the United States to end curbs on technology exports to balance trade.
A spokesman from the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation stated that the two countries should avoid actions that do not help trade expansion.
The United States reported a trade deficit with China of nearly $29 billion in the first nine months of the year, up from $25 billion in the same period last year.
The trade gap with China is the second largest for the U.S. after its deficit with Japan and is projected to reach $40 billion by the end of the year.
American economists indicated that the increasing trade deficit could create new frictions between the U.S. and China.
U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor urged Beijing to fulfill its international trade obligations.
A group of U.S. senators expressed concerns about China's trade practices and opposed allowing China to join the World Trade Organisation on special terms.
Beijing has sought to join the World Trade Organisation under favorable terms for developing nations, but Washington disagrees due to China's large economy.
The Chinese Trade Ministry spokesman claimed that U.S. policy curbs on exports were contributing to the bilateral trade problem.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher mentioned that Washington was considering allowing technical cooperation in peaceful nuclear technology uses.

China is preparing a lobbying campaign to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO) at the ministerial meeting in Singapore this month.
Long Yongtu, assistant minister of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation, will lead China's team at the meetings.
China will be an observer at the WTO meetings in Singapore.
China has been trying to join the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and the WTO for a long time.
China seeks entry to the WTO on favorable terms as a developing nation, but the United States argues that China's economy is too large for such treatment.
A Chinese trade official stated that China will only participate as an observer at the Singapore meeting.
Foreign diplomats believe China will continue to advocate for its case through bilateral talks with member countries.
China views joining the WTO as a symbol of its growing prestige and seeks benefits from fixed mechanisms for settling trade disputes.
China has experienced multiple trade disputes with major trading partners, including issues related to its Most Favoured Nation status and copyright protection.
Diplomats indicated that China must offer more concessions to reach a compromise regarding its WTO membership.

China announced a ban on poultry and poultry products from Missouri and Oklahoma due to an outbreak of Newcastle disease.
The ban is already in effect and was confirmed by an official of the Ministry of Agriculture.
The ban was implemented to prevent damage from Newcastle disease, which is described as very destructive.
Five cases of Newcastle disease were reported between July and September in the United States.
A U.S. embassy official in Beijing could not confirm the outbreak of the disease in the United States this year.
Beijing has banned all U.S. poultry brought into the country by mail or by travelers.
Travelers are prohibited from bringing any poultry goods from the United States into China.
The ban went into effect on Monday, according to an official of the State Bureau of Animal Plant and Quarantine.
Viscerotropic velogenic Newcastle disease (VVND) is considered a deadly disease for poultry.
The last major outbreak of VVND in the United States occurred in California in the 1970s.

China has attempted to influence its stock markets by following the example of U.S. Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan.
China's official People's Daily published a commentary urging investors to act rationally and warning that rising markets can fall.
The commentary advised that the safest investment is in the bank.
Chinese officials and stock market brokers noted similarities between China's actions and Greenspan's comments on 'irrational exuberance' in U.S. markets.
Greenspan's remarks caused a brief decline in global share markets.
A stock market policy official stated that regulators aimed to lower excessively high stock markets.
A spokeswoman for the China Securities Regulatory Commission stated that their goal was to stabilize the market.
Some brokers and investors criticized the commentary for being excessively harsh.
The commentary compared current market conditions to the 1929 Wall Street crash and criticized large investors and brokers.
Last week, the stock exchanges in Shanghai and Shenzhen imposed limits on daily share movements.

China warned against reinforcing military alliances on Monday.
China stated that Cold War ideology still exists.
Vice-Premier Qian Qichen was quoted by the official Xinhua news agency.
Qian claimed that reinforcing military alliances contradicts peace and development.
Qian noted that the Cold War has ended but confrontational thinking remains.
Qian's remarks followed Premier Li Peng's visit to Russia.
Chinese political analysts expressed concerns over NATO's planned expansion.
China criticized closer U.S. military ties with Japan.
Qian mentioned a trend towards economic and political multi-polarisation.
Qian stated that relations between major powers are undergoing significant changes.

China will avoid bold moves in tackling its state enterprises as it focuses on stability ahead of the Communist Party congress.
Analysts believe that policy makers will err on the side of caution in a significant year for the communist era.
Cheng Xiusheng, an economist from the Development Research Centre of the State Council, stated that reform of state enterprises is the nation's biggest economic problem.
Cheng Xiusheng does not expect any major breakthroughs in state enterprise reform this year.
About 75 percent of state firms in China are losing money.
Losses for state firms surged to about 69 billion yuan ($8.3 billion) in the first 10 months of last year, a rise of 45 percent over the same period in 1995.
Halting losses in state firms would require shedding much of the workforce and potentially using bankruptcy laws.
China has set a target of keeping urban unemployment around three percent this year.
China lacks a comprehensive unemployment insurance system and retirement schemes cover only a small portion of the working public.
The loss of a job in China can have a significant impact on individuals and could lead to social unrest.

The Internet Society has backed away from a proposal to expand the number of addresses on the global computer network.
The Internet Society announced it would form a nine-member committee to study the issue instead of moving ahead with the proposal.
The proposal was unveiled in August to address disputes over desirable address names.
Don Heath is the president of the Internet Society.
Objections to the August proposal include technical networking issues and concerns about trademarks and intellectual property.
The new committee is expected to finish its work by early next year.
New names could be distributed four to six months after the committee's work is completed.
The committee may decide not to proceed with any address expansion, but this is considered unlikely by Heath.
Disputes over Internet names are increasing as more companies seek to market their products online.
Every site on the World Wide Web must have a unique address name.

U.S. laws governing the futures markets could be affected by the Supreme Court's interpretation of the word 'in'.
A legislative solution regarding the Commodity Exchange Act is anticipated.
The Commodity Exchange Act was amended in 1974 to regulate trading of futures contracts.
Futures exchanges claim a broad reading of the 1974 amendment would threaten their business.
Major banks argue a narrow reading of the amendment would require them to relocate operations outside the United States.
Congressional action on this issue is expected next year.
Howard Schneider, former Commodity Futures Trading Commission general counsel, believes legislation will ultimately address the issue.
The 1974 expansion of the Commodity Exchange Act included futures on non-agricultural commodities.
The Treasury Department suggested an amendment to exempt certain transactions from the Commodity Exchange Act.
The Treasury Amendment exempts transactions in foreign currency and government securities from the Commodity Exchange Act unless they involve sale for future delivery on a board of trade.

The Internet grew significantly in 2023, according to a survey by Louis Harris and Associates.
An estimated 35 million adults in the United States used the Internet in late September 2023.
This number increased from 27 million at the beginning of 2023.
Humphrey Taylor is the chairman of Louis Harris and Associates.
The number of adult Americans using computers for cyber-activities is increasing.
America Online Inc. and Compuserve Corp. had almost 41 million subscribers, the same level as in January 2023.
Online services faced increased competition from companies like AT&T Corp., which offer cheaper Internet-only access.
Home users reported spending an average of 2.8 hours online per week, down from three hours in April 2023.
Business and other users reported spending an average of 1.8 hours online per week, down from two hours in April 2023.
The poll found that more educated individuals are more likely to use computers and access the Internet.

The Internet could significantly benefit the U.S. economy if the federal government adopts free market policies in cyberspace.
A draft report from a group of President Clinton's top advisers recommends protecting the Internet from new taxes and censorship.
The interagency task force is led by senior presidential adviser Ira Magaziner.
The task force is preparing to issue a report of principles and policies for public comment after seven months of deliberation.
Magaziner stated that the report aims to outline what the government should not do as well as what it should do.
The growth of Internet commerce could enhance U.S. exports of various products and services.
U.S. exports of products such as movies, news, software, and consulting services totaled $40 billion in 1995.
Sales of goods and services online are projected to increase to $7 billion by the year 2000.
The draft report, titled 'A Framework for Global Electronic Commerce,' addresses issues including taxation, customs, privacy, and security.
The report suggests that the United States should advocate for the Internet to be designated a duty-free zone through the World Trade Organisation.

The Federal Reserve voted to allow banks to increase the percentage of revenue bank subsidiaries may earn from underwriting and dealing in securities from 10 percent to 25 percent.
The Fed Board of Governors voted unanimously on this change.
Bank subsidiaries had previously been limited to earning 10 percent of their revenue from these activities.
The Fed cited Swiss Bank Corp. for exceeding the 10 percent cap earlier this year.
The American Bankers Association managing director Larry LaRocca stated that the new rule is a boost for banks that underwrite securities.
Securities firms expressed dissatisfaction with the new rule, with Steve Judge from the Securities Industry Association comparing it to Santa Claus delivering gifts to only one house.
Bruce Thompson from Merrill Lynch and Co. expressed hope that the new rule would not reduce banks' support for Congressional action.
Rachel Robbins from J.P. Morgan & Co. stated that the new rule addresses only part of the need for complete financial reform.
The 1933 Glass-Steagall Act generally prohibits banks from engaging in non-bank activities but allows certain affiliations under section 20.
Currently, 41 bank 'Section 20' subsidiaries have permission to engage in underwriting.

U.S. banks will be able to increase their securities underwriting activities under a new rule adopted by the Federal Reserve.
The Federal Reserve voted unanimously to allow section 20 subsidiaries of banks to derive up to 25 percent of their revenues from underwriting and dealing in securities.
The new rule will take effect in 60 days.
Fed governors called for Congressional action to reform the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act and other laws separating banks from non-bank financial services industries.
Fed vice chair Alice Rivlin stated that the next move should be up to Congress regarding regulatory changes.
Governor Susan Phillips described the Fed's action as a constructive step and appropriate interpretation of existing legislation.
The Glass-Steagall Act prohibits banks from engaging in non-bank activity, but allows banks to affiliate with firms not primarily engaged in such areas under section 20.
The Fed currently authorizes 41 bank subsidiaries to deal and underwrite securities.
Robert Litan from the Brookings Institute stated that the Fed's action will increase pressure on Congress to repeal the Glass-Steagall Act.
Banking industry representatives expressed satisfaction with the Fed's decision, viewing it as a boost for banks involved in underwriting securities.

The Commerce Department will issue final rules on December 30 regarding the export of computer encoding products.
The proposal is unlikely to satisfy the software industry and privacy advocates who opposed a draft version.
Some changes were made in the final rules compared to the earlier draft, but the bulk of the proposal remains the same.
William Reinsch, the Commerce undersecretary, stated that some objections could not be addressed.
Previous rules from the Cold War severely limited the export of products containing encryption.
Under past rules, products could be exported using keys of up to 40 digital bits.
Longer encryption keys have become more common due to advancements in computer speed.
The demand for encryption-capable products is increasing globally due to the growth of the Internet and online commerce.
The new Commerce Department rules aim to balance U.S. competitiveness in the encryption market with law enforcement interests.
Products with key recovery features will be eligible for export after a one-time review under the new policy.

A study released by a coalition of Internet and computer companies claims that Internet users pose little threat to local telephone companies.
The coalition presented the report to counter previous studies by local phone companies that justified new access fees on Internet usage.
Local phone company studies claimed that Internet usage threatened to overwhelm the phone system.
Harris Miller, President of the Information Technology Association of America, stated that the Internet is not crashing the telephone network.
Miller claimed that the phone companies created a 'problem' to protect their own interests.
On December 24, the Federal Communications Commission tentatively decided not to impose access fees on Internet providers similar to those paid by long distance companies.
Lee Selwyn, one of the study's authors, stated that claims of phone network congestion from Internet traffic are greatly exaggerated.
Selwyn also claimed that ordinary consumers using the Internet pay the phone companies enough to cover the cost of increased use.
In 1995, consumers paid more than $1.4 billion for installation and use of six million second phone lines for Internet access.
Bell Atlantic spokesman Harry Mitchell disputed the study's conclusions, stating that the growing demand for phone lines impacts the capacity of the public telephone network.

A U.S. graduate student cracked a powerful computer encryption system.
The Commerce Department announced it would allow three companies to export a stronger encryption system.
Computer encryption programs were classified as munitions and stronger programs could not be exported until this year.
A new policy from the Clinton administration took effect on January 1, allowing companies to receive permission to export stronger programs.
Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration William Reinsch stated that the approvals were achieved without difficulty.
Companies must agree to incorporate features allowing the government to decode encrypted messages within two years to export stronger programs immediately.
The administration's policy has been criticized for not relaxing export limits enough.
Some companies feared that the two-year plan requirement would delay export approvals.
Reinsch indicated that quick approvals should encourage more applicants.
Encryption has become essential for protecting online communications and transactions.

The U.S. financial services industry will discuss bank reform proposals at a hearing on Tuesday before the House Banking Committee's subcommittee on financial institutions.
There is a general consensus in Congress and the industry to reconsider Depression-era laws that separate banking from other financial services.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is considering a proposal to allow combinations between commercial and financial firms.
Savings institutions and insurance companies can already own or be owned by non-financial companies, while banks face stricter regulations.
A Treasury Department task force recommended that the upcoming bank reform proposal allow mixing of commerce and banking.
Rubin informed bankers at a private meeting that no decision has been made regarding the issue of mixing commerce and banking.
House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach opposes the mixing of commerce and banking and warned that banks could be taken over by larger companies.
Insurance and savings groups will oppose restrictions on commercial and financial combinations at the hearing.
The mutual fund industry also opposes restrictions on commercial and financial combinations.
Small banks, represented by the Independent Bankers Association of America, support imposing legal barriers against commercial and financial combinations.

Internet access providers fear that Congress will negatively impact cyberspace.
Company representatives met with members of the Congressional Internet Caucus to discuss concerns about cyberspace legislation.
Tom Evslin, vice president of AT&T Corp.'s WorldNet Internet service, believes it is inevitable that bills will be introduced to legislate Internet content.
Evslin stated that preventing Congress from making mistakes regarding Internet legislation will be difficult.
Bill Schrader, president of Internet provider PSINet Inc., warned that careless legislation could harm the industry.
Members of Congress at the meeting pledged to protect the Internet.
Representative Rick White, co-chairman of the caucus, acknowledged the challenges ahead regarding various Internet issues.
White co-sponsored a bill to relax export restrictions on encryption features in computer hardware and software.
Senator Conrad Burns warned that government legislation will lag behind private sector developments.
Last year, Congress passed the Communications Decency Act, which was opposed by online companies and civil libertarians.

The Supreme Court will decide if a federal regulator properly allowed credit unions to expand their membership over the past 15 years.
This decision addresses a legal dispute between credit unions and banks.
Credit unions support the Supreme Court's reconsideration of a previous Appellate court decision that favored banks.
Bank representatives believe the Supreme Court's action is merely delaying the outcome.
Marc Schaefer, president of AT&T Family Federal Credit Union, stated that the 1934 Federal Credit Union Act was not intended to protect bank markets at the expense of consumers.
Schaefer claimed that consumers would benefit from competition between banks in the marketplace.
Donald Ogilvie, executive vice president of the American Bankers Association, argued that the facts and law support the banks' position.
Ogilvie expressed disappointment over the delay in enforcing a law he believes is clear.
The Supreme Court will hear arguments in the case during its upcoming term starting in October.
The case impacts approximately 3,600 federal credit unions serving 32 million customers.

Shares on most central and eastern European bourses gained ground this week.
Exchanges in Prague, Warsaw, Budapest, Bratislava, and Bucharest all rose.
Zagreb and Sofia traded mixed.
Ljubljana posted slight losses.
The Central European Share Index (CESI) firmed 66.11 points.
Czech share prices were mostly steady on the Prague Stock Exchange throughout the week.
The PX50 index edged up 3.6 points to close at 568.6 on Thursday.
SPT Telecom and Komercni Banka were leading trades on the Prague Stock Exchange.
SPT closed on Thursday at 3,340 crowns.
Polish shares rose for the sixth consecutive session on Thursday.

It's a Snip is competing to become the ninth horse to win the Pardubice steeplechase in consecutive years.
The Pardubice steeplechase has a history of 106 years.
Richard Dunwoody is the jockey for It's a Snip.
The Pardubice steeplechase is a four-and-a-quarter mile event (6.9 km).
The course includes a series of demanding obstacles.
The Pardubice has been compared to the Grand National at Aintree.
Race organisers have made the course easier in recent years.
The Taxis jump has been modified due to past protests and safety concerns.
A total of 21 horses have died in the Pardubice over the years.
Irish Stamp and Veleda II are the other two British horses competing.

Boris Becker, the third seed, won his match against Frederik Fetterlein with a score of 6-3 6-4 at the Czech Indoor Open.
Becker recently won the CA Trophy in Vienna.
Todd Martin, the fifth seed, defeated Cristiano Caratti 6-4 6-1 in his second round match.
Bohdan Ulihrach, the eighth seed, lost to Jiri Novak 6-4 6-2.
Becker experienced soreness in his hand during the match but managed to win in just over an hour.
Becker has faced recurring problems with a ligament injury since Wimbledon.
Becker is currently ranked sixth in the world and is competing for a spot in the ATP Tour Championships.
Wayne Ferreira, ranked second in Ostrava, is ahead of Becker by 46 points for the eighth spot in the ATP Tour Championships.
Martin's match against Caratti lasted 49 minutes.
Ulihrach previously defeated Daniel Vacek but struggled against Novak.

Tim Henman is the only seed in the $475,000 Czech Indoor Open semifinals.
Tim Henman defeated Wayne Ferreira with a score of 6-4 6-3.
David Prinosil defeated Todd Martin with a score of 7-6 7-6.
Martin Damm defeated Michael Stich with a score of 5-7 6-4 6-4.
Petr Korda won against Jiri Novak with a score of 6-1 6-0.
Tim Henman will play David Prinosil in the semifinals.
Wayne Ferreira is ranked seventh in the world.
Tim Henman is ranked 26th in the world.
Todd Martin is currently 199 points behind Wayne Ferreira in the ATP Tour championship race.
Martin, Stich, and Ferreira will compete in Stuttgart next week.

David Prinosil from Germany won the final of the $475,000 Czech Indoor Open against Czech Petr Korda with a score of 6-1 6-2.
Prinosil is 23 years old and was born near Olomouc, Czech Republic, before emigrating to Germany at the age of 14.
Prinosil dominated the match from the start, utilizing his powerful serve and precise groundstrokes.
Prinosil won the first set in 22 minutes by converting both break points he had.
In the second set, Korda attempted to take more risks but was unable to disrupt Prinosil's performance.
Prinosil achieved four consecutive service winners to win a crucial game in the fourth game of the second set.
Prinosil broke Korda's serve in the fifth and seventh games of the second set.
The match lasted a total of 50 minutes.
Prinosil expressed surprise at not losing a set throughout the tournament and stated he played exceptionally well.
Korda mentioned feeling drained from a previous match and noted that the short points limited his ability to control the match.

The Czech September trade deficit is expected to grow by between 13 and 15 billion crowns after a 14.7 billion crown monthly deficit in August.
A Reuters poll of Czech economists indicated the expected growth in the trade deficit.
Czech trade figures for the first nine months will be released by the Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) at 0900 local time on Thursday.
Most economists surveyed expect steady growth in the deficit and few surprises.
Boris Gomez, an analyst at ING Barings, stated that it is too early to talk about a period of stabilization in the deficit.
The nine-month trade gap is expected to be a record, following a January-August figure of 100.9 billion crowns.
The total shortfall for 1995 was 95.7 billion crowns.
The January-September 1995 trade deficit was 62.3 billion crowns.
Analysts agreed that a 13-15 billion September gap would align with prevailing trends and the estimated deficit of 150-160 billion crowns.
The trade balance has been negatively affected by a downturn in the economies of western Europe earlier in the year.

The Prague Stock Exchange experienced a significant one-day decline on Friday due to decreased foreign interest attributed to a lack of market transparency.
Four of the five largest issues on the PSE fell sharply during active trading.
The Reuters RPIX index dropped nearly three percent to 1,052.
Analysts have criticized the PSE for its lack of transparency and regulation.
Jan Sykora of Wood and Company stated that there is a total lack of interest in the market.
Miroslav Nosal of Patria Finance noted that a notable portion of foreign investors are dissatisfied with the current state of the Czech capital market.
The Czech Republic's Securities Act mandates the Securities Registry (SCP) to provide services related to securities transactions.
The SCP does not disclose transaction details, leading brokers to prefer its privacy and faster settlement process.
The average daily stock turnover on the PSE is $4-$6 million, compared to $15 million in Warsaw.
In April, the Czech parliament approved market reforms aimed at increasing transparency and accountability among companies and fund managers.

Investors are shifting from the Czech equity market to the debt market due to a lack of transparency and poor performance.
The official PX50 index of the Prague bourse has lost almost 18 percent in the past two months.
Analysts predict that the downward trend in the equity market will continue until after the New Year.
Michael Gartner, a debt analyst at ING Capital Markets, stated that the bond market is bullish and has a positive outlook.
Estimated daily bond turnover has increased to 900 million to one billion crowns, matching the turnover on the Prague stock exchange.
Alojz Lacko, a bond trader at Patria Finance, noted that the bond market is becoming more important for foreign investors due to reasonable prices.
Investors have complained about the equities market, where 70 percent of trading occurs off-market, affecting minority shareholder rights.
Bourse and Finance Ministry officials are planning to introduce tighter trading rules to address investor concerns.
Analysts believe that these regulatory changes may be too late to retain investors in the equity market.
Gartner highlighted that the bond market is transparent, liquid, and accessible to all types of investors.

Czechs showed low voter turnout for the newly-created Senate elections on Saturday.
The turnout for the elections was expected to be well under 40 percent.
This turnout is the lowest in the four parliamentary elections held since the fall of communism in 1989.
Opposition Social Democrat leader Milos Zeman expressed concern about the apathy towards the upper house.
Zeman predicted that turnout would improve in the second round of elections on November 22-23.
Preliminary data indicated that Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) was performing well despite low turnout.
In Plzen, turnout was reported at 36 percent, with an ODS candidate expected to face a Social Democrat in the second round.
In Most, turnout was reported at 26 percent, with the ODS candidate leading against a Social Democrat candidate.
The Senate elections were viewed as an indicator of the Czech Republic's political situation following inconclusive lower house polls.
Miroslav Sladek, leader of the far-right Republicans, criticized the Senate as a waste of resources.

Senate runoff elections on Friday and Saturday are expected to have little impact on Czech capital markets.
Investors are focusing on macroeconomic fundamentals rather than political influences.
Last weekend's first round of voting provided a mild boost to the Czech crown and the Prague Stock Exchange.
Analysts believe that unless the second round of voting results vary greatly, little further movement in the markets should be expected.
Jay King of Wood and Company stated that the elections will be a non-event from a foreign investor's perspective.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) received over 36.5 percent of the national vote in the first round.
The opposition Social Democrats (CSSD) received 20.3 percent of the vote.
Only 35 percent of the electorate participated in the elections.
The ODS won three outright Senate seats in the first round and had 76 candidates going into the runoff.
The CSSD had 48 candidates going into the runoff.

The Czech governing coalition led by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus won 52 of 81 seats in the newly-created upper house of parliament.
The centre-left opposition Social Democrats won 25 seats in the same election.
The Senate is primarily an advisory body with limited legislative powers.
The election was the first test for Klaus since his coalition lost its lower house majority in June.
Analysts stated that the coalition's strong showing does not address ongoing issues in the capital market.
Charles Robinson of HILFE indicated that the market's reaction would initially be positive but would stabilize without significant changes.
The coalition's performance in the first round of voting increased domestic investor interest and pushed the market up.
Analysts believe that stock prices are unlikely to rise significantly in the near future due to prior expectations being factored in.
The Czech crown gained some value against its dollar/mark basket following the first round results.
Miroslav Nosal of Patria Finance stated that the final election results reflect the current political structure and will not lead to significant changes.

Czech shares increased on Monday after the coalition government's victory in the Senate elections.
Analysts attributed the rise in shares more to a technical correction than a change in investor sentiment.
The Prague Stock Exchange's PX50 index rose 0.86 percent due to gains in seven of the eight most-capitalised shares.
Brokers expressed limited optimism that the rally would last beyond a few days.
The centre-right government's performance was anticipated and already factored into the market prior to the elections.
Jay King from Wood and Company stated that the rally was technically-led and not fundamentally related to the Senate elections.
A local trader noted that the price increases were driven by year-end anticipation and were domestically motivated.
The minority coalition led by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus secured 52 of 81 seats in the new upper house of parliament.
The centre-left opposition Social Democrats won 25 seats in the Senate elections.
Voter turnout was just over 30 percent, making it difficult for the coalition government to claim renewed voter support.

Markets in Eastern Europe experienced a downturn this week.
Stock exchanges in Bratislava, Bucharest, and Zagreb lost ground.
The Prague Stock Exchange remained stable, with the PX50 index increasing by 0.3 points to close at 510.4.
The centre-right governing coalition in the Czech Republic won Senate elections but did not positively impact the Prague Stock Exchange.
Investors are concerned about weak market regulation in the Czech Republic.
The Warsaw Stock Exchange remained flat, with no new signals for market direction.
Analysts believe the positive economic climate may help the Warsaw Stock Exchange rise above 14,000 points next week.
Comments from the central bank deputy head about potential interest rate increases created uncertainty in the Warsaw market.
Hungarian shares initially rose due to a government decision to increase energy prices but lost momentum midweek.
MOL, an oil and gas company, showed signs of weakness, raising concerns among dealers.

Shares in Cable & Wireless (C&W) advanced on Tuesday after news of a deal with NYNEX and Bell Canada International.
The deal creates Britain's largest cable operator by combining C&W's Mercury, Videotron, Bell Cablemedia, and NYNEX CableComms.
C&W shares peaked at 476.5 pence before closing up 25.5 at 466.5 pence.
Richard Brown is the chief executive of C&W and was appointed five months ago.
The deal follows the collapse of merger talks between C&W and British Telecommunications Plc earlier this year.
Analyst John Tysoe stated that the advantages of scope and size from the deal are irrefutable.
BT welcomed the consolidation in the sector but its shares closed down 4.5 at 353.5 pence.
The new merged company will provide integrated telecommunications, information, and entertainment services.
The merger will give C&W's Mercury access to 18 million business and domestic customers.
The number of homes targeted by the new company will be 2.47 million, surpassing Telewest's two million.

Cable & Wireless, NYNEX Corp, and Bell Canada International announced a merger of their British subsidiaries.
The merger includes C&W's Mercury, Videotron, Bell Cablemedia, and NYNEX CableComms.
Videotron is being acquired by Bell Cablemedia in a deal valued at approximately $1.09 billion.
Cable & Wireless is making a $338 million equity investment in Bell Cablemedia.
Cable & Wireless will own 52.6 percent of the new company, Cable & Wireless Communications.
NYNEX will own 18.5 percent and Bell Canada will own 14.2 percent of the new company.
The remaining 15 percent of the new company will be floated.
The new company will provide integrated telecommunications, information, and entertainment services.
Cable & Wireless Communications will serve around six million homes and businesses in Britain.
The company plans to list its shares in London and New York in about six months.

Lloyd's insurance market welcomed a U.S. district court ruling in its favor on Tuesday.
Lloyd's announced it would extend the deadline for acceptances of a 3.2 billion pound recovery plan.
Lloyd's chairman David Rowland stated the offer would remain open following the court's decision.
The district court in Baltimore, Maryland, overturned an injunction by U.S. Names regarding the recovery plan.
Insurance sources indicated the deadline would likely be extended for several days.
Lloyd's spokesman stated the ruling removed the last major legal obstacle to the recovery plan.
Lloyd's reported that over 82 percent of its 34,000 worldwide members had approved the recovery plan.
Only 53 percent of the 2,700 U.S. Names had approved the plan prior to the ruling.
A spokesman for the Merrett 418 Names Association described the successful appeal as beneficial for the recovery plan.
Lloyd's plans to reinsure its liabilities through a new company called Equitas.

Invesco announced a merger with AIM Management Group.
The combined entity will be named AMVESCO Plc.
AMVESCO Plc will manage approximately $150 billion.
The merger values AIM at around $1.6 billion.
Bob McCullough is Invesco's chief financial officer.
Charles Brady is Invesco's chairman and chief executive.
The merger is described as a merger of two companies, not a takeover.
Invesco will issue 290 million new shares to fund the merger.
AIM shareholders will own about 45 percent of the enlarged group.
The merger requires approval from both Invesco and AIM shareholders.

British property company Greycoat is facing pressure from rebel shareholders who want it broken up.
Moorfield Estates has proposed a merger approach to Greycoat.
Analysts believe Greycoat is not in a critical situation.
A proposal to sell Greycoat's assets will be presented to shareholders at a special meeting on Thursday.
The UK Active Value Fund, advised by Brian Myerson's Active Value Advisers, has put forward the asset sell-off proposal.
The UK Active Value Fund owns an 11 percent stake in Greycoat, which it acquired three years ago.
Brian Myerson's relationship with Greycoat's management has been problematic.
Moorfield Estates has made a proposal involving a share exchange offer for Greycoat.
Moorfield Estates aims to add value for shareholders through more active management of Greycoat's assets.
Analysts believe the Moorfield plan is unlikely to succeed, but there may be opportunities for Greycoat to acquire a more profitable company.

British merchant bank Hambros reported a return to first-half profit.
Hambros reported pretax profits of 35.0 million pounds for the first half of the year.
This profit was an improvement from a 7.7 million pound loss for the same period in 1995.
Sir Chips Keswick is the group chief executive of Hambros.
Regent Pacific Group is a Hong Kong investment manager that holds three percent of Hambros.
Regent Pacific Group has called for the breakup of Hambros to realize shareholder value.
Analysts noted that Regent's calls for Hambros to sell its Hambro Countrywide subsidiary were not discussed in their meeting with the company.
Hambros shares closed down 7.5 pence at 245 pence.
Analysts had predicted an interim dividend of 2.5 to 3.0 pence, but the dividend remained unchanged at 2.5 pence.
Hambros is considered one of the less attractive targets for takeover due to recent poor performance.

Robert Fleming announced increased pre-tax profits for the first half of the year.
The pre-tax profit for the first half of the year increased by 16 percent to 92.2 million pounds.
The previous year's pre-tax profit was 79.4 million pounds.
Chief executive John Manser stated that the profit increase showed new businesses were contributing to profitability.
Manser warned of difficult markets in the second half of the year.
An unnamed analyst suggested that the results were not outstanding given market conditions.
Robert Fleming lost investment banking head Bill Harrison in July.
In August, Jardine Fleming revealed a probe by British and Hong Kong regulators into irregular trades.
The probe resulted in fines and voluntary compensation of nearly $20 million to clients.
Regulators withdrew the authorization of Jardine Fleming's London-based fund company.

3i Group Plc reported an increase in its first half net asset value (NAV) per share.
The NAV per share rose to 454 pence from 426 pence for the same period the previous year.
Ewen Macpherson, 3i's chief executive, stated that the increase was partly held back by continental Europe and a strong pound.
Macpherson noted that the UK portfolio performed extremely well, with an 18 percent growth in revenue.
3i invested 327.3 million stg during the period, with 284.2 million stg invested in the UK.
Macpherson indicated that the prospect of a general election in the UK created investment opportunities.
3i realized investments of 122.2 million stg in the UK and 35.9 million stg in continental Europe.
The group plans to expand in Europe and will open an office in Dusseldorf, Germany in January.
3i intends to open additional offices in Hamburg, Munich, and Stuttgart.
The group will also open its first office in South East Asia, in Singapore, early in 1997.

British property group MEPC announced a 14 percent increase in pretax profits for the year.
MEPC's pretax profits rose to 140 million pounds from 122.6 million pounds the previous year.
A writedown on a Los Angeles shopping mall reduced MEPC's net asset value (NAV).
MEPC's net asset value fell to 450 pence per share from 457 pence per share.
MEPC shares were 11p lower at 441-1/2p by 1218 GMT.
The NAV was reported to be below market expectations.
Earnings per share rose nine percent to 22.9 pence.
The total dividend remained at 20 pence.
The NAV drop reflected a marginal fall in values in Britain and elsewhere.
MEPC's UK portfolio accounts for 70 percent of the group.

Ron Baker plans to bring a counter-claim in a lawsuit against him by Dutch bank ING Barings.
Baker's lawyer, Lindsay Hill, stated that the counter-claim will be heard together with the ING Barings case unless an arrangement is reached beforehand.
ING Barings is suing Baker for 113,000 pounds, which includes a 100,000 pound loan and interest.
Barings collapsed in February 1995 due to losses of around $1.4 billion from unauthorized derivatives trades by Nick Leeson.
ING rescued Barings and formed ING Barings as its investment banking arm.
Nick Leeson is serving a six-and-a-half year jail sentence in Singapore for his role in the bank's downfall.
Writs have been filed by administrators of Barings against former auditors and former bosses, including Baker.
Baker's counter-claim will be for an unpaid bonus that he believes is due and outstanding.
Mary Walz, a former Barings executive, had her claim for an allegedly unpaid bonus rejected by a London industrial tribunal.
Hill stated that the tribunal's decision regarding Walz's case has no implications for Baker's case.

CE Electric is a U.S. energy group.
CE Electric made a hostile bid for Northern Electric Plc.
The Takeover Panel ruled against Northern Electric's appeal regarding the bid extension.
CE Electric's bid was valued at 782 million pounds, equivalent to 1.3 billion dollars.
The offer period for CE Electric's bid was extended to 1300 GMT on Tuesday.
CE Electric received acceptances totaling just over 50 percent needed for victory.
The original offer was meant to close last Friday but was extended after CE Electric's appeal.
The extension was granted due to concerns raised by CE Electric about share purchases by its advisers.
Northern Electric launched its own appeal against the extension of the deadline.
The Takeover Panel dismissed Northern Electric's appeal unanimously.

Pearson is a British media and leisure group.
Pearson has a 50 percent stake in Lazard Partners.
Lazard Partners owns three Lazard houses in London, Paris, and New York.
Marjorie Scardino became Pearson's chief executive last week.
There is speculation that Pearson may sell its stake in Lazard Partners.
A pre-emption agreement exists between Lazards and Pearson.
The pre-emption agreement allows Lazards to have first refusal on its shares if Pearson sells its stake.
Lazard has been a profitable venture for Pearson.
Pearson's 50 percent stake in Lazard Partners was negotiated during the 1980s.
Lazard holds 48 million shares of Pearson.

China stated that Japan is heading for confrontation due to its election platform that reiterates claims to disputed islands in the East China Sea.
China Daily commented that Japan is ignoring warnings and protests from China and is on the path to confrontation.
The Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) of Japan announced an election platform that reaffirms Tokyo's claim to the East China Sea islands, known as the Senkakus in Japan and Diaoyus in China and Taiwan.
China Daily suggested that it is not too late for Japan to stop its actions, which it described as a reckless gamble.
The newspaper urged Japan to take measures to prevent further escalation for the sake of the world and its future.
Approximately 300 Taiwanese and Hong Kong protesters challenged Japan's sovereignty claim by raising flags on the disputed islands.
Japan has requested China to help prevent further landings on the islands and has stated it will not recognize a lighthouse built by Japanese rightwingers.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang accused Japan of irresponsibility for encouraging landings by rightwing groups on the islands.
The dispute intensified after a Hong Kong activist drowned during a protest against Japan's sovereignty claim.
Japan's claim to the islands dates back to 1895, following its defeat of imperial China, while China has claimed sovereignty for centuries.

Wang Dan has been charged with plotting to overthrow the government.
Wang Lingyun, Wang Dan's mother, plans to defend him in court.
Wang Lingyun is a 61-year-old researcher at a museum with no legal background.
Chinese laws permit family members to defend accused individuals.
A court spokeswoman confirmed the charges against Wang Dan but did not provide further details.
Wang Dan's trial date has not been confirmed but may occur as early as this week.
Wang Lingyun claims the charge of collaborating with overseas subversive forces is unfounded.
Wang Dan took a correspondence course at the University of California, Berkeley.
Wang Dan was detained in May 1995 but was not formally arrested or charged until last week.
The charge against Wang Dan carries a maximum penalty of death and a minimum sentence of 10 years.

He Ping, a son-in-law of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, has resigned as director of the armament department of the People's Liberation Army.
He Ping is the husband of Deng Xiaoping's youngest daughter, Deng Rong.
He Ping resigned after his hopes for promotion were not realized.
He Ping wanted to become deputy chief of general staff but was offered the position of assistant chief of general staff instead.
The assistant chief of general staff is one rank below the deputy chief of general staff.
A replacement has been named to succeed He Ping as director of the armament department.
The refusal to promote He Ping is seen as a sign of Jiang Zemin's increasing power within the Communist Party.
Jiang Zemin is the chairman of the Central Military Commission.
Deng Xiaoping, who is 92 years old, no longer holds any office but remains influential.
Deng Xiaoping has not been seen in public since early 1994.

China stated that Taiwan is a pawn of hostile Western forces aimed at weakening the country.
The People's Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, published a commentary on this topic.
The commentary was issued to mark the 25th anniversary of Taiwan's ousting from the United Nations.
Taiwan is accused of collaborating with anti-Chinese forces to regain admission to the United Nations.
The commentary claimed that some Western forces use the 'human rights card' and 'Tibet card' to limit China's development.
It suggested that the Taiwan issue is viewed by Western forces as a means to weaken and divide China.
In September, the U.S. House of Representatives approved a resolution supporting Taiwan's efforts to rejoin the United Nations.
China regards Taiwan as a rebel province and believes the issue was settled in 1971 when Beijing replaced Taipei at the United Nations.
The commentary criticized countries that support Taiwan's bid for U.N. admission as shortsighted.
China and its supporters blocked moves to consider U.N. membership for Taiwan for the fourth consecutive year.

Wang Dan is a prominent dissident in China.
Wang Dan faces charges of plotting to overthrow the government.
Wang Dan's trial is set to begin at the Beijing Intermediate People's Court.
Wang Dan's mother, Wang Lingyun, stated that he would plead not guilty.
Wang Lingyun expressed concern that her son may receive a harsh sentence despite his innocence.
Wang Dan has been in detention since May 1995.
Wang Dan could face a minimum of 10 years in prison and a maximum penalty of death.
The court has not provided details about Wang Dan's trial.
Wang Dan's family has found a lawyer to defend him after only one day to prepare.
Human Rights Watch reported that the chances of an acquittal for Wang Dan are slim.

Chinese dissident Wang Dan has appealed against his 11-year jail sentence for plotting to subvert the government.
Wang Dan's mother, Wang Lingyun, expressed little hope for an acquittal or a lighter sentence.
Wang Lingyun hopes U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and German President Roman Herzog will address her son's situation during their upcoming meetings with Chinese leaders.
Wang Lingyun stated that Wang Dan should be acquitted because he is innocent.
Wang Lingyun acted as one of two defense lawyers in her son's case.
Court officials requested Wang Lingyun to submit a written defense for the appeal.
Family members may not be allowed to attend the appeals court trial for Wang Dan.
Experts on China's legal system believe the chances of the appeals court overturning the lower court's verdict are slim.
An official of the Beijing Higher People's Court confirmed that Wang Dan had filed his appeal.
The Beijing Number One Intermediate People's Court convicted and sentenced Wang Dan in less than four hours.

Wang Guangmei auctioned her private antique collection on Tuesday.
Wang stated she would use the proceeds to help impoverished mothers.
The auction took place at a hotel in Beijing.
Wang's collection included porcelain bowls, plates, and an ivory brush holder from the Qing and Song dynasties.
The collection fetched 566,000 yuan ($68,000) at auction.
Wang is the widow of former president Liu Shaoqi, who died in prison during the Cultural Revolution.
The Sungari auction house valued the antiques at up to 510,000 yuan ($61,000).
Some items in Wang's collection were part of her dowry from her wealthy father.
The collection was seized during the Cultural Revolution but was returned to Wang after her release from prison.
Wang expressed emotional ties to the collection but prioritized concerns for impoverished mothers.

China's exports increased in October due to sluggish domestic demand, faster payment of export tax rebates, and expanded credit to exporters.
Wang Jian, a researcher with the cabinet's State Planning Commission, stated that the upturn in exports is expected to continue through the first half of 1997.
Exports rose 23.3 percent to $15.22 billion in October compared to the previous year.
The International Business Daily reported that the increase in exports helped China achieve its largest monthly trade surplus of the year at $3.91 billion in October.
Wang Jian attributed the rise in exports to slow domestic demand and adjustments made by domestic enterprises to a cut in government-paid export tax rebates.
The government reduced the rebate on exports of industrial products from 14.0 percent to 9.0 percent on January 1, 1996.
Exports had declined in the first six months of 1996 due to rising wages and the strength of the renminbi.
The government has been increasing the payment of export rebates to stimulate exports.
Imports rose by three percent year-on-year to $11.31 billion in October.
In the first 10 months of this year, China's exports totaled $119.22 billion, while imports reached $107.21 billion, a rise of 5.5 percent from the previous year.

China's Supreme Court announced that a court has rejected the appeal of Zhou Beifang, upholding a suspended death sentence for bribery.
Zhou Beifang is 43 years old and was the former chairman of Hong Kong-listed affiliates of Capital Iron and Steel Corp (Shougang).
The appellate court showed leniency because Zhou expressed remorse and voluntarily returned ill-gotten wealth during the investigation.
Zhou was convicted of accepting bribes totaling 9.28 million Hong Kong dollars ($1.2 million) between June 1993 and April 1994.
Zhou was also found guilty of paying 1.2 million yuan ($144,600) in bribes to facilitate the relocation of his wife and daughter to the British colony.
Zhou is considered one of China's 'princelings', a term for the children of the ruling party elite.
Zhou's family has close ties to the family of Deng Xiaoping, a paramount leader of China.
Zhou's conviction is part of a highly-publicized anti-graft campaign launched by China last year.
The appellate court also rejected the appeal of co-defendant Chen Jian, who received a 15-year prison sentence for accepting bribes from Zhou.
Zhou Guanwu, Zhou Beifang's father, resigned as chairman and Communist Party secretary of Shougang in February 1995.

Chinese activists protested against American support for Japan's bid to become a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council.
The activists stated that Japan is not qualified to become a permanent member of the Security Council.
The letter opposing Japan's bid was signed by 15 activists.
The activists claimed that many Japanese politicians have been reluctant to apologize for war atrocities and have tried to whitewash history.
China claims that more than 35 million people were killed or wounded during Japan's invasion and occupation from the early 1930s to 1945.
The letter expressed strong protest against U.S. government support for Japan's bid.
Tong Zeng, a leader of the group, stated he would forward the letter to U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
The Chinese government has been reluctant to antagonize Japan due to a desire for more low-interest loans.
The United States has historically supported giving Japan and Germany permanent seats on the Security Council.
The U.N. Security Council currently consists of five permanent members and ten non-permanent members.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin stated that political differences should not interfere with trade and investment between China and Taiwan.
Jiang Zemin emphasized the complementary nature of the economies of China and Taiwan.
Jiang Zemin expressed a commitment to encouraging Taiwanese businessmen to invest in China.
Jiang Zemin assured that the legitimate rights of Taiwanese investors would be protected.
A delegation of nearly 80 Taiwanese business leaders and politicians visited Beijing.
Taiwan has banned direct trade, transport, and mail links with China since 1949.
Indirect trade and investment between Taiwan and China has been allowed since the late 1980s, typically through Hong Kong.
Jiang Zemin indicated that China aims to establish direct trade and transport links with Taiwan.
Beijing has increased pressure on Taiwan to lift the ban on direct links.
Kao Ching-yuan, head of the Taiwanese delegation, urged Beijing to resume talks with Taiwan.

A Chinese court rejected the appeal of Liu Nianchun against a labour camp term for writing petitions.
The Chaoyang District Court in Beijing stated that freedom of speech must not endanger state security.
The court's verdict indicated that Liu's 1995 petition contained attacks against the people's government.
The court ruled that Liu's petition exceeded the limits of the constitution and the law.
Liu argued that the constitution guaranteed his right to freedom of speech, but the court rejected this argument.
Liu's wife, Chu Hailan, plans to appeal the court's decision within 15 days.
Chu Hailan described the court ruling as unfair, not objective, and unjust.
Chu reported that she was sent to a labour camp to prevent her from meeting U.S. officials during a visit by Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
Liu Nianchun is currently serving a three-year term of re-education through labour and has been in detention for nearly one year.
Liu's petition called for the government to re-evaluate its crackdown on student demonstrators from the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989.

Kao Ching-yuan, a Taiwanese business leader, invited Wang Zhaoguo, director of the Chinese cabinet's Taiwan Affairs Office, to visit Taiwan.
Beijing has not confirmed whether it will accept the invitation from Kao Ching-yuan.
If Wang Zhaoguo accepts the invitation, he would be the most senior Chinese official to visit Taiwan since 1949.
Wang Zhaoguo expressed a willingness to visit Taiwan if given the opportunity, but did not make a definite commitment.
The Mainland Affairs Council in Taiwan stated it would welcome Wang's visit but emphasized that procedures must be followed.
The Taiwan Affairs Office did not comment on the remarks made by the Mainland Affairs Council spokesman.
Kao Ching-yuan is leading a delegation of nearly 80 Taiwanese businessmen, economists, and officials on a 12-day visit to Beijing.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin met with the Taiwanese delegation and assured them that political differences would not hinder trade and investment.
Kao raised concerns about tax and labor issues faced by Taiwanese investors in China during his meetings with Chinese officials.
Kao urged Beijing to resume talks with Taiwan, warning that political friction could undermine investor confidence.

Rupert Murdoch is the chairman and chief executive of News Corp Ltd.
Murdoch is visiting Australia for News' annual meeting next week.
Murdoch stated that News Corp aims to increase profits by 20 percent in 1996/97.
Murdoch ruled out a potential bid for John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
Kerry Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd has attempted to sell its 15 percent stake in Fairfax over the last year.
News Corp owns approximately five percent of Fairfax.
Murdoch expressed confidence in winning a lawsuit against Ted Turner and Time Warner.
Turner described Murdoch's lawsuit against the merger of Turner Broadcasting System Inc and Time Warner as frivolous.
Murdoch indicated that the 20 percent profit increase is attainable if the American and British economies remain stable.
News Corp reported a net profit of A$1.02 billion for the year 1995/96.

Rupert Murdoch stated that The News Corp Ltd's first quarter performance was below expectations.
Murdoch expressed confidence in a 20 percent profit rise for the year 1996/97.
In the 1995/96 year, News Corp's net profit decreased to A$1.02 billion from A$1.37 billion in 1994/95.
Murdoch noted that revenues at the Fox U.S. television business started slowly in 1996/97 due to the Atlanta Olympic Games.
He indicated that Australian newspaper revenues would be flat in 1996/97.
Murdoch reported that News Corp's British newspapers were performing well, with The Sunday Times' circulation increasing.
He announced that News Corp had US$2.5 billion in cash after recent U.S. bond issues.
Murdoch stated that News Corp planned to fund future expansion from cash flow where possible.
He mentioned that News Corp would float its British digital media technology company, Digital Media Services, and sell 20 percent of it.
Murdoch indicated that News' Asian satellite pay television operation, STAR TV, was performing well.

Niugini Mining Ltd owns 17.15 percent of the shares in Papua New Guinea's Lihir Gold Ltd.
Niugini Mining Ltd is exploring ways to return Lihir shares to its shareholders.
Ian Goudie is the chief executive of Niugini Mining Ltd.
A straightforward return of the shares to shareholders cannot be approved until late 1998 due to Lihir mine's current debt arrangements.
Niugini Mining Ltd is considering other structures to return the shares before late 1998.
The return of Lihir shares is one of several ways to unlock the true value of the Lihir stake.
The true value of Niugini Mining Ltd's Lihir stake is not reflected in its current share price.
Niugini Mining Ltd's assets can be viewed in two parts: the Lihir stake and other smaller mining assets.
Separating the two parts of Niugini Mining Ltd's assets could appear to have more value to shareholders.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd is likely to benefit from the planned US$20 billion merger of MCI Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc.
News Corp has a partnership with MCI that may strengthen due to the merger.
The merger will create the world's second largest telecommunications group.
Analysts believe the merger will stabilize News Corp's partnership with MCI.
Concerns had arisen about MCI potentially selling its nine percent stake in News Corp.
The merger reduces the risk of MCI selling its stake in News Corp for at least 12 months.
MCI and News Corp announced a broad alliance in May 1995, with MCI acquiring a nine percent stake in News Corp.
MCI's stake in ASkyB will be reduced from 50 percent to 20 percent.
MCI Chief Executive Bert Roberts stated that no major new launches are expected from the venture with News Corp.
Roberts indicated that MCI is unlikely to take up its option to increase its stake in News Corp.

Simsmetal Ltd is an Australian-based metals recycler.
Simsmetal Ltd expects lower net profit for 1996/97 compared to 1995/96.
Simsmetal Ltd's managing director is John Crabb.
Scrap metal prices have decreased to their lowest levels in almost four years.
Simsmetal Ltd anticipates difficult trading conditions due to weak demand in Europe and Asia.
Simsmetal Ltd's net profit for the first quarter of 1996/97 fell 34 percent to A$8.28 million.
Simsmetal Ltd's profit for 1995/96 was A$46.7 million, which was 23 percent lower than the previous year.
Simsmetal Ltd is in talks to acquire a large British scrap metal business.
Simsmetal Ltd ended the first quarter with approximately A$62 million in cash.
Simsmetal Ltd plans to use either cash or unused borrowing lines for the acquisition.

Westpac Banking Corp Ltd is Australia's second largest bank.
Westpac announced a 19.5 percent rise in net profit for the 1995/96 year.
Westpac warned that fierce competition would flatten profits in the year ahead.
Westpac reported a net profit of A$1.132 billion for the year to September 30, 1996.
Bad debt charges fell to A$121 million in 1995/96 from A$330 million in 1994/95.
The drop in bad debt charges contributed about A$200 million to the 12 percent rise in pre-tax and abnormals profit.
Competition from non-bank mortgage originators is pressuring Westpac's margins.
Mortgage originators have taken over 10 percent of the mortgage market from big banks, including Westpac.
Westpac launched an issue of securitised mortgages worth A$340 million.
Westpac plans to multiply the size of securitised mortgage issues in the current year.

An inquiry into Australia's financial system has been established by the government and is headed by Stan Wallis.
The inquiry's interim discussion paper, released on Wednesday, leaves open the option of mergers among Australia's big banks and foreign takeovers of local banks.
The inquiry outlines various options for reform without stating its own preferences.
The key aim of any reforms should be to increase the efficiency of Australia's banks to compete globally.
The inquiry states that new technology will transform the financial sector.
Big banks, such as National Australia Bank Ltd, have lobbied for relaxed merger rules, arguing that such mergers are necessary for global competition.
The former Labor government implemented a policy that prevents mergers or foreign takeovers of Australia's four largest banks and its two largest insurance and superannuation groups.
The current conservative coalition government will maintain the 'six pillars' policy until it reviews the Wallis inquiry's recommendations, expected by the end of March 1997.
The inquiry seeks to identify means to increase the efficiency of the Australian financial system without compromising its safety and performance.
The inquiry asks whether competition and innovation could be stimulated by widening access to traditional banking activities.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) rate cut on Wednesday is expected to squeeze bank margins.
Major banks have previously delayed passing on official rate cuts to variable rate home loan customers by around seven weeks.
Major banks have begun lowering variable and fixed deposit rates immediately after rate cuts, temporarily widening their margins.
The delay in passing on the recent rate cut has been shortened to about five and a half weeks.
Analysts attribute the contraction in delays to increasing competition from non-bank mortgage lenders and regional banks.
ABN AMRO Hoare Govett banking analyst Michael Pulman stated that competition is putting more pressure on margins.
Aussie Home Loans announced it would cut its variable rate to 7.49 percent from 7.99 percent for existing customers starting January 28.
National Australia Bank Ltd plans to cut its variable mortgage rate to 8.25 percent from 8.75 percent for existing borrowers starting January 23.
Westpac Banking Corp's delay in passing on the rate cut has dropped to 37 days.
St George Bank Ltd reduced the time to pass on the rate cut for its major variable rate product to 20 days from 55 days.

Almost 300 students and workers from Kiribati were aboard the MV Maasmond.
The MV Maasmond is a 1,000-tonne charter ship.
The ship lost power due to a fire in the engine room.
The Royal New Zealand Airforce Orion rescue plane located the MV Maasmond drifting about 800 kilometers east of Tarawa.
The MV Maasmond had 290 passengers on board.
The ship has enough food and water for five days.
The MV Maasmond partially restored its electric power but could not start its engine.
The ship's charterer is Kiribati businessman Waysang Kumkee.
The MV Maasmond was chartered to carry passengers and cargo to Christmas Island from Tarawa.
The cargo included rice and tinned food.

Lend Lease Corp and Modern Home Co announced a joint venture to build a markets complex in Northern Bangkok.
The project will cover 160 hectares and cost A$1 billion (US$778 million).
The complex aims to create a new industrial, commercial, and residential hub in Northern Bangkok.
Stage one of the project is 60 percent complete and projected to cost A$700 million.
Stage one is processing 15,000 tonnes of produce a day and has parking for 25,000 vehicles.
The complex, known as the Thai Markets project, will be located on the main northern road from Bangkok, about 20 km from the airport.
The project will include food processing facilities for packaging and processing produce for export.
The second and third stages will cost A$300 million and include factories, retail outlets, and homes.
Lend Lease's Asian unit will contribute up to A$100 million for a 10 percent stake in the joint venture.
The project is expected to take four years to complete and is supported by the Bank for Agriculture and Agricultural Cooperatives and the Thai Ministry of Commerce.

Goodman Fielder Ltd is expected to report a slightly higher annual net profit before abnormals early on Thursday.
Firmer margins in some areas are expected to be offset by higher grain costs.
A Sydney analyst forecasts a pre-abnormals net profit of just under A$100 million.
The median forecast in BZW Australia's Barceps survey is for a A$100.0 million pre-abnormals net profit for the year to June 30, 1996.
Forecasts for pre-abnormals net profit range from A$97.0 million to A$102.3 million.
Goodman Fielder posted a profit of A$97.3 million in 1994/95.
Another Sydney analyst estimates extra grain costs of about A$60 million for the second half of 1996.
Analysts expect the cost of grain to ease back later in calendar 1996.
The higher grain costs were likely offset by lower packaging and palm oil costs in the second half of 1995/96.
Goodman chief executive David Hearn stated that the pre-abnormal profit would be around A$100 million.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp reported a lower than expected profit for the first half of 1996/97.
News Corp remains confident of a 20 percent profit boost for the full year.
Net profits before abnormals increased by 10.3 percent to A$731 million (US$555 million).
The reported profit was below analyst forecasts of A$735 million to A$775 million.
News' shares fell 16 cents to A$6.60 after the result, but closed at A$6.76.
News Corp had previously stated it expected strong movie and television revenues to increase profits by at least 20 percent in 1996/97.
News Corp officials indicated they are still on track for the 20 percent growth.
Operating income from News' Fox Filmed Entertainment unit increased to A$202 million for the first half of 1996/97.
British newspaper profits rose 18 percent in the first half, with gains in circulation revenues at The Sun, The Times, and The Sunday Times.
All of News Corp's newspapers maintained their dominant position in their respective markets despite cover price increases.

Caterpillar Inc. reported record third-quarter profits of $310 million, an increase of 45 percent from $213 million a year ago.
Sales increased to $4.03 billion from $3.73 billion in the same period.
Earnings per share rose 50 percent to $1.61 from $1.07.
The results exceeded Wall Street expectations, leading to a $2.50 increase in Caterpillar stock to $76.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts had forecast profits of $1.34 a share, according to First Call.
For the first nine months of 1997, sales were $12.06 billion, up from $11.86 billion a year ago.
Profit for the first nine months surged to $980 million from $836 million.
Caterpillar Chief Financial Officer Douglas Oberhelman stated that most of the earnings gain was due to improved operations.
Profit margins rose to 25 percent in the quarter from 19 percent a year ago.
Higher machine sales in the United States accounted for most of a 5 percent increase in sales volume in the quarter.

Mercantile Bancorp Inc is a potential target in the Missouri bank merger wave after its planned combination with Mark Twain Bancshares Inc.
Michael Ancell, an analyst at Edward D. Jones & Co, stated that Mercantile is still a buyout candidate.
Mercantile Bancorp Inc is the largest bank holding company in Missouri after Boatmen's Bancshares Inc.
Analysts view Mercantile as attractive to banks seeking to establish a presence in the lower Midwest.
NationsBank Corp agreed to buy Boatmen's Bancshares Inc for $9.5 billion in August.
The deal for Boatmen's Bancshares Inc was valued at 2.7 times book value.
Mercantile's deal values Mark Twain Bancshares Inc at about 2.8 times book value.
The pooling of interests deal is worth $49.62 per share to Mark Twain shareholders.
The combined total assets of the St. Louis-based bank holding companies would be $21.3 billion.
James Schutz, a banking analyst at Chicago Corp, described the transaction as pricey and noted Mark Twain is a profitable franchise.

Olympic Financial Ltd stated it could reach a deal to sell the company by October.
Warren Kantor is the chairman of Olympic's executive committee.
Kantor mentioned that the investment banker Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette is considering strategic alternatives for the company.
Olympic received an indication of interest from a potential buyer.
Kantor noted that others have expressed interest in the company since the announcement.
The first contact from a potential buyer came from a company with investment grade credit.
Olympic's credit is not investment grade.
Kantor stated that Olympic needs capital to expand technology as the business grows.
Olympic's loans serviced increased to $3 billion at the end of June from $1.5 billion a year ago.
Kantor indicated that Olympic aims for Classic loans to constitute 50 percent of its portfolio by the end of the year.

McDonnell Douglas Corp. announced it would consider mergers and acquisitions but not a restructuring.
The Defence Department eliminated McDonnell Douglas from the competition to build a new generation fighter jet.
The new generation fighter jet program could be worth $200 billion or more.
Chief Executive Officer Harry Stonecipher stated that the company continues to look at mergers and acquisitions.
The Pentagon awarded contracts to Boeing and Lockheed Martin Corp. to develop prototype fighter jets.
McDonnell Douglas is the nation's second-largest defence contractor.
Industry analysts suggested that McDonnell Douglas may need to restructure or seek a merger after the Pentagon's decision.
McDonnell Douglas had preliminary merger discussions with Boeing Co. earlier this year.
Stonecipher expressed that he does not think Boeing would be a potential acquisition target for McDonnell Douglas.
British and U.S. forces plan to buy 3,000 new generation fighter jets, with initial delivery scheduled for 2008.

Shoppers lined up outside stores on Friday, some arriving before dawn.
The day after Thanksgiving is traditionally one of the busiest days for retailers.
The day after Thanksgiving marks the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season.
Analysts expect sales gains of about 5 percent over last year's weak sales growth.
There are five fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas this year.
Allen Sinai, chief economist at Primark Decision Economics, forecasts sales growth of 4.5 percent for November and December.
Roni Campos lined up outside Wal-Mart at first Colony Mall in Sugarland, Texas, at 6:30 a.m.
Stephanie Foster began her shopping at 5 a.m. at Mervyns California and noted a line outside Target of at least 200 people.
Rosalee DiGregorio was one of the first customers at Target and mentioned they had 40 Nintendo consoles in stock.
Tracy Mullin, president of the National Retail Federation, stated that Barbie dolls, especially Holiday Barbie, are expected to be hot sellers.

Freight hauler Yellow Corp. announced it could cut 1 percent to 2 percent of its workforce as part of a restructuring of Yellow Freight System.
Yellow Corp. is based in Overland Park, Kansas.
The company has offered early retirement to 153 employees who are 55 and older.
Yellow Corp. will announce layoffs in the first quarter.
The company will take an unspecified charge to fourth quarter earnings to cover expenses related to early retirement, severance, and reorganization costs.
Each geographic unit of Yellow Freight will have a group vice president who reports to Yellow Freight President Bill Zollars.
Five officers at the central office will also report to Bill Zollars.
Bill Zollars stated that the company is decentralizing responsibility to be more responsive to customer needs.
Employees have until January 15 to decide on early retirement.
The number of layoffs will depend on early retirement decisions and the company's needs during reorganization.

Firstar Corp announced it expects to fall short of analysts' fourth-quarter earnings estimates.
Firstar Corp cited temporary factors for the expected shortfall, including a modest decline in commercial loans outstanding.
Firstar Corp has $19.9 billion in assets.
Firstar Corp expects fourth-quarter earnings of about $0.95 a share, which is $0.08 short of the consensus and unchanged from a year ago.
Firstar Corp is implementing a program to trim costs and enhance revenues.
Analysts are uncertain if the decline in commercial loans outstanding will be reversed.
