Boeing's workforce has increased by nearly 15 percent this year after previous layoffs.
As of Sept. 30, Boeing had orders for 435 planes worth $34.9 billion.
Boeing revenues are expected to rise to about $22 billion this year and nearly $36 billion next year.

An outbreak of bacterial food poisoning in the Seattle area has sickened at least 13 children and young adults.
Health officials traced the outbreak to tainted apple juice from Odwalla Inc.
Odwalla Inc. is a fresh juice and beverage company based in Half Moon Bay, California.
Odwalla issued a nationwide recall of products containing fresh apple juice.
Many retailers removed all Odwalla beverages from their shelves.
Ten of the 13 confirmed cases of E. coli food poisoning were traced to unpasteurized Odwalla juice.
Three cases are still under investigation.
At least eight more suspected cases of food poisoning have been reported.
Six children have been hospitalized due to the outbreak, including two who required dialysis.
One 2-year-old boy remains hospitalized but is in satisfactory condition.

Boeing Co. is competing against Lockheed Martin Corp. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. for a Pentagon contract to build 3,000 new joint strike fighters.
The contract could be worth more than $170 billion over the next two decades.
The Pentagon will announce the results of a down select on November 18, which will eliminate one of the three teams.
Lockheed Martin has identified the joint strike fighter as its number one new business opportunity.
Analyst Paul Nisbet stated that winning the contract is more critical for Lockheed Martin and McDonnell Douglas than for Boeing.
Boeing's proposal promises up to 95 percent commonality among the three versions of the jet.
The average 'flyaway' cost for each plane is projected to be less than $30 million, excluding research and development costs.
The joint strike fighter aims to serve the needs of the Air Force, Marines, Navy, and the British Royal Navy with a single common airframe.
The project is intended to replace four existing fighters after delivery begins in fiscal year 2008.

Sierra Semiconductor Corp.'s stock increased by more than 27 percent on Thursday.
The increase in stock price was due to expectations that the company will become more profitable after exiting the computer modem business.
Sierra Semiconductor Corp. is based in San Jose, California.
The company's stock rose $2.625 to $11.875 in late trading on NASDAQ.
Analyst Elias Moosa stated that the company will be smaller but more profitable after the exit from the modem business.
Sierra Semiconductor Corp. plans to cut as many as 150 jobs from its workforce of 500 people.
The company will take a charge against earnings of $50 million to $80 million to write down asset values and cover severance payments.
Scott Randall of Soundview Financial Group indicated that selling the modem-chip business may be difficult.
The market for networking chips is attracting larger competitors like International Business Machines Corp.
Miles Kan of Hambrecht & Quist described the exit from the modem business as a positive strategic move.

Boeing Co announced its planned $13 billion acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp.
Boeing is a leader in commercial aviation and is now among the top military contractors.
Boeing's acquisition is expected to increase competitive pressure on Airbus Industrie.
Analysts believe the main benefits of the acquisition will be on the military side for Boeing.
Cai von Rumohr, an analyst at Cowen & Co, stated that Boeing's military business was previously less significant.
One analyst estimated that the combined company could derive nearly 50 percent of its revenues from government contracts.
Boeing recently completed a $3.2 billion acquisition of Rockwell International Corp's defense and space business.
The Pentagon chose Boeing and Lockheed Martin Corp to build prototype versions of the joint strike fighter plane.
The contract for the joint strike fighter could be worth $200 billion or more to the winning company.
Analyst Nick Heymann stated that McDonnell Douglas was eliminated from consideration for the joint strike fighter program.

Phil Condit is the chief executive officer of Boeing Co.
Phil Condit was elected chairman of Boeing's board of directors on December 9.
Phil Condit began negotiations for a $13.3 billion deal to acquire McDonnell Douglas Corp. one day after his election.
Phil Condit will serve as chairman and chief executive of the merged company if the deal is approved by shareholders and federal regulators.
Phil Condit started his career with Boeing in 1965 and was promoted to chief executive in April after serving as president for over three years.
Frank Shrontz is the current chairman of Boeing and will retire before Condit's promotion to chairman becomes effective on February 1.
Phil Condit is known for changing from a business suit to a sweater and slacks for meetings with workers.
Bill Whitlow, a Boeing analyst at Pacific Crest Securities, stated that Phil Condit is a strong communicator.
Phil Condit aims to cut costs and create a more agile aerospace company.
Boeing has implemented a philosophy of 'working together' to improve collaboration among engineers, contractors, and factory workers.

Microsoft Corp stock is ending 1996 at slightly more than $80 a share.
After adjusting for a stock split, the value of Microsoft shares is up 91 percent.
Bill Gates' stake in Microsoft has risen to about $23.6 billion from $12.4 billion.
Analysts do not predict Microsoft will repeat its 1996 performance in 1997.
Microsoft plans to launch the latest version of Office at the start of the year.
Microsoft intends to expand its package of computer network software for the Internet market.
A new Internet browser is expected to be released by midyear.
Upgrades to Microsoft's core Windows operating systems could be available by the end of the year.
Microsoft's high-end Windows NT system could account for 25 percent of the company's estimated $10.6 billion in revenues for the current fiscal year.
Analysts expect Microsoft's earnings to rise about 20 percent to $2.06 a share in the current fiscal year.

Microsoft Corp. is launching the latest version of its Office suite of applications.
Bill Gates, the Company Chairman, predicts that Office 97 will be the biggest upgrade ever in percentage terms.
The Office suite has an installed base approaching 50 million users, including applications like Word and Excel.
Early reviews of Office 97 have been positive, but corporate users are cautious about upgrading.
The upgrade investment for Office 97 is estimated to be $200 per seat or more.
Michael Pinckney, research director for the Gartner Group, stated that corporations are realizing they do not need to upgrade their office suite environment as often as Microsoft suggests.
Microsoft dominates the market for desktop productivity suites, capturing more than 90 percent of revenues.
Office and its component applications contributed approximately $1.8 billion to Microsoft's $8.4 billion in sales for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1996.
Analyst Scott McAdams projected that Office would account for nearly $3 billion of a total $10.2 billion in revenues this year.
The new Office includes Internet hooks to promote broader acceptance of Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser.

Microsoft Corp is expected to report modest earnings growth for the latest quarter on Friday.
Industry analysts expect Microsoft to report earnings of 51 cents a share for its second quarter ended December 31.
This represents an increase of about 16 percent from the 44 cents a share reported a year earlier.
Sales are expected to rise about 14 percent to more than $2.5 billion.
Analysts consider this a strong performance against tough comparisons with the year-earlier period.
In the 1995 second quarter, sales soared 54 percent and net income jumped 48 percent.
Microsoft executives delayed the earnings report release from Thursday to Friday.
The delay was to coincide with the launch of Office 97, Microsoft's best-selling package of business software.
Analysts estimate that revenues from Office and its applications account for up to 30 percent of Microsoft's total.
Strong growth in personal computer sales and acceptance of Microsoft's Windows NT operating system continue to support profits.

Microsoft Corp.'s share price rose to $90.75 on Monday, an increase of $3.625.
Microsoft reported second-quarter earnings of 57 cents a share, up from 45 cents a year earlier.
The second-quarter earnings surpassed a consensus estimate of 51 cents.
Frank Michnoff of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette stated that Microsoft had a great quarter.
Microsoft executives warned of a slowdown in growth for fiscal 1998, which begins July 1.
Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Mike Brown questioned the high valuation of the company's stock.
Piper Jaffray downgraded Microsoft's stock to hold from buy due to a 100 percent increase over the past year.
Most analysts raised their earnings estimates for Microsoft.
First Call reported that a consensus of 19 analysts estimated Microsoft would earn $2.33 a share for fiscal 1997.
Analysts predict Microsoft will earn $2.71 a share for fiscal 1998, up from a previous consensus of $2.48.

The Ivory Coast 1996/97 cocoa marketing season began on Thursday.
The farm-gate price for cocoa remained unchanged at 320 CFA francs per bagged kilo.
The Droit Unique de Sortie (DUS) export tax was reduced from 160 CFA francs to 150 CFA francs.
Agriculture Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan stated that the government sacrificed about 10 billion CFA francs to maintain the price.
Kouassi Konan indicated that without the tax cut, the farm-gate price would have been affected.
Exporters were not expecting significant price changes.
There were disagreements between shipowners and officials regarding indicative freight rates for 1996/97.
The Office Ivoirien de Chargeurs requested detailed information on proposed freight rates for shipments.
The government approved a decision by the Caisse de Stabilisation marketing board without amendments.
The opening of the cocoa marketing season was delayed by about three weeks.

Shipments of cocoa from Ivory Coast's main port of Abidjan are matching arrivals.
The standing stock of cocoa at the end of October is about 90,000 tonnes.
Some transporters are cautious about shipping cocoa due to unagreed freight rates.
Total cocoa stocks have not changed since last week.
Arrivals of cocoa at the port are increasing with more trucks arriving.
Delays in issuing freight rates and export licenses have blocked some cocoa at Abidjan.
Exporters expect 1996/97 export licenses to be issued this week.
Some exporters are waiting for their licenses and bank finances before making purchases.
Shipping companies will continue shipping at the 1995/96 reference freight rates.
Shipments at the start of the 1995/96 cocoa marketing season were delayed due to freight rate negotiations.

Cocoa buyers in central Ivory Coast report a 30 percent decrease in purchases compared to the same time last year.
Cocoa buyers expect the total cocoa output for Ivory Coast in the 1996/97 season to be under 850,000 tonnes.
One buyer estimates the crop will be about 800-850,000 tonnes for the entire year.
Buyers in the area visited by Reuters agree with the lower estimates.
One buyer with nine purchasing centres states their business is operating at 65 percent of last year's levels.
Cocoa farms between the main towns of Gagnoa and Daloa show varied conditions, with deterioration strongest in the north around Daloa.
Cocoa arrivals reported by exporters are down 25 percent compared to the same time last year.
Exporters and buyers in southwest Ivory Coast expect arrivals of the 1996/97 crop to be no more than 900,000 tonnes.
Private forecasters projected a main crop of 850-900,000 tonnes last summer.
Prime Minister Daniel Kablan Duncan expects the total cocoa crop to shrink to 950,000 tonnes in 1996/97 from 1.2 million tonnes the previous year.

Shipments of cocoa from Ivory Coast's two main ports are estimated to have risen to around 120,000 tonnes by the end of November.
Official figures for cocoa shipments will not be ready until later this month.
Abidjan and San Pedro port stocks have risen over the past week.
About 100,000 tonnes of cocoa had been exported by the same date in the 1995/96 season.
Under 10,000 tonnes were exported in October 1996.
The marketing season for cocoa opened over two weeks later than usual on October 24 this year.
Arrivals in the 1996/97 season had reached 285,000 tonnes by the end of November, with some estimates closer to 300,000 tonnes.
Stocks of cocoa are estimated to be around 150,000 tonnes.
Large shipments in early December are expected to reduce the stock volume.
Shippers expect arrivals to decrease from mid-December to the end of January before increasing until the end of March.

Ivory Coast's coffee industry is facing market reforms and uncertainties regarding returns in 1997.
The Caistab is under pressure to keep farmers interested while fulfilling liberalization obligations for World Bank loans.
Ivory Coast reduced its reference farmgate price from 700 CFA per kilo to 500 CFA per kilo.
The 1996/97 marketing season opened late on November 14.
World prices for coffee fell below the prices guaranteed by the Caistab, raising concerns from the World Bank about a potential repeat in the coming year.
The World Bank is advocating for a rapid end to cross-subsidies from cocoa earnings to the coffee sector.
New Caistab chief Yves-Marie Koissy is expected to present plans in early 1997.
Some exporters predict that coffee output may exceed the 230,000 tonnes forecast by Caistab, which could lead to higher subsidies.
Ivory Coast no longer guarantees a set coffee price to farmers, instead using a guideline minimum price.
Merchants have been paying farmers less than the reference price, with payments reported at 300 to 340 CFA per kilo.

Ivory Coast-based firms and new investors aim to boost local cocoa processing in 1996/97.
Industry sources and analysts state that the 50 percent production target will not be reached by 2000.
The 50 percent target is understood to mean about 400,000 tonnes of cocoa beans.
Ivory Coast can currently process around 180,000 tonnes of cocoa.
Potential investors may increase processing capacity by at least 110,000 tonnes, bringing the total to nearly 300,000 tonnes by 1997.
Ivorian exporter SICC plans to start its first processing project in early 1997.
SICC handles a total of 200,000 tonnes of cocoa in 1996/97 for clients including Cargill's Gerkens.
SICC's Deputy-Director Guillaume Adome stated that processing is necessary for handling large volumes.
Guillaume Adome mentioned that plans depend on government incentives and that a minimum of 50,000 tonnes could be processed at Abidjan or San Pedro.
French group CEMOI expressed interest in processing up to 60,000 tonnes a year in Ivory Coast.

Chad's cotton monopoly Cotontchad forecasts rises in output and processing capacity for the 1996/97 November-October season.
The forecasted increase is attributed to higher world prices.
Cotontchad is seeking new markets in China and Russia to enhance sales.
Mahamet Tahi Kherallah, the company administrative director, states that the industry is affected by external factors.
Kherallah mentions that the future of the industry depends on world cotton price fluctuations, rain levels, and the exchange rate for sales in dollars.
Cotontchad is Africa's fifth largest cotton producer and is majority state-owned.
The company limited the impact of a 1996 drought on production by enlarging the area under cultivation.
Rain levels in southern Chad's cotton areas were largely sufficient, needing four months of good rain between May and September.
Cotontchad's seed cotton purchases are projected to rise to a record 204,600 tonnes in 1996/97 from 157,476 tonnes in 1995/96.
The area under cultivation is projected to increase to 264,557 hectares from 209,750 hectares in 1995/96.

Ivory Coast and other African coffee nations will hold talks with Vietnam on Tuesday regarding robusta output.
An emergency meeting of coffee producers is scheduled in Rio de Janeiro on January 23.
IACO Secretary General Aregu Worku stated that the Vietnam meeting aims to persuade Vietnamese leaders to join the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC).
There will be a fact-finding mission to Vietnamese plantations to observe production and techniques.
Ivorian Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze has traveled to Vietnam for the Asia International Coffee Conference '97 in Ho Chi Minh City from January 14 to 18.
Gauze was accompanied by IACO's chief economist Donald Kaberuka and Ivory Coast's new Caistab marketing board coffee department director Avi Adroh.
Gauze previously blamed non-ACPC member exporters, including Vietnam, for instability in the world robusta price.
Worku indicated that the main discussions will occur in Rio de Janeiro during the January 23 meeting.
African producers plan to renew demands for a 2.5 million bags export quota cut for the first six months of 1997.
Worku noted that Ivory Coast has adhered to its ACPC quota while non-members have increased production.

An Ivory Coast liberalisation study will be ready by January 31.
The study focuses on quality, competition, and reducing bureaucracy.
Four options will be reviewed in the study.
Price stability and self-financing without carryovers will be considered.
The study is sponsored by donors and conducted by Landell Mills Consultants (LMC).
The study aims to avoid issues seen in Cameroon related to coffee quality.
Ivory Coast began coffee and cocoa sector reforms in 1995 as part of a World Bank loan.
The guideline farmgate coffee price was reduced to 500 CFA per kilo for the 1996/97 season.
Coffee exporters are seeking further support from cocoa revenues due to low world prices.
The Caisse de Stabilisation (Caistab) sets a guide price for farmers.

African coffee producers will meet before the end of February to discuss the implementation of world export cuts.
Guy-Alain Gauze is the commodities minister of Ivory Coast and chairman of the Interafrican Coffee Organisation (IACO).
A meeting will be held by the end of February.
African and Asian states agreed to cut robusta exports by one million 60-kg bags between January and June 1997.
This agreement was made during emergency talks of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) in Rio de Janeiro on January 23.
A meeting in Bali on February 6 will discuss sharing the export cuts between the two regions.
The Bali meeting will follow 10 days of informal discussions since January 23.
Donald Kaberuka is the chief economist of the OIC and stated that control and verification mechanisms will be put in place.
Gauze did not specify how export curbs would be distributed between Asian and African regions or individual countries.
Arabica producers at the Rio talks agreed to cut their output by a total of 300,000 (18,000 tonnes).

French chocolate manufacturer Cantalou plans to sign a deal by 1998 to build a cocoa processing plant in Ivory Coast.
Cantalou's public relations manager, Catherine Poirier, stated that a signature will occur by the end of the year.
Cantalou's investment plans have not been finalized despite reports of progress.
Cargill opened an office in Abidjan in late 1996 to explore processing options.
Cargill's representative in Ivory Coast has begun negotiations for a processing plant, with decisions expected from March.
Cantalou representatives visited Ivory Coast in late 1996 to discuss setting up a cocoa processing plant.
Cantalou's proposed processing plant has a budget of 160 million French francs and a capacity of 60,000 tonnes per year.
Ivorian exporter SICC plans to process up to 50,000 tonnes of cocoa per year and expects to finalize a $2 million investment in early 1997.
SICC expects to handle 200,000 tonnes of cocoa exports in 1996/97 for clients including Cargill's Netherlands processing subsidiary Gherkens.
Cocoa processing in Ivory Coast is dominated by UNICAO and Callebaut-Barry, with a current processing capacity of 180,000 tonnes.

Ivory Coast must improve quality controls, enhance farmer training, and market different grades of cocoa separately.
Louis Bensdorp is the head of the Netherlands Cocoa Association (NCV).
Bensdorp stated that Ivory Coast produces high-quality cocoa, but 10 percent of poor quality cocoa affects the overall quality.
Amsterdam is Europe's cocoa processing hub and primarily imports cocoa from Ivory Coast in bulk form.
Bensdorp spoke during Ivorian Consultative Committee cocoa sector reform talks.
Cocoa quality and issues with a new export contract auction system are key topics of discussion.
Bensdorp highlighted a lack of quality control in the cocoa sector.
He proposed three corrective measures to the International Cocoa Organization and other stakeholders.
Bensdorp emphasized the need for quality checks at all stages of the marketing chain and increased farmer cooperative involvement.
He noted that government interference has historically affected cocoa market practices.

Large U.S. newspaper companies are expected to report good third-quarter earnings.
Weak growth in advertising is noted despite the expected earnings.
James Marsh is a newspaper industry analyst at Prudential Securities.
Newsprint costs for newspapers average $550 a ton.
The average forecast for newsprint costs was $600 a ton at the start of 1996.
Newsprint prices peaked at $743 a ton in January.
Edward Atorino is a newspaper industry analyst at Oppenheimer & Co.
Retail advertising rose only about one percent during the first half of the year compared to the first half of 1995.
Classified advertising rose 10 percent in the first half but likely cooled in the third quarter.
Times Mirror Co will benefit from newsprint savings due to its inventory accounting methods and reduced consumption after shutting two big city papers.

Time Warner Inc reported a 32 percent increase in earnings before debt payments in the third quarter compared to the same period last year.
The company attributed its earnings growth to three successful movies, strong magazine advertising sales related to the Olympic Games, and positive results from HBO.
Time Warner's cash flow for the quarter was $964 million.
Revenues for the three months ending September 30 were $4.877 billion, an increase from $4.344 billion a year prior.
Last year's third-quarter cash flow was reported as $729 million.
Time Warner reported a net loss of $167 million, or 43 cents per share, for the quarter.
The net loss in the same quarter last year was $160 million, or 41 cents per share.
Net interest costs for the quarter were $276 million, an increase from $259 million in the previous year.
Preferred dividends increased to $76 million in the third quarter from $16 million last year.
Time Warner is in discussions to restructure its cable-television partnership with U S West Media Group.

Two leading international satellite-television groups plan to enter Argentina.
Argentina has a high penetration of pay-television services.
Nahuelsat holds exclusive satellite-TV rights in Argentina.
Mark Goldman is a vice president of News Corp Ltd.
Galaxy Latin America and Sky Entertainment Latin America are the two groups entering Argentina.
Galaxy is owned by Hughes Electronics Corp, the Cisneros Group, Multivision, and TVA Abril.
Sky Entertainment is owned by News Corp, Tele-Communications Inc, Grupo Televisa, and TV Globo.
Nahuelsat offers a low-cost DTH service in rural areas of Argentina.
52 percent of Argentina's television homes subscribe to pay television.
Business fundamentals in Argentina are challenging for new DTH entrants.

Sunbeam Corp. plans to cut 6,000 jobs, which is half of its workforce.
Sunbeam Corp. will eliminate 87 percent of its product lines.
Albert Dunlap is the chairman of Sunbeam Corp.
Sunbeam Corp. reported its first quarterly loss since 1992.
Sunbeam Corp. lost $28.7 million in the third quarter.
Sales at Sunbeam Corp. fell by 2 percent.
Sunbeam Corp. will reduce its facilities from 53 to 14.
Sunbeam Corp. will take a charge of $300 million for one-time costs.
Only $75 million of the $300 million charge will be in cash.
Sunbeam Corp. aims to double revenues to $2 billion by 1999.

Florida is set to challenge the tobacco industry using an anti-racketeering law.
The challenge could result in larger damages against cigarette makers if Florida prevails.
Florida's lawsuit seeks at least $1 billion for treating smokers' illnesses.
Christopher Mueller, a tobacco-litigation expert, stated that Florida's law allows for winning damage claims but only goes back to 1994.
Florida's RICO law allows officials to seek damages from before 1994.
Florida is one of 16 states that have sued tobacco companies to recoup healthcare costs for poor smokers.
Texas and Florida are using RICO laws to strengthen their claims against Philip Morris Cos. Inc. and other tobacco companies.
Florida filed additional claims under RICO laws on November 4.
Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth is scheduled to appear in county court in West Palm Beach.
A Jacksonville jury awarded $750,000 to a lung cancer sufferer against the Brown & Williamson unit of B.A.T Industries Plc.

A Florida judge stated that tobacco-company lawyers are unlikely to win separate trials for each of the up to 300,000 claims in a secondhand smoking suit.
Tobacco-company lawyers argued that the illnesses attributed to secondhand smoke were too complicated to be combined in one trial.
Hugh Whiting, an attorney for RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co, claimed that a jury could not effectively separate the complexities of the cases.
Dade County Circuit Court Judge Robert Kaye indicated that holding so many trials would be impossible.
Judge Kaye expects a two-part trial process for the class-action suit to begin on June 2.
The first part of the trial will determine if tobacco companies conspired to conceal evidence of the dangers of secondhand smoke.
The second part of the trial will set monetary damages if the tobacco companies lose the first part.
Judge Kaye suggested that the claims by flight attendants could be grouped by category and handled by one jury.
Whiting proposed a national media campaign and a toll-free contact number to reach eligible flight attendants.
Flight-attendants attorneys Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt criticized the proposed campaign as wasteful and expensive.

Tony O'Reilly is best known in America as the chairman of H.J. Heinz.
O'Reilly's family owns 28 percent of Independent Newspapers Plc of Ireland.
Independent Newspapers Plc competes with international media figures such as Rupert Murdoch.
O'Reilly was rumored to be the buyer of Mirror Group Newspapers Plc's 46 percent stake in Independent Newspapers Plc for $100 million.
O'Reilly has expressed interest in buying into John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
Independent Newspapers Plc sells 80 percent of Ireland's nationally distributed newspapers.
Independent has radio partnerships and controlling shares in newspaper businesses in New Zealand and South Africa.
The stock market value of Independent has risen sixfold in five years.
Heinz is in deal talks with prospective buyers and plans to sell substantial businesses by April 30.
Heinz will focus on six business clusters: food-service products, pet food, infant formula outside the United States, condiments, ketchup, and weight-loss services and products.

Republic Industries Inc. agreed to buy National Car Rental System Inc. for about $600 million in stock.
Republic Industries Inc. is based in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and is controlled by Wayne Huizenga.
National Car Rental System Inc. is based in Minneapolis and is owned by an investor group led by William Lobeck.
Republic Industries Inc. previously bought Alamo Rent-a-Car for $625 million in stock.
The acquisitions will give Republic car-rental agencies with 230,000 cars in their fleets.
Analysts believe the National deal will strengthen Republic's position in the car rental business.
AutoNation, a chain owned by Republic, aims to have 80 outlets in place by 2000.
National Car Rental System Inc. has about 800 locations in North America and a fleet of about 100,000 vehicles in the United States.
William Lobeck and other National executives will sign employment agreements with Republic and manage National's daily operations.
Transactions for rental car companies have increased in recent months.

Wayne Huizenga's Republic Industries Inc. acquired Maroone Automotive Group for $200 million.
Maroone Automotive Group operates seven car dealerships, six of which are located in southern Florida.
Republic Industries previously agreed to pay $600 million for the National Car Rental Agency.
Republic Industries is scheduled to complete the acquisition of AutoNation USA.
AutoNation USA is owned by Wayne Huizenga and focuses on consolidating the second-hand car business in the United States.
AutoNation is building superstores for lightly used cars with set prices and warranties.
Republic Industries aims to open between 80 and 100 AutoNation stores by the year 2000.
Maroone Automotive Group owns the fourth largest Chevrolet store, the third largest Dodge location, and the largest Isuzu franchise in the United States.
Michael Maroone will become president of Republic's new-car division.
Republic Industries has acquired several other companies, including Mullinax Inc., Magic Ford, and Bell Dodge.

Quick & Reilly Group Inc expects revenues to potentially double to $120 million by early 1998.
Quick & Reilly Group Inc is acquiring Nash, Weiss & Co, a market maker for retail brokerages.
Quick President Thomas Quick stated that Nash, Weiss will expand its issue roster from 2,500 to over 3,500 or 4,000.
Leslie Quick III, head of Quick & Reilly's U.S. Clearing Corp subsidiary, described the Nasdaq market maker business as a fourth leg for the company.
Quick & Reilly is known as a retail broker and is also involved in backroom processing of Wall Street trading.
Quick & Reilly owns JCC Specialist Corp, the second largest market-maker on the New York Stock Exchange.
The acquisition of Nash, Weiss is expected to improve its capitalization and attractiveness to large institutional clients.
Nash, Weiss is currently on the retail side and is estimated to be the fifth or sixth largest market maker.
The fiscal year for Nash, Weiss ends on the last day of February.
Nash, Weiss will operate as a separate subsidiary in Jersey City, New Jersey, with no planned job cuts or restructurings.

Six top cruise-ship lines agreed to include all fees in the advertised price.
The agreement aims to simplify booking a cruise to be as straightforward as buying an airline ticket.
Add-on fees as high as $150 per person will be included in advertised prices.
Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth stated that there will be no more 'shock at the dock.'
The deals negotiated with Butterworth's staff cover lines operating out of Florida ports.
Florida has two million cruise passengers each year, representing about 60 percent of the North American market.
Two other lines, Princess and Holland America, are likely to adopt full-price policies.
Adam Goldstein, marketing chief for Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd, stated that combining port charges with cruise fare will not change the total price paid by consumers.
Cruise lines had previously added many operating costs to port fees, which passengers believed were government taxes.
Cruise lines, including Norwegian Cruise Line Ltd., Celebrity Cruises Inc., Dolphin Cruise Line, and Majesty Cruise Line, will pay Florida $295,000 as part of the agreements.

A walkout by American Airlines pilots would significantly impact tourist-dependent Caribbean islands.
Latin America's diversified economies would likely withstand a service stoppage by American Airlines.
Antonio Colorado is the executive director of the Caribbean/Latin America Action economic organization.
American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp., dominates U.S. service to the Caribbean and Latin America.
A halt by American Airlines would occur during the peak Caribbean tourist season.
The Caribbean has approximately 160,000 hotel rooms that are 90 percent occupied on average.
Losses from an American Airlines strike could total $15 million each day during the North American winter.
John Bell is the executive vice president of the Caribbean Hotel Association.
American Airlines and its American Eagle subsidiary account for up to 70 percent of flights between the Caribbean and North America.
About 7.2 million North Americans travel to the Caribbean each year.

Florida Panthers Holdings Inc's cash flow losses are narrowing due to strong professional hockey revenues and newly acquired leisure properties.
President Richard Evans stated that games are sold out and advertising and sponsorship revenue is better than expected.
The company is benefiting from hotel and Incredible Ice properties for part of the year.
Evans predicted a cash flow loss of about $3.1 million for the 12 months ending June 30.
Last November, the company forecasted EBITDA losses of about $15 million for the fiscal year through June.
Evans stated that EBITDA should turn positive and total $3.1 million or more in the fiscal year ending June 30, 1998.
EBITDA is expected to total $22.5 million in the following fiscal year when the Panthers hockey team will occupy a new arena.
The new arena, costing $185 million, will seat 19,000 during hockey games and is expected to increase ticket, souvenir, and food revenues.
Panthers Holdings has acquired two marina hotels in Fort Lauderdale and paid $15.5 million for Incredible Ice.
Evans mentioned that all acquisitions would be accretive to cash flow and were likely to be stock transactions.

The family of detained Chinese dissident Wang Dan has found a lawyer to defend him.
Wang Dan is a leader of the 1989 student protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Chinese court officials informed Wang's mother, Wang Lingyun, that she had one day to find a lawyer.
This notification indicated that Wang Dan had been indicted and a trial was imminent.
The lawyer has begun legal formalities at the court handling Wang's case.
Wang Dan has been in detention since May 1995.
It is unclear when the trial of Wang Dan will begin.
Chinese legal experts stated that lawyers are unnecessary in China unless a suspect has been charged.
Wang Dan's family is concerned about his situation after more than 16 months of detention.
Wang Dan could face a sentence of up to seven years in prison if convicted of counter-revolutionary incitement or subversion.

Nantian Electronic Information Group Corp. was founded in 1970.
The company was originally known as the Yunnan Electronic Equipment Factory.
The Cultural Revolution in China occurred from 1966 to 1976.
Nantian's fortunes improved after the economic reforms following Mao Zedong's death.
Nantian supplies computer systems to state banks in China.
In 1995, Nantian reported profits of 42.07 million yuan.
Nantian's sales increased from 510 million yuan in 1994 to 927 million yuan in 1995.
Nantian's sales were 100 million yuan in 1990.
Nantian aimed to increase revenues to 1.2 billion yuan in 1996.
Nantian began making computers in 1974.

China launched a scientific research satellite into orbit using a Long March 2D rocket from Gansu province.
The launch was reported by the Xinhua news agency.
The satellite is designed to spend 15 days in orbit before returning to Earth for retrieval.
This launch was the third successful mission of the Long March 2D rocket.
China's space industry has faced several setbacks in recent years, leading to increased insurance premiums for commercial launches.
In August, a domestic communications satellite launched on a Long March 3 rocket failed to reach its proper orbit.
In February, a Long March 3B rocket carrying an Intelsat satellite exploded shortly after lift-off, resulting in six deaths and 57 injuries.
Chinese officials attributed the explosion to a failure of the rocket's inertia platform.
In January 1995, a Long March 2E rocket explosion killed a family of six and destroyed the Apstar 2 satellite.
China maintains a high success rate for its Long March rocket series, with only a few failures among 43 launches.

China's economy grew by 9.6 percent in the first nine months of 1996.
Many urban family incomes are lagging behind despite economic growth, according to the State Statistical Bureau.
Chinese industrial output increased and farmers were on track for record grain harvests.
Inflation was tamed to a year-on-year rate of 6.6 percent in the first three quarters of 1996.
Gross domestic product was 4.5675 trillion yuan ($550.3 billion) between January and September 1996.
China's GDP grew by 10.2 percent in 1995.
The average income for urban Chinese rose to 3,249 yuan ($391) between January and September 1996, a year-on-year increase of 3.4 percent.
A survey revealed that the incomes per family member of around 40 percent of households had declined.
Some income decline was attributed to the birth of children or the retirement of aging family members.
China's urban unemployment rate was 2.98 percent at the end of September 1996, with 5.3 million unemployed in cities.

A Beijing court sentenced dissident Wang Dan to 11 years in prison.
Wang Dan was convicted of plotting to subvert the government.
Wang Dan's family plans to appeal the verdict.
Wang Dan's father stated that Wang is innocent and received a heavy sentence.
Wang Dan expressed a desire to appeal and believes his actions were for China's democratisation.
Wang Dan was also deprived of his political rights for two years.
The Xinhua news agency reported that sufficient evidence was presented at the trial.
Wang Dan had faced a maximum penalty of death and a minimum 10-year prison term.
Wang Dan was a student leader during the 1989 pro-democracy protests in Beijing.
Human Rights in China criticized the verdict as a show trial that violated Chinese law and international standards.

China stated that the jailing of dissident Wang Dan for 11 years is an ordinary legal matter.
A Chinese court sentenced Wang Dan to 11 years in prison for plotting against the government.
The trial of Wang Dan was described by Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang as a legal procedure in accordance with the law.
Shen Guofang claimed that Wang Dan's case has no connection with human rights issues.
The Beijing Number One Intermediate People's Court stripped Wang Dan of his political rights for two additional years.
Chinese state media hailed Wang Dan's trial as a model of fairness.
International human rights activists condemned the verdict against Wang Dan.
Wang Dan had previously served four years in prison for his role in the 1989 pro-democracy protests.
U.S. officials expressed concern over Wang Dan's sentence and praised him as a voice for human rights.
Sino-U.S. relations have been strained by various issues, but both sides reported easing tensions in recent months.

A committee selected by China chose 340 members for the Selection Committee that will select the first chief executive of post-colonial Hong Kong.
The final appointment of the chief executive will be made in early December.
The Hong Kong Preparatory Committee was established by Beijing to oversee the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule on July 1 next year.
The Selection Committee will consist of 400 members, with the final selection meeting scheduled for December 11 in Hong Kong.
Chinese Vice-Premier Qian Qichen stated that the Selection Committee members have a historic mission and should not disappoint the nation or the people of Hong Kong.
Qian emphasized the need for the selected leader to maintain Hong Kong's stability and prosperity.
The Preparatory Committee selected the 340 members from a list of 409 candidates, primarily consisting of pro-China politicians, businessmen, and community leaders.
Of the 400 Selection Committee members, 26 seats are automatically allocated to delegates from China's National People's Congress.
The remaining 34 members will be appointed by local deputies of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference.
The Selection Committee will also establish a provisional legislature to replace the current elected Legislative Council on July 1, 1997.

China released dissident Chen Ziming on medical parole to seek medical treatment.
Chen Ziming was jailed for his role in the 1989 pro-democracy protests.
Chen arrived home from the Beijing Number Two Prison at around 10.30 pm.
Chen's mother, Wu Yongfen, stated that his wife went to meet him.
Chen was sentenced to 13 years in prison in 1991 for engaging in counter-revolutionary activities.
Beijing authorities identified Chen as a behind-the-scenes organizer of the Tiananmen Square demonstrations.
Chen won medical parole in 1994 as part of efforts to maintain China's Most Favoured Nation trade status with the U.S.
Human rights issues have been a point of tension in Sino-U.S. relations.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher is scheduled to visit Beijing this month.
Chen has been treated for cancer, hepatitis B, heart disease, and other ailments.

China commemorated the 130th anniversary of revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen's birth on Tuesday.
The People's Daily newspaper published an editorial emphasizing Sun Yat-sen's contributions to national unity.
President Jiang Zemin stated that Sun Yat-sen advocated for the safeguarding of China's sovereignty and unity.
The People's Daily claimed that Sun Yat-sen aimed for the return of Taiwan and the unification of China.
The editorial referenced historical Japanese occupation as a factor that separated Taiwan from mainland China.
Chinese state media issued tributes to Sun Yat-sen and urged Taiwan leaders to pursue reunification.
Sun Yat-sen led the 1911 revolution that overthrew China's imperial Qing dynasty and founded the Nationalist Party.
The Nationalist Party fled to Taiwan after losing a civil war against the communists in 1949.
The Communist Party claims to have continued Sun Yat-sen's revolutionary legacy after his death in 1925.
Taipei's Nationalist leaders consider themselves the true heirs of Sun Yat-sen.

European record business executives praised China's crackdown on copyright piracy.
Executives believe Beijing is sincere in its desire to build a legitimate music industry.
European companies are eager to establish cooperative ventures with local firms in China.
EMI Europe President Rupert Perry stated that the Chinese market has enormous potential.
China is making progress in its crackdown on piracy, according to Perry.
Beijing vowed to clamp down on piracy in a June agreement with the United States.
Analysts have expressed doubt about China's commitment to eliminate piracy.
Music executives were encouraged by discussions with Chinese copyright and publishing officials.
The Chinese music market has the potential to grow ten-fold in the coming years.
Music imports into China are currently negligible, while pirate sales are estimated at $170 million a year.

China has launched an ideological campaign against dissent in Tibet.
The campaign targets pro-independence monks and nuns and seeks tighter controls on religion in Tibet.
The official Tibet Daily stated that building 'spiritual civilisation' is strategically important for the region's future.
The ideological campaign aims to reduce the role of religion in Tibet and diminish the influence of the Dalai Lama.
Tibet's communist leadership stated that monks and nuns involved in separatist activities will be dealt with according to the law.
The Tibet Daily reported that activities using religion to threaten public health will be suppressed.
China has attempted to eliminate pro-independence monks and nuns, blaming them for anti-Beijing campaigns.
A Tibetan nun had her prison sentence increased to 18 years for opposing Beijing's choice for the reincarnation of the 10th Panchen Lama.
Beijing has designated a six-year-old boy as the reincarnation of the 10th Panchen Lama, while the Dalai Lama has named another boy as the 11th Panchen Lama.
Local government approval is required for the identification of reincarnations, organization of religious activities, and construction of religious sites in Tibet.

Authorities in Anhui province, China, have ordered three pro-democracy activists to stand trial on charges of counter-revolutionary propaganda and incitement.
The Hefei Intermediate People's Court was scheduled to try dissidents Shen Liangqing, Ma Lianggang, and Huang Xiuming.
Human Rights in China, a New York-based watchdog, reported on the trial.
A court official in Hefei declined to comment on the case, citing that it involved matters not made public.
The trial is part of a state crackdown on dissent in China, where many pro-democracy figures have been imprisoned or detained.
The likely outcome of the trial is seen as predetermined, with the three activists having been detained previously for their involvement in a pro-democracy campaign in 1989.
Shen Liangqing, Ma Lianggang, and Huang Xiuming are all unemployed, with Shen having been a government official, Huang a company manager, and Ma a student.
The evidence against the three activists is based on articles they wrote and distributed in 1991, for which they had already been detained for over a year.
Human Rights in Asia reported that observers were denied access to the trial, despite it being officially open.
China dismisses criticism of its human rights record as interference in its internal affairs.

DirecTV will reduce the price of its entry-level receiver dish to $199 on Monday.
The current cheapest dish offered by DirecTV costs $499, with models available up to $900.
The price cuts are associated with a package of basic programming service costing around $360 a year.
AT&T Corp has a 2.5 percent stake in DirecTV and markets the service directly.
AT&T will not change the price of its own package, which offers the dish for $199 to True Rewards program members.
True Rewards program members must use loyalty points to cover the cost of the service.
The dishes are manufactured by RCA, a subsidiary of Thomson Consumer Electronic Corp.
AT&T is expected to reduce the cost of programming for True Rewards members to $155 a year from $360.
DirecTV is the largest U.S. direct satellite service with 1.7 million subscribers, growing at 20-30 percent annually.
PrimeStar is the second largest satellite service with 1.35 million subscribers, owned by Tele-Communications Inc.

Sprint Corp announced that it has deprioritized its local telephone ventures with cable television companies.
Arthur Krause, Sprint's chief financial officer, stated that there are more immediate opportunities in reselling existing local telephone service.
Sprint's cable partners include Tele-Communications Inc, Comcast Corp, and Cox Communications Inc, which collectively reach 30 million households.
The original plan was to offer bundled local, long distance, and wireless telephone services with cable TV on a single bill across the United States.
Krause mentioned that faster legislative action from the Federal Communications Commission has created opportunities for earlier interconnection deals with incumbent local telephone companies.
Some analysts believe there are technical and strategic difficulties that have led to local services being arranged as separate ventures instead of one common branded service.
Krause predicted that Sprint's first resale deal would occur before any local service offerings in partnership with cable TV companies.
Sprint can only reach 11 million of the 100 million U.S. homes through its own local telephone service unit.
Sprint's third quarter earnings pleased analysts, but concerns remain regarding its ambitious plans, including the Sprint PCS wireless venture.
Krause suggested that the market should view Sprint as two separate companies: its core operations and its new ventures.

GTE Corp. reported a 9 percent increase in earnings for the third quarter.
The increase in earnings was attributed to strong demand for new phone lines.
GTE's earnings results were in line with expectations.
GTE's stock price increased following the earnings report and a favorable court ruling.
A three-judge appeals court panel in St. Louis suspended key parts of federal rules aimed at fostering competition in local phone markets.
The judges expressed doubts about the Federal Communication Commission's authority to impose pricing policies.
The FCC rules would require local carriers to lease phone lines to competitors at discounts of up to 25 percent.
The appellate panel has put the new FCC rules on hold while considering a court challenge.
GTE led the challenge against the FCC rules, supported by some Baby Bells and state regulators.
GTE's net income for the quarter ended September 30 was $756 million, or 78 cents per share.

AT&T Corp operates in the $75 billion long distance telephone market.
AT&T has not shown improvement in earnings performance.
Analysts believe AT&T will face new competition from regional Bells.
Bette Massick from Bear Stearns stated there is no positive medium-term outlook for AT&T.
AT&T's third quarter earnings were in line with analysts' estimates.
AT&T reported a 12 percent decline in earnings per share from $0.96 to $0.84 compared to the previous year.
Increased competition and higher marketing expenses have negatively impacted AT&T's long distance business.
Simon Flannery from J.P. Morgan does not expect earnings improvement for AT&T in the near future.
AT&T has a higher proportion of revenues from the consumer long distance market compared to MCI Communications Corp and Sprint Corp.
GTE Corp and Southern New England Telecommunications Corp are entering the long distance market.

WorldCom Inc. will acquire MFS Communications Co. Inc. in a stock swap worth about $14 billion.
The combined company will be called MFS WorldCom.
MFS WorldCom will provide a full range of local, long distance, Internet, and international services over a fiber optic network.
The merged company will have annualized revenue of about $5.4 billion and more than 500,000 business customers in North America, Europe, and Asia.
MFS WorldCom will have a fiber optic network with 25,000 miles of fiber in service or under construction in major metropolitan areas in the United States.
Bernard J. Ebbers is the president and CEO of WorldCom.
The merger was unanimously approved by both companies' boards.
Each share of MFS common stock will be exchanged for 2.1 shares of WorldCom common stock.
MFS' stock rose 41 percent a year since it went public three years ago.
WorldCom's stock fell $3.75 to $22.625 on Nasdaq after the merger announcement.

AT&T Corp. appointed John Walter as its new president and chief operating officer.
John Walter is the chairman of R.R. Donnelley and Sons.
Walter was unanimously elected to his new positions effective November 1.
Robert Allen is the current chairman of AT&T.
Allen expressed confidence in Walter's leadership qualities for AT&T's success.
Walter stated he is confident in his ability to advance AT&T.
Walter emphasized the importance of having an appropriate cost base for competition.
Industry analysts were surprised by AT&T's choice of Walter as president.
AT&T stock closed at $37.875, down $1.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
AT&T shares have fallen 16 percent this year, adjusted for the spin-off of Lucent Technologies Inc.

WorldCom Inc completed a $14 billion takeover of MFS Communications Co Inc.
Some share analysts are excited about the combined company's strategy to offer end-to-end business services.
Concerns exist regarding the high price of MFS and the potential impact on WorldCom's earnings.
Analyst Guy Woodlief believes the move is strategically beneficial and positions WorldCom as a market leader.
Robert McNamara stated that the merger will provide unmatched service breadth in the telecommunications industry.
Kevin Moore upgraded his rating on WorldCom's stock to strong buy from neutral.
Analysts have not finalized earnings calculations due to MFS's recent acquisition of UUNET.
Bill Vogel described the price of the deal as a high multiple of 20 times trailing earnings.
The merger will result in significant new amortization charges for WorldCom.
Bernard Ebbers stated that the new company should be valued based on discounted cash flow rather than earnings.

CIDCO Inc reported that its sales in the second half of the year were similar to those in the first half.
Sales of caller ID equipment in California were worse than expected, according to Chief Financial Officer Scott McDonald.
McDonald stated that the company's predictions made in July were accurate, but the situation in California is worse than anticipated.
McDonald expressed comfort with analysts' current estimates for 1996, despite a downward revision after the July statement.
In July, CIDCO Inc indicated it was unlikely to meet analysts' sales forecasts for the second half of the year.
The company's lower sales expectations were attributed to weakness in California, uneven sales through Ameritech Corp, and delays in new products.
Caller ID services have gained popularity in the United States, especially after federal approval for long-distance caller ID.
Regulators in California had concerns about caller ID privacy and only approved Pacific Telesis Group's service launch in July 1996.
McDonald noted that negative publicity regarding privacy has hindered sales of caller ID in California.
Sales of caller ID by Ameritech have been inconsistent due to management changes and fluctuating publicity for its service.

MCI Communications Corp. is the second-largest long distance provider in the United States.
MCI is in talks with British Telecommunications Plc regarding a possible merger.
British Telecommunications Plc holds a 20 percent stake in MCI.
An MCI spokesman stated that the talks are expected to conclude over the weekend, but there are no guarantees of an agreement.
Industry analysts believe that a merger between MCI and British Telecom would be beneficial in the competitive U.S. long distance phone industry.
Allen Sinai, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Global Economic Advisors, commented that horizontal mergers make sense in competitive businesses.
MCI's stock was halted for trading at $27.25, having increased by $1.875 on Nasdaq.
MCI's stock price rose to $30.625 after reports of the merger talks.
CNBC reported that Lazard Freres and Morgan Stanley are working on the potential merger deal, which could be valued at over $22 billion.
Kevin Haggerty, senior vice president at Fidelity Investments, expressed that British Telecom is a strong company and that synergy exists between the two companies.

MCI Communications Corp announced a $20 billion merger with British Telecommunications Plc.
The merger is expected to strengthen the combined company in international calling, consulting, and U.S. local calling.
MCI Chief Financial Officer Doug Maine stated that the merger would enable them to compete with any telecommunications company globally.
Maine mentioned that combining MCI's Systemhouse with BT's Syntegra would enhance their consulting and systems integration capabilities.
Analysts believe MCI can provide significant consulting advantages to BT.
Danny Briere from Telechoice commented that BT is struggling in U.K. systems integration.
Maine predicted the merger could expedite the end of the international settlements system, which affects international call rates.
The international settlements system is facing challenges due to market liberalization in countries like Germany.
Analysts suggest that the opening of the international market will lead to lower calling rates for customers.
Maine highlighted the potential profitability in the $90 billion U.S. local market, particularly through MCI Metro.

The merger of MCI Communications Corp. and British Telecommunications Plc is valued at $20 billion.
The new company formed from the merger is named Concert.
Concert will have a market value of $54 billion.
MCI is the second largest long distance company in the U.S. with about 20 percent of the market.
Industry analysts predict that the merger will lead to more mega-mergers among U.S. carriers.
Analyst Guy Woodlief noted that there have been four deals over $10 billion since April.
The merger will require regional Bells, GTE Corp., AT&T Corp., and Sprint Corp. to reassess their market strategies.
Concert plans to enter the $90 billion local calling market through its MCI Metro venture and resale of regional Bell circuits.
Analyst Julie Kennedy stated that the merger increases competition in the telecommunications industry.
Analyst David Goodtree mentioned that WorldCom Inc. is still available for acquisition.

British Telecom and MCI Communications announced a $20 billion merger.
The merger is the largest cross-border takeover deal in history.
The merged company will be called Concert Plc.
Concert Plc will be the world's second-largest telecommunications group by market capitalization.
Concert Plc is valued at $54 billion based on stock prices from the previous Friday.
Concert Plc is comparable in value to AT&T Corp., MCI's main competitor in the U.S. market.
The merger is expected to provide better service and lower international calling charges for customers.
Businesses will benefit from a company that can support them globally.
Analysts predict faster earnings growth for shareholders due to the merger.
The deal values MCI at a total of $25.2 billion.

Excel Communications Inc expects record earnings and sales growth for the third quarter and the year.
Jack McLaine is the chief financial officer of Excel Communications Inc.
Excel plans to offer Internet access, home security monitoring, video service, local telephone services, and wireless telephone.
Excel reported a 350 percent rise in earnings per share in the second quarter of 1996 to $0.36 from $0.08 a year earlier.
Excel is currently covered by only one analyst, so no consensus of expectations is available.
Excel does not own any phone lines and uses WorldCom Inc's long distance network to reach customers.
WorldCom's planned merger with MFS Communications Co Inc will make entering new markets easier for Excel.
Excel is one of approximately 400 telephone service resellers that are gaining market share from industry leaders like AT&T Corp.
These resellers account for $12 billion of the $80 billion long distance market.
Excel had 220,710 sales representatives in the second quarter, an increase from 98,450 a year earlier.

Monsanto Co. is considering several options for its future, including splitting into two separate publicly traded corporations.
One of the proposed corporations would focus on life sciences and the other on chemicals.
Monsanto is based in St. Louis.
Other options include selling or merging its chemical businesses or restructuring them.
Chairman Robert Shapiro stated that the strategies and needs of the chemical and life sciences businesses have become quite different.
Monsanto's stock reached a new 52-week high of $42.75 following news of a possible sale or spin-off of the chemical business.
Analysts believe that Monsanto's life science businesses would have a higher valuation as a separate company.
Monsanto Chief Economist Nicholas Filippello indicated that no options for the chemical operations have been ruled out.
Monsanto's chemical businesses are affected by economic cycles and commodity raw material prices.
Analysts generally favor spinning off the chemical businesses as a separate company due to tax implications.

Archer Daniels Midland Co. agreed to plead guilty to two counts of federal charges of price fixing in the sale of agricultural products.
ADM will pay record fines totaling $100 million, subject to court approval.
The fines include $70 million for fixing prices for lysine and $30 million for citric acid.
The $100 million in fines is the largest ever in a criminal antitrust action.
The fines will have a minimal financial impact on ADM.
ADM has about $1.3 billion in cash and short-term securities and $1.1 billion in long-term securities.
The fate of two top ADM executives, Michael Andreas and Terrance Wilson, remains unclear regarding possible indictments.
The Justice Department's antitrust investigation into ADM is ongoing.
ADM's statement indicated the end of the government probe into alleged misconduct, including practices related to high-fructose corn syrup.
ADM previously settled civil cases for $25 million in the lysine case and $35 million for citric acid.

Archer Daniels Midland Co. pleaded guilty to price fixing.
Archer Daniels Midland Co. agreed to pay $100 million in fines.
Michael Andreas took a temporary leave from his position as vice chairman.
Terrance Wilson retired for medical reasons related to progressive heart disease.
Michael Andreas and Terrance Wilson are under investigation by the Justice Department.
Archer Daniels Midland Co. is based in Decatur, Illinois.
The $100 million fine is the largest penalty in a criminal antitrust case.
Federal authorities are still gathering evidence in the case involving Michael Andreas and Terrance Wilson.
Dwayne Andreas acknowledged the company's guilty pleas during a shareholder meeting.
The company did not officially notify shareholders of its guilty pleas.

McDonald's Corp. reported a 10 percent rise in net income.
Net income rose to $440 million from $400 million.
Earnings per share increased by 11 percent to 62 cents a share from 56 cents.
Earnings for the quarter were about 1 cent below analysts' expectations.
Operating earnings in the United States fell five percent in the third quarter.
Company revenues in the United States rose only one percent.
U.S. same store sales were negative for both the third quarter and nine-month period.
McDonald's operating earnings outside the United States grew 11 percent in the quarter.
Revenue outside the United States jumped 13 percent.
Growth in earnings was strongest in Hong Kong, England, Italy, Spain, Sweden, and Taiwan.

Nalco Chemical Co Chairman Ted Mooney is comfortable with analysts' estimates for fourth quarter earnings from continuing operations of $0.50 to $0.51 per fully diluted share.
The estimated earnings for the fourth quarter are up from $0.45 from continuing operations a year ago.
Nalco expects to increase earnings by a double-digit rate in the future.
Nalco reported third quarter earnings of $0.52 per fully diluted share from continuing operations, which is up 16 percent from $0.45 a year ago.
Nalco plans to continue making strategic acquisitions to increase its business.
Nalco agreed to acquire Nutmeg Technologies Inc, a Connecticut-based water treatment company with $9 million in annual sales.
Nalco's technology treats both water intake and water discharge.
Nalco provides process chemicals to various industries, including paper-making.
Nalco operates in about 20 countries and has a global presence with approximately $1.4 billion in annual sales.
Nalco's European division, which accounts for 25 percent of its foreign business, faces tough economic conditions.

Archer Daniels Midland Co. pleaded guilty to two counts of price fixing.
Dwayne Andreas is the 78-year-old chairman of Archer Daniels Midland Co.
Archer Daniels Midland Co. formed a four-member office of the chief executive.
The office of the chief executive includes Dwayne Andreas, James Randall, Charles Bayless, and G. Allen Andreas.
James Randall is 72 years old and is the president of Archer Daniels Midland Co.
Charles Bayless is 61 years old and is the president of ADM's processing division.
G. Allen Andreas is 53 years old and is a nephew of Dwayne Andreas.
Michael Andreas and Terrance Wilson left the company and are targets for possible criminal indictments.
New York City's deputy controller for pensions, Jon Lukomnik, supports the executive realignment but calls for more changes.
A shareholder proposal for a majority of independent directors on ADM's board was defeated but received 42 percent of the votes.

Agricultural biotechnology is experiencing legal disputes as companies file lawsuits against each other.

Rights to produce and sell genetically enhanced crops are at stake.
Biotech crops, including corn and cotton that produce their own pesticides, are beginning to be commercialized.
Many lawsuits in the biotech industry are expected to be settled out of court.
Bonnie Wittenburg is an analyst at Dain Bosworth.
Timothy Martin is a spokesman for Pioneer Hi-Bred International Inc.
Pioneer Hi-Bred International Inc. has been sued for alleged patent infringement by DeKalb Genetics Corp.
Pioneer claims it has a U.S. patent pending that could supersede DeKalb's claims.

Mark Whitacre, a former executive of Archer Daniels Midland Co. (ADM), filed a lawsuit against ADM seeking back wages and punitive damages.
Whitacre acted as an informant in an antitrust case against ADM.
In his lawsuit, Whitacre denied ADM's charges that he stole $9.0 million from the company.

ADM pleaded guilty to two counts of price fixing related to lysine and citric acid and agreed to pay $100 million in fines.
Whitacre seeks a judgment against ADM of more than $50,000 and punitive damages of more than $50,000.

Whitacre claims lost wages from August 1995, when he was fired, until October 1995, when he was hired by Biomar International Inc.
Whitacre earned $320,000 a year at ADM plus stock options.
Whitacre alleges that ADM denied him the right to exercise stock options, defamed his character, and caused him mental and emotional distress.

A higher minimum wage was signed into law on Tuesday.
The minimum wage will increase by 90 cents an hour to $5.15 next year.
The increase may lead to higher prices for fast-food items, according to some restaurant chains.
Many fast-food chains already pay workers above the federally mandated minimum wage.

Denny Lynch is the spokesman for Wendy's International Inc.
President Clinton signed the first minimum wage increase in five years.
The White House estimates that the new law will raise wages for about 10 million American workers.
Most small businesses opposed the minimum wage increase, fearing it would reduce hiring.
Some economists believe the negative effects of the wage increase will be minimal.

Western Resources Inc stated that its alliance with ONEOK Inc could increase its earnings by $0.10 to $0.15 per share in the first full year of operations.
David Wittig, president of Western Resources, mentioned this potential earnings improvement in a telephone interview.
The Western Resources-ONEOK alliance is expected to become effective in mid-1997, with calendar 1998 being the first full year of operation.

The alliance aligns with Western Resources' strategy to become a brand-name supplier of electricity and home-security products nationwide.
ONEOK has 735,000 gas customers, which presents a marketing opportunity for Western Resources' electricity and home-security businesses.
Western Resources is actively seeking acquisitions to expand its electricity and home-security businesses.

Conseco Inc plans to purchase Pioneer Financial Services Inc for $477 million.
This acquisition is Conseco's seventh announced acquisition in the year.

Conseco is a leading provider of supplemental health insurance, retirement annuities, and life insurance for consumers aged 40 and older.

Pioneer Financial Services Inc is a health and life insurance company based in Schaumburg, Illinois.

Conseco has completed 16 acquisitions involving a total of 29 insurance companies since 1982.
Pioneer shareholders will receive a fraction of a Conseco share worth $25 to $28 for each Pioneer share held.

Morton International Inc. is the maker of Morton Salt.
Morton International has gained a key European presence for two of its businesses due to planned acquisitions.
Morton International is likely to expand in Europe with further purchases.
Morton Chairman S. Jay Stewart stated that there are more opportunities in Europe and Asia than in the U.S. right now.
Morton plans to acquire Italian powder coatings company Pulverlac Spa and French salt company Compagnie des Salins du Midi et des Salines de l'Est.

Stewart noted good demand growth for powder coatings, which are applied to metal parts for protection and coloration.
The acquisition of Pulverlac will result in combined sales of more than $200 million for Morton's North American coatings business.
Morton's total sales for fiscal 1996 were $3.3 billion, including $1.6 billion in specialty chemicals sales.

Wang Xizhe is a Chinese dissident who reportedly fled to Hong Kong from Guangdong province.
Wang's escape occurred over the weekend, shortly after a colleague was sent to a labor camp by Chinese authorities.
Human rights activists stated that Wang was expected to leave Hong Kong soon, possibly for the United States.
The U.S. Consulate did not confirm or deny whether Wang had requested asylum.

Liu Gang fled to the United States from Hong Kong in May after facing police harassment.
