Shen Guofang noted that differences in U.S. and Chinese views on human rights could be resolved through talks.
Shen Guofang warned that a confrontational approach would undermine the basis for dialogue.
U.S. Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright criticized China's human rights record during her Senate confirmation hearing.
Albright mentioned the possibility of co-sponsoring a resolution against China's human rights record at the United Nations Human Rights Commission.
Last April, China successfully blocked a U.S.-backed resolution expressing concern over its human rights violations.

China handed over the remains of U.S. airmen to U.S. military officers on Wednesday.
The airmen died 52 years ago when their bomber crashed in southwestern China during World War Two.
Alan Liotta is the deputy director of the MIA/POW office under the Department of Defence.
A senior Chinese military officer handed over two wooden chests containing remains and a third filled with personal effects.
Four U.S. soldiers in full military uniform took the boxes and placed a folded U.S. flag on each of the three boxes.
A formal ceremony is scheduled to be held in Beijing on Friday.
Liang Ziwei is the director of foreign affairs in the town of Xingan.
A six-man forensic team from the U.S. Department of Defence inspected the crash site on Maoer mountain.
The crash occurred on August 31, 1944, and the human remains will be taken back to the United States for identification.
Local residents discovered the crash site last October while searching for wild herbs.

China announced that Guatemala has pledged not to support Taiwan's bid to enter the United Nations.
Guatemala agreed to abide by a U.N. resolution stating there is only one China and that Beijing is the sole legal representative of China.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang stated that Guatemala pledged to respect the provisions of Resolution 2758 of the General Assembly.
According to Resolution 2758, Guatemala cannot support Taiwan's actions to regain entry to the United Nations.
The U.N. Security Council approved the dispatch of 155 U.N. military observers to monitor peace accords in Guatemala.
China had previously vetoed a similar resolution on January 10 due to Guatemala's ties to Taiwan.
The 14 other Security Council members supported sending peacekeepers to Guatemala, but China's veto prevented the mission.
China and Guatemala held several rounds of negotiations at the United Nations to resolve the impasse regarding Taiwan.
Guatemala recognized the gravity and sensitivity of the Taiwan issue and showed a willingness to take a positive approach.
Guatemala is one of about 30 nations that officially recognize Taipei instead of Beijing.

China issued an anti-corruption communique to the Communist Party on Thursday.
The communique warned party members not to exploit official power for personal profit.
The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection issued the communique.
The communique stated that officials and the 57 million party members should not hold political views that differ from the party line.
The People's Daily published the communique.
The communique acknowledged past successes in battling graft in 1996 but stated that further efforts were needed this year.
The communique noted that corruption still exists and is spreading in some areas.
The communique reminded government officials that they are forbidden from using their political clout for personal gain.
Beijing would punish officials in loss-making state-owned firms for misusing company funds.
Disciplinary authorities punished more than 116,000 officials for exploiting their positions for personal gain in 1996.

British telecoms regulator OFTEL proposed to reduce regulatory demands on Mercury Communications.
Mercury Communications is part of the Cable & Wireless Group.
OFTEL's proposal includes a simplified licence for Mercury covering domestic and international operations.
OFTEL plans to remove several obligations on Mercury due to its non-dominant position in the domestic market.
Mercury Communications holds 11.5 percent of the UK's domestic telecommunications market.
British Telecommunications Plc (BT) holds an 80 percent share of the UK's domestic telecommunications market.
A Mercury official stated that the changes would provide more flexibility on pricing.
OFTEL indicated that competition in the international market may lead to further deregulation.
OFTEL's proposals include replacing Mercury's existing service obligation with standard obligations for non-dominant operators.
International service obligations for Mercury will remain unchanged.

Lloyd Thompson Group and JIB Group are merging in a deal worth 300 million pounds ($496.4 million).
Ken Carter is the chief executive of Lloyd Thompson Group.
The merger is intended to create an international firm focused on profitable growth businesses.
The primary motivation for the merger is business enhancements rather than cost savings.
Ken Carter will become the chief executive of the new group, which will be renamed Jardine Lloyd Thompson Group Plc.
The merger occurs amid declining insurance rates and revenues for brokers.
Increasing competitive pressures are prompting brokers to consider mergers to cut costs and achieve economies of scale.
Under the merger terms, JIB shareholders will receive four new Lloyd Thompson shares for every five JIB shares held.
Jardine Matheson Holdings, which has a 60 percent stake in JIB, supports the merger.
The stock market reacted positively, with JIB shares rising 20-1/2p and Lloyd Thompson shares rising 1-1/2p.

Scottish Amicable announced plans to shed its mutual status in preparation for a 1.0 billion pounds flotation on the London stock market in three to five years.
Scottish Amicable is based in Stirling, Scotland.
The group plans to use capital raised from the flotation to increase its share of the life and pensions market.
Policyholders will receive an initial special bonus of 75 million pounds after demutualising on May 1 this year.
An individual with a 25-year policy maturing this April will receive 1,503 pounds.
A larger payout of at least 200 million pounds is expected upon flotation.
Scottish Amicable's move to seek a flotation follows plans announced last year by Norwich Union.
Chairman Sandy Stewart stated that the group intends to maintain its independence.
Industry analysts believe that policyholders will benefit more by remaining invested in the company rather than selling now.
Scottish Amicable believes the market is entering a growth phase and needs capital and a flexible structure to capitalize on opportunities.

Scottish Amicable plans to float on the stock market.
Abbey National launched a bid for Scottish Amicable, valuing it at up to 1.4 billion pounds.
The bid includes a minimum payout of 400 million pounds to policyholders in cash or Abbey shares.
Scottish Amicable criticized the bid as vague and inadequate.
Scottish Amicable intends to proceed with plans to drop its mutual status and float the group over the next three to five years.
The plans will be detailed in a circular within the next two weeks.
1.1 million policyholders will receive up to 1,500 pounds under the plans.
12 directors of Scottish Amicable stand to share around 14 million pounds.
Scottish Amicable chairman Sandy Stewart indicated interest from other parties had been received.
Stewart stated that Abbey National's offer had not been dismissed and that policyholder interests are a priority.

The head of one of Lloyd's of London's largest corporate investors expects the number of traditional Names at Lloyd's of London to fall to between 4,000 and 5,000.
John Stace is the chief executive of Angerstein Underwriting Investment Trust.
Stace told Reuters that the number of members' agencies looking after Names' interests is likely to drop to four or five.
Angerstein owns Stace Barr, which represents 933 Names.
Stace aims for Stace Barr to remain one of the top surviving members' agencies with around 1,000 Names.
James Illingworth is the operations director at Angerstein.
Illingworth stated that Lloyd's has over 12,000 remaining Names who may resign, convert to limited liability, or remain as unlimited liability backers.
Around half of the remaining Names are expected to resign or convert to limited liability schemes in the coming years.
Conversion schemes for limited liability have been small and unsuitable for mass conversion.
Illingworth commented that the Scottish limited liability Partnership has not been successful for mass conversion.

Scottish Amicable adviser SBC Warburg aims to finalize the first stage of the sale of the life assurance group by signing confidentiality agreements with potential bidders by the weekend.
Three companies, Abbey National, Prudential Corp, and Australian Mutual Provident (AMP), have signed confidentiality agreements regarding the sale of ScotAm.
The confidentiality agreements provide bidders with detailed financial information about ScotAm to help them finalize their offers.
The agreements prevent bidders from publicly disclosing details of their offers and require them to accept the ScotAm board's decision as final.
Several other companies have expressed interest in ScotAm but have not yet signed the confidentiality agreements.
Belgian-Dutch insurer Fortis is rumored to have ruled itself out of the auction process but has not commented on the matter.
Dutch group Aegon has not yet made a bid for ScotAm.
The sale process is expected to take between four and six weeks before the ScotAm board recommends a final offer to policyholders.
ScotAm announced earlier this month that it was seeking definitive offers from parties interested in acquiring it.
Abbey National announced a potential offer of up to 1.4 billion pounds for ScotAm at the end of January.

Scottish Amicable requested firm offers for the company to be submitted by the end of February.
More potential bidders have joined the auction for Scottish Amicable.
Three companies, Abbey National, Prudential Corp, and Australian Mutual Provident (AMP), have signed confidentiality agreements to access ScotAm's financial information.
A source indicated that the number of potential bidders is more than three.
Scottish Amicable will ask all interested parties to submit firm offers by February 28.
A spokesman for Scottish Amicable declined to comment on the number or identity of companies that signed confidentiality agreements.
Dutch insurance group Aegon is a potential bidder for Scottish Amicable.
Belgian-Dutch insurer Fortis has reportedly ruled out a bid for Scottish Amicable.
Lloyds TSB stated it is not interested in bidding for Scottish Amicable.
The Scotsman reported that AMP is considering moving its subsidiary London Life to Scotland if its bid for Scottish Amicable is successful.

Commercial Union (CU) reported a sharp fall in profits for 1996.
CU experienced a 64 million pound currency loss, which contributed to a near 13 percent fall in operating profits.
The operating profits for CU for the year were 444 million pounds.
U.S. weather-related losses amounted to 41 million pounds.
Severe competition in the general insurance market negatively impacted CU's profits.
The life business of CU, which accounts for around 44 percent of premiums, showed healthy growth after adjusting for currency effects.
CU intends to expand its life operations to leverage consistent profit streams and growth prospects.
Finance director Peter Foster stated that CU would consider acquisitions to stimulate growth.
CU reported that the strength of sterling masked significant profit rises in continental Europe.
The net asset value (NAV) of CU decreased to 545 pence at year-end 1996 from 582 pence a year earlier.

Liberty International Holdings may pursue acquisitions to develop its financial services interests.
Liberty International Holdings is 69 percent-owned by Liberty Life.
Liberty International Holdings has a strong balance sheet and is open to acquisitions.
Liberty has approximately 380 million pounds in cash on its balance sheet.
The size of any future acquisition by Liberty depends on the quality of the acquisition.
Liberty has a 72 percent stake in Capital Shopping Centres, Britain's fourth largest quoted property company.
Liberty launched a low-cost pension vehicle called PensionStore in January.
Liberty controls Portfolio Fund Management Limited, which has around 50 million pounds under management.
Liberty announced an alliance with British Telecom and Hermes to improve the British pension market.
Liberty reported a seven percent increase in pre-tax profits for 1996 to 100.4 million pounds.

British insurer General Accident PLC reported a fall in annual profits.
Operating profits decreased by 15 million pounds to 421 million pounds.
Weather-related losses increased by 30 million pounds, contributing to the profit decline.
A change to an average translation of overseas earnings added 10 million pounds to operating profits.
Profits were above market forecasts.
The dividend increased by 10.5 percent to 34.25 pence per share.
Net assets per share rose to 675 pence from 653 pence.
General Accident shares increased by 8.5 pence to 845.5 pence.
Chief executive Bob Scott described the market as increasingly competitive.
Scott stated the group aims to focus life operations in Britain and increase life earnings to cover dividends.

The head of the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) is Sir Andrew Large.
Sir Andrew Large criticized the slow progress in compensating victims of pensions mis-selling in Britain.
Large called for all parties to ensure a speedy conclusion to the compensation situation.
Angela Knight is a British Treasury minister.
Angela Knight urged the pensions industry to expedite payments to individuals affected by pension mis-selling in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
Knight stated that she was looking for rapid and decisive results from the pensions industry.
Large expressed determination to secure redress for those missold personal pensions.
Large emphasized that all parties, including the industry, occupational pension schemes, regulators, and the government, have a responsibility to conclude the review quickly.
As many as 1.5 million people in Britain may have been affected by misadvised personal pensions.
An industry review was launched in 1994, but only a small proportion of affected individuals have been compensated.

Scottish Amicable confirmed that three companies submitted final offers for the insurance group by last Friday's bid deadline.
The bidders are Abbey National plc, Prudential Corp plc, and Australian Mutual Provident (AMP).
The bidders will find out the outcome of their offers at the end of the month.
None of the bidders have made their offers public.
Scottish Amicable's board and advisers SBC Warburg will evaluate the bids privately.
Scottish Amicable agreed to publish offer details if requested by a bidder.
All three bidders have agreed to accept the board's decision at the end of March as final.
Two-thirds of the 1.1 million policyholders must approve the board's recommendation for ownership transfer.
An independent tribunal has been arranged to resolve disputes from the takeover process.
The interests of policyholders will be prioritized in the decision-making process.

Kvaerner ASA is a Norwegian engineering company.
Kvaerner ASA aims to increase its Asia Pacific portfolio in the coming years.
John Fletcher is the chairman and managing director of Kvaerner Corporate Development.
Kvaerner's turnover is expected to increase by about 10 percent in 1997, with 50 percent of that increase coming from Asia.
Total turnover for Kvaerner in 1996 was projected to be US$10 billion, with 35 percent generated from Asia.
In the early 1990s, Asia accounted for less than 10 percent of Kvaerner's annual turnover.
Kvaerner reported a 56 percent fall in pre-tax profit to 706 million crowns on a turnover of 22.94 billion crowns in its half-year results in August.
Kvaerner is Norway's second largest listed company and employs 60,000 people worldwide.
Kvaerner took over British conglomerate Trafalgar House in April and integrated its engineering and construction units.
Kvaerner's business is currently strong in India, Indonesia, Thailand, and China.

China has raised domestic prices on gasoil effective Friday.
Sinopec confirmed the ex-refinery price for diesel was raised to 1,990 yuan per tonne from 1,900 yuan.
This is the first price increase since the introduction of price ceilings on domestic refined products in May 1994.
A trader with Sinopec stated that if prices are not raised, coastal refineries cannot survive.
Refineries have been lobbying for a price increase due to soaring crude bills this year.
Chinese refiners have been holding back on crude oil imports in international markets this year.
Prompt prices of North Sea Brent are currently $24.20 per barrel.
Earlier this week, North Sea Brent prices hit a five-year high of $25.06 per barrel.
Asian benchmark Tapis crude is currently valued at $26.40 per barrel.
Chinese refineries have experienced a 110 yuan increase in domestic crude prices since January.

China held its largest and most expensive airshow, Airshow China '96, to boost its aerospace industry.
Liang Guangda is the vice-chairman of the organising committee of Airshow China '96.
The airshow aims to demonstrate the success of China's reform and improve understanding with global aeronautical communities.
The six-day airshow at Zhuhai airport in Guangdong province started on Tuesday and cost an estimated 350 million yuan ($42 million).
The event featured 300 domestic and foreign aircraft and parts producers, including Boeing, Airbus, and McDonnell Douglas.
China showcased its premier jet fighter, the China F-8II, and the Russian SU-27 fighter jet.
China displayed its Long March Number 2 space rocket at the airshow.
The airshow served as a venue for aviation companies to sign joint venture agreements.
Collins Avionics & Communications Division signed a deal with Shanghai Avionics Corp and Shanghai Broadcast Equipment Factory to develop a tracking system.
The new joint venture company is named Shanghai Rockwell Collins Navigation and Communications Equipment Co Ltd and is located in Pudong, Shanghai.

Pro-democracy demonstrators attempted to disrupt a meeting in Hong Kong to choose future leaders.
The meeting was convened by China and inaugurated by Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.
Protesters gathered outside the Hong Kong Convention Centre before dawn.
The Selection Committee consists of 400 members and is tasked with selecting the Chief Executive and 60 members of a new legislature.
About a dozen demonstrators entered the convention centre but were stopped by police.
Some demonstrators reached the sixth floor before being detained by police.
Eyewitnesses reported that Andrew To, Chan Kwok-leung, and Wong Chung-ki were among those detained.
Scuffles occurred outside the building, resulting in at least one policeman being slightly injured.
Pro-democracy activists criticized the selection process as undemocratic and refused to participate.
Demonstrators chanted slogans calling for a directly elected legislature and opposed the dissolution of the elected legislature.

Hong Kong's Legislative Council speaker, Andrew Wong, announced he is seeking a seat in the Provisional Legislature.
Andrew Wong previously denounced the Provisional Legislature during the 1995 elections.
Wong's decision to join 31 colleagues seeking seats in the Provisional Legislature may increase divisions within the Legislative Council.
Political commentator Chris Yeung stated that divisions within the Legislative Council will widen in the next six months.
Yeung warned that the normal operation of the Legislative Council could be significantly affected or paralyzed.
China plans to disband the current elected legislature and replace it with the Provisional Legislature when Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule in mid-1997.
The Selection Committee, assembled by China, is expected to choose the successor to Governor Chris Patten.
The Selection Committee will also name the 60-member Provisional Legislature on December 21.
Andrew Wong did not confirm his support for the Provisional Legislature but claimed he would remain an impartial leader.
Michael DeGolyer, an associate professor at Hong Kong's Baptist University, stated that having two lawmaking bodies could lead to confusion and disputes.

Emily Lau is a pro-democracy politician in Hong Kong.
Emily Lau was removed by police while protesting against China's methods of selecting a post-colonial leader.
Up to 40 pro-democracy activists clashed with riot police outside the Hong Kong Convention Centre.
A committee of 400 members chosen by Beijing voted for a chief executive to govern Hong Kong.
The vote for the chief executive occurred before the handover of Hong Kong from Britain to China on June 30.
A dozen activists protested by lying down on the road and were removed by police.
Witnesses reported that Emily Lau was among those carried away by police.
It was unclear if the activists were arrested.
John Wing-ling Tse, a legislator of the Democratic Party, expressed that it was a sad day for Hong Kong.
Protesters erected a 'tomb of democracy' outside the Hong Kong Convention Centre.

Tung Chee-hwa returned from a meeting with Chinese leaders in Beijing.
Tung Chee-hwa is the leader-in-waiting of Hong Kong.
Tung Chee-hwa pledged to shape his administration.
Tung Chee-hwa received reassurances from Beijing about Hong Kong's autonomy after the handover.
The handover of Hong Kong from Britain to China is scheduled for June 30.
Tung Chee-hwa's tasks include meeting the governor and chief secretary Anson Chan.
Tung Chee-hwa aims to form an advisory cabinet called the Executive Council.
A poll showed Tung Chee-hwa's popularity rating at 70.1 points after his selection.
Tung Chee-hwa stated he is not merely a yes-man for Beijing.
Tung Chee-hwa hinted at legal endorsement for a China-backed provisional legislature.

Tung Chee-hwa is the future leader of Hong Kong.
A Beijing-approved body will replace the existing elected legislature in mid-1997.
The first sitting of the new body will be held in China, likely in Shenzhen.
The new chamber will hold its first official session soon.
The 60-member provisional legislature was selected by a 400-member committee vetted by China.
The Democratic Party of Hong Kong opposes the provisional legislature.
The Democratic Party claims the provisional body is a travesty of democracy.
The colonial government will cooperate with Tung on the transfer of sovereignty but not with the provisional legislature.
Tung Chee-hwa urged civil servants to accept the reality of the provisional legislature.
Many people in Hong Kong are concerned about the future of stable government and the rule of law after the handover.

Liu Yu Yi is a celebrity painter in Hong Kong.
Liu Yu Yi's portrait subjects include leaders from Beijing.
Liu is creating an oil painting depicting over 200 famous personalities at a feast celebrating the handover of Hong Kong to China.
The painting features Deng Xiaoping as the central figure, flanked by Jiang Zemin, Li Peng, and Tung Chee-hwa.
Deng Xiaoping is recognized as the architect of the 'one country, two systems' formula for Hong Kong.
Liu Yu Yi gained fame in 1993 when he sold 'Liang Xiao' for HK$8.36 million.
He sold 'Song of the Goddess Nu Wa' for HK$8.88 million in 1994 and 'Gathering of Immortals' for HK$10.8 million in 1995.
Liu moved to Hong Kong in 1991 and has gained access to influential circles.
Liu has painted portraits of prominent Hong Kong business figures.
Hong Kong's wealthy individuals are collecting Chinese art and antiques in anticipation of the handover.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind met future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa for the first time since Tung was chosen.
Tung Chee-hwa is a shipping magnate appointed by Beijing in December.
Tung stated that London has not changed its position on aiding a provisional legislature that China plans to install.
Britain argues that the formation of the provisional legislature is illegal under the 1984 Sino-British handover treaty on Hong Kong.
Hong Kong will revert to China at midnight on June 30.
Rifkind's visit to Hong Kong was cut short for him to return to London for a key vote in Parliament.
The South China Morning Post criticized Rifkind for prioritizing domestic issues over Hong Kong's problems.
Britain is scheduled to hold a general election before May 22.
Tung Chee-hwa accused the Democracy Party of damaging Hong Kong's reputation by spreading negative predictions.
Tung described Hong Kong's economy as buoyant and its people as upbeat.

China's state refiner Sinopec is implementing measures to address diesel shortages.
Diesel prices in China have increased since late 1996.
Sinopec's headquarters in Beijing is urging its refineries to increase diesel production from crude oil.
The current gasoline to diesel production ratio at China's refineries is 1:1.3.
Sinopec aims to adjust the gasoline to diesel production ratio to 1:1.4.
The adjustment in production ratio will take several months to implement.
Diesel import quotas were not fully utilized in 1996 due to high international prices.
China may need to import more diesel this year due to supply chain shortages.
Domestic diesel prices were raised from 1,900 yuan per tonne in May 1994 to 2,190 yuan per tonne in December 1996.
Some coastal regions in China have healthy storage levels of diesel, while shortages are reported in some inland provinces.

Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten stated that the territory's economic prosperity is due to its increasingly democratic government.
Patten addressed central bankers and aimed his remarks at official audiences in China.
He claimed that Hong Kong people have developed the institutions and values of a civil society.
Patten noted that the government has welcomed wider public participation in governance.
He highlighted China's commitment to allow the development of democracy in Hong Kong as per the Sino-British accords.
Hong Kong has a population of 6.4 million people and is located on the south China coast.
The territory will revert to China after more than 150 years as a British colony under a 1984 Sino-British treaty.
The Joint Declaration guarantees Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy and freewheeling capitalism for 50 years after the handover.
Hong Kong is the eighth largest trading economy and has foreign reserves of US$66 billion.
China has attempted to scrap Hong Kong's elected legislature and reverse democratic reforms.

Thousands of people in Hong Kong participated in a parade to celebrate the 100-day countdown to the resumption of Chinese rule.
The event took place under rainy weather on a Sunday.
More than 7,000 participants from over 100 pro-Beijing community organizations joined the parade.
The parade featured traditional Chinese symbols such as dragons, lions, and unicorns.
Hong Kong will become a Special Administrative Region (SAR) governed by its own Chief Executive after the handover.
Raymond Wu, the chief organizer, stated that the event marks a grand occasion for the return to China.
Victoria Park, where the rally gathered, is named after Queen Victoria.
The present Queen's image is being removed from coins and stamps in Hong Kong.
Victoria Park will be renamed Central Park after the handover.
Some demonstrators protested against China's military actions during the Tiananmen Square incident in 1989.

Netscape Communications Corp. unveiled a line of low-cost software for corporate networks.
Netscape plans to embrace Microsoft Corp.'s products as part of its strategy in the corporate software market.
Microsoft is competing with Netscape to gain market share in Internet and intranet software.
Netscape holds approximately 80 percent of the Internet browser software market with its Navigator software.
Netscape has between 60 percent to 70 percent of the intranet market.
A corporate intranet is a computer network designed around Internet technology and open standards.
Netscape announced several new products for the corporate market.
Marc Andreessen is the co-founder and senior vice president of technology at Netscape.
Netscape stock decreased by 62.5 cents to $44.25, while Microsoft stock increased by $2.25 to $138.875.
Netscape introduced a new software product called Netscape Communicator, which combines several components.

International Business Machines Corp is expected to report third quarter earnings on Monday.
Analysts do not expect big upside surprises for IBM's earnings.
IBM's new mainframes did not ship in large volumes until the end of the quarter.
First Call estimates IBM's earnings to be in the range of $2.17 to $2.60 a share.
The consensus estimate for IBM's earnings is $2.43 a share.
IBM's earnings last year were $2.30 a share.
IBM is expected to experience a negative impact from currency moves.
The negative impact from currency moves is expected to be less than in the second quarter.

Ross Cooley, a top executive at Compaq Computer Corp., is leaving the company to join an Internet startup called pcOrder.com.
Cooley was in charge of Compaq's $7 billion North American computer business.
At pcOrder.com, Cooley will serve as chairman and chief executive officer with a salary of $1 a year plus stock options.
Cooley's move to a technology startup is similar to the departure of Alex Mandl from AT&T earlier this year.
Cooley's departure is expected to provide credibility to pcOrder.com, which operates an online marketplace for personal computers and related equipment.
Cooley's retirement had been rumored in the industry for several months.
James Schraith will replace Cooley at Compaq.
Eckhard Pfeiffer, president and CEO of Compaq, stated that Cooley's retirement had been discussed for some time.
Compaq has created a new sales infrastructure and hired Richard Snyder from Dell Computer Corp. as general manager of worldwide sales.
All heads of Compaq's five geographical sales regions will now report to Snyder instead of Pfeiffer.

Bill Gates and Larry Ellison are in a competitive dispute over the network computer.
Larry Ellison is the Chairman of Oracle Corp.
Ellison promotes a low-cost, diskless PC for accessing corporate networks and the Internet.
Ellison's vision has gained attention from industry professionals who are concerned about Microsoft's Windows operating systems and Intel's processors.
Sun Microsystems Inc. is collaborating with Oracle on the network computer and plans to introduce the JavaStation.
Microsoft, led by Bill Gates, announced its own low-cost PC solution in response to Oracle and Sun's initiatives.
Eileen O'Brien, an analyst at International Data Corp., noted that Microsoft is reacting to the attention Oracle and Sun are receiving.
Many industry analysts found Microsoft's new PC design underwhelming.
Microsoft's new PC design includes an Intel processor, memory, a hard disk drive, and Windows operating systems.
Some analysts estimate that the total cost of owning a PC can range from $6,000 to $12,000 annually.

America Online Inc. reported a first quarter net loss of $353.7 million.
The loss was attributed to restructuring charges related to changes in accounting practices.
The loss amounted to $3.80 per share for the quarter ending September 30.
AOL included a write-off of $385.2 million in marketing costs in its financial report.
AOL announced a flat-rate pricing plan of $19.95 a month and a corporate realignment into three business units.
AOL's total revenues increased by 77 percent, rising to $349.9 million from $197.9 million a year ago.
Other revenues from advertising and electronic commerce reached a record of $38.8 million.
AOL reported that eight advertisers committed to spend $1 million or more this fiscal year.
Before the accounting charge, AOL earned $19 million, or 17 cents per share.
AOL experienced a one-day service outage in August that analysts estimated cost about $6.5 million in lost revenues.

EchoStar Communications Corp. is a company in the direct broadcast satellite television business.
EchoStar announced a price cut for satellite dishes this month.
Thomson, the U.S. unit of France's Thomson-CS, matched EchoStar's new price of $199 for a satellite dish.
Thomson executives believe the new price will impact the industry and increase sales.
Thomson's price cut reduced the cost of the RCA brand digital satellite system by up to $200 per unit.
A $200 cash back offer from DirecTV and U.S. Satellite Broadcasting Co. reduced the total price to $199 for consumers who pre-pay for one year of programming.
Programming costs on DirecTV range from $29.95 per month for 70 channels to $44.95 per month for 175 channels.
The lower price may hinder new entrants from entering the market profitably.
Other companies, including Uniden America Corp., Toshiba America Consumer Products Inc., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd., and Matsushita Electric Corp of America, plan to introduce new DSS systems later this year.
Thomson holds an estimated 45 percent of the total digital satellite dish market, which was 3.4 million units worldwide at the end of July.

International Business Machines Corp. agreed to buy Edmark Corp. for $80 million in cash.
The acquisition aims to focus IBM's consumer business on learning at home.
IBM will launch a tender offer for all of Edmark at $15.50 a share.
Edmark Corp. is based in Redmond, Wash., and publishes children's education software.
Edmark's software targets students in kindergarten through 12th grade.
Analysts believe the acquisition will strengthen IBM's marketing of personal computers and software to consumers.
Richard Zwetchkenbaum, director of consumer research at International Data Corp., commented on the value of Edmark's properties.
Edmark's titles, including the Mighty Math Series and Thinkin' Things Series, are gaining popularity.
IBM's consumer software titles have had mixed results in the market.
The acquisition will provide Edmark access to IBM's worldwide distribution network.

America Online Inc. announced a major expansion of its online network.
AOL plans to spend $250 million through the end of its fiscal year in June to build capacity and improve service.
AOL is upgrading its network to meet increased demand from its new pricing and marketing initiatives.
As of Sunday, AOL began offering a new flat-rate pricing plan to its 7 million subscribers.
AOL will double its system hardware over the next six months.
AOL has doubled its electronic mail capacity and its capability to connect users to the Internet's World Wide Web since September.
AOL added tens of thousands of new modems to AOLnet since July 1.
AOL's expansion will accelerate through the spring with tens of thousands of new modems being installed monthly.
AOL sent postcards to its members about the new pricing plan of $19.95 a month for unlimited service.
AOL's subscriber growth is rebounding, with 275,000 new members added in October.

Genuity Inc., a subsidiary of Bechtel Corp., will unveil a new Internet gateway on Tuesday.
The new gateway is known as a network access point and is intended to address congestion on the Internet.
Genuity Inc. will announce the network access point and a new service called Hopscotch at the Internet World trade show in New York.
There are currently about eight major network access points that manage most of the world's Internet traffic.
Six major network access points are located in the United States: San Jose, Washington, Chicago, Los Angeles, Palo Alto, and New York.
The National Science Foundation previously funded four of the largest U.S. access points until mid-1995.
After the NSF stopped funding, the access points are now operated by regional and long-distance phone companies.
Rodney Joffe, chief technology officer of Genuity, stated that phone companies are not investing adequately to support Internet growth.
Genuity plans to operate its new network access point as a not-for-profit entity and will not charge Internet service providers for access.
MCI Communications Corp. expressed support for more companies contributing to the Internet.

Louis Gerstner is the Chairman of International Business Machines Corp.
Gerstner warned the computer industry of a potential backlash against the Internet.
Gerstner stated that confusion and feuding among corporate rivals contribute to this potential backlash.
He expressed that there is significant hype in the industry that may lead to corporate and consumer disillusionment about the Internet.
Gerstner emphasized the importance of addressing customer needs to make money on the Internet.
He mentioned that IBM's approach involves working closely with customers to develop necessary products.
Gerstner cited Charles Schwab as an example of a company successfully offering stock trading over the Internet.
He highlighted a conflict involving Microsoft Corp.'s efforts to develop software based on Sun Microsystems Inc.'s Java language.
Gerstner warned against allowing the Java language to become fragmented like Unix did.
Sun Microsystems announced an alliance with IBM and other companies to standardize and certify one version of the Java language.

Digital Equipment Corp.'s top executives are hosting computer industry analysts on Tuesday.
The purpose of the meeting is to present a positive outlook and stimulate interest in the company's stock.
Digital Equipment Corp. reported a significant loss of $433 million in the fourth quarter ended June 30.
The company took a $492 million restructuring charge for job cuts and plant closings.
Analysts expect Digital to discuss its long-term goals of achieving operating margins of 6-7 percent.
Digital is likely to focus on growth areas such as servers using its Alpha chip and Microsoft Corp.'s Windows NT software.
The consensus estimate for Digital's first quarter is a loss of 3 cents per share.
Many analysts anticipate a positive tone during the meeting, highlighting the company's strengths.
Digital's PC business lost approximately $90 million in the fourth quarter, more than previously expected.
Digital is seeking a manufacturing partner to reduce costs in its PC business.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp. will launch a revamped Web site on Monday.
The new strategy for the Web site will focus on the TV Guide.
The entertainment Web site will be renamed The TV Guide Entertainment Network.
The new address for the site will be www.tvguide.com.
The former name of the site was iGuide.
The new site will feature areas including movies, music, sports, and television.
Fox Sports and other Murdoch properties will provide content for the site.
News Corp. expects to turn a profit from the site in three to five years through advertising sales and online transactions.
James Murdoch is the vice president of music and new media at News Corp.
News Corp. will develop customized TV-oriented content for the WebTV Internet access device.

Highland Distilleries reported a 14 percent decrease in full year profits.
Sales of The Famous Grouse blend declined in Britain.
The UK market for Scotch whisky fell by four percent.
Pretax profits for Highland Distilleries were 37.1 million pounds for the year ended August 31, 1996.
Profits before reorganisation costs were 36.5 million pounds, below market forecasts.
Highland's shares decreased by 10p to 332p in early trade.
The Famous Grouse market share in the England and Wales off trade rose by 0.5 percent to 9.3 percent.
Sales of The Famous Grouse in the on-trade fell by one percentage point.
Overall market share for The Famous Grouse increased slightly to 13.3 percent.
Export sales of The Famous Grouse rose by five percent, with European sales increasing by 13 percent.

Matthew Clark reported a one-third decline in sales of its premium brands in the first five months of the financial year.
The premium brands affected include Diamond White, K, and Babycham.
The decline in sales is attributed to the popularity of alcopops among younger drinkers.
Matthew Clark's stock market value decreased by more than 290 million pounds following a profit warning in September.
Sales of draught cider in June and July were 10 percent lower than the previous year's summer.
Sales of premium brands fell by 30 percent.
Draught cider sales were down 15 percent across the entire summer.
Matthew Clark expects underlying growth in the cider market to resume.
The company plans to maintain its interim dividend at nine pence when reporting half-year results.
Matthew Clark's shares closed at 317.5 pence, significantly lower than their year high of 804 pence.

Associated British Foods is expected to report a significant increase in full year profits.
The retail and textile sectors of Associated British Foods are benefiting from increased high street spending.
Analyst Michael Bourke from Panmure Gordon stated that the retail and clothing sectors are driving profit increases.
Analysts forecast pretax profits of 415 million stg, up from 375 million stg from the previous year.
A dividend increase to 9.5p from 8.8p is also anticipated.
Associated British Foods operates as a food processor and manufacturer in Britain, Australia, and the United States.
The company is expected to generate additional cash from British Sugar.
Analyst Charlie Mills from UBS noted that net cash is projected to rise by about 130 million pounds.
Net cash is expected to reach 735 million stg by year end.
PriMark and other Irish retail businesses are expected to perform better.

Associated British Foods reported a 15 percent increase in its full year profits.
Chairman Garry Weston expressed caution about future forecasts due to upcoming elections in the United States and Britain.
ABF posted pretax profits of 430 million pounds for the year ended September 14.
Worldwide sales for ABF increased by 17 percent to 5.707 billion pounds.
Profits were driven by strong performance from ABF's retail operations in Britain and Ireland.
Operating profits rose 25 percent to 69 million pounds.
Primark's performance improved due to refurbishments and better alignment with public demand.
ABF's food manufacturing and processing operations in Britain showed an 8.0 percent sales growth to 3.11 billion pounds.
Operating profits from British Sugar fell to 183 million pounds due to European community quotas and currency strength.
ABF's profits from its Australia and New Zealand operations increased by 20 percent to 38 million pounds.

John McGrath is the chief executive of Grand Metropolitan.
Grand Metropolitan expects to return cash to shareholders in 1998.
The company's debt is projected to be at least one billion pounds lower in 1998.
By early next year, Grand Metropolitan's debt is expected to be in the low to middle two billion pounds range.
Grand Metropolitan's interest cover is projected to be around seven times.
The company cannot afford buybacks at the moment.
Market forecasts for Grand Metropolitan's 1997 pre-tax profits range from 1.04 to 1.06 billion pounds.
Estimates for Grand Metropolitan's 1996 pre-tax profits are around 980 million pounds.
The dollar's exchange rate against the pound was 1.493 on May 1 and rose to 1.638.
Pillsbury and Burger King generate about 60 percent of Grand Metropolitan's group earnings in dollars.

Derek Pretty is the finance director of Kwik Save.
Kwik Save plans to close 107 stores at a cost of 87.5 million stg.
The store closures are intended to ensure the future of Kwik Save.
The closure program will result in less than 200 job losses, with 90 percent of staff redeployed.
About 1,900 employees work in the 107 stores that will be shut.
Graeme Bowler is the chief executive of Kwik Save.
Kwik Save will introduce a new range of chilled foods, health and beauty products, and over-the-counter medicines.
Kwik Save will have 100 own-label products in its stores starting in spring 1997.
Kwik Save aims to maintain its discount pricing strategy.
Kwik Save plans to upgrade its stores based on customer feedback from research conducted by Anderson Consulting.

Unigate Plc is a British dairy and distribution company.
Unigate Plc posted pretax profits of 60.6 million pounds for the half year to September 30.
The pretax profits were up 0.3 percent compared to the previous year.
Unigate Plc's profits exceeded stock market forecasts of 57 to 59 million pounds.
The company held cash of 58 million pounds at September 30.
Unigate Plc raised its interim dividend by 5.3 percent to 7.0 pence.
Unigate shares increased by four pence to 431 pence by late in the session.
Unigate's European foods division reported profits of 44.1 million pounds in the first half.
Fresh foods profits increased from 20.5 million pounds to 26.5 million pounds.
Unigate spent a total of 100 million pounds on acquisitions in the half year.

Britain's independent brewers are advocating for a reduction in the excise duty on beer.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's budget statement is scheduled for November 26.
Clarke's previous budget reduced the duty on Scotch whisky while leaving beer and wine rates unchanged.
The duty on beer was increased by 2p a pint in 1994.
The chairman of the Independent Family Brewers of Britain stated that increasing excise duty has increased divergence with European partners.
The Independent Family Brewers of Britain plans to deliver a petition to the European Parliament regarding excise duty differences among EU member states.
The Brewers and Licensed Retailers Association (BLRA) is advocating for a 20 percent cut in beer duty.
A 20 percent cut in beer duty would reduce the price of a pint by 6p, according to the BLRA.
Oxford Economic Forecasting researcher Adrian Cooper claims a 20 percent cut in beer duty would lower inflation and create more jobs.
The British duty on a pint of beer with 5 percent alcohol by volume is 30 pence.

Lord Douro is the deputy chairman of Vendome Luxury Goods.
Vendome Luxury Goods' products are popular with Japanese consumers.
Lord Douro believes the yen has stabilized against the dollar and may improve.
Chinese demand for products continues to increase strongly.
The yen reached a five year low of 82.52 against the dollar in April 1995.
On April 1, at the start of Vendome's half year reporting period, the yen stood at 107.17 against the dollar.
The yen has risen to around its current level of 111 against the dollar.

Scottish & Newcastle Plc is Britain's largest brewer.
Scottish & Newcastle Plc will benefit from its Courage brands in its half year results.
Center Parcs will negatively impact Scottish & Newcastle Plc's results.
Analyst Dermott Carr from Nikko expressed concerns about Center Parcs and currency strength.
Analysts forecast pretax profits for Scottish & Newcastle Plc to range from 178 to 198 million stg.
Dividend forecasts for Scottish & Newcastle Plc center on 7.0p.
Brewing is expected to contribute approximately 80 million stg to profits.
Courage is anticipated to contribute 45 million stg to the brewing profits.
Courage made an operating profit of 9.0 million stg on a turnover of 298.9 million stg in the first half of 1995.
Scottish & Newcastle Plc acquired Courage from Foster's in August 1995 for about 550 million stg.

Bass Plc plans to spend 670 million pounds ($1.1 billion) on its business next year.
The investment is expected to create approximately 7,000 jobs.
Bass plans a 300 million pound ($500 million) investment program for its Bass Taverns next year.
The investment program will convert many pubs to branded concept bars and refurbish community pubs.
This year, Bass invested 568 million pounds in capital projects, creating at least 6,000 new jobs.
Chairman Sir Ian Prosser declined to comment on the proposed acquisition of brewer Carlsberg-Tetley.
The acquisition is currently being studied by Britain's Board of Trade on competition grounds.
Bass shares were 1p lower at 808p by 1302 GMT.
Analyst Charles Winston stated that Bass needs to resolve uncertainty surrounding Carlsberg-Tetley for the share price to move forward.
In August, Bass announced the acquisition of Allied's 50 percent stake in Carlsberg-Tetley for 200 million pounds in cash.

Gareth Davies is the chief executive of Imperial Tobacco.
Imperial Tobacco de-merged from conglomerate Hanson in October.
Davies stated it is difficult to see growth in the British market due to punitive taxes.
Imperial Tobacco hopes to achieve growth through expansion in the Asia-Pacific region.
Imperial Tobacco posted profits of 303 million stg from Britain for the year ended September 28.
Profits from overseas for Imperial Tobacco grew 55 percent to 70 million stg.
Kenneth Clarke, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, announced a tax increase of 15p on a packet of 20 cigarettes in November.
British cigarette sales fell by 2.5 percent to 81 billion after a similar tax rise in 1995.
Davies expects a similar decline in cigarette sales due to the latest tax rise.
Davies indicated that the tax rise would increase smuggling by widening the tax gap between Britain and mainland Europe.

Bass is attempting to merge with Carlsberg-Tetley to create Britain's largest brewer.
Analysts believe the UK government may be hesitant to approve the merger due to potential job losses.
Ian Lang is the president of the Board of Trade and has the final decision on the merger.
The Monopolies and Mergers Commission is expected to approve the merger if Bass agrees to certain conditions.
Michael Heseltine previously approved S&N's acquisition of Courage without a referral to the MMC.
Britain's Department of Trade and Industry has referred Bass' proposed merger to the MMC for investigation.
An MMC report on the merger is due by March 24.
CAMRA opposes the merger, claiming it has not improved customer choice or reduced beer prices.
Analysts expect the MMC to require Bass to sell about 1,000 of its 4,200 pubs as part of the merger conditions.
A Bass spokeswoman stated that more jobs would be safer if the merger goes ahead.

The race to succeed Alex Trotman for the top office at Ford Motor Co. has begun.
Ford Motor Co. promoted Edward Hagenlocker to vice chairman from executive vice president.
Edward Hagenlocker is in charge of a new auto components organization with 75,000 employees and revenues of $14 billion.
Jacques Nasser was named to head Ford Automotive Operations, replacing Hagenlocker.
Speculation exists about how Ford's board will handle Trotman's succession.
Trotman will reach the mandatory retirement age of 65 in July 1998.
William Clay Ford Jr. may be named a non-executive chairman or chairman when Trotman leaves.
Hagenlocker's tenure at Ford Automotive Operations has been marked by slumping profits.
Hagenlocker oversaw the launch of the successful new F-Series and the new Ford Expedition.
Eugene Jennings stated that Hagenlocker's new role could provide him with necessary experience.

A tentative deal was reached after a 19-day strike by 26,000 Canadian autoworkers.
General Motors Corp. has instructed about 2,000 workers at its Lordstown, Ohio, car assembly plant not to report to work.
There are ongoing material shortages affecting GM's plant operations.
Negotiators for GM and the Canadian Auto Workers union settled disputes over contracting work.
The strike has idled 19,931 workers at various assembly and parts plants in the U.S. and Mexico.
If the deal is ratified, it may take until the end of next week for all affected GM plants to return to pre-strike production levels.
An analyst estimated that the strike could cost GM about 100,000 units of straight-time production in North America.
GM is expected to lose production of about 51,000 units in Canada and 45,000 to 46,000 units in the United States.
Approximately 40 percent of the lost production in Canada consists of GM's full-size C/K pickup trucks made in Oshawa, Ontario.
CAW President Buzz Hargrove stated that GM could restart the Oshawa truck plant as soon as the deal is ratified.

General Motors Corp and the United Auto Workers are facing outsourcing issues.
Analysts do not expect the UAW to stage a prolonged strike against GM.
David Cole is the director of the University of Michigan's Center for the Study of Automotive Transportation.
David Healy is an analyst at Burnham Securities Inc.
Talks for a new three-year labor deal were scheduled to resume on Tuesday at 8:30 a.m. EST.
Bargainers worked for 17 hours into the early morning on Monday before calling a recess.
The UAW represents 215,000 members at GM.
UAW President Stephen Yokich plans to resolve differences with GM at the bargaining table.
Ken Summers is the administrative assistant to the chairman of Local 594 in Pontiac, Michigan.
Harley Shaiken is a labor expert at the University of California at Berkeley.

General Motors Corp. faces labor costs of $43 an hour at its parts plants.
David Healy is an analyst at Burnham Securities Inc.
Joseph Phillippi is an analyst at Lehman Brothers.
Timothy Leuliette is the president and chief executive officer of ITT Automotive.
In 1995, ITT Automotive paid 15 percent of its 35,000 workers worldwide less than $10 an hour.
In 1990, 10 percent of ITT Automotive's employees were paid less than $10 an hour.
GM is negotiating a new three-year labor contract with the United Auto Workers union.
Delphi Automotive Systems has stated that 12 of its U.S. component facilities are underperforming.
Delphi's average U.S. parts worker will earn nearly $19 an hour in the first year of the contract and more than $21 in the third year.
Delphi had revenues of $26.4 billion in 1995.

Ford Motor Co. launched a new computer-aided design project called C3P.
C3P is based on a computer program from Structural Dynamics Research Corp.
Ford claims C3P will cut prototype costs by up to 50 percent.
Ford states C3P will improve investment efficiency by 20 percent to 30 percent.
C3P is expected to eliminate half of costly late development changes.
Paul Blumberg is the director of product development systems at Ford's Product Development Centre.
Three new vehicle programs started in 2023 will use C3P.
Ford plans to merge computer-aided design, manufacturing, and engineering functions into a unified system by 2000.
Structural Dynamics Research Corp. is considered a small player in the CAD/CAM market for the auto industry.
Chrysler Corp. launched a similar design program seven years prior to Ford's C3P announcement.

CMS Energy Co is expected to meet or exceed earnings estimates of $2.40 to $2.45 a share for 1996, according to Chairman and CEO William McCormick.
CMS Energy Co earned $2.27 a share on total revenues of $3.9 billion in 1995.
The Michigan Public Service Commission approved a settlement that removes rate uncertainty related to the Midland Cogeneration Venture L.P.
The settlement allows Consumers Power to include the cost of buying the final 325 megawatts of power from the Midland Cogeneration plant in its customer rates.
CMS was previously allowed to include the cost of buying 915 megawatts of the plant's total 1240 megawatts of power in its rates.
The settlement removes the possibility of future earnings write-downs related to the Midland project.
CMS recorded an after-tax charge of $343 million in the fourth quarter of 1992 from an earlier settlement of Midland Cogeneration issues.
CMS' stock increased by $1 to $32-3/8, with a trading volume of 206,700 shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Midland Cogeneration is the largest cogeneration project in North and South America and is a partnership involving CMS, Dow Chemical Co, Coastal Corp, Asea Brown Boveri Inc, and Fluor Corp.
Standard & Poor's revised its outlook on Consumers Power and CMS to positive from stable following the settlement approval.

General Motors Corp. signed a memorandum of understanding to sell four parts plants to Peregrine Inc.
Peregrine Inc. plans to be a major auto industry supplier with more than $1 billion in annual sales.
Peregrine Inc. was formed by the New York investment firm Joseph Littlejohn & Levy and auto industry executive Edward Gulda.
No terms were announced for the deal involving the sale of the plants.
Edward Gulda stated that Peregrine will be one of North America's premier automotive supply companies.
Peregrine will be based in Southfield, Mich.
Peregrine will pursue business with all car and truck manufacturers in North America and internationally.
Peregrine plans to sign a supply agreement with GM following a final agreement expected by the end of 1996.
The four plants produce a variety of interior parts and generate combined revenue of about $1 billion a year.
The plants employ about 5,500 hourly and salaried workers.

Chrysler Corp. minivans are under investigation by safety regulators for two issues.
One issue involves reports that a 90-pound rear hatch door can close unexpectedly.
Nearly 2 million minivans are involved in the investigations.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has received reports of 39 injuries related to the rear hatch door on 1991-1993 model Caravan, Voyager, and Town & Country minivans.
The rear hatch door issue is caused by bolts holding the door prop cylinders shearing.
NHTSA has received a total of 477 complaints regarding the rear hatch door problem.
The investigation, first launched in May and upgraded on October 31, covers almost 1.3 million minivans.
NHTSA upgraded a preliminary investigation into about 582,000 1996-model Caravan, Voyager, and Town & Country minivans due to reports of sliding doors opening while the vehicle is moving.
NHTSA has received 19 complaints about sliding doors opening at speeds from 15 to 60 mph, but no injuries have been reported.
Chrysler was the first automaker to offer a sliding door on the left side of a minivan.

Chrysler Corp. is exploring the possibility of extending its car production agreement with Mitsubishi Motors Corp.
Chrysler spokeswoman Shawn Williams stated that discussions are ongoing but no conclusions or decisions have been reached.
Mitsubishi Motor Manufacturing of America Inc. builds the Dodge Avenger, Chrysler Sebring, and Eagle Talon coupes at its assembly plant in Normal, Illinois.
The current production agreement between Chrysler and Mitsubishi is set to expire after the 1999 model year.
Chrysler executives have previously indicated a desire to phase out the production arrangement with Mitsubishi.
Richard Recchia, chief operating officer of Mitsubishi's U.S. unit, suggested in October 1995 that the future relationship would focus on components and engineering exchanges.
Automotive News reported that Chrysler Executive Vice President Thomas Gale met with Mitsubishi officials in Tokyo to discuss extending the contract through 2004.
Gail O'Brien, a spokeswoman for Mitsubishi's Normal plant, confirmed that discussions with Chrysler are ongoing.
Analysts believe it would be sensible for Chrysler to continue using Mitsubishi as a production partner due to declining coupe sales.
If Chrysler moves Avenger and Sebring production out of the Normal plant, it may need to convert its plant in Toluca, Mexico.

General Motors Corp is discontinuing the Geo brand seven years after its creation.
The Metro, Prizm, and Tracker models will continue to be sold as Chevrolet vehicles.
Chevrolet General Manager John Middlebrook stated that the Chevrolet brand no longer needs the Geo badge to attract new buyers.
The discontinuation of the Geo brand aligns with GM's efforts to simplify its brand images.
GM created the Geo brand in 1989 as a sub-category of Chevrolet by renaming several Chevrolet vehicles.
The name Geo was intended to signify a world car under the direction of former GM Chairman Roger Smith.
GM plans no changes to the joint venture agreements that produce the Geo vehicles.
The Prizm is produced by NUMMI, a joint venture with Toyota Motor Corp.
The Metro and Tracker are produced at CAMI, GM's joint venture with Suzuki Motor Corp, in Ingersoll, Ontario.
Sales of the Prizm lag behind those of its sister vehicle, the Corolla, with 77,000 units sold compared to 188,000 for the Corolla through November of this year.

Ford Motor Co. announced a new agreement with Republic Industries Inc., the parent company of AutoNation USA.
Under the agreement, AutoNation can submit proposals to acquire existing Ford or Lincoln-Mercury dealerships.
The agreement also covers areas where Ford may want a dealership that it does not currently have.
Mullinax Management, based in Ohio, is reported to be in merger talks with AutoNation.
Ford spokesman John Ochs stated that Ford has not sold any dealerships to AutoNation.
Mullinax is the 11th largest dealer group in the country based on its 1995 retail unit sales of 20,374 cars and trucks.
Robert Rewey, Ford's group vice president of marketing and sales, stated that private entrepreneurs with local community ties will continue to be the backbone of Ford's franchise system.
Ford's deal with Republic is described as a 'framework agreement' that allows AutoNation to submit individual proposals.
Last February, Ford Chairman Alex Trotman stated that Ford had no plans to offer a new-car franchise to an auto superstore.
Chrysler Corp. announced it would grant a new-car franchise to CarMax Auto Superstore in Norcross, Ga.

Chrysler Corp. reported a 9 percent increase in total U.S. sales for August, reaching 186,306 units.
The August sales total broke Chrysler's previous record of 176,184 set in 1989.
Sales of light trucks, including Ram pickups and four-door minivans, totaled 127,870 units, a 16.7 percent increase.
Chrysler experienced 11 consecutive months of rising light truck sales.
Domestic car sales fell 2 percent to 58,255 units.
Chrysler's light truck sales were supported by incentives on some Jeep models.
Sales of the Grand Cherokee rose 42 percent, the Cherokee increased by 52 percent, and Wrangler sales grew by 59 percent.
Total pickup sales were limited by low supplies of the Dakota, which is undergoing a model changeover.
Dealers had a 35-day supply of compact pickups, which is about half of the ideal supply.
Chrysler executives did not expect significant volumes of the new Dakotas until October.

A Chinese appeals court reduced the prison sentence for an International Monetary Fund (IMF) employee to five years.
The employee, Hong Yang, was accused of corruption and accepted bribes totaling 100,000 yuan ($12,000) in 1993.
Hong Yang was sentenced by the Beijing Municipal Higher People's Court.
Hong Yang was arrested in December while on an IMF mission to China.
Hong Yang was found guilty on June 28.
The original sentence for Hong Yang was reported to be 10 years by Beijing sources and 11 years by IMF statements.
Hong Yang appealed the sentence.
Chinese courts rarely reduce sentences on appeal, but an admission of guilt may lead to leniency.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus expressed concern over judicial shortcomings in Hong Yang's case.
The second trial for Hong Yang was held on August 9 and was open to the public.

China needs to extend bank credits to boost its export sector.
Wu Yi is the Minister of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation in China.
Wu Yi requested commercial and subsidised bank credits for machinery and electrical equipment makers.
China's exports for the first eight months of the year were $90.61 billion, a decrease of 4.2 percent from the previous year.
Exports in July and August improved after the government expedited payments of export rebates.
Wu Yi stated that commercial banks should be encouraged to make policy loans.
Wu Yi mentioned that state subsidies would be necessary to support these loans.
Big turnkey projects require significant capital and long completion times.
Exporters face inflationary cost pressures, exchange rate fluctuations, and tax rebate delays during project execution.
Wu Yi expressed confidence that China could achieve its total trade goal of $281 billion this year.

China's leaders have agreed on the need to stimulate the economy.
Fan Gang is an economist and director of the China Reform Foundation.
The central bank of China wants to keep economic policy low-key.
China has relaxed its three-year program of economic austerity.
Retail price inflation in China was 21.7 percent in 1994 and fell to 5.0 percent in September this year.
The government target for inflation for the full year is 10 percent.
China's economic growth has reached about 9.0 percent.
The People's Bank of China has cut interest rates twice this year.
Interest rate cuts are intended to help ailing state industry.
Central bank officials have stated that interest rate cuts do not indicate a loosening of monetary policy.

The choice of Singapore for the listing of Sinochem's shares was influenced by political factors.
Chinese officials and foreign securities analysts noted the close ties between China and Singapore in this decision.
Fu Yong, chairman of Sinochem Asia Holdings, stated that good relations between China and Singapore contributed to the decision.
Fu Yong described Singapore as a stable and prosperous environment.
Hong Kong has attracted most foreign listings of Chinese companies to date.
Sinochem, also known as China National Chemicals Import and Export Corp, is a major state trading company.
Sinochem's trading turnover increased from $14.98 billion in 1994 to $18.21 billion last year.
Sinochem controls 40 percent of all of China's crude oil imports.
Sinochem has a stake in a joint venture oil refinery in Dalian and a newly formed insurance joint venture with Manufacturers Life of Canada.
Sinochem has invested 700 million yuan to build its headquarters in Beijing and is part owner of a commercial tower in Shanghai.

China's foreign debts reached $109.5 billion at the end of June.
The governor of the People's Bank of China is Dai Xianglong.
Dai Xianglong stated that China is confident in paying its foreign debts.
China's foreign exchange reserves are approximately $96 billion.
Dai Xianglong described China's foreign exchange reserves as comfortable but not excessive.
The debt service ratio in China is within international warning levels.
Dai Xianglong indicated that the repayment situation is good overall.
He mentioned that an additional $10 billion in debt is possible each year.
The average annual addition to China's debt level over the past five years has been $10 billion.
Most of Beijing's debt is long term.

China expects talks with the United States soon regarding U.S. sanctions on its textiles.
Beijing has not yet determined which U.S. imports would be banned if Washington does not withdraw penalties on Chinese textiles.
An official from the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation stated that working level talks with the U.S. are anticipated in the near future.
China announced it would temporarily suspend imports of certain U.S. textiles, farm goods, animal husbandry products, fruits, and alcoholic drinks in retaliation for U.S. charges on Chinese textiles.
The temporary import ban from China is set to take effect on December 10.
Washington imposed punitive charges against import quotas for Chinese textile goods in September, accusing China of circumventing U.S. quota restrictions.
China claims the U.S. action was taken without consultation and lacked clear supporting evidence.
China is consulting with its enterprises to determine which products should be included in the ban, with a decision expected in 30 days.
The trade affected by Washington's actions is estimated at $19 million, a small fraction of the overall Sino-U.S. trade.
The United States reported a trade deficit with China of more than $35 billion last year.

China has sent mixed signals to the United States before the visit by Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
The visit by Warren Christopher is the highest level visit by a U.S. official to China in two years.
Diplomats believe the visit is unlikely to encounter major obstacles as both sides aim to repair their relationship.
China and the United States have experienced strained ties due to disputes over human rights, arms proliferation, Taiwan, and trade.
Christopher's visit is expected to be the first in a series of high-level contacts between the two countries.
President Bill Clinton plans to meet with President Jiang Zemin in Manila during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
Plans are being discussed for an exchange of visits between Clinton and Jiang Zemin in 1997 and possibly 1998.
Vice-President Al Gore may visit China in the first half of the following year.
China has publicly rejected the appeal of dissident Wang Dan and upheld his 11-year sentence for subversion.
China released dissident Chen Ziming as a gesture of goodwill after President Bill Clinton's re-election.

Russia plans to expand economic ties with China at a meeting in Moscow next month.
Russian Ambassador Igor Rogachev stated that the goal is to enhance economic cooperation to match political cooperation.
Chinese Premier Li Peng and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin will meet in Moscow to discuss economic steps.
The relationship between China and Russia is described as a strategic partnership.
Rogachev noted that relations between the two countries have not been this smooth since 1949.
Rogachev claimed that relations are currently on a healthy and rational basis.
Russia aims to deliver oil, natural gas, and electricity from Siberia to China.
Russia seeks involvement in China's nuclear power development.
China and Russia have proposed an oil and natural gas pipeline from Siberia to China, but financing is a significant challenge.
Rogachev does not expect an agreement on these issues at the December meeting but anticipates readiness by spring.

U.S. President Bill Clinton appointed Madeleine Albright as the first woman secretary of state and William Cohen as secretary of defense.
Albright and Cohen were seen as capable appointees but were perceived as lacking expertise in Asian affairs.
Asian nations that had faced U.S. pressure on human rights expressed concerns about Albright's appointment.
Senate confirmation for both nominees was widely expected.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto stated he did not expect any changes in U.S.-Japan relations.
Government sources indicated that Albright and Cohen were unfamiliar with Japan.
China welcomed Albright's appointment and expressed hope for improved Sino-U.S. ties.
Sino-U.S. relations had been strained over issues such as Taiwan, arms proliferation, trade, and human rights.
Relations between the U.S. and China had improved recently, highlighted by a meeting between Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
Analysts noted that Albright's past statements on human rights might lead to negative perceptions in Burma.

China announced a ban on poultry and poultry products from Missouri and Oklahoma due to an outbreak of a deadly disease.
The ban is already in effect and was confirmed by an official of the Ministry of Agriculture.
The ban aims to prevent damage from a disease described as very destructive.
China has banned all U.S. poultry brought into the country by mail or carried by travelers.
Travelers are prohibited from bringing any poultry goods from the United States into China.
The ban on poultry products from Missouri and Oklahoma was implemented due to five cases of a deadly poultry flu discovered between July and September.
The quarantine official stated that the ban is unrelated to other trade disputes with the United States.
The virus involved is known as viscerotropic velogenic Newcastle disease (VVND), which is considered very dangerous.
The last major outbreak of VVND in the United States occurred in California in the 1970s, leading to the eradication of the state's entire poultry population.
China had previously announced a ban on imports of poultry from 10 U.S. states due to fears of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI).

The Stone Group is a Chinese high technology company.
The Stone Group plans to inject assets into its Stone Electronic unit to boost trading.
The asset injections could begin next year.
The Hong Kong company is recovering from a decline in profits in 1995.
Duan Yongji is the president of the Stone Group.
Duan Yongji stated that the company wants to expand its float.
The company's stock price-to-earnings ratio is currently about 23.
The company aims to reduce the price-to-earnings ratio to about 10.
A rise in earnings is expected this year and in 1997.
The Stone Group Corp listed shares in 1993 with a flotation of HK$300 million for Stone Electronic Technology Ltd.

China's central bank chief, Dai Xianglong, stated that inflation would be a modest seven percent this year.
Dai Xianglong claimed that the state's economic policies were effective.
Dai criticized companies for lending money at excessively high rates due to tight monetary policies.
Dai stated that appropriately tight monetary policies have achieved clear results acknowledged in China and abroad.
China's retail inflation was 6.9 percent year-on-year in the first seven months and 5.9 percent in July.
Beijing aimed to keep inflation within 10 percent for 1996, down from 14.8 percent the previous year.
Dai mentioned that some monopoly groups and publicly listed companies were lending money at excessively high rates.
Tsingtao Brewery has faced regulatory issues in Hong Kong for lending funds raised from its public offer.
A senior unnamed Chinese economist indicated that several big ministries were cash-rich and earning high returns by lending out their funds.
Dai noted that there are many violations of financial regulations and called for an expansion of supervision over the financial sector.

Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin aims to portray himself as the rightful heir to Deng Xiaoping's legacy.
A television series was created to highlight Deng Xiaoping's contributions and limit the influence of potential challengers to Jiang's authority.
The series was produced by China Central Television over four years.
The series traced Deng's journey from his birthplace in Sichuan province to becoming a leader in China.
The program praised Deng for his pragmatic policies that contributed to China's prosperity.
Approximately 224 million people watched the series, which is 28 percent of the 800 million television viewers in China.
Jiang Zemin is referred to as the 'core' of the third generation of China's leadership.
Jiang described Deng Xiaoping as a 'worthy outstanding Marxist and a stalwart communist.'
Deng Xiaoping has not been seen in public for nearly three years and appeared frail in his last public appearance.
The series did not mention Deng's previous anointed successor, Zhao Ziyang, who was dismissed during the 1989 power struggle.

Two members of Congress criticized the Federal Reserve for its record of hiring and promoting women and minorities.
Representative Henry Gonzalez and Representative Jesse Jackson Jr. wrote a letter to Fed chairman Alan Greenspan.
The letter stated that several discrimination lawsuits against the Federal Reserve indicate a need for reform.
Henry Gonzalez is a Democrat from Texas serving his 19th term in Congress.
Jesse Jackson Jr. is a second-term Democrat from Illinois and the son of a civil rights leader.
A Fed spokesman declined to comment on the criticisms.
Four black secretaries filed a lawsuit against the Federal Reserve in January.
Fifteen other current and former employees have requested to join the litigation related to the lawsuit.
The Federal Reserve's record of diversity in hiring and promotion was described as woefully inadequate by Gonzalez and Jackson.
In 1993, there was one woman and one non-white among the 35 top paid staff at the Federal Reserve, while currently, there are 11 women and five minorities among 72 top paid staff.

Senator Bob Kerrey is preparing legislation regarding computer encryption export policy.
People familiar with Senator Bob Kerrey's plans have reported on this preparation.
The current debate involves the Clinton administration and U.S. software companies.
The Clinton administration favors strict export controls on encryption.
U.S. software companies and civil libertarians want to relax export limits on encryption.
Encryption programs scramble information.
Scrambled information becomes unreadable without a password or software 'key.'

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan urged lawmakers to delay consideration of proposals allowing banks to merge with commercial companies.
Greenspan suggested that Congress should focus on modest financial reforms to remove legal barriers preventing banks from affiliating with insurance companies and securities firms.
Greenspan stated that Congress should widen the permissible range of affiliations for banking organizations to enhance consumer choices and financial market efficiency.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin presented the Clinton administration's plan to allow banks to enter the securities and insurance businesses.
Rubin did not address whether banks should merge with commercial companies and offered Congress two proposals regarding such combinations.
Greenspan acknowledged that barriers between banks and commercial companies will eventually diminish due to technological advancements.
Greenspan advised caution in removing these barriers due to uncertainties regarding their impact on the U.S. financial system.
Greenspan recommended postponing wider authorization of banking and commerce while focusing on financial modernization.
The administration's plan aims to allow banks, securities firms, and insurance companies to compete under a uniform set of regulations.
Rubin estimated that increased competition from the plan could save consumers up to $15 billion a year.

The Czech economy is showing signs of slower growth and a widening trade gap.
Analysts expressed concerns about the pace of industrial restructuring in the Czech economy.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus has been praised for achieving low inflation rates, good GDP growth, and an unemployment rate of about three percent.
The Czech Statistical Bureau reported a record trade deficit of 160.33 billion crowns ($5.75 billion) for 1996.
The trade deficit increased from a 95.7 billion crown shortfall the previous year.
Some economists are concerned about the export competitiveness of Czech industry.
Kamil Janacek, chief economist at Komercni Banka, stated that competition from other transforming economies is increasing.
Since 1992, the Czech economy has transitioned from recession to 4.8 percent consumption-driven real growth in 1995.
Unemployment in the Czech Republic remains around three percent, with nearly 70 percent of the economy in private hands.
The current account showed a deficit of $3.1 billion crowns for the first three quarters, while the capital account was in surplus by approximately $2.0 billion.

The Prague Stock Exchange faced difficulties in 1996.
Analysts predict that the Prague Stock Exchange will recover in the following year.
Government officials previously lacked commitment to strengthen minority shareholder rights and increase market transparency.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and bourse officials have committed to improving the market.
Jan Sykora of Wood and Company stated that foreign investors are under-invested in the Prague Stock Exchange.
The PX50 index reached a year-high of 582.0 in September 1996.
The PX50 index dropped by nearly a quarter to just above 500 points by the end of 1996.
Government officials supported the creation of an independent supervisory body for the market.
Prime Minister Klaus previously showed little enthusiasm for creating a body similar to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
Tomas Jezek stated that creating an SEC-type body is a priority for 1997.

The Prague Stock Exchange fell on Monday from a year high due to profit taking.
