Colombia's military appears to be losing the battle against the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), according to political analysts.
Fighting in a mountain community outside the capital resulted in the deaths of 16 soldiers over four days.
Army commander Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett stated that FARC guerrillas had been driven out of the area.
Bonett claimed that the soldiers were allies of the peasants.
Few peasants believed Bonett's pledge that the army would not take reprisals against civilians.
Most peasants expected FARC to return once the military withdrew.
FARC was established as a pro-Soviet guerrilla group in 1964.
FARC seeks a Marxist revolution for greater social justice and land distribution.
FARC opposes U.S. interference in Colombian affairs.
San Juanito is located 30 miles east of Bogota at an elevation of 6,000 feet.

A German man spoke about his kidnapping experience in Colombia on Wednesday.
He and three companions considered escaping the day before the army attacked the guerrilla camp.
Mardean Muzinic is a construction worker from Munich.
Manfred Kehrer is from Linz, Austria.
Muzinic and Kehrer were freed on Tuesday after being held for a month.
They were kidnapped by a group of 20 Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels.
Kehrer's brother Johann and friend Alexander Scheurer were killed by guerrillas during the army's attack.
Muzinic expressed a willingness to escape, believing that only half of the guerrillas were experienced fighters.
The four friends were separated into two groups after ten days of captivity.
The guerrillas demanded a $15 million ransom, but the German embassy and Austrian ambassador were unaware of the kidnapping until after the release.

The army began stationing troops in strategic areas of Colombia.
Union leaders warned that a state workers' strike could unleash a nationwide civic protest.
The indefinite work stoppage involves about 800,000 state employees.
The strike is expected to be the largest protest since 1977.
The government feared leftist guerrilla movements were planning attacks to coincide with the strike.
Education Minister Jaime Nino cancelled all classes in state-run schools and universities.
State workers are striking for a 21.5 percent wage hike.
The government's wage offer is 13.5 percent.
The strike is also a protest against the reduction of labor rights and plans for privatization.
Defence Minister Guillermo Alberto Gonzalez announced measures to combat street protests.

United News & Media reported a profit rise of more than 20 percent.
The profit rise was reported on Thursday.
The group made significant progress since a merger earlier this year.
The merger effectively doubled the size of United News & Media.
Pre-tax profit before exceptional items totaled 151.9 million pounds in the six months to June 30.
The previous year's restated figure was 125 million pounds.
Chairman Lord Stevens stated that the strategy outlined at the time of the merger is being implemented effectively.
The merger between United News & Media and MAI was completed in April.
The enlarged group has a market capitalization of over three billion pounds.
United News & Media owns British national newspapers including The Daily and Sunday Express and Daily Star.

The UK government referred a bid by London Clubs International for Capital Corp to competition authorities.
Consumer Affairs Minister John Taylor expressed competition concerns regarding the 190 million pound hostile bid.
The bid was referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).
London Clubs International operates seven casinos in London.
London Clubs expressed disappointment over the government's decision.
London Clubs' chief executive Alan Goodenough stated that they provided evidence of no adverse competition issues to the Office of Fair Trading (OFT).
The MMC has until July 7 to make a decision on the bid.
The referral of the bid means it automatically lapses.
London Clubs' board plans to meet to consider future actions regarding the bid.
A merged company would control almost two-thirds of London's 1.7 billion pound casino market.

Granada Group Plc plans to close around 100 of its 560 high street rental and retail stores.
A company spokeswoman stated that the review of stores aims to close the least profitable and least successful ones.
Granada employs approximately 1,500 full-time staff and 430 part-time staff in its stores across Britain.
The company did not specify how many employees would lose their jobs due to the closures.
Locations for the store closures have not yet been identified.
The closures are scheduled to begin in May after a three-month consultation period with workers.
Granada announced it has partnered with BSkyB and Carlton to bid for digital terrestrial television licences.
Granada has become one of Britain's leading companies in recent years.
In January, Granada acquired the Forte catering and hotel empire in a 3.9 billion pounds takeover.
The importance of Granada's rental division has been diminishing compared to the rest of the group.

Quaker Oats Co. agreed to sell its Snapple beverage unit for $300 million.
The selling price is $1.4 billion less than what Quaker paid for Snapple.
Quaker paid $1.7 billion for Snapple in 1994.
The sale of Snapple disappointed Wall Street.
Analysts expressed satisfaction that Quaker decided to sell Snapple.
Snapple's ready-to-drink teas and juices were a pioneer in the premium soft drink market.
Snapple generated more than $500 million in sales in 1996.
Snapple has been unprofitable since Quaker acquired it.
Snapple sales declined by 8 percent in the United States and Canada in 1996.
Quaker Chairman William Smithburg stated that the decision to sell Snapple was made after reviewing shareholder value-building options.

L.D. DeSimone is the chairman and chief executive of Minnesota Mining & Manufacturing Co.
DeSimone stated that the company is comfortable with 1997 earnings estimates ranging from $4.05 to $4.20 per share.
Profits for 3M in 1996 were $3.63 per share.
DeSimone mentioned that the company aims for earnings gains exceeding 10 percent annually.
Giulio Agostini is the chief financial officer of 3M.
About 1,000 employees in the United States and Europe left 3M through voluntary separation in late 1996.
An additional 500 employees in Europe are expected to depart 3M in the first half of 1997 under similar programs.
Agostini stated that raw materials prices are expected to be slightly lower in 1997 than in 1996.
Capital spending for 3M in 1997 is expected to be about $1.3 billion.
The total shares outstanding of 3M is expected to be reduced by about four million in 1997.

WMX Technologies Inc. agreed to sell its 19 percent stake in ServiceMaster L.P. for $626 million.
WMX Technologies Inc. is based in Oak Brook, Illinois.
WMX Technologies Inc. is the largest garbage hauler in the United States.
WMX is undergoing a broad restructuring to address stockholder dissatisfaction.
On February 4, WMX announced plans to divest $1.5 billion in assets, cut 3,000 jobs, and buy back 50 million shares of stock.
Phillip Rooney resigned as Chief Executive Officer of WMX Technologies Inc. on Tuesday.
Rooney's resignation followed demands from an investment group controlled by George Soros.
WMX owns or has rights to acquire 29.035 million restricted shares of ServiceMaster.
The stock sale is expected to be completed on or before April 14.
Following the announcement, WMX's stock price decreased by 37.5 cents to $34.375.

The turnaround in Australia's housing market is expected to occur during 1997.
The expected turnaround is unlikely to signal a repeat of the housing boom seen in the 1980s or the peak in 1993/94.
Lower immigration levels are seen as a major reason for subdued demand for housing in Australia.
The anticipated housing recovery would be welcomed by building material companies, hardware chains, and consumer goods manufacturers.
Building material companies, hardware chains, and consumer goods manufacturers have blamed the recent housing slump for a fall in profits over the past 18 months.
House construction is expected to total 127,200 homes in the 1996/97 year to June 30.
The expected house construction total for 1996/97 is an increase from 124,550 homes built a year earlier.
The Master Builders Association has stated that total building approvals need to rise by around 17 percent to meet the 1996/97 forecast.
The 1996/97 forecast of 127,200 homes is well below the 182,000 homes built in the 1993/94 high point.
The Australian government expects to take in about 86,000 immigrants during 1996/97.

David Jones Ltd reported a 50 percent fall in net profit for the 1996/97 first half.
David Jones expects to appoint a new chief executive officer (CEO) soon.
David Jones reported a net profit of A$22.34 million in the 26 weeks ended January 25.
David Jones reported a net profit of A$44.64 million in the same period a year ago.
David Jones expects the 1996/97 year net profit to be lower than the previous year.
Chairman Richard Warburton stated that the retailer would review five or six underperforming stores.
Warburton did not confirm if the review would lead to store closures.
David Jones is committed to its store expansion programme.
Chris Tideman resigned as CEO on Monday, citing personal reasons.
Warburton stated that Tideman left of his own will and there was no pressure from the board or shareholders.

OzEmail Ltd launched long-distance telephone calls over the Internet at a quarter the cost of Telstra Corp and Optus.
OzEmail is based in Sydney and is listed on the NASDAQ market in the United States.
Users do not need a personal computer to use OzEmail's new service.
Calls can be made from any telephone by dialing a specific number that connects to the Internet.
OzEmail described the new service as a world first.
Former Australian Prime Minister Paul Keating made the first call using the new service.
The first call was made to Mark Roberts, a telecommunications analyst at Montgomery Securities in the United States.
Calls to the U.S. and Britain cost A$21 (US$27) per hour under OzEmail's new service.
OzEmail's service will initially be available to its 100,000-plus Internet customers for calls within Australia and to New Zealand, the United States, and Britain.
The service will be made available to the public after two months, targeting the residential market first.

London telecoms analysts have differing opinions about the prospects of Britain's Cable and Wireless Communications.
Cable and Wireless Communications made its market debut on Monday.
CWC started trading at around 300 pence per share and rose to 309 pence before falling to 299.5 pence.
The valuation of CWC is approximately 4.46 billion pounds.
CWC was formed when the Mercury subsidiary of Cable and Wireless Plc merged with three cable TV units of NYNEX Corp and Bell Canada.
CWC floated a 14.7 percent stake in London and New York.
Brokers Lehman Brothers estimate that a 4.5 billion pound valuation implies an enterprise value of about 6.0 billion pounds.
CWC plans to invest 2.3 billion pounds in capital expenditure to complete its broadband cable and local telephone networks by 2001.
CWC's core business will be telephony provided by Mercury, with 91 percent of revenues coming from telephony.
Some analysts express caution about CWC's prospects due to the lack of profitability among cable television companies in Britain's market.

A parliamentary report stated that some utility regulation in Britain prioritized shareholders over consumers.
The opposition Labour Party is leading in opinion polls ahead of the May 1 election against Prime Minister John Major's Conservative Party.
Labour welcomed the all-party select committee report on the gas and electricity industries.
Labour claims to have found a tax that is popular with consumers upset about high profits and executive pay in monopoly utilities.
The select committee agreed with energy regulators that initial price controls after privatisation favored shareholders over customers.
The report noted that despite significant profit increases, mistakes in regulation may have occurred due to limited experience with utility privatisation globally.
The committee called for increased transparency to help regulators set appropriate price limits.
Electricity and gas prices have decreased since privatisation due to rising competition.
The report supported the British method of linking allowable utility charges to inflation.
Labour plans to fund a 'welfare-to-work' program with a minimum of 3.0 billion pounds from a one-off profits tax.

Telecoms analysts in London found humor in Portugal Telecom SA's statement about Telefonica de Espana SA linking with MCI Communications Corp.
Telefonica denied that a deal had been signed with MCI.
Analysts expect a four-way alliance to be announced involving BT, MCI, Portugal Telecom, and Telefonica.
BT's share price reflects the anticipated four-way alliance.
BT announced a strategic partnership between its Concert venture and Portugal Telecom.
BT declined to comment on a potential deal with Telefonica's international arm Tisa.
Analysts described Portugal Telecom's situation as an 'oops' moment.
Concert's alliance with Portugal Telecom provides exposure to Brazil but has limited presence in other South American countries.
A deal with Telefonica's Tisa would expand Concert's geographic portfolio to include Peru, Argentina, Chile, Venezuela, Colombia, and Puerto Rico.
Analysts believe that without Telefonica, the Unisource alliance led by AT&T would be weakened.

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. began shipping its K6 microprocessor on Wednesday.
AMD's K6 microprocessor is claimed to work faster than Intel's Pentium Pro chip.
The K6 microprocessor is 25 percent cheaper than comparable Intel offerings.
The K6 microprocessor is easier to design a PC around compared to Intel products.
AMD is now considered a strong alternative to Intel for the latest technology.
Jerry Sanders is the chairman of AMD.
AMD makes microprocessors that handle the main calculations of a personal computer.
AMD's chips have historically been about three years behind Intel's technology.
The K6 microprocessor uses technology gained from the acquisition of Nexgen Inc. in 1995.
Analysts expect AMD to ship at least 2 million K6 chips by the end of the year.

Apple Computer Inc. will lay off more employees this year as part of its plan to return to profitability by 1998.
David Harrah is Apple's corporate spokesman.
Apple is reviewing unprofitable product lines with the intention of discontinuing them.
The upcoming job cuts are part of Apple's plan to reduce costs by up to 20 percent due to falling revenue.
Apple has not yet determined how many employees it will lay off.
Apple laid off about 1,300 employees last year as part of a corporate restructuring program.
Apple plans to launch another restructuring program aimed at cutting $400 million in costs.
Harrah confirmed that layoffs will be part of the restructuring plan.
Apple is considering discontinuing the Newton handheld computer and the Pippin home entertainment console.
Apple reported a fiscal first quarter loss of $120 million due to a decline in sales.

Rational Software Corp. agreed to buy Pure Atria Corp. in a stock deal valued at about $839 million.
Both companies' stocks fell after Pure Atria announced its first-quarter earnings would be lower than expected.
Analysts suggested that Rational could face similar difficulties as Pure Atria in managing acquisitions.
Rational Software's stock fell by $10.125, or 43 percent, to $13.25.
Pure Atria's stock fell by $7.375, or 42 percent, to $10.375.
Both stocks were among the biggest percentage losers on the Nasdaq.
Under the acquisition terms, Rational would pay 0.9 of its shares for each of Pure Atria's 39.92 million shares outstanding.
Based on Rational's closing stock price of $23.375, the transaction was initially valued at $839 million.
The stock slide on Monday reduced the deal's value by 43 percent.
Rational specializes in methodology tools, while Pure Atria specializes in development and testing tools.

Hudson's Bay Co named William Fields as chief executive on Monday.
William Fields replaces retiring Chief Executive George Kosich on June 1.
Hudson's Bay shares closed up 0.90 to 27.40 on the Toronto Stock Exchange after the announcement.
William Fields was most recently chief executive of Blockbuster Entertainment Group, a unit of Viacom Inc.
Fields resigned from Blockbuster by mutual agreement on April 22.
Viacom stated that Blockbuster's first quarter performance would fall short of the previous year by 15 to 20 percent.
Fields was chief executive of the stores unit of Wal-Mart from 1995 to 1996.
Hudson's Bay hired another former Wal-Mart executive, Millard Barron, to head its discount department chain Zellers.
Hudson's Bay operates a more upscale chain called the Bay.
Analyst Leonard Kubas stated that having two former Wal-Mart executives would give Hudson's Bay an advantage in merchandising and marketing.

iStar Internet Inc's new chief executive is Craig Wallace.
Craig Wallace stated that iStar would post a reduced third-quarter loss on Friday.
iStar experienced a heavy second-quarter loss.
Wallace claimed that earnings will improve in Q4 compared to Q2.
iStar's net losses in the second quarter were C$10.5 million or C$0.50 a share.
The first-quarter loss for iStar was C$8.1 million or C$0.43 a share.
iStar did not provide previous year comparisons due to acquisitions changing the firm's structure.
Wallace joined iStar in June and became CEO in January.
Before joining iStar, Wallace was the director of marketing at Microsoft Canada Inc.
iStar has not posted a profitable quarter since going public in November 1995.

Corel Corp plans to increase its market share from Microsoft Corp through up to five deals for its office software.
Corel's Chief Executive Michael Cowpland stated that these deals could result in yearly sales of about two million software units.
The announcements for these deals are expected in the next two to three months.
Cowpland mentioned that these sales would bring Corel's total to about seven million units a year when combined with a previous agreement with Packard Bell NEC Inc.
Packard Bell NEC Inc. is a unit of NEC Corp.
Corel acquired WordPerfect from Novell Inc in January 1996 to compete with Microsoft.
Microsoft has yearly revenues of almost $9 billion and is approximately 30 times larger than Corel.
Corel reported revenues of $334 million for the year ending November 30, 1996.
Corel currently holds 20 to 25 percent of total office suite sales.
Corel plans to launch specialized software suites, including one for the legal profession, which will be priced at twice the regular office suite price of $200.

The Shanghai Metal Exchange is China's flagship futures bourse.
The exchange aims to become Asia's premier metals trading floor.
Economic realities are currently hindering the exchange's ambitions.
Total turnover since the exchange opened in May 1992 has exceeded 180 billion yuan ($21 billion).
Regulatory efforts have reduced speculation on the exchange.
The exchange has 120 members, including China's largest base metals producers.
The central government uses the exchange's prices to monitor the market.
Turnover on the exchange decreased from 455.8 billion yuan in 1995 to 230 billion yuan last year due to measures introduced in 1994 and 1995.
The Shanghai Metal Exchange is not yet a significant player on the world trading stage.
Foreign investors are prohibited from trading on China's futures exchanges.

Chinese end-users of copper are buying the metal in small lots.
Chinese trading sources stated that high world prices would prevent significant Chinese buying in the short term.
A fall in copper stocks held in London Metal Exchange (LME) warehouses was not fully due to Chinese buying.
LME copper stocks fell by 9,675 tonnes to 187,777 tonnes last Friday.
Most of the copper material that left LME warehouses was reportedly on its way to China.
A Chinese trader in Hong Kong stated that only one third of the stock moving out of LME warehouses would head to China.
A trader in Beijing indicated that China was more likely to sell copper at current prices.
LME three months prices finished at $2,367 a tonne, down $1 from the previous close.
Figures from the Shanghai Metal Exchange (SME) showed an increase in copper supplies held on warrant of 664 tonnes to 13,522 tonnes.
Another Chinese trading source noted that some end-users were placing small orders of 500 to 2,000 tonnes.

Far East metals traders were focused on whether China would buy copper during the current price rally.
Traders and industry sources polled by Reuters believed that copper prices would continue to rise.
Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) finished higher on Friday, reaching 8-1/2 month highs.
Copper was priced at $2,366 a tonne at the afternoon kerb close on the LME.
Copper prices on the Shanghai Metal Exchange (SME) have been rising in line with the LME since trading resumed after the Lunar New Year holiday.
Shanghai copper futures for the May 1997 contract opened at 23,500 yuan ($2,831) a tonne on Monday.
Shanghai copper futures rose 190 yuan from the previous week's close before falling back to 23,460 yuan in early trading.
Trading sources indicated that Chinese buyers would remain in the market as long as prices on the LME and SME continue to rise.
Shanghai Metal Exchange figures reported copper stocks at 17,524 tonnes.
A trader noted that there had been some signs of Chinese buying, but it was limited to a few hundred tonnes.

Russia sold platinum, palladium, and diamonds in 1995 and 1996.
The sales were intended to save Russia's economy from ruin.
Officials stated that the near-depletion of strategic gold stockpiles does not indicate large bullion exports.
The sales exceeded planned levels.
The exact size of secret stocks of precious metals and diamonds in Russia is unclear.
Russia is a major supplier of precious metals and diamonds to world markets.
A Central Bank official stated that gold had not been exported.
Natalya Khomenko, deputy press director, said that strategic reserves were nearly empty due to bank purchases.
The Central Bank's gold reserves, used to defend the ruble, were reported to be 400 tons.
Russia's Audit Chamber reported that precious metals and diamond exports in 1995 were 50 percent above planned levels.

Chechnya's main oil refinery previously supplied paraffin wax to the Vatican for holy candles.
The refinery is currently inactive and deteriorating after two years of war.
Russian bombs no longer fall on Grozny, the capital of Chechnya.
The refinery faces challenges from local Chechens who steal oil to produce illicit petrol.
The illicit petrol industry in Chechnya is described as unmatched anywhere else in the world.
Many local people collect crude oil from idled wells to produce low-quality gasoline.
The illicit trade provides some income for Chechnya's population, which has been left destitute by fighting.
The illegal oil trade is hindering the reconstruction of the oil industry, which was vital during Soviet times.
Rebel leader Dzhokhar Dudayev promised Chechens a prosperous future with oil riches, which has not materialized.
Black-market refining has become one of the few sources of income in Chechnya.

Russian oil-for-sugar barter deals with Cuba have been a part of trade since Soviet times.
Market economy principles have affected the traditional barter deals between Russia and Cuba.
The last barter arrangement for 1996 has not yet been completed.
One of the Russian commodities houses involved in the 1996 deal has lost money and will likely not engage in future deals.
A source at Alfa-Eko stated that there are currently no discussions about new deals.
Alfa-Eko is involved in resolving issues from the 1996 deal, which has extended into 1997.
Alfa-Eko owes Havana about 200,000 tonnes of oil and is owed about half as much cane sugar.
The barter practice began in the 1960s when Soviet Moscow sold oil to Havana and purchased Cuban sugar at inflated prices.
Havana resells crude oil on world markets, while Russian sugar refineries receive a steady supply of sugar.
Menatep-Impex plans to complete its portion of the 1996 deal in the first quarter of 1997.

French oil groups Total SA and Elf Aquitaine signed contracts with Iraq to buy crude oil under a United Nations oil-for-food deal.
Total SA signed a contract to take 30,000 barrels of oil per day, conditional on United Nations approval.
A spokesman for Total stated that they reached an agreement with Iraq to take 30,000 barrels per day and are awaiting United Nations approval.
Elf Aquitaine signed a three-month deal but did not disclose the amount of oil it would take.
A spokesman for Elf Aquitaine stated that they signed the deal on Friday and submitted it for United Nations approval.
Under the U.N. programme, Iraq may sell $2 billion of crude oil to finance purchases of food and medicine.
The U.N. plan was agreed in principle in May after negotiations but was delayed due to an Iraqi assault on Kurdish rebels.
Oil companies will reimburse Iraq for the oil through payments into an Iraqi account in New York.
Mitsubishi Corp of Japan signed a deal to take 40,000 barrels per day.
The United Nations has approved five contracts for oil sales.

French oil group Elf Aquitaine signed an oil exploration deal with Azerbaijan.
Azerbaijan is described by France as the next oil Eldorado.
The contract is part of a series of Western oil deals in the Caspian Sea region.
The Caspian Sea region contains significant oil reserves despite ethnic conflicts and disputes over pipeline rights.
Elf signed a production sharing contract for the offshore Lenkoran-Talysh Deniz permit with Azeri national oil firm Socar.
The contract was signed in the presence of Azeri President Haydar Aliyev and French President Jacques Chirac.
Elf will hold a 65 percent stake as operator in the field, while Socar will have 25 percent.
Total SA holds a 10 percent stake in the project, with negotiations ongoing for other companies to join.
The oil exploration deal is estimated to be worth around $2 billion, according to Azeri news reports.
The Lenkoran-Talysh Deniz project covers an area of 420 square kilometers in waters up to 100 meters deep.

The French government called off the sale of Thomson SA to Lagardere Groupe.
President Jacques Chirac intends to complete the sale of Thomson SA.
The French government faced employee protests and political opposition regarding the sale.
The Privatisation Commission questioned the terms of a South Korean firm's involvement in the sale.
Catherine Colonna, Chirac's spokeswoman, stated that the French defence electronics industry is world class.
Colonna claimed that the privatisation of Thomson is essential for creating 'poles of excellence'.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis announced that the privatisation process would be delayed by several weeks.
Francois-Michel Gonnot, a parliamentary committee chairman, indicated that the delay could extend to several months or a year.
Lagardere planned to merge Thomson's defence electronics unit with its Matra Defense Espace unit.
The Privatisation Commission reported that the Daewoo deal did not reflect the full value of Thomson's technology.

The Australian state of Victoria announced plans to sell its gas monopoly, Gascor.
Victoria Treasurer Alan Stockdale made the announcement at a gas reform conference.
An industry consultant estimated that the sell-off of Gascor would generate around A$4 billion for the government.
Gascor will be split into three separate, competing distributors by July 1.
The sale of Gascor is planned to occur from mid-1998.
The Victoria government has sold over A$13 billion worth of electricity assets.
Gascor has 1.4 million customers throughout Melbourne, 50 towns in rural Victoria, and some border towns in New South Wales state.
Gascor's balance sheet shows net assets of A$1.14 billion.
Interest in the Gascor businesses is likely to come from private power utilities and new foreign entrants.
Under the terms of the Victoria privatisation, gas prices will be capped below the cost of inflation until the year 2001.

Australia's labour market watchdog is expected to award a wage rise to the nation's lowest-paid workers on Tuesday.
The wage rise is likely to have implications for inflation and interest rates.
The Industrial Relations Commission is preparing to arbitrate between the trade union movement and employers.
The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) has requested a wage rise of A$20 per week for the lowest paid.
The ACTU has also requested rises in minimum rates of pay of up to 8.75 percent.
Employers oppose the wage rise, claiming it will harm the economy.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) estimates that granting the ACTU's claim in full would increase the nation's total wages bill by 1.6 percent.
The RBA's estimate would raise the rate of wages growth to about 5.5 percent, above its comfort zone of 4.0-4.5 percent.
Employers warn that granting the ACTU claim could lead to unemployment exceeding one million and rising inflation.
Australia's jobless rate was 8.7 percent in March and has been above 8.5 percent since early 1995.

Amcor Ltd reported a significant decline in half-year profit.
Amcor's net profit before abnormal items fell by 34 percent to A$140.6 million for the six months ending December 31.
The reported profit was slightly below the average market forecast of A$145 million.
Amcor provided a negative outlook for the remainder of the 1996/97 fiscal year.
The decline in profit was attributed to a steep fall in paper prices from historic highs in the same period of 1995/96.
Amcor experienced a squeeze on margins from customers in the packaging businesses.
Despite an overall increase in production volumes, earnings were negatively impacted.
Amcor managing director Don Macfarlane described the half-year trading conditions as 'limped along.'
Amcor's share price closed 14 cents lower at A$8.35 on Thursday.
Brokers indicated that Amcor's share price decline reflected the company's negative comments about the rest of the 1996/97 fiscal year.

Boeing Co. scrapped plans to build a stretch version of its 747 jumbo jet.
Boeing shares increased by $5.625 to $112.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The rise in Boeing shares contributed significantly to the Dow Jones industrial average.
Boeing is one of 30 stocks in the Dow Jones industrial average.
Industry analysts estimated that scrapping the 747 stretch project could reduce Boeing's research and development costs by over $2 billion in five years.
Analysts also estimated that the decision could boost Boeing's annual earnings by up to $1 per share.
NatWest Securities analyst Nick Heymann stated that the decision removed uncertainty for Boeing as it increases production.
Boeing is preparing to complete a $14 billion purchase of McDonnell Douglas Corp.
Airbus Industrie plans to proceed with the development of the A-3XX superjumbo jetliner.
Heymann expressed doubt about Airbus's ability to fund the A-3XX project.

Starbucks Corp. executives defended the company's coffee buying practices at the annual shareholders meeting.
Chairman Howard Schultz stated that Starbucks has been unfairly targeted due to its high visibility.
Schultz threatened to stop buying Guatemalan coffee if activists continued to criticize Starbucks.
Schultz claimed that Starbucks is committed to improving conditions for Third World farmers.
Schultz mentioned that Starbucks donated $300,000 to the aid group CARE to help workers in Guatemala and other coffee-growing nations.
Starbucks has established a partnership with Appropriate Technology International to assist small-scale producers in Central America.
Bruce Herbert, director of the Northwest Coalition for Responsible Investment, acknowledged Starbucks' contributions but criticized the company for not adhering to its code of conduct.
Schultz announced the establishment of the Starbucks Foundation to support aid projects in cities where Starbucks operates.
The Starbucks Foundation will receive royalties and a $500,000 advance from Schultz's upcoming book.
Schultz expressed concern about rising coffee prices but remained confident that Starbucks would meet Wall Street earnings estimates.

Microsoft Corp. plans to announce a version of its Windows 95 operating system for hand-held consumer devices.
The new Windows CE system for consumer electronics will be available this year.
Microsoft previously abandoned a project called Winpad due to high memory requirements.
The growth of the Internet has increased market possibilities for small wireless devices.
Oracle Corp. has popularized the concept of a $500 consumer device for Internet access.
Microsoft officials declined to comment on the announcement but indicated it would be significant.
Microsoft executives had previously disclosed plans to supply a system for hand-held devices by the holiday season.
The hand-held devices will be marketed by eight companies, including Hewlett-Packard Co., Casio Computer Co. Ltd., and Philips Electronics NV.
The operating system will include stripped-down versions of Microsoft's Word and Excel applications.
Analysts believe the devices will initially be used for accessing electronic mail and personal information.

Land mines may delay Angola's attempts to rebuild its coffee industry for decades.
Output could rise tenfold in the short term with better access to areas once cut off by war.
The last government figure for coffee production before the war was 40,000 tonnes.
Secretary of State for Coffee Gilberto Lutucuta stated the objective is to produce 50-60,000 tonnes over the next four to five years.
Exports through official channels in 1995/96 totalled 5,000-6,000 tonnes.
Lutucuta expressed hope to double production in 1996/97.
Angola's government signed a peace deal with UNITA in 1994.
In the early 1970s, Angola was the world's main supplier of robusta coffee and Africa's second largest coffee producer, yielding 230,000 tonnes in 1973.
Most of the 1995/96 exports came from southern farms, while 70 percent of potential coffee production lay in the north in UNITA areas.
Military mine clearance units set up in 1995 are working in each province under local government control.

The El Nino weather pattern developing in the Pacific could damage West African cocoa crops.
The extent of any losses from El Nino is hard to predict due to local weather and crop patterns.
Industry analysts noted that El Nino sometimes affects yields and sometimes does not.
The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration reported that weather in the Pacific had triggered an El Nino weather pattern.
El Nino is expected to affect world crops.
Cocoa futures for July contracts reached a new high of 1,085 stg a tonne in London trading.
Long-term price effects of cocoa futures depend on traders' views on supply deficits into 1997/98.
El Nino is a reversal of ocean water circulation in the southern Pacific.
El Nino is generally associated with droughts in parts of Africa, Australia, Indonesia, and South America.
In 1976/77, El Nino reduced Nigerian cocoa production from a possible 220,000 tonnes to around 160,000 tonnes.

African coffee producers will meet on March 6-7 to discuss a robusta export limit set in Brazil.
The Interafrican Coffee Organisation (IACO) announced the meeting to Reuters.
IACO Secretary General Arega Worku stated that ministers will discuss exports and implementation decisions.
The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) held an emergency meeting in Rio de Janeiro last month.
Members of the ACPC agreed to cut robusta exports by one million bags and arabica exports by 300,000 bags between January and June 1997.
The IACO Special Ministers Conference will take place in Abidjan, Ivory Coast.
The conference will include ministers from IACO's 25 member states under IACO Chairman Guy-Alain Gauze.
Worku claimed that the initiative of African producers boosted coffee prices.
IACO last met in Abidjan for its 36th General Assembly in November.
Ivory Coast has forecast a 1996/97 crop of 230,000 tonnes but has faced quality problems.

A former U.S. surgeon general will testify in a class-action trial regarding cigarette makers' actions in the 1970s.
Dr. Jesse Steinfeld will testify on behalf of approximately 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants.
The flight attendants claim damages for illnesses allegedly caused by second-hand smoke on passenger jets.
A jury trial in Dade County Court is scheduled to begin on June 2.
This trial will be the first class-action suit against the tobacco industry in the United States.
A second class-action suit on behalf of all Florida smokers is scheduled for trial in Miami in September.
Rosenblatt claims that the tobacco industry impeded public access to information about second-hand smoke.
Steinfeld is also scheduled to testify for Mississippi in a lawsuit against tobacco companies regarding Medicaid costs.
Twenty-one states, including Florida, have filed similar lawsuits against tobacco companies.
Michael York, a lawyer for Philip Morris, stated that there is no credible evidence that second-hand smoke causes disease.

U.S. cigarette makers are diversified cash-generating companies with overseas markets.
Tobacco exports from the United States were worth $5.24 billion last year.
Tobacco exports accounted for roughly 20 percent of the country's total net agricultural surplus.
Cigarette export volumes rose 5.5 percent to a record 243.9 billion.
Japan is the biggest buyer of American cigarettes.
Roy Burry, an analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, stated that overseas demand for cigarettes is increasing.
Most major cigarette companies, except Liggett Corp, are diversified with interests in food and beverages.
Philip Morris Cos Inc and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp generate over half of their revenues from snacks, beer, cereals, and desserts.
Analyst Anton Brenner at UBS Securities noted that U.S. companies are building warehouses and plants overseas.
Liggett, a unit of Brooke Group Ltd, agreed to cooperate with state attorneys general suing tobacco companies.

Cigarette companies will face a class-action anti-smoking case in a Florida court.
The case is known as Broin vs. Philip Morris Co., et al.
Richard Daynard is an anti-smoking activist and heads the Tobacco Products Liability Project at Northeastern University.
The plaintiffs in the case are 60,000 airline flight attendants who are not smokers.
The case claims that the flight attendants' lung cancer and other illnesses were caused by passengers' cigarette smoke.
Smoking was banned on U.S. airliners in 1988.
Professor Michael Zimmer stated that tobacco companies' traditional defense is weakened because the plaintiffs are not smokers.
The case is named for Norma Broin, who is 42 years old and suffering from lung cancer.
Witnesses for the flight attendants will include two former U.S. surgeon generals and experts on secondhand smoke.
A recent Harvard University study found a strong link between heart disease and secondhand smoke.

China will retain controls over the price it pays farmers for grain after reforms.
Minister of state economic restructuring Li Tieying announced plans to unify grain prices.
The reform aims to boost the role of the market in the agricultural sector.
Provincial authorities will have the final say on the price paid for grain.
Wang Lingui of the State Grain Reserve Administration stated that purchasing prices will be based on market prices.
Wang noted that market trends are not the only factors in determining purchasing prices.
Grain traders reported that the difference between state purchase prices and market prices has narrowed.
Analysts expressed concern that future bumper crops could lower market prices and farm incomes.
China's government has historically paid lower-than-market prices for grain to stock state granaries.
The annual state grain-collection quota of 50 million tonnes will remain unchanged under the planned reforms.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin met with future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa in Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
Jiang Zemin pledged support to Tung Chee-hwa and vowed not to interfere with Hong Kong's autonomy.
Tung Chee-hwa is appointed to lead Hong Kong starting July 1 next year.
Tung Chee-hwa is a shipping magnate and will be Hong Kong's first Chinese chief executive after over 150 years of British colonial rule.
Tung Chee-hwa was formally appointed by Premier Li Peng on a Monday prior to the meeting with Jiang.
Jiang Zemin assured Tung that Beijing would adhere to the Basic Law, which grants Hong Kong a degree of autonomy.
Jiang stated that Beijing would not interfere in matters within the scope of Hong Kong's autonomy as a Special Administrative Region.
Tung Chee-hwa's visit to Beijing is being closely monitored by Hong Kong residents interested in his plans for the post-colonial administration.
Tung has not yet provided details about his plans but indicated he would discuss transition issues during his visit.
China stated that it would make the final decision on important civil servants in Hong Kong.

China and the United States signed a new textile agreement on Sunday.
The agreement ended the threat of a cross-Pacific trade war.
Both sides hailed the agreement as a breakthrough.
U.S. officials stated that the main achievement was assured access to Chinese textile markets.
The agreement granted China a U.S. import quota slightly larger than the previous 1994 textile pact.
Penalties imposed by Washington on Chinese imports remained in force under the deal.
Beijing agreed to withdraw its threat of retaliation according to U.S. textile negotiator Rita Hayes.
The four-year textile accord was signed by Rita Hayes and Li Dongsheng.
The negotiations for the agreement extended beyond the original three-day schedule to six days.
The accord aimed to create U.S. jobs by allowing exports while slightly increasing China's U.S. import quota.

Global One is a telecommunications venture owned by Sprint Corp., Deutsche Telekom AG, and France Telecom.
Global One lost almost $370 million in 1996, exceeding the expected loss of $250 million.
Sources indicate that the partners of Global One are considering job cuts due to the losses.
Sprint Corp. owns a 33 percent stake in Global One.
Deutsche Telekom AG and France Telecom own the remaining 67 percent of Global One.
Analysts expect losses of up to $250 million for Sprint, with $85 million attributable to Sprint.
Sprint recorded $51 million of the expected losses in the first nine months of 1996.
Sprint plans to report its fourth quarter results on February 4.
First Call's analyst consensus for Sprint's fourth quarter earnings has decreased to 69 cents per share.
Global One currently employs 2,900 people and has over $800 million in orders expected for the year.

The cable TV industry is valued at $25 billion.
The regional Bells' local phone market is valued at $95 billion.
Many cable TV projects have been abandoned or are on hold.
Analysts believe high-speed Internet services are more appealing than local telephone services.
The threat of satellite TV has caused cable TV firms to defend their market.
Peter Kreisky is a consultant at Mercer Management Consulting.
Most cable TV firms are burdened with debt.
Cable TV firms have deprioritized local phone initiatives due to regulatory and technological uncertainties.
Joann Dobbs is a spokeswoman for Tele-Communications Inc (TCI).
TCI has 15 million customers.

AT&T Corp. announced a 5.9 percent increase in basic U.S. rates for state-to-state calls from a home, effective December 1.
The average increase will add 60 cents a month to the typical residential bill.
AT&T stated that the rate increase is to fund investments in service expansion, technical infrastructure, and customer service improvements.
Small business call rates will rise by 4.8 percent for international, toll-free, and some other services.
The cost of calls made with a calling card will increase by 5 percent.
Calls made with the assistance of an AT&T operator will see a 2.6 percent increase.
Monthly fees for the Reach Out America, SelectSaver, and AnyHour Saver calling plans will increase.
AT&T stopped marketing those plans in 1993 when it introduced the 'True' family of calling plans.
Rates on the True savings plans will also rise because they are based on a percentage discount from the basic rate.
The new One Rate plan introduced this fall will not be affected by the rate increases.

ReliaStar Financial Corp chairman John Turner announced a $488 million merger deal with Security-Connecticut Corp.
The merger aims to broaden the insurance products sold by both firms.
Turner stated that Security-Connecticut has product lines and distribution that complement ReliaStar's offerings.
The merger is a stock-for-stock transaction that values Security-Connecticut at $47 a share.
The merger is expected to result in at least $7.0 million in annual pretax cost reductions.
An additional $2.0 million may be saved through the consolidation of operations in New York.
Turner indicated that the main benefit of the deal will be in cross-selling products.
ReliaStar offers variable life and annuity products, while Security-Connecticut provides second-to-die universal life and term life products.
Turner stated that the deal will not negatively impact earnings in 1997 and will be slightly accretive in 1998.
Security-Connecticut will gain access to a stronger balance sheet to support its life insurance operations.

A 90-cent increase in the U.S. minimum wage will have little short-term impact on most fast food restaurants.
Competition for workers is keeping pay rates above the federally mandated minimum wage standard.
George Goulson is the senior vice president of A&W Restaurants Inc.
Workers already making more than the new minimum wage may seek raises to maintain their pay premium.
President Clinton signed into law a rise in the minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.15 an hour.
Denny Lynch is the spokesman for Wendy's International Inc.
Wendy's average crew wage is about $5.20 an hour.
Higher minimum wages will raise total wages by about $500,000 over the next 12 months at American Restaurant Partners L.P.
American Restaurant Partners L.P. operates 62 Pizza Hut restaurant franchises.
Competition for workers has forced many fast-food chains to pay higher wages, particularly in metropolitan markets.

Bagel sales are increasing as more restaurants open in the United States.
The number of companies involved in bagel baking is expected to decrease.
Howard Penney, a Morgan Stanley analyst, stated that the bagel industry is consolidating.
Smaller, regional chains are expected to be acquired by larger, publicly traded firms.
Access to capital will be a key factor in determining dominant players in the bagel industry.
Allan Hickok, a Piper Jaffray analyst, believes that Einstein/Noah Bagel Corp. will become the dominant chain due to access to capital.
Einstein/Noah Bagel Corp. currently operates more than 315 stores in 27 states and the District of Columbia.
Einstein spokesman Gary Gerdemann stated that the company expects to become No. 1 by the end of 1997 and plans to open 300 to 350 stores this year.
Bruegger's Bagel Bakeries, a unit of Quality Dining Inc., currently ranks No. 1 with 450 units in 37 states.
Chris Romoser, a spokesman for Bruegger's, indicated that the company plans to open a triple-digit number of new stores this year.

A dispute over civil liberties in Hong Kong has led Britain and the United States to warn China to respect a treaty pledge.
A Beijing-controlled panel proposed scrapping Hong Kong laws on civil liberties and elections.
The proposed changes would affect part of Hong Kong's Bill of Rights when China takes over on July 1.
China stated that the issue is an internal affair.
Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, attempted to reduce tensions regarding the controversy.
China plans to replace the elected Legislative Council with a provisional legislature.
China aims to block a British law that would prevent crackdowns on dissent.
Opponents of China argue that these steps violate promises to maintain Hong Kong's freedoms as a Special Administrative Region.
The United States expressed deep concern about attempts to weaken civil liberties in Hong Kong.
Britain's minister for Hong Kong, Jeremy Hanley, summoned the Chinese ambassador to protest the proposals.

Hong Kong's chief judge is Sir Ti Liang Yang.
Sir Ti Liang Yang announced his candidacy for the leadership of Hong Kong on Tuesday.
Yang's announcement has raised concerns about a conflict of interest regarding his role in the judiciary.
Lawyer Martin Lee stated that it is important for the judiciary to be seen as independent.
Emily Lau, a pro-democracy legislator, echoed concerns about Yang's candidacy.
Pro-China politician Tsang Yok-sing suggested that Yang should resign as Chief Justice.
Tsang Yok-sing welcomed Yang's candidacy but emphasized the need for him to step down.
Nihal Jayawickrama, a law professor, stated that Yang should resign now that he has entered politics.
Hong Kong is set to revert to Chinese rule in 300 days.
Other potential candidates for leadership include Anson Chan, Tung Chee-hwa, and T.S. Lo.

Edmund Ho is a banker, community leader, and philanthropist in Macau.
Ho is considered a potential leader of Macau after China's takeover.
Ho stated that he does not think about future greatness.
Ho expressed concern that thinking about greatness would change his character.
Ho is the executive director of Tai Fung Bank, Macau's second-largest bank.
A copy of James Clavell's novel 'Noble House' is in Ho's office.
Ho is widely regarded as a candidate for Macau's chief executive when Portugal returns the territory to China in 1999.
Ho is known as the best-known local public figure in Macau.
Macau has a population of approximately 450,000 people.
Macau's per capita GDP is reported to be US$17,000, but economists believe this figure is distorted by casino earnings.

Rival bidders in the privatisation of Thomson-CSF need to engage Aerospatiale to improve their chances of winning.
France is selling Thomson-CSF as part of a defence industry restructuring that will impact Aerospatiale's business.
The French government will consult Aerospatiale's chairman regarding offers for Thomson-CSF.
The government has excluded Aerospatiale from bidding for Thomson-CSF due to its status as a public sector company.
A defence ministry official stated that Aerospatiale entering the bidding would disrupt the privatisation process.
Alcatel Alsthom has included Aerospatiale and Dassault Industries in its bid for Thomson-CSF.
Lagardere is competing against Alcatel Alsthom for Thomson-CSF.
Aerospatiale has close ties with Thomson-CSF and will be directly affected by its sale.
Lagardere has requested access to financial and industrial information on Aerospatiale to support its bid.
Aerospatiale and Lagardere compete in the markets for missiles and satellites.

Eurotunnel SA/Plc will release first-half results on Monday.
Analysts contacted by Reuters believe forecasting Eurotunnel's figures is futile due to uncertainties over its debt restructuring.
Olivier Machou, an analyst at brokerage Leven, stated that resolving the financial situation is crucial for Eurotunnel.
Machou mentioned that the results are hard to forecast due to price competition with ferries.
One analyst indicated that half-year figures are not reliable for stock evaluation, especially before the summer season.
A London-based broker commented that forecasting is not worthwhile as everything depends on debt negotiations.
An analyst at a large French brokerage estimated a net loss of 2.5 billion francs and an operating loss of around 100 million francs for Eurotunnel.
Eurotunnel needs to finalize a refinancing deal for its bank debt by the end of September.
Eurotunnel reported first-half sales of 1.79 billion francs, an increase from 806 million francs the previous year.
Jeff Summers, head of research at Klesch and Co, noted that Eurotunnel's headline figures may be inflated due to not having all services running a year ago.

Alcatel Alsthom and Lagardere submitted firm offers for Thomson-CSF.
British Aerospace Plc is investing 300 million pounds in Lagardere's offer.
GEC Plc signed memoranda of understanding with both bidders for Thomson-CSF.
The French government is selling its 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF.
The French government set a midday deadline for bidders to submit proposals.
The French government aims to build a national champion before European consolidation.
Alcatel and Dassault Industries submitted a joint bid for Thomson-CSF.
Dassault is offering to merge its Dassault Electronique subsidiary with Thomson-CSF.
Alcatel and Dassault stated they could finance the acquisition without compromising Thomson-CSF's resources.
Lagardere plans to issue a five billion franc bond to help fund its acquisition of Thomson-CSF.

ITT broke into three companies in 1995.
Top executives claimed the move would increase value for stockholders, fuel growth, and enhance competitiveness.
ITT Corp is the hotel, casino, and entertainment division of the former conglomerate.
Industry competition has intensified since the split.
ITT Corp's expansion plan has faced unexpected difficulties.
The company's stock price has significantly declined in recent months.
Hilton Hotels Corp is preparing a $6.5 billion hostile takeover of ITT Corp.
ITT Corp's assets include well-known properties such as the New York Knicks, Sheraton hotels, and Madison Square Garden.
Bruce Raabe of Collins & Co stated that ITT has historically acquired high-quality assets.
Industry analysts believe Hilton's $55 cash and stock offer undervalues ITT Corp.

CSX Corp. amended its merger agreement with Conrail Inc. to increase its offer by $870 million.
The total value of CSX's offer for Conrail is $9.5 billion.
CSX is competing with Norfolk Southern Corp., which has made a $10 billion bid for Conrail.
Conrail has rejected Norfolk Southern's offer, stating that a deal with CSX is a better fit.
The new agreement includes an additional $16 per share for Conrail shareholders, payable in CSX convertible preferred shares.
An industry analyst estimated the value of the new CSX-Conrail deal at $104 per share.
Conrail Chairman David LeVan stated that the merger offers the best result for Conrail.
Norfolk Southern indicated it would continue its efforts to acquire Conrail and may raise its bid.
CSX and Conrail established a voting trust to accelerate payments to Conrail shareholders by 1997.
The revised deal prohibits CSX and Conrail from pursuing a merger with another company before the end of 1998.

CSX Corp made a sweetened bid for Conrail Inc.
The new bid is more appealing to Conrail shareholders than the previous offer.
The new terms are financially more attractive and reduce investor risk.
A provision in the new bid prohibits either company from pursuing another partner until the end of 1998.
Norfolk Southern Corp has a higher offer and is expected to raise its bid.
Peter Gleason, an analyst at Institutional Shareholder Services, stated that the new terms do not guarantee the deal.
The new terms raise the previous bid by about $870 million by offering shareholders convertible preferred shares valued at $16 each.
CSX has already bought 19.9 percent of Conrail in a cash tender offer and seeks to buy another 20.1 percent.
The new terms value Conrail at about $104 per share, or $9.5 billion in cash and stock.
Norfolk Southern's offer is $10 billion at $110 per share in cash.

The Federal Trade Commission approved Time Warner Inc.'s $6.5 billion purchase of Turner Broadcasting System Inc.
The approval was granted after the deal was restructured to meet antitrust laws.
The FTC voted 3-2 to permit the revised transaction.
The original merger proposal was alleged to allow Time Warner to raise cable-TV prices and limit programming choices.
Commissioners Mary Azcuenaga and Roscoe Starek voted against the agreement, stating the deal did not violate antitrust laws.
The merger would create the world's largest media and entertainment company once completed.
The Federal Communications Commission is expected to give its approval soon.
Time Warner and Turner have scheduled meetings for October 10 for their shareholders to approve the transaction.
The merger was restructured to reduce Tele-Communications Inc.'s influence over the new company.
TCI currently owns 21 percent of Turner stock and would own about 7.5 percent of the combined Time Warner-Turner under the merger.

Regulators will host an auction on Tuesday for radio service licenses.
Supporters claim the auction will introduce a new nationwide radio service.
Critics argue the auction may cost U.S. taxpayers millions in lost revenue.
Two licenses for coast-to-coast satellite radio programming are available.
Digital radio will provide CD-quality sound and specialized programming.
William Caldwell is the president of Digital Satellite Broadcasting Corp.
The FCC limited the auction to four companies that applied by the end of 1992.
Chairman Reed Hundt and Commissioner Susan Ness favored opening the auction to more bidders.
Commissioner Rachelle Chong argued that opening the bidding would be unfair to the four applicants.
Digital radio is expected to be subscription-based, costing about $10 a month.

Regulators approved plans to auction two airwave licenses for new nationwide radio services.
The new radio services will be beamed coast-to-coast via satellite and offer CD-quality reception.
The Federal Communications Commission will limit the April 1 sale to four companies that applied by the end of 1992.
The four companies are CD Radio Inc., American Mobile Radio Corp., Digital Broadcast Satellite Corp., and Primosphere LP.
Listeners will need to buy a special radio receiver costing about $200 to access the new service.
The new service is likely to be subscription-based, with an expected cost of about $10 a month.
Operators will be able to offer specialized programming.
CD Radio plans to provide 30 channels of commercial-free music programming if it wins a license.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt and Commissioner Susan Ness favored an open auction for all bidders.
The FCC plans to announce auction plans for a separate airwave slice for wireless technology.

Sun Microsystems Inc. will unveil its first high-end computer servers that can compete with mainframe performance.
Ed Zander is the president of Sun Microsystems Computer Co.
The new servers are capable of more than four times the processing performance of an International Business Machines Corp. mainframe.
The Ultra Enterprise 10000 servers were code named Starfire.
The servers will be formally unveiled on Wednesday morning at a San Francisco news briefing.
The servers will be priced in the $500,000 to $2 million range.
Sun Microsystems reported its second fiscal quarter revenues of $2.08 billion, a 19 percent increase.
Sun's net income for the second fiscal quarter was $178.3 million, a 41 percent increase.
Goldman Sachs analyst Laura Conigliaro estimates that Sun's sales of servers grew in excess of 45 percent in the fourth quarter of last year.
Sun holds a 41 percent stake in the Unix workstation market, according to a preliminary International Data Corp. survey.

Silicon Graphics Inc. will launch a new line of computer workstations on Monday.
The new line of Octane workstations represents the broadest revamp of Silicon Graphics' product line.
The Octane workstations are designed to strengthen Silicon Graphics' No. 3 position in the Unix workstation market.
Silicon Graphics is based in Mountain View, California.
The company will reduce prices of its Indigo2 Impact 10000 workstations by up to 22 percent.
The Indigo2 Impact 10000 workstations will be positioned between the entry-level O2 machines and the new Octane models.
The Octane workstations are used by engineers for tasks such as oil exploration, molecular modeling, flight simulation, computer-aided design, and video and television.
The new Octane workstations share components with a new supercomputing design unveiled in October.
David Weisberg, publisher of Engineering Automation Report, commented on the elimination of chokepoints in the Octane workstations.
Analysts noted that shipments of Wintel-based PCs surpassed traditional workstations for the first time in 1996.

General Magic Inc. demonstrated components of a new service on Monday.
The service is code-named Serengeti.
Serengeti will allow users to track schedules, electronic mail, voice mail, and telephone call processing.
Mobile workers can check and respond to electronic mail and scheduling details using voice commands.
The system may compete with voicemail providers like Octel Communications Inc. and Siemens' Rolm systems.
Serengeti appears to be the first service that integrates multiple components into one.
Users can check their schedules by computer or cellular telephone.
The service will be accessible from most devices, including desktop PCs, telephones, and pagers.
General Magic Chairman Steve Markman stated that a pilot version of the service will enter testing in May.
General Magic announced a joint technology accord with Starfish Software, Inc. to integrate technologies into the Serengeti service.

Tears flowed and eight bells tolled at a farewell for the Royal Navy in Hong Kong on Friday.
Britain shut its HMS Tamar naval base as part of the colony's return to China on July 1.
Eight bells have rung three times a day for more than 100 years at HMS Tamar, except during the Japanese occupation from 1941 to 1945.
First Sea Lord Admiral Sir Jock Slater, Governor Chris Patten, and other dignitaries spoke at the ceremony.
The White Ensign was lowered, furled, and folded at the base on Stonecutters Island in Hong Kong harbour.
Governor Chris Patten expressed hope that the values represented by the White Ensign would remain in Hong Kong.
Commander Oliver Wright stated that the Royal Navy helped provide stability for commerce and industry in Hong Kong.
More than 200 seamen marched through the gates in white uniforms to music from the Royal Marines' brass band.
HMS Tamar closed 100 years after a vessel of the same name first arrived in Hong Kong waters.
The closure ended a 156-year association between the Royal Navy and Hong Kong.

After July 1, Hong Kong's role as a facilitator of China-Taiwan trade will continue and likely expand.
Experts believe that Hong Kong's reversion to mainland rule will heighten sensitivities between China and Taiwan.
George Leung, an economic adviser at Hongkong Shanghai Banking Corp, stated that triangular trade will not see a negative effect after July 1, but handling of issues will become more sensitive.
Direct trade and investment between China and Taiwan have been banned for 48 years.
The ban on direct business, transport, and communication links dates back to 1949.
Hong Kong has acted as a gateway for indirect Taiwan-China trade and investment due to the ban.
Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty is set for midnight on June 30.
Experts believe the 'one country, two systems' policy will allow the continuation of triangular trade.
Under the 'one country, two systems' policy, Hong Kong will remain a separate customs territory.
China and Taiwan recently sealed a pact to ease diplomatic tensions regarding vessel movements.

The jury is undecided on whether China will cut interest rates later this year.
Hong Kong hopes for a rate cut from China.
Only certain sectors in Hong Kong would benefit from a Chinese rate cut.
Trade and investment between China and Hong Kong move easily across the border.
Banking and monetary systems between China and Hong Kong remain separate.
China's currency is inconvertible and has a capital account that creates a divide between banking systems.
Britain and China have agreed to maintain two separate monetary systems under the 'one country, two systems' policy.
George Leung, an economic adviser at Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, stated that a rate cut would not significantly impact Hong Kong's economy.
A rate cut would reduce financing costs for red chips, which are Hong Kong-listed companies with financial backing in China.
In 1996, Hong Kong's total exports were HK$1,397.7 billion, with China accounting for HK$417.8 billion of its re-exports.

Chinese police cordoned off a South Korean embassy compound in Beijing.
North Korean diplomats waited outside the South Korean embassy compound.
A senior official from Seoul was scheduled for talks with Beijing regarding the defection of a top North Korean official.
Hwang Jang-yop, a senior aide to North Korea's leader Kim Jong-il, was inside the embassy compound.
China did not comment on the diplomatic crisis involving North Korea and South Korea.
South Korea sent Kim Ha-jung, a special adviser to Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha, to Beijing for talks.
Hwang Jang-yop sought asylum along with his assistant Kim Dok-hong.
South Korean embassy officials accused North Koreans of attempting to enter the consular office.
North Korean diplomats waited outside the consular compound and observed from behind police cordons.
North Korean officials accused South Korea of kidnapping Hwang Jang-yop.

U.S. and Chinese negotiators were engaged in talks to establish a new textile accord and a deal on market access.
The deadline for the negotiations was extended by one day to avoid a trade war.
Chief U.S. textile negotiator Rita Hayes expressed confidence in reaching an agreement.
Hayes stated that significant progress had been made during the negotiations.
Negotiations included discussions on renewing a 1994 textile accord and resolving U.S. penalties on Chinese exports.
The United States had imposed $19 million in penalties on Chinese textile imports in September.
China threatened to retaliate by banning imports of certain U.S. goods but delayed action for further talks.
Hayes emphasized the importance of market access and a balanced playing field for the textile industry.
Disagreement over market access in China was identified as a major obstacle to reaching an agreement.
Industry representatives remained hopeful for a deal, with Hayes's team reportedly finalizing the agreement text.

A North Korean embassy official warned that Pyongyang would respond with force if South Korea compelled the highest-level defector to go to Seoul.
The North Korean diplomat stated that if South Korea uses force to move the defector, they will respond with force.
The official expressed determination to prevent the defector from being taken to South Korea.
The official questioned why South Korea does not allow journalists to interview the defector if he really defected.
Tensions between North and South Korea heightened after two suspected North Korean agents shot and seriously wounded a defector in Seoul.
The defector, Li Il-nam, known in South Korea as Lee Han-yong, is the nephew of Sung Hye-rim, former wife of Kim Jong-il.
The South Korean government called an emergency meeting of security-related ministers to discuss the attack.
Chinese police surrounded the South Korean embassy in Beijing and laid spikes on roads to prevent cars from approaching.
A bullet-proof car was parked outside the South Korean mission where Hwang Jang-yop sought asylum.
The North Korean diplomat accused South Korea of kidnapping Hwang, while Seoul dismissed the accusation as preposterous.

Lloyd's of London reassured its traditional backers, known as Names, that there was no hidden agenda to force them out of the insurance market.
Outgoing chairman Sir David Rowland stated, 'Trust us,' in response to concerns from a Name.
Rowland promised that there would be no move to eliminate the annual venture where syndicates are reformed each year.
Rowland supported recent changes in the market that shifted members from unlimited to limited liability.
Rowland announced that upon retirement, he would become a limited liability member of Lloyd's.
Rowland expressed that unlimited personal liability has significant consequences for individuals.
Rowland suggested that new trading structures with continuous capital may be a better route for long-term development.
Rowland warned that without embracing change, Lloyd's would experience a steady decline in its fortunes.
The annual venture and reinsurance to close had previously worked well until significant losses occurred between 1988 and 1992.
Critics have questioned the viability of the annual system of raising capital for Lloyd's, citing its cost and impact on long-term planning.

Halifax Building Society is Britain's largest mortgage lender.
Nearly eight million members of Halifax are expected to receive financial benefits from its flotation on the London stock market on June 2.
The basic handout for members will be 200 shares, valued at around 1,400 pounds ($2,270).
The average payout for members is projected to be 2,170 pounds, which is nearly 900 pounds more than initial forecasts made in January.
Bookmakers City Index and IG Index are quoting the Halifax closing price on its first day of trading at 695-705 pence.
The flotation will value Halifax at over 17-1/2 billion pounds, ranking it among Britain's largest dozen companies.
In January, Halifax estimated the share price would be between 390 and 450 pence.
In April, Halifax set a 415 pence 'floor' value on shares sold through its free dealing service.
Around two-thirds of Halifax members will receive the basic 200 shares windfall, with additional shares based on savings levels.
The maximum allocation for members with both a mortgage account and savings account will be just under 10,000 pounds.

The Treasury may take over regulation of insurance companies from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) under the Labour government's plans for reform of Britain's financial services.
Spokesmen for both the DTI and Treasury stated that no decision has been made on the regulatory changes.
The potential regulatory changes could align insurance with the rest of the financial services sector.
An industry executive suggested that it would be sensible for the Treasury to be responsible for all aspects of insurance regulation.
The boundaries between insurance and banking industries have been eroding, increasing pressure to align supervisory regimes.
Many banks are beginning to offer insurance products, while insurers are providing services such as savings facilities, personal loans, and mortgages.
Currently, the DTI regulates insurance companies to ensure they are financially sound and meet solvency requirements.
Regulation of insurance products is separate, with general insurance regulated by an industry code and life products by the Financial Services Act.
The Financial Services Act is set to be replaced by new legislation following framework reforms announced by Chancellor Gordon Brown.
The creation of a single statutory body, the Securities and Investments Board (SIB), could reduce costs and improve transparency in the insurance sector.

The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) signed an agreement with the Hong Kong Futures Exchange (HKFE) to connect to its NYMEX ACCESS trading system.
The agreement may challenge Singapore's trading advantage.
Officials from both exchanges stated that Hong Kong's cash trading base and expertise are inferior to Singapore's, particularly in the energy sector.
There is a growing demand for risk management and hedging opportunities in Asia due to rising oil and metals use, especially in China.
NYMEX president Patrick Thompson expressed potential in China, South Korea, and the rest of Asia during a news conference after the agreement.
The link with Hong Kong is expected to begin operations around the end of March 1997.
The agreement allows HKFE members to trade existing NYMEX futures and options contracts during local Hong Kong trading hours under a mutual-offset system.
The agreement with HKFE raises doubts about NYMEX's previous intention to cooperate with the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX).
Thompson indicated that the link with Hong Kong and Sydney would make a partnership with SIMEX less likely.
A newly formed Oil Advisory Committee will work on new futures and options contracts tailored to the Asian market.

Martin Lee is an internationally-known democracy campaigner from Hong Kong.
Beijing has branded Martin Lee a 'subversive'.
Martin Lee plans to stay in Hong Kong and fight for civil liberties under China's rule.
Martin Lee does not hold a foreign passport.
Martin Lee is the leader of Hong Kong's democracy movement.
Martin Lee has no intention of leaving Hong Kong before or after June 30.
Martin Lee is the leader of Hong Kong's largest political group, the Democratic Party.
Martin Lee questioned Deng Xiaoping in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing.
Martin Lee was born in Hong Kong in 1938 and is the son of a Nationalist general.
Martin Lee graduated from the University of Hong Kong and began his career as a secondary school teacher.

A second wave of Chinese soldiers arrived in Hong Kong on Monday.
The soldiers are preparing garrison facilities before Beijing takes back the territory from Britain on July 1.
Sixty-six uniformed but unarmed soldiers of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) arrived in Hong Kong.
The soldiers drove into Hong Kong in a fleet of 14 staff vehicles from Shenzhen.
This group is the second PLA contingent to arrive in Hong Kong in two months.
Forty soldiers entered Hong Kong on April 21 to prepare logistics and facilities.
Major-General Liu Zhenwu is the commander of the future garrison in Hong Kong.
Liu officiated a send-off ceremony for the soldiers on the Chinese side of the border.
The British garrison is packing up ahead of its departure at midnight June 30.
China plans to station some 10,000 troops in Hong Kong.

International Business Machines Corp. announced that its $23 billion Global Services business will become a separate IBM group.
IBM Chairman Louis Gerstner stated in the company's annual report that the company plans to hire thousands more employees, primarily in Global Services.
IBM indicated to analysts that it will likely add as many new employees in 1997 as it did in 1996, with a significant number in Global Services.
In 1996, IBM's worldwide head count increased to 241,000, up from 225,000 in 1995, largely due to the expanding services business.
In 1995, IBM's employment grew from 220,000 in 1994, marking the first employment growth in 10 years.
Gerstner expressed pride in the job growth resulting from IBM's transformation in his letter to shareholders, describing 1996 as a solid year.
When Gerstner took over IBM in April 1993, he cut 25,000 jobs and took a significant restructuring charge.
The Global Services unit, which designs, installs, and services computers, was previously part of IBM's Sales and Services group.
IBM's Sales and Services group will be renamed the Sales and Distribution Group, still led by Senior Vice President Ned Lautenbach.
Dennie Welsh, the general manager of Global Services, will be promoted to senior vice president and report directly to Gerstner.

Citrix Systems Inc. lost almost 60 percent of its stock value on Thursday.
Concerns about competition from Microsoft Corp. contributed to the decline in Citrix's stock.
Citrix shares fell $15.625 to $10.625 during heavy trading, with over 13.8 million shares traded.
Citrix was informed by Microsoft that it is developing multi-user features for Windows NT.
Microsoft has a product team working on software that would compete with Citrix's WinFrame.
Microsoft Senior Vice President Jim Allchin confirmed the development team is underway.
Microsoft is in discussions with other companies about licensing technology.
Citrix stated that competition from Microsoft could negatively impact its finances.
Microsoft Treasurer Greg Maffei is a member of Citrix's board of directors.
Microsoft owns approximately 6 percent of Citrix.

International Business Machines Corp. is expected to report fourth-quarter earnings on Tuesday.
Analysts expect the stronger dollar will negatively impact IBM's profits.
IBM is based in Armonk, New York.
IBM will report earnings after the stock market closes.
Wall Street analysts predict earnings of $3.13 to $4.32 per share, with a consensus of $3.88 per share.
A year ago, IBM earned $3.09 per share in the fourth quarter, totaling $1.7 billion including special charges.
Morgan Stanley analyst Steve Milunovich believes it will be a good quarter but not a blowout quarter.
Milunovich noted that the dollar strengthened in the fourth quarter and could negatively impact earnings by 25 cents per share.
Analysts expect IBM to report increased restructuring expenses in the fourth quarter.
Dean Witter analyst Jay Stevens stated that IBM's restructuring costs could be twice as much as the previous quarter.

One hundred years after Cadbury launched Britain's first milk chocolate, the average Briton eats 13 kilos of confectionery each year.
Denmark and Ireland have higher average confectionery consumption than Britain.
The Swiss consume more chocolate than the British, averaging 10 kilos per person per year compared to eight kilos in Britain.
British confectionery sales grew by five percent last year to a record 4.9 billion pounds ($8.28 billion).
Cadbury and Trebor Bassett published a review on Tuesday regarding confectionery sales.
Cadbury marketing director Alan Palmer stated that the market will exceed five billion pounds for the first time next year.
Volume sales in Britain rose by two percent to 833,000 tonnes last year.
The Confectionery Market Review reported a growth of more than 12 percent in confectionery sales over the last decade.
Bruce Burnett, Trebor Bassett marketing director, attributed market expansion to major investment in media advertising and new brand innovation.
Milk chocolate accounts for almost 90 percent of chocolate consumed in Britain.

Guinness Plc reported a 60 million pound hit to its trading profits in 1997 due to the pound's strength against foreign currencies.
Guinness shares fell 5p to 430p before recovering to 432-1/2p.
Analysts expressed disappointment regarding the size of Guinness' currency hit.
Merrill Lynch analyst John Beaumont stated that the underlying trading was as expected, with small improvements.
The consensus forecast for Guinness' pretax profits for the year ended December 31, 1997, was 1.017 billion pounds.
Most analysts do not expect Guinness to exceed one billion pounds in pretax profits.
The average forecast for Guinness' pretax profits for 1996 was 958.5 million pounds.
Grand Metropolitan's shares fell 8p to 426-1/2p.
Grand Metropolitan estimated a loss of about 16 million pounds in profit annually due to the pound's rise.
The pound's trade-weighted index rose from 84.0 to 96.1, an increase of more than 14 percent.

H P Bulmer is Britain's biggest cider maker.
H P Bulmer stated that the impact of alcopops on its business has not been significant.
John Rudgard is the chief executive of H P Bulmer.
The total alcopops market accounts for about 60 percent of the sales volume of Strongbow.
Rudgard acknowledged that alcopops have grown quickly and taken sales from various drinks, primarily lager.
There is some substitution from ciders, but the biggest impact is on fashion type ciders, which Bulmer does not produce.
Bulmer has strong brands that provide insulation against competition.
Matthew Clarke issued a profit warning due to tough competition from alcopops and cheap cider products.
