Paul Martin announced an extension of a 12 percent capital tax surcharge on banks until October 31, 1998.
Of Toronto's 14 sub-indices, four declined, including real estate, pipelines, base metals, and oils.
Advances outnumbered declines on the Toronto Stock Exchange by 539 to 469.

Indium is in short supply due to Chinese producers overselling or hoarding stocks.
Traders reported that Chinese producers are unwilling to sell indium at current prices.
Indium is a by-product of zinc and is used in the manufacture of semi-conductors and liquid crystal displays (LCD).
China is the largest producer of indium in Asia.
Japan consumes about two-thirds of the annual world supply of indium.
Eighty percent of Japan's indium consumption is used to make LCDs.
Japanese consumption of indium slumped 38 percent in 1996 to 43.5 tonnes.
Indium demand is increasing due to an improved economic outlook and a revival in the high-end electronics industry.
Chinese producers are currently seeking $290 per kg for indium on a free-on-board (FOB) basis.
The price for 99.99 percent indium ingot was quoted in Rotterdam at $220-250 per kg last week.

Chinese copper trading sources stated that current copper prices are not supported by fundamentals.
A source from the Shanghai Metal Exchange (SME) expressed doubt about the support for copper prices at $2,400 per tonne.
The London Metal Exchange (LME) copper price reached a nine-month high of $2,445 per tonne before falling to $2,390.
Shanghai copper futures ended lower on Monday due to heavy profit-taking.
The most active June 1997 Shanghai copper contract closed at 23,370 yuan, down 50 yuan.
The SME trading source indicated a selling price of 23,300 yuan per tonne.
Monday's intra-day low for Shanghai copper was 23,200 yuan, with expectations of further declines to 22,800 yuan.
London analysts noted that LME copper was set to test a support level at $2,350.
A trader from the Zhuhai Special Economic Zone suggested that LME copper prices should stabilize between $2,320 and $2,380.
The official China Daily Business Weekly reported that China's demand for copper is projected to reach 1.2 million tonnes in 1997.

China's national flag was at half mast along Shanghai's waterfront Bund on Friday in honor of Deng Xiaoping.
Residents of Shanghai remembered Deng Xiaoping as a man who improved their lives.
Shanghai's press reported stability in local share markets following Deng's death.
Both share market indices in Shanghai ended the day higher after Deng's death.
Police increased their presence throughout Shanghai's suburbs on Friday as a precaution.
Shanghai's 14 million residents learned of Deng Xiaoping's death on Thursday.
Deng Xiaoping died on Wednesday night at the age of 92.
Many residents viewed Deng as a reformer and a strong leader.
Deng's market reforms contributed to Shanghai's status as a financial and industrial powerhouse.
Participants at the Shanghai People's Congress paid tribute to Deng Xiaoping.

Russia's new oil majors aim to take control of crude oil exports from traders.
Domestic oil producers export about one third of their total output of 5.86 million barrels per day.
Producers are competing for control over the federal programmes market.
A senior source at Alfa-Eko stated that producers want to remove trading companies from implementing federal programmes.
Federal programmes involve government decrees authorizing companies to export specific amounts of crude oil.
The amounts authorized for export under federal programmes are increasing.
In 1997, federal programme oil exports are expected to reach 60-70 million tonnes, accounting for 60-70 percent of Russia's total oil exports.
Federal programme exporters, primarily trading firms, retain some proceeds from oil exports.
Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov indicated that the government plans to limit the number of companies exporting oil.
LUKoil's president Vagit Alekperov stated that oil producers should handle exports instead of traders.

Russian economic crime officials are investigating Yuri Kolpakov, the general director of Krasnoyarsk, Russia's second largest aluminium smelter.
The investigation concerns the alleged failure to repatriate $20 million from contracts for raw materials supplies.
Olga Semenyaka, a member of an Interior Ministry investigative committee, opened the investigation on Monday.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov is addressing crime in Russia's aluminium industry.
Russia's aluminium industry was the world's biggest exporter of primary metal last year.
Gennady Druzhinin, Krasnoyarsk's board chairman, confirmed the investigation against Kolpakov.
Druzhinin stated that the investigation would not affect output or exports.
Krasnoyarsk produced 770,000 tonnes of aluminium last year, accounting for 27 percent of Russia's total output of 2.87 million tonnes.
Andrei Grigoryev, head of the smelter's information section, stated he was unaware of the charges against Kolpakov.
The investigation is related to a tolling deal with an offshore company identified as Leo Trust Company.

Russia's Norilsk Nickel is struggling to climb out of debt.
Workers at Norilsk Nickel may be unwilling to strike due to their reliance on the company.
Norilsk's main shareholder is attempting to restructure the company.
Restructuring efforts by Norilsk will not yield quick results.
Labour unrest and output disruptions may occur in the future at Norilsk.
Analysts are considering state aid as a solution to labour unrest at Norilsk.
Union leaders have called for strikes at Norilsk's flagship plant on March 27 and April 2 over wage and holiday arrears.
Norilsk's ability to pay overdue salaries depends on regional budget politics rather than cash from Uneximbank.
Norilsk is trying to transfer the cost of social infrastructure to the Krasnoyarsk region.
Norilsk supports 60 percent of the Krasnoyarsk regional budget.

Rhone-Poulenc SA reported a 28.4 percent increase in net income for 1996, totaling 2.74 billion francs.
Rhone-Poulenc SA's chairman, Jean-Rene Fourtou, stated that the net income level was insufficient.
Fourtou denied rumors that Rhone-Poulenc SA was seeking acquisitions, a merger, or a split of its chemicals and pharmaceuticals activities.
Fourtou announced a focus on internal growth for the company.
Rhone-Poulenc SA aims for a 20 percent increase in earnings per share in 1997, from 8.44 francs in 1996.
The company plans to exceed its two-year asset sale program of 10 billion francs, which was at 6.8 billion francs at the end of 1996.
Rhone-Poulenc SA intends to reduce its debt to below 50 percent of equity, down from 61 percent in 1996 and 72 percent in 1995.
Sales for Rhone-Poulenc SA increased by three percent to 85.818 billion francs.
Operating income rose by 38.5 percent to 6.892 billion francs.
The gross dividend was increased by 16.7 percent to 5.25 francs per share.

Shareholders of Thomson SA approved an 11 billion franc state capital injection.
The French government is reviewing how to relaunch the privatisation process of Thomson SA.
A government official stated that they need time to consider their next steps regarding privatisation.
Industry Minister Franck Borotra met with Thomson worker representatives who opposed the privatisation plans.
The French government announced the suspension of the sale of Thomson SA on Wednesday.
Thomson SA owns 58 percent of Thomson-CSF and all of Thomson Multimedia (TMM).
Approximately 200 Thomson workers marched in Paris to support 15 employees who walked from the Angers plant.
The industry ministry stated that Franck Borotra intends to pursue Thomson's privatisation with detailed terms to follow.
The government suspended the sale of Thomson SA to Lagardere Groupe due to disagreements over terms with the Privatisation Commission.
The French Foreign Ministry issued a statement to ease tensions with South Korea regarding the privatisation process.

Total SA reported a 50 percent rise in its 1996 net income to 5.6 billion francs.
The increase in net income was attributed to higher oil prices, a firmer dollar, improved refining margins, and productivity gains.
The profit figure was in line with financial analysts' expectations.
The profit would have shown a 150 percent increase if 1995 special charges of 1.5 billion francs were considered.
Operating income rose by 37 percent to 10.2 billion francs.
Sales increased by 30 percent to 176 billion francs.
Total chairman Thierry Desmarest noted that profit improvement was less than the 25 percent rise at U.S. oil majors.
Elf reported a 1996 net income between 7.3 and 7.5 billion francs, a 40 percent increase from 5.3 billion in 1995.
Total shares closed down 0.55 percent at 471.50 francs after initially rising.
Desmarest expected oil prices to decline in 1997 but not to fall to the 1994/1995 low of $16.40 per barrel.

An Australian biotechnology firm has registered a vaccine against salmonella poisoning in chickens.
The vaccine is registered with Australia's National Registration Authority for Agricultural and Veterinary Chemicals.
Bioproperties Australia Pty Ltd claims it is the only salmonella vaccine that can be used on chicken eggs.
David Tinworth is the managing director of Bioproperties Australia Pty Ltd.
Tinworth estimated total annual sales of tens of millions of dollars if the vaccine is sold internationally.
Bioproperties has successfully trialled the vaccine in both chickens and cattle.
The Genetic Manipulation Advisory Committee confirmed the successful trials of the vaccine.
Bioproperties has applied to register the vaccine for use in cattle.
Vaccine sales into the poultry industry will begin at the end of this year.
Bioproperties plans to begin sales into local dairy and cattle industries within 18 months.

Australia's Industrial Relations Commission (IRC) is set to award a wage rise to the nation's lowest paid workers on Tuesday.
The wage rise is expected to be between A$10 and A$15 per week according to Australian financial markets.
The IRC will announce its decision at 0400 GMT (2 p.m.) in Sydney.
The decision will be monitored by workers, employers, and the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA).
The RBA has warned that real wage rises could threaten the nation's low inflation rate.
The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) has requested a wage rise of A$20 per week and an 8.75 percent increase in minimum pay rates.
The RBA estimates that granting the ACTU's full claim would increase the total wages bill by 1.6 percent.
If the ACTU's claim is fully granted, the RBA predicts wages growth would rise to about 5.5 percent.
A complete victory for the ACTU could lead to a rise in official interest rates and an increase in the unemployment rate.
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry believes the ACTU's claim would increase the national wages bill by 4.8 percent.

The former chief of Australia's biggest retailer was jailed for four years for defrauding the company of A$4.46 million.
Brian Quinn was the former chief executive of Coles Myer Ltd.
Quinn was convicted of using company funds for renovations to his Melbourne mansion.
Judge Geoff Eames described the case as one of greed and excess from the 1980s.
Quinn was ordered not to be eligible for parole until he had served two and a half years in prison.
Judge Eames accused Quinn of greed, vanity, and extravagance.
Quinn was dressed in a grey suit and burgundy tie during the sentencing.
Quinn had denied conspiring to falsely claim renovation expenses as work done on company properties.
Renovations to Quinn's home included adding a storey, building a tennis court, and constructing an eight-car garage.
Bruce Bingham stated that the Quinn family was considering an appeal against the severity of the sentence.

Microsoft Corp.'s fiscal third-quarter profit increased by 85 percent to $1.04 billion.
The profit exceeded analysts' expectations.
The increase in profit was attributed to strong sales of the Office 97 upgrade.
Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Mike Brown expects fourth-quarter results to be similar to the third quarter.
Brown anticipates Microsoft's growth will slow over the next five quarters due to difficult comparisons and a lack of major new upgrades.
Net income rose to 79 cents a share, up from 44 cents a share a year ago.
Revenues for the quarter totaled $3.21 billion, a 45 percent increase from $2.21 billion a year ago.
Analysts had predicted revenues of about $2.9 billion.
In after-hours trading, Microsoft's stock price increased by $4.625 to $102.75.
Brown stated that worldwide acceptance of Microsoft Office 97 contributed to the strong results.

Microsoft Corp.'s stock dropped more than 4 percent on Monday.
The stock fell $3.875 to $90.125.
The stock was the most active issue on Nasdaq.
Reports indicated that the successor to Windows 95, code-named Memphis, would be delayed until 1998.
Industry analysts stated that the delay would have little financial impact on Microsoft.
David Rothschild of Piper Jaffray commented that large organizations prefer software upgrades every three to four years.
The delay was attributed to difficulties in integrating Internet Explorer version 4.0 into the operating system.
Jonathan Roberts, director of Windows product management for Microsoft, did not provide a release date for Memphis.
Roberts mentioned that computer manufacturers would not receive software code in time for holiday season retail shipments.
The Windows 95 update will include several performance-related features, but developers are still working on the new Internet browser.

Nike Inc. reported a 77 percent increase in earnings in the latest quarter.
Nike's net income rose to $237.1 million or 80 cents a share in its fiscal third quarter ended on February 28.
The previous year's net income was $133.9 million or 45 cents a share.
Nike's revenue increased by 53 percent to $2.42 billion from $1.58 billion.
Earnings exceeded Wall Street analysts' expectations, who estimated an average of 72 cents a share.
Worldwide orders for footwear and apparel to be delivered from March through July rose 34 percent to $4.3 billion.
Nike's Chairman Phil Knight expressed satisfaction with the quarter during a conference call.
Revenues rose more than 50 percent in each of Nike's four geographic regions: the United States, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Americas.
U.S. sales of footwear and athletic apparel increased by 51 percent to $1.34 billion.
International sales increased by 67 percent to $983 million, and would have been up 78 percent without currency changes.

Ivorian warehouses are largely full of cocoa due to slow shipments ahead of an expected March export peak.
Some exporters are experiencing a shortage of coffee storage space.
One exporter reported that there is so little space that they are having problems with coffee marketing operations.
Some exporters have to wait 10 days for storage space.
Large cocoa shipments have recently left Ivorian ports, freeing some warehouse space.
A strong February tail to the main cocoa crop has led to rapid replacement of shipped stocks.
As of February 23, 880,000 tonnes of cocoa had been taken to Ivorian ports, leaving warehouse stocks of up to 380,000 tonnes.
Port sources indicate that usually available cocoa warehouse space is 400,000 tonnes.
February cocoa exports are estimated to be up to 100,000 tonnes.
Coffee exports have been sluggish due to lack of demand, low world prices, and poor quality.

Rains spread inland from coastal Ivory Coast cocoa areas this week.
February drought has threatened to stress cocoa trees and reduce late mid-crop potential.
Industry sources indicate that the mid-crop will determine the 1996/97 season harvest.
Government projections estimate the harvest at 950,000 tonnes.
Some industry players predict the harvest could be close to 1.1 million tonnes.
Heavier rains are needed in early March to ensure mid-crop prospects.
Rains are needed to prompt pollinating activity by insects on flower pinheads.
Flowers will give pods maturing in August and September.
Weather data show little rainfall up to February 20.
Heavy rains fell over Abidjan on Thursday after a period of dry weather.

Stowaway deaths in the holds of cargo ships leaving West Africa are prompting calls for international action.
Dockers in Britain found the bodies of seven young Africans in cargo ships carrying cocoa, coconut, and oilseeds.
Three Africans died in the hold of a cocoa ship in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, in February after inhaling toxic pesticides.
The 10,000 tonne cocoa consignment was rejected by American buyers due to the deaths.
Chris Horrocks, Secretary-General of the International Chamber of Shipping, stated that the West African problem is intense.
Horrocks mentioned that Western governments often make token gestures regarding the issue.
British Prime Minister John Major stated that better arrangements are needed to prevent stowaways from hiding on ships.
Shipping officials claim that governments are reluctant to act due to the costs associated with handling stowaways.
The U.N. International Maritime Organisation has set up a committee to consider recommendations for a convention on stowaways.
Ivory Coast has become a magnet for stowaways from neighboring states, with about 200 cases reported in 1996.

Tobacco companies could face a double-digit drop in U.S. sales due to a possible $300 billion deal to settle legal claims.
Analyst Gary Black of Sanford Bernstein predicted a 12 percent drop in U.S. consumption based on past price increases.
Industry analysts stated that the reported $300 billion payment over 25 years was likely on the high side.
Martin Feldman of Smith Barney described the $300 billion figure as much too high and an opening shot by the anti-tobacco lobby.
The negotiations aim to settle government, individual, and class-action suits and include proposals for a $300 billion fund for sick smokers.
The proposals also include sharp limits on advertising and regulation of tobacco by the Food and Drug Administration.
Analysts indicated that a deal may take weeks or months, while Congress may take a year or two to pass laws protecting the industry from lawsuits.
Some anti-tobacco senators in Washington have questioned the terms of the proposed deal.
A 12 percent drop in sales would reduce Philip Morris' pre-tax profits by about $500 million annually and RJR Nabisco's profits by approximately $170 million.
Roy Burry, analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, stated that price increases would likely be gradual, costing the industry $6 billion in the first year after a deal.

North Carolina's attorney general questioned the legal utility of the industry documents Liggett Group has promised to hand over.
Liggett Group, a unit of Brooke Group, agreed to deliver internal documents as part of a settlement with 22 state governments.
The internal documents may help the states in their cases against Philip Morris and other cigarette companies.
North Carolina's attorney general has not filed a suit seeking compensation for state governments' expenses on treating sick smokers.
The attorney general favors a legislative resolution over litigation.
North Carolina is the biggest tobacco-producing state in the United States.
The governor of North Carolina has allied with the tobacco industry against federal marketing limits on cigarettes.
The contents of the Liggett documents have not been made public.
Tobacco company lawyers have secured an order barring the delivery of the documents until at least March 31.
The attorney general dismissed remarks by other attorneys general about the importance of the Liggett documents in proving conspiracy allegations.

Liggett Group has broken away from other cigarette makers.
The breaking away of Liggett Group is not expected to cause significant defections among tobacco farmers in the southern United States.
North Carolina State Attorney General Mike Easley stated that tobacco farmers will continue to have a market regardless of the outcomes of lawsuits.
Tobacco is the single biggest crop in North Carolina.
Tobacco supports 200,000 families in North Carolina, according to Sean Walsh, a spokesman for state Governor Jim Hunt.
Tennessee, Virginia, South Carolina, Kentucky, and Georgia are also major tobacco-growing states.
Liggett, the maker of Chesterfields and L&M branded cigarettes, agreed to settle lawsuits with 22 state attorneys general.
Liggett promised to pay 25 percent of its pre-tax profits for the next 25 years and to label its cigarettes as addictive substances.
Liggett agreed to provide internal documents to the attorneys general that may support claims against other cigarette makers.
No other cigarette company has made a deal similar to Liggett's settlement.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin called for tougher action to curb corruption.
Jiang stated that the war on graft is vital for the nation's destiny and the ruling Communist Party.
Jiang emphasized the importance of unity between the Party and the people to develop China.
Corruption in communist ranks threatens this unity, according to Jiang.
Jiang claimed that the war against corruption is a serious political struggle affecting the Party and the state's destiny.
Jiang has staked much of his political credibility on curbing graft.
Corruption has increased in China during nearly two decades of market-style economic reform.
China's top anti-graft official reported major successes in battling corruption in 1996.
Disciplinary authorities punished more than 116,000 people for corruption in 1997, a 14.3 percent increase from the previous year.
Jiang noted that many Communist Party members are forgetting socialist traditions, leading to extravagance and waste.

More than 250 Chinese citizens have called on Beijing's military leaders to take action in a dispute with Tokyo over a group of islands in the East China Sea.
The petition was organized by Tong Zeng.
The petitioners demand that Beijing send Chinese forces to the Diaoyu Islands to destroy a Japanese lighthouse built by a right-wing group.
The lighthouse was built in July.
Tong Zeng stated that Japan has violated China's territorial integrity.
The petition was addressed to Jiang Zemin and other top military leaders.
The petition was signed by 257 ordinary citizens, including officials, retired servicemen, workers, and students.
The Diaoyu Islands are claimed by both Beijing and Taipei.
Tokyo claims the islands have always been part of Japan.
The dispute intensified after the Nihon Seinen-sha built a lighthouse on one of the islands.

China and the United States began talks on textile trade differences on Tuesday.
Both sides expressed optimism about reaching an agreement before a Friday deadline.
The talks are scheduled to last three days and aim to extend a bilateral textile accord.
The talks also seek to resolve a dispute over U.S. penalties on Chinese exports.
Top U.S. textile negotiator Rita Hayes described the first day of talks as productive.
Hayes stated that many issues remain to be resolved.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang expressed optimism about the talks.
The 1994 Sino-U.S. textile pact was set to expire on December 31 last year but was extended by one month.
Washington imposed $19 million in penalties on Chinese textile imports last September.
China has threatened to retaliate by temporarily banning imports of some U.S. goods.

Top executives in the telecommunications industry are leaving large corporations to start new companies.
Alex Mandl resigned as chief operating officer of AT&T Corp. to become chairman of Associated Communications.
Mandl stated that this career shift requires a willingness to leave the comfort of big Corporate America.
New technology and competition are creating opportunities for executives with key skills in new ventures.
Many executives are leaving their positions while thousands of others are losing their jobs.
Small companies with good technology can compete with established giants due to new wireless licenses and industry convergence.
Jim Barksdale left AT&T wireless to become president and chief executive of Netscape Communications Corp. in January 1995.
George Schmitt took a pay cut to join Omnipoint Corp. after being chief executive of PCS PrimeCo.
Companies expect a winning market strategy and a strong management team when recruiting executives.
AT&T's stock fell $1.375 to $54.125 following Mandl's resignation but increased by 12.5 cents the next day.

AT&T Corp. announced a 5.9 percent increase in basic U.S. rates for state-to-state calls from home, effective December 1.
The average increase will add 60 cents a month to typical residential bills.
AT&T stated the rate increase is to fund investments in service expansion, technical infrastructure, and customer service improvements.
Small business call rates will increase by 4.8 percent for international, toll-free, and some other services.
The cost of calls made with a calling card will rise by 5 percent.
Calls made with the assistance of an AT&T operator will see a 2.6 percent increase.
Monthly fees for the Reach Out America, SelectSaver, and AnyHour Saver calling plans will also increase.
AT&T stopped marketing those plans in 1993 when it introduced its 'True' family of calling plans.
Rates on the True savings plans will increase because they are based on a percentage discount from the basic rate.
The new One Rate plan introduced this fall will not be affected by the rate increases.

MCI Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc merged for $20 billion.
The merger followed a two-year courtship.
A BT insider expressed optimism about the merger's ease.
The merged entity will be named Concert.
Concert was originally the name of a global communications venture created by MCI and BT in July 1994.
Insiders believe the success of the merger will depend on integrating networks, billing, support, and customer service.
Concert Communication Services faced challenges due to internal conflicts and disagreements over standards.
Daniel Briere, a consultant, noted that early conflicts were destructive.
A voicemail system called Callminder developed by BT cannot be upgraded for larger systems.
Concert Communications has $1.5 billion in revenue under contract and operates in 800 cities across 50 countries.

ConAgra Inc reported a decline in profits in its U.S. beef business in the first half of fiscal 1997.
ConAgra Inc stated that its U.S. beef business is showing signs of recovery in the second half of fiscal 1997.
Lee Lochmann is the president of ConAgra Refrigerated Foods Cos.
Lochmann indicated that the beef business has shown significant improvement compared to weak results from the previous year.
ConAgra's U.S. beef operating earnings were negatively impacted by tighter cattle supplies in the first half of fiscal 1997.
Lochmann expects a good supply of cattle in the United States through the summer and into the fall.
U.S. cattle supplies are expected to tighten later in calendar 1997.
Lochmann does not anticipate a severe decline in cattle supplies.
ConAgra's Australian beef business has seen improved operating margins.
ConAgra exports about 93 percent of the beef it processes in Australia to various countries, including Japan, Korea, Canada, and Mexico.

McDonald's Corp. plans to launch its biggest nationwide promotion featuring 55-cent sandwiches.
The price of a Big Mac is currently about $1.95.
The promotion aims to attract customers amid competition in the fast-food industry.
McDonald's has more than 20,000 units worldwide and over 12,000 in the United States.
McDonald's spokesman Jack Daly stated the company hopes to launch a national value-price promotion.
The promotion is expected to feature a different sandwich for 55 cents each month with the purchase of french fries and a drink at regular price.
The promotion is expected to start with the Big Mac hamburger.
Analysts expressed concern that the promotion could lead to a price war in the fast-food industry.
McDonald's stock fell by $2.625 to $44.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Wendy's and Burger King officials stated they do not plan to cut prices in response to McDonald's promotion.

Summit Medical Systems Inc. announced that its 1996 revenues will be substantially less than previously reported.
The reduction in revenues is due to accounting discrepancies discovered by the new chief financial officer, who resigned after less than a week.
Summit Medical Systems Inc. manufactures computer-based information systems for the healthcare industry.
The company expects to revise downward the reported $19.5 million in revenues for 1996.
Summit may also cut revenues for the years 1995 and 1994.
Summit's shares fell by $1.44, or 30 percent, to $3.31 in afternoon trading on the Nasdaq market.
Analyst Chris Paul stated that Summit is believed to have about $40 million in cash and roughly 10.5 million shares.
A preliminary review indicated that revenues for the past three years had been overstated by between $4 million and $6 million.
The overstatement of revenues was attributed to the erroneous recognition of some revenues from software sales and related services.
Summit plans to eliminate an unspecified number of jobs and establish a cost reduction program to reduce annual expenses by 20 percent.

Governor Chris Patten urged Beijing to allow reporters in Hong Kong to write without fear after the territory reverts to China in July.
China released Hong Kong journalist Xi Yang after he served three years of a 12-year prison term on spy charges.
Patten stated that journalists in their system are not imprisoned for revealing information that the government may not want disclosed.
Patten expressed that if the situation were different in Hong Kong, there would not be many journalists free on the streets.
Patten emphasized that the system allowing journalists to write without fear should continue.
Analysts speculated that Xi's release was an attempt by China to address concerns over civil liberties in Hong Kong.
A China-controlled panel proposed repealing laws, including parts of the Bill of Rights and laws allowing political demonstrations.
The plan to repeal laws has faced criticism from Britain, the United States, and pro-democracy parties in Hong Kong.
China plans to eliminate Hong Kong's elected legislature.
Hong Kong democracy activists protested outside China's de facto embassy, demanding the release of at least 13 dissidents jailed in Guizhou province.

China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) plans to use its presence in Hong Kong to improve its image after the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown.
Major-General Liu Zhenwu is the future Hong Kong garrison commander.
British commander Major-General Bryan Dutton will hand over the defense of Hong Kong to the PLA at midnight on June 30.
Roger Goodwin is a spokesman for the British armed forces.
Liu Zhenwu and Bryan Dutton have communicated about the handover of defense responsibilities related to the sovereignty change.
The sovereignty change will end over 150 years of British colonial rule in Hong Kong.
The 'one country, two systems' formula was designed by Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping.
The arrangement allows Hong Kong to maintain its capitalist system for the next 50 years.
General Liu expressed a desire to change the PLA's image and sees Hong Kong as an opportunity to do so.
It is unclear how many PLA troops will be stationed in Hong Kong, but China may deploy up to 10,000 personnel.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind is involved in a political dispute regarding Hong Kong's democratic elections and human rights laws.
China plans to roll back Hong Kong's democratic elections and human rights laws after taking over in July.
Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's future leader appointed by China, criticized the territory's Democratic Party for spreading negative forecasts.
Rifkind is scheduled to arrive in Hong Kong on Saturday night for a visit before the territory is handed back to China.
During his visit, Rifkind will meet with Tung and lawmakers in Hong Kong.
Public opinion has been shifting against Tung due to his increasingly authoritarian statements.
A recent poll indicated Tung's approval rating dropped to 58.5 percent from 64.6 percent in the previous month.
Colonial Governor Chris Patten's approval rating was reported at 59.1 percent, higher than Tung's.
The Far Eastern Economic Review noted a shift in public mood regarding Tung's leadership.
Political analyst Andy Ho suggested that Tung's endorsement of a Beijing-backed move to dilute civil rights could lead to protests.

Lyonnaise des Eaux and Cie de Suez agreed to merge.
The merger will create a new global utilities company.
The new group will have annual sales of more than 200 billion francs.
The market capitalization of the new group will be 75 billion francs.
Suez will pay its shareholders a dividend three times last year's payout.
The companies expect 1997 net profits of at least 3.50 billion francs.
The goal is to double net earnings per share in five years after 1997.
Shareholders will benefit from an immediate eight percent positive effect on net earnings based on 1997 results.
Shareholders will be asked to approve the merger terms on June 11.
Under the agreement, Suez shareholders will receive 20 Lyonnaise shares for every 41 Suez shares.

Thomson-CSF is a French defence electronics firm.
Thomson-CSF posted a net attributable profit of 745 million francs in 1996.
Thomson-CSF reported a net loss of 791 million francs in 1995.
Sales for Thomson-CSF increased by 2.2 percent to 36.27 billion francs in 1996.
The French government is attempting to privatise Thomson-CSF as part of a defence industry restructuring.
Alcatel Alsthom, Dassault Aviation, and Aerospatiale are bidding for Thomson-CSF.
Lagardere, supported by British Aerospace Plc, is also bidding for Thomson-CSF.
Thomson-CSF's operating profit rose by 5.6 percent to 2.07 billion francs in 1996.
Thomson-CSF incurred an exceptional charge of 824 million francs for restructuring costs.
Thomson-CSF's net debt fell to 900 million francs.

Cie de Suez and Lyonnaise des Eaux are expected to announce a merger deal on Friday.
The merger will end the independence of Cie de Suez, which was established in the 19th century to build the Suez Canal.
The boards of Cie de Suez and Lyonnaise des Eaux will meet on Friday to approve the merger terms.
The Lyonnaise board has already backed the merger.
Lyonnaise chairman Jerome Monod stated that the merger with Suez is an excellent plan, but the terms are not yet fixed.
The merger will mark the end of autonomy for Suez, which faced challenges in the 1990s due to a distressed property market.
Cie de Suez was founded in 1858 by Ferdinand de Lesseps to build and operate the Suez Canal.
Discontented Suez shareholders forced out chairman Gerard Worms after a reported loss of four billion francs in 1995.
Gerard Mestrallet was installed as chairman to turn around the company and sold significant assets to improve cash flow.
SGB has a 37 percent stake in Tractebel, which operates in sectors overlapping with Lyonnaise.

Mid-American Waste Systems Inc. filed for bankruptcy.
Mid-American Waste Systems Inc. signed an agreement to sell most of its assets to USA Waste Services Inc.
Mid-American Waste Systems Inc. is based in Canal Winchester, Ohio.
Mid-American Waste Systems Inc. experienced financial losses due to acquisitions and development projects.
Melville Cody of Williams MacKay Jordan & Co. Inc. stated that Mid-American was highly leveraged and losing money.
Mid-American will sell nearly all its assets to USA Waste Services for $180 million in cash and stock.
The transaction is subject to court approval of Mid-American's Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing.
Mid-American's proceeds from the sale and retained assets are expected to total about $227 million.
Mid-American has approximately $323 million of long-term debt.
Mid-American's waste collection and related services will not be interrupted during the bankruptcy process.

A Conrail Inc. director abstained from a vote on the railroad's proposed $9.1 billion merger with CSX Corp.
The abstention was due to a provision prohibiting both parties from seeking another deal until 1999.
Conrail disclosed that board member David Lewis abstained from the vote due to the exclusivity period extending to December 31, 1998.
Conrail noted that Lewis fully supported the proposed transaction despite his abstention.
David Lewis is a partner in the Detroit law firm Lewis Clay & Munday.
CSX and Conrail revised the terms of their merger to provide shareholders with an additional $870 million.
The exclusivity period, extended from July 1997, is controversial.
Norfolk Southern Corp. has challenged the exclusivity period in court, claiming Conrail's board violated its duties.
A hearing on the exclusivity period issue is scheduled for January 9 in U.S. district court.
Conrail's other 11 board members voted in favor of the revised CSX deal.

The top executives of Conrail Inc., CSX Corp., and Norfolk Southern Corp. met on Friday to discuss the takeover battle for Conrail.
The meeting aimed to resolve a stalemate in the three-month takeover battle.
The three companies did not comment on the meeting but indicated that future meetings may occur.
Conrail, CSX, and Norfolk Southern issued a joint statement stating that no further details about the meeting or future meetings would be announced.
The meeting involved chief executives David LeVan of Conrail, John Snow of CSX, and David Goode of Norfolk Southern.
The meeting is considered critical to railroad consolidation on the East Coast.
Conrail rejected a $10.3 billion cash offer from Norfolk Southern in favor of a $9.6 billion cash and stock deal with CSX.
Conrail shareholders defeated a key provision that would have allowed the merger with CSX to proceed.
Norfolk Southern is in the process of purchasing 9.9 percent of Conrail's stock.
Linda Morgan, chairwoman of the U.S. Surface Transportation Board, expressed support for private sector negotiations in railroad mergers.

Opponents of U.S. trade concessions to China are expected to challenge President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's favoured trading status.
Supporters of President Clinton's decision to renew China's most favoured nation (MFN) status for another year are confident of victory.
Opponents include social conservatives and organized labor.
The coalition of opponents criticizes China's policies on human rights, labour rights, religious rights, trade, and abortion.
Opponents are gaining strength from concerns over the transfer of Hong Kong to China and allegations of illegal campaign contributions by Beijing.
A congressional aide stated that the upcoming fight will be tougher due to the issues surrounding Hong Kong and campaign finance.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich indicated that this year's decision will be closer than last year's House vote of 286-141 in support of Clinton on MFN.
Advocates and opponents expect that President Clinton's policy will ultimately survive.
Even if lawmakers reject the president's decision, opponents doubt they could achieve the two-thirds vote needed to override a veto.
Thea Lee from the AFL-CIO stated that a close vote could indicate growing uneasiness among both Democrats and Republicans regarding current China trade policy.

Regulators began auctioning a slice of spectrum for Internet access and wireless local phone networks.
Twenty-four companies are bidding for the rights to offer wireless communications service.
The companies include units of BellSouth Corp., Pacific Telesis Group, Comcast Corp., and a Bell Atlantic Corp./Nynex Corp. joint venture.
The first day of bidding totaled $5.3 million.
Analysts predict that financial problems among wireless carriers will put downward pressure on prices.
This is the Federal Communication Commission's 14th airwave sale.
The FCC is auctioning 128 licenses, with 104 being 10 megahertz licenses and 24 being 5 megahertz licenses.
The FCC is not dictating what services companies can offer over this spectrum.
Potential applications for the spectrum include broadband wireless access, wireless local phone networks, and location services.
The value of wireless spectrum has decreased since last year's $10.2 billion auction for personal communications services.

Regulators approved an overhaul of domestic telephone charges on Wednesday.
The overhaul is expected to lower costs for residential and business customers who make long-distance calls.
Basic local phone rates will remain the same according to Federal Communications Commission (FCC) officials.
Consumers and businesses will pay more for extra phone lines.
Customers who seldom dial long distance will see their bills rise.
The FCC voted to allocate about $2.3 billion a year to wire schools and libraries to the Internet at discounted rates.
An additional $400 million a year will be used to connect rural hospitals to the Internet.
The new rates are a result of last year's communications law.
Consumer advocates generally praised the new rates, while regional Baby Bell companies criticized them.
Small-business advocates expressed concerns about higher phone bills.

Sun Microsystems Inc. will announce its entry into the supercomputing systems market on Tuesday.
The supercomputing market has been dominated by Cray Research, which was acquired by Silicon Graphics Inc. last year.
Sun's new Sun Ultra HPC servers will offer better price performance than Silicon Graphics' Origin 2000 and IBM's RS6000 SP.
Industry analysts believe Sun could become an aggressive new player in the supercomputing market.
The supercomputing market has changed over the last decade due to new massively-parallel computers.
Dataquest analyst Jerry Sheridan stated that Sun's entry is revolutionary and presents a competitive environment.
Sun acquired part of Cray's computing business from Silicon Graphics as part of the Silicon Graphics-Cray deal.
Sun aims to increase its share in the high performance computing market from virtually nothing last year.
International Data Corp. projects the market for powerful computers will reach $5.6 billion by 2000.
Sun's core product is based on the Enterprise Server 3000 to ES 6000 line introduced in April 1996 and adds supercomputing features.

Intel Corp. is the world's biggest maker of computer chips.
Intel's workers received about $820 million in cash bonuses, profit sharing, and retirement pay for the year 1996.
The average employee received a minimum payout of about 33 percent over their base salary for 1996.
An entry-level hourly worker earning $25,000 a year received roughly $8,000 in added compensation and benefits for 1996.
Intel's profits in 1996 soared to $5.2 billion, and revenues hit $20.8 billion.
The $820 million in cash profit-sharing and retirement contributions in 1996 exceeded Intel's total revenues in 1981.
Intel's Chief Operating Officer is Craig Barrett, who will become the company's president in the spring.
Intel ended 1996 with a workforce of around 48,500 employees.
Intel's stock closed at $151.75 on the Nasdaq market, where it was the third most heavily traded stock.
In 1996, Intel paid out $214 million under the Employee Cash Bonus Programme, equivalent to 26.9 days' salary for each employee.

Netcom On-Line Communications, Inc. unveiled a new multi-tier pricing policy on Monday.
The price points for the new pricing policy range from $24.95 to thousands of dollars a month.
Netcom will maintain current customers at the present $19.95 flat rate.
Netcom will introduce a 'fair usage' policy to limit bandwidth usage at peak hours.
David Garrison is the Chairman and CEO of Netcom.
Garrison stated that the company continues to grow rapidly and expects the pricing plan to boost revenues.
Netcom was operating profit positive in the fourth quarter in the United States operations.
The $24.95 a month Netcomplete Advantage service provides 28.8 kilobits per second access.
Netcomplete Advantage Pro costs $29.95 a month and adds premium support and access to online research libraries.
Netcom's pricing plan was developed after collating responses from more than 25,000 subscribers.

Hong Kong's return to China is not a concern for business, according to the official line.
Stewart Aldcroft, director at Templeton, stated that the business perspective sees the situation as a fait accompli.
Brigadier Christopher Hammerbeck, executive director at the British Chamber of Commerce, expressed doubts about Hong Kong retaining its current way of life.
March 23 marks the 100-day countdown to the handover to China on June 30.
Many corporate individuals in Hong Kong view the handover date as an opportunity for celebration.
The business aspects of the handover were addressed years prior.
Deng Xiaoping opened China to foreign investment in the late 1970s.
Hong Kong has established connections with the mainland through investments and joint ventures.
Tai Ming Cheung, analyst at Kim Eng Securities, noted that many companies in Hong Kong are owned by mainland interests.
The property market in Hong Kong has risen more than 40 percent over the past year.

Hong Kong is questioning its ability to maintain prosperity based on traditional strengths.
Hong Kong's traditional strengths include proximity to China, developed markets, and a large free port.
Rival states in Asia, such as Singapore and Jakarta, are rapidly developing.
Hong Kong is concerned about its position as China's primary financial service center.
Challenges facing Hong Kong include an inadequate education system, declining English standards, rising costs, and an under-skilled labor force.
Tokyo and Singapore are identified as immediate threats to Hong Kong's financial dominance.
Tokyo's financial sector is undergoing reforms due to competition from lower-cost rivals.
Analysts believe that Tokyo may take time to regain business from Hong Kong.
Singapore is viewed as having a competitive advantage over Tokyo in the long term.
Kuala Lumpur is emerging as a promising financial center with advantages such as political stability and lower rental costs.

Cathay Pacific's Airbus fleet has been grounded.
Analysts believe the situation for Cathay Pacific is unlikely to improve soon.
Cathay Pacific was starting to represent good fundamental value after five turbulent years.
Cathay Pacific has strong management and a healthy balance sheet.
The new airport at Chek Lap Kok opened in April 1998.
K.Y. Ng at BZW Asia stated that things seem to be going well for Cathay Pacific.
Cathay Pacific's share price has not performed positively.
Many Hong Kong analysts, including K.Y. Ng, have a sell recommendation on Cathay Pacific's stock.
Andrew Fernow at Vickers Ballas believes Cathay Pacific cannot perform in line with the market.
Cathay Pacific's share price has been trading at about HK$12 per share for the past four months.

Chinese culture advises against boasting, as reflected in the saying 'Don't puff up an ox skin.'
The Year of the Ox is expected to be significant for China.
Theodora Lau's 'The Handbook of Chinese Horoscopes' suggests it is a good time for China to settle domestic affairs.
China's communist leaders are preparing for the Year of the Ox with an ambitious agenda.
1997 is considered one of the most significant years in the history of the People's Republic of China.
Hong Kong will revert to Chinese sovereignty on June 30, 1997, after over 150 years of British colonial rule.
A crucial Communist Party congress will be held later in 1997 to determine China's path for the next five years.
Foreign Minister Qian Qichen predicts the Year of the Ox will be auspicious.
Qian Qichen is leading the committee managing Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty.
The horoscope advises sticking to routine and supporting conservative policies for the new year.

Mao Zedong died, which paralyzed China.
Deng Xiaoping's death 20 years later was met with indifference.
There was no significant grief following Deng's death, unlike Mao's.
Mao died at age 82 in September 1976.
When Mao died, crowds expressed deep sorrow.
A woman recalled that Mao's death felt like losing a family member.
A driver near Deng's residence noted that people were indifferent to Deng's death.
Beijing announced six days of mourning for Deng, who died at age 92.
Deng's policies transformed China into an economic powerhouse.
Residents noted that Deng's death did not evoke strong emotional responses.

China is becoming more aware of the importance of human rights in its relationship with the United States.
Washington plans to sponsor a U.N. resolution condemning Beijing unless further progress on human rights is made.
A visiting team of U.S. officials held talks with China on various issues, including human rights.
A Beijing-based diplomat stated that China recognizes human rights as a critical area affecting the relationship with the U.S.
Washington expects to co-sponsor a U.N. draft resolution in Geneva if Beijing does not improve its handling of fundamental freedoms.
Beijing has successfully blocked such resolutions for the past six years with support from developing nations.
The United States is pressuring China to release political prisoners and allow Red Cross inspections of its prisons.
The U.S. State Department released its annual human rights report criticizing Beijing for abuses of basic freedoms.
Beijing released journalist Xi Yang on parole and dissident Chen Ziming for medical treatment in response to international pressure.
There are still strict limits on personal and political freedoms in China, but economic liberalization is gradually reducing authoritarianism.

Lloyd's of London confirmed it will abandon 300 years of self-regulation.
Lloyd's will recommend that supervision be handed over to an external authority.
The Council of Lloyd's endorsed the findings of a working party set up in October 1996.
The proposals aim to align Lloyd's more closely with other regulated markets.
The Council will retain day-to-day responsibility for regulation but will be subject to external oversight.
External oversight will be provided by the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) and the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI).
Lloyd's will ask the government to amend the Insurance Companies Acts and the Financial Services Act.
The government is expected to review all financial services regulation in the coming months, which will likely include Lloyd's.
The report suggests that Lloyd's should mirror best practices from the financial sector with assistance from the SIB.
The report recommends widening powers for the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry regarding the supervision of Lloyd's members.

Lloyd's of London announced it will give backers more time to meet planned increases in capital for underwriting activities.
Lloyd's has dropped proposals preventing Names from using their homes as collateral for underwriting.
The planned capital increases are part of measures to strengthen financial security at Lloyd's.
The changes aim to provide a level playing field between Names and corporate members.
The longer transition period may address concerns raised by Names' representatives.
Names fear being forced out of the market in favor of corporate capital introduced in 1994.
Names will have three years to meet new requirements of showing assets amounting to 50 percent of the premiums they underwrite.
A two-year transition period was proposed but has been extended to the year 2000 after consultations.
The minimum level of means for Names will increase to 350,000 pounds from 250,000 pounds over five years, taking effect in 2002.
The use of principal private residences as collateral for underwriting will continue for homes existing at the end of 1994.

British insurers are preparing for the opening of the Indian market to foreign companies for the first time in over two decades.
Prudential Corp announced plans to explore opportunities in life insurance with Industrial Credit and Investment Corp of India.
The Indian government is expected to outline rules for participation in health insurance and pensions industries soon.
Private and foreign investors will be allowed into the health insurance and pensions sectors through joint ventures with state-run monopolies.
The General Insurance Corp (GIC) and the Life Insurance Corp (LIC) have controlled the insurance industry since nationalisation in 1956 and 1972, respectively.
Inder Kumar Gujral is the new Indian leader who aims to push the February budget through parliament quickly.
Participation in the insurance market is initially limited to firms with majority Indian ownership.
British firms have been forming links with Indian companies since the early 1990s.
Commercial Union has formed a joint venture for general insurance with the Hindustan Times.
Industry analysts expect it to take between six and eight months to pass legislation and award licenses for the health insurance sector.

Hong Kong's colonial government cautioned Beijing not to enact laws for the territory before the handover to China on June 30.
Security Secretary Peter Lai stated that Beijing's actions might lead to lawsuits that would hinder a smooth transition.
Hong Kong's future lawmakers in a China-appointed provisional legislature plan to develop laws for the territory before July 1.
The Hong Kong government opposes China's desire for the provisional legislature to decide on residency rights before the handover.
Peter Lai emphasized that only the current Legislative Council of Hong Kong should legislate before July 1.
The 60-member provisional legislature faces strong opposition from pro-democracy advocates.
Pro-democracy activists have threatened to sue the provisional legislature if it attempts to make laws before July 1.
Britain and China have reached agreements on major provisions regarding right of abode but are deadlocked on actual legislation.
Peter Lai warned that legislation enacted by the provisional legislature before the handover could lead to significant litigation.
The issue of right of abode is important to 750,000 Hong Kong residents who have obtained foreign citizenship but value their residency rights.

China Everbright Holdings Co Ltd is controlled by China's State Council.
CITIC Pacific Ltd sold its 7.74 percent stake in Hongkong Telecom to China Everbright.
Analysts expressed uncertainty about what China Everbright could offer to Hongkong Telecom.
China Everbright Holdings has three listed subsidiaries in Hong Kong.
The subsidiaries of China Everbright Holdings are China Everbright International Ltd, China Everbright Technology Ltd, and China Everbright-IHD Pacific Ltd.
China Everbright Holdings is one of 16 equal shareholders in China United Telecommunications Corp (China Unicom).
China Unicom is China's second largest telecommunications provider.
China Unicom was established in July 1994 at a total cost of 1.28 billion yuan.
Unicom provides basic and long-distance telecommunications services, as well as mobile and paging facilities in China.
Zhu Xiaohua is the chairman of China Everbright and a close associate of Zhu Rongji.

The United States will grant 10-year multiple-entry visas to holders of Hong Kong passports issued after the territory is returned to China.
U.S. Consul-General Richard Boucher stated that future Hong Kong passport holders will receive the same visa treatment as current holders of Hong Kong British travel documents.
Boucher announced the intention to issue maximum validity visas for people with the new Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) passport.
The decision marks a significant step in international recognition of the future SAR passport.
Hong Kong will become a Special Administrative Region of China on July 1, ending 156 years of British colonial rule.
The population of Hong Kong is approximately 6.4 million people.
Easy travel access is considered important for Hong Kong's future prospects as an international business and tourism center.
Nine countries have granted full visa-free entry for SAR passports, including Britain, Singapore, Canada, and the Philippines.
Japan plans to treat SAR passports more favorably than Chinese passports but has not provided specific details.
Hong Kong Director of Immigration Regina Ip welcomed the U.S. decision and viewed it as a confidence booster.

International Business Machines Corp. reported fourth-quarter earnings that were slightly better than expected.
IBM's service business, growth in software sales, and tight expense controls contributed to the earnings.
IBM's net income rose about 18 percent to $2.02 billion in the quarter from $1.71 billion in the 1995 quarter.
Earnings per share increased to $3.93 from $3.09 due to 7 percent fewer shares outstanding.
Wall Street analysts expected profits of $3.88 a share on average.
Some analysts and investors indicated that IBM stock might face profit-taking pressure.
Thom Brown described the results as excellent but suggested a potential brief period of selling.
David Takata noted mixed results, with strong software and services but disappointing mainframe revenues.
IBM reported a 22 percent increase in service revenues and a rise in personal computer sales.
Overall revenues increased 5.6 percent to $23.14 billion from $21.92 billion.

New York State Attorney General Dennis Vacco plans to sue America Online Inc. if negotiations with prosecutors from 20 states break down.
Vacco aims to halt allegedly deceptive business practices and win refunds for frustrated customers of America Online.
America Online has received numerous consumer complaints and several class-action lawsuits since changing its pricing plan.
Many users have reported difficulties accessing the service or being dropped after logging on.
America Online Chairman Steve Case stated that the company is not considering subscriber refunds.
Case claimed that most customers have benefited from a price cut and increased usage under the new plan.
Vacco and attorneys general from 20 states met with America Online officials to discuss subscriber complaints.
Vacco sent notification of New York state's proposed litigation to America Online's headquarters in Dulles, Virginia.
The lawsuit will allege deceptive sales practices, false advertising, and fraud by America Online.
Washington state is considering various options, including filing a lawsuit or negotiating a settlement.

Progressive Networks Inc. unveiled RealVideo, which adds video to its RealAudio software.
RealVideo became available for free on the same day it was announced.
Users can download RealVideo by obtaining Progressive Networks' RealPlayer software from its website.
A more fully featured version of RealPlayer can be purchased for $29.99.
RealVideo delivers live and on-demand video over the Internet and intranets.
Progressive Networks is based in Seattle and is privately held.
The company believes RealVideo will have a similar impact on video as RealAudio had on audio.
More than 50 entertainment, media, and computer companies support RealVideo.
The news conference announcing RealVideo featured film director Spike Lee, who premiered three short films developed using the software.
RealPlayer software will include RealAudio version 3.0.

United Biscuits (Holdings) Plc more than doubled its profits in 1996 to 109 million pounds before tax and exceptional items.
The increase in profits reflects a simpler and slimmed-down portfolio of products.
United Biscuits owns brands such as McVities biscuits and KP nuts.
United Biscuits has exited from its U.S. Keebler subsidiary.
Total exceptional charges in 1996 amounted to 84.7 million pounds compared to 150.3 million in 1995.
Sales rose by three percent to 1.887 billion pounds.
Trading profits grew four percent to 129.2 million pounds.
Underlying profits growth was in line with stock brokers forecasts.
UB's British business increased profits before exceptional items by 12 percent to 113.7 million pounds.
UB expects its margins in Europe to remain firm and to move up over the next two to three years.

Greenalls Plc reported a 48 percent rise in profits before exceptional items to 148.7 million pounds.
The profit increase was driven by the acquisition of brewer Boddington in November 1995.
Chairman and chief executive Andrew Thomas stated that the year saw a good trading performance.
Exceptional items charged in the year ended September 27, 1996, totalled 31.2 million pounds.
The exceptional items included 23.9 million pounds for redundancy payments to former Boddington staff.
Underlying profit before exceptional items and tax, excluding Boddington, increased by 10.7 percent to 111.3 million pounds.
Boddington generated an operating profit of 47.1 million pounds in the 11 months after its acquisition.
Greenalls saved 18 million pounds in costs from integrating Boddington into the group.
Overall group profits before tax and exceptional items were at the top end of analysts' forecasts.
Greenalls plans to spend 170 million pounds on developing its business in 1997/98.

LASMO Plc is a British oil exploration company.
Joe Darby is the chief executive of LASMO Plc.
LASMO Plc expects oil prices to weaken in the short term.
Brent crude is expected to average $19 for the year according to Joe Darby.
Joe Darby stated that prices are not expected to fall below $15 or $16 a barrel.
LASMO realised an average of $18.72 per barrel in 1996.
The average price per barrel for LASMO in 1995 was $17.09.
The average price per barrel for LASMO increased from 1995 to 1996.
Joe Darby provided these statements in an interview.
The expectation for Brent crude is based on the company's analysis.

After 19 months of confrontations, six striking newspaper unions made an unconditional offer to return to work at Detroit's two major daily papers.
Al Derey is the head of the Metropolitan Council of Newspaper Unions.
Derey stated that the action was a tactic to expose the papers to financial losses if they do not agree to a fair contract.
Derey claimed that the strike has not ended and that the new strategy aims to win a fair contract from the newspapers.
About 2,500 workers walked off their jobs at the Detroit Free Press and Detroit News in July 1995 after contract talks collapsed.
The Detroit Free Press and Detroit News are editorially independent and have separate owners.
Knight-Ridder Inc. owns the Detroit Free Press.
Gannett Co. Inc. owns the Detroit News.
The papers have published every day since the strike began, although initially they published a single joint edition.
Since the start of the strike, circulation at the papers has fallen by 30 percent.

Bargaining between union and American Axle Manufacturing Inc. negotiators was expected to continue up to the midnight Friday deadline.
The deadline was set to avoid a strike that would paralyze General Motors Corp.'s U.S. light truck production.
About 7,200 United Auto Workers union members were prepared to strike at five plants in Detroit, Three Rivers, Mich., and Buffalo, N.Y.
The strike would occur if no agreement was reached on a new three-year contract.
American Axle was spun off from GM into a private company in 1994.
American Axle supplies virtually all of the rear axles for GM's pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles.
American Axle also supplies axles for the Camaro and Firebird rear-drive cars, as well as parts for other passenger car lines.
The company makes axles for Chrysler Corp. and axle shafts for Ford Motor Co.
Tight inventories at American Axle and Dana Corp. mean GM's light truck plants would run out of parts by early next week.
Analysts estimate GM could lose $20 million a day in after-tax profits if it suspends light truck production.

A commuter plane crashed in a remote wooded area south of Detroit on Thursday.
The crash killed all 30 people on board.
The plane was an Embraer-120 operated as flight 3272 by Comair.
The crash occurred at 3:50 p.m. EST near the town of Ida, approximately 25 miles from Detroit.
Comair is a regional carrier based in Cincinnati and operates as a feeder for Delta Airlines.
A nearby resident, Thomas Marino, reported hearing a low-flying jet followed by a loud boom.
The region experienced a snowstorm that dropped over half a foot of snow.
There was no confirmation that weather contributed to the crash.
The National Transportation Safety Board reported that the plane had 25 passengers, two pilots, and three flight attendants, all of whom did not survive.
The Brazilian-made Embraer-120 has been involved in 13 other crashes since 1986 that resulted in fatalities.

China has assembled a group of Communist leaders to arrange Deng Xiaoping's funeral.
Analysts described the assembly as a show of unity for Deng's chosen successor.
The 459-member group will obscure the Communist Party's internal politics ahead of a key party congress.
Deng Xiaoping died on Wednesday at the age of 92.
China will hold Deng's funeral next Tuesday in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing.
The funeral ceremonies will not include a lying in state for the public to mourn.
Deng's body parts will be donated to science and his ashes will be scattered at sea.
Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party chief and state President, is the chairman of the funeral committee.
The committee includes all members of the 18-man Politburo and several veterans of the communist revolution.
Political analysts noted that a smaller group for funeral arrangements might reveal too much about the party's internal workings.

U.S. Vice President Al Gore arrived in Beijing on Monday.
Gore's visit aims to heal Sino-U.S. ties and facilitate presidential exchanges.
There is controversy regarding possible Chinese efforts to influence U.S. elections.
Gore stated he would discuss human rights with Chinese leaders during his visit.
Gore has no specific meetings planned with human rights activists.
Gore mentioned he could talk with activists at U.S. embassy functions in China.
The People's Daily reported that the Chinese government did not make payments to the Democratic Party.
Gore is the most senior U.S. official to visit China since President George Bush.
The U.S. State Department's annual report accused Beijing of silencing public dissent in 1996.
Gore's trip is part of an Asian tour that includes South Korea.

China called on Japan to stop encouraging right-wing activities on disputed South China Sea islands.
China warned that failure to stop these activities could escalate the diplomatic row.
China did not specify what actions it would take regarding the disputed islands.
China stated it would exercise restraint in its response to the situation.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang emphasized the seriousness of the matter.
Shen Guofang stated that Japan should take actions to stop illegal activities by right-wing activists.
The dispute over the islands, known as Diaoyus in China and Senkakus in Japan, intensified in July.
Tensions increased after Japanese coast-guard ships barred private Taiwan boats from the area.
Beijing and Taipei criticized Japan's protection of right-wing activities and urged Tokyo to keep people away from the islands.
A group of over 100 Chinese nationalists urged China's military to send warships to the Diaoyu islands.

The Internet Society approved a plan to add seven new top-level domains.
The new top-level domains will include names such as 'firm,' 'arts,' and 'web.'
The implementation of the new domains is set to start in the third quarter of 1997.
America Online Inc. has more than eight million members.
William Burrington is the director of law and public policy at America Online Inc.
Burrington stated that the plan needs more work despite praising its concept.
AT&T Corp's Worldnet service is the largest pure Internet service provider.
Mike Miller is a spokesman for AT&T Corp's Worldnet service.
Online service providers are seeking to delay the implementation of the plan.
Network Solutions Inc. is the sole registration agent for the most popular current domains.

Commuters on the Leesburg Pike in Northern Virginia are near a significant global traffic jam of digital data.
The Internet's data routes are experiencing increased traffic due to thousands of new users signing on daily.
Mark Luker, programme director of the National Science Foundation's network infrastructure project, stated that demand for the Internet is outstripping supply.
Efforts are being made to increase Internet capacity through technical solutions.
There are explorations into rationing Internet access by price based on speed and data quantity.
Mae East is a computer interchange in Northern Virginia where 46 Internet service providers exchange data.
MFS Communications Inc operates Mae East and claims it is the busiest public exchange point on the Internet.
Peak data loads at Mae East can reach 53 million bytes per second.
The National Science Foundation managed the Internet's network backbone until April 1995.
Internet traffic increased from 1.3 trillion bytes per month in March 1991 to 17.8 trillion bytes in late 1994.

The Clinton administration has developed a plan to reform U.S. banking laws.
The administration will announce its positions in the coming weeks.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will present the plan at a House Banking Committee hearing on June 3.
Under Secretary John Hawke is a key architect of the administration's plan.
Hawke is scheduled to speak on Wednesday regarding the administration's stance on banking and commerce.
There is general agreement in Congress and the finance industry to eliminate barriers between banking, securities, and insurance.
There is disagreement about allowing banks to merge with securities and other firms.
The administration's position has changed to favor limited combinations of financial and non-financial activities.
Financial firms may be restricted to a percentage of non-financial activity based on total revenue or capital.
Debate continues regarding the regulation of diverse financial businesses within a single firm.

The Prague Stock Exchange gained ground on Thursday.
Analysts are not convinced that the fortunes of the Prague Stock Exchange have turned around.
The rise in the Prague Stock Exchange is attributed to thin domestic buying.
The bourse has gained in 15 of the past 16 sessions.
Analysts observed little change in market sentiment amid mostly domestic trading.
The PX50 index was up 0.25 percent at 519.5 at its daily price fixing on Thursday.
The bourse is 8.3 percent higher than its low in mid-November.
The Prague Stock Exchange lost close to 20 percent during most of the autumn.
The Czech market has been plagued by poor legislation that fails to protect minority shareholders.
The Securities Registry is bound by law to provide services related to securities transactions.

The Czech crown has recently gained strength due to increased demand from Eurobond issues.
Market speculation exists regarding possible central bank intervention in the Czech crown.
The Czech National Bank (CNB) is monitoring the development of the crown.
The CNB is prepared to allow the market to determine the crown's rate within a fluctuation band.
Since the start of 1997, the Czech crown has gained approximately three percentage points against its fixing basket.
The gain in the crown is mainly attributed to foreign buying for financing new crown Eurobond issues totaling about 30 billion crowns.
Analysts predict the crown may hold steady for a short period but could test 5.5 percent above its parity level next week.
Martin Strauch, a dealer at Citibank, stated that he does not expect significant movement in the crown this week.
The Czech crown is fixed daily at a rate that allows for fluctuations of plus or minus 7.5 percent from the mid-point of a currency basket.
On Wednesday, the CNB fixed the crown at 27.712 to the dollar and 16.846 to the mark, which is 5.05 percent above the mid-point.

The Czech economy is showing signs of slower growth and a widening trade gap.
Analysts expressed concerns about the pace of industrial restructuring in the Czech economy.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus has been praised for achieving low inflation rates, good GDP growth, and a low unemployment rate of about three percent.
The Czech Statistical Bureau reported a record trade deficit of 160.33 billion crowns for 1996.
The trade deficit increased from a 95.7 billion crown shortfall the previous year.
Some economists are concerned about the export competitiveness of Czech industry.
Kamil Janacek, chief economist at Komercni Banka, stated that competition from other transforming economies is increasing.
Since 1992, the Czech economy has transitioned from recession to a consumption-driven real growth of 4.8 percent in 1995.
Unemployment in the Czech Republic remains around three percent, with nearly 70 percent of the economy in private hands.
The current account showed a deficit of $3.1 billion crowns for the first three quarters of the year.

NatWest Markets announced a restructuring of its global debt markets division.
Power has been shifted to managers from Greenwich Capital, which NatWest acquired last year.
The restructuring is not related to a reported loss of 90 million pounds by the investment banking arm of National Westminster Bank Plc.
Gary Holloway and Chip Kruger are the co-chief executives of the new global debt markets division.
Holloway will be based in Greenwich, United States, and will oversee U.S. and Asian operations.
Kruger will be based in London and will manage European debt market operations.
Greg Bowes has been appointed head of government bonds, repos, and futures and options.
Frank Canelas will lead corporate bonds origination, sales, trading, and research.
Bruce Snider has been appointed head of asset-backed origination, structuring, and trading.
Phil Lotz is the chief administrative officer for operations, IT, and finance.

Britain's opposition Labour party does not plan to revolutionise the regulatory structure of the financial services industry if it wins the election.
The ruling Conservative government must call the election by May.
Mike O'Brien is Labour's shadow economic secretary.
O'Brien stated that Labour is discussing a developmental process involving reform rather than revolution.
Labour plans to merge the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) with existing Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs).
The SIB currently supervises frontline regulators that authorise firms to conduct investment business, monitor them, handle complaints, and punish rule-breakers.
O'Brien believes the current regulatory system is overly bureaucratic and expensive.
Labour does not intend to establish an equivalent to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
Labour prefers a regulatory system that is flexible and responsive to changes in the market.
Labour is consulting with industry participants about providing financial services to low-income groups.

A group of U.S. and European firms developed a system for money transactions over the Internet.
The team includes AT & T Corp Unisource, Apple Computer Inc, Nokia Oy, and Mondex UK.
The project will run on a pilot basis.
Julian Wilson, Unisource's director of service development, stated that protocols for shopping and banking have been developed.
The system allows users to pay for electronic services via the Internet.
Wilson claimed the system was a world first involving the transfer of electronic cash from one device to another.
The developers described the system as the world's first trial of fast and safe money transactions over the Internet.
The system will use the GSM network for Internet access.
The system aims to allow Internet users to buy services and access information using smart cards.
The initial pilot is being carried out with National Westminster Bank Plc.

China has pledged to open its insurance, stock, retail, wholesale, and banking sectors to foreign investment.
The pledge is part of China's efforts for entry into the World Trade Organisation.
From 1997 to 2000, China is expected to open its insurance and stock market wider to foreign investment.
The information was reported by the China Daily, quoting Ma Jixian from the State Economic and Trade Commission.
The pledge was included in a unilateral action plan submitted by China to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
Foreign insurers will have access to markets outside Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou before the end of the decade.
China's insurance market was previously monopolized by the state-owned People's Insurance Group.
Currently, only three foreign insurers can write insurance policies in China: American International Assurance Co. Ltd, Tokio Marine and Fire Insurance Co. Ltd, and a joint venture with a domestic insurer.
Foreign stock companies will be allowed to handle A shares, which are currently only available to native Chinese.
China plans to cut its average import tariffs to about 15 percent from the current 23 percent.

China rejected an invitation for its top policymaker to visit Taiwan on Tuesday.
China stated that Taiwan must first abandon its bid to break out of diplomatic isolation.
A spokesman for the Taiwan Affairs Office said it was impossible for Wang Zhaoguo to accept the invitation.
The spokesman indicated that the time for such a visit was not ripe due to Taiwan's foreign policy.
The spokesman advised Taiwan not to seek entry into the United Nations.
Taipei lost its United Nations seat to Beijing in 1971.
China considers Taiwan a rebel province and denies it official links with other states.
If Wang had accepted the invitation, he would have been the most senior Chinese official to visit Taiwan since 1949.
A Taiwanese business leader quoted Wang as saying he would be happy to visit Taiwan if given the opportunity.
China has increased pressure on Taiwan to lift a ban on direct trade and transport links.

Liu Xiaobo has filed a lawsuit against Beijing authorities for sending him to a labour camp without trial.
Liu Xiaobo's wife stated that he urged Beijing's Xuanwu District Court to overturn a decision by the Beijing Re-education through Labour Committee.
Liu Xiaobo's lawsuit claims he refuses to accept the decision to send him to a labour camp for three years.
Liu Xiaobo stated that he is appealing to defend his right to freedom of speech as a law-abiding citizen.
Liu Xiaobo was detained by police in September and sent to a camp in Dalian for three years of re-education through labour.
Re-education through labour is a form of administrative punishment imposed by authorities without a trial.
Western human rights activists claim that re-education through labour is used to remove dissidents from circulation without trial complications.
Liu Xiaobo's wife reported that the court agreed to hear the lawsuit, but no date has been set.
Authorities at the labour camp rejected requests from Liu Xiaobo's family to visit him.
The Re-education through Labour Committee accused Liu Xiaobo of various offences related to a government petition and a newspaper article.

Coles Myer Ltd is expected to report its first profit rise in almost two years on Thursday.
Improved margins are helping to offset sluggish sales growth and boost first half profit by about five percent.
Analysts expect Coles Myer to report a net profit before abnormals of about A$200 million to A$205 million for the 26 weeks to January 26.
This net profit is an increase from A$194.5 million in the first half of 1995/96.
This will be Coles' first profit rise since 1995.
Coles Myer has experienced a two-year period of board turmoil and controversy over corporate governance.
Analysts expect margins to have improved most at Coles' K-Mart discount department store chain in pre-Christmas trading.
K-Mart's improved margins are attributed to a refusal to discount heavily.
