Northern Electric aims to demonstrate it is undervalued by CE Electric's bid of 630 pence per share.
Northern Electric reported pretax profits of 50.7 million pounds for the six months ending September 30.
The pretax profits for the previous year were 58.7 million pounds.
Northern Electric paid an interim dividend of 12.85 pence, an increase from 12 pence.
Northern Electric forecasts full year pretax profits to exceed 112 million pounds.
The company anticipates a final dividend of 29.85 pence.
Northern Electric's gearing is expected to fall to 95 percent by March 31.
Last year, Northern Electric fended off a bid from Trafalgar House with a 560 million pound benefit package.

Britain's Chemical Industries Association (CIA) criticized the electricity wholesale market on Monday.
The CIA called for urgent reforms to the electricity wholesale market.
The CIA stated that electricity prices for industrial consumers should have fallen further.
The CIA's members account for around 20 percent of Britain's industrial electricity use.
Industry observers noted that there may be pressure for an investigation of the pool's operations by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).
A CIA spokesman claimed that the pool is not structured to deliver competitive pricing.
The pool is a system used to set electricity wholesale prices.
Critics argue that the pool gives unfair market control to large generators like National Power and PowerGen.
Many large industrial users purchase electricity directly from the pool instead of through regional electricity companies (Recs).
The CIA reported that prices paid for energy through the pool were 10 percent higher in the first half of the current financial year compared to the same period a year ago.

Shares in Standard Chartered rose sharply on Wednesday.
Standard Chartered is a London-based bank that specializes in the Asia-Pacific region.
Standard Chartered raised its 1996 profits by 32 percent.
Standard Chartered's pretax profit rose to 870 million pounds in 1996.
The pretax profit included exceptional items of 45 million pounds.
Standard Chartered's pretax profit was 661 million pounds in 1995.
By 1030 GMT, Standard Chartered shares were 21.5p higher at 791.5p.
Standard Chartered raised its dividend by 32 percent to 14.5 pence per share.
Trading profit rose to 818 million pounds from 654 million pounds.
Chief executive Malcolm Williamson expects Standard Chartered's cost base to rise by seven percent in 1997.

Prudential Corp Plc is interested in buying a building society.
Peter Davis is the chief executive of Prudential Corp Plc.
Davis stated that Prudential is interested in a building society for its branch network and customer base.
Prudential raised its first half operating profit by 8.0 percent to 421 million stg.
Davis declined to comment on specific names linked to Prudential's potential acquisition.
Industry sources suggest that Prudential is unlikely to be interested in Lloyds Abbey Life.
Prudential's telephone banking operation is set to launch on October 1.
The start-up cost for Prudential's telephone banking operation was around 33 million stg.
Prudential's funds under management have risen by four percent to 85 billion stg since the end of 1995.
Prudential's single contribution sales rose by 50 percent in the first half of the year.

Standard Chartered Plc will increase investment in 1997 and beyond to capitalize on business opportunities.
Malcolm Williamson is the chief executive of Standard Chartered Plc.
Williamson stated that the bank expects to increase costs by seven percent in 1997 after a two percent rise in 1996.
Williamson indicated that the investment will likely continue after 1997 for several years.
The investment will focus on boosting Standard Chartered's core areas of operation.
Core areas of operation include retail banking, consumer banking, and corporate and institutional banking.
Standard Chartered reported a 32 percent rise in pre-tax profits in 1996 to 870 million stg.
The bank raised its dividend by 32 percent to 14.5p per share for the year.
Williamson stated that the increased investment would not affect the bank's progressive dividend policy.
Williamson noted that major banking acquisitions in Asia are challenging due to legal constraints on foreign ownership.

Michael Jackson launched his first concert tour in three years on Saturday in Prague.
The concert aimed to restore Jackson's career, which was affected by allegations of child molestation.
Jackson opened the concert in gold-plated astronaut's armor and performed his song 'Scream'.
The stage design combined elements of a classical Greek temple and a space station.
Jackson performed many hits from his 20-year career during the concert.
The 'HIStory World Tour' will take hundreds of tonnes of equipment to various stops in Europe, Africa, and Asia.
No concert dates are scheduled for the Americas during this tour.
Approximately 120,000 spectators attended the concert on Letna Plain in Prague.
Czech President Vaclav Havel attended the concert but stated that Jackson's music 'isn't close' to him.
The tour is intended to support Jackson's 'HIStory' album, which has not sold as well as his 1982 album 'Thriller'.

The Czech government backed Transport Minister Martin Riman's stance against striking railway workers.
The railway workers have shut down the entire rail network over potential job cuts.
Government spokesman Ivo Strejcek stated that the government expressed support for Riman.
Riman has refused union demands for a long-term railway plan that guarantees jobs.
The rail strike began at midnight on Tuesday and was originally planned for 48 hours.
This strike is the Czech Republic's first major nationwide post-Communist industrial action.
The strike has had little major impact on daily life, but businesses fear it will affect earnings.
Cities have added buses to alleviate commuter pressure due to the strike.
International trains have been stranded at borders with Germany, Poland, Austria, and Slovakia.
The Association of Unions of Rail Workers (OSZ) reported that 75 to 80 percent of railway workers joined the strike.

Standard & Poor's (S&P) gave investment grade ratings to three of the four largest Czech banks.
The high ratings were partly due to an implied safety net for the banks provided by the state.
S&P issued long-term ratings of BBB-minus to Komercni Banka a.s., Ceska Sporitelna a.s., and Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka a.s.
S&P also issued short-term ratings of A3 for counterparty risk to the same three banks.
The ratings for the three banks were lower than the Czech Republic's sovereign rating of A.
The ratings were similar to those issued to the Slovak, Polish, and Greek central banks.
The ratings were one grade above Hungarian sovereign debt.
S&P stated that the size and market position of the three banks made it likely that the Czech government would provide support if needed.
S&P did not give a rating for IPB a.s., the third largest Czech bank, which is awaiting privatisation.
Komercni Banka a.s. held 25 percent of Czech deposits, 26 percent of the credit market, and conducted 10 percent of total trading on the Prague Stock Exchange last year.

Britain's chemical industry predicted three more years of sluggish investment.
The Chemical Industries Association (CIA) reported that spending on new plant and equipment was 2.15 billion pounds ($3.5 billion) last year.
After adjusting for inflation, spending on new plant and equipment fell by 0.6 percent last year.
Britain's investment in the chemical industry is behind that of international competitors.
French chemical companies increased spending by seven percent last year.
U.S. spending in the chemical industry rose by 11 percent last year.
The Netherlands saw a 13 percent increase in chemical industry spending last year.
The CIA projected a five percent increase in spending for 1997.
Nikko Europe analyst Philip Morrish identified global overcapacity and weak European economies as factors affecting investment.
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) stated that weak investment levels are evident across the British economy.

Peptide Therapeutics Plc plans to target North America for further alliances.
John Brown is the new chief executive of Peptide Therapeutics Plc.
John Brown stated that the company seeks partnerships with big pharmaceutical companies in North America.
Alan Goodman will step down as chief executive to lead Peptide's efforts in North America.
Peptide Therapeutics has existing deals with SmithKline Beecham Plc and Medeva Plc.
Peptide agreed to develop vaccines using Medeva's expertise in non-injectable drugs in January.
Peptide licensed its portfolio of allergy vaccines to SmithKline Beecham earlier this month.
John Brown mentioned that there is potential to attract new partners despite existing agreements.
Peptide is interested in developing early stage vaccines against Meningitis B and Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV).
Peptide has increased its staff from 28 to 77 in the past 12 months and plans to grow to between 90 and 100.

Coats Viyella Plc announced a sharp fall in 1996 pre-tax profits.
Pre-tax profits fell 42 percent to 94.4 million pounds in 1996.
A reorganisation charge of 54.9 million pounds contributed to the profit decline.
Excluding charges, profits slid eight percent due to poor demand and economic weakness.
Key divisions, including core thread operations, struggled in important markets such as Europe, Brazil, and Turkey.
Coats Viyella maintained its dividend payout per share at 8.8 pence.
The earnings per share for the group was 6.7 pence.
Shares in Coats rose 4.5 pence to 134.5 in late morning trading.
The stock has fallen 52 percent over the past two years and underperformed the FTSE All Share index by 48 percent.
The stock is currently 84 percent below its 1988 peak of 860 pence.

Colombia's Senate approved a bill to partially lift the country's ban on the extradition of drug traffickers and other criminals.
The bill was approved with a vote of 53-14 in a plenary session.
The bill still faces additional congressional hurdles before it can become a statute.
Justice Minister Almabeatriz Rengifo expressed satisfaction with the vote in favor of the motion.
Critics argue that the bill has been weakened and may not satisfy U.S. anti-drug officials.
The bill must undergo two more debates in the Lower House of Congress before June 20 and four more after mid-July.
If passed, the bill would prohibit extradition if alleged criminals surrender to Colombian authorities or face harsher penalties abroad.
Giovanni Lamboglia, a member of the Liberal Party, expressed opposition to a completely unrestricted extradition law.
Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia indicated that the government may seek to strengthen the proposal after July 20.
The vote coincided with the burial of former president Virgilio Barco, who had previously ordered the extradition of a drug lord.

Colombia is preparing for a nationwide strike on Tuesday.
The strike is expected to be the largest in 20 years.
Labor leaders and security forces reported that talks between union chiefs and government ministers broke down on Sunday.
More than 800,000 state workers are participating in the strike.
State workers are demanding a 21.5 percent pay increase.
The government offered a weighted pay increase of 13.5 percent.
State workers are protesting against the reduction of labor rights and government plans for privatization of state-run industries.
The government stated that the salary demands exceed its current financial capacity.
The police and armed forces announced increased security measures to prevent radical protests and potential guerrilla attacks.
Local authorities in many cities imposed bans on carrying firearms and on motorcyclists carrying passengers.

Colombia will use its coffee stockpiles to meet export commitments due to a lower than expected 1996/97 harvest.
The 1996/97 coffee harvest is estimated to be just over 10 million 60-kg bags according to Jorge Cardenas.
Many private exporters and analysts believe that much of the National Coffee Growers' Federation's stocks are old or damaged.
Semana magazine reported that structural problems are the main cause of falling coffee production levels.
Cardenas predicted that coffee inventories would decrease to 3.5 million bags by the end of September from about five million bags.
Cardenas did not comment on claims that much of the coffee stocks were old.
Semana magazine stated that the decline in coffee output is due to aging plantations and abandonment by growers.
El Espectador reported that the agricultural sector's growth rate in 1996 was 0.21 percent, largely due to poor coffee performance.
Antonio Herron warned that the 'broca' pest could affect all of Colombia's 900,000 hectares of coffee by 1999.
Currently, about 680,000 hectares of coffee plantations are affected by 'broca', which is approximately 75 percent of the country's total.

Shares in United News & Media Plc reached record highs on Friday.
United News & Media Plc reported a 12 percent profit rise in the first year after a merger.
The merger effectively doubled the size of United News & Media Plc.
United News, publisher of The Express and Daily Star, merged with MAI in a three billion pound deal.
The profit before tax and exceptional items for 1996 was 290.2 million pounds.
Earnings per share increased by 15 percent to 40 pence.
Chief executive Clive Hollick stated that the company delivered at the top end of expectations post-merger.
United shares increased by 25.5p to 766p by 1600 GMT.
Several analysts raised their forecasts for 1997 profits to between 310 and 335 million pounds.
United expected annual savings of 43 million pounds by 1998 due to the merger and restructuring.

British Sky Broadcasting Plc emphasized its commitment to digital television on Thursday.
BSkyB warned that the UK was falling behind its European neighbours in the transition to digital television.
David Chance, BSkyB deputy managing director, stated the company's aim is to lead in the digital era.
BSkyB has approximately 5.5 million subscribers and is the leading force in British pay television.
BSkyB plans to launch 200-channel digital satellite services in the UK later this year.
BSkyB has partnered with Carlton Communications Plc and Granada Group Plc to apply for digital terrestrial television (DTT) licenses.
The British Digital Broadcasting consortium is competing with DTN for three key DTT licenses.
The Independent Television Commission (ITC) is expected to announce a decision on the licenses around May.
DTT is scheduled to begin in mid-1998 and will offer around 30 channels.
David Chance expressed hope that regulators would not oppose British Digital Broadcasting if awarded the DTT licenses.

Michael Grade announced he is quitting Channel 4 television.
Michael Grade will become executive chairman of First Leisure Plc by July 31.
John Conlan, the current chief executive of First Leisure, plans to leave the business by the end of the year.
First Leisure was founded in 1982 by Michael Grade's uncle, Lord Delfont.
First Leisure operates various leisure businesses, including bowling alleys, bars, and the Blackpool Tower tourist site.
Michael Grade is already the non-executive chairman of First Leisure.
Michael Grade announced he was quitting as chief executive of Channel 4 after almost a decade.
Michael Grade built Channel 4's audience share to more than 10 percent while maintaining its reputation for distinctive programming.
First Leisure has a market capitalisation of around 600 million pounds.
First Leisure is spending 55 million pounds this year on new bars, nightclubs, and fitness centres as part of a 100 million pound investment programme.

Polaris Industries Inc. is known for its snowmobiles.
Polaris will begin building motorcycles.
No major U.S. company other than Harley-Davidson Inc. has entered the motorcycle market in 40 years.
Polaris is developing a highway cruiser motorcycle named Victory, which will be available in the spring of 1998.
The engine for the Victory motorcycle was designed and will be made in the USA.
Matt Parks will be the general manager of the new Polaris motorcycles unit.
Polaris is the world's largest maker of snowmobiles and among the top three makers of all-terrain vehicles and personal watercraft.
Polaris CEO Hall Wendel stated that entering the motorcycle market is a logical extension of their diversification strategy.
Shares in Polaris rose 37.5 cents to $26.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The worldwide market for cruiser motorcycles is estimated at over 200,000 units annually.

North American garbage companies are expected to continue acquiring each other's assets.
Big firms are selling off unprofitable operations while smaller companies are consolidating.
Top executives from major waste management companies made presentations at a Raymond James conference.
Asset strategy was a key topic in the presentations by trash hauling companies.
WMX Technologies Inc and Browning Ferris Industries Inc control about 25% of the $35 billion solid waste market.
WMX and BFI are shedding non-core and unprofitable operations.
Laidlaw Inc is transitioning into a transportation company and exiting the solid waste and hazardous waste markets.
Mid-sized companies like USA Waste Services Inc, United Waste Systems Inc, and Superior Services Inc are consolidating by acquiring smaller firms.
The trash hauling industry in North America grew significantly in the 1970s due to environmentalism and stricter regulations.
The focus of solid waste handling is shifting from landfill to recycling, which has lower profit margins.

The board of directors of WMX Technologies Inc. expressed support for Chief Executive Phillip Rooney.
An investment group led by financier George Soros called for Rooney's ouster.
The Soros group proposed a slate of nominees for the WMX board.
The WMX board unanimously reaffirmed its support for Phillip B. Rooney.
James Kelleher, an industry analyst, commented on the ongoing struggle involving WMX and Soros.
The Soros group and other investors have been pressuring WMX to improve its performance.
WMX announced it was cutting 3,000 jobs and shedding $1.5 billion in assets.
The Soros group expressed dissatisfaction with WMX's restructuring plan.
WMX reported a fourth-quarter loss of $461 million after charges.
WMX stated that the Soros group's board nominees did not qualify for consideration at the annual meeting.

Telstra Corp reported a 38.4-percent fall in net profit for the 1996/97 first half.
The decline in profit was attributed to the costs of shedding almost a third of its workforce.
Telstra is to be partially privatised by the end of the year.
Telstra is in talks with global telecom carriers about forming possible alliances.
Telstra reported a net profit after abnormals of A$742.0 million in the six months to December 31, 1996.
This net profit is a decrease from A$1.20 billion a year ago.
Redundancy costs were A$1.03 billion in the half-year period.
Staff levels decreased by 7,000 to about 69,500 during the half.
Telstra's plan announced last September includes cutting about 22,000 jobs by the end of fiscal 1998/99.
Revenue grew by 4.6 percent to A$7.77 billion in the December half.

David Jones Ltd is expected to report a sharp fall in half year profit.
David Jones Ltd is searching for a new chief executive.
Chris Tideman resigned as CEO on Tuesday.
Analysts believe Tideman was affected by a weak retail environment.
David Jones has not met investor expectations since its listing in November 1995.
David Jones has been spending more on opening new stores and restructuring.
Analysts noted that Tideman may have been trying to manage too many changes at once.
David Jones is introducing new inventory management systems and increasing its private label merchandise.
David Jones has restructured its South Australian operations and plans to expand into Western Australia and New Zealand.
Analysts expect David Jones to report a net profit before abnormals of between A$20 million and A$22 million.

APEC ministers agreed on further trade and investment liberalisation in the telecommunications sector.
APEC ministers recognized they cannot include China in the forum's agenda of trade liberalisation.
Richard Alston is the Australian telecommunications minister.
Richard Alston stated that China connects 15 million telephone lines a year.
China has one of the lowest penetration rates of fixed telephone lines among APEC members.
Alston compared the scale of operations in China to those in Papua New Guinea and Brunei.
Alston expressed hope that Malaysia would attend future APEC meetings.
Malaysia did not attend the initial APEC telecommunications ministers meeting in Seoul in 1995.
Alston stated that APEC cannot force member countries to adopt a uniform policy.
Ministers agreed on further collaboration on telecommunications for rural development, distance education, information sharing, and the environment.

British Telecommunications Plc stated it might launch a legal challenge if a windfall tax on its profits is imposed by Britain's new Labour government.
BT reported a rise in annual pretax profits to 3.2 billion pounds from 3.02 billion pounds.
Chairman Sir Iain Vallance claimed the group owed it to its shareholders to prevent the government from taxing its earnings.
BT shares increased by two pence to 451-1/2p at 1120 GMT.
Vallance indicated that if BT is significantly affected by the tax and it can be legally challenged, the company would pursue that challenge.
Vallance expressed that the company would be very sad to start a partnership with Labour on such terms.
The government announced it would impose a one-off windfall tax on what it calls the excess profits of privatised utilities.
Some analysts estimated that BT could face a one-off tax of 1.0-1.5 billion pounds.
Vallance argued it would be perverse to categorize BT with privatised utilities for punishment.
BT received approval from European regulators for its proposed merger with MCI Communications Corp, creating a new company called Concert Plc.

Investors in the U.S. and the U.K. are likely to approve a $23 billion merger between British Telecommunications and MCI.
The proposed merger is the largest transatlantic merger to date.
Oliver Ehrenberg, a telecoms analyst at Robert Fleming, expressed caution about the merger, stating that 30 percent is too much of a premium to pay for control of MCI.
Shareholders in MCI Communications Corp were voting on the merger on Wednesday.
BT investors are scheduled to vote on the merger on April 15.
One investment institution in London remains neutral on the merger, citing advantages but also a high price.
BT executives have been meeting with large institutions to discuss the rationale for acquiring the remaining 80 percent of MCI.
BT reported a positive response from investors during a recent road show to market the deal.
The merger is expected to create a company called Concert Plc, with annual revenues exceeding 25 billion pounds and 43 million customers.
BT has projected savings of 1.5 billion pounds over the first five years from the merger, with an annual pre-tax savings of 500 million pounds thereafter.

British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp are reportedly entering South America.
BT announced a strategic alliance with Portugal Telecom SA.
Portugal Telecom's announcement stated that MCI formed a joint venture with Telefonica de Espana.
BT did not mention Telefonica in its statement.
An MCI official stated that the deal with Tisa was announced in error.
A BT spokeswoman confirmed the alliance with Portugal Telecom but did not comment on other rumors.
BT's shareholders are set to vote on a merger with MCI valued at 12.3 billion pounds.
Portugal Telecom will be the exclusive distributor of Concert Communications Services.
BT will acquire a one percent stake and MCI will acquire a 0.5 percent stake in Portugal Telecom.
Portugal Telecom has formed an alliance with Telebras in Brazil, which is a significant telecoms market.

The stock of Apple Computer Inc. rose on Thursday.
The rise in Apple's stock was due to a report about Oracle Corp. chairman Larry Ellison's interest in buying Apple.
Larry Ellison stated he was forming an investor group to raise $1 billion to buy a majority stake in Apple.
Ellison has expressed interest in buying Apple since April 1995.
Ellison's interest in buying Apple is partly to prevent Microsoft Corp. from dominating the computer industry.
Apple's market value is $2.17 billion.
Ellison's stake in Oracle is worth about $6 billion.
Apple's stock rose by $2.25 to $19, while Oracle's stock fell by $1.125 to $39.375.
Ellison is gauging investor support before deciding whether to make a bid for Apple.
Wall Street analysts doubt Ellison will attempt to buy Apple due to a lack of concrete steps taken in the past two years.

Apple Computer Inc. plans to release an operating system that resembles the Macintosh and runs Mac software.
The new operating system will operate on personal computers using Intel Corp. chips.
Apple will release programming tools that allow companies to write software for the Macintosh and convert it for Intel-based PCs running Microsoft Windows.
Apple's strategy aims to prevent software companies from discontinuing Macintosh product development.
Apple Chairman Gilbert Amelio addressed 1,900 programmers at the annual developer conference in San Jose, California.
Amelio stated that the new development environment allows applications to be written once and released for both Mac and Windows platforms with simple recompilation.
The Macintosh operating system has traditionally run only on Apple-designed machines.
Apple's next-generation operating system is code-named Rhapsody and will run on both Apple-designed computers and Intel-based PCs using Microsoft software.
Apple has been working on improvements to the Macintosh for the past two years to differentiate it from PCs.
Apple's stock price decreased by 19 cents to $17.375 on Nasdaq during late trading.

Apple Computer Inc. reported a $708 million second-quarter loss.
The loss was due to a charge for the layoff of a third of its employees and weaker sales of personal computers.
Apple expects strong sales of new PCs and laptops and lower expenses to help achieve profitability by the fiscal fourth quarter ending in September.
The net loss for the fiscal quarter ended March 28 was equivalent to $5.64 a share.
This loss compared to a net loss of $740 million, or $5.99 a share, in the same quarter the previous year.
Apple's loss from operations was $186 million, or $1.48 a share, which was worse than the consensus forecast of $1.22 a share.
The $708 million net loss included a $155 million charge for layoffs and a $375 million charge for the acquisition of Next Software Inc.
Apple expects higher revenue and a reduced operating loss in the third quarter due to its restructuring program.
In March, Apple announced it would lay off 4,100 employees and reorganize operations to cut costs.
The number of Apple computers shipped worldwide in the second quarter decreased by 33 percent to 602,000 units compared to 892,000 units in the same quarter the previous year.

Toronto's stock market ended weaker on Monday.
The Toronto Stock Exchange's 300 Composite Index fell 28.62 points to 5797.65.
64.8 million shares were traded, worth C$1.02 billion (US$730 million).
Fred Ketchen, senior vice-president at ScotiaMcLeod, stated that investors in New York became nervous.
Ketchen claimed that the nervousness in New York affected the Canadian market.
Wall Street fell as investors reconsidered concerns about U.S. interest rate hikes.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained about five percent the previous week.
Toronto's stock market rose nearly 2.5 percent the previous week.
Eleven of Toronto's 14 sub-indexes dropped, with consumer products, pipelines, conglomerates, and retail leading the decline.
Rio Algom Ltd. shares fell 1.80 to close at 34.00.

Toronto stocks gained nearly one percent on Wednesday.
The gain was driven by a rally in the conglomerate and banking groups.
Investors reacted positively to strong first quarter earnings.
The Toronto Stock Exchange's key 300 Composite Index closed at 5789.82 after climbing 55.27 points.
Trading volume was 78.9 million shares worth C$1.27 billion ($909 million).
Fred Ketchen, a senior vice-president at ScotiaMcLeod, stated that the market's overriding influence is shifting from inflationary problems to satisfaction with earnings.
Toronto and New York markets have corrected about 10 percent since mid-March due to concerns over U.S. interest rate hikes.
Stelco Inc reported first quarter earnings of C$0.27 ($0.19) per share, up from C$0.13 ($0.09) per share a year ago.
Of Toronto's 14 sub-indices, 11 gained ground, with consumer products, banks, and conglomerates leading the gains.
Advancing issues outnumbered declines 482 to 468, with 285 stocks trading flat.

Toronto stocks closed flat on Monday.
The Toronto Stock Exchange's key 300 Composite Index added 3.36 points to end at 6217.60.
Turnover was 84.8 million shares worth C$1.13 billion ($836 million).
Investor interest in mergers buoyed Toronto despite declines in Barrick Gold Corp. and Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
Bre-X announced a deal with Freeport-McMoran Copper and Gold Inc. to develop a gold discovery in Busang, Indonesia.
Freeport will own 15 percent of Busang, Bre-X will keep 45 percent, and Indonesian interests will take 40 percent.
Barrick shares fell sharply after being excluded from the Busang development.
U.S. financial markets were closed on Monday for President's Day holiday.
Of Toronto's 14 sub-indices, 12 groups rose, led by conglomerates, media, forestry products, and retail.
Advancing issues outpaced declines 545 to 422 with 297 stocks unchanged.

Chinese soyoil buyers are selling cargoes back to the market.
Traders in the Far East believe these buyers are unlikely to release a large amount of supplies originally meant for China.
Soybeans and soybean meal are being imported into China.
A Hong Kong trader stated that selling back soyoil is logical due to profit margins.
U.S. exporters reported that China resold between 25,000 and 50,000 tonnes of Argentine soyoil to two trading houses recently.
Traders suggested that uncertainty over Chinese government import quotas for soyoil may be causing sell-backs.
A source in Singapore expressed concern that quotas might not be issued.
Traders noted that little soyoil is currently on its way to China.
Trading sources reported that large quantities of soybean meal are arriving at Chinese ports this month.
One trader estimated that soybean meal imports could exceed half a million tonnes, approaching one million tonnes.

Far East metals traders were focused on whether China would buy copper during the current price rally.
Traders and industry sources polled by Reuters believed that copper prices would continue to rise.
Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) finished higher on Friday, reaching 8-1/2 month highs.
Copper was priced at $2,366 a tonne at the afternoon kerb close on Friday.
Copper prices on the Shanghai Metal Exchange (SME) have been rising in line with the LME since trading resumed after the Lunar New Year holiday.
Shanghai copper futures opened higher on Monday at 23,500 yuan ($2,831) a tonne.
Shanghai copper futures fell to 23,460 yuan in early trading on Monday.
Trading sources indicated that Chinese buyers would remain in the market as long as prices on the LME and SME continue to rise.
Shanghai Metal Exchange figures reported copper stocks at 17,524 tonnes.
A trader noted that there had been some signs of Chinese buying, but it was limited to a few hundred tonnes.

Author Shi Young claims that there are documented Japanese war atrocities in China.
Shi Young's book is titled 'The Rape of Nanking (Nanjing): An Undeniable History in Photographs.'
The book documents events from 1937 known as the Rape of Nanking.
Shi Young is collecting material for an exhibition in St. Louis this year.
The exhibition will include video-taped interviews and artifacts from the Nanjing Museum.
Liu Xiuying is one of 10 survivors of the Nanjing massacre seeking compensation from the Japanese government.
Liu Xiuying was attacked and raped by Japanese soldiers in 1937 when she was 19 years old.
Shi Young is updating his book for a second edition.
The first print run of the book was 7,500 copies and is nearly sold out.
Shi and James Yin collected over 400 photographs depicting the Japanese occupation of Nanjing.

Western mines and financiers are not interested in Russia's gold reserves.
Russia is the world's third-largest gold producer.
Ted Reeve is a gold equity analyst at Scotia Capital Markets in Toronto.
Ted Reeve stated that attracting significant foreign investment in Russia's gold sector will be slow.
Russia ranks fifth in gold output and lower in outside investment.
No top joint ventures in Russia have produced gold since launching operations in recent years.
Pas Gido is a board member of Baleyzoloto, a Canadian-Russian project near Chita in Siberia.
Viktor Gritsay is a deputy head of the state committee for precious metals and stones (Komdragmet).
Russia targeted $6 billion in investment for its gold sector by 2000, with 43 percent from foreign investors.
Only $45 million was invested in Russian gold projects last year.

Russia's Norilsk Nickel was created by Stalin using forced labor.
Norilsk Nickel operates under Soviet-style business practices.
Post-Soviet Norilsk is a center of debate over restructuring firms in Russia.
Norilsk was built using the labor of prisoners forced to mine ore.
Norilsk is working to restructure costs, resettle workers and pensioners, and improve its image.
Norilsk is located 200 miles north of the Arctic Circle.
Mikhail Steklov is the director of Norilsk's flagship nickel smelter.
Uneximbank holds 51 percent of Norilsk's voting stock.
Norilsk produces 55 percent of world palladium reserves, 20 percent of platinum, and 35 percent of nickel reserves.
Norilsk aims to regroup into one company focused on maximizing output and profits.

Russian oil barons are competing for control of Rosneft.
Rosneft is one of the last major energy firms in Russia that has not been privatised.
Industry sources reported that Sibneft is attempting to acquire Rosneft.
Boris Berezovsky is known to control Sibneft.
A Russian energy official stated that Berezovsky plans to merge Sibneft and Rosneft.
The merger is intended to control revenue flows from Rosneft's exports.
Sibneft is considering acquiring Rosneft among other energy companies.
Sibneft's management is evaluating the possibility of the acquisition.
Rosneft has significant equity stakes in energy projects worth $40 billion with foreign oil companies.
Rosneft has liabilities including research institutes and defunct equipment producers.

Rhone-Poulenc SA reported a 28.4 percent increase in net income for 1996, totaling 2.74 billion francs.
Chairman Jean-Rene Fourtou stated that the net income level was insufficient.
Fourtou denied rumors regarding potential acquisitions, mergers, or splitting the company's chemicals and pharmaceuticals activities.
The company plans to focus on internal growth.
Fourtou set a target for a 20 percent increase in earnings per share for 1997, from 8.44 francs in 1996.
Rhone-Poulenc expects to exceed its asset sale program of 10 billion francs, which was at 6.8 billion francs at the end of 1996.
The company aims to reduce debt to below 50 percent of equity, down from 61 percent in 1996 and 72 percent in 1995.
Sales increased by three percent to 85.82 billion francs, and operating income rose by 38.5 percent to 6.892 billion francs.
The gross dividend was raised by 16.7 percent to 5.25 francs per share.
Fourtou identified three negative factors affecting results: a recall of albumin products, a crisis in polyester, and low titanium oxide prices.

The French government called off the sale of electronics group Thomson SA.
This decision was made after weeks of defending the choice of buyer.
It was the second privatisation halted in less than a month.
The first privatisation halted was the sale of state-owned bank CIC.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe is experiencing low opinion poll ratings.
The Finance Ministry stated the suspension was due to objections regarding the sale of Thomson's consumer electronics unit to Daewoo Electronics.
Renewed talks about the sale of Thomson could start soon, according to the office of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
The government aims to consult rapidly to facilitate the privatisation of Thomson.
Industry Minister Franck Borotra stated that the privatisation of Thomson is essential for the company's future.
Several thousand workers of Thomson Multimedia protested against the sale on November 20.

Lagardere Groupe does not expect to make a profit on its multimedia activities until 1998.
Lagardere Groupe holds leading market positions in the U.S. and France.
Arnaud Lagardere is the head of multimedia activities at Lagardere Groupe.
Lagardere Groupe anticipates a loss for the years 1996 and 1997.
Lagardere Groupe expects to reach break-even during 1997.
1998 will be the first full year that Lagardere Groupe will be above break-even.
Grolier is the number two interactive encyclopedia publisher in the U.S. behind Microsoft.
Grolier has annual sales of approximately 2.5 billion French francs, equivalent to $448 million.
Lagardere owns the Club Internet access provider, which is number three in France.
Lagardere is involved in projects aimed at developing multimedia satellite services for 2005.

Axa-UAP is to be awarded a licence to sell life insurance in China.
The announcement was made by Axa-UAP's Asian subsidiary.
National Mutual Holdings Ltd is 51 percent owned by Axa-UAP.
Chinese authorities verbally advised National Mutual Holdings that a licence would be granted.
The announcement caused shares of National Mutual to reach a record high.
Shares in National Mutual Asia Ltd, the Hong Kong-listed arm of National Mutual, also increased.
Geoff Tomlinson is the managing director of National Mutual Holdings.
Tomlinson cautioned investors not to get too excited about the announcement.
The licence could take up to 18 months to be granted.
Tony Jackson is an analyst at Macquarie Equities.

Amcor Ltd is an Australian paper and packaging company.
Amcor Ltd reported disappointing profit results and forecasts.
Amcor Ltd stated on Tuesday that it hoped the worst financial performance would be over in 1996/97.
The financial year for Amcor Ltd runs from July to June.
Amcor managing director Don Macfarlane indicated that full-year net profit would be lower than A$338.8 million from 1995/96.
Don Macfarlane predicted that paper prices would rise from early calendar 1998.
Macfarlane made his comments during an interview with Reuters.
Amcor Ltd's second half results are expected to be lower than both the previous year and the first half of 1996/97.
Amcor Ltd announced that there would be significant write-downs.
Macfarlane expressed hope that the current financial situation was the worst.

An Australian state-owned power station and coal mine was sold for A$4.86 billion (US$3.65 billion).
This sale is the largest privatisation in Australia.
A consortium including U.S. utilities CMS Energy Corp and NRG Energy Inc and Australian institutional investors acquired the assets.
David Scaysbrook is the managing director of NRG Australia Ltd.
The sale followed a competitive bidding process involving major global utilities.
The sale of the 2,000 megawatt power station and coal mine surpasses last year's sale of half of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia.
The Commonwealth Bank of Australia sale generated A$4.0 billion for the national government.
Loy Yang A is noted as the most efficient electricity generator in Australia.
CMS Energy holds a 50 percent equity stake in Loy Yang A.
NRG Energy Inc owns a 25 percent stake in Loy Yang A, which includes Australia's largest coal mine.

Boeing Co. reported that its first-quarter profit more than doubled.
Boeing Co. reported a 70 percent increase in sales in the first quarter.
Boeing Co. earned $313 million, or 87 cents a share, in the first quarter.
Boeing Co. earned $119 million, or 35 cents a share, in the same quarter a year earlier.
Boeing Co. reported revenue of $7.32 billion, up from $4.29 billion.
Boeing's net income was 13 percent below the Wall Street consensus of $1 a share.
Boeing's stock price fell by $5.50 to $96.50 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts indicated that Boeing's earnings were affected by higher-than-expected research and development expenses.
Boeing stated that it was incurring significant overtime costs to increase production.
Boeing expects profit margins to be lower for the rest of the year due to growing deliveries of new aircraft models.

Weyerhaeuser Co. reported lower fourth-quarter earnings of $98 million or 50 cents a share.
Weyerhaeuser's fourth-quarter earnings were down from $251 million or $1.25 a share a year earlier.
Weyerhaeuser's revenues for the fourth quarter fell to $2.8 billion from $3.1 billion.
Weyerhaeuser's earnings exceeded the Wall Street consensus of 48 cents a share due to strong operating earnings in its real estate business.
Weyerhaeuser's stock closed at $49.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Weyerhaeuser reported net income of $463 million or $2.34 a share for the year.
Weyerhaeuser's net income for the year was down from $983 million or $4.83 a share before a special charge in 1995.
Weyerhaeuser's revenues for the year fell to $11.1 billion from $11.8 billion.
Louisiana-Pacific Corp. reported a net loss of $14.7 million or 14 cents a share for the fourth quarter.
Louisiana-Pacific's net loss for the year was $201 million or $1.87 a share, primarily due to a pre-tax charge for closing its pulp mill in Ketchikan, Alaska.

Edmark Corp is a U.S. maker of educational computer software for children.
Sally Narodick resigned as chairman and chief executive of Edmark Corp for stress-related health reasons.
Donna Stanger, vice-president for product development, will temporarily assume the duties of chief executive.
Frances Conley, a director of Edmark Corp and principal of Roanoke Capital Ltd, will serve as chairman of the board.
Sally Narodick experienced symptoms including fatigue starting in June and took a two-week holiday.
After returning to work, Narodick suffered from fatigue, insomnia, and weight loss.
Narodick's doctors recommended that she take steps to lower her stress level.
Narodick stated that she needs to take time off to rest and heal.
The market for educational software is increasingly crowded, affecting Edmark and its competitors.
Edmark officials declined to comment on speculation about the company becoming a takeover candidate.

Ivorian coffee exporters are grading a large crop.
Ivorian coffee exporters will pay little attention to the upcoming meeting of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries.
One exporter stated that the meeting means nothing.
Green robusta coffee arrivals at Ivorian ports totalled around 250,000 tonnes by May 9 in the 1996/97 season.
This is an increase from just over 180,000 tonnes by the same time last year.
African producers agreed in January to cut robusta exports from 6.52 million bags to 5.67 million under an ACPC export plan.
The amount to be retained by each country under the ACPC plan was unclear.
Ivory Coast agreed to subtract 15,000 tonnes from its share of the previously agreed African quota.
Ivorian coffee exports and local industry offtake since the start of the season were about 110,000-120,000 tonnes.
Ivorian exporters expect a steady flow of shipments up to the end of the season despite fluctuating world prices.

Ivory Coast plans to discuss further reform of its cocoa industry in May.
A committee of industry, donor, and Ivorian delegates reviewed the cocoa industry from February 5-7.
The review identified quality and marketing problems in the cocoa industry.
Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze stated that the Prime Minister values the committee's deliberations and conclusions.
The state Caistab marketing body will retain a role in the future cocoa industry.
Gauze emphasized that the state must maintain a quality control role.
No solutions to the identified concerns have been agreed upon, but proposals will be discussed in May.
The consultative committee was set up in October and is chaired by Philippe Mian, a technical adviser to Prime Minister Daniel Kablan Duncan.
Findings from the consultative committee will be considered at the cabinet level before May.
World Bank officials indicated they would reconsider ideas put forward by exporters regarding cocoa auctions.

Ivory Coast is expected to have a large coffee crop for the 1996/97 season due to favorable weather and improved farm maintenance.
Industry and port sources reported quality problems with the coffee crop.
Exporters and crop analysts predict a total coffee crop of up to 300,000 tonnes for the 1996/97 season.
The previous year's coffee crop was 180,000 tonnes.
Ivory Coast's official forecast for the 1996/97 coffee crop was 230,000 tonnes.
Port arrivals by April 17 totaled 228,000 tonnes, compared to 150,000 tonnes at the same time the previous year.
Exporters indicated that markets would be found for the increased supply of lower quality coffee.
A quality inspector stated that it was unlikely the full 1996/97 crop would be shipped due to wastage and rejection.
Warehouse stocks were estimated to be well over 150,000 tonnes based on the latest export and arrival figures.
Farmers were reportedly holding back coffee supplies due to low prices offered by buyers.

A Florida judge rejected a request from tobacco companies to delay the start of a class-action lawsuit trial until December.
Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye stated that the trial would begin as scheduled on June 2 in Miami.
The lawsuit was filed on behalf of thousands of flight attendants by Miami lawyers Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt.
The lawsuit claims damages for an estimated 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants suffering from lung diseases and other ailments caused by secondhand smoke on U.S. passenger jets.
Tobacco attorneys warned Judge Kaye that much pretrial examination of witnesses and other work remained to be done.
Hugh Whiting, an attorney for RJ Reynolds Tobacco, stated that only one out of five expert witnesses had been questioned by tobacco company lawyers.
Whiting indicated that as many as 120 other witnesses needed to be questioned before June 2.
Whiting suggested that the trial be postponed to December 15.
Judge Kaye formalized the appointment of Florida lawyers Michael Salmon and Irwin Block to review three batches of industry documents for possible use at trial.
The case is formally known as Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. et al.

Top Citicorp managers have testified before a grand jury investigating allegations of money laundering.
The investigation involves Raul Salinas, the brother of former Mexican President Carlos Salinas de Gortari.
Citicorp Chief Executive Officer John Reed stated that the company is cooperating fully with the grand jury.
Raul Salinas is currently jailed in Mexico on charges of murder and illicit enrichment.
A Swiss prosecutor accused Raul Salinas of receiving large sums of money from drug cartels.
Approximately $100 million was found in Raul Salinas' Swiss bank accounts.
Both Raul Salinas and Carlos Salinas de Gortari deny any connections to illegal drug operations.
John Reed has not been summoned by the grand jury.
Citicorp has spent $4 million on legal fees related to the Salinas inquiry.
Citicorp has not set aside any funds for possible fines related to the investigation.

Philip Morris Cos Inc will hold its annual shareholder meeting on Thursday.
Geoffrey Bible is the Chief Executive of Philip Morris.
The shareholder meeting will take place at Philip Morris' manufacturing plant in Richmond, Virginia.
Questions about Philip Morris' role in historic settlement talks are expected at the meeting.
The settlement talks may result in a payout of $300 billion or more for the cigarette industry.
Activists and industry analysts anticipate the questions regarding the settlement talks.
The phrase 'no comment' is expected to be used during the meeting.
The annual shareholder meeting is a regular event for Philip Morris.
The tobacco industry is involved in the settlement talks.
The outcome of the settlement talks could significantly impact the tobacco industry.

China no longer cares whether it joins the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
Wu Jiahuang is the director-general of the customs administration's tariffs department.
Wu's comments reflect differing internal views on the importance of the global economy.
Wu compared China's bid for entry to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and the WTO to a 'sunken boat' and an 'ailing tree'.
Beijing seeks to join the WTO on favorable terms for developing countries.
Some WTO members, including the United States, argue that China's economy is too large for such treatment.
China's leadership believes negotiations with WTO members on entry terms are politically tainted.
Wu's views on WTO accession may signal that China is not in a hurry to make concessions.
Officials from the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation (MOFTEC) stated that Wu's remarks represent a personal opinion.
MOFTEC's assistant minister An Min stated that early entry into the WTO could boost investment.

A state-sponsored group of Chinese academics criticized a U.S. report that condemned Beijing for silencing dissent.
The group described the U.S. report as malicious and slanderous interference in China's internal affairs.
The U.S. State Department report from 1997 was said to violate United Nations principles and ignore China's progress in human rights.
The People's Daily quoted Tian Dan from the China Society for the Study of Human Rights as saying the report contained groundless accusations.
Tian Dan claimed the U.S. government misleads public opinion and attempts to make its lies seem true through repetition.
The scholars' criticism was widely reported in major Chinese newspapers.
This criticism was a response to a U.S. report released on January 30 that accused Beijing of abusing basic freedoms.
The U.S. report stated that all active Chinese dissidents had been jailed, detained, or exiled in 1996.
Both Washington and Beijing have claimed that relations have improved significantly in recent months.
China's official Xinhua news agency reported that the U.S. report was based on Western media and distorted statements from Chinese officials.

Tung Chee-hwa is the leader-designate of Hong Kong.
Tung Chee-hwa stated that meetings with China's top communist leaders increased his confidence in Hong Kong's future under Chinese sovereignty.
Tung Chee-hwa believes there will be no problems requiring Beijing's assistance after Hong Kong returns to China on June 30, 1997.
Tung Chee-hwa expressed that he would ask for assistance from Beijing if a situation arose that required it.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin pledged full support to Tung Chee-hwa after he takes office.
Jiang Zemin assured that Beijing would not interfere with Hong Kong's autonomy after British colonial rule ends.
Tung Chee-hwa met with Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng in Beijing.
China's leaders emphasized their commitment to granting Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy under the principle of 'one country, two systems'.
Tung Chee-hwa indicated that Hong Kong would have a unique position after its return to China.
Tung Chee-hwa acknowledged the disbanding of Hong Kong's existing elected legislature and the establishment of a Beijing-appointed provisional body.

Four regional Bell telephone companies reported strong fourth-quarter results.
The companies experienced increased demand for extra phone lines, wireless phones, and smartphone services.
Bell Atlantic Corp. and Nynex Corp. produced results close to analysts' expectations.
SBC Communications Inc. and Pacific Telesis Group also met analysts' expectations.
Analyst Richard Klugman stated that demand growth expectations have been raised and should be sustainable for 1997.
The demand for phone lines to connect home computers to the Internet has increased.
Falling costs of mobile phone service have attracted more users.
SBC Chief Financial Officer Don Kiernan expressed surprise at the market's momentum.
Nynex Corp. reported a 10 percent increase in net income to $416.5 million in the fourth quarter.
Bell Atlantic Corp. reported a decrease in profits to $346 million in the fourth quarter.

AT&T Corp. announced an alliance with Shaklee Corp.
The alliance will allow Shaklee's 500,000 sales agents to sell AT&T residential calling plans face-to-face with customers at home.
The alliance is named Shaklee Connections.
AT&T expects the alliance to reach millions of new customers in 1997 and beyond.
No financial details of the alliance were disclosed.
Joseph Nacchio is the executive vice president of AT&T's consumer and small business division.
Shaklee is part of Yamanouchi Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd. of Japan.
Shaklee sells nutritional supplements, personal care products, household cleaners, and water treatment products.
Shaklee's independent sales agents will be eligible to become authorized AT&T distributors.
AT&T's market share in the long-distance market has decreased from 90 percent to about 55 percent over the last decade.

Hughes Electronics Corp is the leading bidder to buy PanAmSat Corp.
A source stated that Hughes' offer is currently the best on the table.
Both PanAmSat and Hughes declined to comment on the reports.
Hughes is a subsidiary of General Motors Corp.
Hughes CEO Mike Armstrong indicated that the company is considering a multi-billion dollar acquisition in aerospace and defense.
Hughes spokeswoman Marcy Garber stated that the company is always looking for ventures to grow its business.
Analysts estimate PanAmSat's value at $3.5 billion or more.
PanAmSat's market capitalization is $2.75 billion.
PanAmSat's majority owners are Grupo Televisa SA and the family of founder Rene Anselmo, each owning 40.5 percent of the company.
Televisa preferred a sale option for PanAmSat, while the Anselmo family had no preference.

Dean Foods Inc reported earnings more than double compared to a year ago in the fiscal third quarter.
Dean Foods expects to make an acquisition in the fourth quarter, potentially in the fluid milk business.
William McManaman is the chief financial officer of Dean Foods.
McManaman stated that Dean Foods is in discussions with more companies than ever before.
Potential acquisition targets for Dean Foods include fluid milk processors and small companies that complement its specialty segment.
McManaman expects Dean Foods to close at least one acquisition in the current fiscal fourth quarter.
Acquisitions have historically been a growth engine for Dean Foods, based in Franklin Park, Illinois.
Dean Foods reported third quarter earnings of $0.51 a share, up from $0.17 a year ago.
Earnings improvements were noted in all segments of Dean Foods, including dairy, vegetables, pickles, and specialty foods.
Prudential Securities analyst John McMillin described the third quarter results as a positive surprise.

Kmart Corp. may merge its Builders Square stores with Waban Inc.'s HomeBase business.
The merger would create the nation's third largest home improvement chain.
The deal reflects consolidation in the home improvement retail sector.
The merger would complete Kmart's exit from specialty retailing.
Michael Conn, a retail analyst at Gruntal & Co., stated that the merger aligns with Kmart's strategy of divesting non-core businesses.
If the deal is completed, Leonard Green & Partners L.P. would hold a majority interest in the new company.
Kmart and Waban would each retain minority interests in the new company.
The proposed new company would have about 250 stores in 25 states and annual revenues of nearly $4 billion.
Builders Square's stores are primarily located in the Midwest and central United States, while HomeBase has 84 stores in 10 Western states.
Marvin Rich, Kmart's executive vice president, stated that the transaction is part of Kmart's plan for Builders Square's disposition.

Michael Foods Inc is considering options for its potato operations.
The options include possibly divesting the business that includes frozen french fries and refrigerated potatoes.
Gregg Ostrander is the president of Michael Foods Inc.
Ostrander stated that the company will evaluate its total potato business over the next couple of quarters.
Michael Foods' largest business is extended shelf-life and processed eggs.
No decisions have been made regarding the potato operations.
Michael Foods presented at an analyst conference.
In 1995, the potato product business accounted for 12 percent of the company's operating earnings.
Michael Foods is currently ranked number seven or eight in frozen french fries.
The refrigerated potato product business is the leader in both retail and food service categories.

A Hong Kong legislator will present a demand to the government on Wednesday.
The demand is for China to clarify the role of the Communist Party in Hong Kong after the handover.
Christine Loh, an independent democrat, will raise the question at a Legislative Council session.
Loh's question will ask the government to press Beijing and Tung Chee-hwa on the Communist Party's representation and role.
Loh hopes to break down the silence about the Communist Party in Hong Kong.
Past efforts to discuss the Communist Party publicly have faced official silence and public dismay.
Loh expressed concern that the Chinese Communist Party will operate in Hong Kong similarly to its operations in China.
Hong Kong is set to revert to China on July 1 after being a British colony for over 150 years.
After the handover, Hong Kong will become a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China with its own capitalist system.
The presence of the Communist Party in Hong Kong has been largely avoided in discussions by the British, Chinese, and Hong Kong governments.

China is implementing a plan to reduce civil rights and democracy in Hong Kong.
The plan is unaffected by the death of Deng Xiaoping.
Deng Xiaoping was the architect of the 'one country two systems' formula for Hong Kong.
Hong Kong is set to become a special, autonomous capitalist zone of China after British rule ends on June 30.
Thousands of Hong Kong residents participated in a mourning ceremony for Deng Xiaoping.
China's parliament approved a plan to amend or eliminate several Hong Kong laws.
The laws affected include those related to democratic elections and civil liberties.
The amendments will reduce protections for rights, political parties, and public protests.
The laws were part of efforts by Britain to establish a democratic framework in Hong Kong.
Beijing has accused Britain of violating treaties regarding Hong Kong's democratic reforms.

Britain's minister handling Hong Kong's 1997 transfer to China is Jeremy Hanley.
Jeremy Hanley is the Minister of State at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.
Hanley arrived in Hong Kong on Friday night to discuss negotiations with officials.
Hanley recently visited Beijing, where relations between Britain and China improved.
Hanley will meet Governor Chris Patten and the Executive Council in Hong Kong.
They will discuss Hanley's talks with China's Hong Kong policy supremo Lu Ping.
They will also discuss Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind's upcoming meeting with China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.
A diplomatic source stated that Hanley's talks in China made progress on the handover ceremony.
The handover ceremony is scheduled for midnight on June 30, marking the end of British rule.
There is hope that Britain's Prince Charles might attend the handover ceremony.

Renault SA reported consolidated revenues of 47.2 billion francs ($8.2 billion) in the first quarter.
Renault's revenues increased by three percent from a year ago or 1.8 percent on a like-for-like basis.
PSA Peugeot Citroen reported turnover of 43.51 billion francs in the first quarter.
PSA's turnover increased by 0.9 percent or 0.6 percent on a like-for-like basis.
Both Renault and PSA stated that exports offset declines in domestic sales.
Renault's sales in the home market dropped 26.5 percent in the first quarter.
PSA's sales in the home market fell 30 percent in the first quarter.
Renault's automobile division revenues increased by 4.7 percent, or 2.7 percent on a like-for-like basis.
The automobile division accounts for 80 percent of Renault's total group revenues.
The French government holds a 46 percent stake in Renault.

Rival bidders Alcatel Alsthom and Lagardere Group are expected to submit final offers on Wednesday for the privatisation of Thomson-CSF.
A source close to Alcatel stated that the final offer would confirm the terms of its joint bid with Dassault Industries.
Alcatel has held talks with Daimler-Benz Aerospace regarding cooperation if it wins Thomson-CSF.
The talks between Alcatel and Dasa are not binding on the French government.
Dasa is in discussions with both Alcatel and Lagardere.
General Electric Company Plc is a major rival to Alcatel and has discussed deals with the two French bidders.
The French government ruled out GEC as a candidate for the Thomson-CSF sale due to national security interests.
The government encouraged Lagardere and Alcatel to engage with GEC while preparing their bids.
Analysts believe GEC aimed to signal its interest in a share of the business plan with the winning bidder.
Industry Minister Franck Borotra stated that the government would consider the prospects for restructuring the defence industry in Europe.

Eurotunnel SA /Plc is seeking a debt deal to refinance its operations.
Debt specialists claim the deal may benefit management and bank lenders but offers little value to shareholders.
Eurotunnel plans to send prospectuses to shareholders next month regarding a restructuring of its 70 billion francs ($12 billion) of bank debt.
Eurotunnel aims to obtain approvals for the restructuring at a meeting in Paris by July 10.
Eurotunnel reported a net loss of 6.1 billion francs in 1996, which is one billion francs less than the previous year.
One debt specialist stated that Eurotunnel has no shareholder value due to its debts eliminating its enterprise value.
Eurotunnel has issued shareholders capital of approximately 10 billion pounds, which it intends to halve to account for past losses.
The debt stock will remain largely unchanged, except for one billion pounds that will be swapped for shares.
A second debt expert noted that the debt deal does not reduce the total debt but extends payment timelines.
Christian Cambier, chairman of the Eurotunnel shareholders association, has four conditions for approving the deal and will seek shareholder proxies for a 34 percent blocking vote.

Conrail Inc. and CSX Corp. amended their $8.5 billion merger agreement to provide Conrail shareholders with an additional $870 million.
The new agreement offers Conrail shareholders an extra $16 per share in CSX convertible preferred shares.
CSX and Conrail are competing with Norfolk Southern Corp., which has made a $10 billion bid for Conrail.
An industry analyst estimated the value of the new CSX-Conrail deal at $104 per share.
Norfolk Southern Corp. stated it remains determined to acquire Conrail and is studying its options.
Conrail has rejected Norfolk Southern's offer, stating that a transaction with CSX is a better fit.
The Conrail-CSX agreement includes $110 per share for 40 percent of the outstanding Conrail shares.
The proposed merger of Conrail and CSX was first announced on October 15.
In early trading, Conrail shares were at $100.375, CSX shares at $44, and Norfolk Southern shares at $86.375.
CSX and Conrail established a voting trust for payment to Conrail shareholders by 1997.

David Goode is the chief executive officer of Norfolk Southern Corp.
David Goode admitted that talks to resolve a stalemate over Conrail Inc will be difficult.
David Goode expressed optimism about the outcome of the negotiations.
Norfolk Southern Corp has made a $10.3 billion bid for Conrail Inc.
Conrail Inc has rejected the Norfolk Southern offer.
Conrail Inc stated that the CSX Corp deal is a better fit.
Conrail shareholders defeated a key provision that would have allowed the merger to proceed.
Norfolk Southern is in the process of buying 9.9 percent of Conrail's stock.
David Goode plans to meet with Conrail and CSX executives on Friday.
Sources indicated that only David Goode, David LeVan, and John Snow are expected to attend the meeting.

CVS Corp expects its proposed $2.8 billion acquisition of Revco D.S. Inc to be slightly accretive in 1997.
CVS Corp expects the acquisition to add 10 to 15 cents to earnings per share in 1998.
Thomas Ryan is the Chief Operating Officer of CVS Corp.
Thomas Ryan stated that CVS aims to be a world-class health-care retailer.
CVS considered acquiring Eckerd Corp but chose Revco as a better fit.
J.C. Penney Co Inc announced a $3.3 billion acquisition of Eckerd in November.
CVS and Revco held talks about the acquisition since early October.
Key criteria for CVS's strategic acquisitions include leadership in new markets, growth potential in pharmacy operations, and earnings accretion.
The planned acquisition of Revco is expected to result in about 1,000 layoffs at CVS's Twinsburg, Ohio headquarters.
CVS will honor Revco severance packages.

Pocket Communications Inc. has filed for bankruptcy protection from its creditors.
Pocket Communications Inc. was the No. 2 bidder at a government wireless phone auction.
Pocket Communications Inc. bid $1.4 billion for 43 licenses to offer a new generation of cellular service.
Pocket Communications Inc. defaulted on $80 million in loans.
The government auction had a total value of $10.2 billion.
NextWave Telecom Inc. was the No. 1 bidder in the auction.
Pocket Communications Inc. is the first company from the 1996 auction to file for bankruptcy protection.
Pocket Communications Inc.'s creditors include Asian entrepreneurs and Siemens AG and L.M. Ericsson.
The Federal Communications Commission suspended a March 31 payment deadline for PCS companies.
Pocket Communications Inc. has postponed initial public stock and bond offerings due to market conditions.

Two Washington-area firms bid a total of $173 million at a government auction for digital audio radio licenses.
American Mobile Radio Corp. won a bid of $89.9 million for one license.
CD Radio Inc. placed a top bid of $83.3 million for the other license.
The auction was limited to four companies and was controversial.
Digital radio is expected to be operational by the latter half of 1999.
The service will be subscription-based and will offer 25 to 50 stations.
A small satellite antenna will be needed to receive broadcasts.
The service is targeted at people who drive frequently or live in remote areas.
CD Radio expects to offer 50 channels of programming, mostly commercial-free music.
The estimated cost of the service will be $10 or less per month.

Regional Baby Bell phone companies have succeeded over long-distance rivals in a regulatory battle.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has decided not to cut the $23 billion that long-distance carriers pay the Bells for access to the local phone network.
Bell executives were concerned that cuts could result in a loss of up to $10 billion in revenues.
Consumer groups and long-distance companies are advocating for immediate cuts of $2 billion to $3 billion.
Analyst Scott Cleland stated that the Bells have avoided significant financial losses.
The FCC plans to rely on competition to reduce access charges over time instead of imposing a large cut.
The FCC may impose a revenue loss on the Bells of no more than $1 billion in the first year.
Customers who make many long-distance calls may see a significant decrease in their bills.
Wireless phone subscribers could face a monthly fee increase of 1 percent to 2 percent.
Customers with multiple phone lines and few long-distance calls may experience a rate increase of around $1 or more.

Hewlett-Packard Co. agreed to acquire VeriFone Inc. in a stock swap worth $1.18 billion.
VeriFone will be operated as an independent unit of Hewlett-Packard.
VeriFone stockholders will receive one HP share for each VeriFone share.
Forrester Research estimates the market for business to business electronic commerce will increase from $600 million last year to $66 billion in the year 2000.
Forrester Research estimates consumer retail business will rise to $7 billion from $530 million in 1996.
Karen Epper, a Forrester Research analyst, stated that VeriFone will be significant in online payment for the foreseeable future.
Hewlett-Packard's acquisition aims to combine its strength as the second-largest U.S.-based computer equipment company with VeriFone's leadership in electronic commerce.
VeriFone had net revenue of $472 million in its 1996 fiscal year.
The acquisition price of $1.18 billion was based on HP's closing stock price of $50.50 a share.
VeriFone estimates that its systems handled more than $520 billion of the $800 billion in electronic transactions conducted in the United States last year.

Novell Inc. named Eric Schmidt as its chairman and chief executive officer on Tuesday.
Eric Schmidt was previously a key architect of Sun Microsystems Inc.'s Internet and Java language strategy.
Schmidt will join Novell on April 7.
Schmidt's role includes re-energizing Novell, which competes with Microsoft Corp.
Novell has disposed of software applications WordPerfect and Quattro Pro in the last 18 months.
These applications were acquired by former Novell CEO Ray Noorda in an unsuccessful attempt to compete with Microsoft.
Analysts believe Schmidt has the energy and intellect to refine Novell's strategy and attract developers.
Schmidt joined Sun Microsystems in 1983 as a software manager.
Schmidt stated that leading Novell fulfills a lifelong dream of running a company in the industry.
Novell claims to have 60 million users worldwide and maintains the No. 1 market share in network operating systems.

Netscape Communications Corp. reported a 119 percent increase in first-quarter profits to $7.9 million.
The profit increase was attributed to new business on its website and corporate sales growth.
CEO Jim Barksdale stated that the company's server business accounted for roughly 38 percent of revenues for the quarter.
Netscape's earnings were 9 cents a share, compared to $3.6 million or 4 cents a share in the first quarter of 1996.
Revenues totaled $120.2 million, a 114 percent increase over the $56.1 million generated a year ago.
Industry analysts had expected Netscape to post earnings of 8 cents a share.
Netscape reported growth in revenues from new businesses that attract viewers to its website.
Netscape entered into a deal with Yahoo! Inc. to provide an Internet information navigation service.
The deal with Yahoo! Inc. contributed to an increase in services revenue from 16 percent to 25 percent of total revenues.
Netscape shares closed up $2.50 at $27.50 in Nasdaq trade after trading at less than a third of their 52-week peak.

Hutchison Whampoa Ltd reported 1996 earnings that met market expectations.
Analysts warned that the outlook for Hutchison Whampoa Ltd remains mixed.
Li Ka-shing is a tycoon associated with Hutchison Whampoa Ltd.
Hutchison Whampoa Ltd is 48.9 percent owned by Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd.
Hutchison Whampoa Ltd has interests in property, energy, telecommunications, container terminal operations, and retailing.
Hutchison Whampoa Ltd maintained earnings momentum by spinning off British mobile phone operator Orange Plc in April 1996.
Hutchison Whampoa Ltd reported a net profit of HK$12.02 billion in 1996, up from HK$9.57 billion in 1995.
Analysts indicated that Hutchison's telecoms and property divisions performed poorly in 1996.
Hutchison's cellular telephone subscriber base is approximately 340,000.
Analysts noted that Hutchison faces increased competition in the telecoms market in Hong Kong.

Western Europe's envoy in Hong Kong is Etienne Reuter.
Etienne Reuter expects most European governments to attend the inauguration of an unelected provisional legislature on July 1.
Reuter stated that he does not know the official position of various European governments yet.
Hong Kong's elected parliament will be scrapped when Britain hands the territory to China.
China has chosen an interim assembly to replace the elected parliament.
Britain and the United States plan to boycott the swearing-in ceremony.
Countries like Australia have refused to boycott the ceremony.
European countries are deciding how to respond to China's invitation regarding the inauguration.
The provisional legislature will govern Hong Kong until elections are held within one year.
Reuter noted that China will likely not issue invitations to those who have stated they will not attend.

There are increasing signs of an economic upswing in China.
Speculation may be responsible for a sudden influx of liquidity in China-related stocks in Hong Kong.
Brokerage W.I. Carr stated that improving economic fundamentals in China could partly explain the rise in Hong Kong's stock market.
W.I. Carr dismissed the idea of a speculative bubble in Hong Kong red chips.
John Mulcahy, managing director of Indosuez W.I. Carr Securities, commented on the market's indication of the future of the Chinese economy and company earnings.
Red chips are gaining due to expectations of high returns from strong connections and asset injections by parent companies.
Many red chips are trading at over 35 times 1997 earnings, while the average Hong Kong blue chip ratio is 15.
Michael Taylor, an economist, stated that corporate restructuring and rising productivity are more responsible for strong Chinese markets than liquidity from central bank credit easing.
Dong Tao, senior regional economist at Schroder Securities, disagreed and attributed market rallies to liquidity seeking better returns.
Tao noted that China's economy is divided between a struggling real economy and excessive liquidity.

Talks in Beijing regarding the fate of senior Pyongyang defector Hwang Jang-yop have made progress but have not resulted in a deal.
Chang Moon-ik is the spokesman for the South Korean embassy in Beijing.
Chang Moon-ik stated that negotiations are ongoing and some headway has been made.
Hwang Jang-yop sought refuge in Seoul's Beijing consulate four weeks ago.
Hwang Jang-yop is a senior North Korean ideological theorist and top aide to Kim Jong-il.
Hwang has been stranded in the consular compound since February 12.
Officials in South Korea expected a breakthrough in talks with China regarding Hwang's passage out of Beijing.
Chang Moon-ik indicated it was unlikely Hwang would be moved in the next few days.
Chinese Foreign Minister Kim Yong-nam visited Beijing last Saturday in an attempt to break the deadlock.
Hwang is the highest North Korean official to flee the country.

A Hong Kong member of the Chinese committee handling the territory's return handed a letter to Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen on Friday.
Frederick Fung is the chairman of the Hong Kong Association for Democracy and People's Livelihood.
Fung protested against Beijing's plan to dilute civil liberties laws.
Fung handed the letter to Qian just before the start of a two-day session of the 150-member Preparatory Committee in Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
Fung expressed a different view on the Preparatory Committee proposal to repeal several provisions of the Bill of Rights.
Beijing plans to repeal or amend a list of 25 Hong Kong laws and ordinances, including parts of its Bill of Rights.
The proposed changes will be debated at the session of the caucus responsible for shaping Hong Kong's future.
The announcement from Beijing stated that the laws contradicted Hong Kong's future mini-constitution, the Basic Law.
Qian defended the proposed changes, stating that only provisions contradicting laws dealing with international affairs or national defense would be removed.
Fung's protest followed an attack by Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten against China's proposal to dilute Hong Kong's civil liberties.

China downplayed concerns about the health of Deng Xiaoping on Tuesday.
Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party chief, cut short an out-of-town trip to visit Deng Xiaoping.
Tang Guoqiang, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, stated there had been no significant change in Deng Xiaoping's health.
Tang Guoqiang did not provide details on what would constitute a major change in Deng's health.
Officials from the State Council stated they were investigating Deng Xiaoping's health situation.
Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng returned to Beijing to visit Deng Xiaoping after cutting short provincial trips.
Diplomats indicated that Deng Xiaoping's health had likely deteriorated recently.
A Western diplomat noted that it had been clear for a while that Deng's health was declining.
Taiwan's United Daily News reported that Chang King-yuh stated Deng's condition was serious.
Deng Xiaoping lives in a tightly-guarded compound in central Beijing.

Lloyd's of London posted profits of more than 1 billion pounds ($1.6 billion) for the second consecutive year.
Lloyd's warned that profits would fall for at least the next two years.
The insurance market had previously faced billions of pounds in losses between 1982 and 1992.
Lloyd's future focus will be on customers, according to Chief Executive Ron Sandler.
Sandler stated that Lloyd's had been too focused on its capital base.
Lloyd's results are reported three years in arrears.
In 1994, Lloyd's profits were 1.01 billion pounds ($1.6 billion), which was slightly below 1993's profits of 1.08 billion pounds ($1.8 billion).
Corporate members were introduced to Lloyd's in 1994 and will share in the profits for the first time.
Corporate capital currently provides 44 percent of Lloyd's market capacity, with expectations for further increases.
Lloyd's chairman, Sir David Rowland, indicated that 1997 results would be under pressure due to declining premium rates.

The number of Names at Lloyd's of London is at 20-year lows.
The insurance market announced it would raise the amount of capital Names must pledge to back their underwriting activities.
This announcement is part of measures to strengthen Lloyd's financial credibility.
There are concerns that Names are being replaced by corporate investors.
Andrew Duguid, secretary of the Lloyd's council, denied any hidden agenda behind the proposals.
Duguid stated that the purpose of the proposals is to bolster the market's financial security.
Duguid does not expect a dramatic impact on the number of Names, but some may reduce their underwriting amounts.
The balance between Names and corporate members is likely to shift due to growth in corporate members.
The number of Names has decreased since significant losses threatened Lloyd's between 1988 and 1992.
Corporate investors now provide around 44 percent of total capacity at Lloyd's.

Lloyd's of London announced it will give Names more time to meet planned capital increases for underwriting activities.
Lloyd's has dropped proposals preventing Names from using their homes as collateral for underwriting.
The planned capital increases are part of measures to strengthen financial security at Lloyd's.
