The longer transition period may address concerns from Names' representatives about new capital requirements.
Names fear they are being forced out of the market in favor of corporate capital introduced in 1994.
Lloyd's denies the claim that Names are being forced out of the market.
Names will have three years to show evidence of assets amounting to 50 percent of the premiums they underwrite.
A two-year transition period was proposed but has been extended to the year 2000 after consultations.
The minimum level of means for Names will increase to 350,000 pounds from 250,000 pounds over five years, starting in 2002.
Names must hold 40 percent of premium capacity at Lloyd's by 2000, with an additional 10 percent from other personal wealth.

Hong Kong yachtsmen voted to adopt a Chinese name two weeks before the territory's return to Chinese rule on July 1.
The name 'Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club' will be kept in English.
The Chinese name translates to 'Hong Kong Yacht Club'.
Club commodore David Kong stated that the Chinese name was a compromise.
The club has fewer ethnic Chinese members than Westerners.
The club was divided last year over the 'Royal' tag on the English name.
Chinese members attempted to remove the 'Royal' tag but were unsuccessful.
The 'Royal' tag is viewed by some as a symbol of British colonialism.
Choi Chung-yung expressed concern that retaining 'Royal' could disadvantage members when seeking help from Chinese authorities.
Other elite clubs in Hong Kong have removed their 'Royal' tags.

Chinese political dissidents living in exile in Hong Kong are seeking sanctuary in Western countries before the July 1 handover to China.
Many dissidents are fleeing Hong Kong due to concerns about China's political influence.
Pro-democracy activists reported that just over 10 dissidents remain in Hong Kong.
Lau Chin-shek is a legislator and spokesman for the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements in China.
The Hong Kong Alliance has assisted many Chinese dissidents in finding refuge in other countries.
Nineteen dissidents left Hong Kong in the week prior to the report.
Many dissidents fled to Hong Kong after the Tiananmen Square crackdown in June 1989.
Lau expressed confidence that remaining dissidents eligible for political refugee status would be able to leave before July 1.
An estimated 40,000 people were expected to attend a candlelit vigil in Hong Kong to commemorate victims of the 1989 crackdown.
Tung Chee-hwa stated that Chinese dissidents who entered Hong Kong illegally cannot remain after the handover.

Investors in China-related stocks are at risk of losses due to the poor health of many mainland state-owned companies.
Kenneth Courtis is a strategist and chief economist at Deutsche Bank Group Asia Pacific.
Demand for Hong Kong-listed companies with mainland ties has increased alongside record highs in the Hang Seng index.
Courtis warned that speculative gains in these stocks could be short-lived due to serious problems with mainland Chinese companies.
A growing number of Chinese and China-backed companies have listed in Hong Kong.
Foreign investors are attracted to China's large domestic market and economic potential.
In Hong Kong, investors have formed long queues to obtain subscription forms for new shares.
Courtis expressed skepticism about the ability of investors to profit from quickly buying subscription forms.
Many mainland state-owned companies are losing money, and Beijing is working to restructure them.
Courtis stated that the losses from state companies are destabilizing the financial system.

AT&T Corp. will end its introductory offer of free Internet access to long-distance customers after March 31.
A revised pricing plan for AT&T's WorldNet Service will go into effect after March 31.
AT&T will continue to offer a flat-rate pricing plan of $19.95 a month for unlimited access.
AT&T has begun posting statistics about the reliability and performance of WorldNet.
AT&T challenged other service providers to match its performance.
Tom Evslin is the vice president of WorldNet.
WorldNet has more than 750,000 members and is the largest 'pure Internet' access provider in the United States.
Starting March 31, long-distance customers who sign up for WorldNet can get a monthly rate of $4.95 for their first five hours.
Long-distance customers who signed up before March 31 will continue to receive their first five hours for free for a year.
Analysts estimated that AT&T would rapidly gain millions of users, but the current subscriber count is over 750,000.

International Business Machines Corp. introduced its next generation mainframe computer family on Tuesday.
The new systems are twice as fast as currently available models.
Ross Mauri is the vice president of System 390 hardware development at IBM.
Mauri reported phenomenal feedback and significant demand for the new servers.
IBM is likely to be sold out of its new mainframe production for the year based on initial customer reaction.
Mainframes are large computers that store data for major corporations worldwide.
Mainframes are used by banks for transactions, airlines for reservation systems, and insurance companies for claims processing.
Despite predictions of their decline, mainframes have seen a resurgence as data repositories accessible via the Internet and intranets.
The new mainframe servers utilize IBM's third generation CMOS processor technology.
IBM introduced two new lines of System 390 servers: the IBM S/390 Parallel Enterprise Server and the IBM S/390 Multiprise 2000.

The stock of International Business Machines Corp fell in heavy trading on Thursday.
The decline was influenced by fears regarding IBM's first-quarter earnings after analysts cut their estimates.
The overall stock market experienced its fourth sharp sell-off in five days.
Investors were concerned that a strong March employment report could lead the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.
IBM's stock price fell to a low of $128.875 before closing down $2.375 at $131.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
IBM was the third most-active stock on the exchange with a trading volume of 4.6 million shares.
The decline in IBM shares began in London after a Wall Street Journal article reported on analysts' estimate cuts.
The article mentioned that a stronger dollar and a transition in mainframe products could negatively impact IBM's earnings.
Two weeks prior, three Wall Street firms made negative comments about IBM and two lowered their earnings estimates.
Morgan Stanley analyst Steve Milunovich reduced IBM's 1997 earnings estimate to $12.30 a share from $12.50.

London Clubs International runs the London Ritz and Les Ambassadeurs casinos.
London Clubs International made a hostile bid of 181 million pounds for Capital Corporation.
London Clubs International described its bid as generous and appropriate.
Alan Goodenough is the chief executive of London Clubs International.
Capital Corporation stated that the offer from London Clubs did not account for its potential.
Alan Hearn is the chief executive of Capital Corporation.
London Clubs International believes it is in the best position to value Capital Corporation.
The decision regarding the bid rests with six institutions that own more than 50 percent of both companies.
Mercury Asset Management owns about 18 percent of shares in both companies.
London Clubs International shares closed at 384-1/2p, while Capital Corporation shares were flat at 203p.

Bass Plc sold 47 Holiday Inn full service hotels and 14 Holiday Inn management contracts in North America to the Bristol Hotel Company.
Bass will take a 36.1 percent stake in Bristol as part of the deal.
Bass will receive loan repayments totaling $300 million and $91 million in cash from Bristol.
The total value of the deal is $640 million, and it is valued at $659 million based on the closing price of Bristol stock.
Bass's decision to sell the hotels aligns with its strategy of expanding its Holiday Inn franchise system.
Bass aims to exit from owning and managing hotels in areas where it has established a presence in franchising.
Richard North, Bass finance director, stated that owning and managing hotels supports their franchising operation.
The 61 hotels transferred have a book value of $638 million and generated profits of $69 million in the financial year to September 30 after franchise fees.
Bristol plans to spend $150 million on refurbishing the properties over the next three years.
Bristol stated that the acquisition should improve earnings slightly in 1997, excluding integration costs and transaction fees.

Compass Group is a food service company.
Francis Mackay is the chief executive of Compass Group.
Francis Mackay stated that there is growth potential from the trend of contracting out catering.
Mackay believes that the outsourcing of catering will continue at least until the year 2000.
The combined catering market in Europe and the U.S. is worth about 100 billion pounds.
Only 30 billion pounds of the catering market is currently outsourced.
Two-thirds of the catering market remains available for outsourcing.
Compass Group is in a strong position to take advantage of the outsourcing market.

Ford Motor Co. reported a profit increase of 82 percent to $1.2 billion in the fourth quarter.
Ford's earnings for the fourth quarter equaled $1 a share.
The fourth quarter results included $132 million in special charges.
Ford cut 3,500 jobs last year, which contributed to the special charges.
In the fourth quarter of 1995, Ford earned $660 million, or 49 cents a share.
Sales for Ford rose to $38.8 billion from $34.6 billion.
Excluding one-time items, Ford's fourth quarter income was $1.10 a share.
Analysts had forecasted Ford's fourth quarter income to be $1.02 a share.
Ford Chairman Alex Trotman stated that automotive earnings will improve in 1997.
Ford expects better results for all of 1997 in Europe and smaller losses in South America.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigators were preparing to examine the wreckage of a Delta Comair plane that crashed in a snowstorm.
The crash occurred on Thursday and resulted in the deaths of all 29 people on board.
The commuter plane was an Embraer Brasilia 120 en route to Detroit from Cincinnati.
The crash site was located in Raisinville Township, approximately 25 miles southwest of Detroit.
NTSB officials arrived in Michigan on Thursday and established a command post in Ann Arbor.
The wreckage was covered with a tarpaulin for protection from snow and was guarded until the investigation began.
Investigators met on Friday to plan their strategy for the probe and were expected to start examining the wreckage later that day.
The plane was carrying 26 passengers and three crew members, according to Cincinnati-based Comair.
The three crew members were Captain Dann Carlsen, First Officer Kenneth Reece, and Flight Attendant Darinda Ogden.
Comair sent 30 members of its emergency response team to Michigan to assist families and authorities during the investigation.

United Auto Workers union bargainers negotiated with American Axle Manufacturing Inc past a midnight strike deadline.
About 7,200 UAW members were prepared to strike at five plants in Detroit, Three Rivers, Mich., and Buffalo, N.Y.
UAW Local 262 in Detroit reported that members had not received official word of an extended deadline.
A strike at American Axle could significantly impact General Motors Corp within days.
The union and American Axle are in disagreement over wages and economic issues.
The union seeks to impose a contract similar to the one agreed upon by the Big Three automakers for about 400,000 UAW members.
The Big Three automakers' contract guarantees jobs for 95 percent of the current workforce and includes $2,000 lump sum payments in the first year and three percent wage hikes in the second and third years.
American Axle supplies nearly all rear axles for GM's pickup trucks and SUVs, as well as parts for other passenger car lines.
Tight inventories at American Axle and Dana Corp could lead to GM's light truck plants running out of parts by early next week.
Analyst David Healy estimated that GM could lose $20 million a day in after-tax profits if light truck production is suspended.

Microsoft Corp entered a licensing agreement with China's Legend Group.
The agreement allows Legend Group to pre-install the Chinese-language version of Windows 95 software.
Yu Zhongyu, chief engineer at the Ministry of Electronics Industry, stated the agreement shows the Chinese government's commitment to protecting intellectual property rights.
Officials described the licensing pact as one of the largest agreements since the U.S. and China reached an intellectual property rights agreement last June.
Beijing agreed to protect intellectual property rights by addressing piracy that was costing American firms $2.3 billion annually in lost sales.
Computer software piracy was a significant topic in Sino-U.S. discussions last year.
The licensing agreement could result in payments of approximately 100 million yuan ($12 million) from Legend to Microsoft over two years if sales targets are met.
Legend Group sold 200,000 personal computers last year and aims to double that figure this year.
Chinese government officials reported that about 1.8 million personal computers were sold in China last year.
Charles Stevens, Microsoft vice president for the Far East, called the agreement the most significant Microsoft has signed in the People's Republic of China.

China has achieved new successes in its fight against inflation.
Economists stated that price rises in China this year could be well below target.
Some economists claim inflation has been squeezed out of the economy with a modest impact on growth.
Chen Dezun is the head of the price research institute of the State Planning Commission.
Chen Dezun stated that inflation could be between three and four percent this year.
The benchmark retail price index rose 1.7 percent in March and 2.6 percent for the first quarter of the year.
China forecast a 6.0 percent rise in retail prices this year.
China's economic growth is expected to exceed 10 percent this year.
The inflation figure for the first quarter was below Premier Li Peng's estimate of 3.0 percent.
Zhong Jiyun is an economist at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.

China provided details on a failed satellite launch aboard its Long March 3B rocket in February.
The failure was attributed to an electrical problem in the power module of the inertial platform.
The inertial platform operated the rocket's direction controls.
A spokesman for China Great Wall Industrial Corp quoted the report stating there was no electric current output from the power module.
All other systems of the Long March 3B operated normally according to the report.
The rocket veered off course seconds after lift-off from the Xichang satellite centre in Sichuan province.
The flight ended in an explosion that destroyed the rocket and the Intelsat satellite it was carrying.
The rocket crashed into a hillside 1.85 km from the launch site.
Official reports indicated six people were killed and 57 were injured in the incident.
China's space programme has faced recent failures, affecting its reputation and commercial satellite launch market prospects.

U.S. Senators criticized a new Securities and Exchange Commission rule requiring companies to disclose their use of derivatives.
The SEC and the Financial Accounting Standards Board proposed increased disclosure about derivatives following significant losses in 1994.
Derivatives are financial instruments like options and futures that derive value from underlying stock or commodity prices.
Derivatives were linked to the bankruptcy of Orange County, California, and over $100 million in losses at Procter & Gamble Co.
The SEC adopted its rules last month, while the FASB is still developing its proposal.
Senators expressed concerns that the new rules would increase costs and complications for companies using derivatives to manage risk.
Senator Lauch Faircloth voiced concerns about unnecessary regulations in the SEC's new rule.
Senator Christopher Dodd stated that the issues in 1994 were due to human error, not the derivatives themselves.
The new rules do not apply to Orange County, which is not subject to most FASB or SEC regulations.
Senator Phil Gramm expressed doubts about the effectiveness of the new rules after hearing from industry representatives.

Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato warned that the Federal Reserve may not be taking adequate precautions for the year 2000.
D'Amato expressed concern after questioning U.S. bank regulators about the year 2000 computer issue in February.
D'Amato was troubled by the responses he received from the Federal Reserve and the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
Problems are expected in computers and software that only record the last two digits of the year.
Such a program might interpret the year 2000 as the year 1900, leading to miscalculations or system crashes.
D'Amato also questioned the Office of the Comptroller and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. in February.
The Office of the Comptroller and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. stated they had detailed plans to address the millennium bug.
D'Amato's office indicated that he was concerned about the responses from the Fed and the NCUA regarding their attention to the year 2000 crisis.
D'Amato sent letters to the Fed and the NCUA asking for additional information.
Estimates for fixing year 2000 problems worldwide have ranged from $300 billion to $600 billion.

The Internet Society announced a plan to provide seven new top-level domains.
The new top-level domains will be added to existing ones such as 'com,' 'net,' and 'org.'
The plan is supported by Digital Equipment Corp., MCI Communications Corp., and UUNET Technologies Inc.
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority endorsed the plan.
The International Telecommunications Union, World Intellectual Property Organisation, and International Trademark Association also backed the plan.
New domain names such as 'firm,' 'arts,' and 'web' will be introduced starting in the third quarter of 1997.
The plan includes an arbitration and mediation procedure for resolving disputes over domain names.
Hasbro Inc. won a lawsuit last year to regain control of the address 'candyland.com.'
MCI Senior Vice President Vincent Cerf stated that sound processes are vital for the Internet's administration.
Network Solutions Inc. currently registers addresses under most existing top-level domains.

The Czech Republic won both reverse singles matches against India in the Davis Cup.
The victory secured a place for the Czech Republic in the second round of the Davis Cup.
Petr Korda announced his retirement from Davis Cup play after the matches.
Jiri Novak won his match against Mahesh Bhupathi with a score of 6-1, 6-4, 6-3.
Korda won his match against Leander Paes with a score of 5-7, 6-3, 6-4, 6-1.
Novak's match against Bhupathi lasted 90 minutes.
Novak was ranked 67th in the world at the time of his match.
Korda was ranked 33rd in the world at the time of his match.
Leander Paes was ranked 105th in the world at the time of his match.
Korda stated that he would no longer play for the Czechs in the Davis Cup due to the demands it placed on him.

Markets in Eastern Europe are experiencing an autumn slump.
Analysts see little potential for improvement in the bearish trend.
Stock exchanges in Warsaw, Prague, Bratislava, Bucharest, Zagreb, and Ljubljana all lost ground this week.
The Budapest Stock Exchange rose slightly but lost momentum by the end of the week.
The PX50 index on the Prague Stock Exchange dipped 0.8 points to close at 509.3.
The centre-right governing coalition in Prague had a strong showing in Senate elections.
Investors are concerned about poor market regulation in the Czech Republic.
Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostenska Banka expressed skepticism about the Senate's ability to effect market changes.
The Warsaw Stock Exchange remained virtually flat this week.
Analysts are divided on the future direction of the Warsaw Stock Exchange.

The Czech December trade deficit is expected to rise to 16 billion crowns from 14.3 billion in December 1995.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) will release the 1996 trade figures at 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Monday.
Most economists surveyed expect steady growth in the trade deficit with few surprises.
Martin Kupka, an economist at Patria Finance, stated that he expects the figures to align with the development throughout 1996.
The full-year trade gap for 1996 is guaranteed to be a record, as the January-November figure reached 140.1 billion crowns.
The 140.1 billion crowns figure is already beyond the 1995 record total shortfall of 95.7 billion crowns.
Most analysts predict a December trade gap of 15-17 billion crowns, following a 16.6 billion crown shortfall in November.
The consensus forecast for the 1996 trade deficit is between 155-165 billion crowns.
The foreign exchange and money markets are expected to show little reaction to the figures unless they vary greatly from estimates.
Czech exporters indicated a desire for a 20 to 25 percent devaluation of the crown against a mark/dollar basket to boost exports in 1997.

NatWest Bank admitted on Thursday that its derivatives losses totalled nearly twice the amount initially thought.
The problem began in December 1994.
NatWest Bank suspended four senior members of staff as a result of initial findings from an internal probe.
NatWest Bank cut millions of pounds from bonuses to restore confidence.
The total loss reported by NatWest Bank was 90 million pounds ($144 million).
Five million pounds had already been provisioned and eight million pounds had been clawed back by not paying bonuses.
This resulted in a loss of 77 million pounds in the accounts.
Martin Owen, chief executive of NatWest Markets, will forego 200,000 pounds of his 500,000 pounds 1996 bonus.
Derek Wanless, NatWest's chief executive, stated that the losses and mis-pricing had gone undetected for a long time.
The losses were confined to the interest rate options area.

Elizabeth Forsyth is a former aide to Asil Nadir, head of Polly Peck Plc.
Forsyth left court on Friday awaiting the outcome of her appeal against a money-laundering conviction.
Forsyth has been in jail for 10 months.
The London Court of Appeal reserved judgment on Forsyth's appeal after a two-day hearing.
Forsyth, 60, was found guilty last year of dishonestly handling 400,000 pounds ($640,000).
Forsyth was freed on bail on Thursday when the court quashed her original five-year sentence.
The court concluded that Forsyth had already served long enough in prison.
The prosecution argued that the money Forsyth was convicted of handling was stolen by Nadir from Polly Peck.
Nadir fled to northern Cyprus in 1993 after jumping bail of 3.5 million pounds.
Forsyth's barrister argued that her conviction was unsafe for several reasons, including the lack of questioning of Nadir.

Britain's commercial property market is improving but is not yet fully healthy.
Pen Kent is an executive director at the Bank of England.
Kent stated that it would be rash to conclude the market is healthy in all respects.
Lease lengths have temporarily stabilized in the commercial property market.
Clauses allowing tenants to break leases are becoming more common.
Many occupiers are expected to reduce their space needs and demand greater flexibility.
There is a sizeable overhang of unlet secondary property in the market.
The pool of unlet secondary property increases when major users move to new offices.
Kent called for solutions to the issues with secondary stock that is unsuitable for conversion or relet.
Institutional investors may resume their longer-term departure from property if market performance declines.

Beijing has pledged to open its doors to imports of U.S. textiles under a new deal.
Washington does not believe it can close its textile trade gap with China.
Chinese and U.S. negotiators signed a new textile agreement in Beijing.
The new textile agreement ended the threat of a cross-Pacific trade war.
The agreement ensures U.S. access to China's textile markets.
China exported $6.5 billion worth of textiles to the United States in 1995.
The United States imported only $64 million worth of textiles from China in 1995.
U.S. textile exports are sluggish due to China's high tariff rates and non-tariff barriers.
The new agreement gave China a U.S. import quota larger than the previous 1994 textile pact.
China pledged to reduce its tariffs on textile imports.

China warned Britain against challenging it in the World Court over its decision to disband Hong Kong's elected legislature.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang stated that challenging China would damage Sino-British relations.
Shen Guofang said that if Britain acts willfully and creates troubles, Sino-British relations will be damaged.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind denounced China's plans to disband the democratically elected legislature.
Rifkind proposed that the International Court of Justice in The Hague rule on the dispute regarding Hong Kong.
Hong Kong, with a population of 6.3 million, will revert to Chinese control at midnight on June 30, 1997.
Beijing's communist leadership promised that almost nothing will change after the handover of Hong Kong.
A Beijing-appointed provisional legislature will take over from the elected Legislative Council after the handover.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten criticized the creation of the provisional legislature, calling it a 'bizarre farce' and a 'stomach-churning' process.
Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first post-colonial chief executive, defended China's decision and criticized Britain's threat to take Beijing to the World Court.

Chinese authorities sealed off the town of Yining in northwestern Xinjiang.
Paramilitary police patrolled the streets of Yining after a separatist riot.
At least 10 people were killed in the riot, including one policeman.
Approximately 100 people were wounded during the riot.
The riot involved around 1,000 Muslim separatists from the Uighur ethnic minority.
The riot was a protest against Beijing rule.
Yining is located in the Yili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture near the border with Kazakhstan.
Authorities closed the airport and railway station in Yining and imposed a curfew.
Local officials reported a lower number of arrests than claimed by residents.
Yining is 50 km from the border with Kazakhstan, where many exiled Uighur separatists reside.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd is expected to report a stagnant net profit for the year to June 30.
The stagnant profit is attributed to soaring newsprint costs and losses from Star TV operations.
The median forecast for News Corp's net profit before abnormals is A$1.343 billion.
The forecasted profit is similar to the A$1.342 billion profit posted in 1994/95.
Analysts believe News Corp may struggle to match last year's profit results.
News Corp posted a A$281 million net profit before abnormals in the third quarter.
The third quarter profit was below expectations of about A$300 million.
Profits for the first nine months of the year totaled A$944 million.
Analysts indicated that higher paper costs and a U.K. cover price war restrained profits.
Star TV is projected to incur losses of US$90 million to US$100 million for the year.

Macquarie Bank Ltd posted a net profit of A$116.94 million for the year to March 31.
Macquarie Bank's net profit rose 25.4 percent compared to the previous year.
The return on average shareholder funds for Macquarie Bank was 25.2 percent.
Macquarie Bank raised its annual dividend to 43 cents from 36 cents the previous year.
Earnings per share for Macquarie Bank increased to 74.9 cents from 61 cents.
Analysts had forecast a net profit of around A$105 million for Macquarie Bank.
Macquarie Bank's Corporate Advisory division had 130 advisory mandates during the year.
Simon Hannes, a senior corporate advisory executive at Macquarie, was charged with insider trading.
Hannes allegedly made a notional profit of A$2 million from buying TNT options before a takeover bid.
Macquarie Bank's Managing Director Allan Moss stated that the Hannes matter did not affect corporate advisory work.

Kerry Packer is a local billionaire.
Packer is interested in acquiring John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
Analysts believe Packer's bid is not guaranteed.
The government must first decide to drop current cross-media rules.
Any legislation must pass through a hostile senate.
Packer would need to offer a takeover premium on top of Fairfax's high share price.
Vince Pepe is a senior media analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
Prime Minister John Howard's cabinet is considering changes to cross-media rules.
Howard has stated that the current rules are outdated.
A successful takeover would result in major newspapers being divided between Packer and Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd.

Shares of Sears, Roebuck and Co fell about six percent on Thursday.
Sears announced it will voluntarily refund some payments from credit card holders who filed for bankruptcy.
Sears stated that the repayments might have a material effect on 1997 earnings.
Analysts indicated that Sears could not quantify its earnings exposure during a conference call.
Sears stock decreased by 3-1/8 to 47-3/4.
The dispute involves reaffirmations, where Sears seeks payments from credit card holders in bankruptcy.
Reaffirmation agreements must be filed with a bankruptcy court.
Sears reported that some reaffirmation agreements were not filed properly.
Sears had $400 million in reaffirmations from 1992 through February 1997.
Sears plans to offer each affected debtor a $100 gift certificate.

William Brandt Jr. is the new chief executive officer of Mercury Finance Co.
Brandt expressed hope for a short-term credit facility from lenders to stabilize the company.
Mercury Finance Co. defaulted on $17 million of commercial debt.
Analysts reported that Mercury has about $100 million of debt due on Thursday.
Brandt aims to avoid filing for bankruptcy reorganization while stabilizing the company.
Brandt stated he is not prepared to file for imminent bankruptcy.
Brandt has a background as a corporate turnaround and bankruptcy specialist.
Mercury's debt ratings were lowered to default status by major rating services.
The company needed to lower its past four years' net income by about $90 million due to accounting irregularities.
Brandt mentioned that if Mercury cannot re-enter the commercial debt market, it would consider securitizing its consumer loans.

First Bank System Inc plans to acquire U.S. Bancorp for $9 billion.
The acquisition will expand First Bank's geographic footprint to the Pacific Northwest.
Analyst James Schutz at ABN AMRO Chicago Corp described the acquisition price as 'very rich'.
The deal will make First Bank the 14th largest bank in the United States based on assets.
The acquisition values U.S. Bancorp at approximately $59.08 per share, or 19.2 times its 1996 earnings.
U.S. Bancorp shares increased by 6-3/16 to 54-7/16 on Thursday.
First Bank's CEO John Grundhofer is known for aggressive cost cutting.
Analyst Frank Barkocy at Josephthal, Lyon & Ross stated that the acquisition is a 'natural fit' for First Bank.
First Bank plans to grow revenues by offering payment systems services to U.S. Bancorp's corporate base.
First Bank expects to reduce combined operating expenses by about 14 percent, resulting in pre-tax cost savings of approximately $340 million.

David Walsh is the chief executive of Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
Bre-X Minerals Ltd. is a Canadian gold prospector.
Walsh stated that Bre-X has the financial resources to endure challenges related to the Busang gold discovery.
Walsh claimed that an audit will confirm that Bre-X made a significant gold strike.
Bre-X has faced scrutiny following reports that the Busang gold deposit may not contain significant amounts of gold.
Canadian regulators are investigating Bre-X and its officials for potential violations of insider trading and disclosure laws.
There are at least eight class action lawsuits against Bre-X in Canada and the United States.
Bre-X's stock market value decreased by more than 80 percent due to panic selling after the preliminary test results.
Bre-X's stock closed at C$2.67 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
An independent audit of the Busang project will be conducted by Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd.

Molson Cos. Ltd. is seeking expansion opportunities in China and Latin America.
Molson has cash from the sale of non-beer assets.
Molson's new President and Chief Executive is Norman Seagram.
Seagram stated that Molson wants to grow its core brewing business.
Molson is not considering a share buyback.
Molson will spend the next three months looking for brewing opportunities.
Analysts and investors are concerned about Molson's track record on acquisitions.
Molson's class A stock closed down C$0.30 at C$20.20 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
Molson's stock has remained around C$20 since earlier speculation pushed it to C$25.
Molson's sale of Diversey Corp. added almost C$1 billion to its finances.

Michael de Guzman was the chief geologist of Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
De Guzman co-discovered a significant gold find this century.
De Guzman may have committed suicide after falling from a helicopter.
He fell 800 feet from a helicopter while en route to the Busang site in Indonesia.
Rescue crews were searching for de Guzman's body in the Borneo rain forest.
An apparent suicide note was found by Indonesian police among de Guzman's belongings.
The note indicated that de Guzman had recently learned he had hepatitis B.
The prognosis for de Guzman's recovery was not good due to his history of malaria.
Foul play was not suspected, and Indonesian police were treating his death as a suicide.
Bre-X has agreed to develop the Busang site, valued at $25 billion, with Freeport-McMoRan and Indonesian partners.

Chrysler Corp Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Robert Eaton announced that the automaker will report record earnings for the full 1996 year.
Chrysler's record earnings are based on record worldwide sales of 2.97 million vehicles.
Chrysler's previous annual profit record was $3.713 billion in 1994.
Chrysler earned $2.025 billion in 1995.
Chrysler's sales in 1995 were limited to 2.61 million units due to the launch of its current line of minivans.
Eaton stated that Chrysler should be able to exceed its 1996 sales results in 1997.
Chrysler plans to produce about 190,000 more trucks in 1997 than it built in 1996.
Chrysler plans to unveil the Dodge Durango at the Detroit auto show.
Chrysler has tentatively planned to add a third production shift to its Bramalea, Ontario, car assembly plant.
Eaton expressed that Chrysler can still earn a profit even if U.S. automotive industry sales fall by 20 percent.

General Motors Corp. informed analysts that its fourth-quarter North American incentive and marketing costs were higher than previously estimated.
As a result of the higher costs, analysts reduced their earnings estimates for GM by hundreds of millions of dollars.
GM's product mix in Europe is expected to be weaker than anticipated, with the low-margin Corsa subcompact comprising a larger share of sales.
New product launch costs for GM remain high.
Analysts lowered their estimates for GM's earnings by 45 cents to 50 cents per share.
GM's stock price decreased by $1.375 over two days, closing at $54.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Burnham Securities analyst David Healy estimates GM will earn $435 million, or 52 cents per share, in the fourth quarter, excluding extraordinary items.
GM plans to take a charge of $170 million, or 22 cents per share, for lump-sum payments to United Auto Workers members as part of a new contract.
Strikes in the United States and Canada during the quarter are estimated to have reduced GM's fourth-quarter profit by about $700 million.
In the fourth quarter of 1995, GM earned $1.87 billion, or $1.98 per share.

The Canadian Auto Workers union has chosen Chrysler Corp as its strike target.
This decision creates competition between General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co for bargaining leadership with the United Auto Workers.
Analysts suggest that Ford is gaining an edge in this competition.
Ford has made offers indicating a willingness to collaborate with the UAW on outsourcing issues.
Sean McAlinden, a labor analyst at the University of Michigan, stated that Ford is working to provide the UAW with a framework agreement.
It is unlikely that UAW President Stephen Yokich will select Chrysler as the U.S. target due to the Canadian union's choice.
The Canadian Auto Workers and UAW traditionally select different targets for negotiations.
Contracts for approximately 400,000 Big Three hourly workers in the U.S. and 53,000 in Canada will expire on September 14.
Ford has offered the UAW opportunities to bring some parts manufacturing back into its plants from outside suppliers.
GM is attempting to shift more parts work to outside suppliers to reduce costs.

AMEC Plc is a British building and engineering group.
AMEC Plc's first half pretax profits doubled to 12.1 million pounds for the six months to June 30.
AMEC Plc's sales increased to 1.32 billion pounds compared to 1.13 billion pounds.
AMEC Plc's interim dividend was frozen at 1.5 pence per share.
AMEC chief executive Peter Mason stated that he hopes to improve the dividend at the year end.
Peter Mason indicated that the conservative payout decision was made to ensure the dividend was covered.
Peter Mason expressed confidence that profits would exceed last year's figures.
AMEC's targeted turnover is 2.75 billion pounds.
AMEC's shares increased by 2.5 pence to 98 at 1104 GMT.
Peter Mason aims to increase international sales to 50 percent of total turnover from the current 30 percent.

The United States and Britain ended their latest round of open skies talks on Friday.
The talks resulted in agreement on some technical issues but did not produce a full deal for trans-Atlantic air travel.
No new date was set for future talks.
Industry sources believe the next discussions could occur in weeks rather than months.
Britain's Department of Trade and Industry announced it would block the proposed British Airways alliance with AMR Corp.'s American Airlines unless certain conditions were met.
Airline industry figures stated that the open skies negotiations would remain deadlocked until there was a British verdict on the proposed alliance.
Conditions for allowing the alliance to proceed were outlined by Britain's Office of Fair Trading.
The Department of Trade and Industry indicated that the alliance's approval was dependent on reaching an open skies agreement.
The U.S. Transportation Department expressed disappointment with the lack of progress in the talks.
A British Department of Transport official reported that useful progress was made on several issues, but not all, and no date was set for further talks.

Go-Ahead Group Plc is a UK bus to rail group.
Dale Campbell-Savours is an opposition Labour MP.
Campbell-Savours alleged that Go-Ahead representatives used inside information to secure a rail franchise.
Go-Ahead Group Plc called the allegations 'rubbish.'
Martin Ballinger is the managing director of Go-Ahead.
Ballinger stated that no one made money from share dealings as no shares were sold.
The allegations were made in the House of Commons, where MPs are protected from libel suits.
Ballinger warned Campbell-Savours to be cautious about statements made outside the House of Commons.
Go-Ahead was shortlisted for the Regional Railways North East franchise on November 15.
Ballinger explained that Go-Ahead's bid was adjusted by the franchise regulator Opraf to align with other bidders.

Bell Atlantic Corp. reported a first-quarter net income of $515.6 million.
This represents an increase of 11.0 percent over the $464.7 million earned in the first quarter of 1996.
Earnings per share rose to $1.17 from $1.06.
This earnings per share figure is slightly more than the First Call consensus estimate of $1.16.
Operating revenues grew to $3.4 billion from $3.2 billion.
J.P. Morgan analyst Simon Flannery commented on the strong performance in new growth areas and productivity.
Bell Atlantic Chairman and Chief Executive Raymond Smith stated that demand for services continues to drive performance.
Smith anticipates a landmark year for the company and the closing of its merger with Nynex.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Bell Atlantic and Nynex Corp. are preparing for a legal counter-attack if their merger is blocked.
The latest earnings report includes results from the Mexican Grupo Iusacell SA de CV investment.

Lucent Technologies Inc. earned $66 million in the first three months of 1997.
Lucent Technologies Inc. reversed a loss of $103 million from the 1996 quarter.
Lucent reported net income of 10 cents a share for the three months ended March 31, 1997.
Lucent's revenues for its fiscal second quarter grew by 12.5 percent to $5.15 billion.
Lucent benefited from strengthened relationships with regional Bell companies after its spin-off from AT&T.
Only consumer products suffered a decline in revenues for the quarter among Lucent's four main businesses.
Lucent's gross profit margin for the quarter rose to 42.1 percent of revenues.
Revenues from systems for network operators increased 23.3 percent to $2.93 billion.
Revenues for microelectronic products increased 18.3 percent to $615 million.
Revenues from consumer products decreased 41 percent to $174 million.

Cisco Systems Inc fell more than two points in active trading on Wednesday.
Analysts stated that the decline in Cisco's stock reflected cautious comments by Cisco officials about the traditionally weak April quarter.
Cisco reported strong growth in revenues and earnings for its second quarter ended in January.
Cisco's quarterly earnings were $0.51, which was a penny above published expectations.
The previous year's earnings were $0.32.
Analysts noted that Cisco management was generally upbeat about company prospects during a conference call on Tuesday evening.
Gruntal analyst David Takata mentioned that the one-to-one book-to-bill ratio going into the seasonally weak Q3 may temporarily concern some investors.
Cisco's year-to-year revenue growth was 73 percent, which was above that of rivals but down from an historic growth rate of over 80 percent.
Merrill Lynch analyst Joe Bellace adjusted his earnings estimates for Cisco to the higher end of his previous range for both the 1997 and 1998 fiscal years.
Bear Stearns analyst Eric Blachno described Cisco's quarterly report as very solid and maintained his buy rating on the stock.

Japan's securities watchdog filed complaints with prosecutors alleging that Nomura Securities Co Ltd made illegal payments to a client.
The client is believed to be one of Japan's sokaiya racketeers.
Japan's commercial law has prohibited payoffs to sokaiya racketeers since 1982.
The complaints allege that Nomura and three former executives made illegal payments totaling 49.7 million yen ($417,600).
This is the first time regulators have charged that Nomura was involved in the scandal.
Nomura has denied any participation in the scam, attributing it to three former executives.
Prosecutors will determine if there is enough evidence to file charges in the case.
The Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission indicated that more junior employees may have handled some improper orders.
Nomura issued a statement apologizing for the scandal and stated it would make a 'fresh start' to prevent recurrence.
Market sources indicate that the Finance Ministry may suspend part of Nomura's operations for about three months as punishment.

The Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd was formed in April 2000 through the merger of two prominent Japanese banks.
The Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd is the world's biggest bank in terms of assets, exceeding 70 trillion yen ($569 billion).
The merger combined Bank of Tokyo's strength in overseas operations with Mitsubishi's domestic network.
The bank has a strong share price and a relatively light burden of bad loans due to conservative lending policies.
Analysts believe the bank faces challenges in becoming a genuinely global player.
The bank must address efficiency and profitability issues to ensure sustained success.
The 'Big Bang' reforms aim to make Japanese financial markets free, fair, and global by 2001.
The proposed deregulation will increase competition from both domestic and international rivals.
A spokesman for Tokyo-Mitsubishi stated that the bank is aware of the challenges and opportunities presented by the Big Bang.
The bank is expected to reveal a three-year management plan next week.

Losses have increased in the Japanese stock market over several years.
Japanese securities brokers continue to operate despite market losses.
Expected liberalization of brokerage fees may negatively impact weaker securities houses.
Small Japanese brokers are considering closing down due to fears of reduced commission revenues.
Foreign brokerages are interested in acquiring local brokers in Japan.
A Japanese securities house official predicts the number of brokers will decrease to half in the next five to ten years.
Many small brokerages in Japan are likely to close or be liquidated.
Analysts predict commission fee revenues in Japan could drop by at least 30 percent within one or two years of deregulation.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto announced a five-year 'Big Bang' plan to reform Japan's financial sector.
Japan will finalize procedures next month to implement reforms related to brokerage fees and financial sector barriers.

China's financial markets are anticipating a central bank interest rate cut in the first quarter of the year.
Analysts believe that a rate cut would benefit debt-ridden state-run enterprises and improve stock and treasury bond markets.
Inflation in 1996 is reported to be lower than the target, according to a Shanghai-based banker.
A second banker stated that a rate cut would alleviate some debt burdens for state-run enterprises.
Officials from the interest rate department of the People's Bank of China have not commented on the matter.
Most state enterprises in China are heavily in debt, impacting the financial system and government budget.
A rate cut would reduce debt servicing payments for state enterprises.
The annual rate for one-year fixed bank deposits is currently 7.47 percent, down from 9.15 percent last May.
Year-on-year retail price inflation for 1996 is expected to be about 6.0 percent, significantly lower than 14.8 percent in 1995.
Personal bank deposits in China increased by about 30 percent year-on-year in 1996, reaching around 3.8 trillion yuan.

China's central bank aims to increase open market operations in 1997.
The increase is partly to absorb state bank funds banned from state debt repurchase and public secondary markets.
The People's Bank of China has not decided how to implement the increase.
The central bank faces a shortage of short-term treasury bills for open market operations.
State banks are banned from the repo and public T-bill spot markets under new rules.
State banks can only purchase T-bills on the primary market and can sell them only to the central bank.
Currently, the central bank is not buying T-bills from state banks.
The lack of liquidity may hinder the market's ability to absorb state bank funds being withdrawn from secondary markets.
The central bank began trial open market operations in April of the previous year.
Accumulated turnover from these operations has only slightly exceeded four billion yuan.

Trading on China's local currency interbank market has increased in recent days.
State banks were directed to withdraw from the state debt secondary markets.
The increased trading volume aligns with Beijing's goal to enhance the interbank market's role in short-term funding and money supply measurement.
Market turnover rose 69.71 percent to 20.938 billion yuan ($2.523 billion) last week compared to the previous week.
The average daily turnover now exceeds four billion yuan, up from around 2.5 billion yuan last year.
Lending by state banks in the interbank market has increased.
Major banks have shifted their short-term surplus lending to the interbank market.
The People's Bank of China ordered state banks to exit the state debt secondary markets to prevent speculation on the stock market.
The interbank market was launched in January last year to facilitate short-term money trading among financial institutions.
The central government plans to focus on the interbank market as part of financial reform in 1997.

Canada's French-language televised debate for the June 2 federal election was cut short when moderator Claire Lamarche collapsed.
Claire Lamarche is a television personality in French-speaking Quebec.
The collapse occurred just before the political party leaders were to discuss national unity.
Arnold Amber, an organizer of the debate, stated that all parties agreed the debate should not continue.
The party leaders left the debate without speaking to the media.
Political scientist Ken McRoberts commented that the moderator's collapse made the debate anti-climactic.
Gilles Duceppe is the leader of the separatist Bloc Quebecois party.
Duceppe was sidelined in the English debate but was expected to rally support in the French-language debate.
The debate was about two hours into its scheduled 2-1/2 hours when the moderator collapsed.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien discussed Canada's high unemployment rate during the debate.

Canada's election campaign intensified on Tuesday.
Party leaders prepared for a French-language debate.
Liberal Prime Minister Jean Chretien faced criticism in Monday's English debate.
The issue of Quebec independence will be a key topic in the French debate.
The French debate is scheduled ahead of the June 2 election.
Reform Party leader Preston Manning stated that national unity is a defining issue.
Manning criticized Chretien for bringing Canada close to separation.
Quebeckers voted 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent to remain in Canada during the 1995 sovereignty referendum.
Manning's participation in the French debate will be limited due to his English-only speaking ability.
Gilles Duceppe, leader of the Bloc Quebecois, faces pressure to perform well in the French debate.

Barrick Gold Corp. is involved in a joint venture proposal for the Busang gold find in Indonesia.
The Indonesian government issued a letter supporting the joint venture between Barrick and Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
The government's support is conditional on meeting the demands of Bre-X's Indonesian partners, PT Askatindo Karya Mineral and PT Amsya Lyna, within a month.
Barrick spokesman Vince Borg stated that the government's reaffirmation of support is a significant step forward.
The Indonesian government previously instructed Barrick and Bre-X to agree on a joint venture to develop Busang.
Barrick and Bre-X submitted a proposal to the government in December for clarification on certain issues.
Placer Dome Inc. made a $5 billion counter-proposal for Bre-X last week due to delays in the agreement.
Placer Dome's proposal includes that 40 percent of Busang would go to Indonesian interests.
The letter from the Indonesian government addressed only the joint venture proposal and did not mention Placer Dome's offer.
Analysts believe that PT Askatindo is crucial for a successful deal between Barrick and Bre-X.

Pope John Paul arrived in Prague on a Friday.
The Pope expressed hope that his visit to the Czech Republic would contribute to the spiritual growth of all Czechs.
The 76-year-old Pontiff was on his third visit to Prague since the fall of communism in 1989.
President Vaclav Havel and other Czech political and religious leaders greeted the Pope at the airport.
Approximately 200 schoolchildren waved yellow and white Vatican flags as the Pope descended the aircraft steps.
The Pope shook hands with Havel and touched a bowl of Czech earth upon arrival.
In a speech, the Pope stated he hoped his visit would promote spiritual and ethical growth among Czechs.
The Pope paid tribute to Havel, recognizing him as a key figure in the country's rebirth after communism.
The Pope's visit was primarily to commemorate the 1,000th anniversary of the death of St Adalbert.
St Adalbert is recognized by Catholics as a significant spiritual figure for Europeans.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus stated that improving the regulation of Czech capital markets is on his agenda.
Klaus criticized foreign critics who claim that improvements in capital market regulation are occurring too slowly.
Klaus spoke at a banking and finance forum in Prague.
Klaus mentioned that he disagrees with critics who expect Czech capital markets to match the quality of Wall Street or the City of London.
Klaus described the critics' attitude as high-brow and doctrinal, which he believes is unhelpful.
Klaus acknowledged that finding the right extent of capital market regulation is an imminent task.
Foreign equity analysts and investors often criticize Czech markets for poor company information and share pricing.
Many analysts compare the Czech capital market unfavorably to Poland's more stringent regulations.
Klaus stated that the country has too many banks and investment funds, many of which are poorly managed.
The Finance Ministry's capital markets oversight office has increased its actions against illegal asset-stripping by managers of smaller investment funds.

Czech consumer prices rose by 0.2 percent in August.
Czech consumer prices rose by 1.0 percent in July.
Czech consumer prices were 9.6 percent higher in August compared to the same month in 1995.
The inflation result in August surprised analysts.
The average inflation rate remained above the government's 1996 target of eight percent.
Radek Maly is an economist with Citibank in Prague.
Radek Maly expected month-on-month inflation to be over 0.6 percent and year-on-year inflation to exceed ten percent.
The Statistical Bureau (CSU) reported a 3.2 percent month-on-month increase in housing prices due to a hike in regulated natural gas and power prices.
Food, beverages, and tobacco products experienced a price drop of 1.4 percent in August.
The CSU raised its average inflation forecast for the year to 9.0 percent in July.

South Korea went on alert for a possible attack by North Korea on Monday.
South Korea expressed a desire for talks to defuse rising tensions.
A high-level defector from North Korea has been stranded in Seoul's embassy in Beijing for six days.
The defector is the most senior official to betray North Korea.
North Korea is facing an imploding economy and food shortages due to two years of floods.
Hwang Jang-yop, a senior North Korean official, turned 74 on Monday.
Hwang Jang-yop remains in Seoul's consulate office in Beijing without progress on his asylum appeal.
South Korea has increased security around its ports, airports, and public places.
Li Il-nam, a prominent defector, is in a coma after being critically wounded by suspected North Korean agents.
South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha stated that the North Korean regime's crisis is likely to deepen.

China appealed for calm amid fears of a diplomatic deadlock over a senior Pyongyang defector in Beijing.
South Korea called for a military alert due to concerns that North Korea might take extreme action.
Signs emerged that North Korea and its leader Kim Jong-il might be ready to give up efforts to recover Hwang Jang-yop.
Beijing may be mediating to end the Cold War crisis related to Hwang Jang-yop.
Hwang Jang-yop is ranked 24th in Pyongyang's hierarchy and spent seven days in Seoul's consulate office in Beijing.
Hwang's defection could lead to more high-level defectors from North Korea.
South Korean Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung called for military readiness against North Korea due to Hwang's defection.
Lee stated that Hwang's defection sent shock waves through the Korean peninsula.
A Seoul newspaper reported documents revealing plans by other North Korean officials to flee.
Lee mentioned that Pyongyang had deployed offensive forces near the border with South Korea despite an economic crisis.

China's President Jiang Zemin pledged to surpass Deng Xiaoping in pursuing capitalist-style reforms.
Jiang Zemin became the most powerful man in China after Deng Xiaoping's death at 92.
Jiang indicated that he intended to complete the reforms initiated by Deng Xiaoping.
Jiang stated that China would run its undertakings better and contribute more to global peace and development.
Jiang's comments were perceived as a criticism of Deng Xiaoping by some ordinary Chinese citizens.
Jiang is the head of the Communist Party and the military in China.
Deng Xiaoping selected Jiang Zemin as his successor.
Some analysts viewed Jiang's quick assumption of Deng's mantle as potentially arrogant and dangerous.
There were signs of discord within China's leadership during Deng Xiaoping's final days.
A magazine called Zhongliu criticized Jiang Zemin, indicating potential leftist opposition.

Philippe Bour is the regional manager for Air France Cargo.
Philippe Bour will meet Hong Kong government officials on Monday.
The meeting will address the refusal of some airlines to withdraw a fuel surcharge on ex-HK air cargo.
Airlines have imposed an 80 Hong Kong cents per kilo fuel surcharge.
The fuel surcharge has caused controversy in Hong Kong.
The Hong Kong Shippers' Council has complained about the surcharge.
The Civil Aviation Department (CAD) has sent warning letters to airlines regarding the surcharge.
Some airlines have withdrawn the surcharge, but Air France, Lufthansa Cargo, Swissair, Air Hong Kong, and Thai Airways International have refused.
Philippe Bour stated that the fuel surcharge is not a rate increase but a separate charge.
The average rate from Hong Kong to Europe is between HK$23-24 per kilo, including the fuel surcharge.

Hong Kong's air cargo industry is experiencing its busiest peak period in many years.
Demand for space on Europe-bound flights is not showing signs of easing.
Trans-Pacific demand has not been sustained after the Thanksgiving peak.
Market analysts predict strong cargo bookings for Europe-bound flights into January and until Chinese New Year.
Cathay Pacific set a new cargo revenue record during the week of November 17-23, with a 19.4 percent increase over the same week last year.
Exceptional cargo performance was reported in Hong Kong, the U.S., Canada, London, and Frankfurt.
James Barrington, Cathay's general manager cargo, stated that the last few weeks have been strong for the airline.
Barrington indicated that rates could rise in a booming environment, although nothing is decided yet.
Trans-Pacific rates have dipped below HK$20 per kg for a 100kg shipment as demand eases.
Polar Air Cargo is cutting capacity due to a weekly demand drop of eight to 10 percent since the end of November.

Cathay Pacific Airways Limited will use Future Air Navigation System (FANS) routes for its Boeing 747-400 freighters.
Cathay Pacific is expected to pioneer the use of FANS routes later this year.
Paul Horsting is the international operations manager at Cathay Pacific.
Cathay Pacific claims to be a leader in the field of FANS technology.
The FANS technology allows aircraft to use GPS satellite navigation instead of radar ground stations.
Airlines expect benefits from FANS technology, including shorter flight times and reduced fuel costs.
Eighteen of Cathay Pacific's 21 Boeing 747-400s have been fitted with Communications Navigation/Air Traffic Management (CNS/ATM) equipment.
Cathay Pacific's entire 747-400 fleet is expected to be fully fitted with FANS technology by March.
Hong Kong's Civil Aviation Department has given engineering approval for the new system.
Los Angeles to Hong Kong is expected to be the first FANS approved route later this year.

Tesco announced plans for a joint venture with Royal Bank of Scotland to enter the banking sector.
Analysts believe that more supermarkets investing in financial services reduces the likelihood of a price war.
The joint venture will take over Tesco's interest-paying ClubCard Plus account and launch a credit card.
Tesco and Royal Bank of Scotland will be equal partners in the venture.
The venture will include Direct Line telephone banking and Scottish Widows fund and life assurance group.
Tesco expects to invest around 40 million pounds ($65 million) in the first year of the venture.
The new venture does not require a banking licence.
The venture could incur a loss of between five and 10 million pounds in the first year.
Tesco's marketing director Tim Mason stated that the venture should become profitable in the second or third year.
Tesco is the third of the big four supermarkets to commit to financial services.

Wessex Water reported a 10 percent increase in half-year pretax profits.
Wessex Water raised its dividend by 14 percent.
Wessex Water's pretax profits for the six months ending September 30 were 75.5 million pounds.
Wessex Water's previous pretax profits were 68.4 million pounds.
Wessex Water declared a dividend of 5.7 pence per share.
Wessex Water's stock price fell three pence to 351 pence.
An analyst stated that the shares fell due to a lack of immediate shareholder benefits.
Wessex Water has a net cash balance of 75 million pounds.
Wessex Water's chief executive Colin Skellett indicated plans for acquisitions or share buybacks in the next six months.
Wessex Water plans to consult with customers to direct investment according to their preferences.

Shares in British supermarkets fell on Monday.
A study indicated that supermarkets are closer to a price war than they have been for 15 years.
Analysts are sceptical that stores will risk a price war.
Supermarkets appear reluctant to sacrifice their profit margins.
The study was conducted by the research group Verdict.
J. Sainsbury Plc warned that its profits would be impacted by efforts to boost sales.
Verdict reported that profits would be 50 million pounds below expectations.
Verdict stated that the risks of a price war are greater than at any time since 1982.
A spokeswoman for Sainsbury said the company is not planning to start a price war.
Sainsbury's sales increased by 4.4 percent over the Christmas trading period.

Britain's markets watchdog banned Ian Hopkins from being a director in the City for at least three years.
The ban was due to Hopkins's involvement in the 1995 collapse of Barings investment bank.
The Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) ordered Hopkins to pay 10,000 pounds towards its costs.
An independent tribunal found that Hopkins was no longer a 'fit and proper person' to be a director of an SFA-regulated firm.
Hopkins was one of nine Barings executives disciplined by the SFA.
Hopkins claimed he attempted to report irregularities in the Singapore operation.
SFA chairman Nick Durlacher rejected Hopkins's interpretation of his role.
The tribunal found that Hopkins did not 'blow the whistle' with clarity, force, or urgency.
Hopkins was responsible for funding Barings's international activities, including its futures operation in Singapore.
The SFA started proceedings against nine former senior executives after the collapse of Barings.

Members of the Halifax Building Society voted to convert the society into a public company.
The Halifax Building Society is Britain's largest mortgage lender.
More than 97 percent of eligible Halifax members voted in favor of the conversion.
The conversion required 50 percent of eligible voters to participate and 75 percent of those votes to be in favor.
The flotation is expected to value the Halifax Building Society at approximately 12 billion pounds.
The flotation is anticipated to occur in June.
Approximately 1,000 Halifax members attended the meeting where the vote took place.
Halifax chairman Jon Foulds stated that the conversion would be in the customers' best interest.
Peter Judge, co-founder of the Halifax Action Group, opposed the conversion and called for the board's resignation.
Halifax members will receive a basic allocation of 200 shares, estimated to be worth around 1,000 pounds.

Prudential Corp Plc won control of Scottish Amicable, a mutually-owned insurance group.
Prudential's acquisition of ScotAm strengthens its position as Britain's number one fund manager.
Prudential's takeover will increase its funds to over 100 billion pounds.
Prudential shares rose by 17 pence to 557 pence following the announcement.
Analysts believe the acquisition will provide strategic and earnings benefits for Prudential.
ScotAm will provide with-profits policyholders with benefits worth over 1.5 billion pounds.
The benefits for policyholders include 600 million pounds in compensation and a special bonus of 470 million pounds.
The remaining ScotAm life fund, valued at approximately 500 million pounds, will be distributed to policyholders.
Policyholders are expected to receive total benefits of around 1,400 pounds, depending on their policy size and age.
Prudential plans to inject 1.3 billion pounds into ScotAm's life fund, which will be closed.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus stated that the Czech National Bank may have gone too far in its attempts to slow inflation quickly.
Klaus claimed that the result of the central bank's actions may have been a slowing in economic growth.
Klaus spoke at Prague's Zofin Forum of business leaders.
Klaus asserted that there is no way to quickly slow inflation.
Klaus indicated that the central bank's steps last year to rein in consumer prices were more than the government wanted.
Klaus identified short-term irremovable inflation factors in the Czech economy.
Klaus criticized the restrictive monetary measures of the Czech National Bank that helped cut inflation to 7.3 percent year-on-year in February.
Klaus noted that the government and the central bank disagreed on whether monetary measures to slow inflation would also slow the economy.
Klaus mentioned that the full-year gross domestic product growth for 1996 ended one percent lower than the government's original expectation of 4.8 percent.
Klaus stated that the Czech trade deficit widened to a record 160.3 billion crowns for the whole of 1996.

Czech President Vaclav Havel underwent major surgery to remove a cancerous lung tumor a month ago.
Havel stated he felt more deeply about the world after facing the possibility of death.
He faced death twice in the previous year, first with the loss of his wife Olga to cancer and second during his hospital stay.
Havel spoke publicly for the first time since his surgery on December 2 in a New Year address on national television.
He reflected on his illness and the suffering caused by both his health issues and the loss of his wife.
Havel expressed that these experiences made him feel the world was unjust.
He perceived these challenges as opportunities for deeper consideration of human existence.
Havel entered a clinic on November 25 with pneumonia, according to his office.
Doctors found a small malignant tumor in his lungs during exploratory surgery a week later.
Havel's condition has been steadily improving, and doctors have indicated good prospects for a full recovery.

A leading Czech economist stated that the Czech central bank should not support the crown if it falls to the low end of its fluctuation band.
Jan Svejnar, director of the Economics Institute at the Czech Academy of Sciences, claimed that without central bank intervention, the crown could drop as low as 20 percent below parity with its mark/dollar basket.
Svejnar suggested that a lower crown would provide natural support to troubled Czech exports.
He clarified that he was not advising for an official devaluation of the currency.
Svejnar called for the central bank to allow a market-driven depreciation in line with the existing macroeconomic situation.
He stated that the central bank should be prepared to let the currency depreciate.
The Czech central bank and government have ruled out devaluation to boost exports.
The Czech National Bank decided in its meeting on Thursday not to change its current policies.
The central bank fixes the crown daily against a mark/dollar basket and allows it to fluctuate within a corridor of plus or minus 7.5 percent of its basket parity.
The crown was fixed at the equivalent of 1.39 percent on Thursday.

Cambridge Antibody Technology Group Plc (CAT) expects to form a major genetics alliance in the next 12 months.
David Chiswell is the chief executive officer of CAT.
Chiswell stated that the alliance would combine CAT's ability to use the body's defenses against disease with genetic research.
Chiswell claimed that CAT will secure at least one major new deal to acquire targets within the next 12 months.
There is speculation that CAT may partner with SmithKline Beecham Plc.
SmithKline Beecham has a strong position in genetic research through a partnership with Human Genome Sciences.
Chiswell did not confirm the identity of any potential partner.
CAT is engaged in pioneering work in human antibodies produced by the immune system.
CAT licenses its technology to major companies including Genentech Inc, Eli Lilly & Co, and Pfizer Inc.
Chiswell stated that CAT's techniques allow for testing potential antibody targets in days, compared to up to six months with other methods.

Glaxo Wellcome Plc announced an 18 percent increase in pre-tax profits.
Pre-tax profits rose to 2.964 billion pounds from 2.505 billion pounds.
Sales increased by 9 percent to 8.341 billion pounds.
Shareholders received a 13 percent increase in the dividend to 34.0 pence.
Shares in Glaxo Wellcome were down 7.5 pence to 10.27.5 pounds.
Sales of Zantac fell 14 percent last year but remained the world's biggest-selling drug at 1.931 billion pounds.
Zantac has been the world's biggest-selling drug since 1986.
Sales of Zovirax were steady at 812 million pounds.
Glaxo expects to at least maintain profits at the 1996 level over the next two years.
Sales of newer products launched since 1990 rose by 650 million pounds to 2.0 billion pounds.

Rentokil Initial Plc announced increases in sales and profits for 1996.
Rentokil Initial's pre-tax profit rose 48 percent to 318 million pounds.
Sales for Rentokil Initial increased by 168 percent to 2.34 billion pounds.
The dividend increased by 20.5 percent to 5.06 pence per share.
A stronger pound reduced profits by just over three million pounds.
An integration charge of 16.4 million pounds was incurred for BET.
The integration charge included nearly 1.5 million pounds paid to former BET chief executive John Clark.
Shares in Rentokil Initial dropped 5.6 percent to 432.5 pence.
Excluding BET, sales increased by 15 percent and profits rose nine percent to 233.4 million pounds.
Rentokil Initial expects another integration charge in 1997 of double-digit millions.

A wave of political violence occurred in Colombia, resulting in at least 24 deaths and numerous injuries within 48 hours.
The northwest banana-growing region of Uraba experienced a massacre where nine civilians were killed by suspected leftist guerrillas.
The Uraba police chief, Col. Anatolio Correa, described the attacks as 'acts of desperation.'
Marxist rebels conducted attacks in central Cundinamarca and eastern Meta provinces to relieve pressure on other fronts.
Col. Anatolio Correa stated that the massacre was a terrorist act and indicated that the guerrillas lack support from the local community.
A gang of 20 FARC rebels attacked the village of Currulao, opening fire on civilians in various locations.
The victims included a 14-year-old student, a funeral parlour owner, a butcher, and peasant farmers.
Six individuals were reported wounded in the Currulao attack.
Two weeks prior, a car bomb in Apartado killed 11 people and injured over 50, also attributed to FARC guerrillas.
Political analysts suggest the violence is linked to control over arms and drug smuggling routes and may have increased due to a pact between right-wing death squads and the military.

A former justice minister, Enrique Parejo, stated that Colombia's moves to lift a six-year extradition ban are a smokescreen to appease the United States while protecting drug barons.
Parejo claimed that the Colombian government does not genuinely intend to push for extradition.
Parejo expressed skepticism about President Ernesto Samper's intentions regarding extradition.
President Samper reaffirmed his commitment to ending the constitutional ban on extradition as part of anti-drug policies.
Parejo accused Samper of merely paying lip service to extradition to placate the United States.
Colombia was blacklisted by the United States for the second consecutive year for failing to combat drug trafficking.
A Senate committee is scheduled to reopen a debate on extradition following a previous hung vote.
Parejo believes that any extradition proposal that passes Congress would be too complex to implement effectively.
Extradition was banned in Colombia in 1991 after violence from Pablo Escobar's Medellin cartel.
When Samper took office in August 1994, he stated that restoring extradition was not part of his political agenda.

The Colombian government reported that 16 soldiers and up to 15 leftist guerrillas were killed in a four-day battle near the capital city.
The battle began late on Friday when about 50 soldiers were airlifted into the area.
The Defence Ministry stated that 13 to 15 Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels were killed during the fighting.
The battle was described as the worst and longest near Bogota in recent memory.
Defence Minister Guillermo Alberto Gonzalez announced the army casualty figure in a national radio interview.
Gonzalez denied reports of missing or unaccounted soldiers in the combat area.
Gonzalez stated that 21 soldiers were stranded early in the firefight but were later rescued unharmed.
Army chief Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett indicated that Bogota was a strategic target for the FARC and National Liberation Army.
Colombia's army announced it was sending hundreds of reinforcements into the mountainous area.
Military sources confirmed that intense aerial bombardments of the area had been ongoing since Sunday.

Investors in Britain's listed soccer clubs have experienced a decline in share prices.
Share prices in the soccer sector have fallen by around 30 percent in the last six weeks.
Smaller clubs like Southampton and Sheffield United have been among the biggest losers in share price.
Manchester United's share price has fallen from 737p in January to 630p currently.
The decline in share prices occurs despite Manchester United's continued success on the pitch.
Share analysts note that the recent declines should be viewed in the context of previous rises of over 200 percent since early 1996.
Analysts suggest that investors should be cautious about investing in clubs outside of soccer's elite.
UBS analysts Guy Feld and Julian Easthope predict a derating of smaller clubs is inevitable.
Pay-per-view television is considered beneficial primarily for top clubs in British and European soccer.
Analysts expect heavy interest in Newcastle United and Aston Villa as they prepare to join the market.

The battle for UK digital terrestrial television (DTT) licences involves three major broadcasting groups and a cable company.
DTN is owned by Nasdaq-listed International CableTel.
DTN is competing against British Sky Broadcasting, Carlton Communications Plc, and Granada Group Plc.
Barclay Knapp is the chief executive of International CableTel.
The Independent Television Commission (ITC) is considering two bids for the DTT licences.
Knapp claims that DTN will create an environment for new British programming and exploit interactive services.
Knapp believes that the successful launch of DTT is essential to challenge BSkyB's dominance in UK pay television.
DTT signals are broadcast from land-based transmitters to aerials, requiring a set-top box or decoder for viewing.
Digital compression allows for improved sound and picture quality and enables the reception of over 30 channels.
DTN and British Digital Broadcasting are bidding for three blocks of frequencies capable of carrying 18 channels.

Channel 5 is Britain's new commercial television station.
Channel 5 launched on a Sunday with an estimated 2.3 million viewers.
The Spice Girls were involved in the launch of Channel 5.
Five of Channel 5's first night shows attracted a million viewers or more.
Channel 5 has a 5.8 percent share of viewing in the 6 p.m. to 10.30 p.m. slot according to initial figures from BARB.
Channel 5 is the first commercial terrestrial station to launch in Britain since 1982.
Channel 5 has a limited budget and aims for an audience share of five percent by the end of the year.
Channel 5 is focusing particularly on viewers under 35 years old.
ITV reported that its Coronation Street soap had 11.6 million viewers for its Sunday evening episode.
Channel 5 is currently available in only six out of 10 British households.

Market confidence exists that St. Jude Medical Inc will proceed with its proposed acquisition of Ventritex Inc.
Both St. Jude Medical Inc and Ventritex Inc stocks were supported on Friday.
Shares in Ventritex were up 1/4 to 18-3/8.
Ventritex confirmed that a third patient implanted with one of its devices died on January 22.
Analyst Jeffrey Barnes from Needham & Co stated that the stock's minimal movement indicates market confidence in the deal proceeding.
Shares in St. Jude were up 5/8 to 37-3/4.
St. Jude Medical Inc has stated it will proceed with the Ventritex deal but will conduct further analysis due to the patient deaths.
Analyst Samuel Navarro from UBS Securities expressed confidence that the transaction will go through, but noted concerns about the terms.
Analysts are assessing the costs for Ventritex to address technical problems with 5,605 implantable defibrillators linked to the deaths.
Estimates for the cost to Ventritex for fixing the devices and potential legal liabilities range from $4 million to $10 million.

Eli Lilly and Co stated it is unaware of issues with physicians switching schizophrenia patients to Zyprexa.
Gary Tollefson, a vice president at Lilly, reported that there are no indications of problems with upgrading patients to Zyprexa.
Zyprexa prescriptions, including refills, are reported to be growing.
Shares of Eli Lilly closed down 2.5 points to 86.625 on Thursday.
Eli Lilly's shares have declined from a 52-week high of 95 on February 24.
Fahnestock & Co analysts Louis Webb and Irena Djurovich issued a report on February 26 claiming physicians are having trouble switching patients to Zyprexa.
The February 26 report suggested that expectations for Zyprexa's sales potential may be inflated.
A follow-up report on February 28 indicated that switching problems persisted after discussions with Lilly.
The Director of Ambulatory Services for Outpatient Psychiatry at Bellevue Hospital reported that about a third of patients switched to Zyprexa experienced a return of psychotic symptoms.
Zyprexa was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for sale in October.

Option Care Inc has a Wall Street 1997 earnings estimate of $0.41 per share.
The previous estimate was $0.33 per share before a one-time charge in 1996.
Erick Hanson is the chief executive of Option Care Inc.
Option Care is based in Bannockburn, Illinois.
The company is targeting annual revenue growth of 25 to 30 percent.
Management owns 70 percent of Option Care's stock.
Option Care was started in California as a home infusion services franchiser.
John Kapoor bought Option Care in 1991 and took it public the following year.
