There are existing systems that allow communication through various methods, including laser beams and facial sensors.
Jacques Charnier from INSERM has been working on tracking eye movements with a fixed camera since 1990.

Comalco Ltd is an Australian aluminium producer.
Comalco's smelting division returned to profit in early 1997.
Comalco experienced a financial loss in 1996 due to low aluminium prices and high costs.
Comalco reported a reasonable profit for the first three months of 1997.
RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd owns 67 percent of Comalco.
RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd is soon to be renamed Rio Tinto.
A new pot line at Comalco's Boyne Island smelter in Queensland will operate at full capacity from the third quarter of 1997.
Comalco's A$1 billion expansion includes a 59.25 percent stake in the Boyne Island smelter.
Comalco's total output is expected to exceed 650,000 tonnes in 1998.
The average price of aluminium on the London Metal Exchange was 74 U.S. cents per pound in 1997.

Colonial Ltd reported a bottom-line loss of A$38 million for calendar 1996.
Colonial Ltd booked A$158 million in abnormal items after tax for 1996.
The result for 1996 was down from a post-abnormal net profit of A$24 million in 1995.
Colonial Ltd's loss was impacted by major restructuring costs from the group's demutualisation.
Changes within Colonial State Bank also affected Colonial Ltd's financial results.
Colonial Ltd announced to the stock exchange that its pre-abnormal net profit fell 28 percent to A$120 million in 1996.
Weaker investment returns contributed to the decline in pre-abnormal net profit for 1996.
The financial results were detailed in Colonial Ltd's accounts.
The loss reported for 1996 was a significant change from the previous year's profit.
Colonial Ltd is an Australian financial services group.

Colonial Ltd is an Australian banking and insurance group.
Colonial Ltd aims for a strong share-market debut on Monday.
Colonial Ltd's float is valued at A$690 million (US$535 million).
The share offer was priced at A$3.10 per share for institutional investors.
The net asset backing of the shares is A$2.48 each.
Colonial Ltd had previously indicated a share price range of A$2.50 to A$2.90.
Institutional bids for shares closed on Friday.
Of the total 235 million shares, institutions could bid for only two-thirds.
Colonial Ltd sold shares to the public for a fixed price of A$2.60 each.
Colonial Ltd has total assets of A$29.7 billion.

Boeing Co. stock increased by $6.875 to $113.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Boeing's stock increase contributed to the rise in the Dow Jones industrial average.
Boeing is one of 30 stocks in the Dow Jones industrial average.
Boeing's decision to halt plans for a stretch version of the 747 jumbo jet could reduce expenses by over $2 billion over five years.
The decision could boost annual earnings by as much as $1 a share.
NatWest Securities analyst Nick Heymann stated that the decision removed uncertainty for Boeing.
Airbus Industrie plans to proceed with the development of the A-3XX superjumbo jetliner.
Heymann expressed doubt about the viability of the A-3XX project due to Airbus's resource limitations.
Boeing estimated that developing new versions of the 747 would cost over $7 billion.
Boeing executives stated that projected demand for very large jets was insufficient to justify the investment.

Boeing Co. stock increased by $7.375 to $113.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Boeing's stock increase contributed to the rise in the Dow Jones industrial average.
Boeing is one of 30 stocks in the Dow Jones industrial average.
Boeing's decision to halt plans for a stretch version of the 747 jumbo jet could reduce expenses by over $2 billion over five years.
The decision could increase annual earnings by up to $1 per share.
NatWest Securities analyst Nick Heymann stated that the decision removed uncertainty for Boeing.
Airbus Industrie plans to proceed with the development of the A-3XX superjumbo jetliner.
Heymann expressed doubt about the viability of the A-3XX project due to Airbus's resource limitations.
Boeing estimated that developing new versions of the 747 would cost over $7 billion.
Only Thai Airways International Ltd. and Malaysian Airline System committed to ordering the proposed new 747 models.

Dennis Fill is the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Advanced Technology Laboratories Inc.
Dennis Fill stated that the company is expected to earn between $1.30 and $1.40 a share this year.
Fill mentioned that earnings of $1.85 a share for 1997 are within reach according to industry analysts' consensus estimates.
Advanced Technology Laboratories Inc. earned $0.74 a share last year.
Fill spoke to Reuters after a presentation at a brokerage conference in New York.
Fill stated that the company aims for a 15 percent return on shareholders' equity by the end of 1998.
Fill noted that the medical-device industry is stabilizing after several turbulent years.
Fill did not expect significant growth in the U.S. ultrasound market before 1998.
ATL's sales are growing by about six to seven percent annually.
ATL's ultrasound imaging product was the first medical device to win premarket approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for diagnosing breast cancer.

CEMOI is building a new cocoa processing factory in Ivory Coast.
The factory is scheduled to open in October 1997.
The factory will have the capacity to process 60,000 tonnes of cocoa beans per year.
The cost of the project is estimated at 160 million French francs.
Ivory Coast aims to process 50 percent of its annual cocoa crop locally by the year 2000.
CEMOI's factory could be upgraded to a capacity of 120,000 tonnes after two years.
The factory will produce cocoa liquor, cocoa cake, and cocoa butter.
Construction began at the site in northern Abidjan (Yopougon) on a Friday.
CEMOI uses 40,000 tonnes of raw cocoa beans annually and plans to sell products from the additional capacity mainly to Europe and possibly China.
Ivory Coast currently has three cocoa processing factories with a total capacity of up to 160,000 tonnes.

Industry and crop analysts forecast a total Ivorian 1996/97 cocoa crop of over one million tonnes.
A major buyer of Ivorian cocoa raised their forecast to 1.07 million tonnes in January from one million tonnes.
The major buyer of Ivorian cocoa suggested the crop could reach 1.1 million tonnes.
Ivorian Agriculture Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan stated that the total 1996/97 crop would be less than one million tonnes.
Kouassi's statement aligns with an earlier estimate from the Ivorian Caistab marketing board of 950,000 tonnes.
It is unclear whether Kouassi's figure refers to total arrivals at ports or beans of sufficient quality for export.
A port source indicated that the figure could represent the export figure rather than total arrivals.
Arrivals of cocoa declared at ports are close to 900,000 tonnes since October 1.
Sources close to the agriculture ministry reported arrivals figures to February 21 at around 850,000 tonnes.
Quality inspectors noted generally good bean quality despite humidity problems.

Gold output from Ivory Coast's second mine, SOMIAF, is set to double over the next two years.
SOMIAF's operations manager, Joe Hinzer, stated that sulphide deposit studies could lead to further increases in gold output.
SOMIAF has started mining a new gold oxide lens of 350,000 tonnes, which will take over a year to mine.
SOMIAF plans to blend a second lens close to the first, which could take one and a half years to mine.
SOMIAF announced two new oxide deposits totaling 510,000 tonnes with a gold content of up to 4.5 grammes/tonne.
Gold production at SOMIAF is projected to rise to 935 kilos in 1996/97 from 600 kilos in 1995/96.
Calendar year yields for SOMIAF are expected to be 950 kilos in 1997 and 622 kilos in 1996.
Output could reach between 1,000 and 1,300 kilos in 1997/98 if new sulphide deposits are found to be exploitable.
SOMIAF is 68 percent owned by Canada's Eden Roc and 32 percent owned by Ivory Coast.
SOMIAF owns one permit of 120 sq km and manages two nearby exploration sites totaling 1,380 sq km.

Pan Am Corp. is open to acquisitions and business opportunities to expand its Pan American World Airways.
Pan Am World Airways is centered in south Florida.
A spokesman for Pan Am declined to comment on a report about acquisition talks with Carnival Air Lines.
Last July, Pan Am agreed to pay about $100 million for Carnival Air, but the transaction was called off after reviewing the carrier's books.
Pan Am sought to rework the terms of the canceled transaction with Carnival Air.
Pan Am spokesman Jeff Kriendler stated that the company would look at opportunities but declined to discuss pending transactions.
Gabriel Gabor, a spokesman for Carnival Air, declined to comment on contacts between the two companies.
Carnival Air has considered several possible deals over the past 18 months.
A combination of Pan Am and Carnival Air would create a regional airline with 31 jets and over 2,200 employees.
Annual revenues for the combined airline would be estimated at $400 million.

Wayne Huizenga is a U.S. billionaire.
Huizenga stated that AutoNation never aspired to control one of every five Toyota and Honda sales in the United States.
Toyota Motor Corp and Honda Motor Co Ltd have filed lawsuits against AutoNation in U.S. courts.
The lawsuits aim to stop AutoNation from buying retailers that sell Toyota and Honda cars.
Honda's lawsuit claims that AutoNation is cheapening its Honda and Acura brands.
Toyota and Honda limit the number of dealerships that can be owned by one proprietor.
Huizenga claimed that AutoNation never said it would control 20 percent of Toyota and Honda's U.S. sales.
Huizenga is the chairman and co-chief executive of Republic Industries Inc.
Republic Industries has bought dozens of small car dealerships and other businesses in the past 18 months.
Ford Motor Co executives are planning to gather Ford and Lincoln-Mercury dealerships into larger sales outlets.

Republic Industries, Inc. agreed to acquire two companies in Florida for a total of $62 million in stock.
The companies being acquired are Gulf Management Inc. and the Steve Moore General Motors automotive group.
Gulf Management Inc. operates Lexus of Tampa Bay and Lexus of Clearwater, Florida.
The Steve Moore General Motors automotive group includes Chevrolet, Cadillac, Pontiac, Oldsmobile, Buick, and Geo brands.
The acquisition includes all related real estate and is subject to manufacturer and government approval.
The owners of the dealerships will retain their responsibilities under long-term employment agreements.
Republic Industries, Inc. is led by Wayne Huizenga.
Republic owns the largest chain of new vehicle dealerships in the United States and is building a chain of used car megastores under the AutoNation USA brand name.
Republic also owns National Car Rental System Inc. and Alamo Rent-A-Car Inc. and has agreed to acquire Spirit Rent-A-Car.
Honda Motor Co. Ltd. and Toyota Motor Corp. have filed lawsuits to block Republic's plan to acquire their outlets in major U.S. markets.

China's last imperial eunuch, Sun Yaoting, died in Beijing at the age of 93.
Sun Yaoting served for seven years in the court of China's last emperor.
Sun Yaoting died on Tuesday evening at his home in a Beijing temple.
Sun Yaoting was born on December 29, 1902, near the northern port city of Tianjin.
Sun Yaoting was castrated at the age of eight by his father to gain power and influence.
The Qing dynasty, which ruled China for almost three centuries, was overthrown shortly after Sun's castration.
Sun's remains were laid out in traditional style at Beijing's Guanghua temple.
Sun Yaoting served China's Emperor Pu Yi during the final years of the Qing dynasty.
After the communist revolution in 1949, Sun was appointed to administer Beijing's temples.
Sun lost his preserved genitals during the Cultural Revolution due to fears of being implicated by the Red Guards.

Chinese authorities closed down 12 illegal compact disc production lines in two weeks.
Beijing has not fully addressed the issue of copyright piracy in the nation.
In 1996, tough actions against intellectual property theft resulted in the seizure of more than 10 million counterfeit products.
Washington recognized China's efforts against intellectual property theft and nearly initiated a trade war over the issue in June.
Guangdong province officials shut down 12 music and video disc production lines since December 10 as part of a national crackdown.
Wang Ziqiang is a representative of the National Copyright Administration of China.
Minister of Culture Liu Zhongde stated that the crackdown on piracy had clear successes.
Liu Zhongde reported the seizure of more than 10 million illegal audio-visual products and the closure of 6,912 illegal work units this year.
U.S. officials indicated that China was improving enforcement of the Sino-U.S. copyright accord.
A Western industry consultant noted that despite the crackdown, pirated Hollywood movies were still widely available.

U.S. President Bill Clinton expressed a commitment to pursue a deeper dialogue with Beijing in his State of the Union address.
Analysts believe Clinton's commitment is likely to reassure China about Washington's seriousness.
Clinton emphasized the importance of improving cross-Pacific relations and vowed to visit China.
A Western diplomat stated that China has felt undervalued by the Clinton administration.
A senior Chinese expert on U.S. policy claimed the Clinton administration has recognized the importance of Sino-U.S. relations.
The expert indicated that the Clinton administration plans to resolve Sino-U.S. problems and implement new policies.
In his State of the Union address, Clinton stated that a deeper dialogue with China is vital for U.S. interests.
Clinton mentioned that an isolated China is not beneficial for America, while a China playing its proper role is.
The improvement in Sino-U.S. relations followed months of warming ties after years of diplomatic disputes.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeline Albright's upcoming visit to China is expected to bring new challenges regarding human rights discussions.

LCI International Inc expects a 75 to 80 percent increase in operating earnings in 1996.
LCI International Inc expects a 65 percent increase in revenue in 1996.
Brian Thompson is the chief executive of LCI International Inc.
Brian Thompson stated he never told analysts to expect lower growth from the company.
Brian Thompson stands by his long-term forecast of 30 to 40 percent annual revenue growth.
Brian Thompson communicated his forecast during a telephone interview with Reuters.
Brian Thompson expects LCI International Inc to perform strongly in 1997.
LCI's stock declined in December after analysts interpreted conversations as indicating slower revenue growth.
Brian Thompson was unable to correct the impression of slower growth initially due to the company being in a quiet period.
Brian Thompson believes LCI International Inc will end up around 65 percent in revenues for the year.

GTE Corp had 800,000 long distance customers at the end of 1996.
This number was six percent above the target of 750,000 set by GTE after entering the long distance market in March 1996.
GTE announced these figures in a press release regarding a new flat rate long distance calling plan.
GTE may increase customer targets for 1997 and advance the expected break-even target.
Rob McCoy, president of GTE long distance, stated that they are evaluating targets on a daily basis.
The current target for end-1997 customers was not disclosed by McCoy.
GTE is expected to break-even by the last quarter of 1998 and contribute a full year profit to the parent company in 1999.
GTE is targeting customers who would spend an average of $25 a month on long distance calls.
Current bills are above $17, approaching $20, and are expected to rise as more users emerge from promotional service.
GTE's new 'Easy One Rate' plan is aimed at users who want simplicity and make many daytime long distance calls.

Fourth quarter results from regional Bells indicate an increase in demand for additional lines, wireless phones, and services like caller ID in the U.S.
There are no signs of demand slowing.
Analysts reported that results from Bell Atlantic Corp, NYNEX Corp, and SBC Communications Inc met market expectations.
Richard Klugman of PaineWebber stated that these companies have raised expectations for demand growth, which should be sustainable for 1997.
Investors are concerned about competition in the Bells' core local markets and its impact on long-distance services.
Bill Vogel, an analyst at Dillon Reed, noted that both Bell Atlantic and NYNEX reported better-than-expected results compared to analysts' consensus.
SBC Communications Inc reported earnings one cent below the First Call consensus of $0.91 for the fourth quarter.
SBC's chief financial officer Don Kiernan stated that the earnings were closer to the fourth quarter consensus when rounding errors were removed.
Bill Deatherage of Bear Stearns mentioned that SBC generally met aggressive revenue expectations despite higher expenses.
NYNEX experienced some pullback due to the weakness of the northeastern economy and had reduced marketing spending.

Quaker Oats Co. reported a profit for the fourth quarter.
Quaker Oats Co. reversed a year-ago loss.
Quaker Oats Co. stated that its Snapple beverage business was unprofitable.
Quaker Oats Co. reported an 8 percent drop in Snapple's U.S. and Canadian sales in 1996.
Quaker Oats Co. reported an 11 percent decrease in Snapple's volume in 1996.
Sales of Quaker's six-flavor Diet Snapple line rose 23 percent in 1996.
Quaker Oats Co. earned $18.1 million, or 12 cents a share, in the fourth quarter.
Quaker Oats Co. had a loss of $47.8 million, or 36 cents a share, in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Quaker Oats Co. reported fourth quarter revenues of $1.06 billion, down 10 percent from $1.18 billion a year earlier.
Quaker Oats Co. earned $244 million, or $1.80 a share, for the full year.

Quaker Oats Co. reported a profit for the fourth quarter.
Quaker Oats Co. reversed a year-ago loss.
Quaker Oats Co. stated that its Snapple beverage business was unprofitable.
Quaker Oats Co. reported an 8 percent drop in Snapple's U.S. and Canadian sales in 1996.
Quaker Oats Co. reported an 11 percent decrease in Snapple's volume in 1996.
Sales of Quaker's six-flavor Diet Snapple line rose 23 percent in 1996.
Quaker Oats Co. earned $18.1 million, or 12 cents a share, in the fourth quarter.
Quaker Oats Co. had a loss of $47.8 million, or 36 cents a share, in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Quaker Oats Co. reported fourth quarter revenues of $1.06 billion, down 10 percent from $1.18 billion a year earlier.
Quaker Oats Co. earned $244 million, or $1.80 a share, for the full year.

Pioneer Hi-Bred International Inc is launching 28 new corn hybrids in 1997.
Pioneer aims to reverse a recent drop in its seed corn market share over the next few years.
Richard 'Rick' McConnell is the senior vice president and director of research at Pioneer.
Eight of the new corn hybrids have the Bt gene to combat the European corn borer.
The Bt corn varieties are part of genetically altered, or transgenic, corn hybrids developed by Pioneer.
Pioneer's share of the North American seed corn market is four times that of its nearest competitor.
Analysts noted that the development of unique biotech crops has leveled the playing field.
Pioneer's other transgenic products include soybeans that can withstand Monsanto Co's Roundup herbicide.
Pioneer will have limited quantities of corn that can resist Liberty herbicide, produced by AgrEvo.
Pioneer's North American corn market share dropped to 44 percent in fiscal 1996 from 45 percent.

Pro-Beijing politicians defeated two motions in Hong Kong's legislature.
The motions aimed to increase pressure on China regarding human rights and the Communist Party's future role.
The first motion was brought by pro-democracy legislator Christine Loh.
Christine Loh urged the Hong Kong government to seek clarification on the Communist Party's role after the handover from Britain.
Legislative Council Chairman Andrew Wong cast a decisive vote in favor of the status quo, breaking a 25-25 tie.
Loh questioned how the Communist Party would be represented and its communication with post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa.
Anthony Cheung of the Democratic Party supported Loh's motion, advocating for greater transparency of the Communist Party's activities.
Ip Kwok-him of a pro-China alliance opposed the motion, stating the Communist Party has no special status in Hong Kong.
Xinhua News Agency, headed by Zhou Nan, represents party authority in Hong Kong.
A separate motion by John Tse of the Democratic Party, urging China to sign international human rights pacts, was defeated by 26 votes to 24.

Western countries plan to grant asylum to around 40 Chinese dissidents and their families living in exile in Hong Kong.
Human rights sources reported this plan on Tuesday.
Countries are concerned that the dissidents may face persecution from Beijing after the handover of Hong Kong on July 1.
Fears among the exiles have increased as China plans to roll back democracy and human rights legislation in Hong Kong.
China has vowed to prevent 'anti-constitutional' activities in Hong Kong.
China has intensified its crackdown on dissenters, resulting in many being jailed over the past year.
A human rights campaigner expressed that there is relief among dissidents about the resettlement plan, but they will not feel safe until they are on the plane.
Hundreds of Chinese dissidents fled to Hong Kong after the Tiananmen Square protests in June 1989.
A dissident support group estimates there are between 100 and 200 dissidents currently in Hong Kong.
The Hong Kong government has not commented on asylum seekers to avoid jeopardizing their situation.

Hong Kong has a Catholic community of 250,000 members.
The Catholic community in Hong Kong is cautious in its relations with Beijing.
Pope John Paul stated that the Vatican would monitor the situation of Catholics in Hong Kong after the 1997 handover to China.
Church sources believe that the Catholic Church in Hong Kong will remain free after 1997.
Some Catholic agencies are leaving Hong Kong to avoid endangering the community after the Chinese flag is raised.
Roman Catholics in Hong Kong make up four percent of the territory's 6.3 million population.
Pope John Paul expressed particular interest in the Catholic community in Hong Kong during his annual address.
Anthony Lam stated that the relationship between the Hong Kong government and the diocese is harmonious.
Hong Kong has been a base for missionary activity aimed at China since its establishment as a British colony.
The Catholic Church in Hong Kong operates under different conditions than churches in mainland China.

Lagardere made a bid for military electronics firm Thomson-CSF.
A senior defence source stated that the competition in naval combat systems is intense.
Lagardere and Alcatel Alsthom submitted rival offers for Thomson-CSF's privatisation.
The privatisation of Thomson-CSF is viewed as a significant step in consolidating the European defence industry.
Lagardere secured 300 million pounds in financing from British Aerospace Plc.
Lagardere plans to combine BAe's and Thomson-CSF's naval businesses into Matra BAe Dynamics.
France and Britain have a history of competition in naval systems.
A defence official claimed that France has a lead in naval combat systems over Britain.
Thomson-CSF and its competitors design and integrate electronic systems for naval weapons and radar.
The submarine sector is considered a sovereignty issue for France.

France is restructuring its defence sector.
State-owned Aerospatiale plays a key role in the restructuring process.
The European Airbus consortium is changing into a limited liability company.
The four national firms in Airbus Industrie are exploring ways to improve efficiency.
The goal is to better compete with U.S. rival Boeing Co.
Boeing Co. is merging with McDonnell Douglas.
Aerospatiale is the French partner in the Airbus passenger plane venture.
Aerospatiale is involved in the merger with Dassault Aviation and the privatisation of Thomson-CSF.
The Dassault merger is expected to be agreed upon this year.
The merger will add 13 billion francs of annual turnover to Aerospatiale.

Lagardere confirmed it will make an offer in the privatisation of Thomson-CSF.
A Lagardere spokesman stated the company would announce its intentions on Friday.
The French government set March 28 as the deadline for intentions to bid for its 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF.
Firm and final offers for Thomson-CSF are due by May 7.
A decision regarding the bids will be made by June 30.
Alcatel Alsthom is making a joint bid with Dassault Industries for Thomson-CSF.
The joint bid includes cooperation with state-owned Aerospatiale if successful.
Thomson-CSF produces missiles, radars, aircraft avionics, training simulators, and telecommunications systems.
In 1996, Thomson-CSF reported a net attributable profit of 745 million francs on sales of 36.27 billion francs.
The French government aims to create the largest possible industrial grouping around Thomson-CSF to enhance research and development efficiency.

Texaco Inc. announced it will exit the chemicals business by selling a Texas facility to Huntsman Corp. for about $600 million.
Texaco is based in White Plains, New York.
Texaco sold the majority of its chemicals business to Huntsman in 1994 for over $1 billion.
The sale will allow Texaco to focus on its core oil and natural gas businesses.
Huntsman Corp. is based in Salt Lake City, Utah, and is the largest privately-held chemicals company in the United States.
Huntsman has operated the Texaco propylene oxide/methyl tertiary butyl ether plant at Port Neches, Texas since 1994.
The Port Neches plant has a production capacity of about 400 million pounds per year of propylene oxide and about 15,000 barrels per day of MTBE.
Propylene oxide is a petrochemical used in various industries including home furnishings and construction.
Huntsman has entered a long-term agreement with BASF AG for a significant portion of the Port Neches propylene oxide production.
Huntsman will acquire Texaco's PO/MTBE manufacturing technology and has negotiated a long-term MTBE supply agreement.

ITT Corp. is preparing for a board meeting on Tuesday to consider a $6.5 billion unsolicited takeover bid from Hilton Hotels Corp.
The board meeting will take place in New York and is the first since Hilton launched its offer last week.
ITT's board has until February 14 to respond to Hilton's offer.
ITT spokesman Jim Gallagher did not disclose the time of the meeting.
A source indicated that the board meeting is likely to last most of the day.
ITT Chairman Rand Araskog declined a request from Hilton CEO Stephen Bollenbach to meet before the board meeting.
Araskog rejected Bollenbach's offer in a faxed letter, stating it would be inappropriate.
The cash and stock transaction values ITT at $55 per share.
ITT stock lost 25 cents to $56.875 in Monday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Bollenbach flew to London on Monday to meet with Hilton's European partner.

Conrail Inc. rejected a $10.5 billion takeover offer from Norfolk Southern Corp.
Conrail believes its proposed $9.3 billion merger with CSX Corp. is a better corporate combination.
Conrail Chairman David LeVan stated that a merger with CSX is in the best interests of Conrail and its constituencies.
The rejection of Norfolk Southern's offer occurred one day after CSX and Norfolk Southern raised their bids for Conrail.
Industry analysts believe CSX and Norfolk Southern are unlikely to increase their offers significantly.
Both CSX and Norfolk Southern will continue their competition in court, before regulators, and in the marketplace.
CSX raised its offer for Conrail to provide shareholders with an additional $870 million.
The revised deal between CSX and Conrail is valued at $9.3 billion, or about $102 per Conrail share.
Norfolk Southern increased its all-cash offer to approximately $10.5 billion, or $115 per share.
Industry experts suggest that Norfolk Southern aims to maintain the price difference while contesting part of the Conrail-CSX agreement in court.

Opponents of U.S. trade concessions to China are expected to challenge President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's favored trading status.
Supporters of President Clinton's decision to renew China's most favored nation (MFN) status for another year are confident of victory.
Opponents include social conservatives, organized labor, and others who criticize China's policies on human rights, labor rights, religious rights, trade, and abortion.
Opponents are gaining support from concerns over the transfer of Hong Kong to China and allegations of Beijing's influence on U.S. elections through illegal campaign contributions.
A congressional aide indicated that the upcoming vote will be more challenging due to issues surrounding Hong Kong and campaign finance.
House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich stated that this year's vote would be closer than last year's 286-141 vote supporting Clinton on MFN.
Advocates and opponents expect that President Clinton's policy will ultimately survive the congressional vote.
Gingrich expressed support for MFN status for China but criticized Clinton for not using the announcement to advocate for human rights and democratic freedoms.
Opponents doubt they can gather enough votes to override a potential veto from President Clinton, even if they manage to reject his decision.
Congress will vote later this summer on whether to overturn Clinton's decision, starting with the House.

Regulators approved plans to auction two airwave licenses for new nationwide radio services.
The Federal Communications Commission will limit the April 1 sale to four companies that applied by the end of 1992.
The four companies are CD Radio Inc., American Mobile Radio Corp., Digital Broadcast Satellite Corp., and Primosphere LP.
Listeners will need to purchase a special radio receiver costing about $200 to access the service.
The new radio service is expected to be subscription-based, costing about $10 a month.
Operators will be able to offer specialized programming.
CD Radio plans to provide 30 channels of commercial-free music programming if it wins a license.
The service is expected to take three to six years to become operational.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt and Commissioner Susan Ness favored an open auction for the licenses.
The FCC agreed to require license winners to offer discounted advertising rates and equal time to political candidates.

Regulators are considering extending consumer safeguards for 900-number phone calls to other pay-per-call services.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) will seek public comment on applying the rules to information and entertainment services that use prefixes other than '900.'
The 900-number rules require clear cost disclosures and a means for settling billing disputes.
Newer services offer callers astrological and travel information, psychic advice, and phone sex.
Scams among 'audio information' or 'audio entertainment' services are a growing problem.
Providers of these services evade the 900 rules by diverting calls to numbers in countries such as Guyana, the Dominican Republic, Sao Tome, or Moldova.
The first three digits of the number can resemble area codes in the United States.
Overseas calls can incur charges of more than $2 a minute.
The FTC has the authority to expand its 900-number rules to cover similar services not accessed by dialing 900.
The FTC has brought cases against alleged international pay-per-call schemes and issued consumer alerts about the costs and risks of such services.

Hewlett-Packard Co. will unveil new products on Monday.
The new products are intended to reduce the difficulties and costs of owning and operating computer networks.
The products include manageability tools and new additions to the HP Vectra line of business computers.
HP is launching a second generation of its HP NetServer E series server devices for small and medium-size businesses.
HP's printer division is adding to its HP OfficeJet 'all-in-one' line of machines.
HP Vectra personal computer models will now come loaded with TopTOOLS, a new management tool provided free.
TopTOOLS enables systems managers to handle configuration, security, and other tasks from any location on a computer network.
Operating networked personal computers can cost up to $12,000 a year, according to some research studies.
HP Vectra PC models will include Intel Corp.'s Pentium processors with MMX technology and enhanced 10/100 Base-T LAN interface.
The HP Vectra VL line will include a 64-bit graphics engine and new S3 Trio64 V2 video controller.

Intel Corp. stock fell for the third straight day on Friday.
Concerns about upcoming price cuts could slow Intel's momentum.
The stock price dropped by $6.75 to $130.50.
The total decline since Tuesday is $16.125, or roughly 11 percent.
The stock's fall contributed to a decline in the entire market.
Analysts are nervous about Intel's first-quarter results, which are due after the market close on Monday.
Intel's quarterly price cuts on Pentium processors are expected to lower personal computer prices.
Some analysts speculate that Intel will cut Pentium prices by 25 percent to 30 percent in anticipation of rival chips.
Analysts expect Intel to report a first-quarter profit of $2.07 a share, up from $1.02 a year ago.
Intel executives expect revenues to be around $6.4 billion, similar to the fourth quarter.

Sun Microsystems Inc. launched initiatives to improve the performance of its Java software on various devices.
The announcements were made at the second annual JavaOne software developers' conference in San Francisco.
Java is a computer language that allows programmers to write software that can run on multiple systems.
Sun plans to introduce a stronger version of Java for Microsoft's Windows operating system in the summer.
Sun aims to enhance Java's performance and security by the end of the year.
Sun has developed Java variants optimized for devices ranging from large data center computers to smaller handheld devices.
Sun announced licensing and partnership agreements with companies like Toshiba Corp. for semiconductors designed around Java.
A version of Java software for older personal computers using Microsoft DOS will be called JavaPC and will be available this fall for under $100.
JavaPC is estimated to provide new life to approximately 180 million older PCs.
The Java software initiative has created an alliance among competitive companies in the industry.

Asian stocks are anticipating a rise in the U.S. Federal funds rate at the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Tuesday.
Concerns about interest rates caused the U.S. Dow Jones index to fall this past week.
The Dow Jones index fell 15 points on Friday to 6805.
Rate fears were not seen as a major factor for the Dow Jones index's decline on Friday.
Local factors are expected to exacerbate rate jitters in Asia, including Taiwan's ban on all pork exports due to an outbreak of hog foot-and-mouth disease.
Singapore is experiencing continued gloom due to poor export figures.
The blue-chip Hang Seng Index fell 247.23 points, or 1.94 percent, in the past week to close at 12,489.30 on Friday.
James Osborn, an ING Barings sales director, stated that if a 25 basis point rise is announced, Hong Kong will probably recover to around the 13,000 level.
Analysts believe that earnings growth is strong and that uncertainty will be cleared after the Fed meeting.
The 225-share Nikkei benchmark index closed up 139.45 points, or 0.75 percent, at 18,633.16 on Friday.

Temperatures are rising in Hong Kong as it prepares for its transition to Chinese rule.
Freedom of speech is a significant issue during the transition.
Hong Kong newspapers are facing accusations of pro-China bias and self-censorship.
The South China Morning Post is Hong Kong's leading English-language daily.
The South China Morning Post was criticized for canceling the cartoon 'The World of Lily Wong' in 1995.
The South China Morning Post has been labeled the 'Pro China Morning Post' by its critics.
The South China Morning Post hired a founding editor of China's state-owned China Daily as a consultant.
Editor Jonathan Fenby of the South China Morning Post denies being influenced by Beijing.
Ming Pao is one of Hong Kong's best-selling Chinese-language newspapers.
A survey conducted by Chinese University of Hong Kong found that one in five journalists hesitated to criticize China.

Financial market pundits in Hong Kong are monitoring the territory's top civil servants for signs of discontent in the government.
Hong Kong is approaching its merger with China on July 1.
The continued tenure of Hong Kong's top civil service is considered key to a successful transition.
Speculation exists about friction between Chief Secretary Anson Chan, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang, and future leader Tung Chee-hwa over policy.
A senior broker expressed concern about maintaining the current status of the civil service to avoid substantial policy mistakes.
The broker suggested that the likelihood of policy mistakes would increase if Donald Tsang were not in office.
Currency analyst Eric Nickerson stated that while he agrees with concerns about individuals, he questions the irreplaceability of any one person.
Anson Chan called for a credible legislature to be established as soon as possible after the handover.
Chan's comments suggested a lack of confidence in the China-appointed provisional legislature that will replace the current council.
Pro-China politician Lau Siu-Kai indicated that Chan's remarks could undermine her future working relationship with the interim body.

Police sealed off South Korea's embassy and consular office in Beijing, China.
The sealing off occurred after a report that North Korean official Hwang Jang-yop sought asylum from Seoul.
Dozens of police were stationed around the South Korean embassy's consular section.
Police sealed roads leading into the area around the embassy.
A policeman informed a Chinese citizen that no one was allowed to enter the sealed area.
Hwang Jang-yop is a senior aide to North Korea's leader Kim Jong-il.
Hwang was reported to have sought asylum at the South Korean embassy in Beijing along with his assistant Kim Dok-hong.
Chinese police prevented access to the fourth floor office of the main South Korean embassy.
An official at the North Korean embassy in Beijing claimed that Hwang must have been kidnapped.
A South Korean unification ministry spokesman described North Korea's claim as preposterous.

A funeral cortege bearing the body of Deng Xiaoping arrived at Beijing's Babaoshan cemetery for cremation on Monday.
The cortege was led by four black cars followed by a white van decorated with black and yellow ribbons.
The white van served as the hearse for Deng's body and was flanked by two Red Flag limousines.
Hundreds of armed police lined the streets along the 2.5 km route to the cemetery from a military hospital.
Deng Xiaoping died last Wednesday at the age of 92.
The cortege consisted of about 30 vehicles and moved at a pace slightly faster than walking.
Thousands of mourners lined the route to get a last glimpse of Deng Xiaoping.
China has heightened security around the capital and especially in Tiananmen Square following Deng's death.
No foreign dignitaries have been invited to the funeral, and Deng's ashes will be scattered at sea.
Deng's family requested that his body not be put on public display and that his corneas be donated to an eye bank.

A funeral cortege carrying Deng Xiaoping's body arrived at Babaoshan cemetery in Beijing for cremation on Monday.
Deng Xiaoping was a paramount leader who transformed China.
The van transporting Deng's body was decorated with black and yellow ribbons.
Babaoshan cemetery is where Chinese communism's heroes are traditionally laid to rest.
A banner reading 'Scatter Hot Tears for Comrade Xiaoping' was displayed outside the military hospital where Deng's body was kept.
Deng Xiaoping died at the age of 92 on the previous Wednesday.
Hundreds of armed police lined the streets along the 2.5-km route to the cemetery.
The cortege moved at a pace slightly faster than walking to allow mourners to see Deng one last time.
Deng Xiaoping ruled China for 18 years with a combination of capitalist-style policies and communist control.
No foreign dignitaries were invited to attend the memorial rites in Beijing's Great Hall of the People.

Lloyd's of London reassured its traditional backers, known as Names, that there was no hidden agenda to force them out of the insurance market.
Outgoing Chairman Sir David Rowland stated, 'Trust us,' in response to a concerned Name.
Rowland promised there would be no move to eliminate the annual reforming of syndicates.
Rowland supported recent changes in the market that shifted members from unlimited to limited liability.
Rowland announced that he would become a limited liability member of Lloyd's upon retirement.
Rowland expressed that unlimited personal liability has significant consequences for individuals.
Rowland suggested that new trading structures with continuous capital may be better for long-term development.
Rowland warned that without embracing change, Lloyd's would face a decline in its fortunes.
The annual reforming of syndicates and reinsurance to close had previously worked well until significant losses occurred between 1988 and 1992.
Critics have questioned the viability of the annual capital raising system at Lloyd's, citing its cost and impact on long-term planning.

Lloyd's of London dismissed concerns about its exposure to possible U.S. tobacco-related insurance claims.
A spokesman for Lloyd's stated that large tobacco liability claims were not regarded as a significant issue for the company.
There had been no substantial volume of tobacco manufacturers' coverage underwritten directly with the Lloyd's market.
Claims applying to years prior to 1993 would be covered by the Equitas reinsurance vehicle.
Equitas was established under last year's Lloyd's rescue plans to manage pre-1993 losses.
Lloyd's stated that no significant exposures related to tobacco were identified during the reserving work for Equitas.
Health-related claims against tobacco companies have been covered by policy exclusions for many years, according to Lloyd's spokesman.
Research by Schroders insurance analyst Paul Hodges questions the sufficiency of exclusion clauses for tobacco-related claims.
Ohio became the twenty-fifth U.S. state to seek recovery of public money spent on treating smoking-related illnesses.
No tobacco company has attempted to claim against its insurer in the U.S. due to costs, fear of losing control of defense, and scrutiny of internal documents.

The Lloyd's insurance market's annual venture has been criticized as costly and damaging to competitiveness in a report by accountants KPMG.
The KPMG report was published on Friday.
The report will be part of the submission by the Lloyd's Corporate Capital Association (LCCA) to the Lloyd's Syndicate Structure working party.
The working party is evaluating different capital structures for syndicates.
The report is viewed as an attack on the position of unlimited liability Names in the insurance market.
Unlimited liability Names are traditional backers of the Lloyd's insurance market.
Lloyd's proposed to raise the amount of capital that Names must pledge to back their underwriting activities.
The number of Names at Lloyd's is already at 20-year lows.
Corporate capital accounts for 44 percent of the market's total capacity.
KPMG estimates the direct costs of the annual venture at 117 million pounds in an average year.

Future Hong Kong lawmakers agreed on a formula to pass laws for the territory.
The provisional legislature met in Shenzhen to decide the format for passing bills.
The bills include those to dilute existing Hong Kong laws protecting civil rights.
The interim chamber agreed that all three required readings of proposed bills could take place before July 1.
The bills would be confirmed and made into laws on July 1.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30.
Tung Chee-hwa launched plans to curb protests and foreign funding of Hong Kong political groups after the handover.
Pro-democracy activists threatened to sue the provisional chamber if it passes any laws before July 1.
Hong Kong democrats regard the interim legislature as a breach of the territory's post-handover constitution.
Hong Kong people will need police permission to demonstrate after July 1.

Hong Kong's future government made minor changes to planned civil rights curbs on Thursday.
The changes were made after Hong Kong reverts to China on July 1.
Michael Suen is an aide to leader-in-waiting Tung Chee-hwa.
Suen unveiled a diluted version of curbs on protests and a modified ban on foreign funding of local political groups.
The concept of 'national security' will not be formally defined until a meeting of the China-backed interim legislature on Saturday.
National security will be defined as the safeguarding of territorial integrity and the independence of the People's Republic of China.
The inclusion of the national security concept in Hong Kong's post-handover laws is expected to outlaw protests advocating independence for Taiwan or Tibet.
Suen stated that changes to the curbs were made after a three-week public consultation marked by strong opposition from the pro-democracy camp.
Local political parties will be barred from taking donations from foreign political groups, but contributions from mainland China are acceptable.
Accepting donations from political groups in Taiwan will be illegal.

Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon will meet with Hong Kong leaders regarding the status of Filipino workers.
Siazon is scheduled to arrive in Hong Kong late on Thursday.
Siazon will meet with Hong Kong governor Chris Patten and future chief Tung Chee-hwa.
Siazon will engage with members of the Filipino community in Hong Kong, which numbers 140,000.
Siazon is expected to announce Manila's decision to waive visas for holders of Hong Kong's post-colonial passport.
Hong Kong will become a Special Administrative Region of China on July 1.
Most Filipino workers in Hong Kong are maids who contribute to the local economy.
There are concerns among Filipinos that they may be replaced by domestic servants from mainland China after July 1.
Cynthia Tellez, director of the Mission for Filipino Migrant Workers in Hong Kong, expressed hope for clear assurances regarding the status of Filipino workers.
The Filipino community in Hong Kong is part of a larger diaspora of four million Filipinos working abroad.

Wall Street's relationship with IBM showed signs of decline after the company's fourth-quarter earnings report.
IBM's stock fell by $13 in early trading and closed $10 lower at $158 on the New York Stock Exchange.
More than 12.2 million shares of IBM changed hands on the New York Stock Exchange.
The decline in IBM's stock contributed to a nearly 34-point drop in the Dow Jones industrial average.
IBM reported fourth-quarter earnings of $2 billion, or $3.93 a share, which was above the average Wall Street estimate of $3.88 a share.
IBM's earnings were boosted by a lower tax rate and lower-than-expected restructuring costs.
IBM's profits were negatively impacted by sluggish mainframe sales and currency fluctuations.
Analysts expressed disappointment with IBM's results for the quarter.
Merrill Lynch analyst Daniel Mandresh raised his price target for IBM stock to $195 in November but later cut his 1997 earnings estimate to $13 a share from $13.40.
IBM earned $5.4 billion, or $10.24 a share, for the entire year of 1996.

After two years of hype about the Internet, investors are questioning its profitability.
The PC Forum conference in Tucson, Arizona, gathered leaders from telecommunications, media, and computer companies.
Attendees expressed increased concern about profits and business models.
Ed Bennett, former president of Prodigy Services, stated that the raw potential of the industry remains unchanged.
It is unclear what business plan will generate significant revenue from the Internet.
American Cybercast filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, raising concerns about Web-based ventures.
Amazon.com, known for pioneering online bookselling, reported a loss of $5.8 million in 1996.
Sheldon Laube, chief technology officer of U.S. Web, noted an increased focus on profitability from analysts and investors.
The PC Forum serves as a platform for discussing industry issues and networking among executives.
The conference featured presentations from 12 early start-ups to attract venture capitalists and analysts.

America Online Inc. is facing scrutiny from 20 state attorneys general due to consumer complaints.
New York threatened to sue America Online for allegedly deceptive business practices and false advertising.
Washington state is considering its options regarding America Online.
Subscribers have reported repeated busy signals when trying to log on after a pricing plan change to unlimited access for $9.95 a month.
New York state Attorney General Dennis Vacco aims to secure refunds or free time for consumers.
America Online Chairman Steve Case is not willing to provide refunds or free time to consumers.
New York has given America Online five business days to respond to the potential legal action.
Prosecutors from 20 states met with America Online to discuss consumer complaints.
AOL stock fell to $36.75, which is not considered significant by technology standards.
AOL is losing new subscribers and is cutting back on its television advertising campaign and mailings of floppy disks.

Reckitt and Colman Plc is expected to report a 15 percent increase in its full year profits.
Analysts forecast 1996 pretax profits for Reckitt and Colman Plc to range from 314 to 320 million stg.
The previous year's pretax profits for Reckitt and Colman Plc were 285 million stg.
Estimates of the total dividend for Reckitt and Colman Plc range from 21.8 to 22.6 pence.
Reckitt and Colman Plc acquired L&F Products for one billion pounds in 1994.
L&F Products is the maker of America's best-selling disinfectant Lysol.
At the half year stage, Reckitt and Colman Plc reported sales up 5.3 percent.
Turnover in the United States for Reckitt and Colman Plc grew by 7.0 percent.
Reckitt and Colman Plc generates about 32 percent of its revenue from Europe.
Reckitt and Colman Plc shares have risen sharply amid rumors of a potential takeover bid by Unilever.

Unilever Plc/NV is unlikely to bid for Danone due to strategic conflicts and regulatory hurdles.
Analysts, including Paribas analyst John Campbell, expressed skepticism about a potential bid for Danone.
Unilever did not comment on rumors regarding a bid for Danone.
Unilever announced the sale of its specialty chemicals division, expected to generate approximately 5 billion stg.
Unilever's name has been associated with various potential takeover targets, including Cadbury-Schweppes and Reckitt and Coleman.
Analysts noted that few of the potential targets align with Unilever's strategy.
Cadbury-Schweppes is considered too large in Britain for Unilever's interests.
Unilever is hesitant to enter the soft drinks market due to competition from Coca-Cola and PepsiCo.
CPC International is identified as a more likely target for Unilever by analysts.
Unilever chairman Niall Fitzgerald stated the company aims to conclude a sale within three to six months.

Reckitt and Colman Plc reported an 11 percent rise in 1996 pretax profits to 316.5 million pounds.
The reported pretax profits equate to $505.5 million.
Chief executive Vernon Sankey stated that the group expected similar growth rates in sales and earnings in 1997.
The company's shares slipped 3p to 782p after the profit figures were released.
Household products accounted for 80 percent of group turnover and posted a nine percent increase in trading profit to 283.9 million pounds.
Earnings from the pharmaceutical division grew 12.2 percent to 67.2 million pounds.
The company benefitted from 27 million pounds in savings from the integration of L&F Products in North America.
Lysol increased its market share across its product range.
The lavatory care category grew by 18.1 percent in Africa and the Middle East.
Reckitt's shares have risen by 14 percent in recent weeks amid market rumors of a potential takeover bid by Unilever.

Ford Motor Co. halted light truck assembly lines at three plants due to a strike at a seat supplier.
Ford signed an agreement with Lear Corp. to help clear a backlog of 7,700 Expeditions built without proper seats.
Lear Corp. Chairman Kenneth Way agreed to produce seats for Ford's Expedition after an appeal from Ford Chairman Alex Trotman.
Lear Corp. will make second and third row seats for the Expedition once the strike is settled.
Front seats for the Expedition are being made by Ford's Chesterfield, Mich., trim plant.
Ford's Chesterfield plant is producing less than 20 seats per hour.
Ford suspended all production at its Michigan Assembly in Wayne due to a strike involving the United Auto Workers and Johnson Controls Inc.
The strike entered its 11th day on Friday and idled about 6,800 workers.
The Expedition is one of Ford's most profitable vehicles, earning an estimated pre-tax profit of $10,000 each.
Ford refused to accept seats made by non-union replacement workers to avoid angering its UAW workers.

U.S. investigators began recovering the bodies of 29 people killed in a commuter plane crash near Detroit.
The crash occurred during a snowstorm on Thursday.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will focus on body recovery before investigating the wreckage.
Monroe County Sheriff Tilman Crutchfield stated that the NTSB briefly examined the site on Thursday night.
The cockpit voice and data recorders had not been located by NTSB officials.
The Comair plane was an Embraer Brasilia 120 en route to Detroit from Cincinnati.
The crash site is located in Raisinville Township, Michigan, about 25 miles southwest of Detroit.
One of the victims was a teacher from Englewood, Colorado, traveling to a memorial service for her brother.
A temporary morgue has been established at Custer Airport near Monroe.
Wreckage from the crash was spread over an area of approximately 200 yards by 100 yards.

Federal-Mogul Corp. has ended its effort to build a global auto parts retail empire.
Federal-Mogul Corp. announced a restructuring that focuses on its core manufacturing and distribution business.
The company is based in Southfield, Michigan.
Federal-Mogul Corp. incurred $264 million in pre-tax charges for the restructuring and special one-time items in the fourth quarter.
Federal-Mogul Corp. has approximately $2 billion in annual sales.
The company will reduce its workforce by about 2,900 jobs, which is 18.5 percent of its total workforce of 15,700.
The restructuring resulted in a net loss of $220.2 million for the fourth quarter, compared to a loss of $49.1 million in the same period in 1995.
For the entire year of 1996, Federal-Mogul Corp. lost $211.1 million, but would have made a profit of $34.7 million before special items.
In 1995, the company reported a loss of $9.7 million.
Federal-Mogul Corp. produces a variety of products for the auto, farm, and construction vehicle industries.

China ordered Boeing jets as a gesture to the United States.
The order includes a pact to sell five 777s to Air China for $685 million.
Beijing is delaying orders for planes it needs while monitoring Sino-U.S. relations.
Diplomats believe that new deals for Boeing or Airbus could be linked to China's World Trade Organisation membership campaign.
The United States advocates for concessions from China to liberalize its domestic market before joining the WTO.
China seeks permanent most favored nation trading status from the United States to avoid annual reviews.
Boeing officials aimed to sell 10 twin-engine 777s to Air China.
The signing ceremony for the Boeing deal took place in the Great Hall of the People.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore's visit to China was the highest-level visit since George Bush in 1989.
Airbus was disappointed by the Boeing order as they were looking to sell the A330-300 in China.

China plans to promote 100 large chemical groups by the year 2000.
The promotion will be supported by a $1.6 billion fund.
Gu Xiulian is the Minister of Chemical Industry in China.
The industry aims for 10 of the promoted groups to compete in the export market and potentially list shares on stock exchanges.
China currently has 13.6 billion yuan, equivalent to $1.6 billion, to support development plans.
Some of the funding was allocated under the previous five-year plan from 1991 to 1995.
The Chinese government is promoting large companies to enhance the competitiveness of its state sector.
There are currently 80 companies capable of exporting $10 million worth of chemicals annually.
The ministry's policy supports companies that are ready to go public, pending approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission.
Tianjin Bohai Chemical Industry (Group) Co Ltd and Jilin Chemical Industry Co Ltd are examples of chemical companies listed in China and abroad.

China's stock regulators are attempting to regain control over backdoor listings of Chinese companies in Hong Kong.
The concerns were triggered by the listing of GITIC Enterprises, a Hong Kong company controlled by the Guangdong International Trust and Investment Corp (GITIC).
GITIC is based in Guangzhou, a city in southern China.
The issue is sensitive due to Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty on July 1 under a Sino-British accord that promises autonomy for 50 years.
A securities industry executive stated that Chinese authorities are worried about the issue and guidelines may emerge soon.
A foreign securities company executive expressed concern that good companies might inject mainland assets into Hong Kong companies and go public without approval.
Chinese companies wishing to list shares abroad, typically in Hong Kong, require clearance from several central government regulatory bodies, including the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC).
Rules for Hong Kong companies controlled by Chinese interests are unclear, but many have recently gained approval from Beijing.
GITIC Enterprises did not obtain prior clearance, and regulatory objections were a last-minute hurdle, but the offer proceeded successfully.
The listing was nearly 900 times subscribed and finished its first day of trading at HK$4.375, compared to its offer price of HK$1.05.
